name: Dynamic Neural Motion Factorization (DynMF)
body: DynMF is a method for representing and rendering dynamic 3D scenes using 3D Gaussian Splatting, where the motion of each Gaussian is modeled as a linear combination of a small set of learned basis trajectories. It solves the problem of efficiently modeling complex, non-rigid deformations in dynamic scenes by sharing a compact set of motion bases across all Gaussians, rather than learning independent trajectories for each point. Unlike methods that use fixed Fourier series bases for temporal decomposition, DynMF employs learned MLP-based basis functions, which are argued to be smoother and more expressive for dynamic scene deformations. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A sequence of images of a dynamic scene captured from varying viewpoints over time; camera poses and intrinsics for each timestamp. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians with time-dependent parameters (mean \mu(t), rotation q(t)) and static parameters (density, spherical harmonics) that can be rendered into novel views at any timestamp t. Data Structures Each Gaussian i stores the following learned parameters: 1. Canonical Mean (\muc): A 3D vector \in \mathbb{R}^3 representing the Gaussian's position in the canonical (static) space. 2. Canonical Rotation (qc): A 4D quaternion \in \mathbb{R}^4 representing the Gaussian's orientation in the canonical space. 3. Motion Coefficients (ci): A vector of size B containing the weights for the basis trajectories. These coefficients are shared between the translational and rotational decompositions for a given Gaussian. 4. Static Attributes: Density and spherical harmonic coefficients, which remain fixed over time. The basis functions are implemented as a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). The MLP takes a normalized time input t/T and outputs the basis values. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize N Gaussians. The means are randomly initialized around the center of the scene (e.g., 2k Gaussians). Canonical means \muc, canonical rotations qc, and motion coefficients ci are initialized as learnable parameters. The MLP weights wj for the basis functions are initialized. 2. Basis Function Definition: Define B basis trajectories. Each basis j is a function of time implemented by an MLP: bj(t) = \text{MLP}\left(\frac{t}{T}; wj\right) where T is the total number of timestamps in the training sequence, and wj are the learnable weights for the j-th trajectory. The MLP consists of 8 linear layers of 256 width. The final two layers produce outputs of size (B, 3) for displacement and (B, 4) for quaternion correction. The input t/T is encoded using positional encoding with 32 frequencies. 3. Time-Dependent Parameter Computation: For a given timestamp t, compute the dynamic mean \mu(t) and rotation q(t) for each Gaussian i using the canonical parameters and the motion coefficients ci: \mui(t) = \mu{c,i} + \sum{j=1}^B c{ij} b^\muj(t) qi(t) = q{c,i} + \sum{j=1}^B c{ij} b^Rj(t) where \mu{c,i} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the canonical mean, q{c,i} \in \mathbb{R}^4 is the canonical quaternion, c{ij} is the j-th motion coefficient for Gaussian i, and b^\muj(t) and b^Rj(t) are the basis functions for translation and rotation, respectively. Note that the same coefficients c{ij} are used for both translation and rotation. 4. Rendering: Render the scene using the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline, substituting the static mean \mu with \mu(t) and the static rotation q with q(t) for the current timestamp. Density and spherical harmonic coefficients are kept fixed along time. 5. Densification and Rigidity: When a Gaussian is split or densified during training, copy the motion coefficients c from the parent Gaussian to the new Gaussian to enforce rigidity. 6. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss, which includes the standard rendering loss (e.g., L1 or SSIM between rendered and ground truth images) and the following regularization losses: L1 Regularization: Penalizes unnecessary basis choices to prevent apparent but nonexistent movements: \mathcal{L}1 = \frac{1}{NB}\sum{i=1}^N \sum{j=1}^B |c{ij}| Sparsity Loss: Enforces strict sparsity in trajectory selection, encouraging each Gaussian to choose only a few trajectories: \mathcal{L}s = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \frac{\|ci\|1}{\|ci\|\infty} Rigidity Loss: Encourages rigidity between nearby Gaussians by minimizing the difference in their motion coefficients, weighted by their spatial proximity at a reference time t^: \mathcal{L}r = \frac{1}{Nk} \sum{i=1}^N \sum{j \in knn{i;k}} w{ij} \|ci - cj\|2 where k is the number of nearest neighbors, and w{ij} = \exp(-\lambdaw \|\mui(t^) - \muj(t^)\|^2). Parameters Number of basis trajectories (B): 10 for D-NeRF dataset; 32 for HyperNeRF and N3DV datasets. MLP Architecture: 8 linear layers of 256 width. Final layers produce (B, 3) for displacement and (B, 4) for quaternion correction. Positional Encoding: 32 frequencies used to encode the time input t/T. Training Iterations: 30k total. Basis functions and motion coefficients are enabled only after the first 3k iterations. Learning Rates: Basis learning rate decays exponentially from 8 \times 10^{-4} to 8 \times 10^{-6}. Coefficients learning rate is fixed at 8 \times 10^{-3}. Initialization: 2k Gaussians' means are randomly initialized around the center of the scene. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class DynMF: def init(self, numgaussians, numbasis, numtimestamps): self.numgaussians = numgaussians self.numbasis = numbasis self.numtimestamps = numtimestamps # Canonical parameters (learnable) # muc: (N, 3), qc: (N, 4) self.muc = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(numgaussians, 3)) self.qc = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(numgaussians, 4)) # Motion coefficients (learnable) # c: (N, B) self.c = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(numgaussians, numbasis)) # Basis MLP # Input: normalized time (scalar), Output: basis values # For translation: output size (B, 3) # For rotation: output size (B, 4) self.mlpbasis = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(32, 256), # Positional encoding expands time to 32 dims nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, numbasis 7) # 3 for trans, 4 for rot) # Positional encoding for time self.freqbands = 32 def positionalencoding(self, tnorm, numfrequencies): """Standard positional encoding for scalar time input.""" # tnorm: (T,) # Output: (T, numfrequencies) scales = torch.tensor([2i for i in range(numfrequencies)], dtype=torch.float32) # tnorm is in [0, 1] scaledt = tnorm.unsqueeze(-1) scales.unsqueeze(0) pe = torch.cat([torch.sin(scaledt), torch.cos(scaledt)], dim=-1) return pe def getbasisvalues(self, tnorm): """ Compute basis values for given normalized timestamps. tnorm: (T,) tensor of normalized times in [0, 1] Returns: basistrans: (T, B, 3) basisrot: (T, B, 4) """ pe = self.positionalencoding(tnorm, self.freqbands) # (T, 32) # MLP output: (T, B7) mlpout = self.mlpbasis(pe) # (T, B7) # Reshape to (T, B, 7) mlpout = mlpout.view(-1, self.numbasis, 7) # Split into translation (3) and rotation (4) basistrans = mlpout[:,:,:3] # (T, B, 3) basisrot = mlpout[:,:, 3:] # (T, B, 4) return basistrans, basisrot def getdynamicparams(self, tnorm): """ Compute dynamic mean and rotation for all Gaussians at given timestamps. tnorm: (T,) tensor of normalized times in [0, 1] Returns: mut: (T, N, 3) qt: (T, N, 4) """ basistrans, basisrot = self.getbasisvalues(tnorm) # (T, B, 3), (T, B, 4) # c: (N, B) -> (1, N, B) for broadcasting c = self.c.unsqueeze(0) # (1, N, B) # mut = muc + sumj cj bj(t) # basistrans: (T, B, 3), c: (1, N, B) # dot product over B: (T, N, 3) transoffset = torch.einsum('tb, nb -> tnb', basistrans, c) # (T, N, 3) mut = self.muc.unsqueeze(0) + transoffset # (T, N, 3) # qt = qc + sumj cj bj(t) # basisrot: (T, B, 4), c: (1, N, B) rotoffset = torch.einsum('tb, nb -> tnb', basisrot, c) # (T, N, 4) qt = self.qc.unsqueeze(0) + rotoffset # (T, N, 4) return mut, qt def computelosses(self, mut, qt, c, gtimages, renderedimages, tnorm, k=5, lambdaw=1.0): """ Compute total loss including rendering, L1, sparsity, and rigidity. """ # Rendering loss (e.g., L1) renderingloss = torch.mean(torch.abs(renderedimages - gtimages)) # L1 Regularization # c: (N, B) l1loss = torch.mean(torch.abs(c)) # Sparsity Loss # c: (N, B) l1norm = torch.norm(c, p=1, dim=1) # (N,) infnorm = torch.norm(c, p=float('inf'), dim=1) # (N,) # Avoid division by zero infnorm = torch.clamp(infnorm, min=1e-8) sparsityloss = torch.mean(l1norm / infnorm) # Rigidity Loss # Use a reference time t (e.g., first timestamp) # mut: (T, N, 3) muref = mut[0] # (N, 3) # Compute pairwise distances for weighting # dist: (N, N) dist = torch.cdist(muref, muref, p=2) # (N, N) wij = torch.exp(-lambdaw dist) # (N, N) # Find k-nearest neighbors for each Gaussian # knnindices: (N, k), knnindices = torch.topk(dist, k=k+1, largest=False, dim=1) # Exclude self knnindices = knnindices[:, 1:] # Remove self (index 0) # Gather coefficients of neighbors # c: (N, B) cneighbors = c[knnindices] # (N, k, B) # Compute difference # ci - cj diff = c.unsqueeze(1) - cneighbors # (N, k, B) # L2 norm of difference diffnorm = torch.norm(diff, p=2, dim=2) # (N, k) # Weighted sum # wij for neighbors: (N, k) wknn = wij.gather(1, knnindices) # (N, k) rigidityloss = torch.mean(wknn diffnorm) totalloss = renderingloss + l1loss + sparsityloss + rigidityloss return totalloss, renderingloss, l1loss, sparsityloss, rigidityloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by Zero in Sparsity Loss: If a Gaussian has all zero motion coefficients, the L\infty norm is zero, leading to division by zero. A small epsilon should be added to the denominator. Quaternion Normalization: The output of the rotation basis function is added to the canonical quaternion. The resulting quaternion q(t) must be normalized to unit length before use in the rendering pipeline to ensure valid rotation. Basis Function Expressiveness: The learned MLP basis functions are not strictly a basis in the mathematical sense, but they empirically span a large enough space to cover deformation variations. If the number of basis trajectories B is too small, the representation may not capture complex motions. A method that uses neural voxels for dynamic scene representation. Choose when voxel-based representations are preferred over Gaussian splatting for volumetric data. A method that learns a deformation field to warp static Gaussians. Choose when explicit motion coefficients are not desired and a continuous deformation field is preferred. A pipeline for dynamic Gaussian Splatting. Choose when a different training or optimization strategy for dynamic Gaussians is required. Time Complexity: Rendering is efficient, comparable to static 3D Gaussian Splatting, as the basis functions are queried per timestamp and the Gaussians are splatted in standard order. Training time is 30k iterations, which takes approximately 20 minutes on the D-NeRF dataset. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the storage of canonical parameters, motion coefficients, and the MLP weights. The number of basis trajectories B is small (10-32), so the memory overhead per Gaussian is minimal. Measured Performance: On the D-NeRF synthetic dataset (400x400 resolution), DynMF achieves 36.89 PSNR, 0.983 SSIM, 0.02 LPIPS, and >300 FPS. Strengths: Compact representation due to shared basis functions; high rendering FPS; good quality on synthetic dynamic scenes; inherent rigidity through coefficient sharing and copying during densification. Limitations: May struggle with highly non-rigid motions or dynamic opacity (e.g., flame or smoke); performance on real-world datasets (HyperNeRF, N3DV) is lower than on synthetic datasets. When to Use: Suitable for real-time dynamic view synthesis of scenes with moderate non-rigid deformations where high FPS is required. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenes with extreme non-rigid deformations or dynamic opacity. DynMF was proposed by A. Kratimenos et al. in the paper "DynMF: Neural Motion Factorization for Real-Time Dynamic View Synthesis with 3D Gaussian Splatting". The method builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting [20] and aims to extend it to dynamic scenes. It was developed to address the limitations of using Fourier series bases for dynamic motion trajectories, arguing that learned MLP bases are smoother and more expressive. The method has been evaluated on synthetic datasets (D-NeRF) and real-world datasets (HyperNeRF, N3DV). name: Gated Second-Order Trajectory
head: Dynamic Modeling, Gated quadratic trajectory, Second-order motion model, Static-Dynamic Partition
body: Gated Second-Order Trajectory is a method for modeling the continuous-time motion of 3D Gaussian primitives in dynamic scenes by applying a second-order kinematic model gated by a binary switch. It solves the problem of efficiently representing temporal dynamics without per-frame neural inference, distinguishing itself from implicit deformation fields by keeping the static subset exactly time-invariant for caching. Inputs and Outputs Input: Canonical Gaussian parameters and a normalized timestamp t \in [0, 1]. Output: Time-dependent position \mui(t) and effective opacity oi(t) for rendering. Data Structures Each Gaussian i stores the following fields: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Canonical center position. \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix (constant over time). oi \in \mathbb{R}: Base opacity. ci: Appearance coefficients (constant over time). vi \in \mathbb{R}^3: Velocity vector. ai \in \mathbb{R}^3: Acceleration vector. t'i \in [0, 1]: Canonical time. \rhoi \in \mathbb{R}: Log-duration parameter. gi \in \{0, 1\}: Binary static-dynamic gate. Numbered Steps 1. Compute the time delta: \Delta ti = t - t'i. 2. Compute the temporal duration: \sigmai = \text{clip}(\exp(\rhoi), \sigma{min}, \sigma{max}). 3. Compute the temporal weight: wi(t) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{\Delta ti}{\sigmai + \epsilon}\right)^2\right). 4. Compute the effective opacity: oi(t) = (1 - gi) oi + gi wi(t) oi. 5. Compute the position: \mui(t) = \mui + gi vi \Delta ti + \frac{1}{2} ai \Delta ti^2. Formulas and Symbol Definitions \Delta ti = t - t'i: Time offset from the Gaussian's canonical time. \mui(t) = \mui + gi vi \Delta ti + \frac{1}{2} ai \Delta ti^2: Second-order trajectory for position. wi(t) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{\Delta ti}{\sigmai + \epsilon}\right)^2\right): Gaussian temporal weight for smooth appearance/disappearance. oi(t) = (1 - gi) oi + gi wi(t) oi: Effective opacity blending static base opacity with dynamic temporal weight. \mui: Canonical position. vi: Velocity vector. ai: Acceleration vector. t'i: Canonical time. gi: Binary gate (0 for static, 1 for dynamic). \sigmai: Temporal duration. \epsilon: Small constant to prevent division by zero. oi: Base opacity. Parameters t: Normalized timestamp of the input frame, t \in [0, 1]. \sigma{min}, \sigma{max}: Bounds for temporal duration clipping. \epsilon: Small constant to prevent division by zero. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Static Caching: When gi=0, the Gaussian remains at \mui for all t. This subset can be cached for mobile rendering. Explicit States: All temporal states are explicit, avoiding per-frame neural inference required by implicit deformation-based methods. Temporal Support: Dynamic Gaussians do not contribute to every frame; they appear/disappear smoothly around t'i based on \sigmai. Precision & Boundaries: The clipping of \sigmai and addition of \epsilon prevent division by zero and unbounded temporal weights. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def gatedsecondordertrajectory(mu, o, v, a, tprime, rho, g, t, sigmamin, sigmamax, epsilon): """ Computes time-dependent position and opacity for a single Gaussian. Args: mu: Canonical position (list of 3 floats) o: Base opacity (float) v: Velocity vector (list of 3 floats) a: Acceleration vector (list of 3 floats) tprime: Canonical time (float in [0,1]) rho: Log-duration parameter (float) g: Binary gate (0 or 1) t: Current normalized timestamp (float in [0,1]) sigmamin: Minimum temporal duration (float) sigmamax: Maximum temporal duration (float) epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability (float) Returns: mut: Position at time t (list of 3 floats) ot: Effective opacity at time t (float) """ deltat = t - tprime sigmai = max(sigmamin, min(sigmamax, math.exp(rho))) weight = math.exp(-0.5 (deltat / (sigmai + epsilon)) 2) if g == 0: ot = o else: ot = weight o mut = [mu[j] + g v[j] deltat + 0.5 a[j] (deltat 2) for j in range(3)] return mut, ot Uses neural voxels for dynamic representation. Choose when high-frequency dynamic details are needed without explicit motion parameters. Uses implicit deformation fields. Choose when continuous deformation is preferred over explicit kinematic models. Focuses on multi-agent Gaussian Splatting. Choose for multi-object scenarios with distinct motion patterns. Factorizes motion into neural components. Choose for complex, non-rigid deformations. Time Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian per frame, as it involves only vector operations and exponentials. No neural network inference is required. Memory Complexity: Adds eight scalars per Gaussian to the static parameters. Strengths: Enables caching of static Gaussians; avoids per-frame neural inference; provides continuous trajectories. Limitations: Assumes piecewise constant velocity and acceleration. When to use: Real-time mobile rendering where static parts can be cached and dynamic parts are relatively simple. Originated in Mobile-4DGS, a method for unified static-dynamic real-time mobile Gaussian Splatting. It extends 3D Gaussian Splatting with a compact set of temporal parameters to model continuous-time motion. name: Neural Parametric Gaussians
body: Neural Parametric Gaussians (NPG) is a two-stage method for monocular non-rigid object reconstruction that imposes a coarse deformation model as regularization for fine-level 3D Gaussian optimization. Unlike concurrent works that apply neural networks directly to all Gaussians, NPG uses a network only to drive an initial coarse point template, while the Gaussians themselves are optimized with static parameters that are deformed by the coarse model. This approach avoids heavy runtime increases for large scenes and ensures temporal consistency in novel views. NPG operates in two stages: first, a coarse neural parametric point model is fitted to monocular video sequences using a low-rank deformation basis; second, 3D Gaussians are initialized and optimized in local volumes defined by the point sets, where Gaussian parameters are shared over time and deformation is driven by the coarse point set. Inputs: A sequence of monocular input views \{Ii\}{i=1}^N. Corresponding segmentation masks \{Mi\}{i=1}^N. Camera poses for each frame, typically obtained via COLMAP. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined in local volumes, with parameters (weights, rotations, scales, spherical harmonic coefficients) shared across the temporal sequence. The coarse point model parameters (basis vectors and MLP weights). Coarse Point Model: Basis Vectors (\mathbf{B}k): Learnable tensors of shape M \times 3, where M is the number of points in the template. Coefficients (\alphak^t): Scalars for each basis vector k at time t, produced by an MLP. MLP (f\theta): Maps temporally encoded time \phi(t) \in \mathbb{R}^d to coefficients \alpha^t \in \mathbb{R}^K. Colors (\mathbf{C}): Coarse colors of shape N \times 3. Random Features (\mathbf{E}): Random features of shape N \times d used for identification. Local Volumes: Volume Definition (\mathcal{V}): A set of oriented local volumes \{(\mathbf{V}^t(i), \mathbf{T}^t(i)) \mid \forall i \in \{1, \dots, M\}\}. Local Volume Points (\mathbf{V}^t(i)): A set of k points (point i plus k-1 nearest neighbors) at time t, shape k \times 3. Local Orientation (\mathbf{T}^t(i)): A rotation matrix in SO(3) determined by the triangle formed by point i and its two closest neighbors. The neighbors defining the triangle are fixed over time. Gaussians: Global List: All Gaussians are stored in a global list. Volume Index: Each Gaussian has an associated volume index. Parameters: Weights \mathbf{w}, rotations \mathbf{R}, scales \mathbf{S}, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{h} are shared across all time steps. Coarse Point Model Representation: The coarse point model \mathbf{P}^t \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times 3} at time t is represented as a sum of basis vectors \mathbf{B}k weighted by coefficients \alphak^t: \mathbf{P}^t = \sum{k=1}^K \alphak^t \mathbf{B}k \quad (1) where \{\mathbf{B}k \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times 3}\}{k=1}^K is the learnable point basis and \alphak^t \in \mathbb{R} are low-rank coefficients. Mask Loss: For each frame i, points \mathbf{P}i^M are sampled uniformly from the input mask Mi. The loss minimizes the Chamfer distance between sampled mask points and the projected point model \pi(\mathbf{P}i): \mathcal{L}M = \text{CD}(\mathbf{P}i^M, \pi(\mathbf{P}i)) \quad (2) where \pi projects the point model to the image plane. Rigidity Loss: This loss keeps neighborhood point distances of a frame t similar to that of a reference frame r: \mathcal{L}R = \sum{i=2}^M \sum{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \| \|\mathbf{P}i^t - \mathbf{P}j^t\|2 - \|\mathbf{P}i^r - \mathbf{P}j^r\|2 \|2^2 \quad (3) where \mathcal{N}(i) denotes neighborhood points of point i within a radius criterion, and r is a manually selected reference frame. Note: The source text contains a typo in the second norm term using t instead of r, but the definition states 'similar to that of a reference frame r'. Optimization Objective (Stage 1): \arg \min (\mathcal{L}M + \mathcal{L}R + \mathcal{L}{\text{OF}}) \quad (4) where \mathcal{L}{\text{OF}} is the optical flow consistency loss. Optical Flow Loss: Let \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{P}^t, \mathbf{E}) render the point cloud \mathbf{P}^t with random descriptors \mathbf{E}. Let \mathcal{R}^B(\mathbf{P}^{t+1}, \mathbf{E}) render \mathbf{P}^{t+1}, apply backward optical flow, and bilinearly sample the result. The flow consistency loss is: \mathcal{L}{\text{OF}}^{t \to t+1} = \| \mathbf{M}^t \circ [\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{P}^t, \mathbf{E}) - \mathcal{R}^B(\mathbf{P}^{t+1}, \mathbf{E})] \|\epsilon \quad (5) where RAFT is used to estimate optical flow. Gaussian Optimization (Stage 2): In stage 2, the optimal weights \hat{\mathbf{w}}, rotations \hat{\mathbf{R}}, scales \hat{\mathbf{S}}, and spherical harmonic coefficients \hat{\mathbf{h}} are found by: \hat{\mathbf{w}}, \hat{\mathbf{R}}, \hat{\mathbf{S}}, \hat{\mathbf{h}} = \arg \min{\mathbf{w}, \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{S}, \mathbf{h}} (1 - \lambda)\mathcal{L}1 + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\text{D-SSIM}} \quad (6) where the Gaussians are rendered using the differentiable rasterizer from Kerbl et al.. K: The number of basis vectors in the low-rank deformation basis. It controls the rigidity of the model. Typically K \ll T (number of frames). k: The number of nearest neighbors defining a local volume. Set to 20 in experiments. \lambda: Weight for the D-SSIM loss component in Stage 2. Not given in the sources. Loss weights for Stage 1: Refer to the supplementals of the source paper. Not given in the sources. Stage 1: Coarse Parametric Point Model 1. Initialize the point basis \{\mathbf{B}k\}{k=1}^K randomly. 2. Initialize the MLP f\theta to map temporally encoded time \phi(t) to coefficients \alphak^t. 3. For each frame t: a. Compute coefficients \alphak^t = f\theta(\phi(t)). b. Compute point positions \mathbf{P}^t = \sum{k=1}^K \alphak^t \mathbf{B}k. 4. Optimize \{\mathbf{B}k\} and \theta by minimizing \mathcal{L}M + \mathcal{L}R + \mathcal{L}{\text{OF}}. a. Mask Loss: Sample points \mathbf{P}i^M from mask Mi. Compute Chamfer distance to projected points \pi(\mathbf{P}i). b. Rigidity Loss: For each point i and its neighbors j \in \mathcal{N}(i), compute the difference between distances in frame t and reference frame r. c. Optical Flow Loss: Render point clouds with random descriptors. Apply backward optical flow to the rendered image of frame t+1 and compare with frame t. Stage 2: 3D Gaussian Optimization 1. Define Local Volumes: For each point i in the coarse model, define volume \mathbf{V}(i) as point i plus its k-1 nearest neighbors. 2. Compute Orientation: Determine local orientation \mathbf{T}(i) from the triangle formed by point i and its 2 closest neighbors. 3. Initialize Gaussians: Fill each volume with a small number of 3D Gaussians. Store Gaussians in a global list with a volume index. 4. Optimize Gaussians: Minimize rendering loss (1 - \lambda)\mathcal{L}1 + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\text{D-SSIM}} by optimizing \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{S}, \mathbf{h}. a. Densification: Apply densification and pruning from Kerbl et al.. b. Splitting: When splitting a Gaussian, assign new Gaussians to the same volume as the original Gaussian. c. Weight Noise: Apply a tiny bit of noise to weights \mathbf{w} of both the original and new Gaussians. Precision: The source notes that the rigidity loss formula in the text contains a typo (\|\mathbf{P}i^t - \mathbf{P}j^t\|2 instead of \|\mathbf{P}i^r - \mathbf{P}j^r\|2). Implementers should use the reference frame r for the second term. Boundaries: The method requires the object to stay in view. No assumptions are made about the 3D location of the object, but it must remain visible. Degenerate Input: Masks obtained from Segment Anything (SAM) are considered a weak assumption but are demonstrated to work. Uses neural voxels for dynamic scenes. Choose when voxel-based representation is preferred over Gaussian splatting. Uses a deformation field for dynamic objects. Choose when explicit deformation fields are needed. A pipeline for dynamic Gaussian splatting. Choose for a comprehensive pipeline approach. Factorizes motion for dynamic scenes. Choose when motion factorization is beneficial. Uses second-order trajectories for motion. Choose when higher-order motion modeling is required. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method avoids heavy runtime increases for larger scenes because it does not apply networks to all Gaussians, only to the initial point template. Strengths: Provides consistent, high-quality novel views from significantly different camera positions. Ensures temporal consistency through the coarse deformation model. Scalable due to shared Gaussian parameters. Limitations: Requires monocular input with masks. Relies on the quality of the coarse point model for regularization. When to use: Monocular non-rigid object reconstruction where temporal consistency and novel view synthesis are critical. When not to use: When multi-view input is available, or when real-time inference with per-Gaussian neural networks is acceptable. Neural Parametric Gaussians (NPG) was introduced in the paper "Neural Parametric Gaussians for Monocular Non-Rigid Object Reconstruction". The method builds on the breakthrough of 3D Gaussian splatting for static scenes and extends it to dynamic objects by using a coarse parametric point model based on low-rank deformation. It addresses the ill-posed nature of monocular non-rigid reconstruction by imposing a two-stage approach. name: Deformable 3D Gaussians
head: Deformable-GS
body: Deformable 3D Gaussians is a framework for high-fidelity, real-time reconstruction of monocular dynamic scenes that extends static 3D Gaussian Splatting by decoupling geometry and appearance from time. Unlike implicit dynamic methods that suffer from slow convergence and overfitting, or entangled methods that condition neural fields directly on time, this approach learns time-independent 3D Gaussians in a canonical space and employs a lightweight deformation field to map them to the deformed space at any given time t. It incorporates an Annealing Smooth Training (AST) mechanism to mitigate temporal jitter caused by inaccurate camera poses in real-world datasets, ensuring smooth interpolation without additional computational overhead. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of images from a monocular dynamic sequence, corresponding time labels, camera poses, and a sparse point cloud derived from Structure-from-Motion (SfM). Outputs: A rendered image for a specific camera pose and time t, and a set of optimized 3D Gaussian parameters and deformation network weights. Data Structures 1. 3D Gaussians (G): Defined in canonical space. Each Gaussian i is represented by: Center position: \mathbf{x}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity: \sigmai \in \mathbb{R} Rotation: Quaternion \mathbf{r}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 Scale: 3D vector \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Appearance: Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients. The 3D covariance matrix \Sigmai is derived from \mathbf{r}i and \mathbf{s}i as \Sigmai = \mathbf{R}i \mathbf{S}i \mathbf{S}i^T \mathbf{R}i^T, where \mathbf{R}i is the rotation matrix from \mathbf{r}i and \mathbf{S}i is the scaling matrix from \mathbf{s}i. 2. Deformation Field (F\theta): A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with depth D=8 and hidden dimension W=256. It takes encoded canonical position and time as input and outputs offsets (\delta \mathbf{x}, \delta \mathbf{r}, \delta \mathbf{s}). Positional Encoding Inputs to the deformation field are encoded using positional encoding \gamma(\cdot): \gamma(\mathbf{p}) = (\sin(2^k \pi \mathbf{p}), \cos(2^k \pi \mathbf{p})){k=0}^{L-1} For canonical position \mathbf{x}: L=10. For time t: L=6 in synthetic scenes, L=10 in real scenes. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians from the SfM sparse point cloud or random generation. Set initial positions \mathbf{x}, opacities \sigma, rotations \mathbf{r}, and scales \mathbf{s}. 2. Warm-up Phase: For the first 3,000 iterations, optimize only the 3D Gaussian parameters (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{r}, \mathbf{s}, \sigma) using the differentiable rasterization pipeline. Do not update the deformation field F\theta. 3. Joint Optimization: After warm-up, jointly optimize the 3D Gaussians and the deformation field F\theta for the remaining iterations (typically up to 40,000). Deformation Calculation: For each Gaussian i at time t, compute the deformation offsets: (\delta \mathbf{x}i, \delta \mathbf{r}i, \delta \mathbf{s}i) = F\theta (\gamma(\text{sg}(\mathbf{x}i)), \gamma(t)) where \text{sg}(\cdot) denotes the stop-gradient operator, preventing gradients from flowing back to the canonical positions \mathbf{x}i through the deformation field. Deformed Parameters: The effective parameters for rendering are: \mathbf{x}'i = \mathbf{x}i + \delta \mathbf{x}i \mathbf{r}'i = \mathbf{r}i + \delta \mathbf{r}i \mathbf{s}'i = \mathbf{s}i + \delta \mathbf{s}i. Annealing Smooth Training (AST): During joint optimization, apply noise to the time input to handle pose inaccuracies. The effective time input becomes t + X(i), where: X(i) = \mathcal{N}(0, 1) \cdot \beta \cdot \Delta t \cdot (1 - i/\tau) Here, \mathcal{N}(0, 1) is standard Gaussian noise, \beta=0.1, \Delta t is the mean time interval between frames, \tau=20,000 iterations, and i is the current iteration index. Rasterization: Project the deformed Gaussians to 2D. The 2D covariance matrix \Sigma'i is computed as: \Sigma'i = \mathbf{J} \mathbf{V} \Sigma'i \mathbf{V}^T \mathbf{J}^T where \mathbf{V} is the view matrix, \Sigma'i is the deformed 3D covariance matrix derived from \mathbf{r}'i and \mathbf{s}'i, and \mathbf{J} is the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the projective transformation. Alpha Blending: Render pixel color C(\mathbf{p}) for pixel \mathbf{p}: C(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} Ti \alphai ci where \mathcal{N} is the set of Gaussians along the ray, ci is the color from SH, \alphai = \sigmai e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{p}-\boldsymbol{\mu}i)^T \Sigma'^{-1}i (\mathbf{p}-\boldsymbol{\mu}i)}, and Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the transmittance. Adaptive Density Control: Pruning: Remove Gaussians with opacity \sigmai below a threshold. Densification: Clone Gaussians with small scales and high positional gradients (threshold t{pos} = 0.0002) and move them in the direction of the gradient. Splitting: Split large, overlapping Gaussians by dividing their scale by \xi = 1.6. 4. Optimization: Use the Adam optimizer. The learning rate for 3D Gaussians follows the standard 3D-GS schedule. The learning rate for the deformation network F\theta decays exponentially from 8 \times 10^{-4} to 1.6 \times 10^{-6}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class PositionalEncoding(nn.Module): def init(self, L): super().init() self.L = L def forward(self, p): # p shape: (..., D) # Output shape: (..., D 2 L) freqbands = 2.0 torch.arange(self.L, device=p.device).float() scaledp = p.unsqueeze(-1) freqbands torch.pi sinvals = torch.sin(scaledp) cosvals = torch.cos(scaledp) return torch.cat([sinvals, cosvals], dim=-1).flatten(startdim=-2) class DeformationField(nn.Module): def init(self, inputdimx, inputdimt, hiddendim=256, depth=8): super().init() self.pex = PositionalEncoding(L=10) # L=10 for x self.pet = PositionalEncoding(L=6) # L=6 for t (synthetic), L=10 for real self.inputdimx = inputdimx self.inputdimt = inputdimt # Calculate encoded dimensions # Original pos: 3, Encoded: 3 2 10 = 60 # Original time: 1, Encoded: 1 2 6 = 12 self.fc = nn.Sequential() currentdim = 60 + 12 for in range(depth): self.fc.addmodule(f'linear{}', nn.Linear(currentdim, hiddendim)) self.fc.addmodule(f'relu{}', nn.ReLU()) currentdim = hiddendim # Output: deltax (3), deltar (4), deltas (3) -> total 10 self.fc.addmodule('output', nn.Linear(hiddendim, 10)) def forward(self, x, t, useast=False, iteration=0, totaliterations=40000, beta=0.1, dt=1.0): """ x: canonical positions (..., 3) t: time (..., 1) """ # Stop gradient on x xsg = x.detach() # Positional Encoding encx = self.pex(xsg) enct = self.pet(t) # AST Noise if useast and iteration < 20000: noise = torch.randnlike(t) beta dt (1 - iteration / 20000) enct = enct + noise # Note: Source adds noise to time input before encoding or after? # Source: gamma(t) + X(i). X(i) is added to t before gamma? # Formula: gamma(sg(x)), gamma(t + X(i)). # So noise is added to t, then encoded. # Correction: Add noise to t, then encode. # Re-encode if AST applied to t if useast and iteration < 20000: # Recalculate enct with noisy t # However, in the source formula (6), X(i) is added to t inside gamma. # gamma(t + X(i)). So we must add noise to t first. pass # Concatenate inputvec = torch.cat([encx, enct], dim=-1) # MLP offsets = self.fc(inputvec) # Split offsets deltax = offsets[...,:3] deltar = offsets[..., 3:7] deltas = offsets[..., 7:10] return deltax, deltar, deltas def rendergaussians(gaussians, cameramatrix, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Simplified rasterization step. gaussians: dict with x, r, s, sigma, shcoeffs cameramatrix: projection matrix """ # 1. Compute deformed parameters # (Assuming deformation field is already called and offsets are available) # xprime = x + deltax # rprime = r + deltar # sprime = s + deltas # 2. Compute Covariance # R = quaterniontomatrix(rprime) # S = scaletomatrix(sprime) # Sigma3d = R @ S @ S.T @ R.T # 3. Project to 2D # J = jacobianofprojection(...) # V = viewmatrix # Sigma2d = J @ V @ Sigma3d @ V.T @ J.T # 4. Alpha blending # Sort gaussians by depth # Render using tile-based rasterizer pass def traindeformable3dgaussians(images, poses, times, sparsepoints): # Initialize Gaussians from sparsepoints gaussians = initializegaussians(sparsepoints) deformationnet = DeformationField(inputdimx=3, inputdimt=1) optimizergs = optim.Adam(gaussians.parameters(), lr=1.6e-4) # Standard 3DGS LR optimizerdef = optim.Adam(deformationnet.parameters(), lr=8e-4) totaliterations = 40000 warmupiterations = 3000 for i in range(totaliterations): # Sample a random image/pose/time from the dataset img, pose, t = samplebatch(images, poses, times) # Get canonical positions x = gaussians['x'] # Compute deformation offsets # Use AST only during joint optimization phase useast = (i >= warmupiterations) deltax, deltar, deltas = deformationnet( x, t, useast=useast, iteration=i, totaliterations=totaliterations) # Compute deformed parameters xprime = x + deltax rprime = gaussians['r'] + deltar sprime = gaussians['s'] + deltas # Render renderedimg = rendergaussians( {'x': xprime, 'r': rprime, 's': sprime, 'sigma': gaussians['sigma'], 'sh': gaussians['sh']}, pose, img.shape[1], img.shape[2]) # Compute Loss (L1 + D-SSIM) loss = computeloss(renderedimg, img) # Backprop optimizergs.zerograd() optimizerdef.zerograd() if i < warmupiterations: # Only optimize Gaussians loss.backward() optimizergs.step() else: # Joint optimization loss.backward() optimizergs.step() optimizerdef.step() # Adaptive Density Control updategaussiandensity(gaussians, optimizergs) # Decay LR for deformation network currentlrdef = 8e-4 (1.6e-6 / 8e-4) (i / totaliterations) for paramgroup in optimizerdef.paramgroups: paramgroup['lr'] = currentlrdef Time Complexity: Training involves joint optimization of Gaussians and a shallow MLP. The deformation field adds minimal overhead compared to implicit NeRF-based methods. Rendering is real-time due to the tile-based rasterization. Memory Complexity: Stores 3D Gaussian attributes (position, rotation, scale, opacity, SH coefficients) and the deformation network weights. The deformation network is small (D=8, W=256). Performance: Achieves higher rendering quality and real-time speeds compared to implicit dynamic methods. Outperforms existing methods in both metrics. Strengths: Decouples geometry and appearance, enabling efficient training and rendering. Handles monocular dynamic scenes effectively. AST mechanism improves temporal smoothness in real-world data with inaccurate poses. Limitations: Relies on SfM for initialization; poor SfM results may affect quality. The deformation field assumes non-dramatic action variations. Deformable 3D Gaussians was proposed to address the limitations of implicit representations (slow convergence, overfitting) and entangled dynamic methods in modeling monocular dynamic scenes. It builds on the success of 3D Gaussian Splatting for static scenes. The method was introduced in the paper "Deformable 3D Gaussians for High-Fidelity Monocular Dynamic Scene Reconstruction". name: Spacetime Gaussian Feature Splatting
head: Spacetime Gaussians
body: Spacetime Gaussian Feature Splatting (STG) is a dynamic scene representation that extends 3D Gaussian Splatting into the 4D spacetime domain to enable real-time novel view synthesis of dynamic scenes. It solves the problem of modeling temporal evolution, emerging/vanishing content, and complex motion by parameterizing Gaussian attributes (position, rotation, opacity) as functions of time, while replacing spherical harmonics with a compact neural feature representation. Unlike sibling methods that rely on deformation fields or linear motion models, STG uses explicit polynomial parameterization for motion and a lightweight MLP for view/time-dependent appearance, offering superior temporal stability and lower memory consumption compared to training independent 3DGS models. Inputs: Multi-view video sequences (images and camera poses) across multiple timestamps. Initialization uses Structure-from-Motion (SfM) sparse point clouds from all available timestamps. Outputs: A set of Spacetime Gaussians (STGs) and a small Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) \Phi, capable of rendering photorealistic images at novel viewpoints and arbitrary timestamps. Each Spacetime Gaussian i stores the following parameters: 1. Spatial Opacity: \sigma{is} \in \mathbb{R} (time-independent base opacity). 2. Temporal Opacity Parameters: \mu{\tau i} \in \mathbb{R} (temporal center), s{\tau i} \in \mathbb{R} (temporal scaling). 3. Position: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 (initial 3D position). 4. Motion Coefficients: \{b{i,k}\}{k=0}^{np} \subset \mathbb{R}^3 (polynomial coefficients for position trajectory). 5. Rotation: qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 (initial quaternion). 6. Rotation Coefficients: \{c{i,k}\}{k=0}^{nq} \subset \mathbb{R}^4 (polynomial coefficients for rotation trajectory). 7. Scaling: si \in \mathbb{R}^3 (3D scaling vector, time-independent). 8. Features: fi(t) \in \mathbb{R}^9 (time-dependent features, see below). f{base} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Base RGB color. f{dir} \in \mathbb{R}^3: View-direction dependent features. f{time} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Time-dependent features. 9. MLP \Phi: A shallow, narrow network mapping splatted features and view direction to final color. Temporal Opacity: The temporal opacity \sigmai(t) is modeled using a 1D Gaussian function: \sigmai(t) = \sigma{is} \exp \left( -s{\tau i} |t - \mu{\tau i}|^2 \right) where \sigma{is} is the spatial opacity, \mu{\tau i} is the timestamp of maximum visibility, and s{\tau i} controls the effective duration. Position Trajectory: The position \mui(t) at time t is defined by a polynomial: \mui(t) = \sum{k=0}^{np} b{i,k} (t - \mu{\tau i})^k In implementation, np = 3. Rotation Trajectory: The rotation is parameterized by a quaternion qi(t) using a polynomial: qi(t) = \sum{k=0}^{nq} c{i,k} (t - \mu{\tau i})^k In implementation, nq = 1. The quaternion is normalized and converted to a rotation matrix Ri(t). Covariance: The scaling matrix Si is kept time-independent. The covariance matrix \Sigmai(t) is computed as: \Sigmai(t) = Ri(t) Si Si^T Ri^T(t) where Si is a diagonal matrix parameterized by si. Spacetime Opacity: The opacity of an STG at spacetime point (x, t) is: \alphai(t) = \sigmai(t) \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} (x - \mui(t))^T \Sigmai(t)^{-1} (x - \mui(t)) \right) Projection: The 3D Gaussian is projected to 2D image space. Let W be the viewing transformation and K be the projection matrix. The 2D center \mu^{2D}i and covariance \Sigma^{2D}i are: \mu^{2D}i = \left( K \left( \frac{W \mui(t)}{(W \mui(t))z} \right) \right){1:2} \Sigma^{2D}i = \left( J W \Sigmai(t) W^T J^T \right){1:2,1:2} where J is the Jacobian of the projective transformation. Feature Splatting: The feature vector fi(t) for each STG is constructed as: fi(t) = \left[ f{base}, f{dir}, (t - \mu{\tau i}) f{time} \right]^T \in \mathbb{R}^9 During rasterization, features are splatted to the image plane. At each pixel, the splatted features are split into F{base}, F{dir}, F{time}. Rendering: The final color I is computed by volume rendering the splatted features through the MLP \Phi, which takes the view direction r as input: I = F{base} + \Phi(F{dir}, F{time}, r) If the "lite-version" is used, \Phi is dropped, and I = F{base}. 1. Initialization: Initialize STGs using SfM sparse point clouds from all available timestamps. 2. Training Loop: a. Sample a timestamp t and camera pose. b. Compute time-dependent parameters \mui(t), Ri(t), and \sigmai(t) using the polynomial and Gaussian formulas. c. Project STGs to 2D and rasterize features fi(t) to the image plane using differentiable splatting. d. Compute final pixel colors using the MLP \Phi (or directly from F{base} in lite-version). e. Calculate loss: L = L{L1} + L{D-SSIM} between rendered and ground truth images. f. Backpropagate gradients to optimize STG parameters and \Phi using Adam optimizer. 3. Density Control: Interleave training with aggressive pruning to reduce Gaussian count and model size. 4. Guided Sampling (Optional): a. After training loss stabilizes, identify pixels with large errors. b. Aggregate errors patch-wise to prioritize substantial errors. c. Use coarse depth maps to determine depth ranges for these patches. d. Sample new Gaussians uniformly along rays within these depth ranges, adding small noise to centers. e. Repeat this process no more than 3 times. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computestgparameters(stg, t): """ Computes time-dependent attributes for a Spacetime Gaussian. """ # Temporal Opacity temporalopacity = stg.sigmais exp(-stg.staui (t - stg.mutaui)2) # Position pos = zeros(3) for k in range(0, 4): # np = 3, so k=0,1,2,3 pos += stg.b[i,k] (t - stg.mutaui)k # Rotation (Quaternion) quat = zeros(4) for k in range(0, 2): # nq = 1, so k=0,1 quat += stg.c[i,k] (t - stg.mutaui)k quat = normalize(quat) rotmatrix = quaterniontorotationmatrix(quat) # Covariance # Si is time-independent Si = diag(stg.si) Sigmat = rotmatrix @ (Si @ Si.T) @ rotmatrix.T return temporalopacity, pos, Sigmat def featuresplatting(stgs, camera, t): """ Rasterizes Spacetime Gaussians to image space. """ imageheight, imagewidth = camera.resolution featuresimage = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 9)) alphasimage = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) # Sort STGs by depth sortedstgs = sortbydepth(stgs, camera, t) for stg in sortedstgs: # Compute time-dependent attributes alpha3d, mut, Sigmat = computestgparameters(stg, t) # Project to 2D mu2d = project2d(mut, camera.W, camera.K) Sigma2d = projectcovariance(Sigmat, camera.W, camera.J) # Compute 2D opacity alpha2d = alpha3d gaussian2dpdf(mu2d, Sigma2d) # Construct feature vector fbase = stg.fbase fdir = stg.fdir ftime = stg.ftime ft = concat([fbase, fdir, (t - stg.mutaui) ftime]) # Rasterize featuresimage, alphasimage = rasterizegaussian( featuresimage, alphasimage, mu2d, Sigma2d, alpha2d, ft) return featuresimage, alphasimage def render(featuresimage, viewdirections): """ Computes final color from splatted features. """ # Split features Fbase = featuresimage[:,:, 0:3] Fdir = featuresimage[:,:, 3:6] Ftime = featuresimage[:,:, 6:9] # Lite version: return base color only # return Fbase # Full version: use MLP # Concatenate Fdir, Ftime and view direction inputtomlp = concat([Fdir, Ftime, viewdirections], axis=-1) color = Fbase + MLPphi(inputtomlp) return color def trainstep(stgs, camera, gtimage, t): # 1. Rasterize features, alphas = featuresplatting(stgs, camera, t) # 2. Render viewdirs = computeviewdirections(camera) predimage = render(features, viewdirs) # 3. Loss l1loss = L1(predimage, gtimage) dssimloss = DSSIM(predimage, gtimage) loss = l1loss + dssimloss # 4. Backprop loss.backward() # 5. Update optimizer.step() return loss Polynomial degree for motion (np): 3. Polynomial degree for rotation (nq): 1. Feature dimension: 9 per STG (3 base, 3 dir, 3 time). Optimizer: Adam. Pruning: More aggressive than standard 3DGS. Guided Sampling: Conducted no more than 3 times. Scaling Matrix: The scaling matrix Si is kept time-independent. Applying time-conditioned functions to scaling did not observe improvement in rendering quality. Temporal Flickering: Training independent 3DGS models per frame causes flickering; STG resolves this by enforcing coherent movement via polynomials. Sparse Initialization: Areas with sparse Gaussians at initialization (often distant) are challenging to converge. Guided sampling is required to address this. Time Complexity: Training time is 40-60 minutes for a 50-frame sequence on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. Memory Complexity: Significantly lower memory consumption than 3DGS, Plenoxels, and Nerfacto because a single model represents all frames. Feature size is 9 parameters per STG vs 48 for 3-degree Spherical Harmonics. Rendering Speed: 140 FPS at 1352 × 1014 resolution on the Neural 3D Video Dataset. 66 FPS at 8K resolution on an Nvidia RTX 4090 GPU (lite-version). Strengths: Real-time high-resolution rendering, compact model size, better temporal stability than independent frame training, handles emerging/vanishing content. Limitations: Requires multi-view video input. Polynomial motion model may be less flexible than deformation fields for highly complex non-rigid deformations, though it offers higher quality than linear models. When to use: Real-time dynamic view synthesis where temporal consistency and rendering speed are critical. When not to use: Scenes with extremely complex, non-polynomial motion that cannot be approximated by low-degree polynomials, or single-view dynamic reconstruction (STG is designed for multi-view). Spacetime Gaussian Feature Splatting was introduced by Zhan Li, Zhang Chen, Zhong Li, and Yi Xu from OPPO US Research Center and Portland State University in the paper "Spacetime Gaussian Feature Splatting for Real-Time Dynamic View Synthesis" (arXiv:2312.16812v2, Apr 4 2024). It builds upon 3D Gaussian Splatting [41] by extending it to the 4D spacetime domain. The method addresses limitations of grid-like representations (e.g., K-Planes, HexPlane) which cannot fully adapt to dynamic scene structures, and linear motion models (e.g., 4D Gaussians) which are less expressive.
