name: CC-4DGS Training Schedule and Hash Encoding Configuration
head: CC-4DGS implementation details, Canonical Deformation Field (CDF) with Compression (CCA) setup
body: CC-4DGS is a training and encoding configuration for dynamic Gaussian splatting that replaces learnable XOR-based hash tables with modulation-based universal hash functions, dense hash encoding, and lightweight neural decoders, combined with a three-stage optimization schedule and dynamic-score gating. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Swift4D by eliminating large XOR-based hash tables to reduce storage, instead mapping hash-encoded integers to continuous features via neural decoders. This approach achieves a superior trade-off among storage efficiency, reconstruction quality, and rendering speed compared to grid-based hash table approaches. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view video sequences (e.g., N3DV or Technicolor datasets), initial COLMAP point cloud, hyperparameters for hash encoding and optimization schedule. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters (position, rotation, scale, opacity, color) in canonical space, deformation field parameters, dynamic scores, and neural decoder weights. Data Structures: Multi-resolution Grids: A set of 4 or 5 hash grids. Hash Function Parameters: m: Bucket size (integer). Must be sufficiently large to limit collisions. P: Prime number (integer). Used alongside m to limit hash collisions. Neural Decoders: Lightweight neural networks, one per grid level, mapping hash-encoded integers to continuous features. Dynamic Score: A learned scalar d per Gaussian. Threshold: Scalar ζ for dynamic score gating. Numbered Steps: 1. Stage 1: Coarse Initialization (5K iterations). Establish the initial canonical point cloud using COLMAP. Optimize base Gaussian parameters (position, rotation, scale, opacity, color) without deformation. 2. Stage 2: Dynamic Score Fitting (3K iterations). Fit the per-Gaussian dynamic score d. This stage prepares the dynamic-score gating mechanism. 3. Stage 3: Main Optimization (20K iterations). Jointly optimize the deformation field and the Gaussian set. Total iterations per N3DV scene: 28K (5K + 3K + 20K). Dynamic-Score Gating: During rendering and optimization, deformation is applied only to Gaussians whose learned dynamic score d exceeds the threshold ζ. This avoids unnecessary computation in static regions. Hash Encoding Configuration: Unlike conventional hash-grid approaches that store vertex embeddings in large XOR-based hash tables, CC-4DGS stores no such learnable hash tables to reduce storage. It employs modulation-based universal hash functions with dense hash encoding. Lightweight neural decoders at each grid level map hash-encoded integers to continuous features. Each grid level uses a sufficiently large bucket size m and a prime P to limit hash collisions. Preliminary tests showed that smaller m values noticeably degrade PSNR. Due to GPU memory constraints, the number of multi-resolution grids is restricted to four or five. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializehashgrids(numgrids=4, bucketsizem=1000000, primeP=1000000007): """ Initialize modulation-based universal hash functions. Note: Exact implementation of modulation-based universal hash function is not provided in sources. We assume a standard hash function h(x) = ((x A) + B) % P, where A, B are random constants. """ grids = [] for i in range(numgrids): # Create a neural decoder for this grid level decoder = LightweightNeuralDecoder() grids.append({ 'level': i, 'decoder': decoder, 'bucketsize': bucketsizem, 'prime': primeP }) return grids def hashencode(position, grids): """ Encode a 3D position using dense hash encoding and neural decoders. """ features = [] for grid in grids: # Hash the position to an integer index # Note: Exact hash function details are not provided. # Assuming a standard hash function for demonstration. x, y, z = position # Modulation-based universal hash function # h = ((x A + y B + z C) % P) % m # Where A, B, C are random constants, P is prime, m is bucket size # This is a placeholder for the actual modulation-based hash function hashindex = (x 12345 + y 67890 + z 11111) % grid['prime'] % grid['bucketsize'] # Map hash-encoded integer to continuous features using neural decoder feature = grid'decoder' features.append(feature) return concatenate(features) def dynamicscoregate(gaussian, thresholdzeta): """ Determine if deformation should be applied based on dynamic score. """ return gaussian.dynamicscore > thresholdzeta def traincc4dgs(dataset, initialpointcloud, numiterationsstage1=5000, numiterationsstage2=3000, numiterationsstage3=20000, thresholdzeta=0.5, bucketsizem=1000000, primeP=1000000007): """ Main training loop for CC-4DGS. """ # Initialize hash grids grids = initializehashgrids(numgrids=4, bucketsizem=bucketsizem, primeP=primeP) # Initialize Gaussians from COLMAP gaussians = initializegaussians(initialpointcloud) # Initialize deformation field and dynamic scores deformationfield = InitializeDeformationField() for g in gaussians: g.dynamicscore = 0.0 # Initialize dynamic score # Stage 1: Coarse Initialization for i in range(numiterationsstage1): # Render image renderedimage = render(gaussians, deformationfield, grids, time=t) # Compute loss (L1 + D-SSIM) loss = computeloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage) # Backpropagate and update base Gaussian parameters updateparameters(gaussians, loss) # Stage 2: Dynamic Score Fitting for i in range(numiterationsstage2): # Render image renderedimage = render(gaussians, deformationfield, grids, time=t) # Compute loss loss = computeloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage) # Backpropagate and update dynamic scores updateparameters(gaussians.dynamicscore, loss) # Stage 3: Main Optimization for i in range(numiterationsstage3): # Render image with dynamic-score gating activegaussians = [g for g in gaussians if dynamicscoregate(g, thresholdzeta)] renderedimage = render(activegaussians, deformationfield, grids, time=t) # Compute loss loss = computeloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage) # Backpropagate and update deformation field and Gaussian parameters updateparameters(deformationfield, loss) updateparameters(gaussians, loss) return gaussians, deformationfield, grids def render(gaussians, deformationfield, grids, time): """ Render image using differentiable Gaussian rasterization. """ # Apply deformation to active Gaussians for g in gaussians: if dynamicscoregate(g, thresholdzeta): # Get hash-encoded features features = hashencode(g.position, grids) # Apply deformation using features and deformation field g.position = deformationfield(g.position, features, time) # Differentiable rasterization image = differentiablerasterize(gaussians) return image Parameters with Typical Values: m (Bucket size): Not given in the sources, but must be sufficiently large. P (Prime): Not given in the sources, but used alongside m. ζ (Threshold): Not given in the sources, but used for dynamic-score gating. Number of multi-resolution grids: 4 or 5. Stage 1 iterations: 5K. Stage 2 iterations: 3K. Stage 3 iterations: 20K. Total iterations per N3DV scene: 28K. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hash Collisions: Smaller m values noticeably degrade PSNR. GPU Memory: The number of multi-resolution grids is restricted to 4 or 5 due to GPU memory constraints. Static Regions: Without dynamic-score gating, unnecessary computation occurs in static regions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Storage cost is significantly reduced compared to Swift4D. The CDF component alone reduces model size to a few tens of megabytes. When combined with CCA, the total storage further decreases to approximately 30 MB. Measured Performance: N3DV Dataset: PSNR in the low 32 dB range, SSIM approximately 0.94. Technicolor Dataset (CDF): PSNR 33.29 dB, SSIM 0.912, rendering speed 64.7 FPS. Technicolor Dataset (CDF+CCA): PSNR 33.30 dB, SSIM 0.912, rendering speed 64.6 FPS, storage ~32 MB. Hardware: Single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Superior trade-off among storage efficiency, reconstruction quality, and rendering speed. Eliminates large XOR-based hash tables to reduce storage. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of m to avoid hash collisions. Limited by GPU memory constraints on the number of multi-resolution grids. When to Use: When storage efficiency is a priority and real-time rendering is required. When Not to Use: When higher reconstruction quality is needed at the cost of increased storage. CC-4DGS was introduced in the paper "CC-4DGS: Computational Deformation and Point-Cloud Compression for Storage-Efficient Dynamic Gaussian Splatting". It builds on prior work such as 4DGS and Swift4D. The method is evaluated on the N3DV dataset and the Technicolor Light Field dataset. CC-4DGS: Computational Deformation and Point-Cloud Compression for Storage-Efficient Dynamic Gaussian Splatting., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2026.3721136, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Rendering-aware QP Offset Modelling
head: Density-based QP scaling, Inter-Sequence QP Modelling, Intra-Sequence QP Modelling
body: This method approximates the optimal Quantization Parameter (QP) distribution for Rate-Distortion Optimized (RDO) RAHT coding in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by linking hierarchical structure to visual impact. Unlike analytical solutions that require per-sequence fitting of multiple parameters, it uses a generalized heuristic based on scene density and resolution to generalize QP offsets across diverse scenes without iterative pre-analysis. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: N{primitives}: Total number of Gaussian primitives in the scene. \{dj\}{j=1}^{N{primitives}}: Euclidean distance from the j-th primitive to its nearest neighbour. W, H: Training resolution width and height. \{\bar{N}i\}: Average number of Gaussian primitives contained by each node at RAHT layer i. Outputs: \beta, \gamma: Sequence-dependent fitting parameters for the QP distribution model. \Delta q{pi}: The QP offset for layer i, derived from the model. Data Structures: Nearest-Neighbour Distances: An array of size N{primitives} storing dj for each primitive. Layer Primitive Counts: An array or map storing \bar{N}i for each RAHT layer i. Steps: 1. Calculate Spatial Density (\rho): Compute the average inverse square nearest-neighbour distance across all primitives: \rho = \frac{1}{N{primitives}} \sum{j=1}^{N{primitives}} \frac{1}{dj^2} Definition: \rho quantifies the aggregation density of primitives in 3D space. A higher \rho implies more overlapping primitives, increasing the likelihood of multi-primitive accumulation per pixel during splatting. 2. Calculate Global Scaling Factor (s): Modulate the QP offset based on scene density and resolution using the regression-derived formula: s = 10 + 0.029 \cdot \rho \cdot (W \cdot H)^{0.2} Parameters: The constants 10 and 0.029 are derived from regression across the dataset. The exponent 0.2 applies to the pixel count (W \cdot H). 3. Derive Sequence-Dependent Parameters (\beta, \gamma): Analytically derive the global offset and scaling parameters from s: \gamma = s^3 \beta = 0.75 \cdot s Definitions: \beta: Accounts for the global offset of the QP distribution. \gamma: Accounts for the scaling of the QP distribution. 4. Compute Layer-wise QP Offsets (\Delta q{pi}): Model the shape of layer-wise QP offsets using \bar{N}i as a proxy for hierarchical impact. Layers closer to the root (smaller index) have higher \bar{N}i and require smaller QP values to mitigate error accumulation. Solve for \Delta q{pi} in the following equation: (\Delta q{pi} + \beta)^3 = \gamma \cdot \bar{N}i Rearranging for implementation: \Delta q{pi} = \sqrt[3]{\gamma \cdot \bar{N}i} - \beta Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeqpoffsets(primitivedistances, layeravgcounts, width, height): """ Compute rendering-aware QP offsets for RAHT coding layers. Args: primitivedistances (list[float]): List of nearest-neighbour distances dj for all primitives. layeravgcounts (dict[int, float]): Map of RAHT layer index i to average primitive count Nbari. width (int): Training resolution width W. height (int): Training resolution height H. Returns: dict[int, float]: Map of RAHT layer index i to QP offset deltaqpi. """ nprimitives = len(primitivedistances) # Step 1: Calculate spatial density rho # rho = (1 / Nprimitives) sum(1 / dj^2) inversesqsum = 0.0 for d in primitivedistances: # Guard against division by zero if a primitive is coincident with its neighbour if d == 0: d = 1e-6 inversesqsum += 1.0 / (d d) rho = inversesqsum / nprimitives # Step 2: Calculate global scaling factor s # s = 10 + 0.029 rho (W H)^0.2 pixelcount = width height s = 10.0 + 0.029 rho (pixelcount 0.2) # Step 3: Derive sequence-dependent parameters beta and gamma # gamma = s^3 # beta = 0.75 s gamma = s 3 beta = 0.75 s # Step 4: Compute layer-wise QP offsets # (deltaqpi + beta)^3 = gamma Nbari # deltaqpi = (gamma Nbari)^(1/3) - beta offsets = {} for layerindex, nbari in layeravgcounts.items(): # Guard against negative values inside cube root if gamma Nbari is negative (unlikely given definitions) val = gamma nbari if val < 0: val = 0.0 deltaqpi = val (1.0 / 3.0) - beta offsets[layerindex] = deltaqpi return offsets Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Nearest-Neighbour Distance: If a primitive coincides with its nearest neighbour (dj=0), the inverse square term becomes undefined. A small epsilon (e.g., 10^{-6}) should be used as a lower bound for dj. Negative Cube Root Argument: Theoretically, \gamma and \bar{N}i are positive, so \gamma \cdot \bar{N}i is positive. However, numerical precision issues or invalid input data could result in negative values. Clamp to zero before taking the cube root. Resolution Scaling: The term (W \cdot H)^{0.2} ensures that higher resolutions increase the scaling factor s, leading to larger \gamma and \beta, which adjusts QP offsets to account for finer sampling. Time Complexity: O(N{primitives}) to compute \rho and O(L) to compute offsets for L layers. This is significantly faster than iterative per-sequence fitting methods. Memory Complexity: O(N{primitives}) to store nearest-neighbour distances. O(L) for layer counts. Strengths: Generalizes across diverse scenes without per-sequence fitting. Accounts for error accumulation during splatting projection by linking hierarchical structure to visual impact. Limitations: Relies on regression-derived constants (10, 0.029, 0.2, 0.75) which may not be optimal for all scene types or hardware configurations. Assumes the relationship between density, resolution, and QP offset holds across the dataset used for regression. When to Use: When coding 3DGS data with RAHT and needing a fast, generalized method to set QP offsets based on scene properties. When Not to Use: When per-sequence optimization is feasible and maximum rate-distortion performance is critical, as analytical solutions with per-sequence fitting may yield better results. This method was proposed in the context of Rate-Distortion Optimized RAHT coding for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the limitation that optimal QP offsets exhibit a linear trend relative to the RAHT layer index, but this relationship cannot be directly generalized due to varying numbers of RAHT layers between sequences. The method builds on the observation that error accumulation in splatting projection is constructive for root layers (leading to visual distortion) and random for leaf layers (cancelling out). It was developed to eliminate the need for per-sequence parameter fitting, enabling robust performance across diverse scenes. A Versatile Rate-Distortion Optimized RAHT Coding Layer for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://centralesupelec.hal.science/hal-05586765v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Closed-Form Triangle Splatting (CF-Splat)
head: CF-Splat, Closed-Form Triangle Splatting with Mesh Priors
body: Closed-Form Triangle Splatting (CF-Splat) is a method for efficient scene appearance estimation over a known mesh geometry using calibrated camera views. It formulates rendered pixel colors as a linear function of per-vertex spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, allowing the global appearance to be solved via a single linear least-squares (LLS) problem rather than iterative nonlinear optimization. Unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting Implementation Details, which relies on gradient-based optimization of millions of coupled Gaussian parameters, CF-Splat eliminates iterative updates, thereby avoiding local minima, reducing computation time by 27.5×–378.0×, and lowering peak GPU memory usage. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A known mesh M = (V, F) with Nv vertices and Nf faces; K calibrated RGB observations O = \{Ik, Kk, Tk\}{k=1}^K, where Ik is the image, Kk is the intrinsic matrix, and Tk = [Rk | tk] is the extrinsic transformation. Outputs: The global SH appearance state X \in \mathbb{R}^{q Nv \times 3}, containing the per-vertex SH coefficients. Data Structures: Mesh: Vertices V = \{vi\}{i=1}^{Nv} and faces F = \{fj\}{j=1}^{Nf}. Each face fj is defined by indices \iota(j, s) \in \{1, \dots, Nv\} for s \in \{0, 1, 2\}. SH Coefficients: For each vertex vi, the SH coefficients for color channel \tau \in \{R, G, B\} are ci^{(\tau)} \in \mathbb{R}^q, where q = (L+1)^2 and L is the maximum SH degree. The global state X stacks these coefficients: X = [C1^\top, \dots, C{Nv}^\top]^\top, where Ci = [ci^{(R)}, ci^{(G)}, ci^{(B)}] \in \mathbb{R}^{q \times 3}. Matrices: A \in \mathbb{R}^{KHW \times q Nv}: Global observation matrix. B \in \mathbb{R}^{KHW \times 3}: Stacked observed RGB colors. W \in \mathbb{R}^{KHW \times KHW}: Diagonal confidence matrix. \Lambda \in \mathbb{R}^{q Nv \times q Nv}: Block-diagonal adaptive SH regularizer. H \in \mathbb{R}^{q Nv \times q Nv}: Normal matrix H = A^\top W A + \Lambda. G \in \mathbb{R}^{q Nv \times 3}: Right-hand side G = A^\top W B. Parameters: L: Maximum SH degree. Typically L=3 for sparse-view evaluations. \epsilonw: Minimum confidence value for grazing-angle observations (0 < \epsilonw < 1). \gammas: Weak regularization weight for SH bands with sufficient directional support (0 < \gammas \ll \gammau). \gammau: Strong regularization weight for SH bands lacking sufficient directional support. Steps: 1. Compute Viewing Directions and SH Basis: For each vertex vi and camera k, compute the camera center in mesh coordinates ok = -Rk^\top tk. The viewing direction is: dk^i = \frac{vi - ok}{\|vi - ok\|2} Evaluate the SH basis vector Y(dk^i) \in \mathbb{R}^q: Y(dk^i) = [y0^0(dk^i), y1^{-1}(dk^i), \dots, yL^L(dk^i)]^\top where yl^m(d) is the SH basis function. 2. Rasterization: For each camera k, rasterize the mesh M using Kk and Tk to find the covering triangle f{\rhok(p{k,r})} for each pixel p{k,r} in the image Ik (where r \in \{1, \dots, HW\}). Compute the barycentric weights \lambda{k,r}^s for the three vertices s \in \{0, 1, 2\} of the covering triangle. 3. Compute Local Observation Features: For each pixel p{k,r} and each vertex s of its covering triangle, let i{s,k,r} = \iota(\rhok(p{k,r}), s) be the global vertex index. Compute the local observation feature: \phi{k,r}^s = \lambda{k,r}^s Y(dk^{i{s,k,r}}) \in \mathbb{R}^q. 4. Construct Per-View Observation Matrix Ak: Construct Ak \in \mathbb{R}^{HW \times q Nv}. For row r (corresponding to pixel p{k,r}), the nonzero blocks are: [Ak]{r, i{s,k,r}} = (\phi{k,r}^s)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times q} \quad \text{for } s=0,1,2 All other entries in row r are zero. 5. Compute Confidence Weights: For each pixel p{k,r}, compute the angle-dependent confidence w{k,r}: w{k,r} = \max\left(\epsilonw, n{\rhok(p{k,r})}^\top \sum{s=0}^2 \lambda{k,r}^s \frac{v{i{s,k,r}} - ok}{\|v{i{s,k,r}} - ok\|2}\right) where n{\rhok(p{k,r})} is the unit normal of the covering triangle. 6. Construct Global Matrices: Stack observed colors: Bk = [Ik(p{k,1}), \dots, Ik(p{k,HW})]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{HW \times 3}. Assemble confidence matrices: Wk = \text{diag}([w{k,1}, \dots, w{k,HW}]) \in \mathbb{R}^{HW \times HW}. Assemble global matrices: A = [A1^\top, \dots, AK^\top]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{KHW \times q Nv} B = [B1^\top, \dots, BK^\top]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{KHW \times 3} W = \text{blkdiag}(W1, \dots, WK) \in \mathbb{R}^{KHW \times KHW}. 7. Compute Adaptive Regularization Weights: For each vertex vi, determine n{\text{view}}^{(i)}, the number of cameras for which the block Ak^{(i)} (associated with vi) contains at least one nonzero row. Compute the regularization weight \gamma{i,l} for SH band l: \gamma{i,l} = \begin{cases} \gammas & \text{if } (l+1)^2 \le n{\text{view}}^{(i)} \\ \gammau & \text{if } (l+1)^2 > n{\text{view}}^{(i)} \end{cases}. 8. Construct Global Regularizer \Lambda: For each vertex i, construct the per-vertex regularizer: \Lambdai = \text{diag}(\gamma{i,0} I1, \gamma{i,1} I3, \dots, \gamma{i,L} I{2L+1}) \in \mathbb{R}^{q \times q}. Assemble the global regularizer: \Lambda = \text{blkdiag}(\Lambda1, \dots, \Lambda{Nv}) \in \mathbb{R}^{q Nv \times q Nv}. 9. Solve the Global LLS Problem: The objective is: X^ = \arg \minX \frac{1}{2} \| W^{1/2}(AX - B) \|F^2 + \frac{1}{2} \| \Lambda^{1/2} X \|F^2. This leads to the normal system: H X^ = G where H = A^\top W A + \Lambda and G = A^\top W B. Solve this system using a matrix-free preconditioned conjugate-gradient (PCG) solver. The solver applies the normal operator H implicitly without explicitly materializing H. It processes observations view-wise, retaining only the current view's features in memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def cfsplat(meshV, meshF, observations, L, epsilonw, gammas, gammau): """ meshV: (Nv, 3) array of vertex coordinates meshF: (Nf, 3) array of vertex indices for each face observations: list of dicts with keys 'image' (H,W,3), 'K' (3,3), 'T' (3,4) L: max SH degree epsilonw: min confidence gammas: weak regularization weight gammau: strong regularization weight Returns: X: (Nv, 3, q) array of SH coefficients, where q = (L+1)^2 """ Nv = meshV.shape[0] K = len(observations) q = (L + 1) 2 # Track unique cameras per vertex for adaptive regularization vertexcameras = [set() for in range(Nv)] allpixeldata = [] for kidx, obs in enumerate(observations): Ik = obs['image'] Kk = obs['K'] Tk = obs['T'] Rk = Tk[:,:3] tk = Tk[:, 3] ok = -Rk.T @ tk H, W = Ik.shape[:2] # Standard z-buffer rasterization to find covering triangle and barycentric weights pixeltriangles, pixelbarycentrics, pixelvertexindices = rasterizemesh(meshV, meshF, Kk, Tk, H, W) for ridx in range(H W): vindices = pixelvertexindices[ridx] lambdas = pixelbarycentrics[ridx] triidx = pixeltriangles[ridx] # Get triangle normal v0, v1, v2 = meshV[vindices[0]], meshV[vindices[1]], meshV[vindices[2]] ntri = np.cross(v1 - v0, v2 - v0) ntri = ntri / np.linalg.norm(ntri) # Compute weighted direction for confidence weighteddirsum = np.zeros(3) for s in range(3): vs = meshV[vindices[s]] dirs = vs - ok norms = np.linalg.norm(dirs) if norms < 1e-8: dirs = np.array([0, 0, 1]) else: dirs = dirs / norms weighteddirsum += lambdas[s] dirs vertexcameras[vindices[s]].add(kidx) conf = ntri.dot(weighteddirsum) w = max(epsilonw, conf) # Compute SH basis vectors for each vertex phis = [] for s in range(3): vs = meshV[vindices[s]] dirs = vs - ok norms = np.linalg.norm(dirs) if norms < 1e-8: dirs = np.array([0, 0, 1]) else: dirs = dirs / norms Yd = computeshbasis(dirs, L) # Standard SH basis evaluation phis = lambdas[s] Yd phis.append(phis) allpixeldata.append({ 'k': kidx, 'r': ridx, 'vindices': vindices, 'phis': phis, 'w': w, 'imagecolor': Ik[ridx // W, ridx % W] }) # Step 7: Compute Regularizer Lambda nviewcounts = [len(cams) for cams in vertexcameras] Lambdablocks = [] for i in range(Nv): nview = nviewcounts[i] Lambdai = np.zeros((q, q)) for l in range(L + 1): dim = 2 l + 1 startidx = l l endidx = startidx + dim weight = gammas if (l + 1) 2 <= nview else gammau Lambdai[startidx:endidx, startidx:endidx] = weight np.eye(dim) Lambdablocks.append(Lambdai) # Step 9: Solve H X = G using PCG def matvecH(xflat): x = xflat.reshape(Nv, q, 3) yblocks = [np.zeros((q, 3)) for in range(Nv)] for pdata in allpixeldata: w = pdata['w'] vindices = pdata['vindices'] phis = pdata['phis'] resr = np.zeros(3) for s in range(3): vidx = vindices[s] phis = phis[s] xv = x[vidx] resr += (phis.reshape(1, -1) @ xv).flatten() resr = w for s in range(3): vidx = vindices[s] phis = phis[s] yblocks[vidx] += np.outer(phis, resr) yflat = np.concatenate([b.flatten() for b in yblocks]) lamxflat = np.zeroslike(xflat) for i in range(Nv): lamxflat[i q 3: (i + 1) q 3] = (Lambdablocks[i] @ x[i]).flatten() return yflat + lamxflat Gblocks = [np.zeros((q, 3)) for in range(Nv)] for pdata in allpixeldata: w = pdata['w'] vindices = pdata['vindices'] phis = pdata['phis'] color = pdata['imagecolor'] for s in range(3): vidx = vindices[s] phis = phis[s] Gblocks[vidx] += np.outer(phis, w color) Gflat = np.concatenate([b.flatten() for b in Gblocks]) x0 = np.zeros(Nv q 3) xsol = pcgsolver(matvecH, Gflat, x0) X = xsol.reshape(Nv, q, 3) return X def rasterizemesh(meshV, meshF, K, T, H, W): """Standard z-buffer rasterization returning covering triangle index, barycentric weights, and vertex indices per pixel.""" # Implementation uses standard graphics pipeline: project vertices, clip, scanline fill, # and compute barycentric coordinates via interpolation. Returns arrays of size HW. # Standard rasterization primitive. pass def computeshbasis(d, L): """Evaluates spherical harmonic basis functions up to degree L for direction d.""" # Standard SH basis evaluation. pass def pcgsolver(matvec, b, x0, tol=1e-6, maxiter=1000): """Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient solver. Uses a triangle-structured preconditioner.""" x = x0.copy() r = b - matvec(x) p = r.copy() rsold = np.dot(r, r) for i in range(maxiter): Ap = matvec(p) pAp = np.dot(p, Ap) if abs(pAp) < 1e-20: break alpha = rsold / pAp x += alpha p r -= alpha Ap rsnew = np.dot(r, r) if np.sqrt(rsnew) < tol: break p = r + (rsnew / rsold) p rsold = rsnew return x Time Complexity: Scales with the number of observations K due to solving the global LLS system, but avoids the iterative overhead of gradient-based methods. Memory Complexity: Governed primarily by the number of mesh vertices Nv, not K. The matrix-free solver retains only the current view's features in memory. Performance: On the Oxford Spires dataset (760 views, 1080x1440, 1.55M vertices), CF-Splat achieved 26.88 PSNR in 1.15 minutes with 4.18 GB memory, compared to 3DGS's 24.04 PSNR in 48.93 minutes with 7.18 GB memory. Scaling: CF-Splat requires approximately 27.5×–378.0× less computation time and 1.8× lower peak GPU memory on average than 3DGS across scenes of different scales. Strengths: Eliminates iterative nonlinear optimization, avoiding local minima and geometric error from view-specific overfitting. Low memory footprint allows scalability to large scenes. Limitations: Requires known mesh geometry and calibrated cameras. CF-Splat was proposed in "CF-Splat: Closed-Form Triangle Splatting with Mesh Priors". It builds on classical surface light field methods and vertex-centered light fields on triangular meshes, which estimated directional radiance using regularized least squares. Unlike iterative splatting methods like 3DGS, which jointly optimize millions of coupled Gaussian parameters, CF-Splat formulates appearance estimation as a global linear least-squares problem, enabling a closed-form solution. CF-Splat: Closed-Form Triangle Splatting with Mesh Priors, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22108, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Softmax-GS
head: Softmax Gaussian Splatting
body: Softmax-GS is a unified rendering and optimization method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that resolves view-inconsistency (popping artifacts) and diffuse boundaries by enforcing a softmax-based competition among overlapping Gaussians. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which assumes non-overlapping primitives, Softmax-GS relaxes this assumption to allow a continuous spectrum of visual behaviors from smooth color blending to sharp, winner-take-all boundaries. It differs from DeSplat and 360 Gaussian Splatting by directly modeling overlap via softmax weights rather than re-sorting or stochastic mixing, and from EVER by maintaining near-real-time rendering speeds while providing controllable boundary sharpness. Inputs: Camera parameters, a set of K 3D Gaussians defined by mean \muk, covariance \Sigmak, opacity exponent pk (where opacity ok \sim \exp(pk)), and color ck. Outputs: Rendered pixel color I(\mathbf{x}) and gradients for optimization. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: For each Gaussian k, store: pk: Exponent (scalar). ak: Integrated 1D absorbance along the ray (scalar, ak = \int ok dl). dk: Depth of the Gaussian center projected onto the ray (scalar). \alphak: Boundary sharpness parameter (scalar, learnable). Intermediate State (per ray/patch): Tk: Current transmittance (scalar). a{past}: Accumulated absorbance of previous Gaussians (scalar). d{past}: Moving average depth of previous Gaussians (scalar). p{past}: Moving average exponent of previous Gaussians (scalar). CUDA arrays of length K (typically 128) to cache intermediate values (a{past}, d{past}, p{past}, Tk) for the backward pass. Parameters: \beta: Softmax competition strength. \beta=0 yields equal blending; large \beta yields sharp boundaries. \gamma: Decay rate for competition based on depth difference. \alpha: Learnable parameter for individual Gaussian boundary sharpness via Generalized Exponential Function (GEF). K: Hyperparameter for the number of closest Gaussians processed with Softmax-GS logic. Typical value: 128. Pruning threshold: Raised to 0.4 to accommodate GEF-shrunk splats. Method Steps: 1. Generalized Exponential Function (GEF) for Absorbance: Replace the standard squared distance \|\cdot\|^2 in the Gaussian kernel with \|\cdot\|^{2\alpha} to control individual boundary sharpness. This modifies the absorbance ak but does not change the exponent pk used in softmax competition. ok(\mathbf{x}, l) \propto \exp(-\|\mathbf{x} - \muk\|^{2\alpha}) Compute ak = \int0^L ok(\mathbf{x}, l) dl. 2. Sequential Processing (Forward Pass): Process Gaussians sorted from nearest to farthest. For each Gaussian k: a. Compute Softmax Weights for Pairwise Competition: Treat all previously processed Gaussians as a single "past" entity with aggregate properties a{past}, d{past}, p{past}. Compute the softmax weight wk between the current Gaussian k and the past entity using their exponents pk and p{past}: wk = \frac{\exp(\beta \cdot pk)}{\exp(\beta \cdot pk) + \exp(\beta \cdot p{past})} w{past} = \frac{\exp(\beta \cdot p{past})}{\exp(\beta \cdot pk) + \exp(\beta \cdot p{past})} Competition operates on pk because ok \in 0, \infty), making \exp(ok) \ge 1, which prevents weights from diminishing. b. Compute Fully Overlapping Absorbances (\hat{a}): Apply the softmax weights to the individual absorbances: \hat{a}k = wk ak \hat{a}{past} = w{past} a{past} c. Interpolate with Depth Decay: Calculate the exponential decay factor s based on the depth difference |dk - d{past}|: s = \exp(-\gamma |dk - d{past}|) Interpolate between the fully overlapping absorbances (\hat{a}) and the original non-softmax absorbances (a): \bar{a}k = s \hat{a}k + (1-s) ak \bar{a}{past} = s \hat{a}{past} + (1-s) a{past} d. Correction for Order Invariance and Transmittance: The interpolation may violate order invariance (second Gaussian's color discounted by (1-\bar{a}{past})) and transmittance consistency (output transmittance higher than original). Solve for corrected absorbances \tilde{a}{past} and \tilde{a}k that satisfy: (1-\tilde{a}{past})(1-\tilde{a}k) = Tk \tilde{a}{past} = \frac{\hat{a}{past}(1-Tk)}{\hat{a}{past} + \hat{a}k} \tilde{a}k = \frac{\hat{a}k(1-Tk)}{\hat{a}k + \tilde{a}{past}Tk} Apply the interpolation step to \tilde{a}{past} and \tilde{a}k to get \bar{a}{past} and \bar{a}k. Finally, scale them by a factor m to restore exact transmittance Tk: (1-m \bar{a}{past})(1-m \bar{a}k) = Tk \bar{a}{past} \leftarrow m \bar{a}{past}, \quad \bar{a}k \leftarrow m \bar{a}k e. Update State: Update the moving averages and transmittance: T{k+1} = Tk (1 - \bar{a}k) a{past} \leftarrow a{past} + \bar{a}k d{past} \leftarrow \text{weighted average of } d{past} \text{ and } dk p{past} \leftarrow \text{weighted average of } p{past} \text{ and } pk Cache these intermediate values in the CUDA arrays. 3. Rendering: The final color is computed using the standard [splatting formulation with the corrected absorbances: I(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{k=1}^K ck \bar{a}k \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \bar{a}j) (Note: In the sequential implementation, this is accumulated incrementally as I \leftarrow I + ck \bar{a}k Tk). 4. Backward Pass: To preserve linear complexity, access the cached intermediate values from the forward pass CUDA arrays directly. Compute gradients for pk, ak, \alphak without recomputing the forward pass. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Each element must have: 'p' (exponent), 'a' (absorbance), 'd' (depth), 'c' (color). """ # Initialize state T = 1.0 apast = 0.0 dpast = 0.0 ppast = 0.0 # Cache arrays for backward pass cacheT = [] cacheapast = [] cachedpast = [] cacheppast = [] renderedcolor = 0.0 for k, g in enumerate(gaussianssorted): pk = g['p'] ak = g['a'] dk = g['d'] ck = g['c'] if k == 0: # First Gaussian: no past entity to compete with barak = ak else: # 1. Compute Softmax Weights exppk = math.exp(beta pk) expppast = math.exp(beta ppast) denom = exppk + expppast wk = exppk / denom wpast = expppast / denom # 2. Compute Fully Overlapping Absorbances hatak = wk ak hatapast = wpast apast # 3. Interpolate with Depth Decay depthdiff = abs(dk - dpast) s = math.exp(-gamma depthdiff) barak = s hatak + (1 - s) ak barapast = s hatapast + (1 - s) apast # 4. Correction for Order Invariance and Transmittance tildeapast = (hatapast (1 - T)) / (hatapast + hatak) tildeak = (hatak (1 - T)) / (hatak + tildeapast T) # Re-apply interpolation to corrected values barak = s tildeak + (1 - s) ak barapast = s tildeapast + (1 - s) apast # 5. Scale to restore exact transmittance T # Solve (1 - mA)(1 - mB) = T for m, where A=barapast, B=barak A = barapast B = barak if A B > 1e-9: disc = (A + B)2 - 4 A B (1 - T) if disc < 0: disc = 0.0 sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) m = ((A + B) - sqrtdisc) / (2 A B) else: # Linear fallback if one absorbance is near zero m = (1 - T) / (A + B) if (A + B) > 1e-9 else 1.0 m = max(0.0, min(1.0, m)) barak = m barapast = m # Accumulate color renderedcolor += ck barak T # Update transmittance T = (1 - barak) # Update past entity state for next iteration apastold = apast apast += barak if apast > 1e-9: dpast = (apastold dpast + barak dk) / apast ppast = (apastold ppast + barak pk) / apast # Cache for backward pass if len(cacheT) < Kcachesize: cacheT.append(T) cacheapast.append(apast) cachedpast.append(dpast) cacheppast.append(ppast) return renderedcolor, cacheT, cacheapast, cachedpast, cacheppast def softmaxgsbackward(g, cacheT, cacheapast, cachedpast, cacheppast, gradout): """ Backward pass concept. Iterates backwards through cached arrays to compute gradients for p, a, alpha. Accesses cached T, apast, dpast, ppast at step k to avoid recomputing forward pass. """ # Gradient computation follows the chain rule through the quadratic correction, # interpolation, and softmax steps using the cached intermediate values. pass Uses differentiable splatting with soft attention weights. Softmax-GS uses a deterministic softmax competition with explicit transmittance correction. Choose Softmax-GS when strict transmittance conservation is required. Focuses on omnidirectional rendering. Softmax-GS focuses on overlap handling. Choose Softmax-GS for standard perspective views with overlapping primitives. Adds geometry priors. Softmax-GS is appearance-focused. Choose Softmax-GS when geometric priors are unnecessary or conflict with appearance optimization. Adds perceptual loss. Softmax-GS can be combined with it. Choose Softmax-GS when perceptual losses are used alongside overlap resolution. Inverse rendering. Softmax-GS can be used here. Choose Softmax-GS when inverse rendering requires stable overlap handling. Texture refinement. Independent. Choose Softmax-GS when texture refinement is combined with boundary sharpness control. Semantics. Independent. Choose Softmax-GS when semantic segmentation requires consistent boundary rendering. Edge detection. Independent. Choose Softmax-GS when edge detection is paired with softmax competition. Density management. Softmax-GS suggests higher pruning threshold. Choose Softmax-GS when aggressive pruning is needed alongside overlap resolution. Quantum computing. Independent. Choose Softmax-GS for classical GPU rendering pipelines. Human avatars. Softmax-GS can be applied. Choose Softmax-GS for human avatars with complex overlapping clothing. Dynamic scenes. Softmax-GS can be applied. Choose Softmax-GS for dynamic scenes with temporal overlap artifacts. Triangle primitives. Independent. Choose Softmax-GS when Gaussian primitives are preferred over triangles. Dropout for regularization. Independent. Choose Softmax-GS when regularization is combined with overlap handling. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussians per ray for both forward and backward passes. Memory Complexity: Requires caching intermediate values (a{past}, d{past}, p{past}, Tk) in CUDA arrays of length K (typically 128) per patch for the backward pass. Performance: Adds approximately 1.2× increase in training time compared to standard 3D GS. Rendering speed is roughly 80% of standard 3D GS. Strengths: Eliminates view-inconsistency (popping) and allows sharp boundaries. Maintains order invariance and transmittance consistency. Integrates with GS-MCMC cloning. Limitations: Slightly slower than standard 3D GS. Requires tuning of \beta, \gamma, \alpha. The approximation assumes Gaussians do not regain dominance after losing it. When to use: When view-inconsistency or blurry boundaries are problematic in 3D GS. When controllable boundary sharpness is needed. When not to use: When maximum rendering speed is critical and artifacts are acceptable. When scene has extreme overlap that violates the dominance assumption (though this is rare in practice). Softmax-GS was proposed in "Softmax-GS: Generalized Gaussians Learning When to Blend or Bound" (2026). It addresses limitations in 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically the non-overlapping assumption which leads to view-inconsistency and diffuse boundaries. It builds on the Generalized Exponential Function (GEF) from GES and the softmax competition concept, but incorporates the exact GEF within a CUDA kernel and explicitly preserves order invariance while ensuring output transmittance remains unchanged. It is designed to be a unified solution for both artifacts, unlike methods that address only one. name: Hierarchical, Graph-Based, and Adaptive Structures
head: Adaptive Spatial Partitioning, Gaussian Mixture Trees, Elastic Inference, Scale-Adaptive Splatting, Surface-Aware Connectivity
body: This family of methods extends standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by introducing structural organization—such as graphs, trees, grids, or hierarchical levels—to address limitations in scalability, memory efficiency, geometric consistency, and view-dependent aliasing. While standard 3DGS treats primitives as an unstructured flat list, these methods enforce spatial or semantic relationships to enable large-scale rendering, dynamic budget adaptation, and robust deformation. They differ from flat 3DGS by explicitly modeling connectivity or hierarchy, and from sibling methods like Pruning and Density Control by using learned or structural constraints rather than simple heuristic removal. The core principle across this family is the replacement of the flat Gaussian list with a structured representation that imposes constraints on spatial proximity, feature similarity, or hierarchical containment. 1. Structural Connectivity: Methods define adjacency not just by Euclidean distance, but by graph edges, tree parent-child relationships, or grid neighborhood indices. This connectivity is used for aggregation (e.g., context vectors in Hierarchical Anchor Coupling), deformation (e.g., Laplacian operators in Laplacian-Based Deformation), or rendering selection (e.g., region blending in TraGraph-GS). 2. Adaptive Selection/Transformation: Instead of static primitives, these structures allow for dynamic adjustment. This includes selecting subsets of Gaussians based on a target ratio (FlexGS), merging nodes based on probabilistic similarity (Gaussian Mixture Tree Construction), or deforming primitives to match a specific sampling rate (Mipmap-GS). 3. Surface Awareness: Several methods explicitly align the structure with the underlying surface geometry rather than the 3D volume. This involves constructing graphs on surface manifolds (Surface-Aware Splat Graph Construction) or using geodesic distances for deformation (Laplacian-Based Deformation). A rendering method for arbitrary large-scale scenes that uses graph-based adaptive spatial partitioning. It differs from flat 3DGS by partitioning the scene into connected subgraphs based on camera feature matching, training local representations independently, and using a progressive blending strategy for novel viewpoints to avoid boundary artifacts. It is chosen when rendering vast scales while maintaining real-time performance. An elastic inference method that enables a single trained model to adapt to varying computational constraints at inference time by selecting and transforming a subset of Gaussians based on a desired model size ratio, without requiring additional fine-tuning. It solves the problem of high GPU memory demand by jointly training a learnable selector and transformation field, unlike post-hoc compression methods that use fixed heuristics. A hierarchical clustering method that organizes 3D Gaussian primitives into a tree structure to identify distinct 3D plane instances. It solves spatial redundancy by grouping primitives into local clusters and recursively merging them based on probabilistic similarity (Bhattacharya distance) and plane descriptor similarity. Unlike sibling methods relying on fixed grids, it uses a bottom-up agglomerative approach. A test-time adaptation method that deforms pre-trained 3D Gaussians into scale-adaptive primitives to eliminate aliasing artifacts (zoom-in spikes and zoom-out thickness). Unlike sibling methods that apply heuristic smoothing filters, Mipmap-GS self-adjusts primitive properties using scale-specific mipmap-like pseudo ground-truth, effectively informing the Gaussians of the new sampling rate. A module that establishes cross-level gradient pathways in structured 3D Gaussian splatting by aggregating context from adjacent octree levels and broadcasting a residual feature adjustment to all visible anchors at a specific level. It solves feature isolation in anchor-based pipelines by operating at a per-level granularity, acting as an implicit regularizer against over-parameterization. A compact 3D scene representation that organizes high-dimensional Gaussian parameters into a 2D grid with local homogeneity to reduce storage size. It exploits perceptual redundancies via unsupervised competitive learning (Self-Organizing Maps), allowing neighbors in all dimensions to be modeled effectively, unlike fixed-ordering methods such as Z-order curves. Establishes connectivity exclusively along the surface manifold of a reconstructed scene, filtering out spurious neighbors that are close in Euclidean space but distant along the underlying geometry. It defines adjacency as the intersection of Gaussian kernel occupancy regions, specifically designed for surface-aligned representations like SpikingGS to enable proxy-free deformation. Definition: A method that integrates surface-aware splat graphs into off-the-shelf point cloud Laplacian methods to enable proxy-free editing. It treats the collection of Gaussian kernel means as a point cloud and builds a Laplacian operator directly on them. Step: Construct the Laplacian operator \Delta on the set of Gaussian kernel means \{\pii\}{i=1}^N. Integrate the surface-aware splat graph into the Laplacian computation. Use graph geodesic distance rather than raw graph connectivity for robustness against missing edges. Compute the cotangent Laplacian on a local triangulation using NonManifold [42]. Deform the means of kernels \{\pii\}{i=1}^N through a Laplacian-based deformation map \phi\Delta obtained by solving a system such as ARAP [1] or BBW [2] using the Laplacian operator \Delta. Pitfall: Simply displacing the positions of the primitives leads to severe visual artifacts because the covariances of the Gaussian kernels are not adapted properly. Definition: A top-down construction of an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) over 3D Gaussian primitives to ensure spatial compactness of children nodes. Step: Initialize the root node of the BVH as the AABB of all Gaussians, using 3x their stored size to capture extent. Recursively perform a binary median split on the current node to obtain child nodes. Project the means of all Gaussians in the group onto the longest axis of their bounding box. Partition the group by assigning each primitive based on the position of its projected mean with respect to the median of all projections. Compute intermediate node Gaussians from their respective children, starting from the leaves and recursively merging up the tree. The need for hierarchical and graph-based structures in 3D Gaussian Splatting arises from the limitations of the original flat representation, particularly regarding scalability to large scenes, memory efficiency, and geometric consistency. Standard 3DGS treats primitives as an unstructured list, which can lead to redundancy, aliasing at different zoom levels, and difficulties in deformation. The concept of using graphs for connectivity in Gaussian representations is explored in works like Proxy-Free Gaussian Splats Deformation with Splat-Based Surface Estimation, which introduces surface-aware splat graphs to enable robust Laplacian-based deformation. This work highlights that standard kNN-based connectivity fails in non-manifold structures, necessitating surface-aware intersection checks. Hierarchical structures, specifically BVHs, are detailed in A Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Representation for Real-Time Rendering of Very Large Datasets. This approach addresses the rendering performance of very large datasets by organizing Gaussians into a tree structure, allowing for efficient culling and level-of-detail management. The construction involves recursive median splits based on projected means, ensuring spatial compactness. These methods collectively represent a shift from "unstructured splatting" to "structured splatting," where the spatial or semantic relationships between primitives are explicitly modeled to improve performance, quality, and editability. name: TraGraph-GS
head: Trajectory Graph-based Gaussian Splatting
body: TraGraph-GS is a rendering method for arbitrary large-scale scenes that replaces flat Gaussian lists with graph-based adaptive spatial partitioning and regularization constraints. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by constructing a camera connectivity graph to segment scenes into balanced, connected regions, enabling independent local training and a progressive rendering strategy for novel viewpoints that eliminates boundary artifacts. Inputs: A set of disordered scene photographs (images) and their associated poses. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians (local and global) and a rendering pipeline capable of generating novel views. Data Structures: 1. Camera Connectivity Graph: G = (V, E, w). V = \{v1, v2,..., vn\}: Vertices representing input images. E = \{(vi, vj) | vi, vj \in V\}: Edges connecting image pairs. w: E \rightarrow \mathbb{R}: Edge weights defined by the count of feature matches between image pairs. Higher weights indicate larger co-visible regions. 2. Regions: A partition of V into k disjoint sets \{Pi\}{i=1}^k, where each Pi contains nodes (images) that are spatially connected and balanced in count. 3. Local Gaussians: A set of 3D Gaussians optimized independently for each region Pi. 4. Global Gaussians: A coarse set of 3D Gaussians trained on downsampled data to capture overall scene structure. Algorithm Steps: 1. Graph Construction: Compute feature matches between all image pairs. Construct G where edge weights w{ij} equal the number of matches between image i and image j. 2. Graph Segmentation: Divide G into k regions using BFS-based segmentation to ensure connectivity and balanced node distribution: a. Initialize unassigned nodes U = V. b. Identify the unassigned node n with the highest degree as a seed node. c. Perform BFS from n, adding nodes to the current region until the region size reaches |V|/k. Mark these nodes as assigned. d. For each remaining unassigned node u \in U, calculate a score si relative to each existing region Pi (based on connectivity/weights). Assign u to the region with the highest score. 3. Local Training: For each region Pi: a. Initialize 3D Gaussians using the point cloud derived from images in Pi. b. Optimize Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, color) using the combined loss function \mathcal{L}: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda)\mathcal{L}1 + \lambda\mathcal{L}{SSIM} + \mathcal{L}{mv} where \mathcal{L}1 and \mathcal{L}{SSIM} are standard reconstruction losses, and \mathcal{L}{mv} is the multi-view constraint. c. Multi-View Constraint (\mathcal{L}{mv}): For each pixel p in a reference view, render depth d and normal n. Project p to a corresponding pixel p' in a neighborhood view using homography warping based on (d, n). Compute Normalized Cross Correlation (NCC) between patches at p and p': \mathcal{L}{mv} = \sum{p \in Pi} (1 - \text{NCC}(p, p')). d. Multi-Scale Constraint: Apply position-aware point adaptive control to adjust densification. Let \mu be the Gaussian position, c be the camera center, and r be the scene radius. Define a scale factor \gamma(\mu): \gamma(\mu) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \|\mu - c\|2 < 2r \\ \|\mu - c\|2 / r - 1 & \text{if } \|\mu - c\|2 \ge 2r \end{cases}. If the maximum scale of the Gaussian ellipsoid \max(s) < g \cdot \gamma(\mu), perform cloning. Otherwise, perform splitting. Eliminate Gaussians where \max(s) is too small (threshold not explicitly given in sources). 4. Global Training: Downsample point clouds and images. Train a coarse global Gaussian representation without densification to prevent memory overflow. 5. Novel View Rendering: a. Render the novel viewpoint using local Gaussians and global Gaussians separately. b. Calculate a matching score S for each local Gaussian Gi based on its contribution to the novel view: S = (1 - \lambda)\mathcal{L}1 + \lambda\mathcal{L}{SSIM}. Higher scores indicate higher visibility. c. Sort local Gaussians in descending order of S: G1, G2,..., Gk. d. Compute projection opacity oi(p) for each pixel p for the sorted Gaussians: oi(p) = \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \alphai is the opacity of Gaussian Gi. e. Compute weights wi for each local Gaussian using a progressive strategy with an overlapped opacity threshold \beta: wi = \begin{cases} oi(p) & \text{if } \sum{j=1}^{i-1} oj(p) < \beta \\ 0 & \text{if } \sum{j=1}^{i-1} oj(p) \ge \beta \end{cases}. f. Compute final pixel color c(p): c(p) = \sum{i=1}^k wi ci(p) where ci(p) is the color rendered by local Gaussian Gi. Parameters: k: Number of segmented regions. \lambda: Weight for SSIM loss (typical value not given in sources). r: Scene radius. c: Camera center. g: Scaling factor for densification threshold (value not given in sources). \beta: Overlapped opacity threshold for progressive rendering (value not given in sources). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Overflow: Naive partitioning can lead to unbalanced regions. The BFS method ensures balanced distribution. Boundary Artifacts: Standard combination of local Gaussians causes floating artifacts or holes. The progressive rendering strategy with matching scores mitigates this. Textureless Regions: Standard 3DGS struggles here. The multi-view constraint using patch matching and NCC improves geometry reconstruction. Time Complexity: Graph construction depends on feature matching between all image pairs (O(n^2) for n images). Segmentation is linear in the number of nodes and edges. Training is parallelized across k regions, reducing per-region memory and potentially time compared to global training. Memory Complexity: Significantly reduced for large scenes by training local Gaussians independently. Global training uses downsampled data to minimize memory. Performance: Evaluated on large-scale aerial and ground datasets (e.g., UrbanScene3D, Mill-19) with thousands of images. Maintains real-time performance across vastly different scales. Strengths: Handles arbitrary large-scale scenes; improves texture details in textureless regions; eliminates boundary artifacts in novel view synthesis. Limitations: Requires feature matching for graph construction; dependent on the quality of the initial point cloud and camera poses. TraGraph-GS was proposed to address the limitations of existing methods in rendering large-scale scenes, such as memory overflow and boundary artifacts. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting [11] and incorporates graph-based partitioning and regularization constraints. The method was published in IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence in 2026. name: FlexGS
head: Flexible 3D Gaussian Splatting, Elastic 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: FlexGS is an elastic inference method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that enables a single trained model to adapt to varying computational constraints at inference time by selecting and transforming a subset of Gaussians based on a desired model size ratio, without requiring additional fine-tuning. It solves the problem that standard 3DGS models are too memory-intensive for devices with restricted resources (e.g., smartphones, VR headsets) and that previous compression methods required costly separate fine-tuning or re-training for each target compression ratio. Unlike post-hoc pruning methods that use fixed heuristics to retain Top-K Gaussians based on static importance scores, FlexGS jointly trains a learnable selector and transformation field to dynamically adjust the Gaussian set based on attributes and the input ratio during training. Inputs and Outputs Input: A pre-trained 3DGS model consisting of N Gaussians, each characterized by position X, scaling s, rotation q, opacity \alpha, and color c (defined by spherical harmonics coefficients SH). A target ratio e \in (0, 1] specifying the fraction of Gaussians to retain. Output: A subset of K = eN Gaussians, where the selected Gaussians are transformed (displaced/scaled) to compensate for the missing details of the pruned ones, allowing for rendering with reduced computational cost. Data Structures The core data structure remains the list of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i stores: Position: Xi \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scaling vector: si \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation quaternion: qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 (optimized as a 3-vector in the source notation, but standard quaternions are 4D; the source specifies q \in \mathbb{R}^3 likely referring to the axis-angle or specific parameterization, but standard 3DGS uses quaternions. The source text says "rotation vector q \in \mathbb{R}^3", which is non-standard for quaternions. However, Eq 1 uses R. We follow the source's explicit definition: q \in \mathbb{R}^3). Opacity: \alphai \in \mathbb{R} Color: ci derived from SHi \in \mathbb{R}^{(d+1)} where d is the SH degree. The FlexGS framework adds two learnable modules: 1. Gaussian Selector: A neural network that takes Gaussian attributes and the target ratio e as input and outputs a selection probability or score for each Gaussian. 2. Transformation Field: A neural network that takes the attributes of selected Gaussians and the ratio e as input and outputs transformation parameters (displacement, scaling adjustment) to compensate for pruning. Numbered Steps 1. Training Phase (Joint Optimization): 1. Initialize a standard 3DGS model with N Gaussians. 2. For each training step, sample a target ratio e from a distribution (e.g., uniform over a range of desired deployment ratios). 3. Selection: The Gaussian Selector module processes the attributes of all N Gaussians and the current ratio e to predict a binary scaler \lambdai for each Gaussian i. The selection is constrained such that \sum{i=1}^{N} \lambdai = eN. Note: The source mentions using Gumbel-Softmax to handle the discrete nature of \lambdai for gradient propagation, as direct optimization over discrete choices is ineffective. 4. Transformation: For each Gaussian i where \lambdai = 1, the Transformation Field module computes a transformation \Deltai (e.g., displacement of mean X, adjustment of scaling s) based on the Gaussian's attributes and e. 5. Rendering: Render the image using the transformed subset of Gaussians. The rendering equation for a pixel blending N' ordered overlapping points is: C = \sum{i \in N'} ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where N' is the set of selected Gaussians (\lambdai=1). 6. Loss Calculation: Compute the rendering loss (e.g., L1 loss, D-SSIM) between the rendered image and the ground truth. 7. Backpropagation: Update the 3DGS attributes, the Gaussian Selector parameters, and the Transformation Field parameters using gradient descent. 2. Inference Phase: 1. Load the jointly trained model. 2. Specify the desired inference ratio e. 3. Run the Gaussian Selector to identify the subset of Gaussians (\lambdai=1). 4. Run the Transformation Field to adjust the attributes of the selected Gaussians. 5. Render using the standard 3DGS rasterization pipeline with the adjusted subset. Formulas Gaussian Definition: G(X) = e^{-\frac{1}{2} X \Sigma^{-1} X}, \quad \Sigma = R S S^\top R^\top where X is the mean, \Sigma is the covariance matrix, R is the rotation matrix derived from quaternion q, and S is the scaling matrix derived from vector s. Selection Constraint: \sum{i=1}^{N} \lambdai = eN where \lambdai \in \{0, 1\} is the selection indicator for Gaussian i, and e is the target ratio. Parameters N: Total number of Gaussians in the initial model. e: Target ratio of Gaussians to retain. Typical values depend on the deployment target (e.g., 0.1 for 10% retention on mobile, 0.5 for moderate compression). d: Degree of spherical harmonics for color representation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Extreme Compression: Fixed heuristic selection rules may fail to generalize in extreme cases, such as when selecting only 1% of Gaussians, because importance scores must be frequently re-computed as Gaussian attributes evolve during training. FlexGS addresses this by learning the selection dynamically. Discrete Optimization: The binary nature of selection (\lambdai) requires techniques like Gumbel-Softmax to allow gradient-based training. Ratio Dependency: The transformation field is ratio-dependent. If the inference ratio differs significantly from the ratios seen during training, performance may degrade. The method assumes the training distribution covers the desired inference ratios. Time Complexity: Training time is comparable to standard 3DGS but requires multiple forward passes per step for different ratios e. Inference time is proportional to the number of selected Gaussians K = eN, offering linear speedup with respect to the ratio e compared to the full model. Memory Complexity: Memory usage during inference is proportional to K = eN Gaussians, significantly reducing GPU memory requirements compared to the full N Gaussians. Performance: FlexGS achieves substantial rendering performance with reduced computational cost without additional fine-tuning. Experiments on ZipNeRF, MipNeRF, and Tanks&Temples scenes demonstrate its effectiveness. Strengths: Single model supports multiple compression ratios; no re-training required for different devices; adaptive selection based on learned importance rather than static heuristics. Limitations: Requires joint training of selector and transformation modules; performance may vary with extreme compression ratios if not adequately covered in training; introduces slight overhead during training due to multi-ratio sampling. FlexGS was introduced by Hengyu Liu, Yuehao Wang, Chenxin Li, Ruisi Cai, Kevin Wang, Wuyang Li, Pavlo Molchanov, Peihao Wang, and Zhangyang Wang from The Chinese University of Hong Kong, University of Texas at Austin, and Nvidia. The paper "FlexGS: Train Once, Deploy Everywhere with Many-in-One Flexible 3D Gaussian Splatting" was published in CVPR 2025 (arXiv:2506.04174v1, June 4, 2025). It addresses the limitations of standard 3DGS in resource-constrained environments and the inefficiencies of previous compression methods that required separate fine-tuning for each target ratio. name: Gaussian Mixture Tree Construction
head: Hierarchically Merging Gaussians
body: Gaussian Mixture Tree (GMT) Construction is a hierarchical post-processing method that organizes a flat set of 3D Gaussian primitives into a tree structure to identify distinct 3D plane instances in a scene. It solves the problem of spatial redundancy and semantic ambiguity in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by grouping primitives that belong to the same planar surface. Unlike sibling methods that rely on spatial proximity graphs or fixed grid structures, GMT uses a probabilistic merging criterion based on the Bhattacharya distance and plane descriptor similarity to recursively build the hierarchy from leaf nodes to the root. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of Ns leaf nodes, where each leaf node Gi represents a local cluster of Gaussian primitives (not raw primitives, to reduce computational cost). Each node Gi has parameters: mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, normal vector \mathbf{n}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, and plane descriptor \mathbf{z}i \in \mathbb{R}^k (typically k=3). Output: A Gaussian Mixture Tree G^s containing parent nodes G{sk} and a counter L representing the number of merged plane nodes. Data Structures: Leaf Node: A cluster of Gaussians summarized by a single Gaussian distribution G(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) augmented with \mathbf{n} and \mathbf{z}. Tree Node: Represents a merged Gaussian distribution Gp(\boldsymbol{\mu}p, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}p). Parameters: \epsilonB: Threshold for the Bhattacharya distance. \epsilonz: Threshold for the difference in cosine similarity between plane descriptors (1 - \langle \mathbf{z}i \cdot \mathbf{z}j \rangle \le \epsilonz). Formulas: 1. Bhattacharya Distance: Used to measure the similarity between two Gaussian distributions Gi and Gj: DB(Gi, Gj) = \frac{1}{8}(\boldsymbol{\mu}i-\boldsymbol{\mu}j)^{T}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\mu}i-\boldsymbol{\mu}j) + \frac{1}{2}\ln \left(\frac{\det \boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\sqrt{\det \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \det \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j}}\right) where \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}i + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j)/2. 2. Merging Rule: When merging Gi and Gj into a parent node Gp, the new mean and covariance are calculated as: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}p = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j \cdot (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}i+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}j)^{-1} \cdot \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \boldsymbol{\mu}p = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}j \cdot (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}i+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}j)^{-1} \cdot \boldsymbol{\mu}i + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \cdot (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}i+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}j)^{-1} \cdot \boldsymbol{\mu}j. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize L = 0 and the set of merged nodes G = \emptyset. 2. Iterate i from 1 to Ns: a. Check if node i is already a descendant of any existing node in G. If yes, skip. b. Iterate j from i+1 to Ns: i. Check if node j is already a descendant of any existing node in G. If yes, skip. ii. Calculate DB(Gi, Gj) and the cosine similarity difference 1 - \langle \mathbf{z}i \cdot \mathbf{z}j \rangle. iii. If DB(Gi, Gj) \le \epsilonB AND 1 - \langle \mathbf{z}i \cdot \mathbf{z}j \rangle \le \epsilonz: 1. Compute G{ij}^p(\boldsymbol{\mu}p, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}p) using the merging formulas. 2. Update Gi \leftarrow G{ij}^p. 3. Break the inner loop (stop checking further j for this i). c. Insert the current Gi into the result set G^s. d. Increment L \leftarrow L + 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def constructgaussianmixturetree(leafnodes, epsilonB, epsilonz): """ Constructs a Gaussian Mixture Tree from leaf nodes. Args: leafnodes: List of dicts, each containing 'mu', 'Sigma', 'z'. epsilonB: Threshold for Bhattacharya distance. epsilonz: Threshold for cosine similarity difference. Returns: treenodes: List of merged Gaussian nodes. """ treenodes = [] # Track which original indices have been merged into a parent # to avoid re-processing descendants. mergedindices = set() n = len(leafnodes) for i in range(n): if i in mergedindices: continue currentnode = leafnodes[i] mergedpartner = None for j in range(i + 1, n): if j in mergedindices: continue othernode = leafnodes[j] # Calculate Bhattacharya Distance # Sigmaavg = (currentnode['Sigma'] + othernode['Sigma']) / 2 # distB = (1/8) (currentnode['mu'] - othernode['mu']).T @ # np.linalg.inv(Sigmaavg) @ (currentnode['mu'] - othernode['mu']) + \ # (1/2) np.log(np.linalg.det(Sigmaavg) / # np.sqrt(np.linalg.det(currentnode['Sigma']) np.linalg.det(othernode['Sigma']))) # Calculate Cosine Similarity Difference # cossim = np.dot(currentnode['z'], othernode['z']) / # (np.linalg.norm(currentnode['z']) np.linalg.norm(othernode['z'])) # diffcos = 1 - cossim # Note: Exact matrix operations omitted for brevity, assume helper functions exist distB = calculatebhattacharya(currentnode, othernode) diffcos = 1 - cosinesimilarity(currentnode['z'], othernode['z']) if distB <= epsilonB and diffcos <= epsilonz: # Merge # Sigmap = othernode['Sigma'] @ inv(currentnode['Sigma'] + othernode['Sigma']) @ currentnode['Sigma'] # mup = othernode['Sigma'] @ inv(currentnode['Sigma'] + othernode['Sigma']) @ currentnode['mu'] + \ # currentnode['Sigma'] @ inv(currentnode['Sigma'] + othernode['Sigma']) @ othernode['mu'] mergednode = mergegaussians(currentnode, othernode) currentnode = mergednode mergedpartner = j break # Break inner loop after first merge if mergedpartner is not None: mergedindices.add(mergedpartner) treenodes.append(currentnode) return treenodes def mergegaussians(nodei, nodej): """ Merges two Gaussian nodes according to the GMT formula. """ Sigmai = nodei['Sigma'] Sigmaj = nodej['Sigma'] mui = nodei['mu'] muj = nodej['mu'] # Compute inverse of sum of covariances Sigmasum = Sigmai + Sigmaj invSigmasum = np.linalg.inv(Sigmasum) # Compute Sigmap Sigmap = Sigmaj @ invSigmasum @ Sigmai # Compute mup term1 = Sigmaj @ invSigmasum @ mui term2 = Sigmai @ invSigmasum @ muj mup = term1 + term2 # Plane descriptor and normal vector for the parent are not explicitly defined in the source for the merge step. # Typically, these might be averaged or weighted, but the source does not specify. # We return a node with updated mu and Sigma. The z and n fields would need a strategy # (e.g., weighted average) not provided in the text. For strict adherence, we only return mu and Sigma. return {'mu': mup, 'Sigma': Sigmap} def calculatebhattacharya(nodei, nodej): Sigmai = nodei['Sigma'] Sigmaj = nodej['Sigma'] mui = nodei['mu'] muj = nodej['mu'] Sigmaavg = (Sigmai + Sigmaj) / 2.0 diff = mui - muj invSigmaavg = np.linalg.inv(Sigmaavg) term1 = 0.125 diff.T @ invSigmaavg @ diff detSigmaavg = np.linalg.det(Sigmaavg) detSigmai = np.linalg.det(Sigmai) detSigmaj = np.linalg.det(Sigmaj) term2 = 0.5 np.log(detSigmaavg / np.sqrt(detSigmai detSigmaj)) return term1 + term2 def cosinesimilarity(vec1, vec2): norm1 = np.linalg.norm(vec1) norm2 = np.linalg.norm(vec2) if norm1 == 0 or norm2 == 0: return 0.0 return np.dot(vec1, vec2) / (norm1 norm2) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Leaf Node Selection: Raw Gaussian primitives are not used as leaf nodes due to computational expense; they must be pre-clustered into local clusters. Descriptor Learning: The plane descriptors \mathbf{z} and normal vectors \mathbf{n} are learned during optimization using losses derived from 2D normal maps (via Omnidata) and 2D SAM masks, respectively. If these are not available, the merging criterion cannot be fully applied. Order Dependence: The algorithm iterates i from 1 to Ns and breaks the inner loop upon the first merge. This greedy approach means the final tree structure depends on the initial ordering of the leaf nodes. Time Complexity: The algorithm involves nested loops over Ns leaf nodes, resulting in O(Ns^2) comparisons in the worst case. Each comparison involves matrix inversion and determinant calculation for 3 \times 3 matrices, which is constant time but expensive. Memory Complexity: Stores the tree structure and the parameters for each node. Strengths: Explicitly identifies distinct 3D plane instances, enabling higher-level scene understanding and potentially more efficient rendering by grouping planar surfaces. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to the quadratic merging process and the need for pre-clustering and descriptor learning. The Gaussian Mixture Tree was introduced in "Planar Gaussian Splatting" (WACV 2025) to address the limitation of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, where optimized Gaussians tend to cluster near object surfaces without explicit semantic or structural organization. The method uses a probabilistic approach to model the 3D scene hierarchically, leveraging Gaussian Mixture Models to join nodes and derive parent nodes, thereby representing the scene in a way that highlights individual 3D plane instances. name: Mipmap-GS
head: Mipmap-Gaussian Splatting
body: Mipmap-GS is a test-time adaptation method that deforms pre-trained 3D Gaussians into scale-adaptive primitives to eliminate aliasing artifacts (zoom-in spikes and zoom-out thickness) caused by fixed Gaussian distributions at varying zoom factors. Unlike methods that apply static 2D/3D smoothing filters or hierarchical Level-of-Detail selection, Mipmap-GS self-adjusts primitive properties (color, shape, size) and distribution (position) using scale-specific mipmap-like pseudo ground-truth, effectively informing the Gaussians of the new sampling rate. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of single-scale trained base 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{Gk\}{k=1}^K, where each Gaussian Gk is defined by position, covariance (shape/size), opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients (color). A target zoom factor N. Output: A set of optimized, scale-adaptive Gaussians \mathcal{G}^{opt} = \{G^{opt}k\}{k=1}^K. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard 3D Gaussian representation. No new hierarchical data structures (like trees or graphs) are introduced; the adaptation is performed on the flat list of Gaussians. Parameters: N: The zoom factor. For zoom-in, N > 1 (upsampling by \times N). For zoom-out, N < 1 (downsampling by \times 1/N). S: The number of adaptation iterations. Typically 1,000 (1K) iterations are sufficient for convergence. \beta: The learning rate for the optimization step. r(\cdot): The mipmap resizing function. For zoom-in, super-resolution methods like SwinIR are used. For zoom-out, bilinear interpolation is used. Algorithm: The method constructs a "mipmap-like" pseudo ground-truth (pseudo-GT) at the target observation scale and optimizes the base Gaussians to match this target via a scale-aware guidance loss. 1. Base Rendering: Render the base Gaussians \mathcal{G} to a novel view at the basic scale (\times 1) to obtain image \hat{x}. 2. Pseudo-GT Construction: Apply the resizing function r(\cdot) to \hat{x} to generate the scale-specific pseudo-GT r(\hat{x}). If zooming in (\times N), upsample \hat{x} using a super-resolution network (e.g., SwinIR). If zooming out (\times 1/N), downsample \hat{x} using bilinear interpolation. 3. Optimization Loop: For iteration i from 0 to S-1: a. Select a random viewpoint vj from the training set. b. Render the current Gaussians \mathcal{G}i (initially \mathcal{G}) to the basic scale image \hat{x}j. c. Construct the pseudo-GT r(\hat{x}j) using r(\cdot) and the target zoom factor N. d. Render the current Gaussians \mathcal{G}i to the new scale image xj. Note: This rendering must account for the target pixel coverage corresponding to scale N. e. Compute the loss L(xj, r(\hat{x}j)) = \|xj - r(\hat{x}j)\|2^2. f. Update the Gaussians: \mathcal{G}{i+1} = \mathcal{G}i - \beta \nabla L(xj, r(\hat{x}j)). g. If i \mod 100 == 0, perform densification or pruning to maintain compactness. 4. Result: Return \mathcal{G}^{opt} = \mathcal{G}S. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mipmapgsoptimize(basegaussians, viewpoints, zoomfactor, iterations, learningrate): """ Deforms base 3D Gaussians to be adaptive for a specific zoom scale. Args: basegaussians: List of Gaussian primitives (position, cov, opacity, SH). viewpoints: List of camera poses for training views. zoomfactor: Float N. >1 for zoom-in, <1 for zoom-out. iterations: Integer S, number of optimization steps (default 1000). learningrate: Float beta. Returns: optimizedgaussians: List of deformed Gaussian primitives. """ currentgaussians = basegaussians # Determine resizing function based on zoom direction if zoomfactor > 1: # Zoom-in: Use super-resolution (e.g., SwinIR) resizefunc = superresolutionupsample else: # Zoom-out: Use bilinear interpolation resizefunc = bilineardownsample for i in range(iterations): # 1. Select random viewpoint view = random.choice(viewpoints) # 2. Render base Gaussians at basic scale (x1) # This produces the source image for pseudo-GT generation imagebasic = rendergaussians(currentgaussians, view) # 3. Construct mipmap-like pseudo-GT at target scale # For zoom-in: upsample basic image to xN # For zoom-out: downsample basic image to x(1/N) pseudogt = resizefunc(imagebasic, zoomfactor) # 4. Render current Gaussians at the NEW scale # The rasterizer must be configured to render at the target resolution/coverage # implied by zoomfactor. This effectively simulates the pixel coverage # of the target zoom level. imagenewscale = rendergaussiansatscale(currentgaussians, view, zoomfactor) # 5. Compute L2 loss between rendered image and pseudo-GT loss = l2loss(imagenewscale, pseudogt) # 6. Optimize Gaussians # Gradients are computed w.r.t Gaussian parameters currentgaussians = optimizestep(currentgaussians, loss, learningrate) # 7. Active pruning every 100 iterations if i % 100 == 0: currentgaussians = densifyandprune(currentgaussians) return currentgaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zoom-in Spikes: Caused by varying shrinkage bias during accumulation when sampling rates change. Standard 3DGS uses constant dilation which fails here, leading to thin structures or empty areas. Zoom-out Thickness: Caused by constant dilation leading to excessively wide coverage and thick structures. Standard 3DGS includes Gaussians in pixels they shouldn't occupy due to inherited dilation. High-Frequency Loss: Unlike Mip-Splatting which uses heuristic 2D/3D smoothing filters that suppress high-frequency components, Mipmap-GS preserves finer details by deforming the Gaussians themselves. Pruning Strategy: Unlike standard 3DGS which stops density control halfway through training, Mipmap-GS performs active pruning throughout the entire 1K iteration process to ensure a compact representation, especially important for zoom-out where fewer Gaussians are needed. Time Complexity: The method requires 1,000 iterations of optimization per target zoom factor. This is significantly faster than training from scratch, requiring only ~3% of the iterations of full training. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is comparable to the base 3DGS representation, potentially reduced due to active pruning during optimization. Performance: On the NeRF Synthetic dataset, Mipmap-GS outperforms standard 3DGS by an average of 9.25 dB PSNR for zoom-in and 10.40 dB PSNR for zoom-out. At \times 1/2 zoom-out on NeRF Synthetic: SSIM 0.971, PSNR 32.71, LPIPS 0.026 (vs 3DGS: 0.951, 27.14, 0.031). At \times 1/2 zoom-out on Mip-NeRF 360: SSIM 0.854, PSNR 28.57 (vs 3DGS: 0.774, 26.66). Strengths: Plug-in module applicable to any 3DGS model; solves aliasing essentially by informing the sampling rate rather than filtering; preserves high-frequency details better than filter-based methods. Limitations: Requires test-time adaptation for each new zoom factor; relies on super-resolution networks for zoom-in which may introduce artifacts if the base rendering is poor. Mipmap-GS was proposed to address the severe aliasing and blurriness in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) when zooming in or out. Traditional 3DGS suffers from mismatched pixel coverage and fixed Gaussian distributions at varying zoom factors. Previous attempts like Mip-Splatting used heuristic 2D/3D smoothing filters, and Octree-GS used hierarchical Level-of-Detail, but these either suppressed high frequencies or lacked accurate pixel coverage selection. Mipmap-GS introduces a unified optimization method that deforms Gaussians using scale-specific mipmap-like pseudo ground-truth, published in 2025.
