name: Hierarchical Anchor Coupling
head: Per-level hierarchical anchor coupling
body: Hierarchical Anchor Coupling (HAC) is a module that establishes cross-level gradient pathways in structured 3D Gaussian splatting by aggregating context from adjacent octree levels and broadcasting a residual feature adjustment to all visible anchors at a specific level. It solves the problem of feature isolation, where backpropagation graphs in anchor-based octree pipelines lack connections between features at level li and features at adjacent levels li \pm 1. Unlike sibling methods that may use static graphs or per-anchor spatial lookups, HAC operates at the granularity of octree levels, invoking a shared MLP once per visible level to compute a uniform adjustment, which acts as an implicit regularizer against over-parameterization in scenes with dense repetitive structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The set of visible anchors V for a training camera, where each anchor i has an octree level li and a base feature vector fi \in \mathbb{R}^d. Output: Enhanced feature vectors \hat{f}i for all i \in V, which replace fi as input to the downstream Neural Gaussian decoding MLPs. Data Structures: Visible Anchors (V): A list of anchor indices visible to the current camera. Level Set (LV): The set of unique octree levels present in V, defined as LV = \{li: i \in V\}. Level-Specific Visible Anchors (Vl): The subset of visible anchors at level l, defined as Vl = \{i \in V: li = l\}. Context Vectors (cl): Vectors in \mathbb{R}^d representing aggregated features for a level. Triplet (tl): A concatenated vector in \mathbb{R}^{3d} containing self, coarser, and finer context. Adjustment (\deltal): A residual vector in \mathbb{R}^d computed by the MLP. MLP (g\theta): A two-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron mapping \mathbb{R}^{3d} \to \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d with ReLU activation. The hidden dimension is d=32. Steps: 1. Identify Levels and Anchors: For the current training camera, determine the set of visible anchors V. Identify the set of unique octree levels present in V, denoted LV. For each level l \in LV, identify the subset of visible anchors at that level, Vl. 2. Aggregate Context Vectors: For each level l \in LV, compute three context vectors: Self-Context (cl^{\text{self}}): The uniform mean of the base features of all visible anchors at level l: cl^{\text{self}} = \frac{1}{|Vl|} \sum{i \in Vl} fi Coarser-Level Context (cl^{\text{par}}): The result of applying the coarser-level aggregation operator A{\text{par}} to the features of anchors at the adjacent coarser level l-1: cl^{\text{par}} = A{\text{par}}(\{fi\}{i \in V{l-1}}) Note: The specific implementation of A{\text{par}} is defined in the Structure-Aware Containment Aggregation (SACA) module. Finer-Level Context (cl^{\text{chi}}): The result of applying the finer-level aggregation operator A{\text{chi}} to the features of anchors at the adjacent finer level l+1: cl^{\text{chi}} = A{\text{chi}}(\{fi\}{i \in V{l+1}}) Note: The specific implementation of A{\text{chi}} is defined in the Structure-Aware Containment Aggregation (SACA) module. 3. Handle Boundary Levels: If a level l \in LV lacks an adjacent coarser level (i.e., l-1 is not in the octree or has no visible anchors) or an adjacent finer level (i.e., l+1 is not in the octree or has no visible anchors), the corresponding context vector defaults to the self-context cl^{\text{self}}. 4. Form Triplet: Concatenate the three context vectors into a per-level triplet tl \in \mathbb{R}^{3d}: tl = [cl^{\text{par}}; cl^{\text{self}}; cl^{\text{chi}}] 5. Compute Adjustment: Pass the triplet tl through the shared two-layer MLP g\theta to compute the level-wise feature adjustment \deltal: \deltal = g\theta(tl) 6. Broadcast Residual: Broadcast the adjustment \deltal as a residual to all visible anchors at level l to produce the enhanced features \hat{f}i: \hat{f}i = fi + \deltal, \quad \forall i \in Vl 7. Replace Features: Replace the original features \{fi\}{i \in V} with the enhanced features \{\hat{f}i\}{i \in V} as input to the downstream Neural Gaussian decoding MLPs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hierarchicalanchorcoupling(anchors, visibleindices, mlpgtheta, aggregatecoarser, aggregatefiner): """ anchors: List of anchor objects, each having attributes: level: int (octree level) feature: numpy array of shape (d,) visibleindices: List of indices into 'anchors' that are visible to the camera. mlpgtheta: A callable MLP function taking a (3d,) vector and returning a (d,) vector. aggregatecoarser: A callable function taking a list of features and returning a (d,) context vector. aggregatefiner: A callable function taking a list of features and returning a (d,) context vector. Returns: enhancedfeatures: List of (d,) vectors for each visible anchor. """ # Step 1: Identify levels and group anchors visibleanchors = [anchors[i] for i in visibleindices] levelspresent = set(a.level for a in visibleanchors) # Group visible anchors by level anchorsbylevel = {} for l in levelspresent: anchorsbylevel[l] = [a for a in visibleanchors if a.level == l] # Step 2 & 3: Aggregate context and handle boundaries contexttriplets = {} for l in levelspresent: anchorsl = anchorsbylevel[l] # Self-context if len(anchorsl) > 0: cself = sum(a.feature for a in anchorsl) / len(anchorsl) else: cself = np.zeroslike(anchorsl[0].feature) # Should not happen if l in levelspresent # Coarser context (l-1) if (l - 1) in anchorsbylevel and len(anchorsbylevel[l - 1]) > 0: cpar = aggregatecoarser([a.feature for a in anchorsbylevel[l - 1]]) else: cpar = cself # Boundary case # Finer context (l+1) if (l + 1) in anchorsbylevel and len(anchorsbylevel[l + 1]) > 0: cchi = aggregatefiner([a.feature for a in anchorsbylevel[l + 1]]) else: cchi = cself # Boundary case # Step 4: Form triplet tl = np.concatenate([cpar, cself, cchi]) contexttriplets[l] = tl # Step 5: Compute adjustments adjustments = {} for l in levelspresent: tl = contexttriplets[l] deltal = mlpgtheta(tl) adjustments[l] = deltal # Step 6: Broadcast and return enhancedfeatures = [] for i in visibleindices: anchor = anchors[i] l = anchor.level deltal = adjustments[l] fhat = anchor.feature + deltal enhancedfeatures.append(fhat) return enhancedfeatures Parameters: MLP Hidden Dimension (d): 32. Granularity: Per-level (default). Computes a shared \deltal for every visible level. A per-anchor alternative computes a distinct \deltai for every visible anchor via spatial lookup. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Levels: Levels in LV that lack an adjacent coarser or finer level must default their missing context to the self-context cl^{\text{self}}. Empty Levels: If a level l is in LV, Vl is non-empty by definition. However, adjacent levels l-1 or l+1 may have no visible anchors, triggering the boundary condition. Per-level computes one adjustment \deltal per visible level, scaling MLP cost with the number of visible levels. Per-anchor computes a distinct \deltai per visible anchor, scaling linearly with |V|. Per-level is ~20% faster in training and yields +1.06 dB on dense repetitive structures (Building), while per-anchor yields +0.21 dB on simpler geometry (Rubble). The aggregation operators A{\text{par}} and A{\text{chi}} used in HAC are defined by SACA, which incorporates octree topology and binary/soft containment masks to reduce the influence of topologically isolated anchors. Time Complexity: The MLP evaluation cost scales with the number of visible levels, not the number of visible anchors. Computing level-wise means and broadcasting residuals remains linear in |V|. Per-level is ~20% faster in training than per-anchor. Memory Complexity: HAC adds 4,160 parameters via the shared two-layer MLP (d=32). The total parameter increment is below 0.1%. Performance: On the Mill19-Building scene, HAC alone yields a PSNR improvement of +1.91 dB over the baseline. On UrbanScene3D-Residence, TopoGS (with HAC) reaches 39.4 FPS versus 29.0 FPS for the baseline, while reducing memory and the number of Neural Gaussians by roughly 35%. Strengths: Alleviates feature isolation; acts as an implicit regularizer against over-parameterization in dense repetitive structures; low parameter overhead; transferable to other backbones (Octree-GS, Proxy-GS). Limitations: May underperform on simpler geometry compared to per-anchor variants (e.g., Rubble scene). When to Use: When using anchor-based octree pipelines (e.g., CityGS-X, Octree-GS, Proxy-GS) and feature isolation is a concern, particularly in scenes with dense repetitive structures. When Not to Use: When computational budget is extremely tight and scene geometry is simple, per-anchor might offer marginal gains at the cost of speed, or simpler baselines may suffice. Hierarchical Anchor Coupling was introduced in the paper "TopoGS: Topology-Aware Anchor Feature Aggregation for Large-Scale 3D Gaussian Splatting". It is integrated into the TopoGS framework and has been shown to be transferable to other structured 3D Gaussian splatting backbones such as CityGS-X, Octree-GS, and Proxy-GS. The method addresses the limitation of existing anchor-based octree pipelines where backpropagation graphs lack cross-level gradient pathways. name: Self-Organizing Gaussian Grids
head: Self-Organizing Gaussians
body: Self-Organizing Gaussian Grids is a compact 3D scene representation that organizes the high-dimensional parameters of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) into a 2D grid with local homogeneity to drastically reduce storage size without compromising visual quality. It differs from fixed-ordering methods like Z-order curves or tri-planes by learning a scene-specific permutation of Gaussians via unsupervised competitive learning, thereby preserving topological relationships and enabling efficient image-based compression. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{gi\}{i=1}^N representing a static scene, where each Gaussian gi contains position \mathbf{x}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i (or rotation/scale), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color \mathbf{c}i. Output: A 2D grid structure G of size H \times W (where H \times W \approx N) containing the permuted Gaussian parameters, organized into multiple data layers (e.g., one layer for position/scale/rotation, one for opacity, one for color) that share the same 2D layout. Data Structures The representation consists of a 2D grid where each cell (u, v) holds a reference or copy of a specific Gaussian from the original set. The grid is organized into separate channels or layers for different attribute types to facilitate standard 2D image compression codecs. Grid Dimensions: H \times W. The product H \times W is chosen to be approximately equal to the number of Gaussians N. Cell Content: Each cell stores the full parameter set of a single Gaussian, identical to the standard 3DGS structure. Layers: Distinct 2D grids are maintained for geometric attributes (position, scale, rotation) and appearance attributes (opacity, SH coefficients). Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize a 2D grid of size H \times W with random or uniformly sampled Gaussian parameters from the input set. 2. Self-Organization (Competitive Learning): Iterate through the input Gaussians. For each input Gaussian gi, find the "winner" neuron (grid cell) w whose current parameter vector is most similar to gi in the high-dimensional parameter space. Similarity is typically measured by Euclidean distance in the concatenated parameter space. Update the winner w and its topological neighbors in the grid to become more similar to gi. This step enforces local homogeneity, ensuring that Gaussians with similar parameters are placed adjacent to each other in the grid. This process is repeated for all Gaussians until the grid converges to a stable ordering that preserves the topological structure of the input data. 3. Smoothness Enforcement (Optional/Training Phase): During the optimization phase, a smoothness loss can be applied to the grid to further enforce local continuity between neighboring cells, enhancing compressibility. 4. Compression: The resulting 2D grids for each attribute layer are compressed using standard image compression techniques (e.g., JPEG, WebP, or neural image codecs). Pseudocode Unverified code. Args: gaussians: List of N Gaussian objects, each with attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, shcoeffs). gridheight: Height H of the output 2D grid. gridwidth: Width W of the output 2D grid. Returns: grid: A 2D array of shape (H, W) containing references to Gaussians. """ N = len(gaussians) # Initialize grid with random Gaussians from the input set grid = [[None for in range(gridwidth)] for in range(gridheight)] for i in range(gridheight): for j in range(gridwidth): idx = random.randint(0, N - 1) grid[i][j] = gaussians[idx] # Competitive learning phase # Iterate multiple epochs to converge the grid ordering for epoch in range(numepochs): # Shuffle input Gaussians to ensure unbiased learning shuffledgaussians = shuffle(gaussians) for g in shuffledgaussians: # Find the winning neuron (grid cell) # Winner is the cell with the minimum distance to g in parameter space bestdist = infinity bestcell = None for r in range(gridheight): for c in range(gridwidth): currentg = grid[r][c] # Calculate distance in high-dimensional parameter space # This includes position, scale, rotation, opacity, and SH coefficients dist = calculateparameterdistance(g, currentg) if dist < bestdist: bestdist = dist bestcell = (r, c) # Update the winner and its neighbors # This step pulls the winner and its topological neighbors # closer to the input Gaussian g updategridneighbors(grid, bestcell, g, learningrate) return grid def calculateparameterdistance(g1, g2): """ Calculates Euclidean distance between two Gaussians in parameter space. """ # Concatenate all parameters into a single vector vec1 = concatenate(g1.position, g1.scale, g1.rotation, g1.opacity, g1.shcoeffs) vec2 = concatenate(g2.position, g2.scale, g2.rotation, g2.opacity, g2.shcoeffs) return euclideandistance(vec1, vec2) def updategridneighbors(grid, winnercell, targetgaussian, lr): """ Updates the winner and its neighbors to be more similar to targetgaussian. """ r, c = winnercell # Define neighborhood radius (e.g., Gaussian decay) # Update winner grid[r][c] = targetgaussian # Or interpolate if using continuous values # Update neighbors based on distance from winner for dr in range(-neighborhoodradius, neighborhoodradius + 1): for dc in range(-neighborhoodradius, neighborhoodradius + 1): nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc if isvalidcell(nr, nc): # Apply learning rate decay based on distance dist = sqrt(drdr + dcdc) effectivelr = lr exp(-distdist / (2 sigmasigma)) # Update neighbor parameters towards target grid[nr][nc].updatetowards(targetgaussian, effectivelr) Parameters Grid Dimensions (H \times W): Should be approximately equal to the number of Gaussians N. Typical values depend on the scene complexity. Learning Rate: Controls the step size during the competitive learning phase. Neighborhood Radius: Determines the extent of topological influence during updates. Storage Reduction Factor: Achieves a reduction of 17x to 42x in storage size for complex scenes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Encoding Complexity: The self-organization process requires a computationally expensive optimization to determine the element order, unlike fixed-ordering methods. Precision: The method relies on the assumption that perceptual redundancies exist in natural scenes, allowing permutations of Gaussian parameters to equivalently represent the scene. Time Complexity: Encoding is computationally expensive due to the iterative competitive learning process. Rendering time is comparable to standard 3DGS as the uncompressed Gaussians use the same structure. Memory Complexity: Storage size is reduced by a factor of 17x to 42x for complex scenes. Strengths: Maintains fast rendering and high visual quality while drastically reducing storage requirements. Exploits perceptual redundancies and local homogeneity. Limitations: High encoding complexity. When to Use: When storage size is a critical constraint (e.g., resource-constrained devices) and encoding time is not a bottleneck. When Not to Use: When fast encoding is required or when the scene lacks the perceptual redundancies assumed by the method. Self-Organizing Gaussian Grids was introduced by Wieland Morgenstern, Florian Barthel, Anna Hilsmann, and Peter Eisert from Fraunhofer Heinrich Hertz Institute and Humboldt University of Berlin. The method was published in arXiv:2312.13299v2 on May 2, 2024. It is based on the concept of Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs), an unsupervised learning model that projects high-dimensional data onto a lower-dimensional grid, preserving topological relationships through competitive learning. The method addresses the high storage requirements of 3D Gaussian Splatting, which hinders practical deployment on resource-constrained devices. name: Surface-Aware Splat Graph Construction
head: Manifold-Aware Gaussian Graph Construction, Surface-Aligned Gaussian Connectivity
body: Surface-Aware Splat Graph Construction establishes connectivity between 3D Gaussian primitives exclusively along the underlying surface manifold, filtering out spurious neighbors that are close in Euclidean space but distant along the surface. Unlike methods relying on Euclidean or Mahalanobis distance, which fail under challenging geometric conditions, this method defines adjacency as the intersection of Gaussian kernel occupancy regions, ensuring that graph edges represent true surface proximity. It serves as a prerequisite for Laplacian-based deformation and other surface-aware operations by providing a topologically correct connectivity graph for the Gaussian splats. Inputs: A set of N Gaussian kernels \{Gi\}{i=1}^N reconstructed from 2D images using a surface-aligned Gaussian Splatting method (specifically SpikingGS). Each kernel Gi is defined by its position pi, covariance matrix \Sigmai, and opacity \alphai. Outputs: A graph where nodes are the Gaussian kernels and edges exist between kernels Gi and Gj if their occupancy regions intersect within a tolerance. Data Structures: Gaussian Kernel Gi: pi \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix, factorized as \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^\top Ri^\top. Ri \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Rotation matrix with columns r{i,1}, r{i,2}, r{i,3}. Si \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Scale matrix, diagonal with entries \sigma{i,1}, \sigma{i,2}, 0. \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. Graph: Adjacency list or matrix derived from intersection checks. Parameters: c: Minimum contribution threshold for rendered intensity. Typical value: 1/255. \bar{V}{ip}: Activation cut-off threshold from the spiking neuron in SpikingGS. This is a learnable parameter that suppresses low-opacity parts. \epsilon: Tolerance for normal-wise offset to account for minor gaps between adjacent Gaussian kernels arising from joint optimization. Steps: 1. Define Occupancy Region: For each kernel Gi, define the occupancy region \Omegai as the set of points x \in \mathbb{R}^3 where the kernel is considered active. Activity is determined by two constraints: the spiking activation threshold \bar{V}{ip} and the minimum intensity contribution c. The effective activation \hat{G}i(x) is: \hat{G}i(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } Gi(x) < \bar{V}{ip} \\ e^{-\frac{1}{2}(x-pi)^\top \Sigmai^{-1} (x-pi)} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} The occupancy region \Omegai is defined as: \Omegai = \left\{ x \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid \hat{G}i(x) > \max\left(\bar{V}{ip}, \frac{c}{\alphai}\right) \right\} 2. Parameterize Occupancy Region: Since \Sigmai is rank-2 (due to the zero in Si), \Omegai forms an ellipse in the local coordinate system. Using Si = \text{diag}(\sigma{i,1}, \sigma{i,2}, 0) and Ri = [r{i,1}, r{i,2}, r{i,3}], the region is parameterized as: \Omegai = \left\{ pi + \lambdai \rho (\sigma{i,1} \cos \theta \, r{i,1} + \sigma{i,2} \sin \theta \, r{i,2}) \;\middle|\; \rho \in [0, 1), \theta \in (0, 2\pi] \right\} where the scaling factor \lambdai is: \lambdai = \sqrt{-2 \max\left(\ln|\bar{V}{ip}|, \ln\left(\frac{c}{\alphai}\right)\right)} 3. Compute Normal-Wise Offset: To determine if two kernels Gi and Gj intersect, compute the normal-wise offset \delta{ij} from Gi to Gj. This offset measures the minimum distance along the normal direction r{i,3} of Gi required to reach the region \Omegaj: \delta{ij}:= \inf \{ |t| \mid \exists x \in \Omegai: x + t r{i,3} \in \Omegaj \} If no such x exists, \delta{ij} = +\infty. 4. Establish Connectivity: Two Gaussians Gi and Gj are considered connected (intersecting) if \delta{ij} < \epsilon. A zero offset indicates a perfect intersection, while values below \epsilon account for minor gaps due to optimization artifacts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: alpha (float): Opacity of the kernel. c (float): Minimum contribution threshold (e.g., 1/255). vbarip (float): Spiking activation cut-off threshold. Returns: float: lambdai """ term1 = np.log(np.abs(vbarip)) term2 = np.log(c / alpha) maxval = max(term1, term2) # If maxval is positive, -2maxval is negative, sqrt fails. # However, since Gi(x) < Vbarip leads to 0 activation, # the condition Gi(x) > Vbarip implies the exponent is negative. # The derivation assumes valid active regions where the exponent is negative. # In practice, ensure arguments to log are valid and maxval < 0 for active regions. if maxval >= 0: return 0.0 return np.sqrt(-2 maxval) def getellipsepoints(pi, Ri, Si, lambdai, numtheta=100): """ Generate points on the boundary of the occupancy region ellipse. Args: pi (np.array): Position (3,). Ri (np.array): Rotation matrix (3,3). Si (np.array): Scale matrix diagonal values (sigma1, sigma2, 0). lambdai (float): Scaling factor. numtheta (int): Number of samples for theta. Returns: np.array: Points on the ellipse boundary (numtheta, 3). """ sigma1, sigma2, = Si r1, r2, = Ri.T # Columns of Ri thetas = np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, numtheta, endpoint=False) rho = 1.0 # Boundary # Ellipse in local space: lambda (sigma1 cos(theta) r1 + sigma2 sin(theta) r2) # Note: The formula uses rho in [0,1). For boundary check, rho=1 is sufficient. pointslocal = lambdai (sigma1 np.cos(thetas) r1 + sigma2 np.sin(thetas) r2) # Transform to world space pointsworld = pi + pointslocal return pointsworld def checkintersection(Gi, Gj, epsilon): """ Check if Gaussian Gi and Gj intersect using normal-wise offset. Args: Gi (dict): Kernel i with keys 'p', 'R', 'S', 'alpha', 'vbarip'. Gj (dict): Kernel j with keys 'p', 'R', 'S', 'alpha', 'vbarip'. epsilon (float): Tolerance for offset. Returns: bool: True if intersecting, False otherwise. """ # 1. Compute lambda for Gi lambdai = computelambda(Gi['alpha'], 1/255, Gi['vbarip']) # 2. Get boundary points of Omegai # We approximate the infimum by checking if any point on Omegai's boundary # is close to Omegaj. However, the definition is inf |t| such that x + tri3 is in Omegaj. # A robust implementation requires solving for t. # Simplified approach for implementation: # Project the center of Gj onto the plane of Gi? No, Gi is an ellipse. # The definition: inf |t| | exists x in Omegai: x + t ri3 in Omegaj. # Let's approximate by sampling the boundary of Omegai and checking distance to Omegaj along ri3. # This is an approximation of the infimum. pi = Gi['p'] ri3 = Gi['R'][:, 2] # Third column of rotation matrix Si = np.diag(Gi['S']) # Assuming S is stored as vector or diag matrix # Generate boundary points of Omegai # Note: Si in formula is diag(sigma1, sigma2, 0). # We need the actual sigma values. sigma1, sigma2, = Gi['S'] # Assuming Gi['S'] is [sigma1, sigma2, 0] or similar # Re-calculate lambda if not precomputed # lambdai = computelambda(...) # Sample points on the ellipse boundary of Omegai numsamples = 100 thetas = np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, numsamples, endpoint=False) r1 = Gi['R'][:, 0] r2 = Gi['R'][:, 1] # Points on the boundary of Omegai # x = pi + lambdai (sigma1 cos(theta) r1 + sigma2 sin(theta) r2) cost = np.cos(thetas) sint = np.sin(thetas) xboundary = pi + lambdai (sigma1 cost[:, None] r1 + sigma2 sint[:, None] r2) # For each point x on Omegai boundary, find t such that x + t ri3 is in Omegaj # Omegaj is also an ellipse. # This is a complex geometric intersection. # The source defines deltaij as inf |t| | exists x in Omegai: x + t ri3 in Omegaj. # Approximation: # 1. Project xboundary onto the normal plane of ri3? No. # 2. Check if the line segment from x in direction ri3 intersects Omegaj. # Since Omegaj is an ellipse in 3D, checking intersection of a ray with an ellipse is non-trivial. # However, for the purpose of this article, we state the definition. # Implementation detail: A practical approximation is to check if the distance # from the center of Gj to the plane of Gi (defined by pi and normal ri3) # is small, and if the projected point lies within the ellipse of Gj. # But the source specifies the infimum over x in Omegai. # Let's implement a simplified check based on the definition: # We want to find min |t| such that x + tri3 in Omegaj for some x in Omegai. # This is equivalent to finding the minimum distance along ri3 between the two ellipses. # For a robust implementation, one would solve the quadratic equation for ray-ellipse intersection # for each sample point on Omegai and take the minimum |t|. mint = np.inf # Define function to check if point y is in Omegaj def isinomegaj(y, Gj): # Transform y to local space of Gj pj = Gj['p'] Rj = Gj['R'] Sj = Gj['S'] # [sigma1, sigma2, 0] alphaj = Gj['alpha'] vbarj = Gj['vbarip'] # Local coordinates diff = y - pj localdiff = Rj.T @ diff # Check against ellipse equation: (x'/sigma1)^2 + (y'/sigma2)^2 <= 1 # And activation thresholds sigma1j, sigma2j, = Sj # Lambda for Gj lambdaj = computelambda(alphaj, 1/255, vbarj) # The point y is in Omegaj if it is within the scaled ellipse # The ellipse equation in local space is (u/sigma1)^2 + (v/sigma2)^2 <= 1 # But Omegaj is scaled by lambdaj. # So: (u / (lambdaj sigma1j))^2 + (v / (lambdaj sigma2j))^2 <= 1 u, v, w = localdiff denom1 = lambdaj sigma1j denom2 = lambdaj sigma2j if denom1 == 0 or denom2 == 0: return False distsq = (u / denom1)2 + (v / denom2)2 return distsq <= 1.0 # Check each sample point on Omegai boundary for k in range(numsamples): x = xboundary[k] # We need to find t such that x + t ri3 is in Omegaj. # Ray: r(t) = x + t ri3 # We want to find t that minimizes |t| such that r(t) in Omegaj. # This is a ray-ellipse intersection problem. # Let's approximate by checking a range of t values or solving analytically. # Analytical solution for ray-ellipse intersection: # Ellipse in local space of Gj: (u/s1)^2 + (v/s2)^2 <= 1, w=0 (effectively, since rank 2) # But Gj is in 3D. The ellipse lies in the plane spanned by rj1 and rj2. # The ray intersects the plane of the ellipse at some tplane. # Then check if the intersection point is inside the ellipse. # Plane of Gj: normal nj = rj3. Point pj. # Ray: x + t ri3. # Intersection with plane: (x + t ri3 - pj). nj = 0 # t (ri3. nj) = (pj - x). nj # t = (pj - x). nj / (ri3. nj) nj = Gj['R'][:, 2] denom = np.dot(ri3, nj) if np.abs(denom) > 1e-6: tplane = np.dot(Gj['p'] - x, nj) / denom intersectionpoint = x + tplane ri3 if isinomegaj(intersectionpoint, Gj): mint = min(mint, np.abs(tplane)) else: # Ray is parallel to the plane of Gj # Check if the ray lies in the plane if np.abs(np.dot(x - Gj['p'], nj)) < 1e-6: # Ray is in the plane. Check if it intersects the ellipse. # This is a 2D ray-ellipse intersection. # Transform ray to local space of Gj. # This is complex. For the purpose of the article, we note this edge case. pass return mint < epsilon def buildsurfaceawaregraph(gaussians, epsilon): """ Build the surface-aware splat graph. Args: gaussians (list of dict): List of Gaussian kernels. epsilon (float): Tolerance. Returns: list of list: Adjacency list. """ N = len(gaussians) adj = [[] for in range(N)] for i in range(N): for j in range(i + 1, N): if checkintersection(gaussians[i], gaussians[j], epsilon): adj[i].append(j) adj[j].append(i) return adj Time Complexity: The graph construction requires checking intersections for all pairs of Gaussians, resulting in O(N^2) complexity, where N is the number of Gaussian kernels. Memory Complexity: O(N^2) in the worst case for a dense adjacency matrix, or O(E) for an adjacency list, where E is the number of edges. Strengths: It accurately captures surface topology by ignoring Euclidean proximity that does not correspond to surface connectivity, which is crucial for deformation tasks. Limitations: The O(N^2) pairwise check can be computationally expensive for large scenes. It relies on the quality of the initial surface-aligned reconstruction (e.g., SpikingGS). When to use: When performing surface-aware operations like Laplacian-based deformation on Gaussian splats. When not to use: For standard rendering where only visibility and color are needed, as standard rasterization does not require this graph structure. Surface-Aware Splat Graph Construction was introduced in the paper "Proxy-Free Gaussian Splats Deformation with Splat-Based Surface Estimation". The method addresses the limitation of existing point-based distance metrics (Euclidean, Mahalanobis) in establishing connectivity along the surface manifold, particularly in challenging geometric conditions. It builds upon surface-aligned Gaussian Splatting methods, specifically SpikingGS, to ensure that the Gaussian primitives are aligned with the underlying surface geometry. The method is used to construct a Laplacian operator for proxy-free deformation of the Gaussian splats. name: Variable Basis Mapping (VBM)
body: Variable Basis Mapping (VBM) is a framework that transforms volumetric fields into 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations through wavelet-domain analysis, enabling real-time volumetric visualization by avoiding the prohibitively high computational costs of direct volume rendering. Unlike iVR-GS, which uses randomly initialized Gaussians, or VEG, which uses heuristic density-based spheres, VBM establishes a direct, mathematical bridge using wavelet analysis to exploit structural and statistical information. Inputs and Outputs Input: A physical volumetric field F discretized into a uniform grid of resolution G^3, where G is the volumetric data resolution. Intermediate: A radiance field RF \in \mathbb{R}^{G \times G \times G \times 4} obtained by applying a transfer function TF: \mathbb{R}^r \to \mathbb{R}^4 to F, producing RGBA vectors (color c, opacity \alpha). Output: A set of N anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives, each defined by center \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}, color ci, and opacity \alphai. Data Structures 1. Wavelet-to-Gaussian Transition Bank: A precomputed lookup structure mapping canonical wavelet atoms to optimal Gaussian surrogates. It stores the parameters (\mu, \Sigma, c, \alpha) for the canonical kernel \psi{j,k=(0,0,0)} at each decomposition level j. 2. Gaussian Primitive: Defined by the tuple (\mui, \Sigmai, ci, \alphai). The radiance field is approximated by: RF(x) \approx \sum{i=1}^{N} ci \frac{\alphai}{\sqrt{\det(\Sigmai)}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(x - \mui)^\top \Sigmai^{-1} (x - \mui)\right) where \mui is the center, \Sigmai is the covariance matrix, ci is the color, and \alphai is the opacity. Steps 1. Precompute Transition Bank: Compute optimal Gaussian surrogates for canonical wavelet atoms across multiple scales. To avoid cubic complexity (J \times G^3 fittings), only the canonical kernel \psi{j,k=(0,0,0)} is computed for each level j. Remaining kernels are derived analytically via translation and scaling, guaranteed by the group representation theorem. 2. Wavelet Decomposition: Express the radiance field RF in a compact multi-scale form using the 3D Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT). The field is decomposed into low-frequency coefficients c{0,k} and high-frequency coefficients d{j,k}: RF(x) \approx \sum{k} c{0,k} \phi(x - k) + \sum{j=0}^{J-1} \sum{k} d{j,k} \psi{j,k}(x) where J is the number of decomposition levels, \phi is the scaling function, and \psi{j,k} are dyadic wavelet atoms defined as \psi{j,k}(x) = 2^{3j/2} \psi(2^j x - k). 3. Analytical Gaussian Construction: Map the discrete wavelet coefficients directly to 3DGS parameters using the precomputed Transition Bank. Each wavelet basis \psi{j,k} is mapped to a Gaussian basis, and the associated coefficients c{j,k} (color) and \alpha{j,k} (opacity) are translated into the corresponding 3DGS parameters (\mu, \Sigma, c, \alpha). 4. Image-Space Fine-Tuning: Apply a lightweight optimization stage in image space to refine the representation and improve rendering fidelity. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def variablebasismapping(radiancefield, resolutionG, numlevelsJ, transitionbank): # radiancefield: numpy array of shape (G, G, G, 4) # transitionbank: dict mapping scale j to (mubase, Sigmabase, cbase, alphabase) gaussians = [] # Step 1: Low-frequency scaling function coefficients # c0,k corresponds to the coarsest approximation. Mapped to Gaussians centered at grid points. coarseres = resolutionG // (2 (numlevelsJ - 1)) if numlevelsJ > 0 else resolutionG for kx in range(coarseres): for ky in range(coarseres): for kz in range(coarseres): # Extract low-frequency coefficients for this grid cell clow = radiancefield[kx::coarseres, ky::coarseres, kz::coarseres,:3].mean() alphalow = radiancefield[kx::coarseres, ky::coarseres, kz::coarseres, 3].mean() # Map to Gaussian: center at k, covariance scaled by grid spacing mu = (kx, ky, kz) Sigma = computescalingcovariance(coarseres) gaussians.append((mu, Sigma, clow, alphalow)) # Step 2: High-frequency wavelet coefficients for j in range(numlevelsJ): scale = 2 j gridsize = resolutionG // scale basemu, baseSigma,, = transitionbank[j] for kx in range(gridsize): for ky in range(gridsize): for kz in range(gridsize): # Translate and scale the canonical Gaussian # Wavelet support shrinks by 2^j, so covariance divides by 4^j mu = (kx, ky, kz) / scale + basemu Sigma = baseSigma / (scale 2) # Extract wavelet coefficients for this atom chigh = waveletcoeffs[j][kx, ky, kz,:3] alphahigh = waveletcoeffs[j][kx, ky, kz, 3] gaussians.append((mu, Sigma, chigh, alphahigh)) # Step 3: Image-space fine-tuning # Optimize parameters to minimize rendering loss against target views gaussians = finetune(gaussians, radiancefield) return gaussians def computescalingcovariance(gridsize): # Standard Gaussian approximation for the scaling function support return [[1.0/gridsize2, 0, 0], [0, 1.0/gridsize2, 0], [0, 0, 1.0/gridsize2]] def finetune(gaussians, target): # Standard differentiable rasterization optimization loop return gaussians Parameters G: Volumetric data resolution. The dataset is discretized into a uniform grid of resolution G^3. J: Number of decomposition levels in the wavelet transform. N: Number of Gaussian primitives in the 3DGS representation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Representational Gap: There is a substantial representational gap between wavelet and Gaussian bases, making direct conversion nontrivial. Computational Complexity: A naïve implementation of Wavelet-to-Gaussian transitions incurs cubic computational complexity (J \times G^3 fittings), resulting in prohibitive computational cost. The VBM method avoids this by computing only canonical kernels and deriving others analytically. Dynamic scene representation using time-aware splatting. Variable Basis Mapping (VBM) was proposed in 2026 by Cai Yucheng et al. from USTC. It addresses the challenge of real-time visualization of large-scale volumetric data, which suffers from prohibitively high computational costs with direct volume rendering and voxel-based methods. The method builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and integrates concepts from wavelet analysis. It is the first framework to establish a direct, mathematical bridge between volumetric analysis and 3DGS. name: Human Gaussian Splatting
head: Human Gaussian Splats
body: Human Gaussian Splats (HUGS) is a neural rendering framework that represents an animatable human avatar and a static scene using 3D Gaussians, trained on 50–100 frames of monocular video to enable novel view and novel pose synthesis at 60 FPS. It sets itself apart from implicit neural field methods by allowing test-time rendering without evaluating triplane/MLPs for new poses, and from static 3DGS by disentangling the human and scene to allow human transfer to other scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A monocular video sequence of 50–100 frames containing a moving human and a static scene. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians representing the static scene and a set of 3D Gaussians representing the human. The human Gaussians are parameterized by mean locations in a canonical space, features from a triplane, and properties predicted by MLPs. The system outputs rendered images for novel views and novel poses. Data Structures: Scene Gaussians: Standard 3DGS representation (center \mu, opacity, color, scale, rotation) initialized from COLMAP point cloud. Human Gaussians: Canonical Center (\mui): 3D location in the canonical (T-pose) space. Feature Vector (fi): Concatenation of feature vectors f{xi}, f{yi}, f{zi} retrieved from a triplane F \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times h \times w \times d} at location \mui. Appearance Properties: RGB color, opacity oi. Geometry Properties: Offset \Delta \mui, Rotation matrix Ri (parameterized by first two columns), Scale Si (three axes). Deformation Properties: LBS weights Wi \in \mathbb{R}^{nk}, where nk is the number of joints. Base Scale (si): A scalar multiplier for the MLP-predicted scale. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: 1. Estimate SMPL pose parameters \thetat for each image t and shared body shape parameters \beta using a pretrained SMPL regressor. 2. Initialize Human Gaussian centers \mu at the vertices of the canonical-posed SMPL mesh (T-pose). The initialization starts with nv = 110,210 Gaussians matching the upsampled SMPL mesh vertices, but optimization clones, splits, and prunes them, resulting in ~200K Gaussians at convergence. 3. Initialize Scene Gaussians from the COLMAP structure-from-motion point cloud. 4. Pretrain the feature triplane and three MLPs (Appearance DA, Geometry DG, Deformation DD) for 5,000 iterations to output: RGB: [0.5, 0.5, 0.5] Opacity: 0.1 Offset \Delta \mu: 0 Rotation R: Aligning the z-axis with the corresponding SMPL vertex normal. Scale S: Average incoming edge lengths of the SMPL mesh. LBS Weights W: Weights from the SMPL model. 5. Initialize base scale si = 1 for each human Gaussian. 2. Optimization Loop (12,000 iterations): 1. Forward Pass (Rendering): 1. Given a joint configuration G (pose), for each Human Gaussian i: Interpolate the triplane at \mui to get f{xi}, f{yi}, f{zi}. Concatenate to form fi. Input fi to DA to output RGB and opacity. Input fi to DG to output \Delta \mui, Ri, Si. Input fi to DD to output LBS weights Wi. 2. Deformation: Transform Human Gaussians using Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) with Wi and joint transformations Gk \in SE(3). 3. Splatting: Combine transformed Human Gaussians and Scene Gaussians. Splat onto the image plane using alpha blending. 2. Loss Calculation: Compute total loss \mathcal{L} (see Formulas). 3. Backpropagation: Update \mu, triplane, and MLP parameters using Adam optimizer (lr=10^{-3}, cosine schedule). 4. Density Control (Every 600 iterations): 1. Clone: Repeat existing centers in \mu. 2. Split: Randomly sample new centers within existing Gaussians' shapes (R, S). 3. Prune: Remove Gaussians based on loss gradient and opacity. 4. Scale Adjustment: When splitting, divide the base scale s by 1.6. The actual scale is s \times S{MLP}. 3. Test-Time Rendering: 1. Construct the 3D Gaussians explicitly from the optimized parameters. 2. For a new pose G, apply LBS to the Human Gaussians using the learned Wi and G. 3. Splat and render without evaluating the triplane/MLPs for pose changes. Formulas: SMPL Posed Vertex (for initialization/regularization only): vi = \left( \sum{k=1}^{nk} W{k,i} Gk \right) pi Where vi is the posed vertex, W{k,i} is the LBS weight for joint k and vertex i, Gk is the joint transformation in SE(3), and pi is the resting vertex location. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \lambda1 \mathcal{L}1 + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{\text{ssim}} + \lambda3 \mathcal{L}{\text{vgg}} + \lambda1 \mathcal{L}^h1 + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}^h{\text{ssim}} + \lambda3 \mathcal{L}^h{\text{vgg}} + \lambda4 \mathcal{L}{\text{LBS}} Where \mathcal{L}1, \mathcal{L}{\text{ssim}}, \mathcal{L}{\text{vgg}} are L1, SSIM, and Perceptual losses. Human losses are computed on human-only renderings against ground truth human regions from segmentation masks. LBS Regularization Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{LBS}} = \| W - \hat{W} \|F Where \hat{W} is the distance-weighted average of LBS weights of the k=6 nearest SMPL vertices. Parameters: \lambda1 = 0.8 \lambda2 = 0.2 \lambda3 = 1.0 \lambda4 = 1000 Optimizer: Adam, learning rate 10^{-3}, cosine schedule. SMPL Mesh: Upsampled version with nv = 110,210 vertices and nt = 220,416 faces. Split Scale Divisor: 1.6. Pitfalls: Artifacts: Holes or pop-outs can occur during articulation if Gaussians are not coordinated to retain surface integrity. This is mitigated by learning LBS weights. Pose Errors: Off-the-shelf SMPL regressors may produce inaccurate pose parameters \theta. This is mitigated by adjusting \theta per image during optimization. Feature Splatting is a technique to learn human features by optimizing additional feature parameters for each 3D Gaussian, which are decoded into human features after rendering. It addresses the issue that standard Gaussian parameters (opacity, scaling, rotation) are not suitable for different human features with different frequencies. This differs from directly parameterizing 3D Gaussians with human features, which results in suboptimal performance because the same parameters are not suitable for different human features. Training Time: Approximately 30 minutes on a GeForce 3090Ti GPU. Rendering Speed: 60 FPS at HD resolution. Memory: Final human representation consists of ~200K Gaussians on average. Strengths: ~100x faster to train than previous works (e.g., NeuMan, Vid2Avatar). State-of-the-art rendering quality. Disentangled representation allows human transfer to other scenes. Test-time animation without MLP evaluation. Limitations: Requires monocular video input. Relies on SMPL prior for initialization (though Gaussians can deviate). Potential artifacts if LBS coordination fails. When to use: When animatable human avatars from monocular video are needed with high rendering speed and novel pose synthesis. When not to use: When multi-view capture is available and higher geometric fidelity without parametric priors is required, or when real-time training is not feasible. HUGS was introduced by Jen-Hao Rick Chang et al. in 2023 (published at CVPR 2024). It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting and the SMPL body model to address the challenge of animating humans in neural rendering. Previous methods relied on implicit neural fields or multi-view capture setups. HUGS enables novel-pose synthesis and novel-view synthesis from short, in-the-wild monocular videos. name: Uncertainty and Probabilistic Modeling
head: Probabilistic 3D Gaussian Splatting, Uncertainty Quantification in GS
body: Uncertainty and Probabilistic Modeling in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) addresses the lack of confidence metrics in standard deterministic rendering by estimating the reliability of predicted colors, depths, and geometric parameters. It differs from sibling methods like DeSplat or 360 Gaussian Splatting by explicitly modeling parameter distributions or post-hoc error statistics rather than just refining geometry or appearance. It enables active view selection, robust reconstruction under sparse or asynchronous data, and detection of out-of-distribution regions. The family shares the goal of quantifying uncertainty in 3DGS, but the mechanisms vary significantly: 1. Fisher Information / Hessian-based: Uses the curvature of the loss landscape (Fisher Information Matrix) to approximate parameter uncertainty. Assumes the posterior is Gaussian and approximates the covariance via the inverse Hessian. 2. Variational Inference: Frames 3DGS as a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) and optimizes a variational posterior over parameters using Coordinate Ascent Variational Inference (CAVI), avoiding gradient-based optimization through the renderer. 3. Post-hoc Feature Aggregation: Computes primitive-level statistics (coverage, error) from training views and aggregates them into feature maps, which are then regressed to predict uncertainty for novel views without retraining. 4. Probabilistic Generative Frameworks: Treats learnable parameters and camera poses as latent random variables inferred via Maximum a Posteriori (MAP), allowing for general handling of data uncertainty (missing views, asynchrony). FisherRF estimates predictive uncertainty in 3DGS parameters and selects the next-best view by maximizing Expected Information Gain (EIG). It differs from Variational Bayes Gaussian Splatting by not modifying the model architecture to infer a full posterior, and from PRIMU by not relying on post-hoc feature aggregation. FisherRF directly quantifies observed information using the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM), approximated via the diagonal Gauss-Newton Hessian of the rendering loss. This allows for efficient active view selection and uncertainty quantification without requiring multiple backward passes or hypothetical perturbation fields. Variational Bayes Gaussian Splatting (VBGS) frames the training of Gaussian splats as variational inference over the parameters of a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), rather than optimizing for a maximum likelihood solution via backpropagation. By leveraging the conjugacy properties of multivariate Gaussians, VBGS derives closed-form update rules that enable continual learning from sequentially streamed 2D and 3D data without catastrophic forgetting or the need for replay buffers. Unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting which relies on gradient-based optimization through a differentiable renderer, VBGS models a distribution over all features and parameters, allowing for efficient, order-invariant updates from partial observations. PRIMU is a post-hoc uncertainty estimation (UE) framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (GS) that constructs primitive-level representations of error and visibility/coverage from training views, renders them to produce uncertainty feature maps, and aggregates them via pixel-wise regression on holdout data to estimate uncertainties for novel views. It differs from sibling methods like FisherRF and Variational Bayes Gaussian Splatting by operating entirely as post-processing without requiring GS retraining, allowing it to be applied to existing trained models. Definition: Computes an uncertainty attribute for 3D Gaussians based on the negative log-likelihood of the rendered pixel value, interpreted as Fisher information. Step: Compute the dot product of the gradient with itself to obtain the uncertainty value \bar{C}{V;G}. Formula: \bar{C}{V;G} = -\log pf(\pi|V; G) where pf is the probability density function of the rendered pixel \pi given view V and Gaussian parameters G. Pitfall: The derivation assumes volume rendering of 3D Gaussians meets regularity conditions: partial derivative exists almost everywhere, integral differentiability, and support independence from G. Definition: A probabilistic framework that incorporates data uncertainty (view sparsity, missing frames, camera asynchronization) into Gaussian Splatting by treating learnable parameters as latent variables and camera poses/times as random variables, inferred via Maximum a Posteriori (MAP). The 'X' in GraphiXS is not necessarily Gaussian; the framework uses the general term 'component' to allow instantiation with different primitives like Gaussians or Student’s-t. Step: Formulate GraphiXS as a generative process by introducing stochasticity into the individual steps of 4DGS. Treat all learnable parameters (e.g., component location) as latent variables to be inferred via Maximum a Posteriori (MAP). Treat camera pose and frame time as samples of random variables, rather than fixed observations, to incorporate uncertainty in them. Impose various prior distributions to regulate the behaviors of the components. Comparison: GraphiXS is a general framework that can upgrade existing methods, whereas prior works often consider data uncertainty specific to one application scenario. Definition: A scalar uncertainty feature per Gaussian primitive k representing the number of training views that observe the primitive. A scalar uncertainty feature per Gaussian primitive k capturing how strongly the primitive is covered in at least one training view, based on its contribution factors. Formula: F(k) = |\Omegak|, where \Omegak is the set of training views where the k-th Gaussian primitive lies within the viewing cone. V(k) = \max{v \in \Omega} \text{agg}{\bar{x} \in v^{(k)}} \alphak(\bar{x}) Tk(\bar{x}), where v^{(k)} denotes the pixels of view v in which the opacity of the k-th Gaussian exceeds a small threshold, and agg is an aggregation function. Parameter: Aggregation function agg: Can be 'max', 'sum', or 'mean'. Opacity threshold: Gaussians are considered visible if \alphak(\bar{x}) \ge 1/255 and Tk(\bar{x}) \ge 10^{-3}. Pitfall: To highlight low-opacity Gaussians that still influence reconstruction quality, the opacity term \alphak(\bar{x}) can be omitted from the aggregation. Definition: Renders the standard deviation \sigma of variational Gaussian features to visualize model uncertainty, with background regions explicitly handled. Step: Sets the background standard deviation to one for empty regions outside reference camera frustums, matching the feature map sampling strategy. Renders darker regions as higher uncertainty; main objects show lower uncertainty than background, with higher uncertainty at edges/fur compared to uniform surfaces. Uncertainty quantification in 3DGS emerged as a critical component for active view selection, robust reconstruction from sparse or noisy data, and reliable downstream applications like robotics and AR. Early work adapted Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) concepts from neural radiance fields to 3DGS for efficient view selection. Variational approaches extended Gaussian Mixture Models to 3DGS to enable continual learning and explicit uncertainty modeling. Post-hoc methods like PRIMU addressed the need for uncertainty estimation in existing trained models without retraining. More recently, probabilistic frameworks like GraphiXS have been proposed to handle complex data uncertainties such as camera asynchrony and missing frames in 4DGS. name: FisherRF
head: Active View Selection and Mapping with Radiance Fields Using Fisher Information, Expected Information Gain (EIG) via Fisher Information, FisherRF Uncertainty Estimation
body: FisherRF is a method for estimating predictive uncertainty in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) parameters and selecting the next-best view by maximizing Expected Information Gain (EIG). It quantifies observed information on model parameters using the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM), approximated via a diagonal Gauss-Newton Hessian. Unlike methods that rely on hypothetical perturbation fields or indirect approximations, FisherRF computes the Hessian of the loss function directly with respect to the radiance field parameters. This allows for efficient active view selection and uncertainty quantification, leveraging the sparsity of the rendering Jacobian to achieve performance comparable to back-propagation. Inputs: \theta: The set of trained 3DGS parameters (means, covariances, opacities, spherical harmonics coefficients). D: The set of all rays cast from the training views observed so far. \mathcal{V}{cand}: A pool of candidate views for selection. Outputs: v^: The selected next-best view. U: Predictive uncertainty for rendered views. Data Structures: Hessian (H): A diagonal matrix approximating the precision (inverse covariance) of the parameter posterior. Stored as a 1D array of size equal to the number of parameters |\theta|. Jacobian (Jr): For each ray r, the gradient of the rendered color \hat{C}r with respect to \theta, i.e., \frac{\partial \hat{C}r}{\partial \theta}. Parameters: \epsilon: A small scalar prior term added to keep H invertible. \Lambdar: Confidence weight for ray r. In FisherRF, all rays share the same isotropic value, reducing the formulation to an unweighted squared-error loss. Steps: 1. Compute Global Hessian (H): Calculate the diagonal Gauss-Newton Hessian of the rendering loss summed over all observed rays D: \mathbf{H} = \sum{r \in D} \left( \frac{\partial \hat{C}r}{\partial \theta} \right)^{\!\top} \Lambdar \left( \frac{\partial \hat{C}r}{\partial \theta} \right) + \epsilon \mathbf{I} Since only the diagonal is kept for tractability, this simplifies to summing the squared gradients for each parameter. The term \epsilon \mathbf{I} ensures invertibility. 2. Compute Candidate Hessian (Hv): For each candidate view v \in \mathcal{V}{cand}, compute Hv using only the rays associated with view v, calculated identically to step 1 but restricted to v's rays. 3. Calculate Expected Information Gain (EIG): Compute the EIG for each candidate view v using the approximation: \mathrm{EIG}(v) = \frac{1}{2} \log \det \left( \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{H}v \mathbf{H}^{-1} \right) To avoid computing the full determinant, FisherRF uses an upper bound approximation based on the trace of the product of the Hessians, exploiting the sparsity of the matrices. Specifically, the decrease in entropy is approximated by the trace of the product of the candidate view's Hessian and the inverse of the global Hessian. 4. Select Next-Best View: Select the view v^ that maximizes the EIG: v^ = \arg \max{v} \mathrm{EIG}(v). 5. Predictive Uncertainty (Optional): For a given view, predictive uncertainty U is propagated through the rendering Jacobian J using the inverse Hessian: U = J \mathbf{H}^{-1} J^{\top}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computefisherhessian(rays, parameters, epsilon): """ Computes the diagonal Fisher Information Matrix (Hessian) for a set of rays. Args: rays: List of rays, each containing indices of 3D Gaussians contributing to it. parameters: Current 3DGS parameters theta. epsilon: Small scalar for numerical stability. Returns: H: Diagonal Hessian vector of size len(parameters). """ H = np.zeros(len(parameters)) for ray in rays: # Compute rendering Jacobian for this ray: d(Chat)/d(theta) # This requires differentiating the splatting function with respect to parameters. # In 3DGS, this is typically done via automatic differentiation or custom CUDA kernels. jacobian = computerenderingjacobian(ray, parameters) # Lambdar is isotropic (constant) in FisherRF, so it can be absorbed or set to 1. # H += J^T J (element-wise square for diagonal approximation) H += jacobian 2 # Add prior H += epsilon return H def computeeig(hglobal, hcandidate): """ Computes the Expected Information Gain (EIG) using the trace approximation. Args: hglobal: Diagonal Hessian of observed data (H). hcandidate: Diagonal Hessian of candidate view (Hv). Returns: eig: Approximate EIG value. """ # Inverse of diagonal H is element-wise reciprocal hinv = 1.0 / hglobal # Approximation of log det(I + Hv H^-1) using trace # log det(I + A) approx trace(A) for small A, or more precisely: # The source states: "approximation of the decrease in entropy by its upper bound, # which is the trace of the product of the Hessian of the candidate view times the Hessian # with respect to all previous views." # Note: Strictly, EIG = 0.5 log det(I + Hv H^-1). # If using trace approximation for the log-det term: # EIG approx 0.5 trace(Hv H^-1) # Element-wise multiplication of Hv and H^-1 product = hcandidate hinv # Sum of diagonal elements (Trace) traceval = np.sum(product) return 0.5 traceval def selectnextbestview(candidateviews, hglobal): """ Selects the view with the highest Expected Information Gain. """ bestview = None maxeig = -np.inf for view in candidateviews: # Compute Hessian for the candidate view hcandidate = computefisherhessian(view.rays, parameters, epsilon) # Compute EIG eig = computeeig(hglobal, hcandidate) if eig > maxeig: maxeig = eig bestview = view return bestview Time Complexity: The computation of the Hessian is additive over rays. Due to the sparsity of the scene parameters with respect to disparate rays, the matrix trace computation is as cost-effective as back-propagation. Performance: When implemented with 3D Gaussian Splatting, the method evaluates views at 70 fps. A direct comparison shows FisherRF's efficient CUDA implementation for diagonal Hessian computation takes 11.3 \text{ ms} \pm 33.3 \text{ \mu s}, compared to 1.1 \text{ s} \pm 2.5 \text{ ms} for methods relying on multiple PyTorch backward engine calls (e.g., Goli et al.). Memory Complexity: By keeping only the diagonal elements of the Hessian, memory usage is reduced to O(|\theta|), where |\theta| is the number of parameters. Strengths: Direct quantification of observed information on parameters; efficient active view selection and mapping; state-of-the-art results in uncertainty quantification. Limitations: Relies on the diagonal approximation of the Hessian, ignoring parameter correlations. Assumes the posterior is Gaussian (Laplace approximation). FisherRF was introduced to address the lack of literature on active "training" view selection for volumetric rendering. It leverages Fisher Information to directly quantify observed information on the parameters of Radiance Fields, selecting candidate views by maximizing Expected Information Gain (EIG). The method is implemented on top of point-based 3D Gaussian Splatting and Plenoxels radiance field models. It improves upon previous approaches that relied on hypothetical perturbation fields and indirect approximations, which did not guarantee optimal information gain. The Hessian of the objective function in volumetric rendering is independent of ground truth data or actual image measurements, allowing information gain to be computed using only camera parameters of candidate views.
