name: Variational Bayes Gaussian Splatting
body:
Variational Bayes Gaussian Splatting (VBGS) is a training method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that frames the optimization of Gaussian mixture model parameters as a variational inference problem rather than a gradient-based maximum likelihood estimation. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which relies on backpropagation through a differentiable renderer and suffers from catastrophic forgetting in continual learning settings, VBGS derives closed-form update rules using Coordinate Ascent Variational Inference (CAVI). This allows for efficient, continual learning from sequentially streamed 2D and 3D data without the need for replay buffers. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A stream of observed data points D = \{(sn, cn)\}{n=1}^N, where sn is the spatial coordinate (2D pixel location for images, 3D Cartesian for point clouds) and cn is the color (RGB). The method requires RGBD data. Outputs: The variational posterior parameters q(\mus, \Sigmas, \muc, \Sigmac, \pi) for K Gaussian components. Data Structures: Each Gaussian component k stores 29 parameters representing the Natural-Inverse-Wishart (NIW) likelihood for color and position, and the Dirichlet prior for assignments. This is in contrast to the 14 parameters (mean, scale, rotation, opacity, SH coefficients) used in the gradient baseline. The parameters per component are structured as follows: 1. Spatial NIW Parameters (q(\mu{k,s}, \Sigma{k,s})): \eta{0,s} = (\kappa{0,s} \cdot m{0,s}, V{0,s} + \kappa{0,s} \cdot m{0,s} \cdot m{0,s}^T) 
u{0,s} = (\kappa{0,s}, n{0,s} + Ds + 1) Where m{0,s} is the mean, \kappa{0,s} is the concentration, n{0,s} is degrees of freedom, V{0,s} is the inverse scale matrix, and Ds is the dimensionality of space (Ds=2 or 3). 2. Color NIW Parameters (q(\mu{k,c}, \Sigma{k,c})): \eta{0,c} = (\kappa{0,c} \cdot m{0,c}, V{0,c} + \kappa{0,c} \cdot m{0,c} \cdot m{0,c}^T) 
u{0,c} = (\kappa{0,c}, n{0,c} + Dc + 1) The covariance \Sigma{k,c} is fixed using a Delta distribution q(\Sigma{k,c}) = 	ext{Delta}(\epsilon I) to prevent color blending. Thus, n{k,c} and V{k,c} are kept fixed at prior values. 3. Dirichlet Parameters (q(\pi)): \eta{0,z} = \alpha (concentration parameters). Algorithm Steps: The training uses Coordinate Ascent Variational Inference (CAVI) to maximize the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO): \mathcal{L} = D{KL}[q(z, \mus, \Sigmas, \muc, \Sigmac, \pi) || p(z, \mus, \Sigmas, \muc, \Sigmac, \pi | s, c)] The algorithm consists of two main steps repeated for each batch or stream of data: 1. Assignment Step (E-step equivalent): Compute the assignment log-probability \log \gamman for each data point n to each component k: \log \hat{\gamma}n = \sum{k=1}^K \left( E{q(\mu{k,s}, \Sigma{k,s})}[\log p(sn | \mu{k,s}, \Sigma{k,s})] + E{q(\mu{k,c}, \Sigma{k,c})}[\log p(cn | \mu{k,c}, \Sigma{k,c})] + E{q(\pi)}[\log p(zn=k)] ight) Normalize to get probabilities: \gamma{n,k} =  rac{\exp(\log \hat{\gamma}{n,k})}{\sum{j=1}^K \exp(\log \hat{\gamma}{n,j})} Note: The sources define \log \gamman generally, but the summation over k is implicit in the normalization step described in the notes. 2. Parameter Update Step (M-step equivalent): Update the natural parameters of the variational posteriors using the sufficient statistics of the data weighted by the assignments \gamma{n,k}: \eta{k} = \eta{0,k} + \sum{n=1}^N \gamma{n,k} T(xn) 
u{k} = 
u{0,k} + \sum{n=1}^N \gamma{n,k} Where T(xn) are the sufficient statistics: T(sn) = (sn, sn sn^T) and T(cn) = (cn, cn cn^T). 3. Continual Learning & Reassignment: Order Invariance: Assignments q(z) are always computed with respect to the initial posterior parameters. This ensures that updates are identical to batch processing and avoids catastrophic forgetting. Reassignment: To handle unused components (where concentration parameters \alphak equal their prior value), replace the means of n components with the location and color of data points sampled proportional to the negative ELBO. n is a fraction (e.g., 0.01 for Replica, 0.05 for Habitat) of the unused components. After reassignment, run CAVI. Rendering: VBGS does not optimize for image reconstruction loss, so standard alpha blending is not sensible. All Gaussians are set to be opaque by setting their alpha value to 1. 3D rendering leverages the 3D renderer from Kerbl et al. [2023], projecting 3D Gaussians to the image plane and combining color values via alpha blending along a casted ray, but with fixed opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def vbgsupdate(datapoints, K, priorparams, reassignfraction=0.0): """ Perform one CAVI update step for VBGS. Args: datapoints: List of (s, c) tuples. s is spatial coord, c is color. K: Number of Gaussian components. priorparams: Dictionary containing initial natural parameters (etas, nus, etac, nuc, alpha) for all K components. reassignfraction: Fraction of unused components to reassign. Returns: Updated variational parameters. """ N = len(datapoints) # 1. Compute Assignments # Initialize log probabilities loggamma = np.zeros((N, K)) for k in range(K): # Extract current variational parameters for component k # Note: In continual learning, these are the INITIAL parameters musk, Sigmask = getmeancovfromniw(priorparams['etas'][k], priorparams['nus'][k]) muck = priorparams['etac'][k][0] # Mean of color # Sigmac is fixed Delta distribution, so we use epsilon I # E[log p(c|mu, Sigma)] for Delta distribution simplifies to log p(c|mu, epsilonI) # Compute log likelihoods for spatial and color # p(s|mu, Sigma) ~ MVN # p(c|mu, Sigma) ~ MVN with fixed covariance logps = mvnlogprob(datapoints, musk, Sigmask) logpc = mvnlogprobcolor(datapoints, muck, epsilon=1e-3) # epsilon from notes # Log prior for component assignment (Dirichlet) logpz = np.log(priorparams['alpha'][k]) loggamma[:, k] = logps + logpc + logpz # Normalize loggammamax = np.max(loggamma, axis=1, keepdims=True) loggamma -= loggammamax # Stability gammahat = np.exp(loggamma) gamma = gammahat / np.sum(gammahat, axis=1, keepdims=True) # 2. Update Parameters updatedparams = copy.deepcopy(priorparams) for k in range(K): # Sufficient statistics # T(s) = (s, s s^T) # T(c) = (c, c c^T) # Update etas and nus # etas = (kappa m, V + kappa m m^T) # nus = (kappa, n + D + 1) # Accumulate weighted stats weighteds = np.sum(gamma[:, k:k+1] np.array([p[0] for p in datapoints]), axis=0) weightedsouter = np.sum(gamma[:, k:k+1] np.array([[p[0] @ p[0].T for p in datapoints]]), axis=0) # Shape (N, D, D) # Update natural parameters # etanew = eta0 + sum(gamma T(x)) # nunew = nu0 + sum(gamma) # For NIW, the update is additive on the natural parameters # etask = etas0k + sumn gammank (sn, sn sn^T) # nusk = nus0k + sumn gammank # Note: The source defines eta and nu as vectors/tuples. # Implementation requires unpacking etas into (kappam, V+kappamm^T) # and updating them. # Simplified update logic based on source Eq 21-22: # etak = eta0k + sum(gamma T(x)) # nuk = nu0k + sum(gamma) # We must unpack the NIW natural parameters to update them correctly. # etas has 2 parts: kappam and V+kappamm^T. # nus has 2 parts: kappa and n+D+1. #... (Detailed NIW update logic omitted for brevity, follows standard NIW conjugacy)... # Update Color Parameters # Sigmac is fixed, so only muc updates. # muc update depends on weighted sum of c. # Update Dirichlet Alpha # alphanew = alpha0 + sum(gamma) updatedparams['alpha'][k] = priorparams['alpha'][k] + np.sum(gamma[:, k]) # 3. Reassignment (Continual Learning) if reassignfraction > 0: unusedcomponents = findunusedcomponents(updatedparams['alpha'], priorparams['alpha']) nreassign = int(reassignfraction len(unusedcomponents)) if nreassign > 0: # Sample data points proportional to negative ELBO # ELBO contribution per data point is roughly loggamma # Negative ELBO implies high error -> sample these errorscores = -np.mean(loggamma, axis=1) # Simplified heuristic indices = sampleindices(datapoints, errorscores, nreassign) for i in range(nreassign): compidx = unusedcomponents[i] point = datapoints[indices[i]] # Reset component to prior, then set mean to data point # Or simply replace mean in the variational posterior # Source: "replace means of n components... with location and color" updatedparams['etas'][compidx] = setmeaninniweta(updatedparams['etas'][compidx], point[0]) updatedparams['etac'][compidx] = setmeaninniweta(updatedparams['etac'][compidx], point[1]) return updatedparams def mvnlogprob(data, mu, Sigma): # Compute log probability of data points under MVN(mu, Sigma) # Returns array of shape (N,) pass def mvnlogprobcolor(data, mu, epsilon): # Compute log probability under MVN(mu, epsilonI) pass def getmeancovfromniw(eta, nu): # Unpack NIW natural parameters to mean and covariance pass def findunusedcomponents(alpha, alphaprior): # Components where alpha == alphaprior pass def sampleindices(data, scores, n): # Sample n indices based on scores pass Time Complexity: The assignment step has complexity O(nm), where n is the number of data points and m is the number of Gaussian components. The parameter update step has complexity O(n). Memory Complexity: Memory requirements are increased by a factor of 2 compared to the gradient baseline (3DGS) for the same number of Gaussians, due to storing the distribution parameters (29 per component vs 14). Performance: On the Tiny ImageNet validation set, VBGS wall-clock time is 0.03 \pm 0.03 s compared to Gradient 0.05 \pm 0.02 s (NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090). In 3D continual learning on the Blender dataset, VBGS (Random Init) average reconstruction error is 11.19 \pm 3.53 dB, while Gradient (Random Init) is 21.26 \pm 1.76 dB. Strengths: Enables continual learning without catastrophic forgetting; no replay buffers needed; closed-form updates are faster than accumulated gradient steps when data fits in memory. Limitations: Relies on RGBD data rather than RGB-only; memory usage is higher; in large-scale 3D datasets, batched processing is necessary, which reduces the speed advantage over gradient methods. VBGS was proposed to address the limitation of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), which uses backpropagation through a differentiable renderer and struggles with catastrophic forgetting in continuous data streams. It leverages the conjugacy properties of multivariate Gaussians to derive closed-form variational update rules. The method is benchmarked on 2D image (TinyImageNet) and 3D point cloud (Blender 3D models, Habitat scenes, Replica, TUM) datasets. Variational Bayes Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03592v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: PRIMU
head: Primitive-based Representations of Uncertainty
body: PRIMU is a post-hoc uncertainty estimation (UE) framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that constructs primitive-level representations of error and visibility/coverage from training views to estimate uncertainties for novel views. It differs from sibling methods like FisherRF and Variational Bayes Gaussian Splatting by operating entirely as post-processing without requiring GS retraining, using 13 optionally direction-dependent features instead of a single uncertainty measure. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A trained 3DGS model (Gaussian primitives with parameters \mu, \Sigma, g, c), a set of training views with known poses, and optionally a small set of holdout views with ground truth for regression training. Outputs: Pixel-wise uncertainty maps for novel views (color and depth), or active view selection (AVS) candidates. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitives: Each primitive k has a 3D mean \muk, a 3x3 covariance matrix \Sigmak (or quaternion/scale representation), a scalar opacity factor g, and view-dependent color coefficients ck (encoded via spherical harmonics). Primitive Features: A vector of 13 features per primitive, optionally direction-dependent. Key features include: Field-of-View (FoV) count F(k). Training-view coverage V(k). Rendering error E(k). Other coverage/error statistics aggregated from training views. Numbered Steps: 1. Project Training Errors and Coverage: For each training view v \in \Omega (where \Omega is the set of training views): a. Render the scene using the trained 3DGS model to obtain predicted color Cv(\bar{x}) and depth Dv(\bar{x}) for each pixel \bar{x}. b. Compute per-pixel reconstruction error e{\bar{x}} (e.g., \ell1 error for color or depth) against ground truth. c. For each Gaussian primitive k visible in view v (i.e., \bar{x} \in v^{(k)} where opacity \alphak(\bar{x}) > \text{threshold}): i. Calculate the contribution factor: w{k, \bar{x}} = \alphak(\bar{x}) Tk(\bar{x}), where Tk(\bar{x}) = \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphaj(\bar{x})) is the accumulated transparency. ii. Aggregate contributions for primitive k in view v using an aggregation function \text{agg} \in \{\text{max}, \text{sum}, \text{mean}\}: \text{Agg}{v}(k) = \text{agg}{\bar{x} \in v^{(k)}} (w{k, \bar{x}}) iii. Compute the rendering error representation for primitive k in view v: Ev(k) = \text{mean}{\bar{x} \in v^{(k)}} (e{\bar{x}} \cdot w{k, \bar{x}}) 2. Construct Primitive-Level Representations: For each primitive k: a. FoV Count: F(k) = |\Omegak|, where \Omegak is the set of training views where primitive k is visible. b. Coverage: V(k) = \max{v \in \Omega} (\text{Agg}{v}(k)). This captures the maximum aggregated contribution across all training views. c. Error: E(k) = \text{mean}{v \in \Omega} (Ev(k)). This captures the mean error-weighted contribution. d. Extract the remaining 10 features (details not fully specified in sources, but noted as optionally direction-dependent). 3. Render Uncertainty Feature Maps: For a novel viewpoint: a. Project all Gaussian primitives onto the image plane using standard 3DGS splatting. b. For each pixel \bar{x}, render the primitive-level features (e.g., F(k), V(k), E(k)) as separate channels. This produces "uncertainty feature maps" where each pixel contains the aggregated features of the contributing primitives. c. The rendering of a feature map M at pixel \bar{x} is computed similarly to color: M(\bar{x}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \alphak(\bar{x}) Tk(\bar{x}) \cdot \text{feature}k where \text{feature}k is the value of the specific feature for primitive k. 4. Aggregate via Regression: a. If holdout data is available, train a gradient boosting regression model on the rendered uncertainty feature maps (from holdout views) to predict the true pixel-wise error (color or depth). b. For novel views, render the uncertainty feature maps and pass them through the trained regression model to obtain the final uncertainty estimate. c. If no regression is used, the uncertainty feature maps can be used directly for Active View Selection (AVS) by prioritizing viewpoints with high uncertainty indicators. Formulas: Opacity: \alpha(\bar{x}) = g \Phi(\bar{x}; \bar{\mu}, \bar{\Sigma}), where \Phi is the 2D Gaussian density, \bar{\mu} is the mean, and \bar{\Sigma} is the covariance. Color: C(\bar{x}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \alphak(\bar{x}) Tk(\bar{x}) ck(\vec{d}), where ck(\vec{d}) is the view-dependent color. FoV Count: F(k) = |\Omegak|. Coverage: V(k) = \max{v \in \Omega} \text{agg}{\bar{x} \in v^{(k)}} (\alphak(\bar{x}) Tk(\bar{x})). Error: E(k) = \text{mean}{v \in \Omega} \text{agg}{\bar{x} \in v^{(k)}} (e{\bar{x}} \alphak(\bar{x}) Tk(\bar{x})). Parameters: Number of Gaussian-primitive features: 13 Regression model: Gradient boosting Aggregation functions: max, sum, or mean Opacity threshold for visibility: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometry Misalignment: Gaussian splats may misalign with scene geometry even when rendered appearance is correct, leading to depth error between true geometry and splat distribution. This affects the accuracy of depth uncertainty estimates. Undefined Depth Error: Regions with undefined depth error (e.g., background) should be handled, potentially represented as light gray or excluded from regression. Generalization: While the method generalizes to unseen scenes to some extent, performance may degrade if the training data distribution differs significantly from the novel scene. Time Complexity: Post-hoc processing. Rendering feature maps is O(N \cdot P) where N is the number of primitives and P is the number of pixels. Regression is fast once trained. Memory Complexity: Requires storing 13 feature values per primitive. No additional model parameters for the UE itself (except the lightweight regression model). Strengths: No retraining required; interpretable features; strong correlation with true errors, especially for depth and foreground objects; generalizes to unseen scenes. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial 3DGS reconstruction; may not capture all sources of uncertainty (e.g., model misspecification); requires holdout data for optimal regression performance (though not strictly necessary for AVS). When to Use: Safety-critical domains (robotics, medical imaging); Active View Selection; when retraining is not feasible. When Not to Use: When real-time uncertainty estimation during training is required; when computational resources for regression are unavailable (though minimal). PRIMU was introduced by Stehr et al. in 2025 (preprint) as a post-hoc uncertainty estimation framework for Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the challenge of reliable uncertainty quantification in 3DGS, which is critical for deploying GS in robotics and medicine. Existing methods often estimate per-primitive uncertainty during training using Fisher information or learned distributions, whereas PRIMU operates entirely as post-processing. PRIMU: Uncertainty Estimation for Novel Views in Gaussian Splatting from Primitive-Based Representations of Error and Coverage, https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02443v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: SCION
head: Scene Composition with Instanced Neural Primitives
body: SCION is a hierarchical compositional scene representation that replaces the millions of independent Gaussians used in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with a compact vocabulary of reusable local primitives and lightweight world-space instances. It solves the redundancy and lack of structural manipulation handles in standard 3DGS by discovering and encoding repetitive structures end-to-end from multi-view captures. Unlike prior codebook methods that share parameters across distinct splats or require manual instance selection, SCION builds shared primitives and recovers structure automatically, enabling compact storage (e.g., 1.2 MB) and instance-level editing without retraining. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of posed RGB images \{Iv\} with calibrated cameras \{\piv\} and a sparse COLMAP point cloud. Output: A scene representation consisting of a primitive vocabulary \mathcal{C} and a set of instances \Phi, optimized to render novel views with high fidelity. Data Structures The representation consists of two main components: 1. Primitive Vocabulary \mathcal{C} = \{ck\}{k=1}^K: A library of K reusable primitives. Each primitive ck is a bundle of Sk local-frame Gaussians (splats). The j-th splat in primitive k has parameters \theta{kj}^L = (\mu{kj}^L \in \mathbb{R}^3, q{kj}^L \in S^3, s{kj}^L \in \mathbb{R}^3, o{kj}^L \in \mathbb{R}, c{kj}^L \in \mathbb{R}^3). \mu^L: Position, q^L: Unit quaternion rotation, s^L: Anisotropic log-scale, o^L: Opacity logit, c^L: RGB color (zeroth-order spherical harmonic). Total parameters per primitive: P{splat} \times Sk, where P{splat} = 14. 2. Instances \Phi = \{\phii\}{i=1}^N: N lightweight world-space placements. The i-th instance has parameters \phii^W = (\mui^W \in \mathbb{R}^3, qi^W \in S^3, si^W \in \mathbb{R}, oi^W \in \mathbb{R}, ai \in \{1, \dots, K\}). \mu^W: World position, q^W: World rotation, s^W: Scalar log-scale, o^W: Opacity logit, ai: Discrete index selecting the primitive c{ai}. Total parameters per instance: P{instance} = 10 (excluding the integer assignment). Rendering Assembly Rendering materializes transient Gaussians by combining local splats with instance transforms. For each instance i and each local splat j in its assigned primitive k=ai, the world-frame Gaussian parameters \tilde{\theta}{ij}^W are computed as: \tilde{\mu}{ij}^W = \mui^W + qi^W \text{rotate}(s{ij}^L, \mu{ai j}^L) \tilde{s}{ij}^W = s{ai j}^L + si^W \mathbf{1} \tilde{q}{ij}^W = qi^W \otimes q{ai j}^L \tilde{o}{ij}^W = o{ai j}^L + oi^W \tilde{c}{ij}^W = c{ai j}^L where q(\cdot) denotes rotation of a vector by a quaternion, \otimes is quaternion composition, and \mathbf{1} is a vector of ones. The total number of assembled Gaussians is T = \sum{i=1}^N S{ai} = \sum{k=1}^K nk Sk, where nk is the number of instances assigned to primitive k. Optimization Procedure The representation is fitted via joint optimization over discrete (assignment) and continuous parameters. The assignment ai is fixed after initialization using frozen DINOv3 features. Optimization proceeds in two alternating phases per iteration. To avoid coupled gradients between primitive and instance parameters, each training iteration renders the same view twice: 1. Splat Pass: Render view with detached instance parameters: \hat{I}\theta = \mathcal{R}(\theta, \text{sg}(\phi)). 2. Instance Pass: Render view with detached primitive parameters: \hat{I}\phi = \mathcal{R}(\text{sg}(\theta), \phi). Here \mathcal{R} is the Gaussian rasterizer and \text{sg} stops gradients. Loss Functions The total loss combines photometric, regularization, and adversarial terms: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{recon}^{(t)}(\hat{I}\theta, I) + \mathcal{L}{reg} + \mathcal{L}{recon}^{(t)}(\hat{I}\phi, I) + \mathcal{L}{reg} + \mathbb{1}{t \ge tD} \lambda{adv} \mathcal{L}{adv}(\hat{I}\theta, I) Reconstruction Loss: \mathcal{L}{recon}^{(t)}(I, \hat{I}) = (1 - \lambda{ssim}) \|I - \hat{I}\|1 + \lambda{ssim}(1 - \text{SSIM}(I, \hat{I})) + \mathbb{1}{lpips}(t) \lambda{lpips} \text{LPIPS}{vgg}(I, \hat{I}) Regularization Loss: \mathcal{L}{reg} = \mathcal{L}{scale} + \mathcal{L}{opac} + \lambda{anch} \sumi |si^W| + \lambda{cap} \sumi [\max(0, si^W - \tau{cap})] + \lambdac \sum{k \in \mathcal{C}{\ge 2}} \frac{1}{|Ak|} \sum{j \in Ak} \|\mu{kj}^L - \bar{\mu}k\|2^2 \mathcal{L}{scale}: Penalizes anisotropic local-frame splat scales. \mathcal{L}{opac}: Caps large local opacity logits. \lambda{anch}: Anchors instance log-scale near initialization. \lambda{cap}: Caps positive instance log-scales to prevent runaway growth. \lambdac: Keeps primitive active splats close to their local-frame mean \bar{\mu}k. \mathcal{C}{\ge 2}: Set of primitives with at least two active splats. Ak is the active subset of primitive k. Adversarial Loss: Added after warmup step tD to preserve per-instance sharpness against averaged reconstruction losses. The discriminator compares randomly cropped real and rendered patches. Densification (Density Optimization) SCION uses two-level densification scoped to primitives and instances. Splat Density Optimization: Uses the MH-3DGS birth rule scoped to one primitive. A dead row in ck is filled with an opacity-weighted alive donor from ck, and new children are written back into ck. 1. Z-scoring: Parent importance score is z-scored within each primitive to respond to local under-fitting. 2. Density Normalization: Acceptance is divided by same-primitive voxel density to prevent births piling up. 3. Mass Correction: When a row is copied into \nu overlapping instances, opacity and scale are corrected to preserve alpha-compositing mass. Instance Density Optimization: 1. Pruning: Remove instances with opacity below threshold or non-finite parameters. 2. Ranking: Rank remaining instances by accumulated gradient magnitude \bar{h}i: \bar{h}i = \frac{\sum{v \in W} \sum{j=1}^{S{ai}} \|\nabla{\piv} (\tilde{\mu}{ij}^W)\|2^2}{\sum{v \in W} S{ai}} 3. Cloning (Small Instances): If linear scale e^{si^W} is below threshold: \mu{i'}^W = \mui^W + \eta{clone} e^{si^W} \xi, \quad \xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) q{i'}^W = qi^W, \quad s{i'}^W = si^W, \quad o{i'}^W = oi^W, \quad a{i'} = ai 4. Subdivision (Large Instances): Split into M children. Children inherit rotation, assignment, and opacity. \mu{i,m}^{W'} = \mui^W + \eta{sub} e^{si^W} \epsilonm, \quad \epsilonm \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) s{i,m}^{W'} = si^W - \frac{1}{3} \log M o{i,m}^{W'} = oi^W Pitfall: Instance children occupy different world positions, so they do not use the alpha-compositing opacity correction applied to splat copying. Reducing opacity here would remove rendered mass. Parameters P{splat} = 14: Parameters per local splat. P{instance} = 10: Parameters per instance. \lambda{anch}, \lambda{cap}, \lambdac: Regularization weights. tD: Warmup step for adversarial loss. M: Number of children when subdividing a large instance. Complexity: Representation space complexity is O(K \bar{S} + N), where \bar{S} is the average number of local splats per primitive, K is the number of primitives, and N is the number of instances. This is significantly smaller than the O(\sum Si) complexity of unshared 3DGS. Storage: SCION maintains high quality even at 1.2 MB storage size. Compression Ratio: Relative to an unshared representation with the same assembled Gaussians: CR = \frac{B{ours}}{P{splat} \sum{k=1}^K nk Sk} where B{ours} = P{splat} \sum{k=1}^K Sk + P{instance} N. Strengths: Compact representation, direct editing/animation handles, end-to-end structure discovery, rate-distortion favorable to existing compression methods. Limitations: Trade-off of per-pixel fidelity for reusable structures; optimization is more complex due to two-level densification and adversarial loss. SCION was introduced to address the redundancy in neural scene representations that model elements independently. Traditional methods treat each Gaussian as unique, storing millions of parameters. SCION leverages the fact that natural and built worlds are full of repetition (e.g., grass blades, bricks, leaves). It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting [Kerbl et al., 2023] and addresses limitations of prior codebook-style methods like Splat and Replace, which require manual instance selection or start from already trained scenes. SCION recovers structure end-to-end from multi-view captures, enabling instance-level scene editing and animation without retraining. SCION: Scene Composition with Instanced Neural Primitives, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2610.02322, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: On-the-Fly GS
head: Gaussian on-the-fly Splatting
body: On-the-Fly GS is a progressive framework for near real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) field optimization that enables robust online training during discrete image acquisition. It addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS, which requires offline training after full Structure-from-Motion (SfM) processing. Unlike SLAM-based methods such as GS-SLAM or RTG-SLAM that require spatial and temporal continuity and often depth priors, On-the-Fly GS handles discrete images captured in an arbitrary manner without spatiotemporal continuity, relying only on a certain degree of overlap with previously registered images. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A stream of discrete RGB images captured in arbitrary order; an On-the-Fly SfM module that estimates camera poses and generates sparse point clouds. Outputs: An optimized 3D Gaussian field that renders the scene with high fidelity as new images arrive. Data Structures: 3D Gaussian Field: A collection of 3D Gaussians representing the scene. Training State: Per-image counters tracking the number of training iterations each image has undergone to manage learning rates. Parameters: N0: The number of initial images used to train the initial 3DGS field before progressive optimization begins. Iteration Limit: A stricter limit on the number of training iterations in Phase 1 to prevent overfitting to the initial few images. Steps: 1. Phase 1: Initial 3DGS Training. The On-the-Fly SfM module estimates poses and generates a sparse point cloud for the first N0 images. An initial 3DGS field is trained using the original 3DGS training method. A stricter limit is imposed on the number of training iterations to prevent overfitting to these initial images. 2. Phase 2: Progressive Optimization (per new image). As a new image arrives, the On-the-Fly SfM module updates the camera poses of both the newly acquired and previously registered images, while refining the sparse point cloud. Based on the updated sparse point cloud, newly optimized Gaussians are appended to the existing 3DGS field. Local & Semi-Global Optimization: Based on overlapping relationships, each local connected image is assigned a weight. This weight determines the number of training iterations each image undergoes, prioritizing the newly added image and its local overlapping images. Adaptive Learning Rate: The learning rate for each image is calculated based on the number of iterations it has undergone. Images with fewer training iterations are assigned higher learning rates, while images with more iterations receive lower learning rates. Load-Balancing Strategy: A load-balancing strategy, inspired by Adr-Gaussian, is incorporated to mitigate the over-accumulation of 3D Gaussians and ensure fast training of newly added regions. Splatting-based Parallel Computation: Back-propagation is re-implemented by transitioning from pixel-based parallelism to splatting-based parallel computation, drawing from Taming-3DGS, to enhance training efficiency. Not given in the sources. gaussians = traininitialfield(sparsepoints, N0) # Not given in the sources. enforcestricteriterationlimit() # return # Phase 2: Progressive Optimization poses, sparsepoints = updateposesandsparsepoints(imagedata, gaussians) # Not given in the sources. newgaussians = initializegaussiansfromsparsepoints(sparsepoints) # Not given in the sources. gaussians.extend(newgaussians) # Local & Semi-Global Optimization overlapweight = computeoverlapweight(imageid, gaussians) # Not given in the sources. numiterations = determineiterations(overlapweight, imageid) # Not given in the sources. # Adaptive Learning Rate currentiters = imageiterationcounts.get(imageid, 0) lr = computeadaptivelr(currentiters) # Not given in the sources. # Optimization Loop for i in range(numiterations): renderedimage = splatandrender(gaussians, poses[imageid]) # Not given in the sources. loss = computeloss(renderedimage, imagedata) # Not given in the sources. gradients = splattingbasedbackpropagation(loss, gaussians) # Not given in the sources. updategaussianparameters(gaussians, gradients, lr) # Not given in the sources. imageiterationcounts[imageid] = currentiters + 1 # Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: Training the initial field with too few images risks overfitting to the initial few images (e.g., 2 or 3 images). Mitigated by a stricter iteration limit in Phase 1. Learning Rate Decay: The standard learning rate decay strategy of original 3DGS, based on complete field quality, is not applicable because acquired images with fewer iterations exhibit lower rendering quality. Discrete Images: The method must handle images without spatiotemporal continuity, requiring only a certain degree of overlap with previously registered images. Time Complexity: Near real-time optimization per new image. The method reduces training time significantly, optimizing each new image in seconds. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Reduces training time significantly compared to offline training. Strengths: Enables robust online training during image acquisition; handles discrete images captured in an arbitrary manner; does not rely on depth priors. Limitations: Requires a certain degree of overlap with previously registered images. When to use: When near real-time 3DGS optimization is needed during image capture, especially for discrete images without spatiotemporal continuity. When not to use: When offline training after full SfM processing is acceptable and real-time updates are not required. On-the-Fly GS was introduced by Cheng and Xin Wang in a paper published in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (LRA) in 2025. It addresses the limitations of existing SLAM-based 3DGS methods (e.g., GS-SLAM, RTG-SLAM) which require spatial and temporal continuity and often depth priors. The method builds on the original 3DGS training method and incorporates strategies from Adr-Gaussian (load-balancing) and Taming-3DGS (splatting-based parallel computation). name: View-Dependent and Appearance Modeling
body: This family extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to model complex, view-dependent lighting effects such as specular highlights and anisotropic reflections, which standard isotropic spherical Gaussians cannot capture accurately. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by replacing or augmenting the static spherical harmonic color representation with physically based rendering (PBR) models, directional anisotropic functions, or neural networks predicting view-dependent attributes. All methods in this family share the goal of decomposing appearance into geometric and directional components to support view-dependent shading. 1. Primitive Representation: Gaussians are augmented with parameters beyond position, covariance, and opacity, such as material properties (roughness, metallic, albedo) or directional spread parameters. 2. Directional Evaluation: The contribution of a Gaussian to a pixel is modulated by the viewing direction relative to the primitive's orientation, achieved through Anisotropic Spherical Gaussians (ASG), neural networks, or refined spherical harmonics. 3. Physical or Approximate Shading: Colors are computed using PBR models (diffuse + specular), directional basis functions, or neural residuals, rather than simple SH evaluation. 4. Differentiable Optimization: All parameters are optimized via gradient descent using a photometric loss, requiring differentiable rendering of the directional components. VDGS produces more faithful view-dependent effects by modeling 3DGS to represent 3D shapes and predicting attributes like view-dependent color and opacity with a NeRF-like neural network instead of spherical harmonic coefficients. NIE applies a neural module to non-Lambertian regions to model view-dependent highlights. Revised Spherical Harmonics dynamically adjust SH coefficients using learned weights to improve color accuracy. name: Anisotropic Reflective Spherical 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: ARS-GS, Anisotropic Spherical Gaussians for 3DGS
body: Anisotropic Reflective Spherical 3D Gaussian Splatting (ARS-GS) is a differentiable rendering method that embeds Anisotropic Spherical Gaussians (ASG) within a Physically Based Rendering (PBR) pipeline to model view-dependent specular reflections and enable accurate mesh reconstruction from multi-view images. Unlike sibling methods that use ASG primarily for appearance fitting, ARS-GS strictly aligns ASG with GGX microfacet models to simulate light transport, providing physical constraints that improve geometric fidelity in highly reflective regions. It solves the problem of vanishing gradients in specular areas by introducing a direct skip connection from specular color to Gaussian position, allowing for the reconstruction of shiny surfaces that traditional spherical harmonics cannot capture. Inputs: A set of N images Xi with known camera poses. Initial Gaussian primitives defined by geometric attributes: opacity \alphak, center position pk, and covariance matrix \Sigmak. Appearance parameters: Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients F{SH} for diffuse lighting and Anisotropic Spherical Gaussian parameters F{ASG} (roughness \rho, metallic m, albedo a, and frame vectors). Outputs: Optimized Gaussian primitives (geometry and appearance). Rendered images and reconstructed meshes via zero-value surface identification. Each Gaussian primitive Gk stores: Geometry: Center pk \in \mathbb{R}^3, Covariance \Sigmak \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, Opacity \alphak \in [0,1]. Appearance: Diffuse SH coefficients F{SH}. Material attributes: Roughness \rho \in [0,1], Metallic m \in [0,1], Albedo a \in [0,1]^3. Anisotropic Frame: Orthonormal basis [x, y, z] where z is the normal, x, y are tangent/bitangent vectors. ASG Bandwidths: \lambda, \mu > 0 derived from roughness. 1. Spatial Gaussian Distribution The spatial probability density function for primitive k is: Gk(x) = \alphak e^{-\frac{1}{2}(x-pk)^T \Sigmak^{-1} (x-pk)} where \alphak is opacity, pk is center, and \Sigmak is covariance. 2. Ray-Gaussian Intersection For a ray r(t) = o + tv, the intersection evaluation E(Gj, o, r) is the maximum 1D Gaussian value along the ray: E(Gj, o, r) = G{j1D}(t^) where t^ is the parameter at which the 1D Gaussian reaches its maximum. The final color C(o,r) is accumulated via alpha compositing: C(o,r) = \sum{j=1}^{J} cj \alphaj E(Gj, o, r) \prod{q=1}^{j-1} (1 - \alphaq E(Gq, o, r)) where J is the number of contributing primitives and cj is the shaded color. 3. PBR Color Model The color cj of a primitive is the sum of diffuse and specular components: cj = c{diffuse,j} + c{specular,j} The BRDF f(\omegai, \omegao) is defined as: f(\omegai, \omegao) = \frac{(1-m)a}{\pi} + \frac{D F G}{4(\omegai \cdot n)(\omegao \cdot n)} where \omegao = -v is the view direction, n is the normal, \omegai is the light direction, m is metallic, a is albedo, D is the microfacet distribution, F is the Fresnel term, and G is the geometry term. 4. Anisotropic Spherical Gaussian (ASG) Definition The ASG lobe is defined as: \Phi(v; [x,y,z], [\lambda,\mu], A) = A \cdot S(v;z) \cdot e^{-\lambda(v \cdot x)^2 - \mu(v \cdot y)^2} where [x,y,z] is an orthonormal frame, \lambda, \mu are bandwidths, A is amplitude, and S(v;z) = \max(v \cdot z, 0) is attenuation. 5. Distribution Term Approximation (D{ASG}) The GGX distribution D(h) = \frac{\rho^2}{\pi (n \cdot h)^2 (\rho^2 - 1) + 1} is approximated using a second-order Taylor expansion for smooth surfaces where h \cdot z \approx 1 - \frac{1}{2}[(h \cdot x)^2 + (h \cdot y)^2]. This yields: D{ASG}(h) \approx \frac{\lambda \mu \pi}{\lambda (h \cdot x)^2 + \mu (h \cdot y)^2 + 2} \approx \Phi(h; [x,y,z], [\lambda,\mu]) The bandwidths are calculated from roughness \rho as: \lambda = \mu = \frac{1 - \rho^2}{\rho^2} [ S1 ] 6. Geometry Term Approximation (G{ASG}) The geometry term G(\omegai, \omegao) = G1(\omegai) G1(\omegao) is reparameterized to share anisotropy with the distribution: G1(\omega) = \frac{2(n \cdot \omega)}{(n \cdot \omega) + \lambda (h \cdot x)^2 + \mu (h \cdot y)^2 + (n \cdot \omega)^2} [ S1 ] 7. Specular Color Calculation (Split-Sum Approximation) The specular integral is decomposed into a Lighting Integral and a BRDF Integral: c{specular,j} \approx \underbrace{\int{\Omega} L(\omegai) D{ASG}(\rho, t) d\omegai}{\text{Lighting Integral}} \cdot \underbrace{\int{\Omega} \frac{D{ASG} F G{ASG}}{4(\omegao \cdot n)} d\omegai}{\text{BRDF Integral}} Lighting Integral: Computed using SH coefficients c{\ell m} and basis Y{\ell m}(t) at the reflection direction t: \int{\Omega} L{SH}(\omegai) D{ASG}(\rho, t) d\omegai = \sum{\ell, m} A\ell(1/\rho) c{\ell m} Y{\ell m}(t) where A\ell(1/\rho) \approx \exp(-2\rho \sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)}). BRDF Integral: Computed using precomputed lookup tables F1, F2 parameterized by roughness: \text{BRDF Integral} = ((1-m) \cdot 0.04 + m \cdot a) \cdot F1 + F2 [ S1 ] 8. Diffuse Color Calculation The diffuse component uses a clamped-cosine kernel: c{diffuse,j} = aj (1 - mj) \int{\Omega} L{SH}(\omegai) \frac{\omegai \cdot n}{\pi} d\omegai [ S1 ] Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeasgbandwidths(roughness): """ Computes ASG bandwidths lambda and mu from roughness rho. Formula: lambda = mu = (1 - rho^2) / rho^2 """ rho = max(roughness, 1e-6) val = (1 - rho2) / rho2 return val, val def evaluategaussian1d(gaussian, rayorigin, raydir): """ Computes the 1D Gaussian value at the point of closest approach along the ray. Returns (maxvalue, tstar). """ # Inverse covariance invcov = np.linalg.inv(gaussian['covariance']) # Project center onto ray to find closest point tstar = np.dot(gaussian['center'] - rayorigin, raydir) pclosest = rayorigin + tstar raydir # Compute exponent diffclosest = pclosest - gaussian['center'] exponent = -0.5 np.dot(diffclosest, np.dot(invcov, diffclosest)) maxvalue = np.exp(exponent) return maxvalue, tstar def computedasg(h, x, y, z, lam, mu): """ Computes the ASG approximation of the GGX distribution DASG. Formula: (lambda mu pi) / (lambda (h.x)^2 + mu (h.y)^2 + 2) """ hx = np.dot(h, x) hy = np.dot(h, y) denom = lam hx2 + mu hy2 + 2 return (lam mu np.pi) / denom def computegasg(n, omega, h, x, y, lam, mu): """ Computes the ASG geometry term G1 for a single direction. Formula: 2 (n.omega) / ((n.omega) + lambda(h.x)^2 + mu(h.y)^2 + (n.omega)^2) """ nomega = np.dot(n, omega) hx = np.dot(h, x) hy = np.dot(h, y) denom = nomega + lam hx2 + mu hy2 + nomega2 return (2 nomega) / denom def shevaluate(shcoeffs, direction): """ Evaluates Spherical Harmonics at a given direction. Assumes 3rd order (9 coefficients) standard basis. """ # Standard SH basis functions for order 2 (9 coeffs) # Y0, Y1, Y2, Y3, Y4, Y5, Y6, Y7, Y8 # Note: Exact basis definition depends on convention. # Using common OpenGL-like convention for demonstration. x, y, z = direction norm = np.sqrt(x2 + y2 + z2) if norm == 0: return np.zeros(9) x, y, z = x/norm, y/norm, z/norm # Basis functions b0 = 0.282095 b1 = 0.488603 y b2 = 0.488603 z b3 = 0.488603 x b4 = 1.092548 x y b5 = 1.092548 y z b6 = 0.315392 (3 z2 - 1) b7 = 1.092548 x z b8 = 0.546274 (x2 - y2) basis = np.array([b0, b1, b2, b3, b4, b5, b6, b7, b8]) return np.sum(shcoeffs basis) def computespecularcolor(lightshcoeffs, roughness, metallic, albedo, normal, viewdir, reflectiondir): """ Computes specular color using split-sum approximation. """ lam, mu = computeasgbandwidths(roughness) # Lighting Integral: SH convolution with ASG lobe # Attenuation factor Al(1/rho) approx exp(-2 rho sqrt(l(l+1))) # For simplicity, assuming lightshcoeffs are already processed or # applying attenuation to basis evaluation. # Here we evaluate SH at reflection direction and apply attenuation. # Note: The source describes summing Al clm Ylm(t). # We approximate this by scaling the SH evaluation or pre-computed tables. # For implementation, we use the lookup table result for BRDF and SH eval for Light. # Lighting Integral Result (simplified as SH eval at reflection dir with attenuation) # In practice, this requires pre-computed SH coefficients for the ASG lobe. # We assume lightshcoeffs are the incident light SH. # The integral is approximated by evaluating SH at reflection direction t. # The attenuation Al is applied to the coefficients or basis. # For this pseudocode, we assume a helper that computes the convolved SH value. lightingintegral = shevaluate(lightshcoeffs, reflectiondir) # Note: Strictly, this should be the result of the integral in, # which involves attenuation. We assume lightshcoeffs are adjusted or # this is a placeholder for the specific SH-ASG convolution. # BRDF Integral # ((1-m)0.04 + ma) F1 + F2 # F1 and F2 are lookup tables. We approximate with simple constants for pseudocode. # In real implementation, these are 2D textures indexed by roughness and NdotV. F1 = 1.0 # Placeholder for lookup table value F2 = 0.0 # Placeholder for lookup table value basecolor = (1 - metallic) 0.04 + metallic albedo brdfintegral = basecolor F1 + F2 return lightingintegral brdfintegral def computediffusecolor(lightshcoeffs, albedo, metallic, normal): """ Computes diffuse color using cosine lobe kernel. """ # Integral of LSH (omega.n)/pi # This is equivalent to evaluating the SH irradiance at the normal. diffuseirradiance = shevaluate(lightshcoeffs, normal) np.pi return albedo (1 - metallic) diffuseirradiance def rendergaussian(gaussian, rayorigin, raydir, lightshcoeffs, roughness, metallic, albedo, normal, viewdir): """ Renders a single Gaussian primitive for a ray. """ # 1. Evaluate spatial Gaussian val, tstar = evaluategaussian1d(gaussian, rayorigin, raydir) if val < 1e-6: return 0.0, 0.0 # 2. Compute reflection direction omegao = -raydir # Reflect view direction around normal t = 2 np.dot(normal, omegao) normal - omegao # 3. Compute ASG parameters lam, mu = computeasgbandwidths(roughness) # 4. Compute Specular # Note: DASG and GASG are used in the split-sum derivation. # The split-sum approximation uses the reflection direction t for the lighting integral. specular = computespecularcolor(lightshcoeffs, roughness, metallic, albedo, normal, omegao, t) # 5. Compute Diffuse diffuse = computediffusecolor(lightshcoeffs, albedo, metallic, normal) # 6. Combine cj = diffuse + specular return cj val, val def optimizegaussianposition(gaussian, loss, lightshcoeffs, roughness, metallic, albedo, normal, viewdir, camerapos): """ Computes gradient for Gaussian position using the skip connection. """ # Direct gradient path for specular component # dL/dpw = dL/dcspecular dcspecular/dpw # Compute specular color raydir = (gaussian['center'] - camerapos) raydir = raydir / np.linalg.norm(raydir) specularcolor, = rendergaussian(gaussian, camerapos, raydir, lightshcoeffs, roughness, metallic, albedo, normal, raydir) # Gradient of loss w.r.t specular color dLdcspecular =... # Provided by upstream loss function # Gradient of specular color w.r.t position # This requires differentiating the rendergaussian function w.r.t gaussian['center'] # Specifically, the reflection direction t depends on normal, which may depend on position, # and the spatial evaluation val depends on position. # The skip connection bypasses the complex diffuse/gradient path. # Simplified: dcspecular/dpw involves d(t)/dpw and d(val)/dpw # t = 2(n.v)v - v. If n is fixed, t doesn't depend on p directly, # but v depends on p. # val depends on p via the Gaussian exponent. # For the purpose of the article, we state the existence of this direct path. # Implementation details of dcspecular/dpw are complex and depend on the specific # differentiable renderer used. pass Vanishing Gradients: In scenes with dense specular reflections, traditional gradient paths from reflectance color loss to Gaussian positions can lead to vanishing gradients. ARS-GS mitigates this with a skip connection linking spatial coordinates directly to ASG color attributes. Roughness Boundaries: When roughness \rho approaches 0, the bandwidths \lambda, \mu approach infinity, potentially causing numerical instability. A minimum roughness (e.g., 10^{-6}) should be enforced. Smooth Surface Approximation: The ASG approximation of GGX relies on a second-order Taylor expansion valid for smooth surfaces where the half-vector aligns with the normal. This may be less accurate for very rough surfaces. Time Complexity: The rendering complexity is linear with respect to the number of Gaussian primitives J per pixel, similar to standard 3DGS, but with higher constant factors due to the PBR calculations (SH evaluation, ASG bandwidth computation). The split-sum approximation allows efficient lighting integration. Memory Complexity: Each primitive stores additional appearance parameters (roughness, metallic, albedo, ASG frame) compared to standard 3DGS, increasing memory usage per primitive. Performance: Evaluated on Ref-NeRF, NeRF-Synthetic, Shiny Blender, and Mip-NeRF-360 datasets. It provides superior performance in accuracy and efficiency for highly specular scenes compared to methods using only SH. Strengths: Accurate modeling of view-dependent specular reflections; improved geometric fidelity in reflective regions; real-time performance via split-sum approximation. Limitations: Relies on the ASG approximation of GGX, which is an approximation rather than an exact equivalence; requires careful handling of roughness parameters to avoid numerical issues. Origin: ARS-GS was introduced in the paper "ARS-GS: Anisotropic Reflective Spherical 3D Gaussian Splatting" (2024). Development: It builds upon 3D Gaussian Splatting and incorporates Anisotropic Spherical Gaussians (ASG) into a PBR pipeline, aligning with GGX microfacet models. It addresses limitations in previous methods like Spec-Gaussian by providing physical constraints for mesh reconstruction. Usage: Used for reconstructing scenes with complex specular reflections and directional lighting, such as real-world environments and synthetic metallic surfaces. name: Spec-Gaussian
body: Spec-Gaussian is a method for modeling complex view-dependent appearance, specifically specular and anisotropic reflections, within 3D Gaussian Splatting by replacing standard spherical harmonics with Anisotropic Spherical Gaussians (ASG). It solves the limitation of standard 3DGS, which struggles to represent high-frequency directional lighting and sharp specular highlights, by approximating the scene's appearance distribution using ASG basis functions. Unlike standard 3DGS which uses isotropic SH for color, Spec-Gaussian decouples the geometric spread from the directional shading, allowing for physically plausible PBR-like shading. Inputs: 3D Gaussian primitives (position, covariance, opacity), material properties (roughness, metallic, albedo), normal vectors, and environment lighting represented as SH coefficients. Outputs: Pixel color and opacity. Data Structures: Each Gaussian stores: center: 3D position. covariance: 3x3 matrix (or 6-vector lower triangle) defining spatial spread. opacity: scalar. roughness: scalar. metallic: scalar. albedo: 3D vector. normal: 3D vector (often derived from covariance or optimized). lightshcoeffs: SH coefficients for the environment map. Steps: 1. Ray-Gaussian Intersection: Compute the point of closest approach p{closest} between the view ray and the Gaussian center. Calculate the maximum Gaussian value V{max} = \exp(-0.5 \Delta^T \Sigma^{-1} \Delta) where \Delta = p{closest} - center. 2. View Direction: Compute the outgoing view direction \omegao = -ray\dir. 3. Reflection Direction: Compute the perfect reflection direction r = 2(n \cdot \omegao)n - \omegao, where n is the surface normal. 4. ASG Bandwidths: Compute ASG bandwidth parameters \lambda and \mu from roughness \rho: \lambda = \mu = \frac{1 - \rho^2}{\rho^2} Clamp \rho to a minimum of 10^{-6} to avoid division by zero. 5. Specular Distribution: Evaluate the ASG approximation of the GGX distribution D(r) using the frame vectors (x, y, z) of the Gaussian and the reflection direction r: D(r) = \frac{\lambda \mu \pi}{\lambda (r \cdot x)^2 + \mu (r \cdot y)^2 + 2} 6. Specular Color: Compute the specular contribution using a split-sum approximation. Evaluate the lighting integral using SH evaluation at the reflection direction r: L{spec} = SH(r) Compute the BRDF integral using the Fresnel-Schlick approximation and the ASG distribution. The final specular color is C{spec} = L{spec} \cdot F \cdot D \cdot G. Note: The provided pseudocode simplifies this to a base color multiplication. 7. Diffuse Color: Compute the diffuse contribution using the cosine lobe kernel. Evaluate the irradiance using SH at the normal n: L{diff} = SH(n) \cdot \pi C{diff} = albedo \cdot (1 - metallic) \cdot L{diff} 8. Composite: The final color for the Gaussian is C = (C{diff} + C{spec}) \cdot V{max}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. rayorigin, raydir) pclosest = rayorigin + tstar raydir diffclosest = pclosest - gaussian['center'] exponent = -0.5 np.dot(diffclosest, np.dot(invcov, diffclosest)) maxvalue = np.exp(exponent) return maxvalue, tstar def computeasgbandwidths(roughness): """Computes lambda and mu from roughness rho.""" rho = max(roughness, 1e-6) val = (1 - rho2) / rho2 return val, val def computedasg(h, x, y, z, lam, mu): """Computes the ASG approximation of the GGX distribution.""" hx = np.dot(h, x) hy = np.dot(h, y) denom = lam hx2 + mu hy2 + 2 return (lam mu np.pi) / denom def computegasg(n, omega, h, x, y, lam, mu): """Computes the ASG geometry term for a single direction.""" nomega = np.dot(n, omega) hx = np.dot(h, x) hy = np.dot(h, y) denom = nomega + lam hx2 + mu hy2 + nomega2 return (2 nomega) / denom def shevaluate(shcoeffs, direction): """Standard SH basis evaluation at direction.""" return np.sum(shcoeffs np.array([1, direction[1], direction[2], direction[0], direction[1]direction[2], direction[0]direction[2], direction[0]direction[1], direction[2]2 - direction[1]2, direction[0]2 - 3direction[1]2 + 3direction[2]2])) def computespecularcolor(lightshcoeffs, roughness, metallic, albedo, normal, viewdir, reflectiondir): """Computes specular color using split-sum approximation.""" lam, mu = computeasgbandwidths(roughness) lightingintegral = shevaluate(lightshcoeffs, reflectiondir) f1 = 1.0 f2 = 0.0 basecolor = (1 - metallic) 0.04 + metallic albedo brdfintegral = basecolor f1 + f2 return lightingintegral brdfintegral def computediffusecolor(lightshcoeffs, albedo, metallic, normal): """Computes diffuse color using cosine lobe kernel.""" diffuseirradiance = shevaluate(lightshcoeffs, normal) np.pi return albedo (1 - metallic) diffuseirradiance def rendergaussian(gaussian, rayorigin, raydir, lightshcoeffs, roughness, metallic, albedo, normal, viewdir): """Renders a single Gaussian primitive for a ray.""" val, tstar = evaluategaussian1d(gaussian, rayorigin, raydir) if val < 1e-6: return 0.0, 0.0 omegao = -raydir t = 2 np.dot(normal, omegao) normal - omegao dasg = computedasg(t, gaussian['framex'], gaussian['framey'], gaussian['framez'], computeasgbandwidths(roughness)) specular = computespecularcolor(lightshcoeffs, roughness, metallic, albedo, normal, omegao, t) diffuse = computediffusecolor(lightshcoeffs, albedo, metallic, normal) cj = diffuse + specular return cj val, val Edge Cases: Roughness Zero: If roughness is 0, \lambda, \mu become infinite. Clamp roughness to 10^{-6}. Degenerate Covariance: If covariance is singular, inverse fails. Add small epsilon to diagonal. A two-pass technique that computes specular reflections in screen space to solve high-frequency radiance fitting issues and normal estimation bottlenecks inherent in forward shading methods like Spec-Gaussian. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of splatted Gaussians. ASG evaluation is slightly more expensive than standard SH but cheaper than full ray tracing. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing Gaussian parameters including material properties and ASG frame vectors. Strengths: Accurately represents sharp specular highlights and anisotropic reflections which standard 3DGS blurs. Limitations: Sensitive to normal estimation errors; requires careful initialization of material properties. Spec-Gaussian was introduced to address the inability of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting to model complex shading like specular and anisotropic components. It utilizes Anisotropic Spherical Gaussians to approximate 3D scene appearance, building on the differentiable rendering framework of 3DGS. name: Deferred Reflection in 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Deferred Reflection, Deferred 3D Gaussian Splatting for Reflection, Deferred Reflection, Deferred Shading with 3DGS, Ours, deferred, Per-pixel Reflection in 3DGS
body: Deferred Reflection is a two-pass rendering technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that computes specular reflections per-pixel in screen space rather than per-Gaussian. It solves the problem of high-frequency radiance fields being difficult to fit stably and accurately, and addresses the bottleneck of normal estimation caused by discontinuous gradients in forward shading. Unlike forward shading methods that compute reflection colors on individual Gaussians, this method separates Gaussian splatting from reflection shading, allowing pixel-precise normal maps to guide gradient propagation and environment map optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters \Thetai (position, covariance, opacity), view-dependent spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for base color, an initial environment map, and a spherical domain \Omega covering the foreground object. Outputs: Final rendered image color C{final}, optimized environment map, and optimized Gaussian parameters including normals and reflection strength. Data Structures: The method uses viewport-aligned textures (screenspace maps) generated in Pass 1. These buffers store: 1. Base Color (C{base}): The diffuse/base color of the Gaussian soup. 2. Normal (N): The surface normal vector. 3. Reflection Strength (R): A scalar parameter weighting the contribution of the reflection. Parameters: Reflection Strength (Ri): A scalar associated with each Gaussian i, learned during training. It weights the base and reflection colors in the final composition. Normal Vector: Regarded as the shortest axis of each Gaussian ellipsoid. Environment Map: A high-frequency lookup table representing lighting, learned during training. Spherical Domain \Omega: A constraint restricting the deferred reflection stage to Gaussians inside this domain to reduce interference from background objects during training. Algorithm Steps: 1. Pass 1: Gaussian Splatting Pass (G-Buffer Generation) For each Gaussian i, compute the Gaussian weight G(\Thetai, \mathbf{v}) and base color ci(\mathbf{v}) from the view-dependent SH coefficients, following the standard 3DGS splatting formulation: C(\mathbf{v}) = \sumi ci(\mathbf{v}) G(\Thetai, \mathbf{v}) where ci(\mathbf{v}) is the base color and G(\Thetai, \mathbf{v}) is the Gaussian weight. Instead of computing the final color, blend the Gaussian properties into the screenspace maps: Accumulate base color C{base} weighted by opacity and Gaussian weight. Accumulate normal N weighted by opacity and Gaussian weight. Accumulate reflection strength R weighted by opacity and Gaussian weight. Normalize the accumulated normal N to unit length. 2. Pass 2: Pixel Shading Pass (Deferred Reflection) For each pixel (u, v) in the image: Retrieve the blended base color C{base}(u,v), normal N(u,v), and reflection strength R(u,v) from the G-buffers. Compute the reflection direction \mathbf{r} using the view direction \mathbf{v} and the normal N(u,v): \mathbf{r} = 2(\mathbf{v} \cdot N(u,v))N(u,v) - \mathbf{v} Query the environment map E(\mathbf{r}) using the reflection direction \mathbf{r} to acquire the specular reflection color C{refl}. Compute the final color C{final} as the sum of the base and reflection colors weighted by the reflection strength: C{final}(u,v) = C{base}(u,v) + R(u,v) \cdot C{refl} 3. Training: Normal Propagation Observation: Gaussians with large reflective strength values Ri have near-correct normal vectors. Expansion: These reflective Gaussians are expanded to propagate their normal vectors to nearby Gaussians. Overlap Mechanism: When a Gaussian with a near-correct normal overlaps a different Gaussian, shared pixels receive near-correct normals. These pixels get meaningful normal gradients from the image color loss, helping to optimize the overlapping Gaussian's normal. Gradient Flow: The deferred shading model blends Gaussian properties into viewport-aligned textures. The blended input values evaluate reflection and compose base/reflection colors into the final color. Image color loss feeds gradient back to input values of the same pixel, creating a gradient channel from color to blended normal to individual Gaussian normal. This facilitates information flow between normals of overlapping Gaussians. 4. Domain Restriction Restrict the deferred reflection stage to Gaussians inside the spherical domain \Omega covering the foreground object. This reduces interference from background objects during training. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def zeros(shape): return np.zeros(shape, dtype=np.float32) def normalize(v): norm = np.linalg.norm(v) return v / norm if norm > 1e-8 else v def projectgaussian(gaussian, camera): # Standard 3DGS projection: returns screen coords, weight, alpha # Simplified for pseudocode completeness pos = gaussian.position viewdir = camera.direction dist = np.dot(pos - camera.origin, viewdir) weight = math.exp(-0.5 dist) # Simplified Gaussian falloff alpha = gaussian.opacity weight screencoords = (pos.xy camera.focallength / dist).astype(int) return screencoords, weight, alpha def getshcolor(shcoeffs, viewdir): # Evaluate SH coefficients for base color return np.array([0.5, 0.5, 0.5]) # Placeholder color evaluation def getshortestaxis(covariance): # Eigenvector corresponding to smallest eigenvalue eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(covariance) return eigenvectors[:, np.argmin(eigenvalues)] def isinsidedomain(position, domaincenter, domainradius): return np.linalg.norm(position - domaincenter) <= domainradius def sampleenvmap(envmap, direction): # Query environment map with reflection direction return np.array([0.8, 0.8, 0.8]) # Placeholder env map query def computeloss(pred, gt): # L1 + SSIM loss standard in 3DGS return np.mean(np.abs(pred - gt)) def pass1gaussiansplatting(gaussians, camera, imagewidth, imageheight, domaincenter, domainradius): basecolorbuffer = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) normalbuffer = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) reflectionstrengthbuffer = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 1)) alphabuffer = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 1)) for gaussian in gaussians: screencoords, weight, alpha = projectgaussian(gaussian, camera) cbase = getshcolor(gaussian.shcoeffs, camera.viewdirection) ni = getshortestaxis(gaussian.covariance) ri = gaussian.reflectionstrength if not isinsidedomain(gaussian.position, domaincenter, domainradius): continue basecolorbuffer[screencoords] += cbase weight alpha normalbuffer[screencoords] += ni weight alpha reflectionstrengthbuffer[screencoords] += ri weight alpha alphabuffer[screencoords] += weight alpha for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): if alphabuffer[y, x] > 0: normalbuffer[y, x] = normalize(normalbuffer[y, x]) return basecolorbuffer, normalbuffer, reflectionstrengthbuffer, alphabuffer def pass2pixelshading(basecolorbuffer, normalbuffer, reflectionstrengthbuffer, envmap, camera): imageheight, imagewidth, = basecolorbuffer.shape finalimage = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): cbase = basecolorbuffer[y, x] n = normalbuffer[y, x] rval = reflectionstrengthbuffer[y, x] v = camera.getviewdirectionatpixel(x, y) rdir = 2 np.dot(v, n) n - v crefl = sampleenvmap(envmap, rdir) finalimage[y, x] = cbase + rval crefl return finalimage def trainstep(gaussians, camera, envmap, gtimage, domaincenter, domainradius): basecolor, normal, reflstrength, alpha = pass1gaussiansplatting(gaussians, camera, 1024, 1024, domaincenter, domainradius) predimage = pass2pixelshading(basecolor, normal, reflstrength, envmap, camera) loss = computeloss(predimage, gtimage) loss.backward() # Gradients flow from color -> blended normal -> individual Gaussian normal # Gradients flow to envmap, reflectionstrength, and gaussian parameters Performance: Runs at a frame rate almost identical to vanilla Gaussian Splatting. On the Shiny Blender Dataset, training time is 16 minutes, and rendering frame rate is 251 FPS. On real-world scenes, training time is 47 minutes, and rendering frame rate is 80 FPS. Quality: Demonstrates consistent improvement in PSNR for both synthetic and real-world scenes compared to forward shading and other baselines. On the Shiny Blender Dataset, it achieves PSNR 33.66, SSIM 0.979, and LPIPS 0.098, compared to forward shading which has lower metrics. Efficiency: Uses significantly fewer Gaussians than forward shading or other baselines. For example, on the 'ball' scene, it uses 27.2k Gaussians vs 76.4k (forward) vs 76.5k (GShader) vs 199k (3DGS). Strengths: Produces sharp reflections with pixel-level details. Eliminates interpolation artifacts caused by discontinuous color changes at Gaussian boundaries. Stabilizes reflection strength and environment map training by smoothing gradients through extra per-pixel samples. Limitations: Environment map queries demand high precision on normal vectors but provide scarcely useful gradients to refine them, making normal estimation difficult. The semi-transparent Gaussian soup has a loosely-defined surface, complicating accurate normal estimation. When to use: For novel view synthesis and real-time rendering of specular reflection effects where high-quality reflections and efficient Gaussian count are desired. When not to use: For non-specular scenes, the method provides negligible benefit over vanilla 3DGS. Origin: Introduced by Keyang Ye, Qiming Hou, and Kun Zhou at Zhejiang University. Publication: Published in SIGGRAPH Conference Papers '24, July 27-August 1, 2024. History: Deferred shading [Deering et al. 1988] is a classical real-time rendering technique that computes high-frequency shading effects like specularity per-pixel in screen space after baking scene properties like normals and colors into buffers. This method combines deferred shading with 3D Gaussian Splatting to effectively render specular reflection, producing accurate estimation of normal and environment maps. It addresses the limitations of per-Gaussian shading (e.g., GaussianShader [Jiang et al. 2023]) which computes reflection on individual Gaussians, leading to independent normal gradients that cannot influence each other and interpolation artifacts. 3D Gaussian Splatting with Deferred Reflection, https://doi.org/10.1145/3641519.3657456, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Optimization and Training Loop
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting Training, 3DGS Optimization
body: This family encompasses the iterative optimization procedures used to adjust the parameters of 3D Gaussian primitives (positions, covariances, opacities, and spherical harmonic coefficients) to minimize the photometric error between rendered images and ground-truth inputs. It differs from sibling methods like TurboGS or Distributed 3DGS Training Loop by relying on standard stochastic gradient descent with fixed iteration budgets and explicit densification/pruning heuristics, rather than adaptive workload division or accelerated rendering pipelines. The core mechanism common to all training loops in this family is the minimization of a composite loss function \mathcal{L} between the rendered image \hat{I} and the ground-truth image I{gt}. The standard photometric baseline is a weighted sum of L1 loss and differentiable Structural Similarity (D-SSIM): \mathcal{L}{img} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}{L1} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} where \mathcal{L}{L1} is the average absolute difference between corresponding pixel colors, and \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} measures local structure, contrast, and texture. The weight \lambda is typically 0.2. The optimization uses the Adam optimizer with \beta1 = 0.9 and \beta2 = 0.99. Training typically runs for a fixed number of iterations, commonly around 30,000 for standard scenes, though specific schedules vary (e.g., Gaussian Primitive Training Schedule uses ~6,000). The process does not stop at a specific loss threshold because the loss curve continues to creep down with diminishing returns; a fixed iteration budget is used instead. Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}{i=1}^N include position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \Sigmai (parameterized by rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 and scale vector \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3), opacity \alphai \in [0, 1], and Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients \mathbf{c}{i, l} for view-dependent color. The standard iterative process minimizing photometric error via Adam optimizer, random view sampling, and periodic densification/pruning heuristics. An error-guided framework that accelerates optimization by dynamically focusing computation on perceptually informative pixels using persistent error and age maps, replacing dense rasterization with tile-wise sparse sampling. A strategy restricting loss evaluation to a sparse subset of pixels per tile, guided by error and age maps, to reallocate computation from well-reconstructed regions. A strategy that dynamically adjusts rendering resolution based on the frequency content (Fourier energy) of training data, allocating high-resolution iterations only after low-frequency structure is captured. Aggregates gradients from multiple views in each step to enforce multi-view coherence, summing gradients rather than averaging them to stabilize descent. Extends the standard loop with subpixel-aware rendering to mitigate aliasing, managing subpixel offsets and adaptive densification schedules. Implements distributed training across multiple GPUs, batching camera selection and dividing rendering workloads based on historical performance. A memory-efficient strategy that initializes all Gaussians with SH order 0 and selectively promotes only those with significant rendering errors to higher orders. Optimizes Gaussians using Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) from a pretrained 2D diffusion model, enabling reconstruction from unstructured images or text prompts without ground-truth 3D geometry. Estimates uncertainty by grouping Gaussian parameter variances into six categories and feeding them into a meta-regression model, rather than aggregating variances directly. Accelerates training by leveraging dense initial point clouds and interrupting the loop with pseudo-view depth optimization, reducing iterations from ~30,000 to ~6,000. Defines the composite loss function \mathcal{L}, establishing the photometric baseline and framework for extending with geometric or semantic constraints. A streaming pipeline for incremental reconstruction from unordered images, maintaining global consistency via loop closure and covisibility graphs. Combines active view selection with residual learning to improve quality under sparse view conditions, using self-augmented pre-filtering to stabilize selection. Amplifies gradient flow to weakly contributing, high-uncertainty Gaussians by combining full-scene renders with uncertainty-intensified renders. Manages incremental construction in SLAM by dividing the scene into submaps, resetting optimization state periodically to prevent drift. Details the optimization schedule, including resolution warm-up (starting at 1/4 resolution) and staged introduction of Spherical Harmonics bands. Adjusts the backward pass to address vanishing gradients for distant primitives or gradient confusion, intercepting gradients to provide non-zero signals. Estimates camera poses by minimizing photometric error, treating poses as learnable parameters rather than fixed inputs. Step: Applies an optimization process during Gaussian extraction to optimize Gaussians to exact locations. Parameter: Truncation function \lambda is introduced when modeling GauPF (Gaussian Probability Function). Projection function \tau is implemented either as \tau(x) = e^{-x} (Exponent) or as a linear projection. Number: 50K Gaussians: PSNR 28.61, SSIM 0.9787, LPIPS 0.0251. 100K Gaussians: PSNR 30.35, SSIM 0.9838, LPIPS 0.0151. 350K Gaussians: PSNR 34.01, SSIM 0.9879, LPIPS 0.0149. Definition: The optimization process using a combined MSE and SSIM loss, along with density control strategies adapted from 3DGS, while preserving the multi-scale structure. Step: Apply splitting and cloning strategies from 3DGS for density control. Newly split/cloned Gaussians remain in their original level and cluster. Routinely reassess and reassign the levels of Gaussians based on their scales to preserve the multi-scale characteristics and balanced distribution across levels. Formula: L = \lambda \cdot MSE(C, \hat{C}) + (1 - \lambda) \cdot SSIM(C, \hat{C}) where \lambda is a hyperparameter balancing the terms, C is ground-truth color, and \hat{C} is rendered color. Definition: A training strategy that gradually increases rendering resolution during training to improve convergence speed and reduce computational overhead, starting from low resolution and increasing toward the target. Formula: Rt = R{max} \cdot (\frac{t}{T})^\gamma, where Rt is the resolution at training step t, R{max} is the final resolution, T is the total training steps, and \gamma controls the growth rate. Parameter: Initial resolution: 540x960. Final resolution: 1080x1920. Definition: A method that uses differences in frequency spectra of rendered and reference images to progressively regularize the model from coarse, low-frequency structures to fine, high-frequency details. Definition: A pipeline to extract meshes from 3D Gaussian Splatting and build hybrid representations that enable easy composition and animation in Gaussian Splatting scenes by manipulating the mesh. Step: 1. Short vanilla 3DGS optimization: optimizing a vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting model for 7k iterations, in order to let Gaussians position themselves in the scene. 2. SuGaR optimization: optimizing Gaussians alignment with the surface of the scene. 3. Mesh extraction: extracting a mesh from the optimized Gaussians. 4. SuGaR refinement: refining the Gaussians and the mesh together to build a hybrid Mesh+Gaussians representation. 5. Textured mesh extraction (Optional): extracting a traditional textured mesh from the refined SuGaR model as a tool for visualization, composition and animation in Blender using our Blender add-on. Definition: Initializing 3D Gaussian primitives directly from the retrieved CAD mesh surface rather than SfM point clouds, providing strong inductive bias. Step: Define target number of primitives N{splats}. Draw area-weighted uniform random sample of points from mesh surface to obtain initial canonical positions \mu{can}^{(i)}. Recover surface normals ni by casting ray from sample toward mesh interior and reading triangle normal of intersected face. Initialize rotation quaternion qi to shortest-arc rotation aligning local z-axis with ni, creating oriented disk tangent to mesh. Pitfall: Standard 3DGS densification/pruning (cloning/splitting) is not employed to maintain strict adherence to the CAD surface geometry. Definition: A compact framework for Language 3DGS that combines semantics-aware Gaussian sparsification and attribute vector quantization in a unified constrained objective, solved via an alternating primal-dual procedure. Step: The optimization alternates among four updates: 1) Primal Update (differentiable scene optimization), 2) Sparsification Update (cardinality projection on opacities), 3) Vector Quantization Update (quantization of attributes), and 4) Dual Update (Lagrange multiplier updates). Formula: Rendering loss: L{RGB} = (1 - \lambda)L1 + \lambda L{D-SSIM}, where \lambda \in [0, 1] balances the terms. Definition: A refinement step that optimizes the spherical harmonic coefficients and Gaussian structures using visual-derived photometric gradients to enhance photorealism and density. Step: Optimize the spherical harmonic coefficients of the Gaussians using photometric gradients derived from captured images. Refine the LiDAR Gaussian structures using images captured from various perspectives. Definition: A modification to the training loss function that adds an L1 sparsity term on opacity to encourage lower opacity values, facilitating effective culling. Step: Add an L1 sparsity term on opacity to the loss function during optimization. The standard 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization loop was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. It relies on a differentiable rasterizer to render images from 3D Gaussians and minimizes a composite loss of L1 and D-SSIM using the Adam optimizer. Subsequent methods have extended this foundation to address specific challenges such as training speed TurboGS, memory efficiency Sparse SH Order Increment, sparse view reconstruction Active View Selection, and integration with other modalities like diffusion models SDS Loss or CAD models Geometric Initialization.
