name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Training Loop
head: Render-Compare-Correct Loop
body: The 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training loop is an iterative optimization process that minimizes the photometric error between rendered images and ground-truth input photos by adjusting the parameters of a set of 3D Gaussians. It differs from sibling methods like TurboGS or Distributed 3DGS Training Loop by relying on the standard stochastic gradient descent with a fixed iteration budget and explicit densification/pruning heuristics, rather than adaptive workload division or accelerated rendering pipelines. The loop operates on a per-image basis, randomly sampling training views to prevent overfitting to camera order. Inputs: Set of training images \{Ik\} with known camera poses \{Ck\} recovered by Structure-from-Motion (SfM). Initial set of Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}{i=1}^N. For standard scenes, this is often a sparse point cloud; for avatars, it may be initialized using SMPL vertex positions and skinning weights. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} (positions, covariances, opacities, SH coefficients) and any auxiliary parameters (e.g., MLP weights for avatar deformation). Data Structures: Gaussian gi contains: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance \Sigmai, parameterized by rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 and scale vector \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients \mathbf{c}{i, l} for view-dependent color. Numbered Steps: 1. Sample View: Randomly select one training image I{gt} and its corresponding camera pose C from the dataset. 2. Transform: Transform canonical Gaussians to the observation space defined by C. If using avatar models, apply deformation (e.g., via SMPL skinning) to positions and orientations. 3. Render: Use the differentiable Gaussian rasterizer to render the image \hat{I} from the current Gaussian set \mathcal{G} and pose C. 4. Compare: Compute the per-image loss \mathcal{L}{img} by comparing \hat{I} and I{gt} pixel-by-pixel. 5. Correct: Compute gradients \nabla{\mathcal{G}} \mathcal{L}{img} and update Gaussian parameters using the Adam optimizer. 6. Densify/Prune: Periodically (e.g., every N iterations), apply densification heuristics (splitting/cloning Gaussians based on gradient magnitude or screen-space size) and pruning (removing low-opacity Gaussians) to adapt the representation density. 7. Repeat: Continue until the fixed iteration budget is reached. Loss Function: The total loss is a weighted sum of L1 loss and differentiable Structural Similarity (D-SSIM): \mathcal{L}{img} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}{L1} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} where \lambda \approx 0.2. \mathcal{L}{L1} is the average absolute difference between pixel colors. \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} measures local structure, contrast, and texture. For avatar reconstruction, additional regularization losses (e.g., perceptual LPIPS) may be added. Parameters: Optimizer: Adam with \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.99. Iteration Budget: Typically 30,000 iterations for standard scenes. Specific schedules may vary (e.g., ~6,000 for primitive training). Stopping Criterion: Fixed iteration count, not a loss threshold, as the loss curve creeps down with diminishing returns. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def train3dgs(trainingimages, initialgaussians, numiterations=30000): # Initialize optimizer with Adam (beta1=0.9, beta2=0.99) optimizer = Adam(initialgaussians.parameters(), lr=1e-4) for iteration in range(numiterations): # 1. Sample a random training view idx = randomchoice(len(trainingimages)) gtimage, camerapose = trainingimages[idx] # 2. Transform Gaussians to observation space # For avatars: apply deformation based on body pose if available transformedgaussians = transformgaussians(initialgaussians, camerapose) # 3. Render the image renderedimage = gaussianrasterize(transformedgaussians, camerapose) # 4. Compute Loss # L1 Loss l1loss = meanabsoluteerror(renderedimage, gtimage) # D-SSIM Loss dssimloss = computedssim(renderedimage, gtimage) # Combined Loss (lambda = 0.2) loss = 0.8 l1loss + 0.2 dssimloss # Optional: Add regularization losses (e.g., LPIPS for avatars) # loss += lambdalpips computelpips(renderedimage, gtimage) # 5. Backpropagate and Update optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # 6. Densify and Prune (every N iterations) if iteration % densifyinterval == 0: initialgaussians = densifyandprune(initialgaussians, gtimage, camerapose) return initialgaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Gradient computation relies on the differentiability of the rasterizer; numerical instability can occur with extremely small or large covariances. Boundaries: Background pixels should be handled explicitly (e.g., setting background to black in ground truth) to avoid artifacts. Degenerate Input: If SfM poses are inaccurate, rendering will fail to align with ground truth, leading to poor convergence. Uses a shorter iteration budget (~6,000) for specific primitive training phases. Accelerates the training loop via optimized rendering but retains the core gradient-based update mechanism. Divides the workload across multiple GPUs for large-scale scenes. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussians N and the number of pixels P per iteration (O(N \cdot P)). Total time scales with the iteration budget (typically 30,000). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store Gaussian parameters and gradients. Performance: Training time varies by hardware but is generally faster than neural radiance field (NeRF) training due to the explicit representation and fast rasterization. Strengths: Simultaneous correction of millions of parameters via gradient descent, avoiding the inefficiency of random search. Limitations: Fixed iteration budget may lead to overfitting or underfitting if not tuned for the scene; densification heuristics can introduce artifacts if not carefully controlled. The 3D Gaussian Splatting training loop was introduced in the original 3DGS paper and popularized by subsequent implementations and tutorials. It builds on the differentiable rendering framework established by 3DGS, enabling end-to-end optimization of explicit 3D primitives. The method has been adapted for various domains, including animatable avatars (Human Gaussian Splatting) and large-scale scenes. name: TurboGS
head: Error-guided training framework for 3DGS
body:
TurboGS is an error-guided training framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that accelerates optimization by dynamically focusing computation on perceptually informative pixels, addressing redundant computation in well-reconstructed regions and loss of fine details. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by replacing dense rasterization with tile-wise sparse pixel sampling guided by persistent error and age maps, while introducing a tile-level structure-aware loss and a moment-damped Levenberg-Marquardt solver to stabilize convergence under sparse supervision. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ground-truth images \{Iv\}, camera poses \{Cv\}, initial Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}0 derived from Structure-from-Motion (SfM), total training iterations T, view budget range [K{min}, K{max}], and hyperparameters \Theta. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}. Data Structures: Error Map (Ev): Stored in contiguous GPU memory with half precision (float16). Initialized by densely evaluating per-pixel reconstruction error for initial Gaussians \mathcal{G}0. Age Map (Av): Stored in contiguous GPU memory with uint16 precision. Tracks the number of iterations since a pixel was last sampled. View Stack: A shuffled list of candidate view indices used for geometry-aware sampling. Parameters: Tile size S: Typically 16 	imes 16 pixels. Pixel sampling rate rt: Dynamic rate queried from a schedule. Number of pixels per tile N{pix}: N{pix} = \max(1, \lfloor rt \cdot S^2 floor). Hard pixel fraction r{hard} and stable pixel fraction r{stable}: N{hard} = \lceil r{hard} \cdot N{pix} ceil, N{stable} = \lfloor r{stable} \cdot N{pix} floor. EMA decay  eta: For error map updates. Geometry-aware weights \lambdad, \lambda	heta: For view selection. Effective learning rate scaling \lambda{base}: Used in difficulty scoring. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize error maps E using \mathcal{G}0, cameras C, and images I. Initialize age maps A to zero. 2. Progress Coefficient: Compute hot = \min(1, t/	au{until}). 3. Sampling Schedule: Query the sampling schedule to obtain the view budget Kt and pixel sampling rate rt based on K{max}, K{min}, E{init}, \Theta, and t. 4. View Selection (GVS): Select an anchor view v^ by maximizing the average error: v^ = \arg \maxv  ar{E}v, where  ar{E}v =  rac{1}{|\Omega|} \sum{p \in \Omega} Ev(p). Sample K-1 remaining views from a candidate stack without replacement using the geometry-aware distribution: \pi(u | v^) \propto \exp(-\lambdad \|cu - c{v^}\|^2 - \lambda	heta (1 - \langle du, d{v^} angle)) where cu, du are the camera center and viewing direction of view u. Maintain a shuffled view stack; refill and reshuffle when fewer than K views remain. 5. Tile-Wise Sparse Pixel Sampling (EPS): Partition the image into tiles of size S 	imes S. A method that prioritizes challenging regions and skips well-reconstructed ones to avoid redundant gradient computation, driven by multi-view reconstruction errors. See Error-Guided Sparse Pixel Sampling. A method that adjusts resolution based on frequency content, distinct from TurboGS's error-guided approach. See Frequency Guided Resolution Scheduler. Focuses on optimizing subsets of Gaussians locally, whereas TurboGS optimizes globally but sparsely. See Local 3DGS Optimization. Time Complexity: TurboGS significantly reduces rasterization cost by only processing a sparse subset of pixels per tile. Limitations: May introduce rippling artifacts in low-frequency regions; sparse supervision can amplify gradient variance across views and tiles. When to use: When training time is a critical constraint and the scene has sufficient texture to guide error-based sampling. When not to use: For scenes with large uniform regions where error signals are weak, leading to potential artifacts. TurboGS was introduced as an error-guided training framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting to address the high computational cost of dense rasterization in standard 3DGS training. It builds on the observation that only a small subset of pixels remains difficult to reconstruct as training progresses. The method was published in 2026. name: Error-Guided Sparse Pixel Sampling
head: Err-SPS, Tile-Wise Pixel Sampling (EPS), Tile-wise Sparse Pixel Sampling, sparse pixel training
body: Error-Guided Sparse Pixel Sampling (Err-SPS) is a training acceleration strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that restricts loss evaluation and gradient computation to a sparse subset of pixels per tile, guided by persistent error and age maps. It solves the problem of redundant gradient computation in well-reconstructed regions by reallocating computation to perceptually informative pixels. It is distinguished from sibling methods like TurboGS by its specific focus on the sampling mechanism itself, whereas TurboGS integrates Err-SPS with additional components like structure-aware loss and density control. Unlike Frequency Guided Resolution Scheduler which targets resolution, Err-SPS targets pixel-level supervision density. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current Gaussian set \mathcal{G}, ground-truth images I{gt}, camera poses Cv, tile configuration (tile size, grid dimensions), error map E, age map A, training progress \rhot, and sampling rate parameters. Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G}', updated error map E', updated age map A', and sparse gradients for the optimizer. Data Structures: Error Map (E): A 2D array matching the image resolution (or tile grid), storing the accumulated reconstruction error per pixel. Initialized to zero or a small constant. Age Map (A): A 2D array matching the image resolution, storing the number of consecutive iterations a pixel has not been sampled. Initialized to zero. Sampled Pixel Set (P{t,v}): A list of pixel coordinates (u, v) for view v in tile t selected for the current iteration. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize: Set E = 0, A = 0. Define tile size T \times T and target sampling ratio rt (e.g., 10-20% of pixels). 2. Iterate: For each training iteration t: 3. View Selection: Select a set of views Vt for the current tile batch. Note: Err-SPS alone does not define view selection; it assumes views are provided. In TurboGS, this is geometry-aware. 4. Tile-wise Sampling: For each tile t and view v \in Vt: 5. Query Error: Retrieve error values E(p) for all pixels p in the tile. 6. Sort: Sort pixels in the tile by error E(p) in descending order. 7. Select: Select the top k = \lfloor rt \times T^2 \rfloor pixels as the sampled set P{t,v}. 8. Increment Age: For all pixels p in the tile not in P{t,v}, increment A(p) \leftarrow A(p) + 1. 9. Reset Age: For all pixels p \in P{t,v}, reset A(p) \leftarrow 0. 10. Forward Pass: Render the scene using the selected pixels P{t,v} for views Vt. This produces rendered colors \hat{I} and depths \hat{D} only for sampled pixels. 11. Loss Computation: Compute the loss L only over sampled pixels: L = \sum{v \in Vt} \sum{p \in P{t,v}} \ell1(\hat{I}p, I{gt,p}) + \lambda\tau^{ncc} L\tau^{S-NCC} where \ell1 is the L1 loss, and L\tau^{S-NCC} is a sparse Normalized Cross-Correlation term. 12. Backward Pass: Compute gradients \nabla \mathcal{G} with respect to the Gaussian parameters using the sparse loss. The backward pass is optimized via a per-Gaussian mechanism to handle sparse pixel updates efficiently. 13. Update Parameters: Update \mathcal{G} using the Adam optimizer with the computed gradients. 14. Update Error Map: Update E using an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of the current pixel-wise losses: E(p) \leftarrow \alpha E(p) + (1 - \alpha) \ell1(\hat{I}p, I{gt,p}) \quad \forall p \in P{t,v} For unsampled pixels, E(p) remains unchanged. 15. Update Age Map: (Already handled in step 9). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def errorguidedsparsepixelsampling(Gaussians, GTImages, Cameras, ErrorMap, AgeMap, Iteration, SamplingRate, AlphaEMA): # 1. View Selection (Assumed external or random for pure Err-SPS) Views = selectviews(Cameras) # 2. Tile-wise Sampling SampledPixels = {} # Dict: (viewidx, tileidx) -> list of (u, v) for viewidx, camera in enumerate(Views): # Get tile grid for this view Tiles = gettilegrid(camera.imagewidth, camera.imageheight) for tileidx, tile in enumerate(Tiles): tilepixels = getpixelsintile(tile) # Get errors for current tile pixels errors = [ErrorMap[p.y][p.x] for p in tilepixels] # Sort pixels by error descending sortedindices = argsortdesc(errors) # Select top k pixels k = int(SamplingRate len(tilepixels)) selectedindices = sortedindices[:k] sampledset = [tilepixels[i] for i in selectedindices] SampledPixels[(viewidx, tileidx)] = sampledset # Update Age Map for p in tilepixels: if p not in sampledset: AgeMap[p.y][p.x] += 1 else: AgeMap[p.y][p.x] = 0 # 3. Forward Pass (Sparse Rasterization) RenderedImages = {} RenderedDepths = {} for (viewidx, tileidx), pixels in SampledPixels.items(): camera = Views[viewidx] # Rasterize only for these pixels renderedcolor, rendereddepth = sparserasterize(Gaussians, camera, pixels) RenderedImages[(viewidx, tileidx)] = renderedcolor RenderedDepths[(viewidx, tileidx)] = rendereddepth # 4. Loss Computation TotalLoss = 0 PixelLosses = {} # Store losses for EMA update for (viewidx, tileidx), pixels in SampledPixels.items(): gtcolor = GTImages[viewidx] renderedcolor = RenderedImages[(viewidx, tileidx)] # Compute L1 loss for sampled pixels loss = 0 for p in pixels: l1 = abs(renderedcolor[p.y][p.x] - gtcolor[p.y][p.x]) loss += l1 PixelLosses[(viewidx, tileidx, p)] = l1 TotalLoss += loss # Add Sparse NCC if required (TurboGS component) # loss += lambdancc sparsenccloss(...) # 5. Backward Pass Gradients = computegradients(TotalLoss, Gaussians) # 6. Update Gaussians Gaussians = adamupdate(Gaussians, Gradients) # 7. Update Error Map (EMA) for (viewidx, tileidx), pixels in SampledPixels.items(): for p in pixels: currentloss = PixelLosses[(viewidx, tileidx, p)] ErrorMap[p.y][p.x] = AlphaEMA ErrorMap[p.y][p.x] + (1 - AlphaEMA) currentloss return Gaussians, ErrorMap, AgeMap, TotalLoss Parameters: Sampling Rate (rt): The fraction of pixels to sample per tile. Typical values are 10-20%. EMA Alpha (\alpha): The smoothing factor for the error map. Not explicitly given in sources, but standard EMA values (e.g., 0.9) are implied. \lambda\tau^{ncc}: Weight for sparse NCC loss. Not given in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Error Maps: If the error map is not initialized properly, early training may sample randomly or bias towards specific regions. Stale Errors: If the error map is not updated frequently enough, it may guide sampling to regions that are no longer challenging. Loss of High-Frequency Details: Relying solely on sparse L1 supervision can degrade reconstruction quality, particularly in high-frequency regions. This requires complementary techniques like sparse NCC regularization or geometry-aware view sampling. Rippling Artifacts: Sparse supervision may introduce subtle rippling artifacts in low-frequency regions with weak texture variations (e.g., walls). A full training framework that incorporates Err-SPS along with structure-aware loss, density control, and a hybrid optimizer. Choose when you need end-to-end acceleration with quality preservation. TurboGS Adjusts resolution based on frequency content. Choose when you want to manage computational load via resolution rather than pixel density. Frequency Guided Resolution Scheduler Adjusts SH order sparsely. Choose when optimizing appearance details rather than geometry/speed. Sparse SH Order Increment Time Complexity: Reduces training time significantly. On Mip-NeRF 360, Err-SPS reduces training time from 891s to 85s. Memory Complexity: Reduces the number of Gaussian splats (NGS) from 2.73M to 0.76M during training, indicating lower memory pressure for gradient accumulation and parameter updates. Performance: Provides substantial acceleration with minimal quality loss when combined with complementary techniques (NCC, density control). Strengths: Efficiently reallocates computation to informative pixels; avoids redundant gradient computation in well-reconstructed regions. Limitations: Can degrade reconstruction quality if used alone; may introduce artifacts in low-texture regions; requires careful tuning of sampling rate and error map update frequency. When to Use: When training time is a bottleneck and you can afford to integrate complementary loss terms (like NCC) to maintain quality. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity reconstruction of fine details is critical and you cannot use additional regularization; or when hardware memory is not the primary constraint. Err-SPS was introduced in the TurboGS paper by Hanson et al. in 2026 (preprint). It is part of the broader effort to accelerate 3D Gaussian Splatting training, building on the observation that most pixels become well-reconstructed early in training, yielding marginal gradients. name: Frequency Guided Resolution Scheduler
head: Frequency-based resolution scheduling
body: The Frequency Guided Resolution Scheduler is a training strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that accelerates optimization by dynamically adjusting the rendering resolution based on the frequency content of the training data. It reduces optimization complexity by allocating more iterations to high-resolution (HR) rendering only when the model has sufficiently captured the low-frequency structure of the scene. Unlike static resolution schedules, this method uses the Fourier energy of the input images to determine the optimal switching points between different resolution levels, ensuring that high-frequency details are fitted only after the coarse geometry is established. The method schedules the rendering resolution r(k) as a function of the iteration index k throughout the total training budget S. It operates by analyzing the frequency domain representation of the training views to determine how much information is contained at different scales. Inputs: N: Number of training views. S: Total number of optimization iterations. \{In\}{n=1}^N: Set of training images at full resolution (H, W). a: Hyperparameter controlling the minimum frequency threshold (default a=4). Outputs: A schedule mapping each iteration k \in [1, S] to a rendering resolution factor r(k), where the rendered image size is (H/r(k), W/r(k)). No persistent data structures are required beyond the standard Gaussian parameters and the pre-computed frequency energy values. The scheduler computes scalar values for each resolution level. 1. Compute Frequency Energy: For each training view In, compute its Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) Fn. Calculate the total frequency energy \mathcal{X}(F) of the full-resolution images: \mathcal{X}(F) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{n=1}^{N} \sum{i=1}^{h} \sum{j=1}^{w} ||Fn(i, j)||^2 where (h, w) = (H, W). 2. Determine Resolution Levels: Define a set of downsampling factors r1, r2, \dots, rm such that 1 = rm < r{m-1} < \dots < r1. The maximum downsampling factor rm (lowest resolution) is determined by the condition: \mathcal{X}(F{rm}) = \frac{1}{a} \mathcal{X}(F) where \mathcal{X}(F{rm}) is the frequency energy of the images downsampled by factor rm. Intermediate energy levels \mathcal{X}(F{r1}), \dots, \mathcal{X}(F{r{m-1}}) are linearly sampled between \mathcal{X}(F) and \mathcal{X}(F{rm}). The corresponding resolution factors ri are solved for these energy levels. Note that downsampling must be performed carefully to avoid aliasing; a common approach is center-cropping the DFT and scaling values by 1/r^2 before inverse transforming. 3. Calculate Switching Iterations: For each resolution transition from ri to r{i-1}, calculate the iteration index s{ri} where the switch occurs: s{ri} = S \cdot \frac{\mathcal{X}(F{ri})}{\mathcal{X}(F)} This formula distributes iterations proportionally to the frequency energy contained in the lower resolution. 4. Interpolate Resolution: For any iteration k, determine the current resolution r(k). If k falls between switching points s{ri} and s{r{i-1}}, interpolate the resolution factor. The sources specify that the resolution r(k) is interpolated with the inverse square of ri and r{i-1}. Specifically, if we define the "inverse square resolution" metric, the interpolation ensures smooth transitions in the effective pixel density. Unverified code. For each Ei, find ri such that X(Fri) = Ei. # Step 2: Sample energies targetenergies = np.linspace(XF, XF / a, numlevels + 1) # targetenergies[0] = X(F) -> r=1 # targetenergies[-1] = X(F)/a -> r=rm # Step 3: Solve for ri # We need a function factorfromenergy(E). # Since we have candidatefactors (factor, energy), we can interpolate. def factorfromenergy(E): # Interpolate factor based on energy # candenergies is decreasing, candfactors is increasing # Use numpy interp. Note: x must be sorted. # candenergies is decreasing, so we reverse or handle carefully. # Let's reverse them for interpolation. erev = candenergies[::-1] frev = candfactors[::-1] # Interpolate f = np.interp(E, erev, frev) return f rvalues = [factorfromenergy(E) for E in targetenergies] # rvalues[0] should be 1.0, rvalues[-1] should be rm. # Step 4: Calculate switching iterations # Switch from ri to r{i-1} happens at s{ri}. # rvalues[i] is the resolution AFTER the switch? # Source: "increase the rendering resolution from (H/ri, W/ri) to (H/ri-1, W/ri-1) at the sri-th iteration." # So at iteration s{ri}, we switch FROM ri TO r{i-1}. # This means for k < s{r1}, we use r1? No, we start at LOW resolution. # Source: "LR rendering... is applied in the early stage... switched to HR". # So we start at rm (lowest res) and go up to r0=1 (highest res). # Let's re-index. # Levels: L0 = rm (lowest), L1 = r{m-1},..., Lm = r0 = 1 (highest). # Switch from Lj to L{j+1} at iteration s{Lj}. # s{Lj} = S (X(F{Lj}) / X(F)). # Let's map rvalues back to this order. # rvalues[0] = 1 (HR). rvalues[-1] = rm (LR). # We want to start at rm. # Switch points: # Switch from rm to r{m-1} at s{rm}. # Switch from r{m-1} to r{m-2} at s{r{m-1}}. #... # Switch from r1 to r0 at s{r1}. switchiterations = [] switchresolutions = [] # Iterate from lowest res (index -1) to highest (index 0) # We have m switches. # Indices in rvalues: m, m-1,..., 1. # rvalues[m] is rm. rvalues[m-1] is r{m-1}. # Switch from rvalues[m] to rvalues[m-1] at s{rm}. for i in range(len(rvalues) - 1, 0, -1): rcurrent = rvalues[i] energycurrent = factorfromenergyinverse(rcurrent) # Need inverse map or just use targetenergies # Actually, we have targetenergies corresponding to rvalues. # targetenergies[i] corresponds to rvalues[i]. si = totaliterations (targetenergies[i] / XF) switchiterations.append(int(si)) switchresolutions.append(rvalues[i-1]) # The resolution we switch TO # Sort switchiterations # They should be increasing. # s{rm} < s{r{m-1}} <... < s{r1} # Build schedule schedule = [] currentres = rvalues[-1] # Start at lowest resolution rm # Add initial segment # From k=1 to s{rm}, use rm. # We need to handle the boundaries. # Let's create a list of (iteration, resolution) events = [] for i in range(len(rvalues) - 1, 0, -1): si = int(totaliterations (targetenergies[i] / XF)) events.append((si, rvalues[i-1])) events.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) currentres = rvalues[-1] schedule = [currentres] totaliterations for k in range(totaliterations): # Check if any switch happens at k # The switch happens AT iteration si. # So for k < si, use old res. For k >= si, use new res. # But multiple switches might be close. # Process events in order. pass # Simpler: currentres = rvalues[-1] eventidx = 0 for k in range(totaliterations): while eventidx < len(events) and events[eventidx][0] <= k: currentres = events[eventidx][1] eventidx += 1 schedule[k] = currentres return schedule def binarysearchfactor(images, targetenergy, low=1.0, high=10.0, tol=0.1): """ Finds the downsampling factor r such that energy(Fr) approx targetenergy. """ while high - low > tol: mid = (low + high) / 2 e = getdownsampledenergy(images, mid) if e > targetenergy: low = mid else: high = mid return (low + high) / 2 a: Hyperparameter controlling the starting significance level for the lowest resolution. Default value is 4. S: Total number of iterations. N: Number of training views. Aliasing: Simple spatial downsampling (e.g., nearest-neighbor subsampling) causes aliasing, which disturbs recoverable low-frequency components and introduces artifacts. The method requires anti-aliasing downsampling, such as center-cropping the DFT and scaling values by 1/r^2 before inverse transforming. Precision: The frequency energy calculation involves summing squared magnitudes, which can be sensitive to numerical precision if not normalized correctly. Degenerate Input: If the training images have very low frequency content (e.g., uniform color), the energy difference between resolutions may be negligible, leading to rapid switching. The hyperparameter a helps mitigate this by setting a floor. Time Complexity: The scheduling itself adds negligible overhead. The primary benefit is a reduction in total optimization time by reducing the number of high-resolution rendering steps. Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required beyond the training images and Gaussian parameters. Performance: DashGaussian reports significant speedups (e.g., optimizing in 200 seconds) while maintaining or improving quality. Strengths: Reduces optimization complexity by focusing high-resolution computation only when necessary. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of frequency energies, which adds a small upfront cost. The Frequency Guided Resolution Scheduler was introduced in the "DashGaussian" paper. It addresses the high computational cost of 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization by recognizing that early-stage optimization primarily fits low-frequency components. By scheduling resolution based on frequency energy, it accelerates training without sacrificing final image quality. name: Multi-View Regulated Gaussian Splatting
head: Multi-View Regulated Training, Multi-view Regulated Learning, Multi-view gradient aggregation
body: Multi-View Regulated Gaussian Splatting (MVGS) is a training strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that aggregates gradients from multiple views in each optimization step to enforce multi-view coherence and stabilize gradient descent. Unlike standard single-view optimization, which updates Gaussians based on one random view per iteration and can lead to conflicting gradients, MVGS jointly updates 3D Gaussians observed by multiple views, resulting in smoother convergence and improved novel view synthesis quality. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{\thetai\}{i=1}^N initialized from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point clouds; a dataset of multi-view images; a number of training views M selected per iteration. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters \thetai = (\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \Sigmai, ci, oi), where \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 is position, \Sigmai \in \mathbb{S}^{3++} is covariance, ci \in \mathbb{R}^3 is view-dependent color (via spherical harmonics), and oi \in [0, 1] is opacity. Data Structures The Gaussian primitive parameters are stored as: \boldsymbol{\mu}i: 3D position vector. \Sigmai: Covariance matrix, parameterized by rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 and scale vector \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. oi: Scalar opacity. ci: Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients for color. Rendering Equation The color \mathbf{C} of a pixel is computed via alpha blending: \mathbf{C} = \sum{i=1}^N ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1}(1-\alphaj) where the opacity \alphai of the i-th Gaussian at pixel location \mathbf{x}i is: \alphai = oi \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} \Delta \mathbf{x}i^T \Sigmai^{-1} \Delta \mathbf{x}i \right) and \Delta \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{x}i - \boldsymbol{\mu}i. Optimization Steps The method employs three core mechanisms: Multi-View Regulated Learning (MVRL), Cross-Intrinsic Guidance (CIG), and Multi-View Cross-Ray Densification. 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians from SfM point clouds. 2. Multi-View Regulated Learning (MVRL): Select M training views for the current iteration. Render images for each of the M views and compute the loss \mathcal{L}m for each view m using the standard photometric baseline: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}{L1} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM}. Compute the gradient chain by summing the gradients of the Gaussian parameters \boldsymbol{\theta} across all M views. Do not average the gradients; sum them to increase gradient magnitude for jointly observed Gaussians: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}{MV}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\theta}} = \sum{m=1}^M \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}m}{\partial \boldsymbol{\theta}} Update \boldsymbol{\theta} using the summed gradient. 3. Cross-Intrinsic Guidance (CIG): Train from low-resolution to high-resolution. In the low-resolution phase, use a larger M (more multi-view images) to capture global/coarse appearances. Initialize finer-scale Gaussians for the high-resolution phase from the coarsely estimated Gaussians of the low-resolution phase, rather than optimizing from scratch. 4. Multi-View Cross-Ray Densification: When input views exhibit minimal overlap, apply multi-view augmented densification. In overlapped 3D space where rays from multiple views intersect, apply cross-ray densification to split Gaussians dynamically, accommodating drastic viewpoint variations. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mvgstrainingloop(gaussians, dataset, numiterations, M, lambdadssim): """ gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes mu, sigma, opacity, shcoeffs dataset: Iterable of image views (camera poses, images) M: Number of views to aggregate gradients from per step lambdadssim: Weight for D-SSIM loss (typically 0.2) """ optimizer = Adam(gaussians.parameters(), lr=initiallr, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.99) for iteration in range(numiterations): # 1. Select M views selectedviews = samplerandomviews(dataset, M) totalgradient = None for view in selectedviews: # 2. Render image for this view renderedimage = rendergaussians(gaussians, view.camerapose) # 3. Compute loss gtimage = view.image l1loss = computel1(renderedimage, gtimage) dssimloss = computedssim(renderedimage, gtimage) loss = (1 - lambdadssim) l1loss + lambdadssim dssimloss # 4. Compute gradients for this view gradients = computegradients(loss, gaussians) # 5. Sum gradients (do not average) if totalgradient is None: totalgradient = gradients else: totalgradient = addgradients(totalgradient, gradients) # 6. Update Gaussians with summed gradient optimizer.step(totalgradient) # 7. Apply densification if necessary (e.g., every K iterations) if iteration % densificationinterval == 0: densifygaussians(gaussians, selectedviews) Parameters M: The number of training views used for gradient aggregation. The sources do not specify a fixed typical value but indicate that increasing M reduces gradient variance. \lambda: Weight for D-SSIM loss, typically 0.2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Minimal Overlap: Standard densification may fail when input views have minimal overlap. MVGS addresses this with multi-view cross-ray densification. Gradient Conflict: Single-view optimization can lead to Gaussians satisfying one view but conflicting with physical restrictions. Summing gradients from multiple views mitigates this by enforcing consistency. Time Complexity: The rendering step has O(N) complexity due to tile-based rasterization. The training complexity increases linearly with the number of aggregated views M per iteration, as M forward/backward passes are performed. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves multi-view consistency, stabilizes gradient updates, and achieves state-of-the-art performance in novel view synthesis. It is a plug-and-play optimizer compatible with many 3DGS variants. Limitations: Requires more computational resources per iteration due to multi-view rendering and gradient aggregation. When to use: When multi-view consistency is critical and single-view optimization leads to unstable gradients or suboptimal rendering quality. MVGS was introduced in the paper "MVGS: Multi-view-regulated Gaussian Splatting for Novel View Synthesis". It addresses the limitation of existing Gaussian-based methods that typically follow a single-view optimization paradigm, which suffers from unstable gradients. The method leverages multi-view coherent (MVC) constraints to enhance 3D Gaussian multi-view consistency. name: Mip-Splatting Training Loop & Evaluation Pipeline
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting Training Schedule, Mip-3DGS Training Loop
body: This article defines the complete training iteration and evaluation procedure for Mip-Splatting, a method that extends 3D Gaussian Splatting by incorporating subpixel-aware rendering to mitigate aliasing artifacts. It handles camera sampling, hybrid loss computation, adaptive densification/pruning, and quantitative metric reporting. It differs from the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting training loop by explicitly managing subpixel offsets for both rendering and ground-truth resampling, and by adjusting the spherical harmonics degree and learning rates on a fixed schedule. Inputs: gaussians: The set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}{i=1}^N with parameters \mathbf{p}i, \mathbf{q}i, \mathbf{s}i, \alphai, \mathbf{c}{i, l}. viewpointstack: A list of training camera poses. trainCameras: The full set of training cameras, indexed by resolution level. gtimage: The ground-truth image for the current camera view. pipe: Pipeline parameters (e.g., convertSHspython, computecov3Dpython). opt: Optimization hyperparameters (learning rates, densification thresholds, intervals). dataset: Dataset configuration flags (e.g., rayjitter, resamplegtimage, kernelsize). Outputs: Updated gaussians parameters. Loss value \mathcal{L} for logging. Quantitative metrics (SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS) during evaluation phases. gaussians.maxradii2D: A tensor of size N storing the maximum image-space radius observed for each Gaussian across all previous iterations. Used for pruning. gaussians.optimizer: An Adam optimizer instance managing gradients for all Gaussian parameters. subpixeloffset: A tensor of shape (H, W, 2) with values in [-0.5, 0.5], representing the subpixel jitter for each pixel. --testiterations: List of iteration numbers for validation. Default: [7000, 30000]. --saveiterations: List of iteration numbers for saving models. Default: [7000, 30000]. --checkpointiterations: List of iteration numbers for saving optimizer checkpoints. Default: []. opt.iterations: Total training iterations. Default: 30,000. opt.positionlrinit: Initial position learning rate. Default: 0.00016. opt.positionlrfinal: Final position learning rate. Default: 0.0000016. opt.positionlrdelaymult: Delay multiplier for position LR. Default: 0.01. opt.positionlrmaxsteps: Steps for position LR decay. Default: 30,000. opt.featurelr: SH feature learning rate. Default: 0.0025. opt.opacitylr: Opacity learning rate. Default: 0.05. opt.scalinglr: Scale learning rate. Default: 0.005. opt.rotationlr: Rotation learning rate. Default: 0.001. opt.lambdadssim: D-SSIM weight. Default: 0.2. opt.densificationinterval: Iterations between densification steps. Default: 100. opt.opacityresetinterval: Iterations between opacity resets. Default: 3000. opt.densifyfromiter: Iteration when densification starts. Default: 500. opt.densifyuntiliter: Iteration when densification stops. Default: 15,000. opt.densifygradthreshold: Gradient threshold for densification. Default: 0.0002. dataset.kernelsize: Kernel size for rendering. Default: 0.1. dataset.rayjitter: Enable subpixel jitter. Default: False. dataset.resamplegtimage: Enable ground truth resampling. Default: False. dataset.samplemorehighres: Prioritize high-res cameras. Default: False. dataset.whitebackground: Use white background. Default: False. 1. Learning Rate Update: Update the learning rates for all Gaussian parameters based on the current iteration. This typically involves a linear decay for position learning rates from opt.positionlrinit to opt.positionlrfinal over opt.positionlrmaxsteps. 2. SH Degree Increment: Every 1,000 iterations, increment the active spherical harmonics degree by one, up to the maximum defined in dataset.shdegree (typically 3). 3. Camera Sampling: Pop a random camera from viewpointstack. If dataset.samplemorehighres is true and a random float < 0.3, override with a high-resolution camera from trainCameras[highresolutionindex]. 4. Subpixel Offset Generation: If dataset.rayjitter is enabled, generate a tensor subpixeloffset of shape (H, W, 2) with uniform random values in [-0.5, 0.5] on CUDA. Otherwise, set subpixeloffset = None. 5. Rendering: Render the scene using the selected camera, Gaussian parameters, and pipeline settings. Pass kernelsize=dataset.kernelsize and subpixeloffset=subpixeloffset to the rasterizer. Extract image (rendered color), viewspacepointtensor, visibilityfilter (boolean mask of visible Gaussians), and radii (image-space radii) from the render output. 6. Ground Truth Resampling: If dataset.resamplegtimage is true, resample the ground truth image I{gt} using the subpixeloffset to align it with the jittered rendering grid. Let this be I{gt}^{resampled}. Otherwise, use the original I{gt}. 7. Loss Computation: Compute the composite loss \mathcal{L}: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda{\text{dssim}}) \mathcal{L}{\text{L1}} + \lambda{\text{dssim}} (1 - \text{SSIM}(I{\text{render}}, I{gt}^{resampled})) where \mathcal{L}{\text{L1}} is the mean absolute error between I{\text{render}} and I{gt}^{resampled}, and \lambda{\text{dssim}} = 0.2. 8. Statistics Tracking: Update gaussians.maxradii2D: For visible Gaussians (visibilityfilter), update the maximum observed radius: \text{max\radii2D}[i] = \max(\text{max\radii2D}[i], \text{radii}[i]) \quad \forall i \in \text{visibility\filter} Add densification statistics: Accumulate gradient norms and other metrics for the visible Gaussians using viewspacepointtensor and visibilityfilter. 9. Densification and Pruning (Conditional): If iteration > opt.densifyfromiter and iteration % opt.densificationinterval == 0: Determine sizethreshold: If iteration > opt.opacityresetinterval, set sizethreshold = 20; otherwise, sizethreshold = None. Call gaussians.densifyandprune(opt.densifygradthreshold, 0.005, scene.camerasextent, sizethreshold) to split, clone, or remove Gaussians based on gradient magnitude, opacity, and size. Call gaussians.compute3Dfilter(cameras=trainCameras) to update the 3D covariance filters for the modified Gaussian set. 10. Opacity Reset (Conditional): If iteration % opt.opacityresetinterval == 0 or (dataset.whitebackground is true and iteration == opt.densifyfromiter), reset the opacities of all Gaussians to a low initial value (e.g., 0.01) to prevent early saturation. 11. 3D Filter Update (Post-Densification): If iteration > opt.densifyuntiliter and iteration % 100 == 0 and iteration < opt.iterations - 100, call gaussians.compute3Dfilter(cameras=trainCameras) to maintain accurate covariance representations after densification has ceased. 12. Optimization Step: Perform the optimizer step: gaussians.optimizer.step(). Zero gradients: gaussians.optimizer.zerograd(settonone=True). 13. Evaluation (Conditional): If iteration is in --testiterations: Render the scene for all test cameras. Load rendered images from testpreds{scale} and ground truth from gt{scale}. Compute per-image SSIM, PSNR, and LPIPS (using a VGG network). Average metrics across all test images. Log to TensorBoard and save to results.json and perview.json. 14. Checkpointing (Conditional): If iteration is in --saveiterations, save the Gaussian model state. If iteration is in --checkpointiterations, save the optimizer state. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mipsplattingtrainingloop(gaussians, viewpointstack, trainCameras, dataset, opt, pipe, iteration): """ One iteration of the Mip-Splatting training loop. """ # 1. Update Learning Rates gaussians.updatelearningrate(iteration) # 2. Increment SH Degree if iteration % 1000 == 0: gaussians.oneupSHdegree() # 3. Sample Camera if dataset.samplemorehighres and random.random() < 0.3: viewpointcam = trainCameras[highresolutionindex] else: viewpointcam = viewpointstack.pop() # 4. Generate Subpixel Offset if dataset.rayjitter: subpixeloffset = torch.rand(H, W, 2, device='cuda') 2.0 - 1.0 # Values in [-0.5, 0.5] else: subpixeloffset = None # 5. Render Scene renderdict = render( viewpointcam, gaussians, pipe, background, kernelsize=dataset.kernelsize, subpixeloffset=subpixeloffset) image = renderdict['render'] viewspacepointtensor = renderdict['viewspacepoints'] visibilityfilter = renderdict['visibilityfilter'] radii = renderdict['radii'] # 6. Resample Ground Truth if dataset.resamplegtimage and subpixeloffset is not None: gtimage = createoffsetgt(gtimage, subpixeloffset) else: gtimage = gtimage # 7. Compute Loss l1loss = (image - gtimage).abs().mean() ssimloss = 1 - ssim(image, gtimage) loss = (1 - opt.lambdadssim) l1loss + opt.lambdadssim ssimloss # 8. Track Statistics gaussians.maxradii2D[visibilityfilter] = torch.max( gaussians.maxradii2D[visibilityfilter], radii[visibilityfilter]) gaussians.adddensificationstats(viewspacepointtensor, visibilityfilter) # 9. Densification and Pruning if iteration > opt.densifyfromiter and iteration % opt.densificationinterval == 0: sizethreshold = 20 if iteration > opt.opacityresetinterval else None gaussians.densifyandprune( opt.densifygradthreshold, 0.005, scene.camerasextent, sizethreshold) gaussians.compute3Dfilter(cameras=trainCameras) # 10. Opacity Reset if iteration % opt.opacityresetinterval == 0: gaussians.resetopacities() elif dataset.whitebackground and iteration == opt.densifyfromiter: gaussians.resetopacities() # 11. 3D Filter Update (Post-Densification) if iteration > opt.densifyuntiliter and iteration % 100 == 0 and iteration < opt.iterations - 100: gaussians.compute3Dfilter(cameras=trainCameras) # 12. Optimization Step loss.backward() gaussians.optimizer.step() gaussians.optimizer.zerograd(settonone=True) # 13. Evaluation (if applicable) if iteration in opt.testiterations: evaluateandlog(gaussians, trainCameras, iteration) # 14. Checkpointing (if applicable) if iteration in opt.saveiterations: savegaussianmodel(gaussians, iteration) if iteration in opt.checkpointiterations: saveoptimizercheckpoint(gaussians.optimizer, iteration) return loss.item() Precision: Subpixel jitter requires floating-point precision for offset generation and resampling. Ensure subpixeloffset is on the same device as the image tensors. Boundaries: When resampling ground truth images, handle boundary pixels correctly to avoid artifacts from interpolation. Degenerate Input: If visibilityfilter is empty (no visible Gaussians), skip densification statistics and loss computation to avoid division by zero or invalid operations. SH Degree: Ensure SH degree does not exceed the maximum supported by the renderer or the data. Time: Dominated by the rasterization step, which is O(N \cdot K) where N is the number of Gaussians and K is the kernel size. Densification adds O(N) overhead every 100 iterations. Memory: O(N) for Gaussian parameters and O(H \cdot W) for intermediate render buffers. maxradii2D adds O(N) memory. Performance metrics (SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS) are reported at iterations 7,000 and 30,000. Specific performance numbers depend on the dataset and hardware. The method is designed to improve visual quality over standard 3DGS by reducing aliasing. Scales with the number of Gaussians N and image resolution H \times W. High-resolution training can be prioritized via dataset.samplemorehighres. Strengths: Reduces aliasing artifacts through subpixel-aware rendering and ground truth resampling. Adaptive densification ensures efficient representation. Limitations: Increased computational cost due to subpixel jitter and resampling. Requires careful tuning of jitter and resampling flags. Use when high-fidelity rendering with minimal aliasing is required. Use when training on high-resolution datasets where standard 3DGS may exhibit jagged edges. Avoid if computational resources are severely limited and aliasing is acceptable. Avoid if ground truth images are not available for resampling. Mip-Splatting was introduced by the autonomousvision group, extending the original 3D Gaussian Splatting method. The codebase is available on GitHub. The method builds upon the differentiable rendering framework of 3D Gaussian Splatting, adding subpixel rendering capabilities to address aliasing issues. Used in 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis tasks where high visual fidelity is critical. autonomousvision/mip-splatting, https://github.com/autonomousvision/mip-splatting, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Distributed 3DGS Training Loop with Adaptive Workload Division
head: Batched Distributed 3DGS Training, Grendel-GS Training Pipeline
body: This method implements a distributed training workflow for 3D Gaussian Splatting that batches camera selection, divides rendering workloads across multiple GPUs using an adaptive strategy based on historical performance, synchronizes losses, and schedules densification and spherical harmonics (SH) degree updates. It differs from standard gradient accumulation by optionally scaling gradients by batch size to avoid explicit accumulation buffers, and by dynamically balancing the computational load of rendering different camera views across the GPU cluster. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A dataset of camera poses and images, initial 3D Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G}, distributed environment configuration (number of GPUs, WORLDSIZE), and training hyperparameters (args). Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian parameters, saved checkpoints, and training logs. Data Structures: batchedscreenspacepkg: A dictionary containing rendering state. Key field: "batchedcudaargs", a list of CUDA argument structures. Each structure contains a "statscollector" field used for adaptive workload division. batchedlosses: A tensor of shape (N, 2), where N is the batch size. Index 0 holds the first loss component (L1), and index 1 holds the second loss component (used for D-SSIM calculation). strategyhistory: A record of past workload division decisions and their resulting performance statistics, used to adaptively select rendering strategies. Parameters: args.bsz: Batch size per iteration step. Controls the loop range and serves as the divisor for gradient scaling. args.lambdadssim: Weight for the D-SSIM loss component. Default value not specified in the sources. args.lrscalemode: String controlling gradient scaling. If not equal to "accumu", gradients are explicitly divided by args.bsz before the optimizer step. args.localsampling: Boolean flag. If true, enables distributed camera index gathering across GPUs using torch.distributed.allgatherintotensor. args.saveiterations / args.checkpointiterations: Lists of iteration numbers triggering Gaussian saves or full checkpoint saves, respectively. args.backend: String specifying the rendering backend, either "gsplat" or another implementation. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the training loop from startfromthisiteration to optargs.iterations with a step size of args.bsz. Update the progress bar every args.bsz iterations. 2. Logging: Log the Exponential Moving Average (EMA) loss to the progress bar every 30 batches (checked via iteration // args.bsz % 30 == 0). 3. State Update: Update the learning rate and increment the trained batch counter. Clear timing accumulators. Start an NVTX range if profiling is enabled. 4. SH Update: Upscale the spherical harmonics (SH) degree by one level every 1000 iterations. This is determined by utils.checkupdateatthisiter(iteration, args.bsz, 1000, 0). 5. Camera Selection: Select cameras for the current batch. If args.localsampling is true: Assert that args.bsz is divisible by utils.WORLDSIZE. Gather local camera indices across all GPUs using torch.distributed.allgatherintotensor, convert to numpy, and fetch the corresponding camera objects. Otherwise: Fetch cameras directly via traindataset.getbatchedcameras(args.bsz). 6. Workload Division Strategy: Initialize the workload division strategy by calling startstrategyfinal(batchedcameras, strategyhistory). This returns batchedstrategies (mapping cameras to rendering strategies) and gpuid2tasks (mapping GPUs to specific tasks). 7. Data Loading: Load camera data from CPU memory to all GPUs using loadcamerafromcputoallgpu(batchedcameras, batchedstrategies, gpuid2tasks). 8. Preprocessing: Preprocess the 3D Gaussian Splatting data and perform all-to-all communication to distribute data across GPUs. If args.backend == "gsplat", call gsplatdistributedpreprocess3dgsandall2allfinal. Otherwise, call distributedpreprocess3dgsandall2allfinal. 9. Rendering: Render images and extract compute locations. Call gsplatrenderfinal or renderfinal with batchedscreenspacepkg and batchedstrategies. Extract the batchstatisticcollector from batchedscreenspacepkg["batchedcudaargs"] for future strategy adaptation. 10. Loss Computation: Compute the loss by calling batchedlosscomputation with the rendered images, cameras, compute locations, strategies, and statistic collectors. 11. Backward Pass: Execute the backward pass: losssum.backward(). 12. Strategy Update: Update the workload division strategy by calling finishstrategyfinal(batchedcameras, strategyhistory, batchedstrategies, batchstatisticcollector) to record performance metrics for adaptive balancing. 13. Loss Synchronization: Synchronize losses across all GPUs using dist.allreduce(batchedlosses, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM, group=utils.DEFAULTGROUP). 14. EMA Update: Update the EMA loss for logging. If emalossforlog is None, set it to the mean of batchedlosscpu. Otherwise, update using: EMA = 0.6 \cdot EMA + 0.4 \cdot \text{mean}(batched\loss\cpu). 15. Evaluation: Trigger evaluation if the current iteration matches testingiterations. Log validation configurations for test and train sets. 16. Densification: Perform Gaussian densification by calling gsplatdensification or densification with the current iteration, scene data, Gaussian parameters, and screenspace package. 17. Saving: Save Gaussians if the current iteration is in args.saveiterations. Write the strategyhistory to a JSON file if args.savestrategyhistory is true. 18. Checkpointing: Save checkpoints if the current iteration is in args.checkpointiterations. Create the directory (handled by Rank 0), synchronize all ranks via torch.distributed.barrier to prevent race conditions, and save gaussians.capture() and the current iteration to a.pth file. Formulas: The combined batch loss is calculated as: L{batch} = (1 - \lambda{dssim}) \cdot L{0} + \lambda{dssim} \cdot (1 - L{1}) where: L{0} is the first loss component (typically L1 loss). L{1} is the second loss component (typically D-SSIM similarity). \lambda{dssim} is args.lambdadssim. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Local Sampling Constraint: When args.localsampling is enabled, args.bsz must be divisible by utils.WORLDSIZE. The code asserts this condition: assert args.bsz % utils.WORLDSIZE == 0. Checkpoint Race Conditions: Checkpoint saving requires rank synchronization. Rank 0 creates the directory, but all ranks must call torch.distributed.barrier to ensure the directory exists before any rank attempts to write to it. Gradient Scaling: The method distinguishes itself from standard gradient accumulation by explicitly dividing gradients by args.bsz when args.lrscalemode != "accumu", avoiding the need for explicit accumulation buffers. Complexity: The method scales with the number of GPUs (WORLDSIZE) and the batch size (args.bsz). The adaptive workload division adds overhead for strategy selection and history management but aims to balance rendering times across heterogeneous or unevenly loaded GPUs. Performance: Specific measured performance metrics (e.g., throughput in it/s, PSNR values) are not provided in the source notes for this specific method's implementation details, though the source references experiments on scenes like "bicycle" and "matrixcity". Strengths: Enables training on large scenes or with large batch sizes that do not fit on a single GPU. The adaptive workload division helps mitigate stragglers caused by varying camera view complexities. Limitations: Requires careful synchronization of data and losses. The adaptive strategy relies on historical data, which may be suboptimal at the very beginning of training. This method is part of the Grendel-GS project, a distributed training system for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the scalability limitations of single-GPU training by distributing the rendering and optimization workload across multiple GPUs. nyu-systems/Grendel-GS, https://github.com/nyu-systems/Grendel-GS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Sparse SH Order Increment
head: SOI, Sparse Order Increment of SH
body: Sparse SH Order Increment (SOI) is a memory-efficient training strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that dynamically increases the Spherical Harmonics (SH) order for a subset of Gaussians based on their view-dependent color error. Unlike standard 3DGS which assigns full 3rd-order SH coefficients to all primitives, SOI initializes all Gaussians with SH order 0 and selectively promotes only those with significant rendering errors to higher orders. This approach significantly reduces GPU memory consumption and storage overhead while maintaining rendering quality comparable to full-order SH, making it suitable for large-scale scenes. Inputs and Outputs Input: The current set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, the rendered images \hat{I}, ground-truth images I{gt}, and the sparse rate parameter rs. Output: Updated Gaussian parameters where the SH order of a subset of Gaussians is incremented by one. Data Structures Each Gaussian gk stores its SH coefficients. Initially, only the 0th-order coefficient (constant color) is allocated. When the order is incremented, additional coefficients for higher degrees (l=1, 2, \dots) are allocated. The exact memory layout of SH coefficients follows the standard 3DGS convention (3 coefficients per degree for l>0), but the number of allocated coefficients per Gaussian varies dynamically. Parameters rs: Sparse rate, the percentage of Gaussians selected for order increment. Typical value: 0.2 (20%). Iteration steps: SOI is executed a fixed number of times (typically 3) during training. For small scenes (30,000 total iterations): Steps at 16,000, 17,000, and 18,000. For large scenes (60,000 total iterations): Steps are scaled proportionately. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: At the start of training, set the SH order to 0 for all Gaussians. This means only the 0th-order SH coefficient (view-independent color) is stored. 2. Pruning: Before executing SOI, perform Gaussian pruning to remove redundant primitives. This minimizes GPU memory overhead during the subsequent order increment. 3. Error Calculation: For each Gaussian gk, calculate the view-based color difference dk across all training views. The formula is: dk = \frac{1}{N \cdot H \cdot W} \sum{p=1}^{N} \mathbb{1}(k \in \mathcal{N}p) \cdot wk^p \cdot |Cp - Cp^{gt}| Where: N is the number of training images. H, W are the image height and width. p iterates over all pixels in the N images. \mathbb{1}(k \in \mathcal{N}p) is an indicator function equal to 1 if Gaussian k overlaps pixel p, and 0 otherwise. wk^p is the contribution weight of Gaussian k to pixel p. Cp is the rendered color at pixel p. Cp^{gt} is the ground truth color at pixel p. | \cdot | denotes the absolute difference (L1 norm). 4. Selection: Sort all Gaussians by their calculated difference dk in descending order. Select the top rs percentage of Gaussians from this sorted list. 5. Increment: Increment the SH order by one for the selected Gaussians. This involves allocating and initializing the next degree of SH coefficients. 6. Repetition: Repeat steps 2-5 every several iterations for a total of 3 times during the training process. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparseshorderincrement(gaussians, renderedimages, gtimages, sparserate, currentiteration, totaliterations): """ Perform Sparse SH Order Increment if the current iteration matches the predefined schedule. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects, each with an 'shorder' attribute. renderedimages: Rendered images for all training views. gtimages: Ground truth images for all training views. sparserate: Fraction of Gaussians to promote (e.g., 0.2). currentiteration: Current training iteration number. totaliterations: Total number of training iterations. Returns: Updated list of Gaussians. """ # Determine if SOI should be executed at this iteration # For small scenes (30k iters): 16000, 17000, 18000 # For large scenes (60k iters): Proportionally scaled if not shouldexecutesoi(currentiteration, totaliterations): return gaussians # Step 1: Pruning to reduce memory overhead before incrementing gaussians = gaussianpruning(gaussians) # Step 2: Calculate color difference for each Gaussian differences = [] for k, g in enumerate(gaussians): dk = 0.0 count = 0 # Iterate over all training views for viewidx in range(len(renderedimages)): renderedimg = renderedimages[viewidx] gtimg = gtimages[viewidx] H, W = renderedimg.shape[0], renderedimg.shape[1] # Get pixels overlapped by Gaussian k # Note: In implementation, this requires access to the rasterization # data or re-rendering to get weights and overlap. # Assuming we have access to per-pixel contributions for gk: for p in range(H W): # Indicator function: 1 if gk overlaps pixel p if gaussianoverlapspixel(g, p): # Weight of gk at pixel p wkp = getgaussianweight(g, p) # Color difference colordiff = abs(renderedimg[p] - gtimg[p]) dk += wkp colordiff count += 1 # Normalize by N H W as per formula # Note: The sum in the formula is over all pixels in all N images. # The denominator is N H W. # If count < NHW, the un-overlapped pixels contribute 0 to the sum. nimages = len(renderedimages) dk = dk / (nimages H W) differences.append((dk, k)) # Step 3: Sort by difference descending differences.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True) # Step 4: Select top rs percentage numtoselect = int(len(gaussians) sparserate) selectedindices = [item[1] for item in differences[:numtoselect]] # Step 5: Increment SH order for selected Gaussians for idx in selectedindices: gaussians[idx].shorder += 1 # Initialize new SH coefficients for the new order initializeshcoefficients(gaussians[idx], gaussians[idx].shorder) return gaussians def shouldexecutesoi(currentiteration, totaliterations): """ Determine if SOI should run based on iteration schedule. """ if totaliterations <= 30000: return currentiteration in [16000, 17000, 18000] else: # Scale proportionately for large scenes (60k iters) # 16000/30000 ~ 0.533, 17000/30000 ~ 0.566, 18000/30000 ~ 0.6 # Approximate scaling: targetiters = [int(32000), int(34000), int(36000)] # Note: Exact scaling factors not specified, but proportional logic is stated. # Implementation should use the specific scaled values from the source. return currentiteration in targetiters Edge Cases and Pitfalls Memory Peaks: Although SOI reduces overall memory, the increment operation itself can cause temporary memory spikes. Pruning before incrementing is critical to mitigate this. Degenerate Input: If a Gaussian has zero contribution to any pixel (e.g., completely occluded or out of view), its color difference dk will be 0. It will not be selected for increment, which is correct behavior. Precision: The color difference calculation involves summing over all pixels. For very large images, this sum can be large. Using floating-point precision consistent with the rendering pipeline is recommended. Time and Memory Complexity Memory: SOI significantly reduces storage and GPU memory overhead compared to full 3rd-order SH. For example, on Mip-NeRF360, storage drops from 742MB (vanilla 3DGS) to 98MB with rs=0.2. Peak GPU memory is also reduced (e.g., from 12.8GB to 8.8GB in ablation studies). Time: Training time is slightly reduced or comparable to vanilla 3DGS. For Mip-NeRF360, training time decreased from 25m57s (vanilla) to 19m41s with SOI (rs=0.2). The overhead of calculating color differences and sorting Gaussians is offset by the reduced memory bandwidth and faster rendering due to fewer parameters. Measured Performance On Mip-NeRF360 dataset: rs=0.1: SSIM 0.815, PSNR 27.27, LPIPS 0.218, FPS 215, Storage 78MB. rs=0.2: SSIM 0.817, PSNR 27.38, LPIPS 0.216, FPS 218, Storage 98MB. rs=0.5: SSIM 0.819, PSNR 27.46, LPIPS 0.213, FPS 220, Storage 158MB. Vanilla 3DGS (for reference): SSIM 0.821, PSNR 27.48, LPIPS 0.209, FPS 229, Storage 259MB. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Drastically reduces storage and GPU memory usage, enabling training of larger scenes. Maintains high rendering quality (SSIM/PSNR close to vanilla 3DGS). Improves rendering FPS due to fewer parameters to blend. Limitations: Requires careful scheduling of the increment steps. The optimal timing may vary with scene scale. The method assumes that view-dependent color errors are a good proxy for the need for higher SH orders, which is generally true but may not capture all geometric nuances. When to Use Use SOI when GPU memory is constrained or when training large-scale scenes with high-resolution images. It is particularly effective for outdoor scenes where ambient light is low frequency, making high-order SH coefficients redundant for many Gaussians. Sparse SH Order Increment was introduced in the paper "EfficientGS: Streamlining Gaussian Splatting for Large-Scale High-Resolution Scene Representation". The method addresses the high memory consumption of 3D Gaussian Splatting, which typically uses 3rd-order SH for all Gaussians. The authors observed that many Gaussians, especially in outdoor scenes, do not require high-order SH to represent their view-dependent color accurately. By starting with SH order 0 and selectively incrementing based on color error, EfficientGS achieves a more efficient representation. name: Gaussian Splatting Training with SDS Loss
head: SDS-based Gaussian Splatting Training, Score Distillation Sampling for 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: This method optimizes 3D Gaussian primitives using a Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss derived from a pretrained 2D diffusion model, enabling reconstruction from unstructured image collections or text prompts where ground-truth 3D geometry is unavailable. Unlike sibling methods that rely on photometric consistency across multiple views, this approach leverages the semantic prior of a diffusion model to guide the Gaussian parameters, making it suitable for single-view or sparse-view synthesis. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} initialized from a point cloud (isotropic covariance). A pretrained diffusion model (e.g., Stable Diffusion 2.1) comprising a VAE, text encoder, UNet, and DDIM scheduler. A text prompt T describing the target scene. Camera poses and image dimensions from the dataset. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters: means \mathbf{p}i, pre-activation scales \log \mathbf{s}i, pre-activation opacities \log \alphai, and colors \mathbf{c}i. Data Structures: Gaussians: Each primitive i stores: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation quaternion (normalized). \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale vector (stored as \log \mathbf{s}i for optimization). \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity (stored as \log \alphai for optimization). \mathbf{c}i: Color coefficients (SH or RGB). Scene: Manages the list of Gaussians and handles rendering calls. Parameters: Learning rates: \eta{\text{opacity}} = 0.01, \eta{\text{scale}} = 0.01, \eta{\text{color}} = 0.01, \eta{\text{mean}} = 0.001. Optimizer: Adam with \epsilon = 10^{-15}. Training iterations: 1,000. SDS Guidance Scale (s): 100. SDS Inference Steps: 50. Timestep Range: t{\min} = 0.02 \times T, t{\max} = 0.98 \times T where T is the total number of training timesteps. Precision: torch.float32. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from a point cloud with isotropic covariance. Enable gradient tracking for \mathbf{p}i, \mathbf{c}i, \log \alphai, and \log \mathbf{s}i. Load the diffusion model components (VAE, text encoder, UNet, scheduler). 2. Rendering: Render the scene from a random camera pose using the Gaussian splatting rasterizer. The rasterizer computes 2D covariance \Sigma{2D} via the Jacobian J of the projection and view transformation W: \Sigma{2D} = J W \Sigma{3D} W^T J^T Add a regularization term of 0.3 to the diagonal elements of \Sigma{2D} to ensure each Gaussian covers at least ~1 pixel. Compute 2D means \mathbf{m}{2D} by projecting 3D means \mathbf{p}i to screen space. Calculate the exponent for each pixel k: E{i,k} = -\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x}k - \mathbf{m}{2D,i})^T \Sigma{2D,i}^{-1} (\mathbf{x}k - \mathbf{m}{2D,i}) Compute alpha values: \alpha{i,k} = \min(0.99, \max(0, \alphai \exp(E{i,k}))) (Clamped to avoid numerical instability; values < 1/255 are set to 0). Compute transmittance Tk for each pixel by accumulating \alpha values in depth order: Tk = \prod{j \le k} (1 - \alpha{j,k}) Render the final image \hat{I} with background color (0,0,0). 3. SDS Loss Computation: Encode: Normalize \hat{I} from [0,1] to [-1,1]. Pass through the VAE encoder to get latent z. Scale by s{\text{vae}} (from vae.config.scalingfactor). Text Embedding: Tokenize prompt T with padding to maxlength. Pass through text encoder to get \mathbf{t}. Noise Prediction: Sample a random timestep t \in [t{\min}, t{\max}]. Add noise \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1) to z. Pass noisy latent and \mathbf{t} through the UNet to predict noise \hat{\epsilon}\theta(zt, \mathbf{t}). Compute SDS: \mathcal{L}{SDS} = \mathbb{E}{t, \epsilon} \left[ w(t) (\hat{\epsilon}\theta(zt, \mathbf{t}) - \epsilon) \right]^2 where w(t) is a weighting function based on the guidance scale s and timestep t (standard SDS weighting). 4. Optimization: Backpropagate \mathcal{L}{SDS} through the rendering pipeline to update Gaussian parameters. Perform an Adam optimizer step. Zero gradients. Repeat for 1,000 iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F from diffusers import StableDiffusionPipeline def traingaussiansplattingsds(gaussians, dataset, prompt, numiterations=1000): # 1. Initialize Optimizer params = list(gaussians.parameters()) optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(params, lr=0.001) # Means use 0.001, others 0.01 in practice # 2. Load Diffusion Model pipe = StableDiffusionPipeline.frompretrained("stabilityai/stable-diffusion-2-1") pipe = pipe.to("cuda") pipe.enablexformersmemoryefficientattention() # Optional for memory # 3. Training Loop for i in range(numiterations): # Random camera from dataset camera, gtimage = dataset.getrandomview() # Render Scene renderedimage = renderscene(gaussians, camera) # Returns RGB [0,1] # Encode to Latent Space renderedimage = (renderedimage 2 - 1) # Normalize to [-1, 1] with torch.nograd(): latents = pipe.vae.encode(renderedimage).latentdist.sample() latents = latents pipe.vae.config.scalingfactor # Text Embedding textinput = pipe.tokenizer(prompt, padding="maxlength", maxlength=pipe.tokenizer.modelmaxlength, returntensors="pt") textembeddings = pipe.textencoder(textinput.inputids.to("cuda"))[0] # Sample Timestep t = torch.randint(0, pipe.config.numtraintimesteps, (1,)).item() noise = torch.randnlike(latents) latentsnoisy = pipe.scheduler.addnoise(latents, noise, t) # Predict Noise noisepred = pipe.unet(latentsnoisy, t, encoderhiddenstates=textembeddings).sample # Compute SDS Loss # Standard SDS weighting: w(t) = (1 - t/T) or similar depending on scheduler # For DDIM, often use simple weighting or variance preserving weights = getsdsweights(t, pipe.config.numtraintimesteps) loss = (weights (noisepred - noise)).pow(2).mean() # Backpropagate loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Update Gaussian Parameters (apply activations if stored as pre-act) gaussians.applyactivations() if i % 20 == 0: visualize(gaussians, camera) def getsdsweights(t, numtimesteps): # Simplified weighting; exact formula depends on specific SDS implementation # Often proportional to (1 - alphat) / sqrt(1 - alphat^2) or similar # For Stable Diffusion, a common choice is: alphat = pipe.scheduler.alphascumprod[t] sigmat = (1 - alphat) / alphat return sigmat The base optimization loop using photometric loss [15139-3d-gaussian-splatting-training-loop.md]. Accelerates training by reducing redundant computations [15697-turbogs.md]. Optimizes training by focusing on high-error pixels [15708-error-guided-sparse-pixel-sampling.md]. Manages resolution during training [15751-frequency-guided-resolution-scheduler.md]. Uses multi-view consistency constraints [15783-multi-view-regulated-gaussian-splatting.md]. Handles mip-mapping for anti-aliasing [17975-mip-splatting-training-loop-evaluation-pipeline.md]. Parallelizes training [18650-distributed-3dgs-training-loop-with-adaptive-workload-divisi.md]. Gradually increases spherical harmonics order [18689-sparse-sh-order-increment.md]. Uses Fisher information for regularization [18747-regression-based-fisherrf.md]. Defines the schedule for primitive addition/removal [18977-gaussian-primitive-training-schedule.md]. Details on loss components [19337-loss-function-design.md]. Optimizes subsets of Gaussians [20073-local-3dgs-optimization.md]. Fast reconstruction methods [20247-immediate-3d-gaussian-splat-reconstruction.md]. Selects views for training [20899-active-view-selection-and-residual-learning-for-3dgs.md]. Uses uncertainty for training [20901-uncertainty-guided-residual-learning-for-3dgs.md]. SLAM integration [21005-submap-based-gaussian-slam-mapping.md]. Neural network-based Gaussian parameters [21236-neural-parametric-gaussians-optimization.md]. General optimization techniques [22286-3d-gaussian-splatting-optimization.md]. Techniques to modify gradients [22461-gradient-modification.md]. Time Complexity: Dominated by the diffusion model inference (UNet forward pass) per iteration. Rendering is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. Memory Complexity: High due to storing the diffusion model in memory and gradients for all Gaussian parameters. Performance: Training is significantly slower than photometric methods due to the heavy diffusion model overhead. However, it produces semantically consistent results from few or single views. Strengths: Does not require multi-view input; leverages powerful 2D priors. Limitations: Slow training; potential for "smearing" artifacts if guidance scale is too high; sensitive to prompt quality. When to use: Single-view reconstruction, text-to-3D, or sparse-view scenarios where photometric loss is insufficient. When not to use: Dense multi-view capture where photometric loss is more efficient and accurate. Originated from the application of Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) to 3D Gaussian Splatting, allowing the optimization of Gaussian primitives using pretrained diffusion models. This approach bridges the gap between 2D generative models and 3D representation learning. The method was popularized by works such as "Diffusion-guided 3D Representations", which demonstrated the feasibility of optimizing Gaussians directly with SDS loss.
