name: Regression-based FisherRF
head: FisherRF with meta-regression, Modified FisherRF
body: Regression-based FisherRF is a variant of the FisherRF uncertainty estimation method that replaces the direct aggregation of color parameter variances with a meta-regression model to predict pixel-wise uncertainty. While standard FisherRF estimates uncertainty by summing the variances of all spherical harmonic parameters to determine color direction-dependence, this method groups Gaussian primitive parameter variances into six distinct categories and feeds them as feature maps into a regression network. It is primarily used as a baseline for comparing uncertainty estimation quality in scene separation and out-of-scene generalization experiments. Inputs: The set of N 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}{i=1}^N optimized during training. For each primitive gi, the variance of its parameters: mean \mathbf{p}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, rotation \mathbf{q}i, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}{i, l}. Outputs: A set of six uncertainty feature maps, one for each parameter group, which serve as input to a regression model to predict pixel-wise uncertainty. Data Structures: The method relies on grouping the variances of Gaussian parameters into six specific categories, originating from the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting implementation: 1. Mean: Variance of the position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. 2. Scale: Variance of the scale vector \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. 3. Rotation: Variance of the rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4. 4. Opacity: Variance of the opacity scalar \alphai \in [0, 1]. 5. SH Degree 0: Variance of the spherical harmonic coefficients for degree zero (view-independent color). 6. SH Higher Degree: Variance of the spherical harmonic coefficients for degrees >0 (view-dependent color). Note that the Scale and Rotation groups correspond to the covariance matrix \Sigmai of the primitive. Steps: 1. Compute Parameter Variances: For each Gaussian primitive gi, calculate the variance of each parameter group. Let Var(\cdot) denote the variance operator. V{mean, i} = Var(\mathbf{p}i) V{scale, i} = Var(\mathbf{s}i) V{rot, i} = Var(\mathbf{q}i) V{op, i} = Var(\alphai) V{sh0, i} = Var(\mathbf{c}{i, 0}) V{sh>0, i} = Var(\{\mathbf{c}{i, l}\}{l > 0}) 2. Aggregate into Feature Maps: Project the variances of all N primitives onto the image plane using the standard differentiable rasterization/splatting pipeline. Aggregate the variances per pixel to form six uncertainty feature maps F1, \dots, F6. For a pixel u, the value of the k-th feature map is the sum of the variances of the k-th parameter group for all Gaussians splatting to u: Fk(u) = \sum{i \in \text{rasterized}(u)} V{groupk, i} where groupk \in \{mean, scale, rotation, opacity, sh0, sh>0\}. 3. Meta-Regression: Feed the six feature maps \{F1, \dots, F6\} into a regression model (e.g., a neural network). 4. Predict Uncertainty: The regression model outputs the predicted pixel-wise uncertainty. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def regressionbasedfisherrf(gaussians, rasterizer, regressionmodel): """ gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives with parameters p, s, q, alpha, csh rasterizer: Function that projects 3D Gaussians to 2D image plane regressionmodel: A neural network taking 6 input channels and outputting uncertainty """ # Step 1: Compute variances for each primitive # Note: In practice, these variances are obtained from the optimizer's state # or accumulated gradients during training. variances = [] for g in gaussians: vmean = computevariance(g.p) vscale = computevariance(g.s) vrot = computevariance(g.q) vop = computevariance(g.alpha) vsh0 = computevariance(g.csh[0]) vshhigh = computevariance(g.csh[1:]) # All degrees > 0 variances.append({ 'mean': vmean, 'scale': vscale, 'rotation': vrot, 'opacity': vop, 'sh0': vsh0, 'shhigh': vshhigh }) # Step 2: Aggregate variances into 6 feature maps # The rasterizer must support accumulating variance values, not just opacity/color featuremaps = [0.0] 6 for g in gaussians: v = variances[g.index] # Project variances to image plane # This step assumes a custom rasterizer that accumulates variance sums # similar to how it accumulates opacity and color projected = rasterizer.projectvariancesum(g, v) # Add projected variance to the corresponding feature map channels # Assuming projected is a tensor of shape (H, W, 6) or similar featuremaps[0] += projected['mean'] featuremaps[1] += projected['scale'] featuremaps[2] += projected['rotation'] featuremaps[3] += projected['opacity'] featuremaps[4] += projected['sh0'] featuremaps[5] += projected['shhigh'] # Step 3: Feed feature maps into regression model # Stack the 6 feature maps into a single tensor of shape (6, H, W) inputtensor = torch.stack(featuremaps, dim=0) # Step 4: Predict uncertainty predicteduncertainty = regressionmodel(inputtensor) return predicteduncertainty def computevariance(param): # Placeholder for the specific variance calculation method. # In the context of FisherRF, this typically refers to the diagonal # entries of the Fisher Information Matrix or the optimizer's # accumulated second-moment estimates. return param.variance Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Variance Calculation: The method assumes access to the variance of the Gaussian parameters. In standard 3DGS, these are not explicitly stored as simple scalars but are derived from the Fisher Information Matrix or optimizer states. The exact computation of Var(\cdot) for quaternion and SH coefficients requires careful handling of their non-Euclidean or high-dimensional nature. Rasterization of Variance: Standard splatting rasterizers accumulate opacity and color. A custom rasterizer is required to accumulate the sum of variances for each parameter group per pixel. Grouping Consistency: The grouping must strictly follow the six categories defined in the original GS implementation to ensure fair comparison with other methods. Complexity: The method adds the overhead of a regression model inference step on top of the standard rasterization. The rasterization step itself must be modified to accumulate six variance channels instead of just opacity and color, increasing memory bandwidth and compute slightly. Performance: No specific quantitative performance metrics (FPS, memory usage) are provided in the sources. Strengths: Aligns the uncertainty estimation pipeline with modern meta-regression approaches (like PRIMU), allowing for fair comparison of feature map quality. Separates uncertainty sources by parameter type (e.g., position vs. color), potentially providing more granular uncertainty signals than the original FisherRF which sums all color variances. Limitations: Requires a custom rasterizer and a trained regression model, adding complexity compared to the direct summation method of original FisherRF. Origin: Regression-based FisherRF was introduced in the study of Uncertainty Estimation (UE) for Gaussian Splatting, specifically in the context of the PRIMU method. History: It is a modification of the original FisherRF method [11], which is based on the Fisher information matrix of a Gaussian Splatting primitive with respect to the gradient of the rendering function. The original FisherRF used the sum of color parameter variances (including all SH parameters) to estimate direction-dependent uncertainty. Usage: It is used as a baseline for UE scene separation studies and out-of-scene generalization experiments. name: Gaussian Primitive Training Schedule
head: Reduced Iteration Schedule with Pseudo-View Depth Optimization
body: This method accelerates the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting by leveraging dense initial point clouds to significantly reduce the required optimization iterations. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by replacing the long, continuous densification process with a two-phase training loop interrupted by pseudo-view depth optimization, reducing total iterations from ~300,000 to ~6,000. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sufficiently dense initial point cloud (e.g., from a structure-from-motion pipeline or generative model), a set of input views, and a target number of iterations. Output: Optimized Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} with refined positions, scales, opacities, and colors. Data Structures: The Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}{i=1}^N are stored as in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting. Each primitive gi contains: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance \Sigmai, parameterized by rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 and scale vector \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Spherical Harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}{i, l} for view-dependent color Parameters: Total iterations: 6,000 (split into two 3,000-iteration phases). Initial densification freeze: First 1,500 iterations. Densification frequency: Once every 500 iterations after the initial phase. Optimizer: Adam (\beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.99). Loss: \mathcal{L}{img} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}{L1} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} with \lambda = 0.2. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussian primitives from the dense point cloud. 2. Phase 1 Training: Train for 3,000 iterations. Disable densification (growing/pruning) for the first 1,500 iterations. Apply densification once every 500 iterations for iterations 1,501–3,000, following the strategy from AbsGS. 3. Pseudo-View Generation: Render RGB images for a set of "pseudo views" (additional camera poses not present in the input dataset). 4. Depth Optimization: Perform depth optimization specifically for these pseudo views to refine the geometry and depth consistency. 5. Phase 2 Training: Continue training for another 3,000 iterations. Maintain the densification schedule (once every 500 iterations). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traingaussianprimitives(points, inputviews, pseudoviews, totaliters=6000): # Initialize Gaussians from dense points gaussians = initializegaussians(points) # Phase 1: Initial Training for iter in range(3000): # Densification control if iter < 1500: densify = False elif (iter - 1500) % 500 == 0: densify = True else: densify = False # Standard training step with densification if enabled renderimage = render(gaussians, inputviews) loss = computeloss(renderimage, inputviews.gt) optimize(gaussians, loss, densify=densify) # Intermediate Step: Pseudo-View Depth Optimization renderpseudorgb = render(gaussians, pseudoviews) optimizedepth(gaussians, pseudoviews, renderpseudorgb) # Phase 2: Final Training for iter in range(3000, 6000): # Densification control if (iter - 1500) % 500 == 0: densify = True else: densify = False renderimage = render(gaussians, inputviews) loss = computeloss(renderimage, inputviews.gt) optimize(gaussians, loss, densify=densify) return gaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dense Initialization Dependency: This schedule relies on "sufficiently dense point clouds" for initialization. If the initial point cloud is sparse, the reduced iteration count may lead to under-converged results. Densification Timing: Applying densification too early (before 1,500 iterations) is explicitly avoided to prevent instability or unnecessary primitive proliferation. The CompGS training loop is the optimization procedure for 3D Gaussian Splatting that incorporates auxiliary parameters and adaptive control mechanisms to refine Gaussian primitives. Time Complexity: Significantly reduced training time. Requires ~6,000 iterations compared to ~300,000 for conventional 3D Gaussian Splatting. Memory Complexity: Similar to standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, as the number of primitives is determined by the initial dense cloud and densification schedule. Performance: Achieves satisfactory results with the reduced iteration budget. Hardware: Experiments conducted on NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. Strengths: Drastic reduction in training time; effective for scenes with good initial geometry. Limitations: Relies on high-quality dense initialization; may not generalize well to sparse input scenarios without modification. This method is described in the context of Generative Bundle Refinement (GBR) for high-fidelity Gaussian Splatting with enhanced mesh reconstruction. It builds on the observation that dense initial point clouds allow for faster convergence, enabling a truncated training schedule with intermediate geometric refinement via pseudo views. name: CompGS Training Loop
head: CompGS Training
body: The CompGS training loop is the optimization procedure for 3D Gaussian Splatting that incorporates auxiliary parameters and adaptive control mechanisms to refine Gaussian primitives. It solves the problem of static Gaussian initialization by iteratively updating positions, scales, opacities, colors, and auxiliary features through a differentiable rendering pipeline. It is distinguished from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by the explicit management of auxiliary parameters (updated via a separate optimizer) and a specific adaptive control schedule for pruning and growing primitives based on view-dependent error metrics. Inputs: Dataset of training views, where each sample contains: image tensor, image dimensions (H, W), tangent half-FOV (\tan(\text{fov}x), \tan(\text{fov}y)), camera center, camera index, world-to-view matrix, and world-to-image projection matrix. Initial Gaussian model initialized from sparse point clouds (Structure-from-Motion). Configuration parameters: maxiterations, ssimweight, stopiteration, controlbaseinterval, numtrainingviews, auxupdateenable, controlstartbaseinterval, voxelsize, derivefactor, and ref/res feature/hyper dimensions. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian model parameters (means, scales, opacities, colors, auxiliary features). Evaluation metrics (per-view PSNR calculated via MSE). GaussianModel: Stores parameters for N Gaussians. Fields include means (\mathbb{R}^3), scales (\mathbb{R}^3), opacities (\mathbb{R}), colors (\mathbb{R}^3 or spherical harmonics coefficients), and auxiliary parameters (dimensions defined in config). RenderSettings: Struct containing camidx, imageheight, imagewidth, tanfovx, tanfovy, campos, viewmatrix, projmatrix. RenderResults: Struct containing renderedimg (tensor), predicttime, rendertime. Optimizers: WarpedAdam instances for main Gaussian parameters and auxiliary parameters. 1. Initialization: Initialize dataset, Gaussian model (with voxelsize, derivefactor, ref/res feature/hyper dimensions), and optimizers (WarpedAdam for main and auxiliary params). 2. Model Initialization: Initialize the Gaussian model from sparse SfM point clouds. 3. Training Loop (for iteration i from 0 to maxiterations): Select a random view sample. Update learning rate. Render the scene with specific camera settings (camidx, image dimensions, FOV, camera position, view/projection matrices). Retain gradients only if iteration < stopiteration. Compute rendering loss as weighted sum of L1 loss and SSIM loss: L{\text{render}} = (1 - \text{ssim\weight}) L{\text{L1}} + \text{ssim\weight} L{\text{SSIM}}. Compute regularization loss as 0.01 \times \text{mean}(\prod \text{scales}) (volume proxy) across all Gaussians. Update auxiliary parameters if auxupdateenable is true and iteration is within range (controlstartbaseinterval to stopiteration). Remove auxiliary parameters if iteration == stopiteration. Step and zero gradients for both gaussianoptimizer and auxoptimizer. Perform adaptive control (pruning/growing) if enabled, iteration is within range, and iteration % (controlbaseinterval numtrainingviews) == 0. 4. Evaluation: After training, evaluate by rendering all views, saving original and rendered images, and calculating per-view PSNR using MSE: \text{PSNR} = 10 \log{10}(1 / \text{MSE}). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F class RenderSettings: def init(self, camidx, imageheight, imagewidth, tanfovx, tanfovy, campos, viewmatrix, projmatrix): self.camidx = camidx self.imageheight = imageheight self.imagewidth = imagewidth self.tanfovx = tanfovx self.tanfovy = tanfovy self.campos = campos self.viewmatrix = viewmatrix self.projmatrix = projmatrix class WarpedAdam: def init(self, params): self.params = params def step(self): for p in self.params: if p.grad is not None: p.data -= p.grad def zerograd(self): for p in self.params: if p.grad is not None: p.grad.zero() def ssim(rendered, target, datarange=1.0): # Computes structural similarity index; returns value in [0, 1] return 1.0 - F.mseloss(rendered, target) def updatelrmeans(optimizer, lrupdateconfigs, maxiterations, iteration): # Updates learning rates for Gaussian means based on schedule pass def adaptivecontrolstep(model, iteration): # Prunes low-opacity Gaussians and grows high-error Gaussians pass def evaluateandsave(dataset, model, config): # Renders all views, saves images, calculates per-view PSNR pass def traincompgs(dataset, gaussianmodel, config): gaussianoptimizer = WarpedAdam(gaussianmodel.mainparams) auxoptimizer = WarpedAdam(gaussianmodel.auxparams) if config.auxupdateenable else None stopiteration = config.adaptivecontrol.stopiteration ssimweight = config.training.ssimweight numtrainingviews = dataset.numtrainingviews controlbaseinterval = config.controlbaseinterval controlstartbaseinterval = config.controlstartbaseinterval for iteration in range(config.maxiterations): sample = dataset.getrandomsample() updatelrmeans(gaussianoptimizer, gaussianmodel.getlrconfigs(config), config.maxiterations, iteration) rendersettings = RenderSettings( camidx=sample.camidx, imageheight=sample.imageheight, imagewidth=sample.imagewidth, tanfovx=sample.tanhalffovx, tanfovy=sample.tanhalffovy, campos=sample.cameracenter, viewmatrix=sample.worldtoviewprojmat, projmatrix=sample.worldtoimageprojmat) retaingrad = iteration < stopiteration renderresults = gaussianmodel.render(rendersettings, retaingrad=retaingrad) l1loss = F.l1loss(renderresults.renderedimg, sample.img) ssimloss = 1.0 - ssim(renderresults.renderedimg.unsqueeze(0), sample.img.unsqueeze(0), datarange=1.0) renderingloss = (1.0 - ssimweight) l1loss + ssimweight ssimloss volumeproxy = torch.prod(gaussianmodel.scales, dim=-1) regloss = 0.01 torch.mean(volumeproxy) totalloss = renderingloss + regloss if auxoptimizer is not None and config.auxupdateenable and iteration >= controlstartbaseinterval and iteration < stopiteration: totalloss.backward(retaingraph=True) auxoptimizer.step() auxoptimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() gaussianoptimizer.step() gaussianoptimizer.zerograd() if config.adaptivecontrol.enabled and iteration < stopiteration and iteration % (controlbaseinterval numtrainingviews) == 0: adaptivecontrolstep(gaussianmodel, iteration) if iteration == stopiteration and auxoptimizer is not None: gaussianmodel.removeauxparams() evaluateandsave(dataset, gaussianmodel, config) Gradient Retention: Gradients must not be retained after stopiteration to save memory, but must be retained during the adaptive control phase if it occurs after the main optimization loop's gradient-free phase. Auxiliary Parameter Timing: Auxiliary parameters are only updated within a specific iteration range (controlstartbaseinterval to stopiteration). Precision: PSNR calculation involves \log{10}(1/\text{MSE}). If MSE is zero (perfect reconstruction), this results in infinity. A small epsilon should be added to MSE in practice. Separates backward stages and releases intermediate buffers early to reduce peak working set while retaining direct gradient accumulation. Raster caches are released before projection backward while retaining 3DGS’s direct gradient accumulation. Reduces mean working set to 7.64 GiB and warm-pass time from 12.19 to 11.35 seconds on the Bicycle 15K model. Separates raster and later gradient peaks, unlike the Original method where they overlap, allowing coordinated buffer lifetime management. Time Complexity: Dominated by the differentiable rendering step per iteration; adaptive control adds overhead proportional to the number of primitives. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of Gaussians and auxiliary parameter dimensions. Performance: Uses WarpedAdam optimizer; stage separation variant reduces mean working set to 7.64 GiB and warm-pass time to 11.35 s on Bicycle 15K. Strengths: Adaptive control allows dynamic refinement of the Gaussian set; auxiliary parameters enable more complex feature representations. Limitations: Complexity of managing two optimizers and specific iteration schedules. The CompGS training loop is part of the CompGS (Compressed Gaussian Splatting) framework, which extends 3D Gaussian Splatting with compression and auxiliary parameter handling. It was introduced in the unofficial repository by Liu Xiangrui. name: Loss Function Design
body: This article defines the composite loss function \mathcal{L} minimized during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting models, which drives the optimization of Gaussian primitives to match ground-truth observations. It establishes the standard photometric baseline and provides the structural framework for extending this baseline with geometric, semantic, or consistency constraints via sibling methods. It differs from 3D Gaussian Splatting Training Loop by focusing specifically on the mathematical formulation and weighting of the loss terms rather than the iteration schedule or densification logic. The core mechanism common to all training loops in this family is the minimization of a composite loss function \mathcal{L} between the rendered image \hat{I} and the ground-truth image I{gt}. The standard photometric baseline is a weighted sum of L1 loss and differentiable Structural Similarity (D-SSIM): \mathcal{L}{img} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}{L1} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} where \mathcal{L}{L1} is the average absolute difference between corresponding pixel colors, and \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} measures local structure, contrast, and texture. The weight \lambda is typically 0.2. The optimization uses the Adam optimizer with \beta1 = 0.9 and \beta2 = 0.99. Training typically runs for a fixed number of iterations, commonly around 30,000 for standard scenes, though specific schedules vary (e.g., Gaussian Primitive Training Schedule uses ~6,000). The process does not stop at a specific loss threshold because the loss curve continues to creep down with diminishing returns; a fixed iteration budget is used instead. Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}{i=1}^N include position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \Sigmai (parameterized by rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 and scale vector \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3), opacity \alphai \in [0, 1], and Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients \mathbf{c}{i, l} for view-dependent color. Enforces geometric and photometric agreement between matched Gaussians across different views to solve sparse-view ambiguity. Unlike standard photometric losses, it operates directly on Gaussian parameters (centroids, covariances, opacities, SH) using world-space transformations and log-eigenvalue comparisons to prevent geometric degeneracy. Aligns rendered 3D semantic fields with distilled 2D vision-language feature maps. It extends the loss composite with a contrastive semantic loss and spatial total variation regularization to handle noise in distilled features and enable open-world scene representation. A regularization term that encourages the 3D Gaussians to align well with the surface of the scene. It is applied after a short vanilla 3DGS optimization phase to prepare for mesh extraction via Poisson reconstruction. A composite loss for Gaussian updates consisting of a guided subset term (L{sub}) and a full loss (L{full}). The variant without full loss tends to oversmooth low-confidence regions and cause high-frequency detail loss, while the variant with full loss reinforces these regions to prevent under-updated Gaussians from collapsing. The standard photometric loss formulation (L1 + SSIM) is the foundational training objective for 3D Gaussian Splatting. The SuGaR regularization term was introduced to address the difficulty of extracting meshes from unorganized 3D Gaussians by enforcing surface alignment. The SA-ResGS loss was developed to improve next-best-view selection and reconstruction in sparse or ambiguous regions by combining residual supervision with uncertainty-guided view selection. name: Multi-Attribute Consistency (MAC) Loss
head: MAC loss
body: The Multi-Attribute Consistency (MAC) loss is a regularization objective for 3D Gaussian Splatting that enforces geometric and photometric agreement between matched Gaussians across different views. It solves the ambiguity problem in sparse-view reconstruction by using high-confidence 2D pixel correspondences as anchors to jointly constrain position, shape, and appearance in a common world coordinate frame. Unlike standard photometric losses that only compare rendered pixels, MAC loss operates directly on the underlying Gaussian parameters, providing robust supervision that respects the geometry of covariance matrices and prevents geometric degeneracy. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pair of training images (I1, I2), their camera-to-world transformation matrices T{wc}^v = [\mathbf{R}^v | \mathbf{t}^v] (ground truth during training, estimated at test time), and a set of matched pixel pairs \mathcal{M} = \{(\mathbf{p}1^k, \mathbf{p}2^k)\}{k=1}^K with associated joint confidence scores wk. Outputs: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{MAC} and gradients with respect to the Gaussian parameters (centroids, covariances, opacities, SH coefficients) predicted by the network. Data Structures: For each view v \in \{1, 2\}, the method predicts dense parameter maps aligned with a descriptor grid. At any grid coordinate (u, v), the predicted Gaussian primitive G^v(u,v) consists of: Centroid: \boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{cam}}^{v} \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance: \mathbf{\Sigma}{\text{cam}}^{v} \in \text{Sym}^+(3) (symmetric positive-definite 3 \times 3 matrix) Opacity: \alpha^v \in [0, 1] Spherical Harmonics coefficients: \mathbf{c}^v Numbered Steps: 1. Gaussian Sampling: For each matched pixel pair k with coordinates (\mathbf{p}1^k, \mathbf{p}2^k), bilinearly sample the predicted parameter maps at these coordinates to obtain two Gaussians G1^k and G2^k. Gk^v = \left( \boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{cam}}^{v,k}, \mathbf{\Sigma}{\text{cam}}^{v,k}, \alpha^{v,k}, \mathbf{c}^{v,k} \right), \quad v \in \{1, 2\} 2. World-Space Transformation: Transform the sampled parameters from the camera frame to the common world coordinate system using the camera-to-world matrix T{wc}^v = [\mathbf{R}^v | \mathbf{t}^v]. Centroid: \boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{world}}^{v,k} = \mathbf{R}^v \boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{cam}}^{v,k} + \mathbf{t}^v Covariance: \mathbf{\Sigma}{\text{world}}^{v,k} = \mathbf{R}^v \mathbf{\Sigma}{\text{cam}}^{v,k} (\mathbf{R}^v)^\top 3. Positional Consistency: Compute the L1 distance between the world-space centroids. Apply Huber loss \mathcal{H}(\cdot) to the distance. This term is evaluated only if the camera-space z-coordinate of both centroids is positive (z{\text{cam}} > 0). \mathcal{L}{\text{pos}}^{(k)} = \mathcal{H}\left( \|\boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{world}}^{1,k} - \boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{world}}^{2,k}\|1 \right) 4. Shape Consistency: Compare the covariance matrices in the world frame. To respect the geometry of the manifold \text{Sym}^+(3) and ensure invariance to rotation and uniform scaling, the loss uses the difference of log-eigenvalues rather than Euclidean distance between matrices. Let \lambda1^{v,k} and \lambda2^{v,k} be the eigenvalues of \mathbf{\Sigma}{\text{world}}^{1,k} and \mathbf{\Sigma}{\text{world}}^{2,k} respectively. The shape loss is defined as the Huber loss of the difference of the log-eigenvalues: \mathcal{L}{\text{shape}}^{(k)} = \mathcal{H}\left( \|\log(\lambda1^{v,k}) - \log(\lambda2^{v,k})\|1 \right) (Note: The source specifies comparing log-eigenvalues to prevent geometric degeneracy, where the gradient scales as 1/\lambda.) 5. Appearance Consistency: Compute the L1 distance between the opacities and the Spherical Harmonics coefficients. \mathcal{L}{\text{app}}^{(k)} = \|\alpha^{1,k} - \alpha^{2,k}\|1 + \|\mathbf{c}^{1,k} - \mathbf{c}^{2,k}\|1 6. Aggregation: Combine the terms using the joint confidence wk of the match and scalar weights \lambdap, \lambdas, \lambdaa. A small constant \epsilon prevents division by zero. \mathcal{L}{\text{MAC}} = \frac{\sum{k=1}^{K} wk \left( \lambdap \mathcal{L}{\text{pos}}^{(k)} + \lambdas \mathcal{L}{\text{shape}}^{(k)} + \lambdaa \mathcal{L}{\text{app}}^{(k)} \right)}{\sum{k=1}^{K} wk + \epsilon} Parameters: \lambdap, \lambdas, \lambdaa: Scalar weights for positional, shape, and appearance consistency. Values not given in the sources. \epsilon: Small constant to prevent division by zero. Value not given in the sources. wk: Joint confidence of the k-th matched pixel pair. Derived from the semantic fusion module and confidence gating threshold \tau{\text{conf}}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometric Degeneracy: As a Gaussian's smallest eigenvalue \lambda{\min} approaches zero, the gradient of the log-eigenvalue shape loss scales inversely with \lambda (|\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial \lambda| \propto 1/\lambda). This creates a strong repulsive effect that pushes \lambda{\min} away from zero, preventing collapsed, needle-like artifacts. Ambiguous Regions: If no match survives the confidence gating (wk > \tau{\text{conf}}), the MAC loss for that region falls back to zero, allowing the network to rely solely on photometric supervision. Coordinate System: Covariance matrices must be transformed using the rotation component \mathbf{R} only, not the full affine transform, to maintain symmetry. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of matched pixel pairs K and the number of attributes (position, shape, appearance). The bilinear sampling and eigenvalue decomposition are the dominant operations per match. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the dense parameter maps for the input views and the set of matches \mathcal{M}. Strengths: Robust to outliers due to Huber loss and confidence weighting; prevents geometric degeneracy; improves performance in sparse-view and low-overlap regimes. Limitations: Requires reliable 2D correspondences (provided by MASt3R/DINOv3); relies on accurate camera poses (ground truth during training). When to use: Sparse-view reconstruction where photometric loss alone leads to ambiguities or artifacts. When not to use: Dense-view scenarios where photometric loss is sufficient, or when 2D correspondence estimation is unreliable. The MAC loss was introduced in "MAC-Splat: Multi-Attribute Consistency for High-Fidelity Sparse-View Reconstruction" by J. Yang et al.. It builds on the MASt3R geometric backbone and a frozen DINOv3 encoder to obtain semantically informed 2D correspondences. The method was developed to address the limitations of conventional losses in sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting, particularly under different overlap regimes. Experiments on ScanNet++ demonstrated that MAC-Splat outperforms strong baselines like Splatt3R, improving average PSNR by more than 4.5 dB and reducing LPIPS. name: Cross-Modal Alignment Optimization Strategy
head: Semantic Gaussian Alignment, Vision-Language Gaussian Optimization
body: This strategy aligns rendered 3D semantic fields with distilled 2D vision-language feature maps to enable open-world scene representation. It distinguishes itself from standard photometric-only training by incorporating a contrastive semantic loss and spatial regularization, preventing the optimization instabilities caused by noise in distilled features. It builds on Loss Function Design by extending the loss composite with semantic and geometric terms. Inputs: Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}{i=1}^N initialized from a sparse point cloud. Ground-truth images I{gt}. Distilled dense feature maps F{gt} obtained from a fine-tuned vision transformer processing multi-view input images. Camera parameters for rendering. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients, and semantic embeddings). Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive gi: Contains position \mathbf{p}i, covariance \Sigmai (from quaternion \mathbf{q}i and scale \mathbf{s}i), opacity \alphai, SH coefficients \mathbf{c}{i,l}, and a semantic embedding vector \mathbf{e}i. The dimensionality of the distilled vision-language vectors is 512. Distilled Feature Map: A dense 2D map of 512-dimensional vectors aligned with image pixels. Parameters: Photometric Loss Weight: 0.8. Optimizer: Adam (\beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.99). Iterations: 100 iterations are cited for specific feature distillation phases, though general training may vary. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussian primitives using a sparse point cloud generated by standard Structure-from-Motion (SfM) algorithms. 2. Feature Distillation: Process input images through a modified vision transformer fine-tuned for dense prediction to generate multi-scale, localized semantic feature maps F{gt}. 3. Rendering: Rasterize the Gaussian primitives to produce a rendered color image \hat{I} and a rendered semantic embedding map \hat{E}. 4. Photometric Loss: Compute the discrepancy between \hat{I} and I{gt} using a combination of L1 loss and Structural Similarity (SSIM). 5. Semantic Alignment Loss: Compute a contrastive loss between the rendered pixel embedding \hat{e}p and the ground truth feature vector f{gt} at the corresponding pixel location. 6. Geometric Regularization: Apply spatial total variation regularization to the semantic embeddings of neighboring Gaussians to encourage regional smoothness. 7. Optimization: Update all Gaussian parameters via stochastic gradient descent using the Adam optimizer. 8. Adaptive Densification: Periodically identify under-reconstructed regions (high gradients or errors) and clone small Gaussians or split large ones. Formulas: The total loss \mathcal{L}{total} is a weighted combination: \mathcal{L}{total} = \lambda{photo} \mathcal{L}{photo} + \lambda{sem} \mathcal{L}{sem} + \lambda{reg} \mathcal{L}{reg} Where: \mathcal{L}{photo} is the photometric loss (L1 + SSIM). The weight \lambda{photo} is 0.8. \mathcal{L}{sem} is the semantic alignment loss. It uses a contrastive mechanism: \mathcal{L}{sem} = - \cos(\hat{e}p, f{gt}) + \sum{j \in \mathcal{N}{neg}} \cos(\hat{e}p, fj) Where \cos(\cdot, \cdot) is cosine similarity, \hat{e}p is the rendered embedding, f{gt} is the ground truth feature, and the sum is over negative samples fj from spatially distant or visually dissimilar regions. \mathcal{L}{reg} is the spatial total variation regularization on semantic embeddings of neighboring Gaussians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def crossmodalalignmentstep(gaussians, images, featuremaps, cameras): # 1. Render renderedcolor, renderedsemantics = rendergaussians(gaussians, cameras) # 2. Photometric Loss # L1 and SSIM between renderedcolor and images l1loss = meanabsoluteerror(renderedcolor, images) ssimloss = 1.0 - ssimindex(renderedcolor, images) lphoto = l1loss + ssimloss # 3. Semantic Alignment Loss (Contrastive) # For each pixel, compare rendered semantic embedding with distilled feature # and minimize similarity with negative samples lsem = 0.0 for pixel in pixels: erendered = renderedsemantics[pixel] fgt = featuremaps[pixel] # Maximize similarity with ground truth possim = cosinesimilarity(erendered, fgt) # Minimize similarity with negative samples (distant/dissimilar regions) negsamples = getnegativesamples(pixel, featuremaps) negsim = sum(cosinesimilarity(erendered, fneg) for fneg in negsamples) lsem += -possim + negsim lsem /= numpixels # 4. Geometric Regularization (Spatial Total Variation) # Encourage smoothness in semantic embeddings of neighboring Gaussians lreg = 0.0 for gaussian in gaussians: neighbors = getneighboringgaussians(gaussian) for neighbor in neighbors: lreg += abs(gaussian.semanticembedding - neighbor.semanticembedding) # 5. Total Loss lambdaphoto = 0.8 lambdasem = 1.0 # Not specified, assumed 1.0 for normalization or relative weighting lambdareg = 0.1 # Not specified, assumed small weight for regularization totalloss = lambdaphoto lphoto + lambdasem lsem + lambdareg lreg # 6. Update updategaussianswithgradients(gaussians, totalloss) # 7. Adaptive Densification (Periodic) if step % densificationinterval == 0: densifygaussians(gaussians, gradients, errors) return totalloss Complexity: Adds overhead for feature map generation and contrastive loss computation. The contrastive loss requires identifying negative samples, increasing per-step computation compared to simple L1 semantic loss. Strengths: Prevents optimization instability caused by noise in distilled feature maps by using relative similarity (contrastive) rather than absolute distance (MSE). Eliminates boundary bleeding issues in semantic fields by leveraging photometric loss for spatial accuracy. Limitations: Requires pre-computed dense feature maps from a vision-language model, adding a preprocessing step. Sensitive to the choice of negative sampling strategy for the contrastive loss. When to use: When open-world semantic understanding is required alongside geometric reconstruction. When not to use: When only photometric accuracy is needed, or when computational resources for feature distillation are unavailable. Originated in the paper "Open-World 3D Vision-Language Scene Representation with Gaussian Splatting and Cross-Modal Alignment". It addresses the limitation of global image embeddings from vision-language models by using multi-scale feature distillation for localized semantic granularity. It replaces simple MSE for semantic loss with contrastive loss to handle noise in distilled features. Open-World 3D Vision-Language Scene Representation with Gaussian Splatting and Cross-Modal Alignment, https://doi.org/10.66238/jaiec72, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Immediate 3D Gaussian Splat Reconstruction
head: Immediate 3D Gaussian Splat Reconstruction Pipeline, Incremental 3D Gaussian Splatting Reconstruction, Incremental 3DGS with Loop Closure, Main Pipeline for Immediate 3D Gaussian Splat Reconstruction, Real-time 3DGS Reconstruction, Streaming 3D Gaussian Splatting Pipeline, Two-Level Matching 3DGS
body: Immediate 3D Gaussian Splat Reconstruction is a streaming pipeline that processes an unordered sequence of RGB images to produce a real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model. It solves the problem of incremental reconstruction from unordered inputs by maintaining global consistency through loop closure and a covisibility graph, while optimizing Gaussian primitives in real-time. Unlike batch reconstruction methods, it interleaves matching, pose estimation, and Gaussian placement with a fixed local optimization window, keeping the delay between capture and processing start below the time to handle two keyframes (<0.8 s). It distinguishes itself from other training loops by its explicit handling of disjoint sequences via shelving and its linear-scaling fast bundle adjustment, which restricts landmark observations to covisibility-based subsets rather than all keyframes in the window. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A stream of unordered RGB images \{I1, I2, \dots\}. Output: A 3DGS reconstruction consisting of optimized Gaussian primitives and camera poses. Data Structures: 1. Registered Keyframes (M): A set of camera poses and images that have been successfully integrated into the global map. 2. Covisibility Graph (G{graph}): A triple (M, E, W) representing the set of registered keyframes, edges E between them, and edge weights W. 3. Active Gaussian Primitives (G{prims}): The set of 3D Gaussians currently in the scene. 4. Gaussian Hierarchy (H): A structure managing the spatial organization of Gaussians. 5. Shelf (Shelf): A buffer for unmatched frames that fail initial registration. Parameters: N=20: The fixed number of keyframes selected for local bundle adjustment. \tau{lc} = 5: The threshold for the minimum graph distance (hops) between clusters to trigger loop closure. \tauv: The threshold for the minimum number of valid matching pairs required to trigger loop closure. Welding Window (W): Defined as the union of the top N/2 keyframes from cluster C1 and the top N/2 keyframes from cluster C2. Implementers must distinguish them (e.g., G{graph} vs G{prims}) to avoid overwriting. Accumulated Drift: Without loop closure, accumulated drift causes Gaussians to be optimized incorrectly, introducing spiky artifacts and superimposition. Memory Constraints: While this method is efficient, related feed-forward methods like AnySplat run out of memory on high-end hardware (H100) for large scenes due to VRAM limitations and image size constraints (448x448). Initialize data structures M = set() # Registered keyframes Ggraph = (set(), set(), set()) # Covisibility graph (M, E, W) Gprims = set() # Active Gaussian primitives H = set() # Gaussian hierarchy Shelf = set() # Shelved unmatched frames # 2. Bootstrap the reconstruction # Process the first 8 well-connected keyframes to initialize the map bootstrapkeyframes = getfirst8wellconnectedimages(imagestream) for Iq in bootstrapkeyframes: processimage(Iq, M, Ggraph, Gprims, H, Shelf) # 3. Iterate over remaining incoming images for Iq in imagestream: processimage(Iq, M, Ggraph, Gprims, H, Shelf) def processimage(Iq, M, Ggraph, Gprims, H, Shelf): # 4. Two-Level Matching # Extract MixVPR and XFeat features for four rotations (0, 90, 180, 270 degrees) # Use MixVPR to detect orientation, then select corresponding XFeat features V, Kprime = TwoLevelMatching(Iq, M) # 5. Handle unmatched frames if not V: Shelf.add(Iq) return # 6. Update Covisibility Graph UpdateGraph(Ggraph, Iq, V) # 7. Loop Detection loop, C1, C2 = LoopDetection(Iq, Kprime, Ggraph) # 8. Local Bundle Adjustment # Select N=20 keyframes for optimization S = SelectKeyframes({Iq}, Ggraph, N=20) LocalBA(S, Gprims) # 9. Loop Closure Handling if loop: # Welding BA aligns the disjoint clusters WeldingBA(C1, C2, Ggraph) # Propagate corrections through the graph BackbonePropagation(Ggraph, C1, C2, Gprims) # 10. Place New Gaussians PlaceGaussians(Iq, Ggraph) # 11. Update State M.add(Iq) UpdateHierarchy(Ggraph, H, Iq) OptimizeGaussians(M, Ggraph) # 12. Retry Shelved Frames RetryShelved(Shelf, M, Ggraph) def TwoLevelMatching(Iq, M): # Extract features for 4 rotations features0 = ExtractFeatures(Iq, rot=0) features90 = ExtractFeatures(Iq, rot=90) features180 = ExtractFeatures(Iq, rot=180) features270 = ExtractFeatures(Iq, rot=270) # Detect orientation using MixVPR orientation = MixVPRDetect(Iq, M) # Select correct feature set based on orientation selectedfeatures = features0 if orientation == 0 else \ features90 if orientation == 90 else \ features180 if orientation == 180 else features270 # Match using XFeat V, Kprime = XFeatMatch(selectedfeatures, M) return V, Kprime def LoopDetection(Iq, Kprime, Ggraph): # Identify disjoint clusters in the visual neighborhood C1, C2 = FindClusters(Iq, Kprime, Ggraph) # Calculate graph distance between clusters dG = minshortestpathhops(C1, C2, Ggraph) # Check loop closure conditions if dG > 5 and min(len(C1), len(C2)) > tauv: return True, C1, C2 return False, None, None def WeldingBA(C1, C2, Ggraph): # Select anchor keyframes based on connectivity Ia1 = argmax{I in C1} connectivity(I, W) Ia2 = argmax{I in C2} connectivity(I, W) # Compute rigid transform between optimized and initial poses Tdelta = Taopt inverse(Tainit) # Estimate scale change from landmark depth variations sdelta = EstimateScaleChange(C1, C2) # Compose similarity transform Sdelta = Sim3(Tdelta, sdelta) # Optimize poses in the welding window LocalBA(W, Gprims) def BackbonePropagation(Ggraph, C1, C2, Gprims): # Build backbone path using Dijkstra's algorithm B = Dijkstra(Ia1, Ia2, Ggraph) # Interpolate transformation along backbone for Ib in B: alpha = distance(Ib, Ia2) / distance(Ia1, Ia2) # Interpolate rotation using 6D representation # Interpolate scale linearly: sdelta,b = sdelta ^ alpha Sdeltab = InterpSim3(Sdelta, alpha) # Apply to keyframes not in welding window for Ii not in W: Ibstar = argmin{Ib in B} distance(Ii, Ib) Tinew = Sdeltabstar Tiold # Update Gaussians based on new poses UpdateGaussians(Gprims) def LocalBA(S, Gprims): # Fast BA: Restrict landmark observations to covisibility-based subset # This scales linearly with N, unlike quadratic scaling in previous methods OptimizePosesAndGaussians(S, Gprims) Time Complexity: The method scales linearly with the number of keyframes in the local window by restricting landmark observations to a covisibility-based subset, avoiding the quadratic growth of previous fast BA solutions. The delay between capture and processing start is kept below 0.8 seconds. Memory Complexity: Efficient enough to run on standard GPUs, unlike feed-forward methods like AnySplat which require excessive VRAM for large scenes. Strengths: Real-time incremental reconstruction, robust to rotation via two-level matching, handles disjoint sequences via shelving, and corrects drift via loop closure. Limitations: Requires a bootstrap phase of 8 keyframes; performance depends on the quality of feature matching; shelved frames may delay full reconstruction if matching is poor. name: Active View Selection and Residual Learning for 3DGS
head: SA-ResGS (Self-augmented Residual 3D Gaussian Splatting), Self-augmented Residual 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: SA-ResGS is a training framework that combines active view selection with residual learning to improve 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstruction quality under sparse view conditions. It addresses the limitation that standard training with few views often fails to converge to high-fidelity models due to ambiguous geometry and lack of coverage. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Uncertainty-Guided Residual Learning for 3DGS by explicitly integrating a self-augmented pre-filtering mechanism (SA-HashGS) to stabilize the view selection process, ensuring that the residual supervision is applied to reliable, high-quality views rather than noisy candidates. SA-ResGS operates as an iterative training loop that alternates between Gaussian optimization and view selection. The method relies on the standard 3DGS optimization principles defined in Optimization and Training Loop, specifically the composite loss \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}{L1} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} with \lambda = 0.2. Inputs: A set of candidate training images V{cand}, a COLMAP SfM initialization (positions \mathbf{p}i, scales \mathbf{s}i, rotations \mathbf{q}i), and a fixed iteration budget. Outputs: A final set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} optimized for the selected subset of views V{sel} \subseteq V{cand}. The method maintains the standard 3DGS parameter set \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}{i=1}^N. Additionally, it utilizes a hash grid or point-based structure for the SA-HashGS component to estimate uncertainty, though the exact internal layout of the hash grid is not specified in the provided sources. The view selection mechanism relies on a direction-dependent coverage feature map with max aggregation and dropped opacity to guide selection. 1. Initialization: Initialize the Gaussian model \mathcal{G} using the provided COLMAP SfM points. Set the initial training view set V{sel} to 4 uniformly distributed views from the candidate set. 2. Training Loop: a. Render images from the current views V{sel} using the current \mathcal{G}. b. Compute the composite loss \mathcal{L} between rendered images and ground truth. c. Update \mathcal{G} using the Adam optimizer (\beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.99) for a fixed number of iterations (typically 20,000 total iterations are reported for the full schedule). 3. View Selection (Active View Selection): a. Evaluate the remaining candidate views V{cand} \setminus V{sel}. b. Use the SA-HashGS mechanism to estimate uncertainty/coverage for each candidate. This involves a self-augmented pre-filtering step that restricts the candidate set for Fisher uncertainty estimation. c. Select the view with the highest uncertainty/lowest coverage metric. 4. View Addition: Add the selected view to V{sel}. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-4 until V{sel} reaches the maximum limit (typically 20 views). 6. Residual Learning Integration: Throughout the training, the "ResGS" component applies residual supervision. This involves comparing the current reconstruction against a reference or previous state to guide optimization in sparse or ambiguous regions. The synergy between SA-HashGS and ResGS ensures that residual updates are based on stable view sequences. Initial Views: 4 uniformly distributed views. View Addition Schedule: Add 1 view every 100 epochs until reaching 20 training views. Total Iterations: 20,000 iterations per experiment. Random Seed: Fixed for reproducibility. SfM Initialization: Standard COLMAP SfM points. Uncertainty Quantification Error: Purely dynamic selection without the SA-HashGS stabilization (†+ResGS) can lead to poor performance if uncertainty estimates are noisy, especially under large uncertainty quantification errors. Hold-out Views: Unlike some other active view selection methods (e.g., PRIMU-AVS), SA-ResGS does not require a hold-out view for training a regressor, relying instead on the single direction-dependent coverage feature map. A specific view selection strategy used within SA-ResGS that uses a direction-dependent coverage feature map with max aggregation and dropped opacity, omitting the gradient boosting regressor found in other methods like PRIMU-AVS to avoid needing a hold-out view. Time Complexity: The method requires multiple training phases (one for each view addition), significantly increasing total training time compared to single-view-set training. Each phase runs for a portion of the 20,000 iterations. Memory Complexity: Standard 3DGS memory usage plus overhead for the SA-HashGS uncertainty estimation structures. Performance: SA-ResGS outperforms baselines like FisherRF, ACP, and random selection, as well as variants like †+ResGS (without SA-HashGS) and †+SA-HashGS (without ResGS). The full SA-ResGS configuration shows synergy, providing the best reconstruction quality in sparse view scenarios. Strengths: Improves reconstruction quality with fewer views; stabilizes view selection; avoids need for hold-out views. Limitations: Increased training time due to iterative view selection and re-optimization; sensitivity to the quality of the initial SfM reconstruction. SA-ResGS was introduced in the paper "SA-ResGS: Self-augmented Residual 3D Gaussian Splatting for Next Best View Selection". It builds upon the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework and addresses challenges in active view selection for 3D reconstruction. The method integrates concepts from residual learning and self-augmented pre-filtering to enhance the robustness of the view selection process. name: Active View Selection for 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: PRIMU Active View Selection, PRIMU-AVS
body: Active View Selection (AVS) for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) identifies a subset of training views that maximizes final reconstruction quality while limiting the total number of views used. PRIMU-AVS distinguishes itself from the full PRIMU method by omitting the gradient boosting regressor, thereby avoiding the need for an additional hold-out view for training. It relies on a single direction-dependent coverage feature map with max aggregation and dropped opacity to guide view selection. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of candidate training views with camera poses, and the current state of 3D Gaussian primitives (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) after a specified number of training iterations. Output: A selected training view from the candidates. Data Structures Coverage Feature Map (V{max}): A 2D image buffer with the same resolution as the target rendering. Each pixel stores a scalar value representing the maximum direction-dependent coverage of Gaussian primitives. Candidate Views: A list of camera poses excluding the currently selected training views and the reserved evaluation views. Parameters Total Training Views (N{\text{total}}): 20. Initial Views: 4 (1 fixed + 3 distance-maximized). Selection Interval: A new view is added after 100 \times N{\text{current}} iterations, where N{\text{current}} is the number of views already selected. Opacity Drop: Opacity is set to \alpha=1 (dropped) during coverage calculation. Steps 1. Initialization: Select one fixed view as the first training view, then select three additional views by maximizing the Euclidean distance to the camera centers of the existing views. 2. Initial Training: Begin training with these 4 views. 3. Iterative Selection: Continue training until the iteration count reaches the threshold for the next view selection. 4. Coverage Rendering: For each candidate view, render the V{max} feature map. 5. Scoring: Calculate the mean value across all pixels of the rendered map. 6. Selection: Select the candidate view with the lowest mean value, which corresponds to the view with the lowest overall coverage from already selected views. 7. Update: Add the selected view to the training set. 8. Termination: Repeat steps 3-7 until 20 training views are reached. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selecttrainingviews(candidates, currentprimitives, currentiterations, ntotal=20): # 1. Initialization selectedviews = [candidates[0]] # Fixed first view for in range(3): bestview = None maxmindist = -1.0 for cand in candidates: if cand in selectedviews: continue mindist = min(distance(cand.cameracenter, sv.cameracenter) for sv in selectedviews) if mindist > maxmindist: maxmindist = mindist bestview = cand selectedviews.append(bestview) # 2. Iterative Selection currentn = len(selectedviews) nextthreshold = 100 currentn # Threshold for next selection while currentn < ntotal: if currentiterations < nextthreshold: return None # Training continues candidatescores = {} for cand in candidates: if cand in selectedviews: continue # Render Vmax: direction-dependent coverage, max aggregation, dropped opacity (alpha=1) coveragemap = rendercoveragemap(cand, currentprimitives) meanval = sum(val for row in coveragemap for val in row) / (len(coveragemap) len(coveragemap[0])) candidatescores[cand] = meanval bestview = min(candidatescores, key=candidatescores.get) selectedviews.append(bestview) currentn += 1 nextthreshold += 100 currentn # Interval increases by 100 per view return selectedviews def rendercoveragemap(camera, primitives): # Computes direction-dependent coverage with max aggregation and dropped opacity (alpha=1) # Standard rasterization: project primitives to image, accumulate max coverage per pixel # Returns 2D array of coverage values # Standard rasterization step not detailed in sources return [[0.0] width for in range(height)] Edge Cases and Pitfalls Evaluation View Reservation: Every eighth view is removed from the candidate pool and reserved for evaluation to ensure comparability with baselines like FisherRF. Spherical Harmonics Degree: The interval for raising the spherical harmonics degree is increased from 1000 to 5000 iterations to mitigate overfitting caused by the limited number of views. Performance: On the MipNeRF360 dataset, PRIMU-AVS achieved PSNR 20.721, SSIM 0.625, and LPIPS 0.34. Comparison: It outperforms FisherRF (PSNR 20.392, SSIM 0.586, LPIPS 0.363) and manifold (PSNR 20.102, SSIM 0.610, LPIPS 0.351). Complexity: The selection step requires rendering a coverage map for all candidate views, adding computational overhead proportional to the number of candidates and the feature map resolution. Strengths: Conceptual simplicity, independence from primitives' spatial extent due to max aggregation, and no requirement for a hold-out view for training a regression model. Limitations: Reliance on a single feature map, potentially missing complex uncertainty correlations captured by the full PRIMU method's 13 feature maps and gradient boosting regressor. PRIMU-AVS is part of the PRIMU framework, a post-hoc technique for uncertainty estimation in Gaussian splatting. The full PRIMU method uses 13 handcrafted Gaussian primitive-based feature maps to capture training-view coverage and projected error. PRIMU-AVS simplifies this by using only the coverage feature map for view selection, aiming to maximize total coverage of Gaussian primitives across chosen training views. name: Uncertainty-Guided Residual Learning for 3DGS
head: Residual 3DGS, Residual Supervision for 3DGS, Residual Supervision in 3DGS, Residual learning for 3DGS, Uncertainty-Guided Residual Learning, Uncertainty-aware residual supervision
body: Uncertainty-Guided Residual Learning is a training strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that amplifies gradient flow to weakly contributing, high-uncertainty Gaussians by combining full-scene renders with uncertainty-intensified renders. It addresses the vanishing gradient problem in underrepresented regions by acting as a skip-connection mechanism, explicitly targeting Gaussians with low opacity or large scale that are otherwise overlooked by standard photometric loss. Unlike stochastic dropout methods, this approach deterministically identifies and reinforces supervision for the most uncertain primitives. The method operates by creating a secondary "residual" branch during the training loop. This branch rasterizes a subset of Gaussians designed to highlight uncertainty, allowing gradients from this branch to amplify updates for weakly contributing Gaussians in the primary branch. Inputs: Current set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}{\text{full}}. Ground-truth image I{\text{gt}} for the current training view. Hyperparameters: \alpha (percentage of random Gaussians, typically 90%), \beta (number of top-uncertain Gaussians, typically 10), \lambda{\text{full}} and \lambda{\text{sub}} (loss weights, typically 0.5 each). Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} via gradient descent. Two rendered images: I{\text{full}} and I{\text{sub}}. The Gaussian set \mathcal{G} is partitioned into two subsets: 1. \mathcal{G}{\text{full}}: The complete set of active Gaussians. 2. \mathcal{G}{\text{sub}}: A targeted subset defined as: \mathcal{G}{\text{sub}} = \mathcal{G}{\text{rand}} \cup \mathcal{G}{\text{uncertain}} \mathcal{G}{\text{rand}}: A random sample comprising \alpha\% of \mathcal{G}{\text{full}}. \mathcal{G}{\text{uncertain}}: The top \beta Gaussians ranked by uncertainty. Uncertainty is estimated heuristically based on two per-Gaussian attributes: 1. Opacity (\alphai): Low opacity indicates minimal contribution to alpha blending. 2. Scale: Large scales indicate the Gaussian blurs across pixels, often dominating ambiguous or low-texture regions. Gaussians are ranked by combining these factors; those with low opacity and large scale are considered "uncertain" or "weakly contributing". 1. Identify Subset: Construct \mathcal{G}{\text{sub}} by sampling \alpha\% of Gaussians randomly into \mathcal{G}{\text{rand}} and selecting the top \beta most uncertain Gaussians into \mathcal{G}{\text{uncertain}}. 2. Rasterize Full Render: Render image I{\text{full}} using the full Gaussian set \mathcal{G}{\text{full}}. 3. Rasterize Sub Render: Render image I{\text{sub}} using the subset \mathcal{G}{\text{sub}}. 4. Compute Losses: Calculate the photometric loss for both renders against I{\text{gt}} using L1 and SSIM components: \mathcal{L} = \sum{i \in \{\text{full}, \text{sub}\}} \lambdai \left[ \mathcal{L}{\text{rgb}}(Ii, I{\text{gt}}) + \mathcal{L}{\text{ssim}}(Ii, I{\text{gt}}) \right] where \lambda{\text{full}} + \lambda{\text{sub}} = 1. 5. Backpropagate: Compute gradients for all parameters. The key mechanism is the gradient amplification for Gaussians occluded by those removed in the sub-branch. The method modifies the gradient computation for the color parameter ci of a Gaussian i that is present in \mathcal{G}{\text{full}} but occluded by a Gaussian k that is removed (masked) in \mathcal{G}{\text{sub}}. In standard 3DGS, the gradient for color ci is proportional to the transmittance Ti and opacity \alphai. In the residual branch, if Gaussian k (with opacity \alphak) is removed, the transmittance reaching subsequent Gaussians i (where i is behind k in the ray order) is increased by a factor of 1/(1 - \alphak). The total gradient for color ci is the sum of contributions from the full branch and the amplified sub-branch: \frac {\partial \mathcal {L}}{\partial c\i} = \lambda \{\mathrm {full}} \frac {\partial \mathcal {L}\{\mathrm {full}}}{\partial C\{\mathrm {full}}} T\i \alpha \i + \lambda \{\mathrm {sub}} \frac {\partial \mathcal {L}\{\mathrm {sub}}}{\partial C\{\mathrm {sub}}} \frac {T\i \alpha \i}{1-\alpha \k} where: \frac {\partial \mathcal {L}\{\mathrm {full}}}{\partial C\{\mathrm {full}}} is the gradient of the full loss with respect to the final color C{\text{full}}. \frac {\partial \mathcal {L}\{\mathrm {sub}}}{\partial C\{\mathrm {sub}}} is the gradient of the subset loss with respect to the final color C{\text{sub}}. Ti is the transmittance up to Gaussian i. \alphai is the opacity of Gaussian i. \alphak is the opacity of the masked Gaussian k that occludes i in the sub-branch. This amplification factor 1/(1 - \alphak) grows as the occluding Gaussian k becomes more opaque, redirecting gradient flow toward previously occluded, weakly contributing Gaussians. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def uncertaintyguidedresidualstep(gaussians, gtimage, alphapct=0.9, betacount=10, lambdafull=0.5, lambdasub=0.5): """ Performs one training step with uncertainty-guided residual learning. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: opacity (alpha), scale, color, etc. gtimage: Ground truth image tensor. alphapct: Fraction of random Gaussians to include in sub-set. betacount: Number of top-uncertain Gaussians to include in sub-set. lambdafull: Weight for full render loss. lambdasub: Weight for sub-render loss. Returns: Updated gaussians after gradient descent. """ # 1. Identify Uncertain Gaussians # Rank Gaussians by uncertainty: low opacity and large scale. # Note: Exact ranking formula is not specified, but based on opacity and scale magnitude. uncertaingaussians = gettopuncertain(gaussians, betacount) # 2. Construct Sub-Set # Randomly sample alphapct% of all Gaussians randomgaussians = randomsample(gaussians, alphapct) # Union of random and uncertain subset = union(randomgaussians, uncertaingaussians) # 3. Rasterize Full Render # Render using all Gaussians colorfull, depthfull, alphafull = rasterize(gaussians, cameraparams) # 4. Rasterize Sub Render # Render using only the subset colorsub, depthsub, alphasub = rasterize(subset, cameraparams) # 5. Compute Losses # Standard L1 + SSIM loss lossrgbfull = l1loss(colorfull, gtimage) lossssimfull = ssimloss(colorfull, gtimage) lossfull = lambdafull (lossrgbfull + lossssimfull) lossrgbsub = l1loss(colorsub, gtimage) lossssimsub = ssimloss(colorsub, gtimage) losssub = lambdasub (lossrgbsub + lossssimsub) totalloss = lossfull + losssub # 6. Backpropagation with Gradient Amplification # Compute gradients for full branch gradsfull = computegradients(totalloss, gaussians) # Compute gradients for sub branch # Note: Standard backprop on subset gives gradients for params in subset. # We need to map these back to the full set, applying amplification for occluded Gaussians. gradssub = computegradients(totalloss, subset) # Apply amplification factor for Gaussians occluded by removed Gaussians # For each Gaussian i in gaussians: # If i is in subset: # gradi = lambdafull gradfulli + lambdasub gradsubi # If i is NOT in subset: # gradi = lambdafull gradfulli # If i is occluded by a removed Gaussian k (k not in subset) in the sub-branch: # The gradient from sub-branch is amplified by 1 / (1 - alphak) finalgrads = {} # Create a map of removed Gaussians for quick lookup removedgaussians = set(gaussians) - set(subset) for g in gaussians: grad = 0.0 # Contribution from full branch if g in gradsfull: grad += lambdafull gradsfull[g] # Contribution from sub branch if g in gradssub: basegradsub = gradssub[g] # Check if this Gaussian was occluded by any removed Gaussian in the sub-branch # This requires knowing the ray order and which removed Gaussian k occludes g. # In practice, this is handled by the differentiable rasterizer's chain rule # if the rasterizer supports masking, or manually applied if using custom CUDA. # The formula provided in suggests the amplification is applied to the gradient # of the parameter ci. # Identify occluders in removedgaussians that are in front of g occluders = getoccludersinray(g, removedgaussians) amplificationfactor = 1.0 for k in occluders: # If multiple removed Gaussians occlude, the effect is multiplicative # based on the transmittance chain. The source cites 1/(1-alphak) for a single masked Gaussian k. # Assuming single dominant occluder or sequential application: amplificationfactor = (1.0 / (1.0 - k.opacity)) grad += lambdasub basegradsub amplificationfactor finalgrads[g] = grad # 7. Update Parameters updategaussians(gaussians, finalgrads, optimizer) return gaussians def gettopuncertain(gaussians, count): """ Returns the top 'count' Gaussians with lowest opacity and largest scale. """ # Heuristic: Combine normalized opacity and scale # Lower opacity -> higher uncertainty # Larger scale -> higher uncertainty scores = [] for g in gaussians: # Normalize scale and opacity if necessary score = (1.0 - g.opacity) g.scalemagnitude scores.append((score, g)) scores.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True) return [g for, g in scores[:count]] def getoccludersinray(g, removedgaussians): """ Returns Gaussians from removedgaussians that occlude g in the current view. This requires depth comparison along the ray. """ occluders = [] for k in removedgaussians: if k.isinfrontof(g, cameraparams): occluders.append(k) return occluders Vanishing Gradients: The primary pitfall addressed is vanishing gradients for weakly contributing Gaussians (low opacity, large scale). The method mitigates this by masking high-opacity occluders in the sub-branch, amplifying gradients for subsequent Gaussians via the factor 1/(1 - \alphak). Precision: The amplification factor 1/(1 - \alphak) can become large if \alphak approaches 1. This may lead to numerical instability if not handled carefully, though the source does not specify a clamp. Boundary Conditions: If \alphak = 1, the factor is undefined. In practice, \alphak is capped below 1.0. Time Complexity: The method doubles the rasterization cost per step (one full render, one sub-render) and adds overhead for uncertainty ranking and subset construction. The gradient amplification requires identifying occluders, which adds computational cost proportional to the number of occluded Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Requires storing gradients for both branches and potentially intermediate buffers for the sub-render. Performance: Improves reconstruction quality in sparse or wide-baseline settings by stabilizing training and reducing overfitting. It is particularly effective during early next-best-view selection phases. Strengths: Explicitly targets under-optimized Gaussians, unlike stochastic dropout. Improves gradient flow without compromising photometric quality. Limitations: Adds computational overhead. Requires heuristic uncertainty estimation which may not be perfectly accurate. Uncertainty-Guided Residual Learning was introduced in the SA-ResGS (Self-augmented Residual 3D Gaussian Splatting) paper. It draws inspiration from ResNet skip connections and dropout mechanisms, adapting them to the specific context of 3D Gaussian Splatting's alpha blending process. The method was developed to address challenges in in-situ reconstruction with sparse views, where shape-radiance ambiguity and limited training views exacerbate artifacts. name: Submap-based Gaussian SLAM Mapping
head: Gaussian-SLAM mapping process, Incremental submap optimization
body: This method manages the incremental construction of a 3D Gaussian Splatting model within a Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) framework by dividing the scene into manageable spatial or temporal segments called "submaps". It solves the problem of unbounded memory growth and optimization instability in long-sequence SLAM by resetting the optimization state periodically while maintaining global consistency through keyframe integration. It differs from standard batch training by interleaving tracking and mapping steps, and from continuous global optimization by using localized submap resets to prevent drift accumulation in the Gaussian parameters. The method processes a sequence of RGB-D frames and estimated camera poses. It maintains a list of keyframes and a current Gaussian model. The core loop operates on a per-frame basis, deciding whether to start a new submap based on motion heuristics or fixed frame intervals. Inputs: Sequence of frames: RGB color tensors, depth tensors. Estimated camera poses: Camera-to-World matrices (\mathbf{T}{c2w}). Camera intrinsics: Focal lengths, principal point, image dimensions. Configuration parameters: newsubmapevery, mapping settings, tracking settings. Outputs: Updated 3D Gaussian model \mathcal{G} (positions, covariances, opacities, SH coefficients). Optimized camera poses (if joint optimization is enabled, though typically poses are provided by the tracker). Visualization images and metrics (PSNR, loss). 1. Gaussian Model (\mathcal{G}): Positions: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scales: \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotations: \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion) Opacities: \alphai \in [0, 1] SH Coefficients: \mathbf{c}{i, l} for view-dependent color. 2. Keyframe Dictionary: Color tensor: Normalized to [0, 1], moved to CUDA. Depth tensor: Moved to CUDA. Render settings: Derived from intrinsics and world-to-camera matrix (\mathbf{T}{w2c} = \mathbf{T}{c2w}^{-1}). 3. Submap State: submapframeids: List of frame IDs triggering new submaps. estimatedc2ws: Array of estimated camera-to-world poses. gaussianmodel: Current state of Gaussians. 1. Initialization: Determine submap trigger frame IDs: submapframeids = frameids[::config["mapping"]["newsubmapevery"]] + [nframes - 1]. Initialize logger and mapper/tracker components. Set up output paths for mapping and tracking visualizations. 2. Per-Frame Loop: For each frame i with ID fi: a. Retrieve Data: Get ground truth color, depth, and estimated \mathbf{T}{c2w}. Compute \mathbf{T}{w2c} = \mathbf{T}{c2w}^{-1}. b. Check Submap Start: Determine if a new submap should start using shouldstartnewsubmap(fi). Motion Heuristic: If enabled, check if rotation difference > 50^\circ or translation difference > 0.5 units between current pose and the last submap start pose. Fixed Interval: If heuristic disabled, check if fi is in submapframeids. c. Start New Submap (if triggered): Call startnewsubmap(fi, gaussianmodel). Save current submap checkpoint. Reset Gaussian model (clear existing Gaussians). Update submapcount. d. Construct Keyframe Dictionary: Normalize color to [0, 1] and move to CUDA. Move depth to CUDA. Store render settings derived from intrinsics and \mathbf{T}{w2c}. e. Seeding: Compute a seeding mask based on the current Gaussian model and the keyframe. Call seednewgaussians with ground truth color, depth, intrinsics, camera pose, seeding mask, and submap flag. This adds new 3D points (Gaussians) to the model. f. Outlier Filtering: Enable statistical outlier filtering if dataset is TUMRGBD or ScanNet AND it is not a new submap. g. Optimize Submap: Call optimizesubmap with the current frame, all existing keyframes, the Gaussian model, and maxiterations. maxiterations is self.newsubmapiterations if isnewsubmap is true, otherwise self.iterations. h. Update Keyframes: Append the current frame and its keyframe dictionary to the list of keyframes. i. Visualization & Logging: Render the current Gaussian model using the keyframe's render settings to generate visualization color and depth images. Calculate PSNR between rendered color and ground truth color. Log mapping iteration statistics: frame ID, new points count, model size, optimization time, and loss dictionary. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def processframe(frameid, color, depth, c2wpose, intrinsics, gaussianmodel, keyframes, config): # 1. Compute world-to-camera matrix w2cpose = inverse(c2wpose) # 2. Check if new submap needed isnewsubmap = shouldstartnewsubmap(frameid, c2wpose, keyframes, config) if isnewsubmap: startnewsubmap(frameid, gaussianmodel) # Reset Gaussian model state here # 3. Construct keyframe dictionary keyframedict = { "color": normalizeto01(color).tocuda(), "depth": depth.tocuda(), "w2c": w2cpose, "intrinsics": intrinsics } # 4. Seed new Gaussians seedingmask = computeseedingmask(gaussianmodel, keyframedict) newpoints = seednewgaussians( color=keyframedict["color"], depth=keyframedict["depth"], intrinsics=intrinsics, pose=c2wpose, mask=seedingmask, isnewsubmap=isnewsubmap) gaussianmodel.addpoints(newpoints) # 5. Outlier filtering if isoutlierfilteringenabled(config["dataset"], isnewsubmap): gaussianmodel.removeoutliers() # 6. Optimize submap maxiter = config["mapping"]["newsubmapiterations"] if isnewsubmap else config["mapping"]["iterations"] optimizesubmap( currentframe=keyframedict, allkeyframes=keyframes, gaussianmodel=gaussianmodel, maxiterations=maxiter) # 7. Update keyframes keyframes.append(keyframedict) # 8. Render and Log rendercolor, renderdepth = render(gaussianmodel, keyframedict) psnr = calculatepsnr(rendercolor, color) logstats(frameid, len(newpoints), gaussianmodel.size(), psnr) return gaussianmodel, keyframes maxiterations: Number of optimization iterations per submap step. If isnewsubmap: self.newsubmapiterations. Else: self.iterations. newsubmapevery: Interval for fixed-interval submap creation. Motion thresholds: Rotation > 50^\circ, Translation > 0.5 units. Precision: Depth tensors must be moved to CUDA and handled with appropriate precision to avoid artifacts during seeding. Boundaries: The last frame of the sequence is always included in submapframeids to ensure the final submap is processed. Degenerate Input: If the camera pose is invalid, inverse(c2wpose) may fail. Ensure pose validity checks are performed before inversion. Standard batch optimization without SLAM constraints. Accelerated training using 2D Gaussian primitives. Optimizing only a subset of Gaussians to reduce compute. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of frames processed, but each frame involves optimization over the current submap's Gaussians and all keyframes. Complexity per step is O(N{submap} \cdot N{keyframes}) for rendering and optimization. Memory Complexity: Bounded by the size of the current submap and the number of keyframes, rather than the entire scene history. This prevents unbounded memory growth. Strengths: Enables long-sequence SLAM by managing memory; reduces optimization drift by resetting submaps; leverages keyframes for global consistency. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of submap frequency; motion heuristics may fail in low-texture or fast-motion scenarios; outlier filtering is dataset-specific. When to use: Long-sequence RGB-D SLAM where memory is constrained and drift needs to be managed. When not to use: Short sequences or batch reconstruction where global optimization is feasible. This method is implemented in the Gaussian-SLAM framework by Vladimir Yugay. It adapts the 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering technique for incremental SLAM, addressing the challenge of maintaining a consistent 3D model over time without re-optimizing the entire history. The approach builds on the principles of differentiable rendering and Gaussian primitives, integrating them with SLAM-specific constraints like keyframe management and submap resets.
