name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Optimization
head: 3DGS Training Procedure
body: This article details the specific optimization schedule, initialization strategies, and hyperparameter configurations required to train a 3D Gaussian Splatting model from scratch. It addresses the problem of converging anisotropic Gaussian primitives to represent a scene's geometry and appearance while maintaining training stability and rendering speed. It differs from general differentiable rendering by employing a staged introduction of Spherical Harmonics (SH) and a resolution warm-up to mitigate artifacts caused by missing angular information and gradient instability. Inputs: A set of M input images with known camera poses (intrinsics and extrinsics). Scene bounds (for synthetic bounded scenes) or a bounding volume. Outputs: A set of N optimized 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}{i=1}^N, where each gi contains: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance \Sigmai (parameterized by rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 and scale vector \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3) Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Spherical Harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}{i, l} for view-dependent color. The implementation uses Python/PyTorch with custom CUDA kernels for rasterization. Gaussian Attributes: Stored in contiguous arrays or PyTorch tensors for batched operations. Sorting: Uses NVIDIA CUB sorting routines for fast Radix sort to order Gaussians by depth for alpha blending. Rasterization: Custom CUDA kernels extended from Kopanas et al. [2021]. 1. Initialization: Synthetic Bounded Scenes: Initialize with 100,000 Gaussians uniformly distributed within a volume enclosing the scene bounds. These are automatically pruned to 6,000–10,000 meaningful Gaussians during early training. Real-World/Unbounded Scenes: Typically initialized from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points, though the specific initialization count for real-world scenes is not explicitly detailed in the provided notes beyond the synthetic case. 2. Resolution Warm-up: Start optimization at an image resolution 4 times smaller than the target resolution. Upsample the resolution twice: first after 250 iterations, and second after 500 iterations. 3. Spherical Harmonics (SH) Band Introduction: To prevent incorrect diffuse color values due to missing angular regions in captures, optimize only the zero-order (DC) SH component initially. Introduce one additional SH band every 1,000 iterations. Continue until all 4 bands of SH are represented. 4. Gradient Computation: Compute gradients for all visible Gaussians contributing to the pixel color. Pitfall: Limiting gradient computation to only the front-most N points (e.g., N=10) causes unstable optimization and severe quality degradation (e.g., an 11dB PSNR drop in the Truck scene). 5. Densification (Implicit in Optimization Loop): Cloning: Small Gaussians are cloned to better/faster converge on thin structures. Splitting: Large Gaussians are split to improve background reconstruction. Note: The specific thresholds and frequency for cloning/splitting are part of the broader "Gaussian Primitive Training Schedule" [18977-gaussian-primitive-training-schedule.md] and are not detailed in the optimization-specific notes. 6. Pruning: Gaussians with low opacity are pruned during the training process to maintain compactness. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def train3dgaussiansplatting(inputimages, cameraposes, targetresolution, totaliterations=30000): """ Optimizes 3D Gaussian Splatting parameters. """ # 1. Initialization # For synthetic bounded scenes: 100K random points in bounding volume # For real-world: Typically SfM initialization (details in parent article) gaussians = initializegaussians(scenebounds="bounded") # 2. Setup Optimizer # Adam optimizer with beta1=0.9, beta2=0.99 (from Shared Principles) optimizer = Adam(gaussians.parameters(), lr=initiallr) # 3. Setup Rendering Pipeline # Custom CUDA rasterization extended from Kopanas et al. [2021] # Radix sort via NVIDIA CUB rasterizer = CustomCUDARasterizer() # 4. Training Loop currentshband = 0 # Start with 0-order only currentresolution = targetresolution / 4 # 4x smaller for iteration in range(1, totaliterations + 1): # Resolution Warm-up if iteration == 250: currentresolution = currentresolution 2 elif iteration == 500: currentresolution = currentresolution 2 # Sample a batch of images and cameras image, camera = samplebatch(inputimages, cameraposes) # Render image using current resolution # All visible Gaussians contribute to gradients (do NOT limit to N front-most) renderedimage = rasterizer.render(gaussians, camera, currentresolution) # Compute Loss # Composite loss: (1-lambda)L1 + lambdaD-SSIM (from Shared Principles) loss = computecompositeloss(renderedimage, image) # Backpropagation loss.backward() # Update SH Bands # Introduce one band every 1000 iterations if iteration % 1000 == 0 and currentshband < 4: currentshband += 1 enableshband(gaussians, currentshband) # Step Optimizer optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Densification and Pruning # (Specific logic delegated to Gaussian Primitive Training Schedule) densifyandprune(gaussians, iteration) return gaussians Total Iterations: 30,000 for standard scenes. SH Band Interval: 1,000 iterations per band. Total SH Bands: 4. Initial Resolution Factor: 4x smaller than target. Resolution Upsample Steps: At iteration 250 and 500. Gradient Depth Limit: None (all visible points). Missing Angular Information: In captures with missing regions (e.g., corners, inside-out), optimizing all SH bands simultaneously produces incorrect zero-order (diffuse) color values. Mitigated by optimizing only zero-order initially. Gradient Limiting: Limiting gradients to the front-most N points (e.g., N=10) leads to unstable optimization and significant quality loss (11dB PSNR drop in Truck scene). Popping Artifacts: Large Gaussians can cause popping artifacts, partly due to trivial rejection via guard bands in the rasterizer and depth order switches. Training Time: Synthetic NeRF scenes: ~35-45 minutes on a single A6000 GPU. Mip-NeRF360 scenes: 48 hours on a single GPU (equivalent to 12 hours on a 4-GPU A100 node). Tanks & Temples: ~7 minutes on a single A6000 GPU. Rendering Speed: Trained synthetic scenes: 180-300 FPS on A6000 GPU. Mip-NeRF360: 10 seconds per frame. Model Size: Synthetic scenes: 200,000–500,000 Gaussians per scene after 30,000 iterations. Compactness: Uses ~1/4 the point count of Zhang et al. [2022] with 3.8 MB model size vs 9 MB. Strengths: Anisotropic covariance significantly improves surface alignment and rendering quality compared to isotropic models. Achieves comparable quality to InstantNGP/Plenoxels in 5-10 minutes, surpassing them with additional time. Fast convergence for thin structures via cloning small Gaussians. Limitations: Artifacts in poorly observed regions (e.g., elongated "splotchy" Gaussians). Popping artifacts in regions with view-dependent appearance. Training time for large unbounded scenes (e.g., Mip-NeRF360) is significantly longer than for synthetic bounded scenes. Use when real-time rendering speed is required after training. Use when high-quality view-dependent effects are needed (SH bands). Avoid if training time is strictly constrained for very large unbounded scenes without access to multi-GPU setups. The method was introduced in the paper "3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering". The rasterization kernels are extended versions of methods by Kopanas et al. [2021], and the sorting uses routines from Merrill and Grimshaw [2010]. The optimization procedure was refined to address specific issues in Gaussian Splatting, such as the instability caused by limited gradient depth and the sensitivity of SH coefficients to missing angular data. The staged introduction of SH bands and resolution warm-up were key innovations to stabilize training. Evaluated on 13 real scenes (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, Hedman et al.) and synthetic Blender dataset. Hardware used: A6000 GPU for most results, 4-GPU A100 node for Mip-NeRF360. 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering [pdf], https://repo-sam.inria.fr/fungraph/3d-gaussian-splatting/3dgaussiansplattinglow.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Gradient Modification
body:
Gradient modification techniques adjust the backward pass of 3D Gaussian Splatting to address specific optimization failures, such as vanishing gradients for distant or "dead" primitives, discontinuities in geometric boundaries, and gradient confusion from imperfect supervision. Unlike standard training which relies on direct backpropagation through the rasterizer, these methods intercept gradients to provide non-zero signals to primitives that would otherwise receive none, or to stabilize update directions. This family sets itself apart from sibling methods like TurboGS (which focuses on acceleration) or Error-Guided Sparse Pixel Sampling (which focuses on data selection) by directly altering the gradient values or paths computed for Gaussian parameters. The core mechanism common to all gradient modification techniques is the interception of the standard gradient  rac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial 	heta} (where 	heta represents Gaussian parameters like mean \mu, opacity \sigma, or control points) to replace or augment it with a modified gradient 	ilde{
abla}. This is typically done to: 1. Enable optimization of parameters that are otherwise disconnected from the loss (e.g., due to rasterization culling or piecewise constant functions). 2. Stabilize training by filtering out noisy or conflicting gradient signals. 3. Extend the range of influence for primitives that have low contribution to the current pixel but are geometrically relevant. All methods operate within the standard Adam optimizer framework defined in the parent Optimization and Training Loop, modifying the input gradients before they are passed to the optimizer step. A technique for handling discontinuities in geometric boundaries by approximating gradients for Bézier curve control points. It solves the problem where standard automatic differentiation yields zero gradients for piecewise constant indicator functions, preventing the optimization of geometric parameters defining scene edges [13137-b-zier-boundary-gradient-approximation]. It sets itself apart from Truncated Gradient Updates for 3D Gaussian Splatting by focusing on geometric boundary approximation via Bézier curves rather than magnitude truncation for distant primitives [13137-b-zier-boundary-gradient-approximation]. See Bézier-boundary gradient approximation for implementation details. A technique that applies truncated gradient updates to "dead" Gaussians (those with low opacity) to enable long-range movement and convergence. It addresses vanishing gradients in dynamic scenes or poor initialization by intercepting the backward pass to provide non-zero gradients to Gaussians rasterization-filtered out due to distance or low opacity, while restricting these updates to prevent divergence in well-fitted primitives [18661-truncated-gradient-updates-for-3d-gaussian-splatting]. See Truncated Gradient Updates for 3D Gaussian Splatting for implementation details. An optimization strategy that augments Gaussian primitives with a flag gradient attribute to mitigate gradient confusion and perturbations caused by imperfect supervision from pseudo-views. Augments canonical Gaussian primitives \{\mu, s, q, \sigma, c\} with an additional per-Gaussian attribute flag gradient 
abla \in \mathbb{R}^{11+kc}, where 
abla records gradient trends for \mu, s, q, \sigma, and kc SH coefficients. 1. For each Gaussian in one optimization step, compute the cosine similarity between the current gradient for each attribute g{ic} and the corresponding flag gradient 
abla(gi) stored in 
abla. 2. If the cosine similarity is greater than zero, indicating aligned gradient update trends, use the current gradient g{ic} directly. 3. If the cosine similarity is less than or equal to zero, indicating potential disturbances, scale the current gradient by a factor \epsilon and update the flag gradient: g{ic} = \epsilon g{ic}, \quad 
abla(gi) = (1 - \epsilon)
abla(gi) + \epsilon g{ic} Pass the modified gradients to the gradient-based optimizer (e.g., Adam). 4. Eliminate the flag gradient attribute 
abla after optimization is complete to avoid affecting rendering speed and storage consumption. \epsilon: The scaling factor for gradients with negative cosine similarity, set to 0.1. Gradient modification in 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged as a response to specific failure modes in the standard optimization loop, such as the inability to optimize geometric boundaries defined by discontinuous functions and the vanishing gradients for primitives that do not contribute to the current view. The Bézier-boundary approach addresses the non-differentiability of indicator functions in geometric modeling [13137-b-zier-boundary-gradient-approximation]. Truncated gradient updates address the issue of "dead" Gaussians in dynamic scenes or sparse initialization, allowing them to move towards relevant pixels [18661-truncated-gradient-updates-for-3d-gaussian-splatting]. Gradient Flag Optimization was introduced to handle gradient confusion caused by imperfect supervision from pseudo-views in super-resolution tasks. S2Gaussian: Sparse-View Super-Resolution 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.00075, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Bézier-boundary gradient approximation
head: Bézier-boundary gradient approximation strategy, DisC-GS gradient approximation
body: A gradient modification technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that enables the optimization of control points defining discontinuous indicator functions (used for rendering edges and boundaries) by approximating the non-differentiable gradient of a cubic Bézier curve. It solves the problem where standard backpropagation fails because the indicator function g(\cdot) is piecewise constant, yielding zero gradients that cannot guide the learning of control point coordinates. It sets itself apart from standard Gaussian Splatting by explicitly handling discontinuities via Bézier curves, and from sibling methods like Truncated Gradient Updates by focusing on the geometric boundary of the curve rather than truncating magnitude. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current control point coordinates c{\text{curve}}, the pixel location p=(xp, yp), the current output of the Bézier curve function g{sc}(p), the gradient of the loss with respect to the curve output \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial g{sc}}, and the hyperparameter \epsilon (small constant). Output: The approximated gradient \frac{\partial g}{\partial c{\text{curve}}[0,0]} (and similarly for other coordinates) to be used in the optimizer step. Data Structures: c{\text{curve}}: Attribute storing control point coordinates. For 2D Gaussian Splatting: Shape \mathbb{R}^{4M \times 2}. For 3D Gaussian Splatting: Shape \mathbb{R}^{4M \times 3}. M: Hyperparameter for the number of control points per Gaussian. Value: 3. c{\text{curve}}[i, j] denotes the j-th coordinate of the i-th control point. Method Steps: The method approximates \frac{\partial g}{\partial c{\text{curve}}[0,0]} using the chain rule: \frac{\partial g}{\partial c{\text{curve}}[0,0]} = \frac{\partial g}{\partial g{sc}} \times \frac{\partial g{sc}}{\partial c{\text{curve}}[0,0]} where g{sc}(p) is the cubic Bézier curve function evaluated at p. The core difficulty is approximating \frac{\partial g{sc}}{\partial c{\text{curve}}[0,0]}. 1. Check Modification Necessity: Determine if g{sc}(p) needs modification by checking if the current state is already optimal or saturated. If any of the following conditions hold, set \frac{\partial g{sc}}{\partial c{\text{curve}}[0,0]} = 0 and terminate: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial g{sc}} = 0 (Optimal state). \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial g{sc}} > 0 and g{sc}(p) = 0 (Already at minimum). \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial g{sc}} < 0 and g{sc}(p) = 1 (Already at maximum). 2. Solve for Target Control Point: If modification is needed, identify the target value \phi for c{\text{curve}}[0,0] such that the Bézier curve passes through p. Solve the system of equations derived from the cubic Bézier definition for parameter t and target \phi: xp = (1-t)^3 \phi + 3(1-t)^2 t c{\text{curve}}[1,0] + 3(1-t)t^2 c{\text{curve}}[2,0] + t^3 c{\text{curve}}[3,0] yp = (1-t)^3 c{\text{curve}}[0,1] + 3(1-t)^2 t c{\text{curve}}[1,1] + 3(1-t)t^2 c{\text{curve}}[2,1] + t^3 c{\text{curve}}[3,1] Collect all real number solutions for \phi into a set S\phi. This is solved in O(1) time. 3. Approximate Gradient Based on S\phi: No Side: If S\phi = \emptyset, set \frac{\partial g{sc}}{\partial c{\text{curve}}[0,0]} = 0. No real value of c{\text{curve}}[0,0] can cause the curve to pass through p. Single Side: If all solutions in S\phi lie on the same side of the current c{\text{curve}}[0,0], let \phie be the solution nearest to c{\text{curve}}[0,0]. Approximate the gradient via linear interpolation: \frac{\partial g{sc}}{\partial c{\text{curve}}[0,0]} = \frac{g{sc}(p) - \hat{g}{sc}(p)}{\phie - c{\text{curve}}[0,0] + \epsilon} where \hat{g}{sc}(p) = 1 if g{sc}(p)=0 else 0. The epsilon \epsilon is set to 10^{-5} if \phie > c{\text{curve}}[0,0] and -10^{-5} otherwise. Both Sides: If solutions exist on both left and right sides of c{\text{curve}}[0,0], let \phi1 be the nearest solution from the left and \phi2 be the nearest from the right. Approximate the gradient as the sum of two interpolation terms: \frac{\partial g{sc}}{\partial c{\text{curve}}[0,0]} = \frac{g{sc}(p) - \hat{g}{sc}(p)}{\phi1 - c{\text{curve}}[0,0] + \epsilon1} + \frac{g{sc}(p) - \hat{g}{sc}(p)}{\phi2 - c{\text{curve}}[0,0] + \epsilon2} where \epsilon1, \epsilon2 follow the same sign rule as \epsilon above. 4. Final Gradient: Multiply the result by \frac{\partial g}{\partial g{sc}} to obtain the final gradient for the control point. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def bezierboundarygradientapproximation( ccurve, # Array of shape (4M, 2) or (4M, 3) p, # Pixel coordinate (xp, yp) gsc, # Current output of Bézier curve at p dLdgsc, # Gradient of loss w.r.t. gsc M=3 # Hyperparameter for control points): """ Approximates the gradient of the discontinuous indicator function with respect to the first control point's x-coordinate. """ # 1. Check modification necessity if dLdgsc == 0: return 0.0 if dLdgsc > 0 and gsc == 0: return 0.0 if dLdgsc < 0 and gsc == 1: return 0.0 # 2. Solve for target phi # Extract fixed control points for x and y # ccurve[0,0] is the variable we are solving for (phi) # ccurve[1,0], ccurve[2,0], ccurve[3,0] are fixed x-coords # ccurve[0,1], ccurve[1,1], ccurve[2,1], ccurve[3,1] are fixed y-coords c0x = ccurve[0, 0] c1x = ccurve[1, 0] c2x = ccurve[2, 0] c3x = ccurve[3, 0] c0y = ccurve[0, 1] c1y = ccurve[1, 1] c2y = ccurve[2, 1] c3y = ccurve[3, 1] xp, yp = p # We need to solve for t and phi such that: # xp = (1-t)^3 phi + 3(1-t)^2tc1x + 3(1-t)t^2c2x + t^3c3x # yp = (1-t)^3c0y + 3(1-t)^2tc1y + 3(1-t)t^2c2y + t^3c3y # From the y-equation, we can solve for t (cubic equation in t) # yp = c0y(1-t)^3 + c1y3t(1-t)^2 + c2y3t^2(1-t) + c3yt^3 # This is a standard cubic Bezier evaluation for y. # We find roots t in [0, 1] for this equation. # Coefficients for cubic polynomial in t: At^3 + Bt^2 + Ct + D = 0 # y(t) = c0y(1 - 3t + 3t^2 - t^3) + 3c1y(t - 2t^2 + t^3) + 3c2y(t^2 - t^3) + c3y t^3 # y(t) = -c0y + t(3c0y - 3c1y + c3y) + t^2(-3c0y + 6c1y - 3c2y) + t^3(c0y - 3c1y + 3c2y - c3y) # Wait, standard form: y(t) = (1-t)^3 c0 + 3(1-t)^2 t c1 + 3(1-t) t^2 c2 + t^3 c3 # Let's expand: # (1-3t+3t^2-t^3)c0 + (3t-6t^2+3t^3)c1 + (3t^2-3t^3)c2 + t^3 c3 # t^3: -c0 + 3c1 - 3c2 + c3 # t^2: 3c0 - 6c1 + 3c2 # t^1: -3c0 + 3c1 # t^0: c0 Ay = -c0y + 3c1y - 3c2y + c3y By = 3c0y - 6c1y + 3c2y Cy = -3c0y + 3c1y Dy = c0y # Solve Ay t^3 + By t^2 + Cy t + (Dy - yp) = 0 coeffsy = [Ay, By, Cy, Dy - yp] troots = np.roots(coeffsy) # Filter real roots in [0, 1] validt = [] for t in troots: if np.isreal(t) and 0 <= np.real(t) <= 1: validt.append(np.real(t)) Sphi = [] for t in validt: # From x-equation: xp = (1-t)^3 phi + K # K = 3(1-t)^2tc1x + 3(1-t)t^2c2x + t^3c3x K = 3(1-t)2 t c1x + 3(1-t) t2 c2x + t3 c3x denom = (1-t)3 if abs(denom) > 1e-9: phi = (xp - K) / denom Sphi.append(phi) # 3. Approximate gradient if len(Sphi) == 0: dgscdc0x = 0.0 else: # Check sides leftsols = [phi for phi in Sphi if phi < c0x] rightsols = [phi for phi in Sphi if phi > c0x] # Define target output for interpolation # If gsc is 0, we want to move it to 1 (if gradient encourages increase) # If gsc is 1, we want to move it to 0 (if gradient encourages decrease) # The formula uses gsc(p) - ghatsc(p) # ghatsc(p) = 1 if gsc(p)==0 else 0 if gsc == 0: ghatsc = 1 else: ghatsc = 0 numerator = gsc - ghatsc if len(leftsols) == 0 and len(rightsols) > 0: # Single side (right) phie = min(rightsols) # Nearest to c0x if phie > c0x: eps = 1e-5 else: eps = -1e-5 dgscdc0x = numerator / (phie - c0x + eps) elif len(rightsols) == 0 and len(leftsols) > 0: # Single side (left) phie = max(leftsols) # Nearest to c0x if phie > c0x: eps = 1e-5 else: eps = -1e-5 dgscdc0x = numerator / (phie - c0x + eps) elif len(leftsols) > 0 and len(rightsols) > 0: # Both sides phi1 = max(leftsols) # Nearest from left phi2 = min(rightsols) # Nearest from right if phi1 > c0x: # Should not happen, but for safety eps1 = 1e-5 else: eps1 = -1e-5 if phi2 > c0x: eps2 = 1e-5 else: eps2 = -1e-5 term1 = numerator / (phi1 - c0x + eps1) term2 = numerator / (phi2 - c0x + eps2) dgscdc0x = term1 + term2 else: # All solutions are exactly equal to c0x? Or empty? # If Sphi is not empty but no left/right, they are equal. # This is a degenerate case. Set to 0. dgscdc0x = 0.0 return dLdgsc dgscdc0x Parameters: \epsilon: Small constant to prevent gradient explosion. Value: 10^{-5} if target \phi > current c{\text{curve}}[0,0], else -10^{-5}. M: Number of control points per Gaussian. Value: 3. Initial learning rate for c{\text{curve}}: 2 \times 10^{-4}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Side: If S\phi is empty, the gradient is set to 0. This occurs when the curve geometry cannot be adjusted by changing c{\text{curve}}[0,0] to pass through p. Precision: The epsilon value is critical. Using a fixed sign based on the direction of movement prevents division by zero and stabilizes training. Cloning/Splitting: When Gaussians are cloned or split during densification, the new Gaussians inherit the same c{\text{curve}} attribute as the original. A method to jointly optimize a binary gate gi and motion parameters to classify Gaussians as static or dynamic, using a hard-concrete relaxation with straight-through estimator. It solves the problem of incorrectly treating moving Gaussians as static, which leaves frozen copies of moving objects in the scene, by learning a sparse static-dynamic partition. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly maintaining a binary classification per Gaussian that is committed and frozen after training, enabling efficient rendering of static background without temporal overhead. Time Complexity: The core approximation step (solving for t and \phi) is O(1) per control point coordinate. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the control point attributes c{\text{curve}} with shape \mathbb{R}^{4M \times 2} (2D) or \mathbb{R}^{4M \times 3} (3D) per Gaussian. Strengths: Enables differentiable rendering of discontinuities (edges, boundaries) which standard Gaussian Splatting cannot handle natively. Consistently outperforms existing methods on PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS metrics on novel view synthesis tasks. Limitations: Relies on the approximation of non-differentiable functions, which may introduce artifacts if the approximation is poor. Requires careful tuning of \epsilon and learning rates for the control points. When to Use: When rendering scenes with sharp discontinuities, edges, or boundaries that standard smooth Gaussian Splatting fails to represent accurately. Originated in DisC-GS: Discontinuity-aware Gaussian Splatting. The method addresses the limitation of standard Gaussian Splatting, which assumes differentiable rendering, by incorporating a discontinuous indicator function g(\cdot) into the \alpha-blending process. Since g(\cdot) is piecewise constant, its gradients are zero, preventing the optimization of the control points c{\text{curve}} that define the discontinuity boundaries. The Bézier-boundary gradient approximation strategy was proposed to bridge this gap by approximating the gradient of the Bézier curve function with respect to its control points, allowing the network to learn the geometry of discontinuities. DisC-GS: Discontinuity-aware Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15196v2, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Learned Static–Dynamic Partition
head: Binary gate optimization, Hard-concrete relaxation gating
body: A method to jointly optimize a binary gate gi and motion parameters to classify Gaussians as static or dynamic, using a hard-concrete relaxation with straight-through estimator. It solves the problem of incorrectly treating moving Gaussians as static, which leaves frozen copies of moving objects in the scene, by learning a sparse static-dynamic partition. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly maintaining a binary classification per Gaussian that is committed and frozen after training, enabling efficient rendering of static background without temporal overhead. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color, velocity), photometric loss gradients, temperature schedule parameters. Outputs: Binary gate values gi \in \{0, 1\} for each Gaussian, where gi=1 indicates dynamic and gi=0 indicates static. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i maintains: \elli: Learnable gate logit (scalar). gi: Binary gate value (scalar, 0 or 1). g{bi}: Relaxed gate value for gradients (scalar, continuous). ei: Promotion evidence accumulator (scalar, exponential moving average). forceddynamic: Boolean flag. committedlabel: Boolean flag indicating if the partition is frozen. Parameters: T: Temperature, annealed from T{init}=2.0 to T{final}=0.1. [\gamma, \zeta] = [-0.1, 1.1]: Relaxed range bounds. \taum: Velocity threshold for forced dynamic classification. \eta: Momentum factor for evidence EMA. Training phases: Logistic noise for first 5k iterations; deterministic evaluation after; partition committed at 25k iterations. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize \elli for all Gaussians. If velocity initialization vi is available and \|vi\|2 > \taum, set forceddynamic = True and gi = 1. If no velocity initialization, start with strong dynamic prior (or static prior depending on implementation details, but typically dynamic to avoid freezing). Initialize ei = 0. 2. Forward Pass (Training): Sample ui \sim U(0, 1). Compute relaxed sigmoid: si = \text{sigmoid}\left(\frac{\elli + \log \frac{ui}{1-ui}}{T}\right) Clamp to relaxed range: \tilde{s}i = \text{clamp}(si(\zeta - \gamma) + \gamma, 0, 1) Compute binary gate: gi = \mathbb{I}[\tilde{s}i \geq 0.5] Compute straight-through estimator for gradients: g{bi} = \text{sg}(gi) - \text{sg}(\tilde{s}i) + \tilde{s}i Use g{bi} in motion parameter updates (Eqs. 19 and 22 in source). 3. Backward Pass: Compute loss gradients \frac{\partial L}{\partial \elli}. Remove gradient contribution from gate regularizers before computing evidence. 4. Evidence Update (Motion Evidence and Promotion): Update exponential moving average of evidence: ei \leftarrow \eta ei + (1 - \eta) \text{ReLU}\left(-\frac{\partial L}{\partial \elli}\right) Negative gradient indicates evidence for motion. After 2k warmup, check static population every 500 iterations. Promote Gaussians with ei above the 0.995 quantile, up to 1% of all Gaussians per step. Once promoted or forced, a Gaussian cannot revert to static. 5. Sparsity Regularization: Apply sparsity loss to free Gaussians (excluding forced/promoted dynamic ones): L{sparse} = \frac{1}{|F|} \sum{i \in F} \text{sigmoid}\left(\frac{\elli - T \log \frac{-\gamma}{\zeta}}{T}\right) L{bin} = \frac{1}{|F|} \sum{i \in F} pi(1 - pi), \quad pi = \text{sigmoid}(\elli) Introduce sparsity loss gradually from iterations 5k to 20k. 6. Densification: When cloning or splitting Gaussians, new copies inherit \elli, forceddynamic, committedlabel, and ei from the parent. 7. Commitment: At iteration 25k, freeze the static-dynamic partition. Renderer and compression operate on fixed binary partition gi. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updategate(gaussian, lossgrad, T, eta, iteration, totalgaussians): """ Update the static-dynamic partition for a single Gaussian. gaussian: object with attributes li, gi, gbi, ei, forceddynamic, committedlabel lossgrad: gradient of loss w.r.t. li (after removing regularizer contributions) T: current temperature eta: EMA momentum iteration: current training iteration totalgaussians: total number of Gaussians in scene """ if gaussian.committedlabel: return # Partition is frozen # Forward pass ui = random.uniform(0, 1) si = sigmoid((gaussian.li + log(ui / (1 - ui))) / T) gamma, zeta = -0.1, 1.1 stilde = clamp(si (zeta - gamma) + gamma, 0, 1) gaussian.gi = 1 if stilde >= 0.5 else 0 gaussian.gbi = gaussian.gi - stilde + stilde # Straight-through: sg(gi) - sg(stilde) + stilde # Evidence update (only if not forced dynamic) if not gaussian.forceddynamic: # Remove regularizer gradient contribution from lossgrad here evidencegrad = -lossgrad gaussian.ei = eta gaussian.ei + (1 - eta) max(0, evidencegrad) # Promotion check (every 500 iterations after 2k warmup) if iteration > 2000 and iteration % 500 == 0: if not gaussian.forceddynamic and gaussian.gi == 0: # Check if this Gaussian should be promoted # Note: In practice, this requires global quantile calculation # Here we simulate the logic for a single Gaussian pass # Global promotion logic handled externally # Forced dynamic initialization if gaussian.forceddynamic: gaussian.gi = 1 gaussian.gbi = 1 def promotegaussians(gaussians, iteration, totalgaussians): """ Promote static Gaussians to dynamic based on evidence. """ if iteration <= 2000 or iteration % 500 != 0: return # Collect static, non-forced Gaussians staticcandidates = [g for g in gaussians if not g.forceddynamic and g.gi == 0] if not staticcandidates: return # Calculate 0.995 quantile of evidence evidencevalues = [g.ei for g in staticcandidates] threshold = np.percentile(evidencevalues, 99.5) # Promote up to 1% of total Gaussians maxpromotions = int(0.01 totalgaussians) promoted = 0 for g in staticcandidates: if g.ei > threshold and promoted < maxpromotions: g.forceddynamic = True g.gi = 1 g.gbi = 1 promoted += 1 def commitpartition(gaussians, iteration): """ Freeze the static-dynamic partition at iteration 25k. """ if iteration == 25000: for g in gaussians: g.committedlabel = True g.gbi = g.gi # Ensure forward pass uses binary value A mechanism to prevent moving Gaussians from being incorrectly classified as static by using velocity initialization and reconstruction evidence. A Gaussian is forced to be dynamic if its initialized velocity satisfies \|vi\|2 > \taum. Once forced/promoted, it cannot revert to static. Evidence ei is updated as ei \leftarrow \eta ei + (1 - \eta) \text{ReLU}\left(-\frac{\partial L}{\partial \elli}\right). Promote Gaussians whose evidence is above the 0.995 quantile, at most 1% per step, after 2k warmup, checking every 500 iterations. Time Complexity: O(N) per iteration for gate updates, where N is the number of Gaussians. Promotion check is O(N \log N) due to quantile calculation, but only every 500 iterations. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing \elli, gi, ei, and flags per Gaussian. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of Gaussians. The commitment at 25k iterations allows for efficient rendering without temporal overhead for static Gaussians. Strengths: Prevents frozen artifacts of moving objects; enables efficient rendering of static scenes; sparse dynamic partition reduces computational cost for temporal updates. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of temperature schedule and promotion thresholds; commitment is irreversible, so misclassifications after 25k cannot be corrected. When to use: When rendering scenes with both static and dynamic elements, especially on mobile or resource-constrained devices where temporal updates are expensive. When not to use: When all Gaussians are known to be static or dynamic, or when real-time adaptation to changing dynamics is required after training. Originated in Mobile-4DGS: Unified Static-Dynamic Real-time Mobile Gaussian Splatting. The method addresses the inefficiency of modeling temporal variation for static background elements like floors and stationary objects, while avoiding the artifact of frozen moving objects. It builds on Bézier-boundary gradient approximation to handle the non-differentiable binary gate. Mobile-4DGS: Unified Static-Dynamic Real-time Mobile Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05289, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Truncated Gradient Updates for 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: TruncGradGS
body: Truncated Gradient Updates is a gradient modification technique that applies a surrogate "truncated" gradient to 'dead' Gaussians (those with low opacity) to enable long-range movement and convergence, addressing vanishing gradients in dynamic scenes or poor initialization. It sets itself apart from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by intercepting the backward pass to provide gradient signals to primitives that are rasterization-culled due to distance or low density, while distinguishing itself from siblings like Bézier-boundary gradient approximation by focusing specifically on the Mahalanobis distance threshold and opacity-based dead Gaussian filtering to prevent divergence. Inputs: Gaussian parameters: Mean \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, Opacity \sigma \in [0, 1], Alpha \alpha (derived from density and scale). Pixel center p \in \mathbb{R}^2 in the image plane. Loss gradient with respect to alpha: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alphai}. Pruning threshold \tau{pruning} (typically used in Adaptive Density Control). Slope parameter m controlling the decay of the truncated gradient. Coefficients a, b, c derived from the Gaussian covariance structure (Eq. 8 of). Outputs: Modified gradient \tilde{\nabla}\mu for the Gaussian mean \mu. Modified gradient \tilde{\nabla}\sigma for the opacity \sigma (only in specific low-opacity cases). The method operates on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting data structures. Key fields accessed during the backward pass include: mu: 3D mean position. sigma: Opacity scalar. alpha: Alpha value (often \alpha = \sigma \cdot \text{density}). covariance: Used to derive a, b, c for the Mahalanobis distance. 1. Calculate Squared Mahalanobis Distance: Compute the squared Mahalanobis distance rs between the Gaussian mean \mu and the pixel center p in the image plane: rs = \|\mu - p\|2^2 The threshold condition for truncation relies on a value K defined as: K = a(\mux - px)^2 + 2b(\mux - px)(\muy - py) + c(\muy - py)^2 where a, b, c are coefficients from the Gaussian's 2D projection covariance. 2. Determine Gradient Update Path: Evaluate the product of opacity \sigma and alpha \alpha against the threshold 1/255 and compare rs against a cut-off threshold \tau (derived from K and the slope m). Three paths exist: Normal Path: If \sigma\alpha \ge 1/255 (high-pass filter), the Gaussian receives standard gradients from the loss. No truncation is applied. Truncated Path: If \sigma\alpha < 1/255 (low density or low opacity) AND the Mahalanobis distance is above the threshold (rs > \tau), the Gaussian receives the truncated gradient. If the low contribution is due to low density \alpha, compute the truncated gradient for the mean \mu. If the low contribution is due to low opacity \sigma, compute the gradient only for the opacity \sigma. Skip Path: If \sigma\alpha < 1/255 AND the Mahalanobis distance is below the threshold (rs < \tau), the Gaussian receives no gradients. 3. Check Gradient Sign: Only apply the truncated gradient if \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alphai} < 0. If the gradient is positive, applying the truncated gradient would cause a long-range push, making Gaussians repel each other. 4. Compute Truncated Gradient: For Gaussians on the Truncated Path, the cut-off gradient is defined as G'(x), where x is the solution to G(x) = \tau. The solution for the displacement is given by: rs = \|\mu - p\|2^2 \left( 1 \pm \sqrt{\frac{-2 \log \tau}{K}} \right) The choice of slope m influences the range of action: a lower m yields a near-constant long-range gradient approximating the cut-off gradient, while a higher m yields a sharp decay from the cut-off gradient. 5. Apply Dead Gaussian Filter: To prevent divergence, the truncated gradient is applied only to "dead" Gaussians, defined as those where \sigmai < \tau{pruning}. This prevents the accumulated truncated gradient from surpassing the true gradient for well-fitted Gaussians. 6. Interleaved Optimization: Alternate between optimization via the truncated gradient and normal optimization with Adaptive Density Control (ADC) turned on. This prevents perturbations to the accumulated viewspace gradient from affecting ADC. 7. Delay Pruning: Delay the pruning of primitives until the end of training. This allows dead Gaussians to receive long-range gradients and converge to distant pixels before being pruned. 8. Expand Tile-Coverage Radius: Expand the tile-coverage radius of each dead Gaussian if its radius is below a threshold. This addresses tile-based culling of the rasterizer, enabling long-distance pixel error contributions using the truncated gradient field. 9. Dynamic Scene Handling (Optional): For dynamic methods, create viewpoint-dependent motion masks via frame-difference and image processing on input videos. Ignore contributions of static pixels to reduce computation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetruncatedgradient(gaussian, pixel, lossgradalpha, taupruning, m, a, b, c): """ Computes the modified gradient for a Gaussian based on truncated gradient logic. Args: gaussian: Object containing mu (3D), sigma (opacity), alpha (alpha/density product). pixel: 2D pixel center (px, py). lossgradalpha: Gradient of loss w.r.t alpha (dL/dalpha). taupruning: Pruning threshold for opacity. m: Slope parameter for truncated gradient decay. a, b, c: Coefficients from Gaussian covariance projection. Returns: gradmu: Modified gradient for mean. gradsigma: Modified gradient for opacity. """ # Step 1: Calculate Mahalanobis-related term K dx = gaussian.mu[0] - pixel[0] dy = gaussian.mu[1] - pixel[1] K = a dx2 + 2 b dx dy + c dy2 # Step 2: Determine Path # Threshold for high-pass filter alphathreshold = 1.0 / 255.0 # Check if Gaussian is "dead" (low opacity) isdead = gaussian.sigma < taupruning # Check if Gaussian contributes significantly contributes = (gaussian.sigma gaussian.alpha) >= alphathreshold # Initialize gradients gradmu = 0.0 gradsigma = 0.0 if contributes: # Normal Path: Return standard gradients (handled by upstream backprop) # This function is only called for modification, so we return 0 or pass through return None, None else: # Gaussian does not contribute via standard rasterization # Check Mahalanobis distance threshold condition # The cut-off threshold tau is implicitly handled by the distance check # In practice, we check if distance is "large enough" to warrant truncation # Based on, if distance < threshold, it's a Skip Path # Simplified logic based on description: # Truncated Path: sigmaalpha < 1/255 AND distance > threshold # Skip Path: sigmaalpha < 1/255 AND distance < threshold # We need to determine if distance is above threshold. # The threshold is derived from tau and K. # For implementation, we assume a function isdistanceabovethreshold exists # which checks if rs > tau(K, m). if isdistanceabovethreshold(K, m): # Truncated Path if not isdead: # Only apply to dead Gaussians to prevent divergence return None, None # Check sign of alpha gradient if lossgradalpha >= 0: # Positive gradient causes repulsion; do not apply truncated gradient return None, None # Compute Truncated Gradient # The cut-off gradient G'(x) where x is solution to G(x) = tau # The displacement is proportional to the gradient of the surrogate loss # Calculate the magnitude based on slope m and distance # Lower m -> near-constant long-range gradient # Higher m -> sharp decay # Note: Exact formula for G'(x) requires solving G(x)=tau. # The source gives the solution for rs: # rs = ||mu - p||^2 (1 +/- sqrt(-2 log(tau) / K)) # The gradient direction is towards the pixel p. direction = pixel - gaussian.mu[:2] # 2D projection of mean dist = np.linalg.norm(direction) if dist == 0: return 0.0, 0.0 unitdirection = direction / dist # Compute the truncated gradient magnitude # This is a surrogate gradient. The exact scaling depends on the loss function L. # Typically, it scales with the loss value or a constant factor related to tau. # defines the cut-off gradient as G'(x). # Placeholder for the specific derivative of the surrogate loss function # In practice, this is often a constant or linearly decaying value truncatedgradmag = computetruncatedgradientmagnitude(m, K, taupruning) gradmu = truncatedgradmag unitdirection # If low opacity is the cause, also compute gradient for sigma #: "In the latter case, we only compute the gradient for the opacity sigma." # This implies if alpha is high but sigma is low, we might only update sigma. # However, the condition is sigmaalpha < 1/255. # If alpha is high, sigma must be very low. if gaussian.alpha > 0: # Check if alpha is the limiting factor or sigma # If the low contribution is primarily due to low sigma # We compute gradsigma. # The gradient for sigma is typically the loss gradient w.r.t alpha # scaled by the derivative of alpha w.r.t sigma. gradsigma = lossgradalpha gaussian.alpha # Simplified chain rule return gradmu, gradsigma else: # Skip Path: No gradients return None, None def isdistanceabovethreshold(K, m): """ Determines if the Mahalanobis distance is above the cut-off threshold. The threshold depends on K and the slope m. """ # The source states: "The choice of slope m influences the range of action... # a lower value of m yields a near-constant long-range gradient... # a higher value of m yields a sharp decay." # The threshold tau is the point where the gradient is cut off. # We assume a threshold function tau(K, m). # If the actual squared distance rs > tau, we apply truncated gradient. # Since the exact tau function is not explicitly given as a simple formula # in the provided text (it refers to Eq 8 and supplementary material), # we note that this check is implementation-specific. # However, the condition is simply: rs > tau. # For the purpose of this article, we assume the rasterizer or a helper # provides the threshold. return True # Placeholder: In real implementation, compare rs with tau(K, m) def computetruncatedgradientmagnitude(m, K, taupruning): """ Computes the magnitude of the truncated gradient. """ # The source defines the cut-off gradient as G'(x). # This is likely a constant or a function of m. # A lower m yields a near-constant gradient. # We assume a base magnitude related to the loss or a hyperparameter. return 1.0 / m # Simplified approximation for the article Slope parameter m: Influences the range of action of the truncated gradient in the image plane. A lower m yields a near-constant long-range gradient approximating the cut-off gradient; a higher m yields a sharp decay from the cut-off gradient. Pruning threshold \tau{pruning}: Used to identify "dead" Gaussians. Only these Gaussians receive truncated gradients to prevent divergence. Threshold 1/255: Used to distinguish between high-pass (normal) and low-pass (truncated/skip) paths. Model Divergence: Accumulated truncated gradients may surpass the true gradient, especially for "very bad fits" (no normal gradients) or "good fits" (true gradient near zero). This is prevented by applying the truncated gradient only for dead Gaussians (\sigmai < \tau{pruning}). Repulsion: If the sign of \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alphai} is positive, applying the truncated gradient causes a long-range push, making Gaussians repel each other. The method checks for negative gradients before applying. Tile Culling: Dead Gaussians with small radii may be culled by the tile-based rasterizer, preventing them from receiving any gradient. Expanding the tile-coverage radius for dead Gaussians addresses this. Performance Overhead: The method is 1–10× slower to train than the baseline, depending on the scene and primitive count. Inference speed is unaffected. Time Complexity: Training is 1–10× slower than the baseline 3DGS due to the additional gradient computation and radius expansion for dead Gaussians. Memory Complexity: No significant additional memory overhead compared to standard 3DGS, as it modifies the gradient computation rather than adding new data structures. Measured Performance: Static Scene (Mip-NeRF360, Random Init): 3DGS + Truncated Gradient achieves PSNR 25.16 (vs 24.74), SSIM 0.8511 (vs 0.8351), LPIPS 0.1974 (vs 0.2106), and #GS 0.799M (vs 1.126M). Dynamic Scene (Neural 3D Video): 4DGS + Truncated Gradient achieves PSNR 31.70 (vs 30.22), SSIM 0.9493 (vs 0.9443), LPIPS 0.1339 (vs 0.1360), and #GS 1.733M (vs 2.806M). Scaling: The method scales with the number of primitives, but the overhead is mitigated by only applying the truncated gradient to dead Gaussians and using motion masks for dynamic scenes. Strengths: Improves reconstruction quality for poorly initialized scenes and dynamic scenes with large spatio-temporal divergence. Reduces the number of Gaussians needed for high-quality reconstruction. Limitations: Slower training time. Requires careful tuning of the slope parameter m and pruning threshold. Not effective if the initial camera poses are extremely poor (though it helps convergence). When to Use: Use for static and dynamic scene reconstruction where standard 3DGS fails to converge due to vanishing gradients or poor initialization. It is a plug-and-play module for 3DGS, 2DGS, 4DGS, CEM-4DGS, and 4DScaffold. When Not to Use: Avoid if training time is a critical constraint and the scene is well-initialized. Avoid if the scene has no dynamic elements and standard 3DGS converges well. Origin: The method was introduced by T. Morales, N.-Q. Le-Pham, R. Atkins & B.-S. Hua in the paper "TruncGradGS: Improved 3D Gaussian Splatting via Truncated Gradient Updates". History: It was published in the Proceedings of Eurographics - The European Association for Computer Graphics in 2026. Development: The method builds on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting framework, addressing its limitations in handling "dead" Gaussians and long-range optimization. It integrates with existing dynamic Gaussian Splatting methods like 4DGS and CEM-4DGS. TruncGradGS: Improved 3D Gaussian Splatting via Truncated Gradient Updates, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03534v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Pose and Camera Optimization
head: Camera Pose Optimization, View Pose Estimation
body: Pose and Camera Optimization refers to the family of methods that estimate the relative or absolute camera poses (rigid transformations) by minimizing the photometric error between rendered images and ground-truth views using a 3D Gaussian Splatting representation. It solves the problem of recovering camera motion without relying on external Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines, enabling incremental or global pose estimation directly from differentiable rendering. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting Training Loop by treating camera poses as learnable parameters rather than fixed inputs, and distinguishes itself from Local 3DGS Optimization and Neural Parametric Gaussians Optimization by encompassing both local incremental estimation and global non-rigid deformation contexts. The core mechanism common to all methods in this family is the minimization of a photometric loss \mathcal{L} between the rendered image \hat{I} and the ground-truth image I{gt}. The standard photometric baseline is a weighted sum of L1 loss and differentiable Structural Similarity (D-SSIM): \mathcal{L}{img} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}{L1} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} where \mathcal{L}{L1} is the average absolute difference between corresponding pixel colors, and \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} measures local structure, contrast, and texture. The weight \lambda is typically 0.2. The optimization uses the Adam optimizer with \beta1 = 0.9 and \beta2 = 0.99. Training typically runs for a fixed number of iterations, commonly around 30,000 for standard scenes, though specific schedules vary (e.g., Gaussian Primitive Training Schedule uses ~6,000). The process does not stop at a specific loss threshold because the loss curve continues to creep down with diminishing returns; a fixed iteration budget is used instead. Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}{i=1}^N include position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \Sigmai (parameterized by rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 and scale vector \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3), opacity \alphai \in [0, 1], and Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients \mathbf{c}{i, l} for view-dependent color. Local 3DGS Optimization is an iterative method for estimating the relative camera pose (transformation) between two nearby images by optimizing a local 3D Gaussian Splatting representation against photometric loss. It solves the problem of camera pose estimation without requiring external Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines like COLMAP, relying instead on monocular depth estimation and differentiable rendering. It sets itself apart from global optimization methods by freezing the Gaussian attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, SH) after initialization and optimizing only the pose parameters, making it suitable for incremental or local sequence processing [20073-local-3dgs-optimization.md]. Neural Parametric Gaussians (NPGs) is a two-stage optimization procedure for monocular non-rigid object reconstruction that combines a coarse parametric point model regularized by a low-rank deformation basis with 3D Gaussians to model fine geometric and appearance details efficiently. It sets itself apart from siblings like Local 3DGS Optimization by explicitly decoupling the learning of global non-rigid deformation (via the parametric basis) from local detail fitting (via Gaussians), ensuring coarse geometry remains intact over time. A method to handle photometric inconsistencies (automatic exposure/white-balance) by co-optimizing a per-view latent vector mapped via an MLP to a linear transformation of spherical harmonic coefficients. \hat{c}i = a \odot ci + b, where \hat{c}i are the transformed coefficients, ci are the original spherical harmonic coefficients, \odot is the Hadamard product, b models brightness changes, and a provides white-balance expressive power. a, b = Q(zn; \thetaQ), where Q is an MLP taking latent zn \in \mathbb{R}^{64}. zn \in \mathbb{R}^{64}, a latent vector per input camera view. \thetaQ, trainable parameters of the MLP Q that maps zn to a and b. A reduced model prevents zn from explaining distractors as per-image adjustments, which would happen in a simpler GLO. The concept of optimizing camera poses within differentiable rendering frameworks has evolved from traditional Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines to end-to-end differentiable approaches. Early works like [Martin-Brualla et al. 2021b] (referenced in) proposed Global Latent Optimization (GLO) to handle per-image adjustments, but suffered from explaining distractors as photometric changes. [Rematas et al. 2022] (referenced in) provided an analysis of such models. The adaptation of these concepts to 3D Gaussian Splatting, as seen in [SpotLessSplats], allows for robust pose estimation and photometric consistency handling in casual captures with automatic exposure and white-balance. Local methods, such as those described in [20073-local-3dgs-optimization.md], leverage monocular depth estimation (e.g., DPT) to initialize local Gaussians, enabling pose estimation without external SfM. Non-rigid extensions, like Neural Parametric Gaussians, extend this to dynamic scenes by coupling parametric deformation bases with Gaussian splats. name: Local 3DGS Optimization
head: Local 3DGS Pose Optimization
body: Local 3DGS Optimization is an iterative method for estimating the relative camera pose (extrinsic transformation) between two nearby images by optimizing a local 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation against photometric loss. Unlike global reconstruction methods that optimize scene geometry and camera poses simultaneously, this method keeps the local Gaussian attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, and spherical harmonics) fixed after initialization, learning only the pose parameters. It is distinct from Neural Parametric Gaussians Optimization by relying on explicit 3D Gaussian primitives rather than neural field representations for the local scene model. Inputs: Two nearby images: current view It and target view I{t+1}. Monocular depth estimation model (e.g., DPT). Camera intrinsic parameters (or heuristics if unknown). Outputs: Estimated relative pose Qt representing the transformation from the coordinate system of It to I{t+1}. Data Structures: Local 3DGS Representation (Gt): A set of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian gi contains: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Covariance \Sigmai, parameterized by rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 and scale vector \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1]. Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients \mathbf{c}{i, l} for view-dependent color. Pose Parameter (Tt): A learnable transformation matrix (or quaternion/translation pair) representing the relative pose. Initialized as Identity I. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Local 3DGS: Compute monocular depth map Dt for image It using the depth estimation model (e.g., DPT). Initialize the local 3DGS representation Gt from It and Dt using InitGauss(It, Dt). Note: The source mentions downsampling the point cloud before fitting to handle high-resolution inputs. Optimize Gt on the input view It via photometric loss for 500 iterations to fit the local geometry. 2. Initialize Pose: Set the relative pose parameter Tt to the Identity transformation I. 3. Optimize Pose: While not converged: Render the target view image \hat{I}{t+1} by rasterizing the transformed Gaussians Tt \odot Gt. Compute the photometric loss \mathcal{L} between the target image I{t+1} and the rendered image \hat{I}{t+1}. Update the pose parameter Tt using the Adam optimizer on the gradient \nabla \mathcal{L}. Constraint: All attributes of Gt (position, SH, opacity, scale, rotation) are frozen during this step; only the pose parameters (quaternion and translation vector) are updated. The pose optimization runs for 300 steps. 4. Output Pose: The final relative pose Qt is the accumulated transformation Tt. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def local3dgsoptimization(It, Itplus1, depthmodel, cameraintrinsics): """ Estimates relative pose between It and Itplus1 using Local 3DGS. Args: It: Current view image. Itplus1: Target view image. depthmodel: Monocular depth estimation model (e.g., DPT). cameraintrinsics: Camera intrinsic parameters. Returns: Tt: Estimated relative pose transformation. """ # Step 1: Initialize Local 3DGS # Compute depth for current view Dt = depthmodel.predict(It) # Initialize Gaussians from image and depth # Note: Source mentions downsampling point cloud before fitting Gt = InitGauss(It, Dt) # Optimize local 3DGS attributes on It for 500 iterations # Loss is photometric loss between rendered It and It for in range(500): Irendered = rasterize(Gt, cameraintrinsics) L = photometricloss(It, Irendered) # Update Gt attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, SH) Gt = adamupdate(Gt, L) # Step 2: Initialize Pose # Tt represents the transformation from It coordinate system to Itplus1 Tt = Identity() # Step 3: Optimize Pose # Freeze Gt attributes, only optimize Tt for in range(300): # Transform Gaussians by current pose estimate Gtransformed = transform(Gt, Tt) # Render target view Irenderedtarget = rasterize(Gtransformed, cameraintrinsics) # Compute loss against target image L = photometricloss(Itplus1, Irenderedtarget) # Update only pose parameters (quaternion and translation) Tt = adamupdate(Tt, L) return Tt def photometricloss(Igt, Ipred): """ Computes weighted sum of L1 loss and D-SSIM. Lambda = 0.2 """ lambdaweight = 0.2 l1loss = meanabsoluteerror(Igt, Ipred) ssimloss = 1.0 - ssim(Igt, Ipred) return (1 - lambdaweight) l1loss + lambdaweight ssimloss Parameters: Local 3DGS Optimization Iterations: 500 iterations. Pose Learning Optimization Steps: 300 steps. Monocular Depth Estimation Model: DPT (Vision Transformers for Dense Prediction). Camera Intrinsic Heuristic: If intrinsic parameters are unknown, Field of View (FoV) is set to 79^\circ and principal points are set to the image center. Optimizer: Adam with \beta1 = 0.9 and \beta2 = 0.99. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unknown Intrinsics: Using heuristic intrinsics (FoV 79^\circ, center principal point) leads to slight degradation in novel view synthesis and camera pose estimation accuracy compared to known intrinsics. High-Resolution Inputs: High-resolution images can generate a huge amount of points; downsampling the point cloud before fitting is necessary to manage memory and computation. Dramatic Camera Motion: The method is designed to handle dramatic camera motions (large relative rotation angles, up to 180^\circ in tested sequences like CO3D-V2 and Tanks and Temples). Time Complexity: The method involves two optimization phases: 500 iterations for local 3DGS fitting and 300 steps for pose optimization. The complexity is dominated by the rasterization and loss computation per iteration. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians N in the local representation. Downsampling is used to mitigate memory issues with high-resolution inputs. Strengths: Capable of handling dramatic camera motions (large relative rotation angles) without requiring COLMAP or initial pose estimates. It provides photo-realistic rendering with detailed geometry. Limitations: Performance degrades slightly when camera intrinsics are unknown and must be heuristically set. It is limited to "nearby" images as defined by the local window assumption. When to Use: When initial camera poses are unavailable (COLMAP-free) and relative pose estimation between consecutive or nearby frames is required. When Not to Use: When global consistency across a large scene is needed in a single step, or when high-precision intrinsics are unknown and cannot be estimated separately. Local 3DGS Optimization was introduced in the supplementary material of "COLMAP-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting" by Zhou et al. (CVPR 2024). It addresses the challenge of view synthesis and pose estimation without relying on Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines like COLMAP. The method builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting and adapts them for local, iterative pose refinement. It was evaluated on datasets such as CO3D-V2 and Tanks and Temples, demonstrating robustness to large camera rotations. name: Neural Parametric Gaussians Optimization
head: two-stage optimization for monocular non-rigid reconstruction
body: Neural Parametric Gaussians (NPGs) is a two-stage optimization method for monocular non-rigid object reconstruction that combines a coarse parametric point model regularized by a low-rank deformation basis with 3D Gaussians to model fine geometric and appearance details. It solves the ill-posed problem of reconstructing dynamic objects from single-camera video by preventing the geometric collapse common in purely implicit or unregularized explicit methods. Unlike sibling methods such as Local 3DGS Optimization which may lack global structural priors, NPGs explicitly maintains a consistent coarse template across timesteps, enabling high-fidelity novel view synthesis on challenging monocular datasets like Unbiased4D. The method optimizes a hybrid representation in two distinct stages. Stage 1 learns a coarse parametric point model using a low-rank deformation basis. Stage 2 refines this representation using 3D Gaussians, leveraging the coarse model as a structural prior. Inputs: Monocular video sequence of a non-rigid object. Masks for dynamic objects (optional, used for sequences with static backgrounds like Lego/T-Rex). Hyperparameters: Deformation basis size K, learning rates, iteration counts. Outputs: Optimized coarse parametric point model (positions, deformation coefficients). Optimized 3D Gaussian fields (positions, covariances, opacities, SH coefficients) aligned with the deformed template. 1. Coarse Parametric Model: Points: Np = 1500 points modeling coarse geometry. Deformation Basis Coefficients: Computed by a 6-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). The MLP maps input features (e.g., time, spatial coordinates) to coefficients for the low-rank basis. Basis Size: K (scalar). Controls regularization strength. Optimal value found to be 25 for synthetic cactus. 2. 3D Gaussian Fields: Parameters \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}{i=1}^N as defined in Pose and Camera Optimization: position \mathbf{p}i, covariance \Sigmai (from quaternion \mathbf{q}i and scale \mathbf{s}i), opacity \alphai, and SH coefficients \mathbf{c}{i, l}. Interpolation Weights: w used to blend or interpolate between Gaussian states or template points (specific definition of interpolation mechanism not detailed in sources, but w is optimized). Stage 1: Coarse Parametric Model Optimization 1. Initialize Np = 1500 points to model the coarse object geometry. 2. Initialize a 6-layer MLP to compute deformation basis coefficients. 3. Define the deformation basis size K. Set K=25 for standard synthetic sequences (e.g., cactus). 4. Apply Rigidity Loss during optimization to keep the template consistent across timesteps. 5. Optimize point positions and MLP coefficients using the Adam optimizer. Batch size: 10. Learning rate: 0.0005 with cosine annealing and warm-up. Iterations: 100,000. Stage 2: 3D Gaussian Refinement 1. Initialize 3D Gaussians based on the Stage 1 template. 2. Adopt the learning rate schedule from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for most parameters. 3. Optimize Gaussian parameters and interpolation weights w for 70,000 iterations. Learning rate for interpolation weights w: Matches the default point position learning rate in 3DGS. Learning rate for Gaussian scales: 0.0005. Scale Scheduler: Exponential decay from a high initial value down to 0.0005. 4. (Optional) Finetuning: Continue optimizing Stage 1 parameters (point positions, MLP coefficients) alongside Stage 2 parameters. Learning rate for Stage 1 parameters during finetuning: 0.0001. This step is not strictly necessary but improves template accuracy. The optimization minimizes a photometric loss \mathcal{L}, consistent with the parent method Pose and Camera Optimization: \mathcal{L}{img} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}{L1} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} where \lambda = 0.2. Additionally, Stage 1 employs a Rigidity Loss \mathcal{L}{rigid} to enforce temporal consistency of the coarse template. The exact mathematical formulation of \mathcal{L}{rigid} is not provided in the sources, but its purpose is to prevent the template from deforming inconsistently across timesteps. Deformation Basis Size (K): 25 (optimal for synthetic cactus; smaller K over-regularizes, larger K overfits). Number of Coarse Points (Np): 1500. MLP Depth: 6 layers. Stage 1 Learning Rate: 0.0005 (cosine annealing + warm-up). Stage 1 Iterations: 100,000. Stage 1 Batch Size: 10. Stage 2 Iterations: 70,000. Stage 2 Scale Learning Rate: 0.0005. Stage 2 Finetuning LR: 0.0001 (for Stage 1 params). Template Collapse: If the camera is very static, the optimized template may collapse to a flat surface, leading to incorrect deformation. This is a critical failure mode in highly ill-posed monocular scenarios. Static Backgrounds: For sequences with large static ground planes (e.g., Lego, T-Rex), masks for dynamic objects only are required to prevent the model from optimizing static background elements incorrectly. Basis Size Selection: Choosing K incorrectly leads to either over-regularization (restricting non-rigid deformations) or overfitting (hindering novel view synthesis). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def npgoptimization(videoframes, masks=None): # Hyperparameters K = 25 # Deformation basis size Npoints = 1500 stage1iters = 100000 stage2iters = 70000 lrstage1 = 0.0005 lrstage2scale = 0.0005 lrfinetune = 0.0001 batchsize = 10 # Stage 1: Coarse Parametric Model # Initialize 1500 points coarsepoints = initializepoints(Npoints) # Initialize 6-layer MLP for deformation basis coefficients deformationmlp = initializemlp(layers=6) # Optimizer for Stage 1 optimizerstage1 = Adam([coarsepoints, deformationmlp.parameters()], lr=lrstage1) schedulerstage1 = CosineAnnealingWarmup(optimizerstage1) for iter in range(stage1iters): # Sample batch of frames/views batchframes = samplebatch(videoframes, batchsize) # Compute deformation coefficients using MLP # Inputs to MLP (e.g., time, spatial coords) are derived from batch coeffs = deformationmlp(batchframes.inputs) # Apply deformation basis of size K to coarse points deformedpoints = applydeformationbasis(coarsepoints, coeffs, K) # Render intermediate representation (not fully detailed in sources, # but implied to be part of the loss calculation) renderedimgs = render(deformedpoints) # Calculate Loss # 1. Photometric Loss (standard L1 + D-SSIM) lossimg = computephotometricloss(renderedimgs, batchframes.gt) # 2. Rigidity Loss (keeps template consistent across timesteps) # Exact formula not given in sources lossrigid = computerigidityloss(deformedpoints, batchframes.timesteps) loss = lossimg + lossrigid # Backprop and update optimizerstage1.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizerstage1.step() schedulerstage1.step() # Stage 2: 3D Gaussian Refinement # Initialize 3D Gaussians from Stage 1 results gaussians = initializegaussians(deformedpoints) # Optimizer for Stage 2 # Note: Different LRs for different parameters paramsgaussians = [ {'params': gaussians.positions, 'lr': lr3dgsdefault}, # Matches 3DGS default {'params': gaussians.scales, 'lr': lrstage2scale}, {'params': gaussians.opacities, 'lr': lr3dgsdefault}, {'params': gaussians.shcoeffs, 'lr': lr3dgsdefault}, {'params': gaussians.interpolationweights, 'lr': lr3dgsdefault} # w ] optimizerstage2 = Adam(paramsgaussians) # Exponential scheduler for scales schedulerscales = ExponentialDecay(optimizerstage2, targetlr=lrstage2scale) # Optional: Include Stage 1 params in optimizer for finetuning if finetunestage1: paramsstage1 = [ {'params': coarsepoints, 'lr': lrfinetune}, {'params': deformationmlp.parameters(), 'lr': lrfinetune} ] optimizerstage2.addparamgroup({'params': paramsstage1}) for iter in range(stage2iters): batchframes = samplebatch(videoframes, batchsize) # Get deformation coefficients coeffs = deformationmlp(batchframes.inputs) # Deform coarse points deformedpoints = applydeformationbasis(coarsepoints, coeffs, K) # Render 3D Gaussians (blended/interpolated using weights w) renderedimgs = rendergaussians(gaussians, deformedpoints) # Photometric Loss loss = computephotometricloss(renderedimgs, batchframes.gt) optimizerstage2.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizerstage2.step() # Update scale scheduler schedulerscales.step() return coarsepoints, deformationmlp, gaussians Performance: NPGs outperforms baselines like Nerfies, HyperNeRF, TiNeuVox, and HexPlane on the Unbiased4D dataset (PSNR 22.348 vs 15.92–18.56). Strengths: Successfully keeps coarse geometry intact over the sequence and fits high-frequency details, which is critical for monocular non-rigid reconstruction. Limitations: Highly sensitive to camera motion; static cameras can cause template collapse. Requires careful tuning of the deformation basis size K. Complexity: Uses a fixed iteration budget (100k + 70k) rather than loss convergence. NPGs was introduced in "Neural Parametric Gaussians for Monocular Non-Rigid Object Reconstruction" (CVPR 2024). It addresses the limitations of previous methods that fail to capture geometry correctly in monocular settings by introducing a two-stage optimization with a low-rank deformation basis. name: BAD-Gaussians
head: Bundle Adjusted Deblur Gaussian Splatting
body: BAD-Gaussians recovers a sharp 3D scene representation by jointly learning camera motion trajectories and 3D Gaussian parameters from a sequence of motion-blurred images, inaccurate poses, and sparse point clouds. It solves the problem of reconstructing high-quality geometry and appearance from blurry inputs where standard 3D Gaussian Splatting fails due to unmodeled motion blur. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like DeSplat and 360 Gaussian Splatting by explicitly modeling the physical motion blur formation process via virtual camera poses and optimizing the camera trajectory (start and end poses) alongside the Gaussians, rather than assuming static sharp inputs or using different blur kernels. Inputs: A sequence of N motion-blurred images \{Bk\}{k=0}^{N-1}, their corresponding inaccurate initial poses and sparse point clouds estimated from COLMAP. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians (mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity o, color c) and optimized camera start (T{start}) and end (T{end}) poses for each blurred image. Data Structures: 3D Gaussian: Parameterized by \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, o \in \mathbb{R}, and c \in \mathbb{R}^3. Camera Pose: T{start} and T{end} are parameterized by their corresponding Lie algebras of SE(3), represented by a 6D vector each. Virtual Poses: n discrete virtual camera poses interpolated between T{start} and T{end} to approximate the exposure time. Parameters: n: Number of discrete samples (virtual camera poses) used to approximate the motion blur integral. Typical value: 10. Learning rate for Gaussians: Identical to original 3D-GS. Learning rate for camera poses (T{start}, T{end}): Exponentially decreased from 1 \times 10^{-3} to 1 \times 10^{-5}. Optimizer: Adam. Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians and camera poses using estimations obtained from COLMAP. 2. Virtual Pose Generation: For each blurred image k, define the start pose T{start}^{(k)} and end pose T{end}^{(k)}. Generate n virtual poses Ti^{(k)} for i=0 \dots n-1 by interpolating between T{start}^{(k)} and T{end}^{(k)}. The interpolation method can be linear or cubic B-spline. 3. Virtual Image Synthesis: For each virtual pose Ti^{(k)}, render a sharp virtual image Ci^{(k)}(u) using standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization. The pixel value at location u is computed by sorting Gaussians front-to-back and compositing their contributions. The opacity contribution of a Gaussian i is given by: \alphai = oi \cdot \exp(-\sigmai) where oi is the learned opacity and \sigmai = \frac{1}{2} \Deltai^\top \Sigma'^{-1} \Deltai, with \Deltai being the offset between the pixel center and the 2D Gaussian center projected onto the image plane. 4. Blur Model Approximation: Compute the synthesized blurred image Bk(u) by averaging the virtual sharp images: Bk(u) \approx \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=0}^{n-1} Ci^{(k)}(u) \quad (7). 5. Loss Computation: Calculate the photometric loss between the synthesized blurred image Bk(u) and the input blurred image Bk^{input}(u). 6. Gradient Backpropagation: Compute gradients with respect to Gaussian parameters \theta and camera poses T. Gradient w.r.t. Gaussian parameters \theta: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} = \sum{k=0}^{K-1} \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial Bk} \right) \cdot \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=0}^{n-1} \left( \frac{\partial Bi}{\partial Ci} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{\partial Ci}{\partial \theta} \right) \quad (10) where \frac{\partial Bi}{\partial Ci} = \frac{1}{n}. Gradient w.r.t. Camera Poses T: \frac{\partial L}{\partial T} = \sum{k=0}^{K-1} \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial Bk} \right) \cdot \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=0}^{n-1} \left( \frac{\partial Bk}{\partial Ci} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{\partial Ci}{\partial \theta} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{\partial \theta}{\partial T} \right) \quad (11) Note: The source text contains a typo in the second term of the sum for Eq. 11, listing \frac{\partial Ci}{\partial \theta} instead of \frac{\partial Ci}{\partial T}, but the formula provided is used as written. The term \frac{\partial \theta}{\partial T} represents the Jacobian of the Gaussian parameters with respect to the camera pose. 7. Optimization: Update \theta and T using the Adam optimizer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def interpolatepose(Tstart, Tend, t): """Linear interpolation of 6D Lie algebra vectors.""" return (1.0 - t) Tstart + t Tend def renderblurredimage(gaussians, Tstart, Tend, nsamples, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Renders a motion-blurred image by averaging nsamples virtual sharp images. """ virtualimages = [] for i in range(nsamples): t = i / (nsamples - 1) Tvirtual = interpolatepose(Tstart, Tend, t) # Standard 3D-GS rasterization: project 3D Gaussians to 2D using Tvirtual, # sort front-to-back, compute alpha via αi = oi exp(-0.5 Δi^T Σ'^-1 Δi), # and composite color contributions. sharpimage = torch.zeros(imageheight, imagewidth, 3, device=gaussians.device) virtualimages.append(sharpimage) blurredimage = torch.stack(virtualimages, dim=0).mean(dim=0) return blurredimage def trainbadgaussians(blurredimages, initialgaussians, initialTstart, initialTend, nsamples=10, numtrainingsteps=10000): """ Training loop for BAD-Gaussians. """ gaussians = initialgaussians.clone().requiresgrad(True) Tstart = initialTstart.clone().requiresgrad(True) Tend = initialTend.clone().requiresgrad(True) # Learning rate for Gaussians identical to original 3D-GS; poses decay exponentially optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([{'params': gaussians}, {'params': [Tstart, Tend]}], lr=1e-3) for step in range(numtrainingsteps): currentposelr = 1e-3 (1e-5 / 1e-3) (step / numtrainingsteps) for paramgroup in optimizer.paramgroups: if paramgroup['params'] == [Tstart, Tend]: paramgroup['lr'] = currentposelr else: paramgroup['lr'] = 1e-3 optimizer.zerograd() totalloss = 0 for blurredimg in blurredimages: renderedblur = renderblurredimage(gaussians, Tstart, Tend, nsamples, blurredimg.shape[1], blurredimg.shape[2]) loss = F.l1loss(renderedblur, blurredimg) totalloss += loss totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return gaussians, Tstart, Tend Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance Saturation: Increasing n beyond 10 yields diminishing returns. Performance reaches a saturation point, so n=10 is recommended for the trade-off between performance and efficiency. Trajectory Representation: Cubic interpolation (B-spline) improves performance in scenes with complex camera trajectories (e.g., MBA-VO and Deblur-NeRF-R) compared to linear interpolation. Pose Accuracy Sensitivity: The method is sensitive to the accuracy of initial poses. Methods like Deblur-NeRF and DP-NeRF show a significant performance gap when trained with COLMAP poses versus ground-truth poses, highlighting the importance of good initialization. Time Complexity: Training time is approximately 30 minutes on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. This is significantly faster than competing methods like Deblur-NeRF, DP-NeRF, and BAD-NeRF, which take more than 10 hours. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Rendering Efficiency: Achieves over 200 FPS rendering efficiency. In contrast, Deblur-NeRF, DP-NeRF, and BAD-NeRF fall below 1 FPS. Strengths: High rendering speed, fast training time, ability to handle motion blur and inaccurate poses jointly. Limitations: Sensitive to initial pose accuracy. Performance gains from increasing n saturate quickly. When to use: When reconstructing scenes from motion-blurred images with inaccurate camera poses and sparse initialization. When not to use: When high-precision camera poses are already available and images are sharp (standard 3D-GS is sufficient and simpler). BAD-Gaussians was introduced in the paper "BAD-Gaussians: Bundle Adjusted Deblur Gaussian Splatting". It builds upon the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework [15] and addresses the limitations of NeRF-based deblurring methods (Deblur-NeRF [26], BAD-NeRF [46]) which are computationally expensive and slow to render. The method leverages the geometry within multi-view blurry images to reconstruct a high-quality 3D scene by minimizing the photometric error between input blurred images and synthesized blurred images based on a physical motion blur image formation model.
