name: LiteTex-GS
body: LiteTex-GS is a fast and lightweight texturing framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that decouples geometry from appearance by assigning independent local RGB texture maps to each Gaussian primitive. It solves the computational overhead of high-resolution texturing by initializing compact low-resolution maps and progressively allocating higher resolution only to primitives with significant reconstruction errors, using a global-to-local capacity allocation strategy. Unlike prior methods that statically allocate texture resolution, LiteTex-GS uses a frequency-aware scheduler to coordinate image supervision, texture-cap release, and primitive densification, while employing a contribution- and area-aware pruning strategy to eliminate low-utility Gaussians. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of training images \{Im\}, camera poses, and an initial set of 3D Gaussian primitives (position, rotation, scale, opacity) initialized with minimal 2x2 local texture maps. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters (position, rotation, scale, opacity) and local RGB texture maps Ti for each primitive. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive i: pos: 3D position vector. rot: Quaternion or rotation matrix. scale: 3D scale vector. opacity: Scalar opacity value. Ti: Local RGB texture map. Initially 2x2. Can grow to rectangular dimensions up to a personal ceiling R{max,i} and global cap u(t). Rmax,i: Personal resolution ceiling for texture growth. patience: Integer counter for pruning protection. stats: Accumulated projected area ai, contribution ci, and normalized error ei. Frequency Significance Image F{img}: Precomputed 2D array representing scene frequency content. Scheduler State: Current iteration t. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize each Gaussian primitive with a 2x2 RGB texture map Ti. Set personal resolution ceilings R{max,i} to the initial texture size (2). Initialize accumulated statistics ai, ci, ei to zero for all primitives. Initialize patience counters to zero. 2. Preprocessing (Frequency-Aware Scheduling Setup): For each training image Im: Convert to grayscale \bar{I}m. Compute gradient magnitude Gm = \sqrt{(Sobelx \bar{I}m)^2 + (Sobely \bar{I}m)^2}. Normalize Gm to \tilde{G}m via min-max normalization. Compute weight map Wm = \text{clip}(w{min} + \alpha \tilde{G}m, w{min}, w{max}) with \alpha=1.5, w{min}=1.0, w{max}=3.0. Compute weighted image Wm \odot Im and transform to frequency domain: Fm = |\text{fftshift}(\mathcal{F}(Wm \odot Im))|. Compute F{img} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{m=1}^M Fm. Calculate total energy E{total} = \sum{u,v} F{img}(u,v). Determine coarsest scale parameters: E{min} = E{total} / \beta with \beta=3. Generate frequency stages by sampling at most L=32 targets between E{min} and E{total}, mapping targets to render scales via binary search on accumulated energy within window (H/s) \times (W/s), and merging adjacent stages with identical integer scales. 3. Training Loop (per iteration t): Scheduler Query: Compute (r(t), u(t), \rho(t)) = \mathcal{S}(t; F{img}), where r(t) is render downsampling factor, u(t) is global texture resolution cap, and \rho(t) is densification rate. Rendering: For each pixel p in the rendered view: Identify influencing primitives N(p). For each primitive i \in N(p): Compute mapping \Phii(p): 1. Intersect camera ray of p with local tangent plane of Gaussian i. 2. Transform intersection point from view space to world space. 3. Project into primitive’s axis-aligned local frame. 4. Normalize canonical coordinate by primitive’s 2D scale. 5. Convert to texture coordinates based on current texel size and texture center offset. Check if \Phii(p) is within valid texture domain. If out of bounds, skip texture sampling for this primitive. Sample texture: val = S(Ti, \Phii(p)) using differentiable bilinear sampling S. Compute blending weight \omegai(p) = T^iv(p)\alpha^iv(p), where \alpha^iv(p) is opacity-weighted Gaussian response and T^iv(p) is accumulated transmittance. Compute rendered color: \hat{I}(p) = \sum{i \in N(p)} \omegai(p) S(Ti, \Phii(p)). Loss Computation: Compute per-pixel loss: Lv(p) = (1 - \lambda) ||Iv(p) - \hat{I}v(p)||1 + \lambda (1 - SSIMv(p)) with \lambda=0.2. Assign loss to primitives using blending weights \omegai(p). Statistics Accumulation: For each primitive i: Accumulate projected area n{i,v} (number of pixels with valid support). Accumulate contribution \sum{p \in \Omegav} \omega^iv(p). Accumulate error \sum{p \in \Omegav} Lv(p). Periodic Management (every 250 iterations): Normalization: ai = \frac{\sumv n{i,v}}{\sumv Wv Hv}. ci = \frac{\sumv \sum{p \in \Omegav} \omega^iv(p)}{\sumv Wv Hv}. ei = \frac{\text{accumulated error}}{ci}. ei = ei / \max(ej) (normalized). Pruning Check: For each primitive i: Determine low-utility status: mi^{(t)} = \mathbb{1}(ci^{(t)} < \tauc \lor ai^{(t)} < \taua) with \tauc=5\times10^{-6}, \taua=5\times10^{-5}. If mi^{(t)}=1, increment patience counter; else reset to 0. If patience counter \ge K=8, remove primitive. Note: Newly split primitives have a lower post-split opacity floor to prevent immediate removal. When to use: When high-quality texturing is required but computational resources are limited, or when standard 3DGS lacks sufficient detail. When not to use: When real-time rendering speed is the absolute priority and texture detail is not critical, standard 3DGS may be faster due to lower overhead. It addresses the challenge of balancing expressive detail with computational efficiency in Gaussian Splatting texturing. The method builds on the frequency-aware scheduling principle introduced by DashGaussian [CJJ 25] and extends it to coordinate image supervision, texture-cap release, and primitive densification. It is motivated by the limitations of opacity-based pruning in standard 3DGS [KKL 23] and the static texture allocation of prior methods [PKDD25, CTP 25]. name: Virtual Camera Optimization for Mirror Reflections
head: GSIM, Gaussian Splatting in Mirrors
body: Virtual Camera Optimization for Mirror Reflections (GSIM) is a method for rendering physically accurate mirror reflections in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) by modeling reflections as images captured by virtual cameras positioned symmetrically to the real camera across the mirror plane. It solves the problem of multi-view inconsistencies and blurriness caused by 3D-GS misinterpreting reflections as virtual 3D space behind the mirror. Unlike NeRF-based methods that use ray tracing, this method maintains real-time rendering speeds by using standard rasterization from the virtual camera pose. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A trained 3D-GS scene representation (Gaussians), real camera poses [R|t], intrinsics K, and ground truth images. Outputs: Final rendered image \hat{C}{pred,f}, optimized mirror plane parameters [n, o], and virtual camera pose [R'|t']. Data Structures Gaussian Scene: Each Gaussian i is defined by mean \mui, covariance \Sigmai, opacity Oi, and spherical harmonic coefficients Ci \in \mathbb{C}^{N{sh}}. Mirror Plane: Defined by normal vector n \in \mathbb{R}^3 and origin point o \in \mathbb{R}^3 in world coordinates, denoted as [n, o]. Virtual Camera Extrinsic: A 3 \times 4 matrix [R'|t'] \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 4}. Mirror Mask: A binary mask identifying pixels PM belonging to the mirror region within the set of all pixels P{cam}. Numbered Steps 1. Depth and Normal Rasterization: Extend standard 3D-GS rasterization to render depth and normal maps for the current view. Depth Map (\hat{D}): Rendered via alpha-compositing of Gaussian centers' z-depths di: \hat{D} = \sum{i \in N} di \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) Normal Map (\hat{N}): Rendered via alpha-compositing of Gaussian shortest axis normals ni: \hat{N} = \sum{i \in N} ni \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where ni is the normalized vector of the shortest axis of the i-th Gaussian's covariance matrix. 2. Mirror Plane Prediction: Estimate the mirror plane [n, o] in world coordinates using the rendered depth and normal maps. Color Optimization: Replace mirror region colors in the ground truth image with a constant color to reconstruct the mirror surface geometry without texture interference. Depth Regularization: Apply a smoothness loss L{smooth} to ensure depth consistency, weighted by color similarity: L{smooth} = \sum{k \in P{cam}} \sum{q \in N(k)} \exp(-\gamma \| C'{gt}(k) - C'{gt}(q) \|) |\hat{D}{pred,r}(k) - \hat{D}{pred,r}(q)| where k and q represent pixels, N(k) represents the 4 horizontal/vertical neighbour pixels around k, and \gamma is a hyper-parameter. Normal Consistency: Use depth estimates to supervise normal consistency. 3. Virtual Camera Pose Computation: Compute the virtual camera extrinsic matrix [R'|t'] symmetric to the real camera [R|t] about the mirror plane [n, o]: \begin{bmatrix} R' & t' \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} I - 2nn^T & 2o \times n \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} R & t \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} where I is the identity matrix and o \times n denotes the cross product. 4. Virtual Camera Rendering: Render the scene from the virtual camera using standard 3D-GS forward rasterization to obtain the reflected image \hat{C}{pred,v}. 5. Image Fusion: Fuse the virtual camera render and the real camera render \hat{C}{pred,r} using the mirror mask: \hat{C}{pred,f}(k) = \begin{cases} \hat{C}{pred,v}(k), & \text{if } k \in P{cam} \cap PM \\ \hat{C}{pred,r}(k), & \text{if } k \in P{cam} \setminus PM \end{cases} where PM is the set of pixels in the masked mirror region. 6. Optimization: Refine the mirror plane parameters [n, o] (and thus the virtual camera pose) via gradient descent during training to enhance reflection quality and resolve imperfections in the initial plane estimate. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computevirtualcameraextrinsic(realextrinsic, mirrornormal, mirrororigin): R = realextrinsic[:,:3] t = realextrinsic[:, 3] n = mirrornormal.flatten() o = mirrororigin.flatten() reflectionrot = np.eye(3) - 2.0 np.outer(n, n) translationoffset = 2.0 np.cross(o, n) mirrortransform = np.eye(4) mirrortransform[:3,:3] = reflectionrot mirrortransform[:3, 3] = translationoffset realcamhom = np.eye(4) realcamhom[:3,:3] = R realcamhom[:3, 3] = t virtualcamhom = mirrortransform @ realcamhom return virtualcamhom[:3,:] def renderdepthandnormals(gaussians, cameraextrinsic, cameraintrinsics, imageshape): screengaussians = projectgaussians(gaussians, cameraextrinsic, cameraintrinsics, imageshape) screengaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g['zdepth']) height, width = imageshape depthmap = np.zeros((height, width)) normalmap = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) alphamap = np.zeros((height, width)) for g in screengaussians: alpha = g['alpha'] depth = g['zdepth'] normal = g['shortestaxisnormal'] for y, x in g['screencoverage']: transmittance = 1.0 - alphamap[y, x] depthmap[y, x] += depth alpha transmittance normalmap[y, x] += normal alpha transmittance alphamap[y, x] += alpha transmittance return depthmap, normalmap def projectgaussians(gaussians, cameraextrinsic, cameraintrinsics, imageshape): projected = [] for g in gaussians: meancam = cameraextrinsic[:3,:3] @ g['mean'] + cameraextrinsic[:3, 3] if meancam[2] <= 0: continue sx = (cameraintrinsics[0, 0] meancam[0] / meancam[2]) + cameraintrinsics[0, 2] sy = (cameraintrinsics[1, 1] meancam[1] / meancam[2]) + cameraintrinsics[1, 2] eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(g['covariance']) normal = eigenvectors[:, np.argmin(eigenvalues)] coverage = [(int(sy), int(sx))] projected.append({'alpha': g['opacity'], 'zdepth': meancam[2], 'shortestaxisnormal': normal, 'screencoverage': coverage}) return projected def fitmirrorplane(depthmap, normalmap, mirrormask): n = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) o = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) return n, o def fuseimages(realrender, virtualrender, mirrormask): return np.where(mirrormask[..., np.newaxis], virtualrender, realrender) Parameters \gamma: Hyper-parameter for the RGB-weighted depth smoothness regularization loss. n: Normal vector of the mirror plane in world coordinates. o: Origin point of the mirror plane in world coordinates. PM: Set of pixels belonging to the masked mirror region. P{cam}: Set of all pixels in the rendered image. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Misinterpretation of Reflections: Standard 3D-GS treats reflections as virtual 3D space, causing blurriness and multi-view inconsistencies. Imperfect Plane Estimates: Initial mirror plane estimates may be inaccurate, necessitating the optimization step to refine the virtual camera pose. Textureless Areas: Depth predictions may be unreliable in textureless regions, requiring the color replacement strategy during optimization. Time Complexity: Real-time rendering speeds are maintained, comparable to standard 3D-GS, as it avoids the computational expense of ray tracing. Memory Complexity: Requires storing additional depth and normal maps during training, but no significant increase in scene representation size. Performance: Achieves comparable or superior results to state-of-the-art methods while significantly reducing training time compared to NeRF-based approaches like Mirror-NeRF. Strengths: Physically-based reflection rendering, real-time capability, no need for additional depth supervision tailored specifically for mirrors (unlike Mirror-3DGS). Limitations: Relies on accurate mirror plane estimation; performance may degrade if the mirror mask is inaccurate. When to Use: Scenes with mirrors where high-quality, multi-view consistent reflections are required, and real-time rendering is desired. When Not to Use: Scenes without reflective surfaces, or where computational resources are extremely limited and even the overhead of depth/normal rendering is prohibitive. The method was proposed by Zihan Wang, Shuzhe Wang, Matias Turkulainen, Junyuan Fang, and Juho Kannala from Aalto University, University of Oulu, and ETH Zurich. It was published in the BMVC 2024 paper "Gaussian Splatting in Mirrors: Reflection-Aware Rendering via Virtual Camera Optimization". The work addresses the limitations of 3D-GS in handling specular reflections, which prior NeRF-based methods like Mirror-NeRF attempted to solve using ray tracing, but at the cost of training time and rendering speed. The method builds on the observation that mirror reflections can be modeled as images from a virtual camera symmetric to the real camera. name: ParetoGS Continuous-Budget Decoding
head: ParetoGS budget decoding, ParetoGS residual atlas encoding
body: ParetoGS Continuous-Budget Decoding is a runtime procedure that returns parameters for exactly K Gaussians at any valid integer budget by interpolating between nested adapted anchors using a compressed residual atlas and calibrated exponents. It differs from static compression methods like Data Compression and Storage Optimization by enabling smooth, continuous trade-offs between quality and performance without retraining, and from discrete pruning methods like Pruning and Density Control by preserving the full geometric fidelity of the original model through residual interpolation rather than hard selection. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of nested adapted anchors (including a Full model), the global nested member ordering, and pre-calibrated interval exponents (p, q). Outputs: Standard K-Gaussian parameters (position, log scale, quaternion, opacity logit, DC color, higher-order SH coefficients) for a specified integer budget K. Data Structures: Global Nested Ordering: A permutation of Gaussian IDs derived from concatenating entry sequences of contracted anchors. Full-model parameters are reordered to match this sequence. Compressed Residual Atlas: Stores orthogonal decompositions of non-full anchor residuals relative to the Full model. Layout: Stacked by member layer and parameter field. Precision: Quantization scales, anchor combination coefficients, and SH channel bases are stored in FP16. Quantization: Symmetric INT8 quantization applied independently to each channel within blocks of 64 Gaussian rows. Interval Exponents: For each interval between neighboring anchors, a pair (p, q) is stored. Member-Order Metadata: Tracks the entry sequence of Gaussians as budget increases. Runtime Cache: By default, caches the two most recently used endpoints. Numbered Steps: 1. Construct Global Nested Ordering: When contracting an upper anchor U to a lower anchor L, record the IDs of deleted Gaussians. Reverse each deletion trace to determine the order in which members enter as budget increases. Starting with the smallest anchor, concatenate these entry sequences to form the global nested ordering. Reorder full-model parameters and align all anchors to this ordering by ID. 2. Compute and Encode Residuals: Compute residuals of non-full anchors relative to the Full model in raw parameter coordinates (position, log scale, quaternion, opacity logit, DC color, higher-order SH coefficients). Convert non-full anchor residuals to FP16 and stack them by member layer and parameter field. Perform orthogonal decomposition along the anchor-state dimension for each layer. Retain all available components along the state dimension (maximum rank 10). For the 45 higher-order SH channels, use a rank-36 channel subspace, while ensuring decoding outputs all 45 channels. Apply symmetric INT8 quantization independently to each channel within blocks of 64 Gaussian rows using the following formulas: s{bc} = \frac{\max{i \in b} |x{ic}|}{127} q{ic} = \text{clip}\left(\text{round}\left(\frac{x{ic}}{s{bc}}\right), -127, 127\right) \hat{x}{bic} = q{ic} s{bc} where b is the block of 64 rows, c is the channel, x{ic} is the input value, s{bc} is the scale, and q{ic} is the quantized value. If a block is all-zero, the scale s{bc} defaults to 1. 3. Calibrate Interval Exponents: For each neighboring anchor pair, enumerate shared-state exponent p and entering-member gate exponent q from predefined discrete sets: P = \{0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6\} Q = \{0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 3\} At rounded budgets corresponding to normalized progress t \in \{0.25, 0.5, 0.75\}, compare all 72 (p, q) pairs on up to ten training views. Views are midpoint selections from equally partitioned intervals of the training-camera list. Calculate the reconstruction loss \ell{v,h} for view v at the lower endpoint, three intermediate budgets, and upper endpoint, indexed by h=0, \dots, 4, using image loss \ell = 0.8 L1 + 0.2 (1 - SSIM). Compute loss delta, delta variance, and negative delta mean for each view: d{v,h} = \frac{1}{3} \sum{h=1}^{3} \frac{\ell{v,h} - \ell{v,h+1}}{t{h+1} - th} sv = \frac{1}{3} \sum{h=0}^{3} |d{v,h} - (\ell{v,0} - \ell{v,4})| mv = \frac{1}{4} \sum{h=0}^{3} \max(-d{v,h}, 0) Define Q^+ as the mean of the largest \lceil V/4 \rceil values in a set. Minimize the calibration objective: J(p, q) = \frac{1}{3V} \sum{v=1}^{V} \sum{h=1}^{3} \ell{v,h} + Q^+(\{mv\}) + 0.25 Q^+(\{sv\}) Store the minimizing p and q for each interval. Exact ties favor larger p, then larger q. Pitfall: Calibration must not update Gaussian parameters or use test views to avoid overfitting and ensure deployment stability. 4. Decode at Runtime for Budget K: If K matches an exact anchor, restore that anchor directly. If K=N (full count), use the Full model. For other counts, identify the two neighboring anchors between which K falls. Interpolate shared members in raw parameter coordinates using the shared-state exponent p. For entering members, use their upper-anchor state and multiply their activated opacity by t^q, where t is the normalized progress within the interval. Clip scaled opacity to [10^{-6}, 1 - 10^{-6}], convert back to logit, and output standard K-Gaussian parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def decodeparetogs(K, fullmodel, anchors, ordering, atlas, exponents): """ Decode ParetoGS parameters for budget K. Args: K: Integer budget (number of Gaussians). fullmodel: Array of parameters for the full model, reordered by globalnestedordering. anchors: List of adapted anchors, each containing parameters for a subset of Gaussians. ordering: Global nested ordering of Gaussian IDs. atlas: Compressed residual atlas containing orthogonal decompositions. exponents: Dictionary mapping anchor intervals to (p, q) tuples. Returns: Parameters for exactly K Gaussians. """ N = len(ordering) # Case 1: Exact anchor match for anchor in anchors: if anchor.count == K: return anchor.parameters[ordering] # Case 2: Full model if K == N: return fullmodel[ordering] # Case 3: Interpolation between neighboring anchors # Find the two anchors between which K falls based on their counts # Assuming anchors are sorted by count loweranchor = None upperanchor = None for i in range(len(anchors) - 1): if anchors[i].count < K < anchors[i+1].count: loweranchor = anchors[i] upperanchor = anchors[i+1] break if loweranchor is None or upperanchor is None: raise ValueError("K does not fall within any anchor interval") # Get exponents for this interval p, q = exponents[(loweranchor.id, upperanchor.id)] # Calculate normalized progress t # t is the relative position of K between lower and upper anchor counts # Note: The source defines t based on normalized progress, # but for interpolation between discrete anchors, we assume t represents # the fraction of the way from lower to upper in terms of member inclusion. # The source mentions t in {0.25, 0.5, 0.75} for calibration, # implying t is a continuous variable in [0, 1] for decoding. t = (K - loweranchor.count) / (upperanchor.count - loweranchor.count) # Identify shared and entering members # Shared members are those present in both lower and upper anchors # Entering members are those present in upper but not lower lowerids = set(loweranchor.memberids) upperids = set(upperanchor.memberids) sharedids = lowerids & upperids enteringids = upperids - lowerids # Initialize output parameters # We need to reconstruct the full set of K parameters # The global ordering helps us map IDs to positions # Create a mapping from ID to index in the global ordering idtoidx = {gid: idx for idx, gid in enumerate(ordering)} # Parameters for shared members: interpolate in raw coordinates # The source says "shared members follow Equation (4) in raw parameter coordinates" # Equation (4) is not provided, but typically this implies linear interpolation # or interpolation based on the exponent p. # Given the context of "shared-state exponent p", it likely modulates the # contribution or the interpolation weight. # However, without Eq (4), we assume standard linear interpolation for shared members # as is common in such atlases, or that p affects the opacity/weighting. # Let's assume linear interpolation for raw parameters for shared members. # Parameters for entering members: use upper-anchor state, scale opacity by t^q # Opacity is stored as logit. outputparams = {} for gid in sharedids: idx = idtoidx[gid] # Interpolate raw parameters between lower and upper # Assuming parameters are aligned by ID in the anchors lowerp = loweranchor.parameters[gid] upperp = upperanchor.parameters[gid] # Linear interpolation for raw parameters # Note: The source mentions "shared-state exponent p". # If p is an exponent for the shared state, it might mean: # param = lowerp + t^p (upperp - lowerp) # Or it might affect the opacity specifically. # Given the ambiguity of Eq (4), and the explicit instruction for entering members, # we will use linear interpolation for shared parameters as a safe default # for "raw parameter coordinates" unless p is explicitly defined as a power law. # However, "shared-state exponent p" strongly suggests a power law interpolation. # Let's use t^p for the interpolation weight. weight = t p interpolatedp = lowerp + weight (upperp - lowerp) outputparams[gid] = interpolatedp for gid in enteringids: idx = idtoidx[gid] # Use upper-anchor state upperp = upperanchor.parameters[gid] # Scale opacity by t^q # Opacity is the 4th component (index 3) in the 59 scalar components # It is stored as a logit. opacitylogit = upperp[3] opacity = sigmoid(opacitylogit) # Scale opacity scaledopacity = opacity (t q) # Clip opacity scaledopacity = max(1e-6, min(1 - 1e-6, scaledopacity)) # Convert back to logit scaledopacitylogit = logit(scaledopacity) # Update the opacity logit in the parameter vector newp = upperp.copy() newp[3] = scaledopacitylogit outputparams[gid] = newp # Assemble the final parameter array in the global ordering finalparams = np.zeros((K, 59)) for i, gid in enumerate(ordering[:K]): finalparams[i] = outputparams[gid] return finalparams def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-x)) def logit(x): return np.log(x / (1 - x)) Parameters: Scalar components per Gaussian: 59 at SH degree 3 (position, log scale, quaternion, opacity logit, DC color, higher-order SH coefficients). Quantization block size: 64 Gaussian rows per channel. All-zero block scale fallback: 1. Precision for quantization scales, anchor combination coefficients, and SH channel bases: FP16. Image loss composition: 0.8 L1 + 0.2 (1 - SSIM). Opacity clip range: [10^{-6}, 1 - 10^{-6}]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Calibration Overfitting: Calibration must not update Gaussian parameters or use test views to avoid overfitting and ensure deployment stability. No Per-Gaussian Progress Correction: Only interval-level exponents are cached; no per-Gaussian progress correction is stored. Precision: Quantization scales and coefficients are FP16; INT8 quantization is used for the atlas data. Time Complexity: Decoding is O(K) for assembling the K Gaussian parameters, assuming constant-time lookup of anchors and exponents. Calibration is O(V \cdot |P| \cdot |Q| \cdot H), where V is the number of views, |P| and |Q| are the sizes of the exponent sets, and H is the number of intervals. Memory Complexity: The compressed residual atlas reduces storage by using orthogonal decomposition (rank 10 for state, rank 36 for SH channels) and INT8 quantization. The exact memory savings depend on the number of anchors and the compression ratio of the atlas. Measured Performance: The method achieves high-quality continuous-budget rendering, with PSNR results comparable to full models at lower budgets. Strengths: Enables smooth quality-performance trade-offs without retraining; preserves geometric fidelity through residual interpolation; efficient runtime decoding. Limitations: Requires pre-calibration; calibration must be done carefully to avoid overfitting; no per-Gaussian progress correction. When to Use: When continuous budget control is needed for deployment on devices with varying capabilities or when dynamic quality adjustment is required. When Not to Use: When static compression is sufficient, or when per-Gaussian adaptive quality is needed. ParetoGS Continuous-Budget Decoding was introduced in the paper "ParetoGS: High-Quality Continuous-Budget 3D Gaussian Splatting with Sparse Adapted Anchors". It builds on the concept of adapted anchors and residual encoding to provide a flexible rendering pipeline. name: TruncGradGS
head: Piecewise truncated gradient, Truncated Gradient Updates
body: TruncGradGS is a modification to the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) rasterization gradient computation that replaces near-zero Gaussian derivative tails with a linear surrogate to solve the vanishing gradient problem in dynamic scenes with large inter-frame displacements. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by ensuring that Gaussians discarded by the alpha-blending threshold still receive gradient updates, thereby maintaining gradient flow for primitives that are distant or rapidly moving. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters (mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \sigma), 2D pixel coordinates p, the alpha-blending discard threshold \tau, and the linear slope parameter m. Outputs: Modified gradient \nabla G with respect to the Gaussian parameters (specifically the mean \Delta x). Data Structures: The method operates on the standard 3DGS primitive representation: Mean \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3. Covariance \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (positive definite). Opacity \sigma \in \mathbb{R}. Color c \in \mathbb{R}^3 (view-dependent). Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Squared Mahalanobis Distance: For a query pixel p and a Gaussian with mean \mu, calculate the squared Mahalanobis distance d(p)^2 using the inverse covariance matrix \Sigma^{-1}: d(p)^2 = (\mu - p)^T \Sigma^{-1} (\mu - p) In the context of the 2D projection used for rasterization, \Sigma refers to the projected 2D covariance, and p, \mu are 2D coordinates. 2. Determine Boundary Point (xb): The truncation boundary is defined by the Gaussian isocontour where the density equals the threshold \tau: G{2D}(xb) = \tau. This corresponds to a squared Mahalanobis distance of -2 \log \tau. To find the scalar distance s from the pixel p to the boundary point xb along the ray direction, parametrize the ray as: xb = p + s \frac{\mu - p}{\|\mu - p\|} Substitute this into the distance equation (\mu - xb)^T \Sigma^{-1} (\mu - xb) = -2 \log \tau to form a quadratic equation in s. The solution for s is: s = \|\mu - p\| \sqrt{1 \pm \frac{-2 \log \tau}{K}} where K is defined as: K = a(\mux - px)^2 + 2b(\mux - px)(\muy - py) + c(\muy - py)^2 The coefficients a, b, c come from the un-normalized general Gaussian 2D function (conic form): f(x, y) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} [a(\mux - x)^2 + c(\muy - y)^2] - b(\mux - x)(\muy - y)\right) Select the appropriate root for s that places xb on the Gaussian splat. 3. Calculate True Gradient: Compute the true partial derivative of the 2D Gaussian function G{2D} with respect to the mean parameter \Delta x (representing the mean offset). The derivative contains interaction terms with the Gaussian function: \frac{\partial G}{\partial \Delta x} (Specific analytical forms depend on the exact parameterization of \Delta x, but it is the standard backpropagated gradient from the rasterizer). 4. Apply Piecewise Truncated Gradient: Determine the gradient update g based on the squared Mahalanobis distance d(p)^2 relative to the threshold -2 \log \tau and the sign of the gradient: Case 1 (Inside Threshold): If -2 \log G < -2 \log \tau (i.e., the pixel is within the effective support), use the true partial derivative: g = \frac{\partial G}{\partial \Delta x} Case 2 (Outside Threshold): If the Gaussian is outside the threshold, apply a linear surrogate. First, calculate the bias b to ensure continuity at the boundary xb: b = \frac{\partial G}{\partial \Delta x}(xb) - m xb Then, apply the piecewise rule based on the sign of the gradient at the boundary \frac{\partial G}{\partial \Delta x}(xb): If \frac{\partial G}{\partial \Delta x}(xb) < 0: g = \min(m \cdot x + b, \frac{\partial G}{\partial \Delta x}) If \frac{\partial G}{\partial \Delta x}(xb) > 0: g = \max(-m \cdot x + b, \frac{\partial G}{\partial \Delta x}) The variable x in the linear terms mx+b represents the distance coordinate along the ray from the pixel to the boundary, effectively scaling the linear surrogate. 5. Loss Sign Guard: Only apply the truncated gradient if the Gaussian is decreasing the loss via alpha-blending, i.e., \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alphai} < 0. If \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alphai} \ge 0, do not apply the truncated gradient. Applying it when the loss is increasing causes long-range push forces that make Gaussians repel each other. Parameters: \tau: The density threshold determining the boundary point. Set to the alpha-blending discard threshold of the rasterizer (typically 1/255). m: The slope of the linear surrogate gradient. A model parameter controlling the linear scaling of the gradient magnitude. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Repulsion: Applying the truncated gradient when \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alphai} \ge 0 causes Gaussians to repel each other due to long-range push forces. Discontinuity: The method ensures gradient continuity at the boundary xb by matching the linear surrogate to the true gradient value at that point. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computegaussianandgrad(mean2d, covinv2d, point2d): """Computes G and dG/dDeltax at a given point using the conic form.""" dx = mean2d[0] - point2d[0] dy = mean2d[1] - point2d[1] a, b = covinv2d[0, 0], covinv2d[0, 1] c = covinv2d[1, 1] exponent = -0.5 (a dx2 + c dy2) - b dx dy G = math.exp(exponent) dGdx = G (a dx + b dy) dGdDeltax = -dGdx return G, dGdDeltax def truncgradgsgradientupdate(mean2d, covinv2d, pixel2d, currenttruegradient, alpha, sigma, tau, m, lossgradalpha): """ Computes the truncated gradient for a 3D Gaussian splat at a specific pixel. Args: mean2d: np.array, 2D mean of the Gaussian [mux, muy] covinv2d: np.array, 2x2 inverse covariance matrix of the projected Gaussian pixel2d: np.array, 2D pixel coordinate [px, py] currenttruegradient: float, the standard backpropagated gradient dG/dDeltax at pixel alpha: float, the projected density of the Gaussian at the pixel sigma: float, the opacity of the Gaussian tau: float, the alpha-blending discard threshold (e.g., 1/255) m: float, the slope parameter for the linear surrogate lossgradalpha: float, the gradient of the loss with respect to alpha (sigma alpha) Returns: float: The modified gradient to be used for optimization """ # Step 1: Compute Squared Mahalanobis Distance (K) diff = mean2d - pixel2d K = float(diff @ covinv2d @ diff) # Step 2: Determine if we are inside or outside the threshold thresholdval = -2.0 math.log(tau) if K < thresholdval: # Case 1: Inside threshold, use true gradient return currenttruegradient # Step 3: Loss Sign Guard if lossgradalpha >= 0: # Do not apply truncated gradient if it increases the loss return 0.0 # Step 4: Determine Boundary Point distance s distmup = np.linalg.norm(diff) if distmup < 1e-8: return currenttruegradient # s = ||mu - p|| sqrt(1 + (-2 log tau) / K) s = distmup math.sqrt(1.0 + thresholdval / K) # Step 5: Calculate bias b for continuity at boundary # Boundary point coordinate along ray pointb = pixel2d + (s / distmup) diff gradatboundary, = computegaussianandgrad(mean2d, covinv2d, pointb) b = gradatboundary - m s # Step 6: Apply piecewise rule if gradatboundary < 0: linearval = m s + b return min(linearval, currenttruegradient) else: linearval = -m s + b return max(linearval, currenttruegradient) TruncGradGS is designed to be compatible with dynamic frameworks like 4DGS, addressing the specific challenge of large temporal divergence where primitives move significantly between frames. Standard 3DGS discards Gaussians with contribution scalar \sigmai \alphai below a threshold, resulting in zero gradients. TruncGradGS applies the linear surrogate to these discarded Gaussians to maintain gradient flow. Time Complexity: The method adds a constant-time overhead per Gaussian-pixel interaction to compute the Mahalanobis distance, solve for the boundary, and apply the piecewise logic. It does not change the asymptotic complexity of the rasterization pass. Memory Complexity: No additional memory structures are required beyond the standard Gaussian parameters and the scalar parameters \tau and m. Strengths: It solves the vanishing gradient problem in dynamic scenes, allowing Gaussians to receive updates even when they are distant or rapidly moving, which improves optimization stability and final reconstruction quality for dynamic content. Limitations: Incorrect application (ignoring the loss sign guard) can cause Gaussians to repel each other, leading to instability. It is specifically beneficial for dynamic scenes; for static scenes with small displacements, the benefit may be marginal compared to the added computational overhead. TruncGradGS was introduced in the paper "TruncGradGS: Improved 3D Gaussian Splatting via Truncated Gradient Updates" by T. Morales, N.-Q. Le-Pham, R. Atkins & B.-S. Hua, published in the Proceedings of Eurographics (2026). It addresses limitations identified in standard 3DGS rasterization where the exponential falloff of the Gaussian distribution causes gradients to vanish for pixels outside the immediate support, a problem exacerbated in dynamic methods like 4DGS. name: EfficientGS
body: EfficientGS is an optimized adaptation of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) designed for efficient large-scale, high-resolution scene representation. It reduces redundancy in 3DGS to alleviate computational and storage demands without sacrificing quality. Unlike vanilla 3DGS, which suffers from redundancy and low FPS/high storage in large-scale high-resolution scenes, EfficientGS allows for more efficient scene representation with fewer Gaussians. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Sparse point cloud obtained via Structure-From-Motion (SFM). Output: A set of 3D Gaussians representing the scene, optimized for size and rendering speed. Data Structures: Each 3D Gaussian g is defined by: Mean position \mu. Covariance matrix \Sigma. Opacity. View-dependent color represented by Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients. The covariance matrix \Sigma is decomposed into rotation and scaling components to ensure positive semi-definiteness during optimization: \Sigma = R S S^T R^T where R is the rotation matrix and S is the scaling matrix. The Gaussian function is defined as: G(x) = e^{-\frac{1}{2} (x-\mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x-\mu)} where x is an arbitrary position in the scene. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from sparse SFM points. 2. Iterative Optimization: Perform differentiable rasterization and optimize Gaussian parameters using color loss. 3. Selective Densification: Every few iterations, determine if a Gaussian has reached a steady state. If not (non-steady state), densify it. This focuses on non-steady state Gaussians based on their gradient modulus sum to minimize unnecessary cloning and splitting. 4. Pruning: After several densifications, remove auxiliary Gaussians that have minimal contribution to sight rays. This eliminates representational redundancy and optimizes the Spherical Harmonics (SH) of remaining Gaussians. 5. Sparse SH Order Increment: Do not start increasing SH order until after pruning. Every few iterations, assess the need for higher-order SH for each Gaussian based on color disparity from different viewing angles. Gradually increase the SH order only where needed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def efficientgstraining(sfmpoints, images, cameraposes, numiterations, densificationinterval, pruninginterval, shincrementinterval): # 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from sparse SFM points gaussians = [] for p in sfmpoints: gaussians.append({ 'mu': p.position, 'R': identitymatrix(), 'S': scalevector(1.0), 'opacity': 0.8, 'SHcoeffs': zerovector(), 'gradmu': zerovector(), 'gradR': zeromatrix(), 'gradS': zerovector(), 'gradopacity': 0.0, 'gradSH': zerovector() }) # Parameters densificationthreshold = 0.0001 # Gradient modulus sum threshold pruningthreshold = 0.01 # Ray contribution threshold shdisparitythreshold = 0.05 # Color disparity threshold pruningstartiteration = 3000 # Iteration to begin pruning phase for iteration in range(numiterations): # 2. Iterative Optimization: Differentiable rasterization and color loss renderedimage = zeroslike(images[0]) for g in gaussians: # Project 3D covariance to 2D image plane projectedcov = projectcovariance3dto2d(g['mu'], g['R'], g['S'], cameraposes) # Render and blend renderedimage = alphablend(renderedimage, g['opacity'], projectedcov) loss = meansquarederror(renderedimage, images[0]) # Backpropagate gradients computegradients(loss, gaussians, cameraposes) # 3. Selective Densification: Every few iterations, check steady state via gradient modulus sum if iteration % densificationinterval == 0: gradsums = [sum(abs(g['gradmu']) + abs(g['gradR']) + abs(g['gradS'])) for g in gaussians] nonsteadyindices = [i for i, s in enumerate(gradsums) if s > densificationthreshold] newgaussians = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): if i in nonsteadyindices: newgaussians.append(clonegaussian(g)) newgaussians.append(splitgaussian(g)) else: newgaussians.append(g) gaussians = newgaussians # 4. Pruning: After several densifications, remove auxiliary Gaussians with minimal ray contribution if iteration >= pruningstartiteration and iteration % pruninginterval == 0: raycontributions = [0.0] len(gaussians) for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): raycontributions[i] += g['opacity'] toremove = [i for i, c in enumerate(raycontributions) if c < pruningthreshold] gaussians = [g for i, g in enumerate(gaussians) if i not in toremove] optimizesh(gaussians) # Optimize SH of remaining Gaussians # 5. Sparse SH Order Increment: Do not start until after pruning. Assess need based on color disparity if iteration > pruningstartiteration and iteration % shincrementinterval == 0: colordisparities = [] for g in gaussians: maxdisp = 0.0 for img, cam in zip(images, cameraposes): disp = abs(rendergaussiancolor(g, cam) - sampleimageatgaussian(img, g)) maxdisp = max(maxdisp, disp) colordisparities.append(maxdisp) toincrement = [i for i, d in enumerate(colordisparities) if d > shdisparitythreshold] for i in toincrement: gaussians[i]['SHcoeffs'] = increaseshband(gaussians[i]['SHcoeffs']) return gaussians Parameters: Densification Trigger: Based on gradient modulus sum to identify non-steady state Gaussians. SH Order Increment Trigger: Based on color disparity from different viewing angles. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: GPU Memory Pressure: Starting SH order increment too early increases GPU memory pressure. EfficientGS delays this until after pruning to mitigate this. Redundancy: Vanilla 3DGS suffers from redundancy in large-scale high-resolution scenes. EfficientGS addresses this through selective densification and pruning. Model Size: Approximately tenfold smaller than conventional 3DGS. Performance: Expedites training and rendering times for large-scale, high-resolution scenes (e.g., 4K+ aerial images). Quality: Maintains high rendering fidelity despite the reduction in Gaussian count. Strengths: Reduces computational and storage demands; improves rendering quality by focusing on non-steady state Gaussians; streamlines scene representation by eliminating non-dominant Gaussians. Limitations: Not given in the sources. EfficientGS was introduced to address the challenges posed by the proliferation of high-resolution aerial photography (often exceeding 4K) in 3DGS training and rendering for large-scale scenes. Traditional mesh-based methods struggle with non-Lambertian surfaces, while vanilla 3DGS suffers from redundancy and high storage requirements in such contexts. EfficientGS leverages the representational capacity of individual Gaussians to significantly reduce redundancy. name: Variational 3D Gaussians
head: Variational Gaussian Splatting, latentSplat
body: Variational 3D Gaussians encode a scene as a set of N semantic 3D Gaussians where uncertainty is modeled by storing parameters for a normal distribution of spherical harmonic coefficients rather than explicit feature vectors. This approach allows the representation of a distribution of possible 3D reconstructions conditioned on reference views, enabling consistent multi-view rendering of specific samples while providing plausible details in regions outside the reference view frustums. It differs from standard Gaussian Splatting by replacing deterministic feature vectors with probabilistic distributions over spherical harmonic coefficients, facilitating gradient backpropagation through sampling operations. Inputs: Two reference view images I1, I2 and their corresponding camera poses. A target camera pose for novel view synthesis. Outputs: A set of N variational Gaussians \mathcal{G}. Rendered feature images \mathbf{F} and RGB images for the target view. The scene is represented as a set of N variational Gaussians: \mathcal {G} = \{(\mathbf {x}, \mathbf {S}, \mathbf {R}, o, \mathbf {c}, \mathbf {h}\mu, \mathbf {h}\sigma)i\}{1\leq i \leq N} Each Gaussian i contains the following fields: \mathbf {x} \in \mathbb {R}^3: Three-dimensional location (mean). \mathbf {S} \in \mathbb {R}^{3\times 3}: Diagonal scale matrix. \mathbf {R} \in \mathbb {R}^{3\times 3}: Orientation matrix. o \in [0, 1]: Opacity. \mathbf {c} \in \mathbb {R}^K: Spherical harmonic coefficients for view-dependent colors. \mathbf {h}\mu \in \mathbb {R}^4: Mean of the normal distribution for semantic features. \mathbf {h}\sigma \in \mathbb {R}^4: Standard deviation of the normal distribution for semantic features. The covariance matrix \mathbf{C} is derived from scale and rotation as: \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{R}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{S}^\top \mathbf{R}^\top The feature distributions are modeled as \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{h}\mu, \text{diag}(\mathbf{h}\sigma)). 1. Encoding: An encoder (adapted from pixelSplat) predicts the parameters \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{S}, \mathbf{R}, o, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{h}\mu, \mathbf{h}\sigma for N Gaussians based on the input reference views I1, I2 and their poses. The encoder predicts Gaussians within the field of view of the two reference views. 2. Sampling Semantic Gaussians: To render a specific reconstruction, explicit spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{h} for the semantic features are sampled from the variational distributions using the reparameterization trick: \mathbf {h} = \mathbf {h}\mu + \epsilon \cdot \mathbf {h}\sigma \quad \quad \epsilon \sim \mathcal {N}(0, \mathbf {1}) This step produces a set of "semantic Gaussians" with deterministic features \mathbf{h}, allowing consistent multi-view rendering of one possible reconstruction. Gradients backpropagate from the sampled coefficients to the reference view encoder. 3. Rendering: The set of semantic Gaussians is rendered using an efficient Gaussian splatting renderer. The renderer is extended to handle feature vectors in addition to RGB colors. The spherical harmonic basis is used to decode the per-Gaussian coefficients \mathbf{h} into view-dependent features. These features are splatted into pixel space. 4. Filling Empty Regions: Regions in the rendered image that have no Gaussians (because they are outside all reference view frustums) are filled by sampling from a normal distribution: \mathbf {F} = \mathbf {F}^\textnormal {ren} + \sqrt {1-\mathbf {O}}\odot \epsilon \,, \quad \quad \epsilon \sim \mathcal {N}(\mathbf {0}, \mathbf {1}) where \mathbf {F} is the final feature image, \mathbf {F}^\textnormal {ren} is the rendered features from existing Gaussians, and \mathbf {O} is the opacity. This provides plausible reconstruction details for empty areas, supported by a GAN-based decoder. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def samplesemanticgaussians(variationalgaussians): """ Converts variational Gaussians to semantic Gaussians by sampling features. Args: variationalgaussians: List of dicts, each containing: 'x': (3,) location 'S': (3,3) diagonal scale matrix 'R': (3,3) orientation matrix 'o': float opacity 'c': (K,) color SH coefficients 'hmu': (4,) feature mean 'hsigma': (4,) feature std dev Returns: semanticgaussians: List of dicts with same structure, but 'h' replaces 'hmu'/'hsigma' """ semanticgaussians = [] for g in variationalgaussians: # Sample epsilon from standard normal distribution epsilon = np.random.normal(0, 1, size=4) # Reparameterization trick h = g['hmu'] + epsilon g['hsigma'] # Create semantic Gaussian semanticg = { 'x': g['x'], 'S': g['S'], 'R': g['R'], 'o': g['o'], 'c': g['c'], 'h': h # Explicit feature vector } semanticgaussians.append(semanticg) return semanticgaussians def renderwithfilling(semanticgaussians, camerapose, imageshape): """ Renders semantic Gaussians and fills empty regions. Args: semanticgaussians: List of semantic Gaussians (output of samplesemanticgaussians) camerapose: Camera extrinsics/intrinsics imageshape: (H, W, C) target image shape Returns: F: (H, W, C) final feature image O: (H, W, 1) opacity mask """ # Initialize rendered features and opacity to zero Fren = np.zeros(imageshape) O = np.zeros((imageshape[0], imageshape[1], 1)) # Splat semantic Gaussians into pixel space # Note: In practice, this involves projecting 3D Gaussians to 2D, # computing 2D covariance, and accumulating contributions. # Here we assume a function that performs standard Gaussian splatting # for both color (c) and features (h). for g in semanticgaussians: # Decode view-dependent features using spherical harmonics # h is the sampled feature mean; c is for color # This step produces a feature vector per pixel covered by the Gaussian viewdependentfeatures = decodesphericalharmonics(g['h'], camerapose, g['x']) viewdependentcolor = decodesphericalharmonics(g['c'], camerapose, g['x']) # Splat into Fren and O # Accumulate weighted features and opacity # This is a simplified representation of the splatting process splatmask, weights = projectandcomputeweights(g, camerapose, imageshape) Fren += weights[:,:, np.newaxis] viewdependentfeatures O += weights[:,:, np.newaxis] g['o'] # Normalize opacity if necessary (depending on alpha compositing implementation) # O is typically the accumulated opacity # Fill empty regions # Sample epsilon epsilon = np.random.normal(0, 1, size=imageshape) # Reparameterization trick for empty areas # sqrt(1 - O) ensures that where opacity is high, less noise is added F = Fren + np.sqrt(np.maximum(1 - O.squeeze(), 0))[:,:, np.newaxis] epsilon return F, O def decodesphericalharmonics(coefficients, camerapose, location): """ Decodes spherical harmonic coefficients into a view-dependent vector. Args: coefficients: (K,) SH coefficients camerapose: Camera orientation relative to Gaussian location: 3D location of Gaussian Returns: vector: (C,) view-dependent feature/color vector """ # Compute spherical harmonic basis functions for the viewing direction # This depends on the order of SH (e.g., order 3 has 16 coefficients) # For simplicity, assume coefficients are already ordered and basis is computed basis = computeshbasis(camerapose, location) # Dot product to get the value vector = np.dot(basis, coefficients) return vector def computeshbasis(camerapose, location): """ Computes spherical harmonic basis functions for a given viewing direction. Args: camerapose: Camera orientation (e.g., rotation matrix or quaternion) location: 3D location of Gaussian Returns: basis: (K,) array of SH basis values """ # Extract viewing direction from camera pose and location # direction = normalize(cameraposition - location) # Convert direction to spherical coordinates (theta, phi) # Compute SH basis functions Yl^m(theta, phi) # This is a placeholder for the actual SH math # For order 3, K=16 K = 16 basis = np.zeros(K) #... actual SH basis computation... return basis N: Number of Gaussians. Not given in the sources. K: Dimension of spherical harmonic coefficients for color. Not given in the sources. Feature dimension: 4 (for \mathbf{h}\mu, \mathbf{h}\sigma). \epsilon: Standard normal noise \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{1}). Empty Regions: When rendering novel views, regions may have no Gaussians because they are outside all reference view frustums. These areas must be filled by sampling from a normal distribution based on rendered features and opacity to provide plausible reconstruction. Gradient Flow: The reparameterization trick is essential for backpropagating gradients from the sampled coefficients to the reference view encoder. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Models uncertainty in feature space; provides plausible details in unseen regions via probabilistic filling; allows consistent multi-view rendering of specific samples. Limitations: Requires a GAN-based decoder for plausible filling in empty areas; uncertainty modeling adds complexity to the representation. When to use: When dealing with limited reference views (e.g., two views) and needing to synthesize novel views with plausible details in occluded or unseen regions. When not to use: When high-fidelity deterministic features are required without probabilistic modeling; when computational resources for GAN decoding are unavailable. Variational 3D Gaussians were introduced in the paper "latentSplat: Latent 3D Gaussian Splatting for Memory Efficient Novel View Synthesis" by C. Wewer et al.. The method adapts the encoder from pixelSplat to predict variational Gaussian parameters. It is used for novel view synthesis from a small number of reference views, leveraging the efficiency of Gaussian splatting. latentSplat, https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16292, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: EnvMap-GS
head: two-stage outdoor Gaussian reconstruction with background-to-environment map baking
body: EnvMap-GS is a two-stage Gaussian Splatting framework designed to reconstruct outdoor "inside-out" captures where a camera moves within a restricted navigation area while looking outward at a distant environment. It explicitly separates foreground and background regions to eliminate "floaters" (large, erroneous Gaussians in the far field) caused by incorrect initialization and limited view ranges. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which struggles with far-field reconstruction, EnvMap-GS constrains background primitives to a spherical shell and allows the background to be baked into an environment map for faster rendering. Inputs: A sequence of images or video frames captured in a restricted area; a metric monocular depth estimation model (e.g., Video Depth Anything). Outputs: A set of foreground Gaussians, a set of background Gaussians, and optionally an inpainted environment map. Data Structures: Camera Poses: 4 \times 4 transformation matrices from COLMAP. Sparse Point Cloud: 3D points from Structure-from-Motion (SfM). Dense Metric Depth Maps: Per-image depth maps from MMDE. Distance-from-Center (DFC) Maps: Image-aligned maps storing the Euclidean distance of unprojected 3D points to the scene center O. Gaussian Primitives: Defined by mean \mu, covariance \Sigma (or rotation R and scale S), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients c{lm}. Steps: 1. Pre-processing: Run Structure-from-Motion (COLMAP) on input images to obtain camera poses and a 3D sparse point cloud. Set the world center O to the barycenter of the camera positions. 2. Depth Estimation: Estimate dense metric depth maps for each input image using a metric monocular depth estimation (MMDE) method, such as Video Depth Anything. 3. Distance Map Creation: For each image, unproject every pixel's depth value into 3D space using the corresponding camera pose. Compute the Euclidean distance of each resulting 3D point to the center O. Store these distances in image-aligned Distance-from-Center (DFC) maps. 4. Segmentation: Determine the threshold Ri. Estimate the histogram of distances in the DFC maps with a binning interval of 10 meters. Set Ri to the distance value corresponding to the first bin where the point count is less than 2.5% of the total reconstructed points. Classify points with distance < Ri as foreground and points with distance \ge Ri as background. 5. Stage 1 Initialization (Background): Create a geodesic sphere point cloud. Initialize background Gaussians within a spherical shell defined by inner radius Ri and outer radius Ro. 6. Stage 1 Optimization: Optimize the background Gaussians using a loss function combining: a background-only photometric term; a shell constraint loss L{shell}, constraining Gaussians to remain inside the shell [Ri, Ro]; a planarity loss L{planarity}, aligning Gaussians with local tangential planes. 7. Stage 1 Pruning: Apply a modified pruning strategy that preserves large, stable Gaussians necessary for representing distant scenery. 8. Stage 2 Initialization (Foreground): Initialize foreground Gaussians from the filtered SfM sparse point cloud, containing only the foreground points identified in Step 4. 9. Stage 2 Optimization: Add and refine foreground Gaussians using the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering loss. The background set remains fixed during this stage but contributes to the final image formation. 10. Environment Map Conversion (Optional): Render the background Gaussians to an object-free environment map. Inpaint the map to fill missing parts. This map can replace the Gaussian-based background for faster rendering. Formulas: Shell constraint: L{shell} = \sum{g \in \text{BG}} \left( \max(0, Ri - \|\mug\|) + \max(0, \|\mug\| - Ro) \right). Planarity constraint: L{planarity} = \sum{g \in \text{BG}} \left( 1 - \frac{|\mathbf{n}g \cdot \mathbf{v}{\min}|}{\|\mathbf{v}{\min}\|} \right), where \mathbf{n}g is the local surface normal and \mathbf{v}{\min} is the eigenvector of \Sigmag corresponding to the smallest eigenvalue. Parameters: O: World system center, placed at the barycenter of camera positions. Ri: Inner radius threshold for foreground-background segmentation. Ro: Outer radius of the background spherical shell. Binning interval: 10 meters. Threshold cutoff: 2.5% of total reconstructed points. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Threshold Sensitivity: While the heuristic for Ri works for most scenes, it is scene-dependent. Changing Ri within reasonable ranges does not significantly affect novel view synthesis metrics. Metric Scale: MMDE methods are independent of the SfM reconstruction, so global metric scale alignment is not required. Floaters: Standard GS fails in the far field due to densification choices and limited view ranges. EnvMap-GS addresses this by constraining background Gaussians to a shell. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Step 1: Pre-processing cameraposes, sparsecloud = runcolmap(images) O = barycenter(cameraposes) # Step 2: Depth Estimation depthmaps = [mmdemodel.predict(img) for img in images] # Step 3: Distance Map Creation dfcmaps = [] for imgidx, (img, pose, depthmap) in enumerate(zip(images, cameraposes, depthmaps)): points3d = unprojectdepth(depthmap, pose) distances = computedistances(points3d, O) dfcmaps.append(distances) # Step 4: Segmentation alldistances = [d for dm in dfcmaps for d in dm.flatten()] histogram = computehistogram(alldistances, binsize=10.0) totalpoints = len(alldistances) Ri = 0 for bincenter, count in histogram: if count < 0.025 totalpoints: Ri = bincenter break foregroundpoints = [p for p in sparsecloud if distance(p, O) < Ri] backgroundpoints = [p for p in sparsecloud if distance(p, O) >= Ri] # Step 5: Stage 1 Initialization geodesicsphere = creategeodesicsphere(O, Ri, Ro) backgroundgaussians = initializegaussians(geodesicsphere, shellrange=(Ri, Ro)) # Step 6: Stage 1 Optimization for epoch in range(numepochsstage1): bgimage = rendergaussians(backgroundgaussians, cameraposes) photometricloss = computephotometricloss(bgimage, images) shellloss = computeshellconstraintloss(backgroundgaussians, Ri, Ro) planarityloss = computeplanarityloss(backgroundgaussians) totalloss = photometricloss + shellloss + planarityloss backgroundgaussians = optimize(backgroundgaussians, totalloss) # Step 7: Stage 1 Pruning backgroundgaussians = prunegaussians(backgroundgaussians, preservelarge=True) # Step 8: Stage 2 Initialization foregroundgaussians = initializegaussians(foregroundpoints) # Step 9: Stage 2 Optimization for epoch in range(numepochsstage2): fullimage = rendergaussians(backgroundgaussians + foregroundgaussians, cameraposes) loss = computerenderingloss(fullimage, images) foregroundgaussians = optimize(foregroundgaussians, loss) # Step 10: Environment Map Conversion envmap = rendergaussians(backgroundgaussians, sphericalcameraposes) envmap = inpaint(envmap) return foregroundgaussians, backgroundgaussians, envmap def runcolmap(images): return estimateposesandpoints(images) def barycenter(poses): return sum([pose[:3, 3] for pose in poses]) / len(poses) def unprojectdepth(depthmap, pose): return [depthmap[y, x] invK @ [x, y, 1] for y, x in pixelcoords()] def computedistances(points, center): return [norm(p - center) for p in points] def computehistogram(values, binsize): bins = {} for v in values: binidx = int(v // binsize) bins[binidx] = bins.get(binidx, 0) + 1 return [(binidx binsize + binsize / 2, count) for binidx, count in bins.items()] def distance(p, center): return norm(p - center) def creategeodesicsphere(center, rmin, rmax): return generatespherepoints(center, rmin, rmax) def initializegaussians(points, shellrange=None): return [creategaussian(p) for p in points] def rendergaussians(gaussians, poses): return splat(gaussians, poses) def computephotometricloss(rendered, target): return L1(rendered, target) def computeshellconstraintloss(gaussians, rmin, rmax): return sum(max(0, rmin - norm(g.mu)) + max(0, norm(g.mu) - rmax) for g in gaussians) def computeplanarityloss(gaussians): return sum(dot(g.normal, g.covarianceeigenvector) for g in gaussians) def optimize(params, loss): return gradientdescent(params, loss) def prunegaussians(gaussians, preservelarge): return [g for g in gaussians if g.scale > threshold or preservelarge] def computerenderingloss(rendered, target): return L1(rendered, target) + 0.2 SSIM(rendered, target) def inpaint(image): return fillgaps(image) Converting the optimized background Gaussians into a 2D environment map to accelerate rendering. This replaces the Gaussian-based background with a static texture, reducing computational load during novel view synthesis. Using a geodesic sphere point cloud to initialize background Gaussians ensures uniform coverage of the spherical shell, avoiding clustering artifacts common in random initialization. Time Complexity: Two-stage optimization increases training time compared to single-stage GS. Stage 1 optimizes background Gaussians with additional geometric losses; Stage 2 optimizes foreground Gaussians with standard loss. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for foreground and background Gaussians separately, plus DFC maps and depth maps during preprocessing. Performance: Reduces background artifacts and improves perceptual quality of novel view renderings compared to state-of-the-art baselines, specifically removing floaters in the navigation region. Strengths: Effective for outdoor "inside-out" captures; eliminates far-field floaters; enables faster rendering via environment map baking. Limitations: Requires metric depth estimation; assumes a restricted navigation area; background is constrained to a spherical shell, which may not fit all outdoor scenes perfectly. EnvMap-GS was introduced to address the challenges of reconstructing outdoor environments from "inside-out" captures, where a camera moves within a restricted area but looks outward. Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting suffers from "floaters" in the far field due to incorrect initialization and densification choices, as well as limited view ranges. The method builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting [7] and extends it with geometric constraints and a two-stage optimization process. It is particularly relevant for real-time applications requiring high-fidelity novel view synthesis of large outdoor scenes. name: Thermal-Physics-Informed 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: TPI-GS
body: Thermal-Physics-Informed 3D Gaussian Splatting (TPI-GS) is a framework that embeds infrared radiative transfer modeling into the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation, transforming Gaussian primitives into thermophysical radiative elements to enable physically interpretable infrared scene representation and novel view synthesis. Unlike standard 3DGS, which relies on view-dependent color blending via spherical harmonics to approximate photometric appearance, TPI-GS replaces this with physics-driven radiance integration based on Planck’s law, explicitly modeling atmospheric attenuation and sensor response. This approach bridges classical infrared simulation theory with neural point-based rendering, allowing for joint optimization of geometric structure and thermal radiation fields under multi-view supervision. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view infrared images of a scene; initial 3D Gaussian point cloud (position, covariance, opacity) derived from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) or similar initialization. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives parameterized by geometric attributes and thermophysical fields, capable of rendering novel-view infrared images with radiometric coherence. Data Structures: Each 3D Gaussian primitive i is augmented with the following learnable parameters in addition to the standard 3DGS geometric parameters (position \mathbf{p}i, rotation \mathbf{q}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, opacity \alphai): 1. Emissivity (\epsiloni): A scalar or vector parameter modeling surface thermal radiation properties. 2. Temperature (Ti): A scalar parameter modeling the thermal state of the primitive. 3. Thermal Texture (\mathbf{t}i): A parameter modeling spatial thermal variations. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Thermophysical Parameterization: Initialize each Gaussian primitive with learnable emissivity \epsiloni, temperature Ti, and thermal texture \mathbf{t}i. These parameters are optimized jointly with geometric parameters. 2. Spectral Radiance Calculation: For each Gaussian primitive, compute the spectral radiant exitance M{\lambda, i} using Planck’s law: M{\lambda, i} = \epsiloni \frac{2hc^2}{\lambda^5} \frac{1}{e^{\frac{hc}{\lambda kB Ti}} - 1} Where h is Planck’s constant, c is the speed of light, kB is Boltzmann’s constant, \lambda is the wavelength of the infrared radiation, Ti is the temperature of the primitive, and \epsiloni is the emissivity of the primitive. 3. Radiance Accumulation (Rendering): Render the infrared image by accumulating radiance along the viewing ray. Unlike standard 3DGS which blends spherical harmonic coefficients, TPI-GS performs physics-driven radiance integration. The total radiance L{total} reaching the camera is computed by summing the contributions of all splatted Gaussians using front-to-back alpha compositing, modified by atmospheric attenuation and sensor response: L{total} = \sum{i \in \text{sorted}} M{\lambda, i} \cdot \tau{atm}(di) \cdot \alphai \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj) + L{sensor} Where \alphai is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian, M{\lambda, i} is the spectral radiant exitance of the i-th Gaussian, \tau{atm}(di) is the atmospheric transmittance factor at distance di explicitly modeled to account for path-dependent attenuation, and L{sensor} accounts for sensor response. 4. Frequency-Domain Supervision: To mitigate the inherent smoothing effect of Gaussian splatting and improve high-frequency texture fidelity, apply a Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) to the rendered infrared images and the ground truth. Compute a loss in the frequency domain to supervise the reconstruction. 5. Joint Optimization: Optimize the geometric parameters (\mathbf{p}i, \mathbf{q}i, \mathbf{s}i, \alphai) and thermophysical parameters (\epsiloni, Ti, \mathbf{t}i) simultaneously using gradient descent. The loss function combines photometric error in infrared space and the DWT-based frequency supervision loss under multi-view constraints. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def planckradiance(wavelength, temperature, emissivity): h, c, kB = 6.62607015e-34, 299792458.0, 1.380649e-23 exponent = torch.clamp((h c) / (wavelength kB temperature), max=700.0) return emissivity (2 h c2) / (wavelength5) / (torch.exp(exponent) - 1) def rendertpigs(gaussians, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics, wavelength, attenuationcoeff): # 1. Project 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space and sort by depth centers3d = gaussians.position centerscam = (cameraextrinsics @ torch.cat([centers3d, torch.oneslike(centers3d[:,:1])], dim=1).T).T[:,:3] centers2d = (cameraintrinsics @ centerscam.T).T centers2d = centers2d[:,:2] / centers2d[:, 2:] depths = centerscam[:, 2] sortidx = torch.argsort(depths) sortedgaussians = gaussians[sortidx] sortedcenters2d = centers2d[sortidx] sorteddepths = depths[sortidx] H, W = int(cameraintrinsics[0, 0]), int(cameraintrinsics[1, 1]) renderedimage = torch.zeros((H, W), device=gaussians.position.device) accumulatedalpha = torch.zeros((H, W), device=gaussians.position.device) # 2. Front-to-back alpha compositing with physics-driven radiance for i in range(len(sortedgaussians)): g = sortedgaussians[i] center = sortedcenters2d[i] depth = sorteddepths[i] # Compute spectral radiance via Planck's law Llambda = planckradiance(wavelength, g.temperature, g.emissivity) # Apply atmospheric attenuation tau = torch.exp(-attenuationcoeff depth) Leff = Llambda tau # Compute 2D Gaussian weights for pixels in bounding box xmin, ymin = max(0, int(center[0] - 3 torch.sqrt(g.cov2d[0, 0]))), max(0, int(center[1] - 3 torch.sqrt(g.cov2d[1, 1]))) xmax, ymax = min(W, int(center[0] + 3 torch.sqrt(g.cov2d[0, 0]))), min(H, int(center[1] + 3 torch.sqrt(g.cov2d[1, 1]))) for y in range(ymin, ymax): for x in range(xmin, xmax): dx, dy = x - center[0], y - center[1] weight = torch.exp(-0.5 torch.tensor([dx, dy]) @ torch.linalg.inv(g.cov2d) @ torch.tensor([dx, dy])) alphacontribution = g.opacity weight if accumulatedalpha[y, x] < 1.0: renderedimage[y, x] += Leff alphacontribution (1.0 - accumulatedalpha[y, x]) accumulatedalpha[y, x] += alphacontribution return renderedimage def computedwtloss(rendered, groundtruth): def haardwt2(img): h, w = img.shape cA = F.avgpool2d(img.unsqueeze(0), 2).squeeze(0) cH = F.avgpool2d((img[:,:-1] - img[:, 1:]).unsqueeze(0), 2).squeeze(0) cV = F.avgpool2d((img[:-1,:] - img[1:,:]).unsqueeze(0), 2).squeeze(0) cD = F.avgpool2d(((img[:-1,:-1] - img[1:, 1:]) - (img[:-1, 1:] - img[1:,:-1])).unsqueeze(0), 2).squeeze(0) return cA, cH, cV, cD coeffsr = haardwt2(rendered) coeffsgt = haardwt2(groundtruth) return sum(torch.mean(torch.abs(cr - cg)) for cr, cg in zip(coeffsr, coeffsgt)) def computeloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage): photometricloss = torch.mean(torch.abs(renderedimage - groundtruthimage)) freqloss = computedwtloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage) return photometricloss + 0.1 freqloss Thermal-physics-informed 3D Gaussian Splatting for infrared images rendering, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infrared.2026.106593, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Environment Map Generation from Gaussian Background
head: Baking Gaussian Background to EnvMap, SH0 Environment Map Extraction
body: This method converts the distant background components of a 3D Gaussian Splatting scene into a static 2D equirectangular environment map, replacing explicit Gaussian primitives in those regions. It solves the rendering overhead and visual instability (floaters) associated with distant background Gaussians in interactive applications like VR. It is distinguished from sibling methods like DeSplat or 360 Gaussian Splatting by explicitly decoupling the scene into a dynamic foreground (Gaussians) and a static background (EnvMap), trading motion parallax for performance and stability. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scene model containing a set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}, each defined by position \mathbf{t}, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma} (or rotation \mathbf{R} and scale \mathbf{S}), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}{lm} for view-dependent color. Output: A static equirectangular environment map texture E of resolution 8192 \times 4096 pixels, and a modified scene representation where background Gaussians are removed. Data Structures: Environment Map: A 2D texture of size 8192 \times 4096 pixels (8K equirectangular) storing RGB color values. Gaussian Sets: The foreground set \mathcal{G}{FG} is retained for active rendering. The background set \mathcal{G}{BG} is discarded or marked inactive after baking. Parameters: Resolution: 8192 \times 4096 pixels. Foreground/Background Threshold (Ri): A distance cutoff from the camera origin. Gaussians with centers beyond Ri are classified as background. The rendering effect of Gaussians is limited beyond 20 meters, making Ri = 20 m a typical value, though it can be adjusted to preserve parallax for specific mid-distance regions. Steps: 1. Segmentation: Partition \mathcal{G} into foreground \mathcal{G}{FG} and background \mathcal{G}{BG} based on the Euclidean distance of each Gaussian's center \mathbf{t}i from the camera origin. \mathcal{G}{BG} = \{ gi \in \mathcal{G} \mid \|\mathbf{t}i\| > Ri \} \mathcal{G}{FG} = \{ gi \in \mathcal{G} \mid \|\mathbf{t}i\| \le Ri \} 2. SH0 Extraction: For each Gaussian gi \in \mathcal{G}{BG}, retain only the base spherical harmonic band (SH0) to represent the view-independent base color c0. 3. Rasterization/Baking: Render \mathcal{G}{BG} onto an equirectangular projection by mapping Gaussian centers to spherical coordinates and splatting them onto the 2D grid. For each pixel (u, v) in the 8192 \times 4096 map, compute the corresponding view direction \mathbf{d}{uv}. Sort contributing \mathcal{G}{BG} Gaussians by depth along \mathbf{d}{uv}. Accumulate contributions using standard alpha compositing: C{bg}(u,v) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{G}{BG}} \alphai \cdot c{0,i} \cdot \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj) where the sum iterates over depth-sorted Gaussians, \alphai is opacity, and c{0,i} is the SH0 color. 4. Texture Generation: Store the accumulated color C{bg}(u,v) into the environment map texture E. 5. Scene Update: Remove \mathcal{G}{BG} from the active rendering list. The renderer uses \mathcal{G}{FG} for near-field rendering and samples E for the background. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generateenvmap(gaussians, Ri, width=8192, height=4096): # Step 1: Segment Gaussians by distance from camera origin bggaussians = [g for g in gaussians if math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in g.center)) > Ri] # Step 2: Initialize Environment Map envmap = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(height width)] # Step 3: Bake Gaussians to Equirectangular Map for v in range(height): for u in range(width): # Map pixel to spherical coordinates lon = (u / width) 2 math.pi - math.pi lat = (v / height) math.pi - math.pi / 2 # Convert to Cartesian view direction dirx = math.cos(lat) math.sin(lon) diry = math.sin(lat) dirz = math.cos(lat) math.cos(lon) viewdir = (dirx, diry, dirz) # Sort background Gaussians by depth along view direction sortedbg = sorted(bggaussians, key=lambda g: g.center[0]viewdir[0] + g.center[1]viewdir[1] + g.center[2]viewdir[2]) accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedalpha = 0.0 for g in sortedbg: # Extract SH0 color (view-independent base color) color = g.shcoeffs[0] alpha = g.opacity # Project 3D Gaussian to 2D tangent plane at viewdir centerdir = (g.center[0]/math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in g.center)), g.center[1]/math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in g.center)), g.center[2]/math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in g.center))) cosangle = centerdir[0]viewdir[0] + centerdir[1]viewdir[1] + centerdir[2]viewdir[2] cosangle = max(-1.0, min(1.0, cosangle)) angle = math.acos(cosangle) # Approximate angular spread for spherical splatting depth = g.center[0]viewdir[0] + g.center[1]viewdir[1] + g.center[2]viewdir[2] if depth <= 0: continue sigmaang = g.scale[0] / depth pdf = math.exp(-0.5 (angle / sigmaang)2) / (2 math.pi sigmaang2) contribution = alpha pdf if contribution <= 0: continue # Alpha compositing newalpha = accumulatedalpha + contribution (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) if newalpha > 0: accumulatedcolor = [ (accumulatedcolor[0] accumulatedalpha + color[0] contribution (1.0 - accumulatedalpha)) / newalpha, (accumulatedcolor[1] accumulatedalpha + color[1] contribution (1.0 - accumulatedalpha)) / newalpha, (accumulatedcolor[2] accumulatedalpha + color[2] contribution (1.0 - accumulatedalpha)) / newalpha ] accumulatedalpha = newalpha envmap[v width + u] = accumulatedcolor return envmap The pseudocode implements standard 3D-to-spherical projection and 2D Gaussian evaluation in the tangent plane, which is required to correctly splat 3D Gaussians onto an equirectangular grid. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parallax Artifacts: A static environment map cannot reproduce motion parallax for mid-distance objects, causing standard metrics (PSNR/SSIM) to drop compared to ground truth, though it remains acceptable in VR. Visual Gap: A visual gap may appear at the boundary Ri under certain viewing conditions, particularly when the camera moves outside the intended navigation area. Floaters: The method produces a floater-free background, avoiding pop-up effects common in distant Gaussian reconstructions. The primary method described, focusing on two-stage outdoor reconstruction with background-to-environment map baking. It is chosen when performance and stability in VR are prioritized over perfect parallax. EnvMap-GS A sibling method that may handle background differently, potentially retaining Gaussian structure or using different compression. DeSplat Focuses on 360-degree scene representation, possibly using different primitives or projections. 360 Gaussian Splatting Time Complexity: Rendering time is significantly reduced. Replacing background Gaussians with an environment map reduces average frame time and increases throughput, as background Gaussians introduce significant rendering overhead even when visually static. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is reduced by removing \mathcal{G}{BG} from the active Gaussian list, while adding the environment map texture to the footprint. Performance: The method boosts rendering throughput, making it suitable for interactive VR navigation. Strengths: Floater-free background, reduced rendering overhead, stable frame rates in VR. Limitations: Loss of motion parallax for mid-distance objects, potential visual gaps at Ri, lower PSNR/SSIM for distant regions compared to ground truth. When to Use: Interactive VR applications, semi-bounded environments with well-defined navigation areas, scenes with significant distant background elements that cause floaters or performance issues. When Not to Use: Applications requiring precise motion parallax for mid-distance objects, or where high-fidelity novel view synthesis metrics for distant regions are critical. The method originates from the work on "EnvMap-GS: two-stage outdoor Gaussian reconstruction with background-to-environment map baking" by D. Pintani et al.. It addresses the challenges of rendering large-scale outdoor scenes with 3D Gaussian Splatting, where distant background elements often suffer from noise (floaters) and high computational cost. By baking the background into a static environment map, the method leverages the efficiency of traditional environment map rendering while maintaining the high-quality foreground reconstruction of 3DGS.
