name: MAC-Splat
body: MAC-Splat is a training framework for sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting that resolves depth and correspondence ambiguities by enforcing direct 3D consistency supervision. Unlike methods relying on 2D photometric losses or proxy geometry, it uses semantically informed 2D correspondences to anchor and jointly regularize the position, shape, and appearance of matched Gaussians in a shared world coordinate frame. Inputs: Sparse-view image set, initial 3D Gaussian primitives (centroids, covariances, opacities, colors), and camera poses. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian scene representation. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitives: Standard 3DGS attributes: centroid \mathbf{c}, covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma} (parameterized by rotation \mathbf{R} and scale \mathbf{s}), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color \mathbf{c}{sh}. Correspondence Anchors: Pairs of 2D pixel coordinates (u1, v1) and (u2, v2) from different views, associated with a confidence score and semantic feature vector. Steps: 1. Geometric Correspondence Extraction: Use the MASt3R geometric backbone to extract sparse 2D correspondences between image pairs. 2. Semantic Enrichment: Enrich the geometric matches with part-level features from a frozen DINOv3 encoder via a lightweight Residual Semantic Fusion module to improve correspondence reliability and confidence estimation. 3. 3D Lifting: Lift the 2D anchor pairs into 3D space. During training, use ground-truth camera poses. At test time, use MASt3R-estimated poses. 4. Multi-Attribute Consistency (MAC) Loss Calculation: Identify the Gaussians in the scene that project to the corresponding 2D anchors. Enforce direct, confidence-weighted consistency on these matched Gaussians in a common world coordinate frame. The loss jointly regularizes positional consistency (distance between centroids), shape consistency (agreement between covariance parameters, respecting covariance geometry), and appearance consistency (agreement between opacity and color attributes). The formulation is robust to outliers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemacloss(gaussians, matches, poses): """ Computes the Multi-Attribute Consistency loss for matched Gaussians. matches: list of tuples (u1, v1, u2, v2, confidence) poses: dict mapping viewid to camera-to-world transformation gaussians: list of dicts with keys 'centroid', 'covariance', 'opacity', 'color' """ posloss = 0.0 shapeloss = 0.0 apploss = 0.0 totalweight = 0.0 for u1, v1, u2, v2, conf in matches: # [Comment: MASt3R backbone extracts sparse 2D correspondences and confidence scores.] # [Comment: Residual Semantic Fusion enriches matches with DINOv3 part-level features.] # Project 2D pixels to 3D rays using camera poses ray1 = backprojectpixel(u1, v1, poses['view1']) ray2 = backprojectpixel(u2, v2, poses['view2']) # Find Gaussians whose 2D projection is closest to the pixel centers g1 = findclosestgaussian(gaussians, u1, v1, poses['view1']) g2 = findclosestgaussian(gaussians, u2, v2, poses['view2']) if g1 is None or g2 is None: continue # Positional Consistency: Euclidean distance between centroids deltapos = [g1['centroid'][i] - g2['centroid'][i] for i in range(3)] posterm = sum(d2 for d in deltapos) # Shape Consistency: Covariance alignment respecting geometry deltacov = [[g1['covariance'][i][j] - g2['covariance'][i][j] for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] shapeterm = sum(val2 for row in deltacov for val in row) # Appearance Consistency: Opacity and color agreement deltaalpha = g1['opacity'] - g2['opacity'] deltacolor = [g1['color'][i] - g2['color'][i] for i in range(3)] appterm = deltaalpha2 + sum(c2 for c in deltacolor) # Weight by confidence posloss += conf posterm shapeloss += conf shapeterm apploss += conf appterm totalweight += conf if totalweight > 0: posloss /= totalweight shapeloss /= totalweight apploss /= totalweight # Combines positional, shape, and appearance terms with equal weighting. loss = posloss + shapeloss + apploss return loss def backprojectpixel(u, v, pose): # Standard pinhole camera inverse projection to a unit depth ray. return (u, v, 1.0) def findclosestgaussian(gaussians, u, v, pose): # Projects all Gaussian centroids to 2D screen space and returns the closest one. bestg = None mindist = float('inf') for g in gaussians: # Simplified orthographic projection for demonstration; real implementation uses perspective projection. center2d = (g['centroid'][0], g['centroid'][1]) dist = (center2d[0] - u)2 + (center2d[1] - v)2 if dist < mindist: mindist = dist bestg = g return bestg Parameters: Encoder: DINOv3, kept frozen during training. Backbone: MASt3R, used for geometric matching. Camera Poses: Ground-truth during training; MASt3R-estimated at test time. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Outliers: The MAC loss formulation is designed to be robust to outliers in correspondences. Pose Accuracy: Performance depends on the quality of camera poses, as the method uses ground-truth poses during training but must rely on MASt3R-estimated poses at test time. Sparse View Ambiguity: The method specifically targets sparse-view settings where 2D photometric losses are insufficient. Performance: On ScanNet++, MAC-Splat improves average PSNR over Splatt3R by more than 4.5 dB. It also reduces LPIPS and maintains performance as the camera pose gap increases. Strengths: Resolves geometric ambiguities in sparse-view reconstruction, produces geometrically coherent and semantically plausible reconstructions, and is robust to outliers. Limitations: Relies on external geometric backbones (MASt3R) and semantic encoders (DINOv3), increasing computational overhead during the correspondence extraction phase. When to use: Sparse-view 3D reconstruction where standard 3DGS fails due to depth ambiguity. When not to use: Dense-view settings where photometric losses are sufficient, or real-time applications where the overhead of MASt3R/DINOv3 inference is prohibitive. Origin: MAC-Splat was introduced to address geometric artifacts in sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting caused by the inability of 2D photometric losses to resolve depth and correspondence ambiguities. Development: It builds on the MASt3R geometric backbone and a frozen DINOv3 encoder to obtain semantically informed 2D correspondences. The core contribution is the Multi-Attribute Consistency (MAC) loss, which enforces holistic 3D consistency. Usage: Applied to sparse-view reconstruction tasks, with experiments conducted on ScanNet++. name: Heat Kernel Textures (HKTex)
head: HKTex, Geodesic Gaussians
body: Heat Kernel Textures (HKTex) is an intrinsic, UV-free texture representation that uses anisotropic heat kernels as geodesic equivalents to Gaussians, defined directly on any manifold surface discretized as a triangular mesh. It solves the problems of UV mapping—such as seams, distortions, wasted memory, and vertex duplication—by operating natively on the manifold rather than in ambient Euclidean space. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which detaches from geometry, HKTex kernels bend to conform to the surface, and unlike UV mapping, it eliminates artifacts by construction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangular mesh M (geometry), and optionally a target UV texture or a set of multi-view images for optimization. Output: A set of optimized heat kernel parameters \mathcal{K} = \{\kappas\}{s=1}^S representing the texture, integrated into a physically based rendering (PBR) pipeline. Data Structures: Each kernel \kappas is defined by the following parameters: p\star: Position of the heat source on the manifold. \theta: Angle of anisotropy. \eta: Anisotropy strength. \tau: Threshold controlling the scale of the kernel. \varsigma: Sharpness of the kernel border. c: RGB color. Mathematical Background: The heat diffusion on a manifold is governed by the heat equation ut = e^{-tL} u0, where L is the Laplace-Beltrami Operator (LBO). The solution is approximated spectrally as: \mathbf{u}t = e^{-t\mathbf{L}} \mathbf{u}0 \approx \mathbf{\Phi} e^{-t\mathbf{\Lambda}} \mathbf{\Phi}^T \mathbf{M} \mathbf{u}0 where \mathbf{M} is the mass matrix, \mathbf{\Phi} are eigenvectors, and \mathbf{\Lambda} are eigenvalues. The stiffness matrix weights w{ij} for the LBO are defined as: w{ij} = \begin{cases} -\frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{\langle \hat{e}{kj}, \hat{e}{ki} \rangle{\mathbf{H}{\eta, \theta}}}{\sin(\alpha{ij})} + \frac{\langle \hat{e}{hj}, \hat{e}{hi} \rangle{\mathbf{H}{\eta, \theta}}}{\sin(\beta{ij})} \right] & (i,j) \in \text{Edges}, \\ -\sum{k \neq i} w{ik} & i=j, \\ 0 & \text{else}. \end{cases} The inner products are weighted by a shear matrix \mathbf{H}{\eta,\theta} = \mathbf{R}\theta \mathbf{U}{ijk} \mathbf{D}\eta \mathbf{U}{ijk}^T \mathbf{R}\theta^T, where \mathbf{U}{ijk} is a local reference frame, \mathbf{R}\theta is a rotation matrix, and \mathbf{D}\eta = \text{diag}(\frac{1+\eta}{1}, 1, 1) controls anisotropy. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Multi-view fitting: Initialize S kernel positions uniformly over the mesh surface. Initialize colors c randomly from a uniform distribution. UV-texture fitting: Initialize 50% of positions uniformly and 50% based on UV-texture image gradients, transferring sampled 2D points to the manifold. Initialize colors from the UV texture at corresponding coordinates. Parameter Initialization: Let u \sim U(0,1). \theta = u \cdot \pi. \eta = 1.0 + 99.0 \cdot u. \varsigma = 10 + 40 \cdot u^{0.5} (range [10, 50]). \tau = \tau{\min} + (1.0 - \tau{\min} - 10^{-8}) \cdot u^{0.7} (range \tau{\min}, 1.0)), where \tau{\min}=0.7 for UV and 0.9 for multi-view. 2. Mass Estimation ([Kernel Density Estimation): Compute pairwise biharmonic distances D between all sources. Compute adaptive bandwidth \sigmam as the median of all non-zero pairwise distances. Compute local density for each source s: \varrhos = \sum{i=1}^S \exp(-D{i,s}^2 / \sigmam^2). Define masses as inverse density: ms = 1/\varrhos. Normalize masses so \sum ms equals the total surface area. 3. Optimization Loop: Importance Sampling: Pre-sample a pool of 10M points uniformly on the mesh. For the first 250 steps, draw samples uniformly from the pool. After warm-up, update sampling weights \epsilon(p) using exponential moving average: \epsilon{\text{new}}(p) = \gamma \epsilon{\text{old}}(p) + (1 - \gamma) L(p) with \gamma = 0.99, where L(p) is photometric loss. Ray Sampling (Multi-view): Sample random cameras (azimuth, elevation, distance). Generate primary rays per pixel; resample until intersection with the object. Concatenate, shuffle, and partition rays into mini-batches of B=1024 rays. Re-evaluate each ray with N{\text{spp}}=8 gradient samples. Rendering & Loss: Evaluate kernels dynamically at ray intersections (not splatted). Compute predicted linear RGB \hat{\mathbf{c}}i = \frac{1}{N{\text{spp}}} \sum{s=1}^{N{\text{spp}}} \mathbf{L}{i,s}. Clip prediction and target to [0, 1] and convert to gamma space (unless HDR). Optimise a per-ray photometric loss (L1 loss averaged across the mini-batch). Update & Projection: Perform gradient descent step. Projected Gradient Descent (PGD): Clamp parameters to valid ranges: \theta \in [0, \pi]. \varsigma \in [10, 200]. \tau \in [0.3, 1.0 - 10^{-8}]. \eta \in [1, 200]. Individual kernel colors c \in [-1, 1]^3. Global mean color c{\text{base}} \in [0, 1]^3. 4. Adaptive Density Control (Kernel Splitting): If a kernel requires splitting, interpolate the principal direction \hat{v}M at the old position p{\text{old}} using barycentric interpolation from mesh vertices. Define new major axis \hat{d} by rotating \hat{v}M by \theta{\text{old}} + \pi/2 around face normal \hat{n}: \hat{d} = \hat{v}M \cos(\theta{\text{old}} + \pi/2) + (\hat{n} \times \hat{v}M) \sin(\theta{\text{old}} + \pi/2) Remove old kernel. Create two new kernels displaced along \hat{d} using the exponential map: p{\text{new}}^{(\pm)} = \text{Exp}(p{\text{old}}, \pm \hat{d} (1 - \tau{\text{old}}) r{\text{base}}) where r{\text{base}} is a base scaling radius. Shrink new kernels by reducing spatial extents by factor 1.6: \tau{\text{new}} = 1.0 - 1.0^{-\tau{\text{old}}/1.6} Zero out optimizer states (momentum/variance) for new kernels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def initializehktex(mesh, numkernels, mode='multiview'): kernels = [] for in range(numkernels): u = random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) if mode == 'multiview': pstar = sampleuniformonsurface(mesh) c = [random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0) for in range(3)] else: if < numkernels // 2: pstar = sampleuniformonsurface(mesh) c = [random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0) for in range(3)] else: uvpoint = sampleuvgradient(mesh.uvmap) pstar = uvtosurfacepoint(mesh, uvpoint) c = sampleuvcolor(mesh.uvmap, uvpoint) theta = u math.pi eta = 1.0 + 99.0 u varsigma = 10.0 + 40.0 (u 0.5) taumin = 0.7 if mode == 'uvtexture' else 0.9 tau = taumin + (1.0 - taumin - 1e-8) (u 0.7) kernels.append({ 'pstar': pstar, 'theta': theta, 'eta': eta, 'tau': tau, 'varsigma': varsigma, 'c': c, 'momentum': [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 'variance': [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] }) return kernels def computemasses(kernels, mesh): D = computepairwisebiharmonicdistances([k['pstar'] for k in kernels]) nonzerodists = [d for row in D for d in row if d > 0] nonzerodists.sort() sigmam = nonzerodists[len(nonzerodists) // 2] densities = [] for s in range(len(kernels)): density = sum(math.exp(-(D[i][s] 2) / (sigmam 2)) for i in range(len(kernels))) densities.append(density) masses = [1.0 / d for d in densities] totalarea = mesh.totalsurfacearea() currentsum = sum(masses) masses = [m (totalarea / currentsum) for m in masses] return masses def optimizehktex(mesh, kernels, masses, numsteps, numkernels): pool = sampleuniformpointsonsurface(mesh, count=10000000) epsilon = [0.0] len(pool) gammaema = 0.99 B = 1024 Nspp = 8 for step in range(numsteps): if step < 250: rayindices = random.sample(range(len(pool)), B) else: rayindices = weightedsample(pool, epsilon, B) for idx in rayindices: # L(p) is computed during rendering pass rays = [] for in range(B): cam = samplerandomcamera() ray = generaterayfromcamera(cam, randompixel()) while not rayintersectsmesh(ray, mesh): cam = samplerandomcamera() ray = generaterayfromcamera(cam, randompixel()) rays.append(ray) totalloss = 0.0 for i, ray in enumerate(rays): samples = [] for in range(Nspp): color = evaluatehktexatpoint(mesh, kernels, masses, ray.intersectionpoint) samples.append(color) predictedcolor = [sum(s) / Nspp for s in zip(samples)] targetcolor = gettargetcolor(ray) predclipped = [max(0.0, min(1.0, c)) for c in predictedcolor] targetclipped = [max(0.0, min(1.0, c)) for c in targetcolor] predgamma = [c (1.0/2.2) for c in predclipped] targetgamma = [c (1.0/2.2) for c in targetclipped] lossi = sum(abs(p - t) for p, t in zip(predgamma, targetgamma)) / 3.0 totalloss += lossi avgloss = totalloss / B # gradients = computegradients(avgloss, kernels) # for k in kernels: applyoptimizerstep(k, gradients) for k in kernels: k['theta'] = max(0.0, min(math.pi, k['theta'])) k['varsigma'] = max(10.0, min(200.0, k['varsigma'])) k['tau'] = max(0.3, min(1.0 - 1e-8, k['tau'])) k['eta'] = max(1.0, min(200.0, k['eta'])) k['c'] = [max(-1.0, min(1.0, c)) for c in k['c']] for k in kernels: if needssplit(k): vhatM = barycentricinterpolate(mesh.vertices, k['pstar']) dhat = [vhatM[0]math.cos(k['theta']+math.pi/2) - vhatM[1]math.sin(k['theta']+math.pi/2), vhatM[1]math.cos(k['theta']+math.pi/2) + vhatM[0]math.sin(k['theta']+math.pi/2), 0.0] pnewplus = exponentialmap(k['pstar'], dhat, (1 - k['tau']) rbase) pnewminus = exponentialmap(k['pstar'], [-x for x in dhat], (1 - k['tau']) rbase) taunew = 1.0 - (1.0 (-k['tau'] / 1.6)) replacekernel(k, pnewplus, pnewminus, taunew) k['momentum'] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] k['variance'] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def evaluatehktexatpoint(mesh, kernels, masses, point): contributing = [] for k in kernels: dist = geodesicdistance(mesh, point, k['pstar']) if dist < effectiveradius(k['tau'], k['eta']): contributing.append(k) if not contributing: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] totalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] totalweight = 0.0 for k in contributing: value = evaluateheatkernel(mesh, k['pstar'], point, k['eta'], k['theta'], k['varsigma']) weight = value k['mass'] totalcolor = [totalcolor[j] + weight k['c'][j] for j in range(3)] totalweight += weight if totalweight == 0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return [c / totalweight for c in totalcolor] def sampleuniformonsurface(mesh): return mesh.randompointonsurface() def uvtosurfacepoint(mesh, uvpoint): return mesh.barycentricuvtoxyz(uvpoint) def sampleuvcolor(mesh, uvpoint): return mesh.uvtexture.sample(uvpoint) def computepairwisebiharmonicdistances(points): return mesh.computebiharmonicdistancematrix(points) def weightedsample(pool, weights, k): return random.choices(pool, weights=weights, k=k) def samplerandomcamera(): return Camera(azimuth=random.uniform(0, 2math.pi), elevation=random.uniform(0, math.pi), distance=random.uniform(1, 5)) def generaterayfromcamera(cam, pixel): return cam.generateprimaryray(pixel) def rayintersectsmesh(ray, mesh): return mesh.rayintersect(ray) is not None def gettargetcolor(ray): return ray.targetimage.sample(ray.pixel) def needssplit(k): return k['density'] > threshold def replacekernel(oldk, p1, p2, taunew): oldk['pstar'] = p1 oldk['tau'] = taunew newk = {oldk, 'pstar': p2, 'momentum': [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 'variance': [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]} return newk Time Complexity: The spectral approach for solving heat diffusion is one order of magnitude faster than simulating diffusion by solving a sparse linear system, scaling to high-resolution meshes. Memory Complexity: Eliminates UV coordinates and vertex duplication, lowering memory footprint compared to UV mapping. Strengths: Intrinsic to geometry, no UV seams/distortions, differentiable, integrates with PBR. Limitations: Requires a triangular mesh; optimization is constrained to the surface. When to use: When UV mapping artifacts are unacceptable, or for compressing existing UV textures and inverse rendering from 2D photos. When not to use: If the input is not a manifold mesh or if ambient Euclidean operations are required. HKTex was introduced by Foti et al.. It addresses the limitations of UV mapping and standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (which operates in Euclidean space) by using discrete Riemannian geometry to define textures on manifolds. It is applicable to games, VR, AR, and VFX. Heat Kernel Textures the Geodesic Gaussians That Do Not Splat, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37595-717, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Gaussian Splatting in Style
body: Gaussian Splatting in Style (GSS) is a method for stylizing complex 3D scenes by learning a mapping between 3D Gaussians and a queried style image, generating novel views conditioned on an input style image while preserving geometric consistency. Unlike methods that apply 2D stylization post-rendering or train separate models per style, GSS learns a unified 3D color module that predicts stylized RGB colors based on scene geometry and a style latent code, enabling real-time rendering of arbitrary styles. It sets itself apart from post-rendering approaches by conditioning the color prediction on the style rather than applying AdaIN to rendered views, and from per-style training approaches by learning a generalizable mapping rather than training on 2D stylized images for specific styles. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D Gaussian scene parameters (mean positions \mu, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics for base geometry), a style image I{style}, and training views (ground truth images I{gt}). Outputs: Stylized novel views I{gen} rendered from the 3D Gaussian scene with colors predicted by the 3D Color module. Data Structures: 1. 3D Gaussians: Standard 3DGS representation. Mean positions \mu are used as input to the color module. 2. Multi-Resolution Hash Grid (MHG): Used to encode spatial information from \mu. Configuration: 16 levels, with each level having a feature vector of length 2. 3. Style Latent Code: A vector representing the style image, obtained from a pretrained encoder. 4. 3D Color Module: An MLP consisting of 2 fully connected layers with 64 neurons each. Numbered Steps: 1. Warm-up Phase (Geometry Initialization): Initialize the scene using vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting without the 3D Color module for the first 3000 iterations to establish geometric consistency. Fix the number of Gaussians in the scene after this phase. 2. 2D Stylization Module Setup (Guide Generation): Pass the input style image I{style} and the original ground truth view I{gt} through a pretrained VGG encoder to obtain feature representations. Pass these features through an Adaptive Instance Normalization (AdaIN) layer and a convolutional decoder to obtain the 2D stylized image I{style2d}. This image serves as a guide for the 3D color module. 3. 3D Color Module Training: For each training iteration, compute the input to the 3D Color module: encode the style image using a pretrained image encoder to get the style latent code. Extract mean positions \mu of the 3D Gaussians. Feed \mu into the MHG to get spatial features. Feed the style latent code into a Fully Connected (FC) layer. Concatenate the MHG features and FC features. Pass the concatenated tensor through the MLP to predict the new RGB color for each Gaussian. Render the scene using the 3DGS pipeline with the predicted RGB colors to generate the stylized view I{gen}. Compute the Guide Loss Lg: Lg = ||I{style2d} - I{gen}|| where I{style2d} is the 2D stylized image from the 2D stylization module and I{gen} is the stylized view from the pipeline. Optimize the 3D Color module parameters using the Guide Loss. 4. Inference: To generate a novel view for a new style image: encode the new style image to get its latent code. Pass the scene's mean positions \mu and the new style latent code through the trained 3D Color module to get RGB colors. Render the scene using the standard 3DGS pipeline. Parameters: Optimizer: Adam optimizer. Learning Rate: 1e-4. Training Iterations: 150,000 iterations for the 3D Color module, starting after the 3000-iteration warm-up phase. Hardware: Experiments run on Nvidia A4500 GPU. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class MHG(nn.Module): """Multi-Resolution Hash Grid encoder. Not given in the sources: Exact hashing and interpolation logic. """ def init(self, numlevels=16, levelchannels=2): super().init() self.numlevels = numlevels self.levelchannels = levelchannels self.grid = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(numlevels, 256, levelchannels)) def forward(self, positions): # Returns features: (N, numlevels levelchannels) # Not given in the sources: Exact hashing and interpolation logic. return self.grid[0] class FCStyleEncoder(nn.Module): """Fully Connected layer for style latent code.""" def init(self, latentdim=512, outdim=64): super().init() self.fc = nn.Linear(latentdim, outdim) def forward(self, stylelatent): return self.fc(stylelatent) class ColorMLP(nn.Module): """2 fully connected layers with 64 neurons each.""" def init(self, inputdim, hiddendim=64, outputdim=3): super().init() self.fc1 = nn.Linear(inputdim, hiddendim) self.fc2 = nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim) self.fc3 = nn.Linear(hiddendim, outputdim) self.relu = nn.ReLU() def forward(self, x): x = self.relu(self.fc1(x)) x = self.relu(self.fc2(x)) return torch.sigmoid(self.fc3(x)) def adain(stylefeat, contentfeat): """Adaptive Instance Normalization. Not given in the sources: Exact AdaIN implementation details. """ # Standard AdaIN operation return stylefeat def rasterizegaussians(gaussians, colors, cameraparams): """Applies the standard differentiable Gaussian rasterizer. Not given in the sources: Exact rasterization kernel implementation. """ # Projects Gaussians to screen space, sorts by depth, and accumulates colors return torch.zeroslike(colors[:,:2]) class GaussianSplattingInStyle: def init(self, gaussians, styleencoder, vggencoder, decoder): self.gaussians = gaussians self.styleencoder = styleencoder self.vggencoder = vggencoder self.decoder = decoder self.mhg = MHG(numlevels=16, levelchannels=2) self.fcstyle = FCStyleEncoder() self.colormlp = ColorMLP(inputdim=96) self.optimizer = optim.Adam(list(self.mhg.parameters()) + list(self.fcstyle.parameters()) + list(self.colormlp.parameters()), lr=1e-4) def getstylelatent(self, styleimage): return self.styleencoder(styleimage) def get2dstyleguide(self, styleimage, gtview): stylefeat = self.vggencoder(styleimage) gtfeat = self.vggencoder(gtview) styledfeat = adain(stylefeat, gtfeat) istyle2d = self.decoder(styledfeat) return istyle2d def trainstep(self, gtviews, styleimage, cameraparams): istyle2d = self.get2dstyleguide(styleimage, gtviews) stylelatent = self.getstylelatent(styleimage) means = self.gaussians.means mhgfeatures = self.mhg(means) stylefeatures = self.fcstyle(stylelatent).unsqueeze(0).expand(means.shape[0], -1) combined = torch.cat([mhgfeatures, stylefeatures], dim=-1) rgb = self.colormlp(combined) igen = rasterizegaussians(self.gaussians, rgb, cameraparams) loss = torch.norm(istyle2d - igen) self.optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() self.optimizer.step() return loss.item() def render(self, styleimage, cameraparams): stylelatent = self.getstylelatent(styleimage) means = self.gaussians.means mhgfeatures = self.mhg(means) stylefeatures = self.fcstyle(stylelatent).unsqueeze(0).expand(means.shape[0], -1) combined = torch.cat([mhgfeatures, stylefeatures], dim=-1) rgb = self.colormlp(combined) return rasterizegaussians(self.gaussians, rgb, cameraparams) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: 2D Stylization Insufficiency: Simply applying 2D stylization to rendered novel views (GS-Ada) is insufficient for 3D consistency, resulting in lower consistency metrics. Over-smoothing: Methods like StylizedNeRF may generate views with high blur and loss of details, leading to artificially high consistency scores despite poor visual quality. Aggressive Style Transfer: Methods like ARF may be too aggressive, leading to loss of scene information and neglecting far-away objects. Geometry Consistency: The warm-up phase is critical; skipping it may result in poor geometric consistency. Time Complexity: Training requires roughly 4 hours per scene on an Nvidia A4500 GPU. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: GSS achieves an average rendering speed of 157 FPS, approximately 4x faster than the second fastest method (LSNV at 40 FPS). Scaling: The use of MHG and a tiny MLP allows handling large scenes with millions of Gaussians, such as those in the Tanks and Temples (TnT) dataset. Strengths: Preserves geometric details, faithful to style images, real-time rendering, 3D consistency. Limitations: Requires a warm-up phase; relies on pretrained encoders for style and VGG features. When to use: When real-time stylized novel view synthesis is required with high geometric consistency. When not to use: When per-scene style optimization is acceptable and real-time performance is not critical (e.g., ARF). Gaussian Splatting in Style (GSS) was introduced by A. Saroha et al. in a paper published in 2025. It builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting and previous work in neural radiance field stylization such as StylizedNeRF and StyleRF. The method addresses the limitations of existing 3D stylization techniques, which often suffer from blurriness, over-smoothing, or lack of 3D consistency. It is used for stylizing complex 3D scenes from real-world datasets like LLFF and TnT, using style images from the WikiArt dataset. Gaussian Splatting in Style, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-85187-215, fetched 2026-10-26

name: EOGS (Earth-observation Gaussian Splatting)
head: Gaussian Splatting for Efficient Satellite Image Photogrammetry
body: EOGS is a method for digital elevation modeling and appearance recovery from remote sensing images, adapting the standard 3DGS framework for satellite photogrammetry to achieve state-of-the-art performance with significantly faster training times (minutes vs. days). It models remote sensing requirements such as shadow modeling and camera-specific corrections to achieve comparable accuracy to EO-NeRF while being over 300 times faster. Unlike its siblings which often focus on general scenes or specific artifacts, EOGS is specialized for earth observation, replacing complex RPC pipelines with affine approximations and introducing regularizations for sparsity, consistency, and opaqueness to handle semi-transparent shadows and low-visibility regions. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: N non-orthorectified satellite images, their corresponding RPC camera model coefficients, and metadata including 3D satellite attitude and position. Outputs: A set of K Gaussian primitives representing the 3D geometry and appearance of the scene, including elevation maps and orthorectified imagery. Data Structures The method relies on the standard 3DGS primitive structure but modifies initialization and rendering parameters: Gaussian Primitives (\gammak): Defined in world-space coordinates. Center (\muk): 3D position vector. Covariance (\Sigmak): 3x3 symmetric positive-definite matrix representing shape and orientation. Opacity (\alphak): Scalar. Color: The method disables per-Gaussian view-direction color dependency (SH coefficients). Camera Parameters: Affine Color-Correction (\phiA): Camera-dependent affine transformation for radiometric correction. Ambient Color (\psiA): Camera-dependent ambient color term. Coordinate System: World-space is a uniformly rescaled and recentered version of the Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) system. The scene center coincides with the origin, the scene is contained in a unit cube, and it is east-north-up aligned. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussian centers uniformly in the 3D scene such that the initial density is 0.13 Gaussians per cubic meter. Initialize all Gaussians with white color and opacity set to the lowest possible value of 1% (0.01). 2. Camera Approximation: Compute a per-scene affine approximation of the transformation from world-space to NDC-space, replacing the full RPC-based transformation pipeline. For an affine camera model A: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow A\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^2, the projection of a Gaussian center \muk and covariance \Sigmak simplifies to: \mu{A,k} = A\muk + \mathbf{a} \Sigma'{A,k} = A \Sigmak A^T This eliminates the need for the local first-order approximation used in the original 3DGS method, as the approximation is moved to the camera models. The mean error of this approximation is negligible (\approx 0.012 pixels). 3. Rendering with Shadows: Render the scene using the affine camera model Ai and sun camera Si for each input image i. The synthesized view \hat{I}i is denoted as I{Ai, Si}, indicating dependence on both the satellite camera and the sun position. Implement shadow mapping to render shadows in a physically accurate manner. 4. Optimization: Run optimization for 5000 iterations. Use the same optimizer and scheduler as 3DGS for the primitive parameters (centers, covariances, opacities). Use a second Adam scheduler with a learning rate of 10^{-2} for learning camera-dependent parameters: the affine color-correction \phiA and the ambient color \psiA. Enable shadow mapping and all three regularizations (sparsity, consistency, opaqueness) starting at iteration 1000. 5. Loss Calculation: Minimize the final loss function defined as: \min \sum{i=1}^{N} \left( \ell(\hat{I}i, Ii) + 0.1 Lo + 0.1 L{cc} + 0.01 L{ac} + 0.01 Ls \right) where \ell is the photometric distance function (typically L1 + SSIM as in 3DGS). Lo: Opacity loss. L{cc}: Color correction loss. L{ac}: Ambient color loss. Ls: Shadow entropy loss. Formulas Optimization Problem: \arg \min{(\gammak){k=1}^K} \sum{i=1}^{N} \ell(\hat{I}i, Ii) where Ii is the i-th input satellite observation, \hat{I}i is the corresponding synthesized view, and \ell is the photometric distance function. Shadow Entropy Loss (Ls): Defined as an entropy-based penalty for incorrect use of shadows to handle semi-transparent objects casting semi-transparent shadows: Ls = \sum{u} H(s{A,S}(u)) where H is entropy and s{A,S} relates to the shadow map for camera A and sun S. Parameters N: Number of non-orthorectified satellite images used as input. K: Number of Gaussian primitives used to represent the scene. Opacity initialization: 1%. Initial Gaussian density: 0.13 Gaussians per m³. Total iterations: 5000. Regularization enablement iteration: 1000. Learning rate for camera-dependent parameters (\phiA, \psiA): 10^{-2}. Loss coefficients: 0.1 for Lo and L{cc}, 0.01 for L{ac} and Ls. Pitfalls Semi-transparent Shadows: Semi-transparent objects casting semi-transparent shadows cause geometry misuse where texture is embedded in geometric shadows. This is handled by the entropy-based penalty Ls. Low Visibility: EOGS struggles in regions observed in only a few images (low visibility), performing worse than in high-coverage regions. Time Complexity: Training time is approximately 3 minutes on tested datasets, compared to 15 hours for EO-NeRF and 25 minutes for SAT-NGP. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On the IEEE GRSS Data Fusion Contest (DFC2019) and IARPA Multi-View Stereo 3D Mapping Challenge (IARPA2016) datasets, EOGS achieves elevation MAE comparable to EO-NeRF (e.g., 1.45m vs 1.37m on DFC2019 no-mask, 0.89m vs 1.02m on DFC2019 foliage-mask). Scaling: EOGS is Pareto-optimal with respect to elevation MAE and training time. Strengths: High efficiency (300x faster than EO-NeRF), state-of-the-art accuracy in minutes, handles radiometric correction and shadow modeling. Limitations: Struggles in regions with low image coverage (few visible cameras). Performance is slightly worse than EO-NeRF on full AOIs without foliage masking, though equivalent when foliage is ignored. When to use: Large-scale earth observation datasets requiring fast digital elevation modeling and appearance recovery. When not to use: Scenes with very low visibility or sparse camera coverage. EOGS was introduced in the paper "Gaussian Splatting for Efficient Satellite Image Photogrammetry". It is the first method for digital elevation modeling based on 3DGS. The method builds on the efficiency of 3DGS [23] and incorporates remote-sensing improvements from EO-NeRF [32], such as radiometric correction and shadow modeling, while introducing novel components including sparsity, view consistency, and opacity regularizations. It differs from SatNeRF and EO-NeRF by learning colors and not resampling input images that may contain transients or color shifts, and by not requiring pre-trained models for RGB renders or priors on elevation renders. name: HDR Gaussian Splatting
head: HDR-GS, High Dynamic Range Gaussian Splatting
body: HDR Gaussian Splatting (HDR-GS) is a framework for 3D High Dynamic Range (HDR) imaging that renders novel HDR views and reconstructs Low Dynamic Range (LDR) images with user-controllable exposure time. It solves the problem of long training times and slow inference speeds associated with existing NeRF-based HDR Novel View Synthesis (NVS) methods. It sets itself apart by employing a Dual Dynamic Range (DDR) Gaussian point cloud model and two Parallel Differentiable Rasterization (PDR) processes to handle HDR and LDR rendering simultaneously. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of posed LDR images, camera poses (recalibrated from Normalized Device Coordinates to world coordinates), and an optional user-defined exposure time \Delta t for LDR reconstruction. Outputs: A rendered HDR image and a rendered LDR image corresponding to the input camera pose. Data Structures: The scene is represented by a set of Np Dual Dynamic Range (DDR) Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{Gi \mid i = 1, \dots, Np\}. Each Gaussian Gi contains the following attributes: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position. \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix. \alphai \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. c{l,i} \in \mathbb{R}^3: LDR color. c{h,i} \in \mathbb{R}^3: HDR color. \Delta t \in \mathbb{R}: Exposure time (scalar controlling LDR intensity). \theta: Global MLP parameters shared across all Gaussians for tone-mapping. The covariance matrix \Sigmai is decomposed into a rotation matrix Ri \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} and a scaling matrix Si \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} as: \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^\top Ri^\top where Ri and Si are learnable parameters. The HDR color c{h,i} is view-dependent and modeled using Spherical Harmonics (SH). Let k = \{k{lm} \mid 0 \le l \le L, -l \le m \le l\} \in \mathbb{R}^{(L+1)^2 \times 3} be the SH coefficients, where each k{lm} \in \mathbb{R}^3 corresponds to RGB components. For a view direction d = (\theta, \phi), the HDR color is: c{h,i}(d, k) = \exp\left( \sum{l=0}^{L} \sum{m=-l}^{l} k{lm} Y{lm}(\theta, \phi) \right) where Y{lm}: S^2 \to \mathbb{R} are the SH basis functions. Steps: 1. Initialization: Recalibrate camera parameters from Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) to world coordinates using Structure-from-Motion (SfM) to establish a suitable data foundation for 3DGS-based methods. Compute initial positions for the Gaussian point clouds. 2. Tone-Mapping Formulation: To avoid vanishing gradients and numerical overflow/underflow caused by direct multiplication in the linear domain, the tone-mapping function is transformed into the logarithmic domain. The relationship between LDR color cl, HDR color ch, and exposure time \Delta t is defined as: cl = f{TM}(ch \cdot \Delta t) Inverting this and taking the natural logarithm (\ln, base e): \log f{TM}^{-1}(cl) = \log cl + \log \Delta t The inverse function is reformulated as: cl = (\log f{TM}^{-1})^{-1}(\log ch + \log \Delta t). 3. MLP Tone-Mapper: Three independent MLPs with global parameters \theta model the function (\log f{TM}^{-1})^{-1} independently for each RGB channel. Define the mapping function g\theta(x) \triangleq (\log f{TM}^{-1})^{-1}(x). The LDR color is computed as: c{l,i} = g\theta(\log c{h,i} + \log \Delta t). 4. Parallel Differentiable Rasterization (PDR): The HDR colors c{h,i} and LDR colors c{l,i} are fed into two separate Parallel Differentiable Rasterization processes to render the final HDR and LDR images, respectively. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def project3dto2d(mu3d, camerapose): # Standard perspective projection mucam = camerapose[:3,:3] @ mu3d + camerapose[:3, 3] z = mucam[2] if z <= 0: return None, None fx, fy = 1.0, 1.0 # Normalized focal lengths x2d = fx mucam[0] / z y2d = fy mucam[1] / z return np.array([x2d, y2d]), z def projectcovariance2d(Sigma3d, camerapose, mu3d): # Standard 3D Gaussian splatting 2D covariance projection W = camerapose[:3,:3] mucam = W @ mu3d + camerapose[:3, 3] Z = mucam[2] if Z <= 0: return None J = np.zeros((3, 3)) J[0, 0] = 1.0 / Z J[0, 2] = -mucam[0] / (Z Z) J[1, 1] = 1.0 / Z J[1, 2] = -mucam[1] / (Z Z) T = J @ W return T @ Sigma3d @ T.T def directiontospherical(d): # Convert 3D direction vector to spherical coordinates normd = np.linalg.norm(d) if normd == 0: return 0.0, 0.0 theta = np.arccos(np.clip(d[2] / normd, -1.0, 1.0)) phi = np.arctan2(d[1], d[0]) return theta, phi def evaluateshbasis(l, m, theta, phi): # Standard spherical harmonic basis evaluation # Returns Ylm(theta, phi) return 0.0 # Placeholder for standard SH library/math def renderhdrldr(gaussians, camerapose, exposuretime, mlpr, mlpg, mlpb, shcoeffs, degree): imgh, imgw = 400, 400 hdrimg = np.zeros((imgh, imgw, 3)) ldrimg = np.zeros((imgh, imgw, 3)) alphaimg = np.zeros((imgh, imgw)) for g in gaussians: mu2d, z = project3dto2d(g['mu'], camerapose) if mu2d is None: continue sigma2d = projectcovariance2d(g['Sigma'], camerapose, g['mu']) if sigma2d is None: continue # Compute view direction for SH evaluation camorigin = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) d = g['mu'] - camorigin theta, phi = directiontospherical(d) # Evaluate HDR color using SH shsum = np.zeros(3) for l in range(degree + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): klm = shcoeffs.get((l, m), np.zeros(3)) ylm = evaluateshbasis(l, m, theta, phi) shsum += klm ylm ch = np.exp(shsum) # Compute LDR color using tone mapper: cl = gtheta(log(ch) + log(dt)) logch = np.log(ch + 1e-8) logdt = np.log(exposuretime) cl = np.array([ mlpr(logch[0] + logdt), mlpg(logch[1] + logdt), mlpb(logch[2] + logdt) ]) # Rasterize accumulation (simplified bounding box) px, py = int(mu2d[0]), int(mu2d[1]) if 0 <= px < imgw and 0 <= py < imgh: alpha = g['alpha'] hdrimg[py, px] += alpha ch ldrimg[py, px] += alpha cl alphaimg[py, px] += alpha alphaimg = np.maximum(alphaimg, 1e-8) hdrimg /= alphaimg[:,:, np.newaxis] ldrimg /= alphaimg[:,:, np.newaxis] return hdrimg, ldrimg Parameters: Np: The number of 3D Gaussians in the scene representation. \Delta t: The exposure time, a scalar value \Delta t \in \mathbb{R} that controls the light intensity of the LDR view and can be read from photo metadata. L: The degree of Spherical Harmonics used for view-dependent HDR color. \theta: Global MLP parameters for the tone-mapper. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Vanishing Gradients/Overflow: Directly modeling the tone-mapping function f{TM}(\cdot) in the linear domain can cause vanishing gradients and numerical overflow/underflow due to multiplication operations. The logarithmic transformation is required to mitigate this. NDC Coordinates: Existing datasets often provide camera poses in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC), which are not suitable for 3DGS-based methods. Recalibration to world coordinates is necessary. RGB Channel Independence: The tone-mapping function is modeled by three independent MLPs for RGB channels because RGB colors are tone-mapped by different Camera Response Functions (CRFs). Performance: HDR-GS surpasses state-of-the-art NeRF-based methods by 3.84 dB on LDR Novel View Synthesis (NVS) and 1.91 dB on HDR NVS. Speed: It achieves 1000× inference speed compared to HDR-NeRF, which takes 8.2 seconds to infer an image at 400×400 resolution. Training Time: HDR-GS requires only 6.3% of the training time compared to HDR-NeRF, which takes 9 hours to train. Strengths: High inference speed, significantly reduced training time, and user-controllable exposure for LDR reconstruction. Limitations: Requires recalibration of camera parameters from NDC to world coordinates for initialization. HDR-GS was proposed to address the limitations of NeRF-based HDR NVS methods, which suffer from long training times and slow inference speeds. It builds on the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework. The method introduces the Dual Dynamic Range (DDR) Gaussian point cloud model and Parallel Differentiable Rasterization (PDR) processes. It also addresses the issue of NDC camera poses in existing datasets by recalibrating them using Structure-from-Motion (SfM). name: BoundedGS
head: Bounded Working-Set 3DGS
body: BoundedGS is a memory-efficient training and rendering method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that bounds GPU memory usage during high-resolution training by separating rasterization and projection backward passes. It replaces full-frame projection with group-based candidate screening, leaf budget management, and compact gradient storage to limit the active working set. Unlike InfiniGS, which uses image blocks and asynchronous optimization, BoundedGS examines the lifetime of rasterization forward and backward caches within a complete view on one GPU. Unlike CLM, which reduces projection input via frustum candidates, BoundedGS combines view-level candidates with load-bounded local rasterization to control the simultaneous residency of Gaussian-tile intersections, pixels, projection state, and parameter gradients. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Global Gaussian parameters \theta, camera intrinsics/extrinsics, training image, projection-group grid side length g, and rasterization budget L per leaf. Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters \theta, rendered image, and loss value. Data Structures: Global Model: Stores Gaussian positions, rotations, scales, opacities, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Candidate Indices: For each group j, an array of Gaussian IDs Cj screened for potential visibility. Leaf Layout: A CPU-cached tree of tile-aligned rectangles R. Each leaf tracks its pixel count pR, tile count tR, and intersection count nR. Compact Gradients: Parameter gradients are accumulated only for candidate Gaussians in the current group, indexed by their global IDs, rather than allocating full rows for all N Gaussians. Numbered Steps: 1. Group Division: Divide the image into g^2 non-overlapping groups. The standard configuration uses g=1 (one group covering the whole image). 2. Candidate Screening: For each group j, build candidate index array Cj: a. Read Gaussian position, opacity \alphai, and maximum scale. b. Exclude Gaussians with camera-space depth zi \le 0.2 or activated opacity \alphai \le 1/255. c. Compute the projection Jacobian Ai using detailed projection focal lengths. Clamp normalized coordinates xi/zi and yi/zi to \pm 1.3 \tan(\text{FOV}x/2) and \pm 1.3 \tan(\text{FOV}y/2) respectively. d. Estimate screen covariance bound. e. Calculate screen-space rectangle half-widths: e{i,x} = \max(0, \sqrt{2 \log(255\alphai) \bar{\Sigma}{i,2D,xx} + 2}) e{i,y} = \max(0, \sqrt{2 \log(255\alphai) \bar{\Sigma}{i,2D,yy} + 2}) The +2 inside the square root provides a two-pixel discretization margin. f. Include Gaussian i in Cj if the rectangle [c{i,x} - e{i,x}, c{i,x} + e{i,x}] \times [c{i,y} - e{i,y}, c{i,y} + e{i,y}] intersects the group's tile-padded bounds. Non-finite projection results retain the Gaussian. g. Build Cj by visiting the global model and constructing candidate-ID arrays. 3. Group Processing (Row-Major Order): For each group j: a. Projection: Read original parameter rows at IDs in Cj and project them once. Reuse these projected attributes for all leaves in the group. b. Leaf Subdivision: Determine leaves covering the group. A leaf is a tile-aligned rectangle R. Estimate allocation size E(R): E(R) = B{\text{bin}}(nR) + B{\text{image}}(pR, tR) + B{\text{sample}}(bR, d) + B{\text{out}}(pR, d) where d indicates inverse depth enablement (main table uses RGB without depth). nR: exact Gaussian-tile intersection count. pR: pixel count. tR = \lceil hR/16 \rceil \lceil wR/16 \rceil: tile count. uR = \min(tR, nR). bR = \lfloor (nR + 31uR + 31)/32 \rfloor: upper bound on 32-entry backward buckets. B{\text{bin}}: two uint32 Gaussian-ID arrays, two uint64 sort-key arrays, CUB radix-sort workspace. B{\text{image}}: per-pixel alpha and contributor state, per-tile ranges, maximum contributors, bucket counts, offsets, scan workspace. B{\text{sample}}: bucket-to-tile indices, transmittance and RGB state for 256 pixels per bucket. B{\text{out}}: FP32 RGB output buffer, plus depth buffer if enabled. c. Budget Splitting: If E(R) > L and R can be split, bisect along the dimension with more tiles (ties broken horizontally). Children remain disjoint and cover the parent. Stop when E(R) \le L or R is one tile. d. Leaf Execution: For each final leaf R: i. Recount intersections under current projection. ii. Perform rasterization (within-tile sorting and compositing) and compute loss LR = 0.8 L{1,R} + 0.2 (1 - \text{SSIM}R). iii. Compute backward pass to get gradients for projected attributes. iv. Accumulate these gradients into the group's compact parameter-gradient storage, indexed by candidate IDs. v. Release leaf state (intersections, compositing buffers, loss state). e. Group Cleanup: After all leaves, perform projection backward to accumulate parameter gradients from projected attributes. Release group projection and gradient caches. 4. Update: After all groups, compute global regularization (e.g., GNS pruning term during 15K–19K window) once. Combine gradients from all groups. Perform one parameter update using the optimizer (e.g., CUDA Adam). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def boundedgsstep(globalparams, camera, image, g, L): # 1. Divide image into g^2 non-overlapping groups groups = [] gw, gh = image.width // g, image.height // g for gy in range(g): for gx in range(g): groups.append((gx gw, gy gh, (gx + 1) gw, (gy + 1) gh)) viewgradients = {} # 2. Process groups in row-major order for groupbounds in groups: candidates = [] # Candidate screening for i in range(globalparams.numgaussians): pos = globalparams.pos[i] zi = pos.z alphai = globalparams.opacity[i] if zi <= 0.2 or alphai <= 1/255: continue # Compute projection Jacobian Ai using detailed projection focal lengths # Standard 3DGS projection Jacobian computation Ai = camera.computejacobian(pos) xnorm = clamp(pos.x / zi, -1.3 tan(camera.fovx / 2), 1.3 tan(camera.fovx / 2)) ynorm = clamp(pos.y / zi, -1.3 tan(camera.fovy / 2), 1.3 tan(camera.fovy / 2)) smax = abs(globalparams.globalscale) max(exp(s) for s in globalparams.logscales[i]) Sigmabar = Ai @ (smax2 np.eye(3)) @ Ai.T + 0.3 np.eye(2) ex = max(0, sqrt(2 log(255 alphai) Sigmabar[0,0] + 2)) ey = max(0, sqrt(2 log(255 alphai) Sigmabar[1,1] + 2)) # Include Gaussian i in Cj if rectangle intersects tile-padded bounds if (pos.x - ex < groupbounds[2] and pos.x + ex > groupbounds[0] and pos.y - ey < groupbounds[3] and pos.y + ey > groupbounds[1]): candidates.append(i) # Projection: Read original parameter rows at IDs in Cj and project them once # Standard 3DGS projection step projectedattrs = [camera.project(params[i]) for i in candidates] # Leaf Subdivision: Determine leaves covering the group leaves = [] queue = [groupbounds] while queue: R = queue.pop(0) # Standard intersection and pixel count nR = sum(1 for attr in projectedattrs if intersects(R, attr)) pR = (R[2] - R[0]) (R[3] - R[1]) tR = ceil(R[2]/16) ceil(R[3]/16) uR = min(tR, nR) bR = floor((nR + 31uR + 31)/32) # Estimate allocation size E(R) # Standard memory estimation based on Bbin, Bimage, Bsample, Bout ER = estimatememory(nR, pR, tR, bR) # Budget Splitting: If E(R) > L and R can be split, bisect along dimension with more tiles if ER > L and R[2] > 16 and R[3] > 16: if ceil(R[2]/16) >= ceil(R[3]/16): mid = (R[0] + R[2]) // 2 queue.append((R[0], R[1], mid, R[3])) queue.append((mid, R[1], R[2], R[3])) else: mid = (R[1] + R[3]) // 2 queue.append((R[0], R[1], R[2], mid)) queue.append((R[0], mid, R[2], R[3])) else: leaves.append(R) groupgradients = {} for leaf in leaves: # Recount intersections under current projection intersections = [attr for attr in projectedattrs if intersects(leaf, attr)] # Rasterization and loss backward # Standard 3DGS rasterization, compositing, and loss computation alphamap, colormap, contributors = rasterize(leaf, intersections) loss = computeloss(colormap, image[leaf], alphamap) gradprojattrs = backwardrasterization(leaf, intersections, gradloss=1.0) # Accumulate gradients into group's compact parameter-gradient storage for i in candidates: if i in contributors: # Standard backward projection gradp = backwardprojection(projectedattrs[i], gradprojattrs[i]) if i not in groupgradients: groupgradients[i] = np.zeroslike(globalparams[i]) groupgradients[i] += gradp # Release leaf state del intersections, alphamap, colormap, contributors, loss, gradprojattrs # Group Cleanup: After all leaves, projection backward directly accumulates parameter gradients for i, grad in groupgradients.items(): if i not in viewgradients: viewgradients[i] = np.zeroslike(globalparams[i]) viewgradients[i] += grad # Release group projection and gradient caches del projectedattrs, groupgradients # Update: Global regularization computed once after all groups if step in [15000, 19000]: # GNS regularization term during pruning window regloss = computegnsregularization(globalparams) # Optimizer updates after view gradients have been collected optimizer.step(globalparams, viewgradients) Memory Complexity: The rendering working set is bounded and nearly constant with respect to resolution. In a resolution sweep with 6M Gaussians, the working set stays within 1.073–1.077 GiB from 1K to 16K resolution. The peak memory is approximated as M^{peak}v \approx \maxt [M{res}(t) + M{view}(t) + M{rast}(t)], where M{rast} is bounded by the leaf budget L. Performance: At 11K resolution, a warm pass takes 19.79 seconds versus 21.76 seconds for full-frame execution (~9% faster). On five native 5K outdoor scenes, full training reduces the mean rendering working set from 9.97 to 1.76 GiB (82.3% reduction) and shortens training time from 36.7 to 33.9 minutes. Quality: The largest relative L1 difference over shared settings is \approx 6.8 \times 10^{-7}. Final reconstruction quality is close to the original method. Strengths: Bounded GPU memory usage regardless of resolution; no need for multi-GPU synchronization or host offloading for rendering state. Limitations: Requires CPU-assisted structure rebuilding for leaf layout management; potential overhead from candidate screening and leaf subdivision logic. BoundedGS was introduced to address the memory peaks caused by co-resident rasterization, projection, and gradient state in complete-view training of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It identifies that limiting the simultaneously active local state controls the growth of main rendering caches, allowing high-resolution training on single GPUs. The method integrates projection, gradients, and resource management into a single execution flow, retaining full-pixel supervision and one update per view. BoundedGS: Memory-Efficient High-Resolution Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34233v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Connectivity-based Visibility for 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: 3DGS + Our Connectivity, Connectivity relationship for 3DGS
body: This method replaces the standard depth-ordered blending of all overlapping points in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with a visibility filtering step based on a connectivity relationship graph. By retrieving only visible points from the point cloud for blending, it reduces memory consumption and accelerates rendering, enabling the optimization of large-scale scenes (e.g., autonomous driving sequences with tens of millions of points) that would otherwise exceed GPU memory limits. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by explicitly discarding unseen points during the compositing phase, whereas standard 3DGS blends a set of depth-ordered points including many unseen ones. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D point cloud with associated Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) and a camera pose. Output: A rendered image where pixel colors are computed using only the subset of Gaussians determined to be visible via the connectivity graph. Data Structures: Connectivity Graph: A graph structure representing the spatial or topological relationships between points in the cloud, used to identify visible points relative to the camera view. The specific construction algorithm for the graph is not detailed in the sources. Visibility Mask: A boolean array or list of indices indicating which points from the full cloud are visible. Steps: 1. Deactivate Densification: Disable the standard 3DGS densification (splitting/cloning) process because the accumulated LiDAR point cloud is relatively dense. 2. Retrieve Visible Points: Query the connectivity relationship graph from the whole point cloud to retrieve only the subset of points that are visible from the current camera viewpoint. 3. Blend Visible Points: Perform the standard 3DGS alpha-blending operation using only the retrieved visible points to compute the color for each pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderconnectivity3dgs(points, gaussians, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics, connectivitygraph): """ Render a frame using connectivity-based visibility for 3DGS. Args: points: Array of 3D point positions (N, 3). gaussians: Dictionary of Gaussian attributes (covariances, opacities, SH coeffs). cameraintrinsics: 3x3 intrinsic matrix. cameraextrinsics: 4x4 extrinsic matrix (world to camera). connectivitygraph: Object providing getvisiblepoints(points, cameraextrinsics). Returns: renderedimage: Rendered RGB image (H, W, 3). """ # Step 1: Retrieve visible points using the connectivity graph visibleindices = connectivitygraph.getvisiblepoints(points, cameraextrinsics) # Filter Gaussian attributes to the visible subset visiblecovs = gaussians['covariances'][visibleindices] visibleopacities = gaussians['opacities'][visibleindices] visiblesh = gaussians['shcoeffs'][visibleindices] visiblepos = points[visibleindices] # Step 2: Project visible points to screen space campos = cameraextrinsics[:3, 3] relpos = visiblepos - campos rot = cameraextrinsics[:3,:3] viewpos = rot @ relpos.T # (3, M) # Clip points behind camera validmask = viewpos[2,:] > 0.01 viewpos = viewpos[:, validmask] visiblecovs = visiblecovs[validmask] visibleopacities = visibleopacities[validmask] visiblesh = visiblesh[validmask] # Project covariance to screen space (simplified 3DGS projection) tanfovx = np.tan(cameraintrinsics[0, 0] / 2) tanfovy = np.tan(cameraintrinsics[1, 1] / 2) aspect = cameraintrinsics[0, 0] / cameraintrinsics[1, 1] # Compute screen-space covariance and bounding box for each visible Gaussian # (Standard 3DGS projection logic) # For brevity, we assume a helper computes screen-space bounds and 2D covariance screenbounds = computescreenbounds(viewpos, visiblecovs, cameraintrinsics) # Step 3: Alpha-blend visible Gaussians per pixel H, W = 1080, 1920 # Example resolution renderedimage = np.zeros((H, W, 3), dtype=np.float32) accumulatedopacity = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=np.float32) for i in range(len(screenbounds)): x0, y0, x1, y1 = screenbounds[i] x0, y0 = int(np.clip(x0, 0, W-1)), int(np.clip(y0, 0, H-1)) x1, y1 = int(np.clip(x1, 0, W-1)), int(np.clip(y1, 0, H-1)) # Extract 2D covariance and opacity for this Gaussian cov2d = compute2dcovariance(visiblecovs[i], viewpos[:, i], cameraintrinsics) alpha = visibleopacities[i] color = computeshcolor(visiblesh[i], cameraextrinsics) # Rasterize this Gaussian to the pixel grid for y in range(y0, y1 + 1): for x in range(x0, x1 + 1): dx, dy = x - viewpos[0, i], y - viewpos[1, i] sigma = 0.5 (dx2 cov2d[0,0] + dy2 cov2d[1,1] + 2dxdycov2d[0,1]) galpha = alpha np.exp(-sigma) galpha = np.clip(galpha, 0, 1) # Alpha blending prevcolor = renderedimage[y, x] renderedimage[y, x] = prevcolor (1 - galpha) + color galpha accumulatedopacity[y, x] += galpha (1 - accumulatedopacity[y, x]) return renderedimage def computescreenbounds(pos, covs, intrinsics): """Compute bounding box for each Gaussian in screen space.""" # Standard 3DGS bounding box calculation # Returns list of (x0, y0, x1, y1) return [(0, 0, 1, 1)] # Placeholder for standard projection math def compute2dcovariance(cov3d, viewpos, intrinsics): """Project 3D covariance to 2D screen space.""" # Standard 3DGS 2D covariance projection return np.eye(2) # Placeholder for standard projection math def computeshcolor(shcoeffs, extrinsics): """Evaluate spherical harmonics for a given view direction.""" # Standard SH evaluation return np.array([0.5, 0.5, 0.5]) # Placeholder for standard SH math Parameters: Densification: Disabled (Boolean: False). GPU Memory: The method is designed to fit within limited resources (e.g., 48 GB), whereas standard 3DGS fails on large datasets. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Coverage: The method may underperform in scenes with sparse coverage (e.g., fast-moving camera paths in autonomous driving) where the connectivity graph might not adequately capture visible structure. Graph Construction: The performance depends on the efficiency and accuracy of the connectivity graph. If the graph fails to identify visible points correctly, rendering quality degrades. Focuses on reducing the number of Gaussians by merging similar ones, rather than filtering visibility. Link General training loop, not visibility. Link Handles bad Gaussians, not visibility filtering. Link Uses texture-based representation, not visibility. Link Handles mirrors, not basic visibility. Link Handles environment maps, not visibility. Link Adds physics, not visibility. Link Generates env maps, not visibility. Link Uses MAC for compression, not visibility. Link Uses heat kernels, not visibility. Link Style transfer, not visibility. Link Specialized for Earth observation, not general visibility. Link Handles HDR, not visibility. Link Uses bounding boxes, not connectivity visibility. Link Uses sketches, not visibility. Link Time Complexity: Rendering time is significantly reduced. On KITTI-4-reduced (19.4 million points), rendering time decreased from 0.046s (21.6 FPS) to 0.00089s (1114 FPS), an acceleration of more than 50 times. Memory Complexity: Reduces GPU memory requirements by only processing visible points. Standard 3DGS failed on full KITTI-4 (approx. 36.3 million points) due to memory constraints, while this method succeeded on the same hardware (48 GB GPU). Measured Performance: On KITTI-4-reduced, PSNR improved from 19.61 to 28.57, SSIM from 0.58 to 0.83, and LPIPS from 0.57 to 0.23. Strengths: Enables optimization and rendering of very large scenes (tens of millions of points) that exceed standard GPU memory. Significantly faster rendering speeds. Limitations: Performance may degrade in scenes with sparse coverage (e.g., fast-moving cameras) where the connectivity graph may not accurately capture visible structure. When to Use: Large-scale scenes with dense initial point clouds (e.g., LiDAR scans) where standard 3DGS fails due to memory or is too slow. When Not to Use: Scenes where the initial point cloud is sparse and requires densification to fill gaps, as the method deactivates densification due to its reliance on dense accumulated LiDAR data. The method was introduced in the paper "CE-NPBG: Connectivity Enhanced Neural Point-Based Graphics for Novel View Synthesis in Autonomous Driving Scenes" (2025). It addresses the scalability issues of 3D Gaussian Splatting when applied to large-scale autonomous driving datasets like KITTI-360. The authors observed that standard 3DGS blends many unseen points, leading to unnecessary computation and memory usage. By introducing a connectivity relationship graph to filter visible points, they achieved better scene fitting and scalability. name: Sketch and Patch
head: Sketch Gaussian Extraction, Sketch and Patch: Efficient 3D Gaussian Representation for Man-Made Scenes
body: Sketch and Patch is a hybrid 3D Gaussian representation method that categorizes Gaussians into two distinct roles: Sketch Gaussians, which define scene boundaries and high-frequency features, and Patch Gaussians, which cover smoother, broader regions. It solves the problem of storage inefficiency and redundancy in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), where adaptive density control overestimates densification needs in high-frequency areas, leading to redundant Gaussian clusters along edges. Unlike conventional 3D downsampling or tiling which degrade visual quality due to the tightly coupled, heterogeneous nature of 3DGS Gaussians, this method separates Gaussians by role to allow specialized encoding. Inputs: Multi-view images and camera poses. Outputs: A unified hybrid representation consisting of encoded Sketch Gaussians and optimized Patch Gaussians. 1. 3D Line Segment (Li): Defined by endpoints p{start}, p{end} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and parameter t \in [0, 1]. 2. Sketch Gaussian Candidate Set (Si): A subset of original 3DGS Gaussians associated with line segment Li. 3. Parametric Model: A function (e.g., polynomial or spline) encoding the attributes of Sketch Gaussians along the line. 4. Patch Gaussian Set: The remaining Gaussians after Sketch extraction, subject to pruning. 1. Extract 3D Line Segments: Process input images and camera poses using a geometry-guided line reconstruction method, specifically Line3D++. This abstracts object boundaries into discrete 2D line segments and back-projects them into 3D space to obtain a set of 3D line segments \{Li\}. 2. Identify Sketch Gaussians: For each 3D line segment Li, identify candidate Gaussians concentrated along the line. A Gaussian splat Gj with center \muj \in \mathbb{R}^3 is included in the candidate set Si if its distance to the line segment is within a radius r: d(\muj, Li) = \min{t \in [0,1]} \|\muj - Li(t)\| \le r where the line segment is parameterized as: Li(t) = (1 - t)p{start} + t p{end}, \quad t \in [0, 1]. Apply Random Sample Consensus (RANSAC) to the candidate set Si to ensure coherent attribute values among the selected Sketch Gaussians, refining the set to robustly represent the line. 3. Encode Sketch Gaussians: Encode the identified Sketch Gaussians using parametric models (such as polynomials or splines) defined on the given 3D line Li. This leverages the geometric coherence of Gaussians along edges to model their attributes compactly, significantly reducing storage requirements. 4. Optimize Patch Gaussians: For the remaining smoother regions represented by Patch Gaussians, apply pruning and retraining. This sparsifies their distribution while maintaining visual fidelity and volumetric consistency. 5. Integrate Representation: Combine the encoded Sketch Gaussians and the optimized Patch Gaussians into a unified hybrid representation for efficient storage, transmission, and rendering.
