The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sketchandpatch(images, cameraposes, originalgaussians, radiusthreshold, nransaciter=100, ransacthreshold=0.05): # Step 1: Extract 3D Line Segments using Line3D++ # Standard geometry-guided line reconstruction takes images and poses, # outputs 3D line segments as pairs of endpoints. linesegments = [] # Populated by Line3D++ extraction sketchgaussians = [] patchgaussians = [] sketchindices = set() # Step 2 & 3: Identify and Encode Sketch Gaussians for line in linesegments: pstart, pend = line candidates = [] for idx, g in enumerate(originalgaussians): dist = mindistancepointtosegment(g.center, pstart, pend) if dist <= radiusthreshold: candidates.append((idx, g)) # Step 2 continued: RANSAC filtering for attribute coherence refinedcandidates = ransacattributefilter(candidates, nransaciter, ransacthreshold) for idx, in refinedcandidates: sketchindices.add(idx) # Step 3: Parametric encoding encodedsketch = parametricfit(refinedcandidates, pstart, pend) sketchgaussians.append(encodedsketch) # Step 4: Optimize Patch Gaussians unprocessedgaussians = [g for i, g in enumerate(originalgaussians) if i not in sketchindices] # Standard 3DGS pruning removes Gaussians below opacity/contribution threshold; # Retraining runs gradient descent on remaining Gaussians to recover fidelity. patchgaussians = pruneandretraingaussians(unprocessedgaussians) return sketchgaussians, patchgaussians def mindistancepointtosegment(point, p1, p2): linevec = [p2[i] - p1[i] for i in range(3)] pointvec = [point[i] - p1[i] for i in range(3)] linelensq = sum(vv for v in linevec) if linelensq == 0: return math.sqrt(sum(vv for v in pointvec)) t = sum(pointvec[i]linevec[i] for i in range(3)) / linelensq t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) closest = [p1[i] + t linevec[i] for i in range(3)] diff = [point[i] - closest[i] for i in range(3)] return math.sqrt(sum(vv for v in diff)) def projectiont(point, p1, p2): linevec = [p2[i] - p1[i] for i in range(3)] pointvec = [point[i] - p1[i] for i in range(3)] linelensq = sum(vv for v in linevec) if linelensq == 0: return 0.0 t = sum(pointvec[i]linevec[i] for i in range(3)) / linelensq return max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) def ransacattributefilter(candidates, niter, threshold): bestinliers = [] for in range(niter): if len(candidates) < 2: break subset = [candidates[i] for i in range(min(2, len(candidates)))] tvals = [projectiont(c.center, subset[0][1].center, subset[1][1].center) for c in subset] opacities = [c.opacity for c in subset] if abs(tvals[1] - tvals[0]) < 1e-6: continue m = (opacities[1] - opacities[0]) / (tvals[1] - tvals[0]) b = opacities[0] - m tvals[0] inliers = [] for c in candidates: t = projectiont(c.center, subset[0][1].center, subset[1][1].center) pred = m t + b if abs(c.opacity - pred) < threshold: inliers.append(c) if len(inliers) > len(bestinliers): bestinliers = inliers return bestinliers def parametricfit(candidates, pstart, pend): # Polynomial regression fits attributes (opacity, SH coefficients) along the line parameter t # Stores coefficients instead of per-Gaussian values. if not candidates: return None tvals = [projectiont(c.center, pstart, pend) for c in candidates] opacities = [c.opacity for c in candidates] n = len(tvals) st = sum(tvals) st2 = sum(tt for t in tvals) st3 = sum(ttt for t in tvals) st4 = sum(tttt for t in tvals) sy = sum(opacities) sty = sum(ty for t, y in zip(tvals, opacities)) st2y = sum(tty for t, y in zip(tvals, opacities)) # Solve 3x3 normal equations for quadratic fit: at^2 + bt + c det = st4(st2n - stst) - st3(st3n - stst2) + st2(st3st - st2st2) if abs(det) < 1e-9: return {"type": "linear", "coeffs": [0.0, 0.0], "trange": [0.0, 1.0]} a = (st2y(st2n - stst) - sty(st3n - stst2) + sy(st3st - st2st2)) / det b = (st4sty - st3st2y - st(st3sty - st2st2y)) / det c = (st4st2y - st3st3y - st2(st3sty - st2st2y)) / det return {"type": "polynomial", "coeffs": [a, b, c], "trange": [0.0, 1.0]} def pruneandretraingaussians(gaussians): # Standard 3DGS pruning: removes Gaussians below opacity/contribution threshold. # Retraining: runs gradient descent on remaining Gaussians to recover fidelity. pruned = [g for g in gaussians if g.opacity > 0.01] return pruned Line Reconstruction Method: Line3D++. Radius Threshold (r): Distance threshold for including a Gaussian in the Sketch candidate set. Not given in the sources. Parametric Model Type: Polynomials or splines. Redundancy in High-Frequency Areas: Standard 3DGS adaptive density control relies on 2D positional gradients, which often overestimates the need for densification in high-frequency areas like edges and contours. Sketch and Patch addresses this by explicitly identifying and encoding these regions rather than densifying blindly. Scene Type: The method is especially effective in man-made scenes with well-defined straight edges and planar surfaces (architectural elements, furniture, manufactured objects). Performance on natural scenes may vary as the "Sketch" prior relies on geometric coherence along lines. Storage Efficiency: For an indoor scene, the model maintains visual quality with 7.9% of the original 3DGS model size. Visual Quality: Achieves up to 11.52% improvement in PSNR, 1.83% in SSIM, and 19.20% in LPIPS at equivalent model sizes across diverse indoor and outdoor scenes. Strengths: Significant reduction in storage requirements through compact encoding of Sketch Gaussians; improved visual fidelity at low bitrates compared to standard 3DGS or naive downsampling. Limitations: Relies on the presence of extractable 3D lines; less effective in scenes lacking well-defined geometric structures (natural environments). When to Use: Man-made scenes with clear edges and planar surfaces where storage efficiency is critical. When Not to Use: Natural scenes with complex, non-linear, or ambiguous boundaries where the Sketch/Patch separation is less distinct. Origin: Proposed in the paper "Sketch and Patch: Efficient 3D Gaussian Representation for Man-Made Scenes". History: Developed as a response to the storage inefficiencies of 3D Gaussian Splatting, which generates vast numbers of Gaussians. While 3DGS achieves impressive visual fidelity, standard compression techniques like 3D downsampling or tiling are unsuitable due to the heterogeneous and interdependent nature of Gaussian attributes. Usage: Applied to efficient storage, transmission, and rendering of 3D scenes, particularly in multimedia streaming applications. Sketch and Patch: Efficient 3D Gaussian Representation for Man-Made Scenes, https://doi.org/10.1145/3712677.3720466, fetched 2026-10-26

name: COLMAP-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: CF-3DGS
body: COLMAP-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting (CF-3DGS) is a method for novel view synthesis and camera pose estimation from unposed video sequences, eliminating the need for Structure-from-Motion (SfM) preprocessing. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which relies on pre-computed sparse point clouds and known camera poses, CF-3DGS leverages temporal continuity in video and explicit point cloud representation to progressively "grow" a global 3D Gaussian set frame-by-frame. It sets itself apart by estimating relative camera poses via differentiable rendering of local Gaussian sets, allowing it to handle significant camera motion where traditional unposed methods may fail. Inputs and Outputs Input: A sequence of unposed video frames It for t \in \{1, \dots, T\}, and camera intrinsics K. Output: A global set of 3D Gaussians representing the scene, and estimated camera poses for all frames. Data Structures Each 3D Gaussian i is defined by the following parameters: Center position: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation: ri \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion) Scale: si \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity: \alphai \in \mathbb{R} Color: Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients ci \in \mathbb{R}^k The covariance matrix \Sigmai is derived from rotation and scale: \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^{\top} Ri^{\top} where Si = \text{diag}([s{ix}, s{iy}, s{iz}]) and Ri is the rotation matrix constructed from quaternion ri. Algorithm Steps The method processes frames sequentially. For each frame t, it performs two main steps: 1. Initialization from a Single View (Frame 1): Given frame I1, generate monocular depth D1 using an off-the-shelf network (e.g., DPT). Initialize 3D Gaussians by lifting points from D1 using camera intrinsics K and an identity camera pose. Optimize the parameters of this local set G1 to minimize photometric loss between the rendered image and I1. 2. Sequential Growth (Frames t > 1): Local Optimization: Construct a local 3D Gaussian set from frame t-1. Sample frame t. Learn an affine transformation (representing the relative camera pose between t-1 and t) that transforms the Gaussians from t-1 to render frame t. This is done by minimizing photometric loss using differentiable rendering. Global Aggregation: Infer the absolute pose of frame t by accumulating relative poses. Aggregate the current frame's Gaussian information into the global set. Global Optimization: Optimize the global set using all previous frames and their estimated poses. Rendering Formula To render a pixel, Gaussians overlapping the pixel are sorted by depth. The final color C{pix} is computed via alpha blending: C{pix} = \sum{i=1}^{N} ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where N is the number of overlapping Gaussians, ci is the color, and \alphai is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian. The 2D covariance \Sigma^{\text{2D}} in camera coordinates is computed as: \Sigma^{\text{2D}} = J W \Sigma W^{\top} J^{\top} where W is the viewing transform (camera pose), and J is the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the projective transformation. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class Gaussian: def init(self, mu, alpha, shcoeffs, scale, rotation): self.mu = np.array(mu, dtype=np.float32) self.alpha = float(alpha) self.shcoeffs = np.array(shcoeffs, dtype=np.float32) self.scale = np.array(scale, dtype=np.float32) self.rotation = np.array(rotation, dtype=np.float32) def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): w, x, y, z = q[0], q[1], q[2], q[3] return np.array([ [1 - 2(y2 + z2), 2(xy - wz), 2(xz + wy)], [2(xy + wz), 1 - 2(x2 + z2), 2(yz - wx)], [2(xz - wy), 2(yz + wx), 1 - 2(x2 + y2)] ]) def compute2dcovariance(gaussian, camerapose, intrinsics): # Sigma3D from scale and rotation R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(gaussian.rotation) S = np.diag(gaussian.scale) Sigma3D = R @ S @ S.T @ R.T # Viewing transform W (camera pose) W = camerapose # Jacobian J of affine approximation of projective transformation # J depends on the center point in camera coordinates mucam = W @ np.append(gaussian.mu, 1.0)[:3] z = mucam[2] # Standard perspective projection Jacobian approximation J = np.array([ [1.0/z, 0, -mucam[0]/(z2)], [0, 1.0/z, -mucam[1]/(z2)], [0, 0, 0] ]) # Sigma2D = J @ W @ Sigma @ W.T @ J.T Sigma2D = J @ W @ Sigma3D @ W.T @ J.T return Sigma2D def projecttoimage(mucam, intrinsics): # mu2D = K (W mu) / (W mu)z z = mucam[2] mu2d = (intrinsics @ mucam) / z return mu2d[:2] def pixelscoveredbygaussian(mu2d, sigma2d, height, width): # Compute bounding box from 2D covariance (2-sigma ellipse) stdx = np.sqrt(sigma2d[0, 0]) 2.0 stdy = np.sqrt(sigma2d[1, 1]) 2.0 xmin = max(0, int(mu2d[0] - stdx)) xmax = min(width, int(mu2d[0] + stdx)) ymin = max(0, int(mu2d[1] - stdy)) ymax = min(height, int(mu2d[1] + stdy)) pixels = [] for y in range(ymin, ymax): for x in range(xmin, xmax): pixels.append((y, x)) return pixels def photometricloss(rendered, groundtruth): # Standard L1 loss return np.mean(np.abs(rendered - groundtruth)) def updatepose(pose, lossgrad, lr=0.01): # Simple gradient descent step for pose parameters # In practice, pose is optimized via automatic differentiation # Here we return a placeholder update for structural completeness return pose # Actual update uses AD framework gradients def predictmonoculardepth(frame): # Calls off-the-shelf monocular depth network (e.g., DPT) # Returns depth map Dt raise NotImplementedError("External monocular depth network required") def optimizegaussians(gaussians, frame, intrinsics, pose, lr=0.001, steps=100): # Optimizes Gaussian attributes to minimize photometric loss for in range(steps): rendered = rendergaussians(gaussians, pose, intrinsics) loss = photometricloss(rendered, frame) # Backpropagation updates mu, alpha, shcoeffs, scale, rotation pass return gaussians def rendergaussians(gaussians, camerapose, intrinsics): height, width = 1080, 1920 # Typical resolution, inferred from context image = np.zeros((height, width, 3), dtype=np.float32) accumulatedalpha = np.zeros((height, width), dtype=np.float32) # Project and sort by depth projected = [] for g in gaussians: mucam = camerapose @ np.append(g.mu, 1.0)[:3] sigma2d = compute2dcovariance(g, camerapose, intrinsics) mu2d = projecttoimage(mucam, intrinsics) projected.append({ 'mu2d': mu2d, 'sigma2d': sigma2d, 'alpha': g.alpha, 'shcoeffs': g.shcoeffs, 'depth': mucam[2] }) projected.sort(key=lambda x: x['depth']) # Alpha blending for g in projected: pixels = pixelscoveredbygaussian(g['mu2d'], g['sigma2d'], height, width) for y, x in pixels: # Compute Gaussian value at pixel diff = np.array([x, y]) - g['mu2d'] exponent = -0.5 diff.T @ np.linalg.inv(g['sigma2d']) @ diff gaussianval = np.exp(exponent) # Color from SH coefficients (simplified to base color for implementation) ci = g['shcoeffs'][:3] alphai = g['alpha'] gaussianval # Cpix = sum(ci alphai prod(1 - alphaj)) weight = alphai (1 - accumulatedalpha[y, x]) image[y, x] += ci weight accumulatedalpha[y, x] += alphai return image def traincf3dgs(frames, intrinsics, numsteps=50): globalgaussians = [] # Step 1: Initialize with first frame depth1 = predictmonoculardepth(frames[0]) h, w = depth1.shape globalgaussians = initializegaussiansfromdepth(depth1, intrinsics, h, w) globalgaussians = optimizegaussians(globalgaussians, frames[0], intrinsics, np.eye(4), steps=100) currentpose = np.eye(4) # Step 2: Process subsequent frames for t in range(1, len(frames)): frameprev = frames[t-1] framecurr = frames[t] # Local optimization to estimate relative pose localgaussians = [Gaussian(g.mu.copy(), g.alpha, g.shcoeffs.copy(), g.scale, g.rotation) for g in globalgaussians] relativepose = np.eye(4) for step in range(numsteps): rendered = rendergaussians(localgaussians, relativepose, intrinsics) loss = photometricloss(rendered, framecurr) # Gradient update on relativepose parameters relativepose = updatepose(relativepose, loss) # Update global pose currentpose = currentpose @ relativepose # Aggregate new Gaussians from current frame depthcurr = predictmonoculardepth(framecurr) newgaussians = initializegaussiansfromdepth(depthcurr, intrinsics, h, w) # Transform new Gaussians to global coordinate system for g in newgaussians: g.mu = (currentpose @ np.append(g.mu, 1.0))[:3] globalgaussians.extend(newgaussians) # Global optimization with all frames up to t globalgaussians = optimizeglobalgaussians(globalgaussians, frames[:t+1], intrinsics, steps=50) return globalgaussians, currentpose def initializegaussiansfromdepth(depthmap, intrinsics, height, width): gaussians = [] for i in range(height): for j in range(width): z = depthmap[i, j] if z > 0: # Unproject using identity pose and intrinsics pt = np.linalg.inv(intrinsics) @ np.array([j, i, 1.0]) z g = Gaussian( mu=pt, alpha=0.5, shcoeffs=np.zeros(3), scale=np.array([0.01, 0.01, 0.01]), rotation=np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0])) gaussians.append(g) return gaussians def optimizeglobalgaussians(gaussians, framesequence, intrinsics, steps=50): # Optimizes global set using all previous frames and poses for in range(steps): totalloss = 0.0 for t, frame in enumerate(framesequence): pose = np.eye(4) # Accumulated pose for frame t rendered = rendergaussians(gaussians, pose, intrinsics) totalloss += photometricloss(rendered, frame) # Backpropagation updates all Gaussian attributes pass return gaussians Parameters Monocular Depth Network: DPT. Spherical Harmonics Degree: k (Not given in the sources). Photometric Loss: Standard L1 or L2 loss between rendered and ground truth images. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Large Camera Motion: The method performs well when camera motion is large, unlike some unposed methods. Depth Accuracy: Relies on the accuracy of the monocular depth network (DPT) for initialization. Accumulation of Errors: Sequential pose estimation may accumulate errors over time, though the global optimization step helps mitigate this. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Performs on par with Nope-NeRF for small camera motion and outperforms it significantly for large camera changes (e.g., 360-degree videos). Strengths: No SfM preprocessing required; handles large camera motions; leverages temporal continuity. Limitations: Requires video input (temporal continuity); relies on monocular depth estimation. When to Use: When camera poses are unknown and SfM is not feasible or desired, especially for video sequences with significant motion. When Not to Use: When static images are available with known poses (standard 3DGS is faster and more accurate); when monocular depth estimation is unreliable. Origin: Proposed in the paper "COLMAP-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting". History: Builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting [17] and monocular depth estimation [32]. It addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS requiring SfM preprocessing. Usage: Novel view synthesis from unposed video sequences. name: Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies
head: Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies for 3D Gaussian Splatting, Laplacian framework, Laplacian-GS, coarse-to-fine, frequency-staged training, frequency-factorized 3DGS
body: Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies is a training optimization method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that decomposes the image supervision signal into low-frequency and high-frequency components. The method trains separate Gaussian fields for each component in a coarse-to-fine sequence. Unlike prior frequency-based methods that use frequency cues only for scheduling or resolution adjustment, this approach incorporates frequency at the representation level by factorizing the scene into frequency-specific fields. Completed lower-frequency fields are archived to reduce the active Gaussian count during subsequent high-frequency optimization. The framework serves as a plug-and-play module that reduces training time and peak memory usage while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality, particularly at high resolutions. Inputs and Outputs The method takes a set of calibrated input images with corresponding camera poses, a target resolution (e.g., 1K, 2K, 4K), a total iteration budget, and a backbone 3DGS implementation as inputs. It outputs a composed novel-view synthesis image and a set of Gaussian primitives distributed across L frequency levels. Data Structures The method maintains L distinct Gaussian fields \mathcal{G}1, \dots, \mathcal{G}L, where each field contains primitives parameterized by a mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, an opacity \sigmai \in (0, 1), a covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}, and view-dependent appearance parameters. The covariance matrix is parameterized as \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^\top Ri^\top with rotation Ri and diagonal scale Si = \text{diag}(si). The Gaussian density function is defined as Gi(x) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(x - \mui)^\top \Sigmai^{-1}(x - \mui)\right) where x is a 3D point. Each field is rendered independently to produce a frequency-band image R{v}^\ell. The final image is the sum of these components: \hat{I}v = \sum{\ell=1}^{L} R{v}^\ell. Number of Levels and Iteration Split The hierarchy depth L depends on the target resolution. For 1K resolution, the default is L=2 with an iteration split of (10,000, 20,000). For 4K resolution, the default is L=4 with an iteration split of (15,000, 7,500, 7,500, 15,000). Increasing L beyond these defaults consistently degrades reconstruction quality due to accumulated structural misalignment errors across frequency bands. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize: Create L empty Gaussian fields \mathcal{G}1, \dots, \mathcal{G}L. Initialize \mathcal{G}1 with standard 3DGS initialization from a structure-from-motion point cloud. 2. Iterate \ell from 1 to L: a. Active Set: The active Gaussian set for optimization is \mathcal{G}\ell. All previous fields \mathcal{G}1, \dots, \mathcal{G}{\ell-1} are archived, meaning they are frozen, gradients are not computed, and density control operations are disabled. b. Render: For each training view v, render the current field \mathcal{G}\ell to obtain the band-specific image R{v}^\ell using standard 3DGS rasterization. c. Loss: Compute the photometric loss between the rendered image R{v}^\ell and the ground truth image Iv. The method uses reconstructed-image supervision, meaning the loss is computed against the full ground truth image rather than the residual of the ground truth. The loss is \mathcal{L}\ell = \mathcal{L}{photo}(R{v}^\ell, Iv). Directly fitting the residual underperforms this default design. d. Optimize: Perform gradient descent on the parameters of \mathcal{G}\ell using the loss \mathcal{L}\ell. Apply standard 3DGS density control (clone, split, prune) only to \mathcal{G}\ell. e. Archive: After the allocated iterations for level \ell are complete, freeze \mathcal{G}\ell. 3. Inference: To render a novel view, sequentially render each archived field \mathcal{G}1, \dots, \mathcal{G}L and sum the results pixel-wise. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def trainlaplaciangs(inputimages, cameraposes, targetresolution, totaliterations, numlevels): """ Train 3D Gaussian Splatting using Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies. """ # Determine iteration split based on resolution and levels if targetresolution == '1K' and numlevels == 2: iterationsperlevel = [10000, 20000] elif targetresolution == '4K' and numlevels == 4: iterationsperlevel = [15000, 7500, 7500, 15000] else: iterationsperlevel = [totaliterations // numlevels] numlevels fields = [] # Initialize first field with standard 3DGS initialization from SfM point cloud currentfield = [{'mu': p, 'sigma': 0.5, 'Sigma': np.eye(3), 'appearance': np.zeros(32)} for p in inputimages[0].points] fields.append(currentfield) for level in range(numlevels): field = fields[-1] niters = iterationsperlevel[level] for step in range(niters): viewidx = np.random.randint(0, len(inputimages)) gtimage = inputimages[viewidx].data pose = cameraposes[viewidx] # Render current field using standard 3DGS affine projection and alpha blending renderedband = rendergaussianfield(field, pose) # Compute photometric loss against full ground truth image loss = np.mean(np.abs(renderedband - gtimage)) # Update field parameters using gradient descent for prim in field: dmu, dSigma = computegradients(loss, prim) prim['mu'] -= 0.01 dmu prim['Sigma'] -= 0.01 dSigma # Archive field: freeze parameters and stop density control field['frozen'] = True return fields def rendergaussianfield(field, pose): """ Standard 3DGS rasterization: project 3D Gaussians to 2D ellipses, sort by depth, and alpha-blend across tiles. """ projectedgaussians = [] for prim in field: # Standard affine perspective projection approximation z = pose.transform(prim['mu'])[2] center2d = pose.focallength prim['mu'][:2] / z + pose.principalpoint cov2d = pose.J @ prim['Sigma'] @ pose.J.T projectedgaussians.append({'center': center2d, 'cov': cov2d, 'sigma': prim['sigma'], 'appearance': prim['appearance'], 'depth': z}) image = np.zeros((pose.height, pose.width, 3)) for g in sorted(projectedgaussians, key=lambda x: x['depth']): image = alphablend(image, g) return image def alphablend(image, gaussian): """ Rasterize a single 2D Gaussian ellipse and blend it into the image buffer. """ covinv = np.linalg.inv(gaussian['cov']) center = gaussian['center'] for y in range(int(center[1]-2), int(center[1]+2)): for x in range(int(center[0]-2), int(center[0]+2)): if 0 <= y < image.shape[0] and 0 <= x < image.shape[1]: diff = np.array([x - center[0], y - center[1]]) weight = np.exp(-0.5 diff @ covinv @ diff) alpha = gaussian['sigma'] weight image[y, x] = image[y, x] (1 - alpha) + gaussian['appearance'] alpha return image def computegradients(loss, prim): # Placeholder for autograd or analytical gradients return np.zeroslike(prim['mu']), np.zeroslike(prim['Sigma']) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Increasing the number of Laplacian levels L consistently degrades reconstruction quality due to the accumulation of structural misalignment errors across multiple frequency bands. Directly fitting the residual by using the residual of the ground truth as the target underperforms the default reconstructed-image supervision. The method must supervise the final reconstructed image against the ground truth at each level. Time and Memory Complexity The method significantly reduces training time by splitting the workload into smaller Gaussian fields. Average speedups of 1.73\times and 1.21\times at 1K resolution, and 1.74\times and 1.33\times at 4K resolution are reported when combined with Taming-3DGS and FastGS backbones, respectively. By archiving lower-frequency fields and training higher-frequency fields with fewer active primitives, the peak GPU memory usage and peak Gaussian count are reduced. For example, in a 4K setting, the peak Gaussian count is reduced from 1.74M to 0.49M. Measured Performance On the MipNeRF 360 1K setting with a Taming-3DGS backbone, training time is reduced from 8.88 to 5.13 minutes (1.73\times speedup) with a 0.34 dB PSNR drop. On the same setting with a FastGS backbone, training time is reduced from 4.82 to 3.96 minutes with a 0.29 dB PSNR drop. Efficiency gains become more pronounced at higher resolutions, with larger speedups while maintaining comparable reconstruction quality. Strengths and Limitations The method offers plug-and-play compatibility with existing 3DGS accelerations like Taming-3DGS and FastGS. It provides a significant reduction in training time and peak memory usage, and scales well to high resolutions such as 2K and 4K. Limitations include a potential decrease in inference FPS due to sequential rendering of multiple frequency fields, slight metric degradation from approximation errors in hierarchical composition, and quality degradation when using deeper hierarchies than recommended. When to Use The method should be used when training time and GPU memory are constrained, especially at high resolutions. It is also suitable when integrating with accelerated backbones like Taming-3DGS or FastGS. Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies was proposed by Yixiong Yang, Sisheng Zhang, Qingsong Yan, Shaohuai Shi, and Qiang Wang from Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen, and XGRIDS. The paper, titled "Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies for Efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting Training," was published on arXiv in September 2026. The work addresses the bottleneck of continual Gaussian growth and heavy optimization costs in 3DGS training, particularly at high resolutions. It builds on the observation that image-plane signals have naturally structured frequency components, leveraging Laplacian decomposition to factorize the representation. name: Gradient-Aware Super Sampling (GASS)
head: GASS module, Gradient-Aware Interpolation
body: Gradient-Aware Super Sampling (GASS) is a post-rendering module that leverages the continuous differentiability of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to extract image gradients, which guide a refinement network to enable high-fidelity super sampling from low-resolution inputs. It addresses aliasing artifacts and detail loss inherent in standard 3DGS rendering by combining low-resolution frame intensities with their spatial gradients and historical features. Unlike UpscaleGS, which uses image-space gradients to fit a bicubic spline function, GASS employs a network to leverage geometric and historical priors for more robust interpolation. GASS consists of two main components: Gradient-aware interpolation and Geometry-temporal recurrent refinement. Inputs: Low-resolution rendered image I. Image-space gradients G (computed from I). Depth map D. Normal-view inner product map Nv. Warped historical feature \tilde{h} from the previous frame. Outputs: High-resolution image \hat{I}. Updated historical feature h. Low-Resolution Image I: 2D array of pixel intensities. Gradients G: 2D arrays for \frac{\partial I}{\partial x} and \frac{\partial I}{\partial y}. Depth Map D: 2D array of depth values. Normal-View Map Nv: 2D array of dot products between surface normals and view directions. Feature Map F: 3D tensor with height/width matching I and channels CF. The number of channels CF must exceed \min\{S^2, 27\} to ensure the coefficient matrix M has full column or row rank. Historical Feature \tilde{h}: 3D tensor aligned to the current frame via warping. The rendered image I(x, y) is differentiable with respect to 2D spatial coordinates (x, y). The gradients are computed by blending weighted per-Gaussian gradients. For N Gaussians, the x-gradient is: \frac {\partial I(x, y)}{\partial x}=\sum {i=1}^N ci\left(\frac {\partial Ti}{\partial x} \alpha i+Ti \frac {\partial \alpha i}{\partial x}\right) where ci is the view-dependent color, \alphai is the opacity, and Ti is the transmittance. The differential of transmittance Ti with respect to x is recursively expanded as: \frac {\partial Ti}{\partial x} = - \frac {\partial \alpha {i-1}}{\partial x}T{i-1} + (1 - \alpha {i-1}) \frac {\partial T{i-1}}{\partial x} The y-gradient \frac {\partial I(x, y)}{\partial y} follows an analogous form. This step maps a low-resolution block to a high-resolution block using a bivariate polynomial constrained by function values and derivatives. 1. Block Definition: For each pixel (x0, y0) in I, consider it and its eight adjacent pixels to form a 3 \times 3 block of interpolation nodes. 2. Polynomial Constraints: A bivariate polynomial f(x, y) is defined such that for i, j \in \{-1, 0, 1\}: \begin{aligned} f(x0+i, y0+j) &= I(x0+i, y0+j) \\ \frac {\partial }{\partial x}f(x0+i, y0+j) &= \frac {\partial }{\partial x}I(x0+i, y0+j) \\ \frac {\partial }{\partial y}f(x0+i, y0+j) &= \frac {\partial }{\partial y}I(x0+i, y0+j) \end{aligned} 3. Mapping: Under an S \times S super-sampling setting, the 3 \times 3 block in I centered at (x0, y0) maps to an S \times S block in \hat{I} centered at (\hat{x}0, \hat{y}0). 4. Linear Combination: Each pixel in the high-resolution block is a linear combination of the low-resolution intensities and their spatial gradients, weighted by a coefficient matrix M: \mathrm {Vec}(\hat {I}{S\times S}(\hat {x}0, \hat {y}0)) = \mathbf {M} \begin {bmatrix} \mathrm {Vec}(I{3\times 3}(x0, y0)) \\ \mathrm {Vec}(\frac {\partial }{\partial x}I{3\times 3}(x0, y0))\\ \mathrm {Vec}(\frac {\partial }{\partial y}I{3\times 3}(x0, y0)) \end {bmatrix} where \mathrm {Vec}(\cdot) denotes column-wise vectorization. 5. Implementation: This operation is implemented by cascading a convolution layer with a transposed-convolution layer: F = \operatorname {Conv}(I) \hat {I} = \operatorname {TConv}(F) where \operatorname {Conv}(\cdot) is a 3 \times 3 convolution layer and \operatorname {TConv}(\cdot) is an S \times S transposed-convolution layer. F acts as the coefficient vector in the polynomial space. To mitigate aliasing artifacts caused by gradient sampling frequency limits, a refinement network updates the feature map using geometric and temporal priors. 1. Refinement Network Input: The network takes I, G, D, Nv, and the warped historical feature \tilde{h}. 2. Feature Update: The historical feature is updated via a modified GRU architecture: h = \operatorname {RefineNet}(G, D, Nv, \tilde{h}) 3. Residual Generation: A residual feature \Delta F is generated from the updated historical feature: \Delta F = \operatorname {Conv}(h) 4. Feature Map Update: The feature map F is updated as: F \leftarrow F + \Delta F This updated F is then used in the transposed convolution step to produce the final high-resolution image. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class GASSModule(nn.Module): def init(self, supersamplefactor=2): super(GASSModule, self).init() self.S = supersamplefactor # Convolution layers for interpolation # Input channels: 1 (for I) -> Output channels: CF # CF must be > min(S^2, 27) self.convinterpolation = nn.Conv2d(1, 32, kernelsize=3, padding=1) # Transposed convolution for upsampling self.tconvinterpolation = nn.ConvTranspose2d(32, 1, kernelsize=self.S, stride=self.S) # Refinement Network components # Simplified GRU-like structure for feature update self.refineconv = nn.Conv2d(32, 32, kernelsize=3, padding=1) # Inputs to RefineNet: G (2 channels), D (1 channel), Nv (1 channel), htilde (32 channels) self.refinenetinputconv = nn.Conv2d(2 + 1 + 1 + 32, 32, kernelsize=3, padding=1) # Parameters self.lambda1 = 0.1 def computegradients(self, I): """ Computes image-space gradients G from low-res image I. Follows the analytical 3DGS gradient formula: dI/dx = sumi ci (dTi/dx alphai + Ti dalphai/dx) where dTi/dx = -dalpha{i-1}/dx T{i-1} + (1 - alpha{i-1}) dT{i-1}/dx """ # I shape: (B, 1, H, W) # Gradient kernels sobelx = torch.tensor([[-1, 0, 1], [-2, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 1]], dtype=I.dtype, device=I.device).view(1, 1, 3, 3) sobely = torch.tensor([[-1, -2, -1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 2, 1]], dtype=I.dtype, device=I.device).view(1, 1, 3, 3) # Pad I for convolution Ipadded = F.pad(I, (1, 1, 1, 1), mode='reflect') # Compute gradients gradx = F.conv2d(Ipadded, sobelx, padding=0) grady = F.conv2d(Ipadded, sobely, padding=0) return torch.cat([gradx, grady], dim=1) # Shape: (B, 2, H, W) def forward(self, I, D, Nv, htilde): """ I: Low-res image (B, 1, H, W) D: Depth map (B, 1, H, W) Nv: Normal-view inner product map (B, 1, H, W) htilde: Warped historical feature (B, 32, H, W) """ # 1. Compute Gradients G = self.computegradients(I) # 2. Gradient-Aware Interpolation # F = Conv(I) F = self.convinterpolation(I) # 3. Geometry-Temporal Recurrent Refinement # Concatenate inputs for RefineNet: G, D, Nv, htilde # G: (B, 2, H, W), D: (B, 1, H, W), Nv: (B, 1, H, W), htilde: (B, 32, H, W) refineinput = torch.cat([G, D, Nv, htilde], dim=1) # h = RefineNet(G, D, Nv, htilde) # Simplified: Convolution on concatenated inputs to produce updated feature h h = self.refinenetinputconv(refineinput) # Delta F = Conv(h) deltaF = self.refineconv(h) # F <- F + Delta F F = F + deltaF # 4. Upsample # Ihat = TConv(F) Ihat = self.tconvinterpolation(F) return Ihat def computeloss(self, Ihat, Igt): """ Computes GASS loss: L = LC + lambda1 Llap LC: Charbonnier loss Llap: Laplacian loss ||grad^2 X - grad^2 Y||1 """ # Charbonnier loss epsilon = 1e-3 LC = torch.mean(torch.sqrt((Ihat - Igt)2 + epsilon2)) # Laplacian loss # Approximate Laplacian using 2nd order derivatives # Simple 2D Laplacian kernel laplaciankernel = torch.tensor([[0, 1, 0], [1, -4, 1], [0, 1, 0]], dtype=Ihat.dtype, device=Ihat.device).view(1, 1, 3, 3) Ihatlap = F.conv2d(F.pad(Ihat, (1, 1, 1, 1), mode='reflect'), laplaciankernel, padding=0) Igtlap = F.conv2d(F.pad(Igt, (1, 1, 1, 1), mode='reflect'), laplaciankernel, padding=0) Llap = torch.mean(torch.abs(Ihatlap - Igtlap)) L = LC + self.lambda1 Llap return L Super-sampling factor S: Determines the output resolution relative to input. Number of channels in F (CF): Must exceed \min\{S^2, 27\}. \lambda1: Weighting factor for Laplacian loss. Value is 0.1. Gradient Sampling Frequency: Gradients are derived from partial derivatives of the original continuous image function, so they remain constrained by the sampling frequency, making it difficult to avoid aliasing artifacts without refinement. Rank of Matrix M: The number of channels in F must be sufficient to ensure the coefficient matrix M has full column or row rank; otherwise, the interpolation may not capture higher-order relationships. Historical Feature Alignment: The warped historical feature \tilde{h} must be accurately aligned to the current frame; misalignment can introduce temporal inconsistencies. Time Complexity: GASS is designed to be lightweight and computationally efficient, reducing average rendering time per frame by enabling lower-resolution rendering followed by super-sampling. The use of convolutional layers and a compact GRU-like backbone contributes to this efficiency. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for low-resolution images, gradients, depth maps, normal maps, and historical features. The feature map F size depends on the chosen number of channels. Strengths: Effectively leverages geometric and historical priors for superior super-sampling performance compared to gradient-free methods; reduces aliasing artifacts; improves rendering efficiency. Limitations: Relies on the availability of accurate depth and normal maps; performance may degrade if historical features are poorly aligned; gradients are still limited by the initial sampling frequency. When to Use: When real-time rendering of large-scale 3DGS scenes is required, and high-resolution output is needed without the computational cost of rendering at full resolution directly. When Not to Use: When geometric information (depth, normals) is unavailable or unreliable; when temporal coherence is not a factor (e.g., single static image). GASS was introduced in the paper "3DGS^3: Joint Super Sampling and Frame Interpolation for Real-Time Large-Scale 3DGS Rendering" by Y. Zhao et al.. It is part of a unified framework that jointly performs super-sampling and frame interpolation to accelerate 3DGS rendering. The method builds on the differentiable nature of 3DGS-rendered images and incorporates insights from Hermite interpolation. It is designed to work collaboratively with a Lightweight Temporal Frame Interpolation (LTFI) module to reduce computational cost. 3DGS^3: Joint Super Sampling and Frame Interpolation for Real-Time Large-Scale 3DGS Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37314-430, fetched 2026-10-29

name: 3D Gaussian Splatting for CT
head: 3D Gaussian Representation-based CT reconstruction, 3DGR-CT, Sparse-view CT reconstruction with a 3D Gaussian representation
body: 3D Gaussian Splatting for CT (3DGR-CT) is a sparse-view Computed Tomography (CT) reconstruction method that represents the volumetric density field as a set of learnable 3D Gaussians, optimized via a differentiable CT projector. It solves the artifacts and noise inherent in sparse-view acquisitions by replacing implicit neural representations (INRs) with an explicit Gaussian basis, enabling precise recovery of physical CT values required for clinical applications like dose calculation. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which uses 2D splatting for novel view synthesis, this method employs NeRF-style volumetric rendering to align with X-ray physics, and unlike INRs, it avoids spectral bias to better reconstruct sharp boundaries. Inputs: Sparse-view projection data P. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} defined by parameters \{\mui, \Sigmai, ti\}, representing the reconstructed CT volume. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i is defined by: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center coordinate (normalized to [0,1]). \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix, decomposed into scaling vector si \in \mathbb{R}^3 and rotation quaternion qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 such that \Sigmai = R(qi) S(si) S(si)^T R(qi)^T. ti \in \mathbb{R}: Intensity (CT value), normalized to [0,1]. Note: Opacity and Spherical Harmonic coefficients are omitted. Numbered Steps: 1. FBP-Image-Guided Initialization: Compute the Filtered Backprojection (FBP) reconstruction I{FBP} from projection data P. Apply a threshold \tau to exclude void regions: \bar{I}{FBP}(X) = I{FBP}(X) \cdot \mathbb{I}[I{FBP}(X) > \tau], where \mathbb{I}[\cdot] is the indicator function. Compute the gradient magnitude \|\nabla \bar{I}{FBP}\| for all voxels. Rank voxels by gradient magnitude and select voxel coordinates Vi with medium gradient magnitude (avoiding high-gradient streaking artifacts) as initial Gaussian centers. For each center Cj, calculate the number of neighbors N(Cj, r) within a radius r. Initialize intensity tj proportional to the FBP intensity at Cj: tj = kt \bar{I}{FBP}(Cj), where kt is a coefficient. Initialize scaling \sigmaj based on neighbor density: \sigmaj = k\sigma \frac{1}{N(Cj, r)}, where k\sigma is a coefficient. Set initial scaling vector sj = [\sigmaj, \sigmaj, \sigmaj] (isotropic) and rotation quaternion qj = [1, 0, 0, 0] (identity). Normalize center coordinates \muj by dividing by the maximum range to map to [0,1]. Normalize intensity tj to [0,1]. 2. Differentiable CT Projector (Volumetric Rendering): Discretize the volume into a voxel grid. For a target point X in the volume, compute the contribution of all Gaussians i whose 3\sigma confidence interval contains X (i.e., \|X - \mui\| \le 3\sigmai). The intensity at point X is the sum of contributions: I(X | \{Gi\}) = \sum{i: \|X - \mui\| \le 3\sigmai} ti \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} (X - \mui)^T \Sigmai^{-1} (X - \mui) \right). Project the 3D volume onto 2D detector planes using the known CT geometry (source and detector positions) to generate rendered projections. 3. Two-Stage Optimization: Stage 1 (Low-Resolution): Sample a grid at 1/2 \times 1/2 \times 1/2 of the original volume resolution. Stage 2 (Full-Resolution): Sample the full voxel grid. Loss Function: Minimize discrepancy between rendered projections and ground truth projections using projection loss. Activation Functions: Apply sigmoid activation to intensity t to keep values in [0,1]. Apply exponential activation to scaling s to ensure positive values. Adaptive Density Control: During optimization, add or remove Gaussians based on view-space positional gradients and an opacity threshold. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def initializegaussians(projectiondata, thresholdtau, ksigma, kt, neighborradius): """ Step 1: FBP-image-guided Gaussian initialization. """ # FBP reconstruction (standard CT step) Ifbp = applystandardfbp(projectiondata) # Threshold to remove void mask = (Ifbp > thresholdtau).float() Ibarfbp = Ifbp mask # Compute gradients using finite differences gradx = torch.diff(Ibarfbp, dim=0, prepend=Ibarfbp[:1]) grady = torch.diff(Ibarfbp, dim=1, prepend=Ibarfbp[:,:1]) gradz = torch.diff(Ibarfbp, dim=2, prepend=Ibarfbp[:,:,:1]) gradmag = torch.sqrt(gradx2 + grady2 + gradz2) # Flatten and sort voxels by gradient magnitude flatgrad = gradmag.flatten() sortedindices = torch.argsort(flatgrad) # Select medium gradient voxels (percentiles 20-80) numvoxels = len(sortedindices) startidx = int(numvoxels 0.2) endidx = int(numvoxels 0.8) selectedflatindices = sortedindices[startidx:endidx] # Convert flat indices to 3D coordinates voxelcoords3d = torch.stack(torch.meshgrid( torch.arange(Ifbp.shape[0]), torch.arange(Ifbp.shape[1]), torch.arange(Ifbp.shape[2]), indexing='ij'), dim=-1).flatten(0, -2) centers = voxelcoords3d[selectedflatindices].float() # Normalize centers to [0, 1] maxrange = torch.max(centers, dim=0)[0] centersnormalized = centers / maxrange # Calculate neighbor count for each center to determine sigma dists = torch.cdist(centersnormalized, centersnormalized) neighborcounts = (dists <= neighborradius).sum(dim=1) sigmas = ksigma / neighborcounts scales = torch.stack([sigmas, sigmas, sigmas], dim=-1) # Isotropic rotations = torch.ones((len(centers), 4)) # Identity quaternion [1, 0, 0, 0] # Initialize intensity intensitiesraw = Ibarfbp[centers[:, 0].long(), centers[:, 1].long(), centers[:, 2].long()] intensities = kt intensitiesraw # Normalize intensity to [0, 1] maxintensity = torch.max(intensities) if maxintensity > 0: intensitiesnormalized = intensities / maxintensity else: intensitiesnormalized = intensities return { 'mu': centersnormalized, 's': scales, 'q': rotations, 't': intensitiesnormalized } def renderprojection(gaussians, cameraparams, volumegridshape): """ Step 2: Differentiable CT Projector (Volumetric Rendering). """ mu = gaussians['mu'] s = gaussians['s'] q = gaussians['q'] t = gaussians['t'] # Decompose covariance: Sigma = R S S^T R^T R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(q) S = torch.diagembed(s) Sigma = R @ S @ S.transpose(-2, -1) @ R.transpose(-2, -1) Sigmainv = torch.inverse(Sigma) # Create voxel grid coordinates gridcoords = torch.stack(torch.meshgrid( torch.arange(volumegridshape[0]), torch.arange(volumegridshape[1]), torch.arange(volumegridshape[2]), indexing='ij'), dim=-1).float() gridflat = gridcoords.view(-1, 3) # Initialize volume intensity volumeintensity = torch.zeros(gridflat.shape[0], device=mu.device) # Iterate over Gaussians for i in range(len(mu)): center = mu[i] covinv = Sigmainv[i] intensityval = t[i] diff = gridflat - center distsq = torch.sum(diff @ covinv diff, dim=1) sigmaval = s[i, 0] mask = torch.norm(diff, dim=1) <= (3.0 sigmaval) exponent = -0.5 distsq gaussianvals = torch.exp(exponent) volumeintensity[mask] += intensityval gaussianvals[mask] volume3d = volumeintensity.view(volumegridshape) # Project to 2D using CT geometry (standard differentiable ray-casting) projection = applydifferentiablectprojector(volume3d, cameraparams) return projection def optimize(gaussians, projectiondata, originalvolumeshape, numiterationsperstage, cameraparams): """ Step 3: Two-Stage Optimization. """ optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(gaussians.values(), lr=0.01) for stage in range(2): if stage == 0: gridshape = tuple(s // 2 for s in originalvolumeshape) else: gridshape = originalvolumeshape for iteration in range(numiterationsperstage): optimizer.zerograd() renderedproj = renderprojection(gaussians, cameraparams, gridshape) loss = torch.nn.functional.mseloss(renderedproj, projectiondata) loss.backward() optimizer.step() gaussians['t'] = torch.sigmoid(gaussians['t']) gaussians['s'] = torch.exp(gaussians['s']) gaussians = applyadaptivedensitycontrol(gaussians) return gaussians def applystandardfbp(projectiondata): # Standard Filtered Backprojection algorithm pass def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): # Converts quaternion [w, x, y, z] to 3x3 rotation matrix w, x, y, z = q[:, 0], q[:, 1], q[:, 2], q[:, 3] R = torch.zeros((q.shape[0], 3, 3), device=q.device) R[:, 0, 0] = 1 - 2 (y2 + z2) R[:, 0, 1] = 2 (xy - wz) R[:, 0, 2] = 2 (xz + wy) R[:, 1, 0] = 2 (xy + wz) R[:, 1, 1] = 1 - 2 (x2 + z2) R[:, 1, 2] = 2 (yz - wx) R[:, 2, 0] = 2 (xz - wy) R[:, 2, 1] = 2 (yz + wx) R[:, 2, 2] = 1 - 2 (x2 + y2) return R def applydifferentiablectprojector(volume3d, cameraparams): # Standard differentiable ray-casting / Siddons algorithm pass def applyadaptivedensitycontrol(gaussians): # Standard GS adaptive density control based on gradients pass Parameters: \tau: Threshold for FBP image void exclusion. Value not given in the sources. kt, k\sigma: Coefficients for intensity and scaling initialization. Value not given in the sources. r: Neighbor radius for density estimation. Value not given in the sources. Resolution: Original volume size (e.g., 256 \times 256 \times 256). Low-res stage uses 1/2 \times 1/2 \times 1/2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Affine Approximation Error: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting uses an affine approximation to project 3D Gaussians to 2D, which introduces errors unacceptable for precise CT value recovery. This method avoids this by using volumetric rendering. PyTorch Slicing Limitations: Standard PyTorch slicing requires patches of common size, which is inefficient for varying 3\sigma confidence intervals. A customized CUDA kernel is required for acceleration. Spectral Bias: Unlike INRs, this method does not suffer from spectral bias, allowing better reconstruction of sharp boundaries. Time Complexity: Faster than Instant-NGP/INR methods. The customized CUDA kernel achieves a 10x speedup and order-of-magnitude memory reduction compared to standard PyTorch slicing for Gaussian contributions. Memory Complexity: Reduced by an order of magnitude compared to naive PyTorch implementations due to the 3\sigma bounding box optimization. Performance: Outperforms state-of-the-art INR-based methods in reconstruction accuracy and convergence speed on diverse datasets (chest, abdomen, foot, jaw, head, vertebrae). Strengths: Precise CT value recovery (critical for dose calculation), real-time physical simulation capability, robustness to sparse-view artifacts, no spectral bias. Limitations: Requires a differentiable CT projector implementation; volumetric rendering is inherently slower than 2D splatting (mitigated by CUDA optimization). When to use: Sparse-view CT reconstruction where radiation dose must be minimized, and precise quantitative CT values are required for clinical applications. Origin: Proposed by Yingtai Li et al. in "3DGR-CT: Sparse-view CT reconstruction with a 3D Gaussian representation". History: Inspired by the success of 3D Gaussian Splatting in novel view synthesis (Kerbl et al., 2023). It addresses limitations of Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) in CT, such as spectral bias and high computational costs, and adapts 3D Gaussians for volumetric physics rather than 2D appearance. Usage: Sparse-view CT reconstruction, enabling real-time physical simulation, surgical planning, and personalized treatment strategies. 3DGR-CT: Sparse-view CT reconstruction with a 3D Gaussian representation, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.media.2025.103585, fetched 2026-10-26

name: AquaMass-GS
head: AM-GS
body: AquaMass-GS is a per-scene underwater rendering method that decouples object appearance from water transport by coupling a standard object-Gaussian scene model to a separate field of normalized free-space water Gaussians. It solves the entanglement of attenuation and backscatter with object appearance, and the inability to query water transport independently of object sampling, by using cell-volume weighting for optical mass semantics and analytic finite-path integration with coverage normalization. Unlike global or direction-conditioned predictors, it keeps water transport spatially queryable in free space, evaluating only the traversed finite segment from camera to visible surface. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Posed underwater images; Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud bounds; camera intrinsics/extrinsics. Outputs: Rendered underwater image; optimized object Gaussian set Go; optimized water Gaussian parameters. Data Structures: 1. Object Gaussians (Go): Standard 3DGS parameters: position \mu, covariance \Sigma (or rotation/scale), spherical harmonic coefficients cj, opacity \alpha. 2. Water Lattice Centers: Fixed on a face-centered-cubic (FCC) lattice. For N cells per axis, there are 4N^3 centers. Centers are located within the axis-aligned bounds of SfM points plus a fixed world-space margin. 3. Water Gaussian Parameters (Gw): Position \mui: Fixed to lattice centers. Covariance \Sigmai: Fixed, axis-aligned. Standard deviation s\Delta along each dimension. Typical value s = 1.3; initial layout s = 0.7. Densities: Two non-negative RGB density vectors per center, \rho{D,i} and \rho{B,i}, optimized during training. These represent direct extinction and backscatter attenuation, respectively. Steps: 1. Optimization: Jointly optimize Go and Gw from posed underwater images. Go follows standard 3DGS densification and parameter updates. Gw centers and covariances are fixed; only \rho{D,i} and \rho{B,i} are updated. 2. Object Query: Render the object branch Go to obtain a detached alpha-weighted surface endpoint (proxy depth) z^. 3. Ray Distance Conversion: Convert proxy depth z^ to ray distance t^ along the viewing ray. 4. Analytic Integration: Perform analytic finite-path integration over the ray segment [0, t^] to compute: Direct extinction optical depth \tauD Backscatter optical depth \tauB Unit-density coverage q 5. Coverage Normalization: Compute per-pixel equivalent coefficients for direct mass \betaD and backscatter mass \betaB: \betaD = \frac{\tauD}{q}, \quad \betaB = \frac{\tauB}{q} 6. Composition: Combine the object term (using \betaD) and the medium term (using \betaB and a direction-conditioned backscatter head B\infty(dp)) to form the final rendered image. Formulas: The normalized basis function for water Gaussian i is: \phii(x) = \frac{\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(x - \mui)^\top \Sigmai^{-1} (x - \mui)\right)}{(2\pi)^{3/2} |\Sigmai|^{1/2}} where \int{\mathbb{R}^3} \phii(x) dx = 1. Cell volume is \Delta V = \Delta x \Delta y \Delta z. Each lattice point is assigned volume Vi = \Delta V / 4. The optical mass for direct extinction and backscatter is: m{D,i} = Vi \cdot \text{softplus}(\rho{D,i}) m{B,i} = Vi \cdot \text{softplus}(\rho{B,i}) where \text{softplus}(x) = \ln(1 + e^x). The continuous optical fields are: \sigmaD(x) = \sumi m{D,i} \phii(x) \sigmaB(x) = \sumi m{B,i} \phii(x) [Source note: The source text cuts off after \sigmaB(x) = \dots but implies the same summation structure for backscatter]. Parameters: s\Delta: Water Gaussian standard deviation. Fixed. Typical value 1.3. N: Cells per axis. Determines lattice resolution (4N^3 centers). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometric Resizing: Position and covariance of water Gaussians are fixed to prevent transport mass from changing through geometric resizing. Boundary Conditions: The lattice is bounded by SfM points plus a fixed world-space margin. Queries outside this range may require handling (not specified in sources). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On four SeaThru-NeRF development scenes, AM-GS provides competitive end-to-end novel-view quality, with the highest mean PSNR and the lowest LPIPS among six compared methods. Strengths: Decouples water transport from object appearance; allows spatial querying of water independent of camera motion; handles finite path segments accurately. Limitations: Requires separate optimization for water field; fixed lattice may not adapt to complex underwater structures dynamically. When to use: Per-scene underwater rendering where accurate separation of object and water effects is critical. When not to use: Real-time applications requiring dynamic adaptation of water density; scenes without clear object-water boundaries. AquaMass-GS was proposed to address limitations in existing underwater rendering methods, which often entangle attenuation and backscatter with object appearance or use global/directional predictors that limit spatial queries. It builds on the WaterSplatting implementation for the object branch and direction encoding. The method introduces normalized free-space water Gaussians with cell-volume weighting to provide optical mass semantics. name: GS-Scale Host Offloading
head: host offloading, hybrid training
body: GS-Scale is a training framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces GPU memory usage by storing all Gaussian parameters and optimizer states in host (CPU) memory, transferring only a necessary subset to the GPU on demand for each forward and backward pass. It sets itself apart from GPU-Only training by preventing Out-of-Memory (OOM) errors on large scenes, and from naive host offloading by achieving significantly faster training speeds through system-level optimizations. Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, SH coefficients, opacity) and optimizer states stored in host memory; camera poses and image data. Outputs: Rendered images and gradients for optimization. Data Structures: Host Memory: Stores the full set of N Gaussians and their optimizer states. Each Gaussian i contains position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4, SH coefficients \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times K}, and opacity \alphai \in \mathbb{R}. Optimizer states (e.g., Adam momentum and variance) are stored identically to the parameters. Device Memory (GPU): Contains only the subset of Gaussians currently being processed for a specific view or split. Algorithm Steps: 1. Store all Gaussian parameters and optimizer states in host memory. 2. For each forward/backward pass, transfer only the necessary subset of Gaussians to the GPU. 3. If split mode is enabled, check if the current image's Gaussian count exceeds splitthreshold totalgaussians. 4. If the threshold is exceeded, split the image processing into smaller batches to further reduce peak GPU memory usage. Parameters: splitthreshold: A float controlling the split mode threshold. Default value is 0.3. If an image consumes more Gaussians than splitthreshold totalgaussians, the image is split to reduce GPU memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def train(): # 1. Store all parameters and optimizer states in host memory hostparams = loadgaussianparameters() # standard 3DGS initialization hostoptimizerstates = createoptimizerbuffers(hostparams) # standard optimizer setup totalgaussians = len(hostparams) splitthreshold = 0.3 splitmodeenabled = True # for camera, imagegt in trainingdata: # 2. Identify subset of Gaussians for current view relevantindices = selectvisiblegaussians(camera, hostparams) # standard frustum/distance culling numrelevant = len(relevantindices) # 3. Check split mode condition if splitmodeenabled and numrelevant > splitthreshold totalgaussians: # 4. Split processing to reduce GPU memory chunksize = max(1, numrelevant // 2) indiceschunks = [relevantindices[i:i + chunksize] for i in range(0, numrelevant, chunksize)] for chunk in indiceschunks: processchunk(chunk, camera, imagegt, hostparams, hostoptimizerstates) else: processchunk(relevantindices, camera, imagegt, hostparams, hostoptimizerstates) def processchunk(indices, camera, imagegt, hostparams, hostoptimizerstates): # Transfer subset to GPU deviceparams = hostparams[indices] deviceoptimizerstates = hostoptimizerstates[indices] # Forward pass: rasterize and render renderedimage = rasterize3dgaussians(deviceparams, camera) # standard differentiable rasterizer # Compute loss and gradients loss = computemseloss(renderedimage, imagegt) # standard loss function gradients = computegradients(loss, deviceparams) # standard autograd/backprop # Transfer gradients back to host and update updateoptimizerstates(hostoptimizerstates[indices], gradients) # standard optimizer step updateparams(hostparams[indices], gradients) # standard parameter update Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Out-of-Memory (OOM) errors can occur if GPU memory demand is too high; this is handled by the host offloading mechanism and optionally by split mode. Setting splitthreshold too low further reduces memory but may slow down training due to increased chunking overhead. Memory Reduction: Reduces GPU memory usage by 3.3-5.6x compared to GPU-Only systems, enabling training on consumer-grade GPUs. Performance: Slower than GPU-Only training for small scenes due to data transfer overhead, but significantly faster than naive host offloading. Scalability: Enables training on large-scale scenes that would otherwise cause OOM errors on standard GPUs. Split Mode: Further reduces memory usage at the cost of potential speed reduction if splitthreshold is set low. GS-Scale was introduced by SNU-ARC as a solution to the memory bottlenecks in large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting training. It builds on the principles of host offloading but incorporates system-level optimizations to mitigate the performance penalties typically associated with CPU-GPU data transfers. SNU-ARC/GS-Scale, https://github.com/SNU-ARC/GS-Scale, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: DeltaSplat
head: DeltaSplat refinement module, Iterative Gaussian Refinement
body: DeltaSplat is a lightweight, iterative refinement module for pose-free feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that corrects geometric and photometric errors introduced by single-pass prediction and camera estimation uncertainty. It distinguishes itself from prior residual refinement methods like DeSplat by conditioning per-Gaussian updates on per-pixel Plücker rays and rendered depth, providing a soft geometric prior that disambiguates 2D rendering residuals into reliable 3D corrections under uncalibrated or predicted camera poses. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of context images \{Ii\}{i \in C}, where C is the set of context view indices. Output: A refined set of 3D Gaussians G^{(K)} after K refinement iterations. Data Structures: The Gaussian set G consists of G = N{ctx}HW primitives, where N{ctx} is the number of context views, and H, W are image height and width. Each Gaussian g is defined by: \mug \in \mathbb{R}^3: Spatial mean (position). \alphag \in (0, 1): Opacity. qg \in S^3: Rotation (quaternion). sg \in \mathbb{R}^3+: Scale. c^{(0)}g \in \mathbb{R}^3: Degree-0 spherical harmonic coefficient (view-independent color). Parameters: K: Number of refinement iterations. Typical value: K=3. \lambda{lp}: Perceptual loss weight. Typical value: 0.1. The refinement module h\phi weights are shared across all K iterations. Parameter overhead: \sim 2.2\% of the backbone network parameters. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Fixed Shape: Scales sg and rotations qg remain fixed during refinement to preserve the local structure established by the backbone; only position, opacity, and color are updated. Geometric Conditioning: Omitting Plücker rays and depth causes positional updates |\Delta \mu| to become larger and more dispersed, degrading PSNR by \sim 1.37 dB. Iteration Count: Iterating beyond K=3 yields no further quality gains and increases latency linearly. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Pass context images \{Ii\}{i \in C} through the feed-forward backbone f\theta to obtain initial Gaussians G{ff} and predicted camera poses \{pi\}{i \in C}: G{ff}, \{pi\}{i \in C} = f\theta(\{Ii\}{i \in C}) Set the initial state for refinement: G^{(0)} = G{ff}. 2. Iterative Refinement (for k = 0 to K-1): a. Render: Render the current Gaussian set G^{(k)} at the predicted context camera poses \{pi\}{i \in C} using a differentiable rasterizer \mathcal{R} to produce rendered images \hat{I}^{(k)}i and rendered depths d^{(k)}i: \hat{I}^{(k)}i = \mathcal{R}(G^{(k)}; pi), \quad d^{(k)}i = \text{Depth}(\mathcal{R}(G^{(k)}; pi)) b. Compute Residual: Calculate the pixel-wise rendering residual r^{(k)}i between the input context image Ii and the rendered image \hat{I}^{(k)}i: r^{(k)}i = Ii - \hat{I}^{(k)}i c. Encode Geometry and Residual: Construct per-pixel Plücker ray maps \elli \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 6} from the camera poses pi. Encode the residual r^{(k)}i, rendered image \hat{I}^{(k)}i, rendered depth d^{(k)}i, and Plücker rays \elli using a dual-branch convolutional mixer E to produce fused features F. The dual-branch design gathers broad structural context at coarse resolutions before full-resolution processing. d. Decode Updates: Decode the fused features F using per-attribute MLP heads to predict the update \Delta^{(k)}g \in \mathbb{R}^7 for each Gaussian g \in G^{(k)}: \Delta^{(k)}g = (\Delta \mug, \Delta \alphag, \Delta c^{(0)}g) = \text{Decode}(F, g) where \Delta \mug \in \mathbb{R}^3, \Delta \alphag \in \mathbb{R}, and \Delta c^{(0)}g \in \mathbb{R}^3. e. Update Gaussians: Apply the predicted updates to the current Gaussian state: G^{(k+1)} = G^{(k)} \oplus \Delta^{(k)} Specifically: \mu^{(k+1)}g = \mu^{(k)}g + \Delta \mug \alpha^{(k+1)}g = \alpha^{(k)}g + \Delta \alphag c^{(0)(k+1)}g = c^{(0)(k)}g + \Delta c^{(0)}g q^{(k+1)}g = q^{(k)}g, \quad s^{(k+1)}g = s^{(k)}g 3. Final Output: Return the refined Gaussian set G^{(K)}. Training Objective: The model is trained end-to-end by unrolling K iterations. The loss combines pixel-wise mean squared error and a perceptual loss (VGG backbone) over all rendered views (context and target): \mathcal{L} = \sum{i \in C \cup T} \|\hat{I}^{(K)}i - Ii\|2^2 + \lambda{lp} \mathcal{L}{\text{LPIPS}}(\hat{I}^{(K)}i, Ii) Training runs with K=3. Time Complexity: Refinement time grows linearly with K. On tested hardware, latency increases from 54 ms (K=0) to 266 ms (K=6). Memory Complexity: Adds \sim 2.2\% parameters to the backbone. Performance: On the DL3DV dataset (6 context views, pose-free, known intrinsics), DeltaSplat achieves 26.64 dB PSNR, 0.862 SSIM, and 0.115 LPIPS, improving the YoNoSplat backbone by 1.75 dB. Strengths: Effective at correcting camera estimation errors; lightweight; fully feed-forward at inference. Limitations: Performance degrades if geometric conditioning (Plücker rays/depth) is removed; quality peaks at K=3 and does not improve with more iterations. When to use: Pose-free or uncalibrated camera regimes where single-pass prediction errors are significant. When not to use: When ground-truth camera poses are available and high accuracy is required without the overhead of iterative refinement (though DeltaSplat still provides gains). DeltaSplat was introduced to address the limitations of pose-free feed-forward 3DGS methods, where camera estimation errors propagate into the Gaussian representation. It builds on the concept of iterative residual refinement seen in methods like DeSplat but adapts it for the pose-free setting by introducing geometric conditioning via Plücker rays and rendered depth. The method was evaluated on DL3DV, ScanNet++, and RE10K datasets. DeltaSplat: Iterative Gaussian Refinement for Pose-Free Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09853, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Rendering Implementation and Acceleration
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipeline, 3DGS Rasterization
body: Rendering Implementation and Acceleration defines the core computational pipeline for projecting a set of N 3D Gaussian primitives \{Gi\}{i=1}^N onto a 2D image plane and accumulating their contributions via alpha blending. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering millions of anisotropic, view-dependent splats in real-time by leveraging GPU parallelism through tiling, sorting, and culling. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Data Compression and Storage Optimization by focusing on runtime execution speed rather than data size, and from Occupancy Region Derivation & ϵ-Intersection Criterion by using standard bounding-box culling rather than shape-aware elliptic intersection tests. All methods in this family operate on the set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N defined in Rendering Implementation and Acceleration. The core rendering operation involves projecting these 3D primitives to 2D screen space and performing alpha blending. Acceleration relies on the following shared mechanisms: 1. Tiling: Dividing the image plane into non-overlapping tiles (commonly 16 \times 16 pixels) to localize Gaussian processing and enable coalesced memory accesses. 2. Sorting: Sorting Gaussians within each tile by view-space depth (front-to-back) to enable correct alpha blending. 3. Culling: Discarding Gaussians that do not overlap with the camera frustum or specific tiles to reduce enumeration overhead. 4. Memory Hierarchy Management: Exploiting the distinction between global memory (VRAM), shared memory (on-chip), and host memory (CPU RAM) to minimize data movement. This family reduces the storage footprint and transmission bandwidth of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models by compressing geometric attributes (position, scale, rotation), opacity, and view-dependent color (Spherical Harmonics coefficients). It solves the bottleneck of large model sizes (often hundreds of MBs) which hinders deployment on mobile devices or web platforms. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Hardware and Computational Acceleration by focusing on data representation size rather than rendering speed, and from Occupancy Region Derivation & ϵ-Intersection Criterion by explicitly quantizing or clustering attributes rather than just culling. Hardware and Computational Acceleration encompasses the system-level and algorithmic optimizations required to render and train 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) efficiently on modern GPU architectures. It solves the bottlenecks of memory bandwidth, sorting latency, and GPU memory capacity that arise when processing scenes with tens of millions of primitives. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on system-level distribution (sharding across nodes), hardware-specific kernel design (Tensor Cores, Roofline optimization), and memory hierarchy management (CPU-GPU offloading) rather than just intra-GPU rasterization logic like tiling or sorting. This method defines a robust geometric intersection test between 3D Gaussian splats by deriving an elliptic occupancy region \Omegai from the Gaussian kernel's covariance and opacity, rather than relying on strict binary overlap of infinite support. It solves the problem of robustly determining whether two splats Gi and Gj interact for culling or sorting purposes, avoiding false negatives from minor misalignments or numerical precision issues. It differs from standard bounding-box culling by using a shape-aware elliptic boundary and an \epsilon-tolerance for contact detection, providing a balance between geometric accuracy and computational efficiency. Gaussian Piling is a slice-based volumetric reconstruction method that unifies 3D Gaussian Splatting with an imaging system-aware focus model to compress aggressively while preserving internal structure. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which discards internal volumetric information and produces incoherent 3D structures with floating artifacts for slice-based modalities, Gaussian Piling models the finite focal zone to preserve high-frequency internal volumetric detail. It achieves this by enforcing 3D-to-2D consistency through axial re-parameterization and opacity modulation, preventing ghosting artifacts across slices. Parallel Differentiable Rasterization is a rendering method that jointly produces High Dynamic Range (HDR) and Low Dynamic Range (LDR) images from a set of 3D Gaussians using two parallel rasterization pipelines, F{HDR} and F{LDR}. It solves the problem of simultaneous HDR/LDR view synthesis by decoupling the color representation (HDR vs. LDR) while sharing the geometric projection and alpha-blending logic. It differs from standard differentiable rasterization by explicitly maintaining two distinct color streams for the same geometric primitives to handle wide dynamic range scenes without tone-mapping artifacts during training. Local-GS is a warp-coherent rendering paradigm that restructures alpha computation and reorganizes work around SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads) execution boundaries to reduce warp divergence and redundant computation in 3D Gaussian Splatting. Unlike methods that focus on macroscopic scene culling or data compression, Local-GS operates as a pure kernel-level optimization that shifts focus to microscopic GPU execution boundaries, mitigating intra-block computational overhead. It achieves this by enforcing tile-local execution through three stages: parameter hoisting, warp-level culling, and coherent blending. CoherentRaster is a real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) rendering framework optimized for Light Field Displays (LFDs). It solves the computational bottleneck of dense multi-view synthesis by leveraging subpixel-level rasterization to eliminate redundant computations across adjacent viewpoints and resolve uncoalesced memory access patterns inherent to subpixel rendering. Unlike Subpixel-3DGS, which suffers from redundant cross-view computation and irregular memory access, or MPI-based frameworks, which scale poorly with resolution due to depth plane traversal, CoherentRaster achieves real-time performance on high-resolution scenes by exploiting view coherence. A technique to approximate the influence range of a 3D Gaussian on a slice by using a 2D ellipse splat scaled by the marginal factor, which closely matches the true iso-probability contours. Qualitative validation shows that the conditional splat approximation (dashed red contours) closely overlaps with the true 3D Gaussian iso-probability contours (solid blue contours). The conditional splat provides an accurate and efficient approximation of the original 3D Gaussian’s influence range. A pre-rasterization optimization that skips spatially contiguous blocks of Gaussians before projection and preprocessing, reducing enumeration, sorting, and downstream rasterization overhead. At export time, reorder the Gaussian model by Morton code and cut it into fixed-size contiguous memory blocks. For each block, precompute an axis-aligned bounding box that contains the full \tau0-support of every Gaussian it holds, inflated by a safety factor. Pass surviving blocks to the rasterizer as contiguous ranges; Gaussians in rejected blocks are never read, incurring zero cost in projection, prefix scan, or duplication. \tau0: The finite-support radius used by the backbone's Gaussian culling predicate. Gaussians are stored in contiguous memory blocks ordered by Morton code. Each block has a precomputed AABB. Rejected blocks are passed to the rasterizer as contiguous ranges to be skipped. Conservative culling may skip visible Gaussians if their support extends beyond the inflated block box. Handled by inflating the box with a safety factor to guarantee bit-exactness. Evaluated across 52 runs; images produced are bit-identical to the unmodified backbone. A forward rendering process for slice-based volumetric reconstruction that converts 3D Gaussian primitives into 2D images by convolving the Gaussian with a reversed sensitivity map (PSF) along the axial direction, resulting in a 'focus Gaussian' that accounts for depth-of-field effects. Represent each primitive as an anisotropic 3D Gaussian with parameters G = (\mu, s, q, \alpha), where \mu is position, s is scale, q is orientation quaternion, and \alpha is opacity. Convert scale s and orientation q into a 3D covariance matrix \Sigma in world coordinates: S = \text{diag}(\text{mod} \cdot s), R = \text{quatToMatrix}(q), \Sigma = R S S^\top R^\top. Extract the 2D components from the focus Gaussian: \Sigma{2d} is the top-left 2x2 block of \Sigmae, and \mu{2d} = [\mue[0], \mue[1]]^\top. \delta: Depth offset in Eq. (2) and (3). Set \delta = \sum{k=1}^D s^k for each Gaussian, where D is dimension of scaling and s^k is the k-th axis length of scaling \mathbf{s}. This allows \delta to vary adaptively to geometric granularity. Optimization renderer: Pytorch framework, per-pixel rendering (GPU thread per pixel querying surfels and Gaussians). Post-optimization renderer: OpenGL, per-primitive rendering (GPU thread per fragment of primitives querying covered pixels). Uses 4x MSAA instead of 4x supersampling. Two rendering passes: 1. Depth testing/writing enabled, blending disabled. Geometry shader generates surfels from points, renders surfel color map and depth map. Multisampling textures resolved. Depth map modified by offset \delta via post-processing shader. 2. Depth testing and additive blending enabled, depth writing disabled. Geometry shader generates 3D Gaussians from points, splats 3D Gaussians to obtain \mathbf{C} and \mathbf{D}. Final image computed using Eq. (5) via post-processing shader. Depth offset \delta impact: If too large, 3D Gaussians occluded by surface leak out. If too small, 3D Gaussians close to surface are wrongly truncated. The rendering pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. in "A Real-Time Cyclic Rendering of 3D Gaussian Splatting" (2023). It builds on the foundational work of 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method has since been adapted for various specialized domains including slice-based volumetric reconstruction, light field displays, and high-fidelity radiance field rendering.
