name: Data Compression and Storage Optimization
head: 3DGS Compression, Gaussian Quantization, Codebook-Based Compression
body: This family reduces the storage footprint and transmission bandwidth of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models by compressing geometric attributes (position, scale, rotation), opacity, and view-dependent color (Spherical Harmonics coefficients). It solves the bottleneck of large model sizes (often hundreds of MBs) which hinders deployment on mobile devices or web platforms. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Hardware and Computational Acceleration by focusing on data representation size rather than rendering speed, and from Occupancy Region Derivation & ϵ-Intersection Criterion by explicitly quantizing or clustering attributes rather than just culling. All methods in this family operate on the set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N defined in Rendering Implementation and Acceleration. The core rendering operation involves projecting these 3D primitives to 2D screen space and performing alpha blending. Acceleration relies on the following shared mechanisms: 1. Tiling: Dividing the image plane into non-overlapping tiles (commonly 16 \times 16 pixels) to localize Gaussian processing and enable coalesced memory accesses. 2. Sorting: Sorting Gaussians within each tile by view-space depth (front-to-back) to enable correct alpha blending. 3. Culling: Discarding Gaussians that do not overlap with the camera frustum or specific tiles to reduce enumeration overhead. 4. Memory Hierarchy Management: Exploiting the distinction between global memory (VRAM), shared memory (on-chip), and host memory (CPU RAM) to minimize data movement. This method accelerates data transmission during training by compressing numerical attributes into ASCII strings. It solves the bottleneck of transmitting large volumes of floating-point and integer data between processing units or across networks by reducing the byte count per value. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Sensitivity-Aware Vector Clustering and Compact 3D Gaussian Representation (C3DGS) by its focus on transmission speed via character-level encoding rather than geometric quantization or structural simplification. Sensitivity-Aware Vector Clustering is a compression scheme for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces storage requirements by clustering Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients and Gaussian shape parameters (scale and rotation) into compact codebooks using sensitivity-aware vector quantization. It distinguishes itself from standard post-training quantization by deriving a sensitivity measure for each scene parameter to guide the clustering process, prioritizing the preservation of parameters that significantly affect image quality. Compact 3D Gaussian Representation (C3DGS) is a compression framework that reduces the storage and computational cost of 3D Gaussian Splatting by pruning redundant Gaussians and compressing their attributes via spatial redundancy exploitation. It achieves over 25× storage reduction and faster rendering compared to standard 3DGS by replacing per-Gaussian color storage with a grid-based neural field and quantizing geometric attributes into a codebook. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on global significance scoring or 2D grid sorting, C3DGS specifically targets the spatial correlation of color and the geometric similarity of scales/rotations to minimize memory footprint. The Monte Carlo Specular Energy Aggregator (MC-SEA) is a compression technique that maps high-order (e.g., third-order) Spherical Harmonics (SH) radiance energy into a compact lower-order (e.g., first-order) subspace without pre-training or distillation. It preserves specular features by extracting directional moments of the specular residual via Monte Carlo projection, preserving magnitude and spatial direction without pretraining or distillation. Unlike Mobile-GS which uses distillation from a high-order teacher model, Flux-GS compresses energy directly without costly distillation or pre-training. A compression method that utilizes vector clustering to encode color and geometric attributes. Reduces storage footprint of 3DGS scenes by quantizing per-Gaussian attributes and using codebooks, achieving ~10x smaller sizes without significant quality loss. Per-Gaussian attribute storage: position (FP16), scales (FP16), opacity (INT8), spherical harmonic coefficients (INT8 or codebook-based). The need for compression in 3DGS arises from the large number of Gaussians required for high-fidelity novel view synthesis, leading to model sizes that are impractical for many applications. Early work focused on pruning and quantization. C3DGS introduced grid-based color representation and geometric codebooks. Sensitivity-aware methods were developed to prevent quality degradation during quantization by identifying critical parameters. MC-SEA addressed the inefficiency of high-order SH for specular highlights by aggregating energy into lower-order representations. Recent surveys highlight various techniques including VQ-NeRF, LightGaussian, and CompGS as part of the broader effort to make 3DGS production-ready. name: ASCII-Based Data Compression
head: Anywhere Compression, Base 94 Floating-Point Compression, Base 95 Integer Compression
body: This method accelerates data transmission during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting models by compressing floating-point and integer values into ASCII strings. It differs from sibling methods like Sensitivity-Aware Vector Clustering and Compact 3D Gaussian Representation (C3DGS) by operating on the serialization layer rather than the geometric representation or clustering logic, specifically targeting the bottleneck of transferring model parameters between devices or processes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Floating-point numbers (e.g., Gaussian parameters) and integer numbers (e.g., indices or counts) intended for data transmission. Output: ASCII-encoded strings representing the compressed values. Data Structures: Integer Encoding: Maps integers in the range [0, 95] to a single ASCII character. Floating-Point Encoding: Maps the integer component to a single ASCII character in the range [0, 94] and uses a delimiter to separate the fractional part. Steps: 1. Integer Compression (Base 95): Select ASCII characters with codes 32 to 126. Map each integer value v \in [0, 95] to the character at index v within this range. Result: A single character representing the integer. 2. Floating-Point Compression (Base 94): Select ASCII characters with codes 32 to 125 for the integer component. Select ASCII character 126 (~) as the delimiter connecting the integer and fractional parts. Encode the integer part I of the floating-point number using the Base 94 mapping. Encode the decimal places d (number of decimal digits) as a separate integer or string component. Note: The source describes splitting the string into integer part I and decimal places d, then calculating f = I \times 10^{-d}. 3. Decoding: Integer: Convert the ASCII character directly back to the decimal integer. Floating-Point: Split the ASCII string at the delimiter (ASCII 126). Let the left part be the integer component I and the right part represent the decimal precision d. Calculate the final value f using the formula: f = I \times 10^{-d} 4. Color Matrix Optimization: The color matrix values are constrained to the range [0.0, 2.0] with only one decimal place. This reduces the possible values to 21 alternatives (0.0, 0.1, \dots, 2.0). These values are compressed using the ASCII compression algorithm to significantly reduce data size. Parameters: Integer Base: 95 (ASCII 32–126). Floating-Point Integer Base: 94 (ASCII 32–125). Delimiter: ASCII 126 (~). Color Precision: 1 decimal place. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Matrix Traversal Overhead: Compressing large color matrices via ASCII string conversion is computationally expensive due to the traversal time required. Using PyTorch internal functions like torch::where and torch::indexselect to replace explicit loops improves speed but is not fast enough to fully replace standard transmission methods. Line Breaks: Using line break characters in ASCII strings adds extra operators during writing and decoding, increasing overhead. Densification: Adjusting the densifyandprune process, specifically removing densifyandsplit operations where appropriate, can improve speed without impacting rendering quality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compressintegerbase95(value: int) -> str: """ Compress an integer in range [0, 95] to a single ASCII character. ASCII 32 maps to 0, ASCII 126 maps to 95. """ if not (0 <= value <= 95): raise ValueError("Integer out of range [0, 95]") # ASCII 32 is the start of the range return chr(value + 32) def decompressintegerbase95(char: str) -> int: """ Decompress a single ASCII character back to an integer. """ code = ord(char) if not (32 <= code <= 126): raise ValueError("Invalid ASCII character for integer compression") return code - 32 def compressfloatbase94(value: float) -> str: """ Compress a floating-point number. Integer part is encoded in Base 94 (ASCII 32-125). Delimiter is ASCII 126 (~). Fractional part is handled by specifying decimal places d. Formula: f = I 10^-d """ # Determine decimal places d to preserve precision # Note: The source implies d is the number of decimal places. # For simplicity in this implementation, we assume a fixed precision or # derive d from the input string representation if needed. # Here we assume the caller provides the precision or we round to 1 decimal. # Extract integer part I I = int(value) # Determine d (decimal places). # If value is 1.5, I=1, d=1. f = 1 10^-1 = 0.1? # Wait, the source says f = I 10^-d. # If I=1 and d=1, f=0.1. name: Sensitivity-Aware Vector Clustering
head: Niedemayr et al. compression, Niedermayr, Sensitivity-Aware Scene Compression, Sensitivity-Aware Vector Clustering for 3DGS Compression, Sensitivity-aware k-Means
body: Sensitivity-Aware Vector Clustering is a compression scheme for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces storage requirements by clustering spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients and Gaussian shape parameters (scale and rotation) into compact codebooks using sensitivity-aware vector quantization. It distinguishes itself from post-training quantization methods by deriving a sensitivity measure for each scene parameter to guide the clustering process, prioritizing the preservation of parameters that significantly affect image quality. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of optimized 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N with positions, opacities, scales, rotations, and SH coefficients for color, along with a set of training images and their camera parameters. Output: Two codebooks (one for SH coefficients, one for shape parameters) and a compressed representation of the scene where each Gaussian is defined by indices into these codebooks, alongside uncompressed position, opacity, and other attributes. Data Structures: Codebook Entry (Shape): 4 scalar values for a quaternion (rotation) plus 3 scalar values for scaling. Codebook Entry (Color): SH coefficients (e.g., 48 coefficients for degree 3). Indices: 32-bit unsigned integers storing the index into the respective codebook for each Gaussian. Sensitivity Calculation: The sensitivity S(p) of a parameter p is calculated based on its contribution to the training images. The total image energy E is the sum of RGB components over all pixels in all training images. The sensitivity is defined as: S(p) = \frac{\sum{i=1}^{N} \frac{\partial Ei}{\partial pi}}{\sum{i=1}^{N} Pi} where N is the number of training images, Pi is the number of pixels in image i, and Ei is the energy contribution of image i. The gradient \frac{\partial Ei}{\partial pi} is computed via a single backward pass over each training image. For a vector x with components xd, the sensitivity is the maximum over its component sensitivities: S(x) = \maxd S(xd) Clustering Algorithm: The method uses two separate codebooks: one for SH coefficients (color) and one for Gaussian shape features (scale and rotation). 1. Initialization: Codebooks are initialized randomly with a uniform distribution within the minimum and maximum values of each parameter. The codebook size K is typically 4096. 2. Sensitivity Thresholding: SH vectors (and shape vectors, if a separate threshold \betag is used) with sensitivity higher than a threshold \betac are identified. These high-sensitivity vectors are not clustered but are added directly to the codebook after the clustering process to preserve critical details. Typical value for \betac is 6 \cdot 10^{-7}. 3. Weighted Distance: For the remaining vectors, the distance between a vector x and a centroid ck is weighted by the sensitivity of x: D(x, ck) = S(x) \|x - ck\|2^2 4. Assignment: Each vector is assigned to the centroid with the minimum weighted distance. 5. Centroid Update: The centroid ck is updated using the weighted average of the assigned vectors A(k): ck = \frac{1}{\sum{xi \in A(k)} S(xi)} \sum{xi \in A(k)} S(xi) xi 6. Batched Clustering: To handle large datasets, a batched strategy is used. In each update step, a random subset of vectors is picked. Centroids are updated using a moving average with a decay factor \lambdad (typical value 0.8). Batch size for color features: 2^{18}. Batch size for Gaussian parameters: 2^{20}. 7. Normalization: Clustering normalized covariance matrices can lead to non-unit scaling vectors due to floating-point errors. Each codebook vector is re-normalized after each update step by dividing it through the trace of the covariance metric. 8. Decomposition: After clustering, each codebook entry for shape is decomposed into rotation (quaternion) and scale parameters using eigenvalue decomposition, as direct optimization of the matrix is not possible. Quantization-Aware Training: To recover information lost during clustering, parameters are fine-tuned on the training set using quantization-aware training. Forward Pass: Quantization is simulated considering a certain number of bits and the moving average of each parameter's min/max values (Min-Max Quantization). Backward Pass: The simulated quantization is ignored, and the gradient is calculated for the parameter without quantization. Optimization: Typically 5000 optimization steps are performed. The D-SSIM loss weight \lambda is typically 0.2. Compression and Encoding: 1. Linearization: Gaussians are ordered by their positions along a Z-order curve (Morton order) to exploit spatial coherence. 2. Entropy Encoding: The set of Gaussians and codebooks are compressed using DEFLATE (LZ77 + Huffman coding). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computesensitivity(groundtruthimages, renderedimages, parameters): """ Compute sensitivity S(p) for each parameter p. E is the sum of RGB components. """ # Calculate total image energy E for each training image # Ei = sum(RGB components of image i) energies = [np.sum(img) for img in groundtruthimages] # Compute gradients of energy with respect to parameters # This requires a backward pass through the differentiable renderer gradients = computegradients(groundtruthimages, renderedimages, parameters) # Sum of gradients and normalization factors sumgradients = np.sum(gradients, axis=0) # Sum over images sumpixels = np.sum([img.size for img in groundtruthimages]) # Sum of pixels Pi # Sensitivity S(p) sensitivity = sumgradients / sumpixels return sensitivity def sensitivityawarekmeans(vectors, sensitivities, k, decayfactor=0.8, batchsize=218): """ Perform sensitivity-aware k-Means clustering. """ # Initialize centroids randomly within min/max of vectors centroids = np.random.uniform(vectors.min(), vectors.max(), (k, vectors.shape[1])) numupdates = 800 # For Gaussians, 100 for SH for step in range(numupdates): # Pick random subset (batch) indices = np.random.choice(len(vectors), size=batchsize, replace=False) batchvectors = vectors[indices] batchsensitivities = sensitivities[indices] # Compute weighted distances # D(x, ck) = S(x) ||x - ck||^2 distances = np.zeros((len(batchvectors), k)) for j in range(k): diff = batchvectors - centroids[j] distances[:, j] = batchsensitivities np.sum(diff2, axis=1) # Assign to nearest centroid assignments = np.argmin(distances, axis=1) # Update centroids using moving average newcentroids = np.zeroslike(centroids) for j in range(k): clustervectors = batchvectors[assignments == j] clustersensitivities = batchsensitivities[assignments == j] if len(clustervectors) > 0: # Weighted average totalweight = np.sum(clustersensitivities) weightedsum = np.sum(clustervectors clustersensitivities[:, np.newaxis], axis=0) newcentroid = weightedsum / totalweight # Moving average update centroids[j] = decayfactor centroids[j] + (1 - decayfactor) newcentroid else: # Keep old centroid if no vectors assigned newcentroids[j] = centroids[j] centroids = newcentroids # Re-normalize shape codebook entries if necessary # Divide by trace of covariance metric to counteract floating point errors centroids = renormalizeshapecentroids(centroids) return centroids def compressscene(gaussians, shcodebook, shapecodebook, betac=6e-7): """ Compress the 3D Gaussian scene. """ # 1. Calculate sensitivities for SH coefficients and shape parameters shsensitivities = computesensitivityforsh(gaussians.shcoeffs) shapesensitivities = computesensitivityforshape(gaussians.shapeparams) # 2. Identify high-sensitivity vectors highsensshindices = np.where(shsensitivities > betac)[0] highsensshapeindices = np.where(shapesensitivities > betac)[0] # betag typically 3e-6 # 3. Cluster remaining vectors remainingsh = np.delete(gaussians.shcoeffs, highsensshindices, axis=0) remainingshape = np.delete(gaussians.shapeparams, highsensshapeindices, axis=0) shcentroids = sensitivityawarekmeans(remainingsh, shsensitivities[~(shsensitivities > betac)], k=4096) shapecentroids = sensitivityawarekmeans(remainingshape, shapesensitivities[~(shapesensitivities > betac)], k=4096) # 4. Add high-sensitivity vectors to codebooks finalshcodebook = np.vstack([shcentroids, gaussians.shcoeffs[highsensshindices]]) finalshapecodebook = np.vstack([shapecentroids, gaussians.shapeparams[highsensshapeindices]]) # 5. Decompose shape codebook entries into quaternion and scale finalshapecodebook = decomposeshapecodebook(finalshapecodebook) # 6. Assign indices to each Gaussian # Find nearest centroid for each Gaussian's SH and shape params shindices = findnearestcentroidindices(gaussians.shcoeffs, finalshcodebook) shapeindices = findnearestcentroidindices(gaussians.shapeparams, finalshapecodebook) # 7. Linearize Gaussians by Morton order sortedindices = getmortonorder(gaussians.positions) # 8. Compress using DEFLATE compresseddata = deflateencode(sortedindices, shindices, shapeindices, finalshcodebook, finalshapecodebook) return compresseddata Compression Ratio: Achieves up to 31× compression on real-world scenes with minimal visual degradation. Rendering Speed: Enables real-time rendering on lightweight GPUs, up to 4× higher framerates than optimized GPU compute pipelines for uncompressed scenes. Memory: Significantly reduces VRAM usage by replacing high-dimensional SH coefficients and shape matrices with small integer indices and compact codebooks. Strengths: Preserves visual quality better than uniform quantization by focusing on sensitive parameters; efficient hardware rasterization support. Limitations: Requires an initial training phase to compute sensitivities and perform quantization-aware fine-tuning; batched clustering may introduce approximation errors if batch sizes are too small. Sensitivity-Aware Vector Clustering was proposed by Niedemayr et al. in 2024. It builds on the observation that 3D Gaussian splatting representations contain significant redundancy in SH coefficients and shape parameters. The method draws inspiration from volumetric radiance field compression and deep network weight quantization. It is designed to make 3D Gaussian representations suitable for network streaming and rendering on low-power devices. name: Compact 3D Gaussian Representation (C3DGS)
head: Compact3DGS, Compact 3D Gaussian Representation for Radiance Field
body: Compact 3D Gaussian Representation (C3DGS) is a method for compressing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes by reducing the number of Gaussian primitives and compacting their attributes, addressing the high memory and storage costs of unbounded scenes. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by exploiting spatial redundancy: instead of storing per-Gaussian attributes, it uses a grid-based neural field for view-dependent color and a codebook for geometric attributes, combined with a learnable volume-based mask to prune redundant Gaussians. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on global significance scoring or vector clustering, C3DGS explicitly regularizes Gaussian volume via binary masks during training to iteratively eliminate non-essential primitives. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N initialized from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points, along with camera poses and training images. Output: A compact representation consisting of: 1. A reduced set of active Gaussians defined by position, a binary mask, and codebook indices. 2. A hash-based grid neural field for color. 3. A geometric codebook. 4. (Optional) Quantized and entropy-coded bitstream for final storage. Data Structures: 1. Gaussian Attributes: position: 3D vector (x, y, z). mask: Binary scalar mi \in \{0, 1\}. If mi=0, the Gaussian is pruned. colorcodeidx: Integer index into the color grid (implicit via position query). geocodeidx: Integer index into the geometric codebook. 2. Color Representation: grid: Hash-based multi-resolution grid (Instant-NGP style) mapping 3D coordinates to feature vectors. The grid stores features that are decoded into spherical harmonics coefficients or directly into RGB values. 3. Geometric Codebook: codebook: A small lookup table of size K containing learned scale and rotation parameters. Each Gaussian stores only an index ci \in \{1, \dots, K\}. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from SfM points with standard 3DGS attributes (position, opacity, scale, rotation, spherical harmonics coefficients). Initialize the hash grid and geometric codebook. 2. Volume-Based Masking (Pruning): Introduce a learnable binary mask mi for each Gaussian i. Define a volume metric Vi based on the Gaussian's opacity \alphai and scale (covariance determinant). Gaussians with low contribution to the scene reconstruction are identified. During training, optimize the masks such that mi \to 0 for redundant Gaussians. The rendering loss includes a regularization term on the mask to encourage sparsity. Pitfall: Aggressive pruning can remove high-frequency details. The mask optimization must be balanced with the reconstruction loss. 3. Color Attribute Compression: Replace per-Gaussian spherical harmonics coefficients with a query to the hash grid. For a Gaussian at position \mathbf{p}, query the grid to obtain a feature vector. Decode this feature vector into view-dependent color (RGB) or lower-degree spherical harmonics coefficients. This exploits spatial redundancy where neighboring Gaussians share similar colors. Parameter: Use a hash-based grid representation (Instant-NGP) for compactness and fast processing. 4. Geometric Attribute Compression: Replace per-Gaussian scale and rotation parameters with codebook indices. Cluster similar geometric patterns (scale/rotation combinations) across the scene. Store only the index ci for each Gaussian. Retrieve scale and rotation from the codebook at index ci during rendering. Note: The codebook size K is kept small to minimize overhead. 5. Training: Optimize positions, masks, grid parameters, and codebook entries jointly using differentiable rendering. The loss function typically includes photometric loss (L1 or SSIM) and mask regularization. 6. Post-Processing (Optional): Apply quantization to the remaining parameters (positions, codebook indices, grid features). Apply entropy coding to the quantized data for final storage compression. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def querycolorgrid(grid, position): """ Query the hash-based grid for color features at a given 3D position. Returns: RGB color or SH coefficients. """ # Implementation details of Instant-NGP hash grid query # 1. Hash position to grid indices # 2. Trilinear interpolation of features # 3. Decode to color pass def getgeometryfromcodebook(codebook, index): """ Retrieve scale and rotation from the geometric codebook. """ return codebook[index] def rendergaussian(gaussian, camera, grid, codebook): """ Render a single Gaussian primitive. """ # 1. Check if Gaussian is active if gaussian.mask == 0: return None # 2. Retrieve attributes position = gaussian.position # Color is not stored per Gaussian, but queried color = querycolorgrid(grid, position) # Geometry is retrieved from codebook geoindex = gaussian.geocodeidx scale, rotation = getgeometryfromcodebook(codebook, geoindex) # 3. Project to 2D and splat (standard 3DGS splatting logic) #... (standard projection and alpha blending)... return splat def trainstep(gaussians, images, grid, codebook, optimizer): """ One step of training. """ optimizer.zerograd() renderedimage = renderscene(gaussians, camera, grid, codebook) # Compute photometric loss loss = photometricloss(renderedimage, images) # Add mask regularization to encourage pruning maskloss = lambda gaussians: sum(g.mask for g in gaussians) loss += regularizationweight maskloss(gaussians) loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Update codebook and grid parameters #... (standard gradient descent updates)... Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Hash grid collisions may affect color accuracy. Use sufficient grid resolution. Boundaries: Pruning near object boundaries may cause artifacts. The mask regularization should be tuned to preserve boundary Gaussians. Degenerate Input: If the scene has very low redundancy, the codebook may not compress well. The method assumes spatial redundancy in color and geometric similarity in scale/rotation. OMG extends C3DGS by retaining per-Gaussian parameterization for geometry to handle sparsity better, while using a small neural field and Sub-Vector Quantization (SVQ) for appearance. It achieves higher compression (>300×) by addressing C3DGS's weakness in sparse settings where neural fields struggle due to larger distances between Gaussians. Time Complexity: Rendering speed is linearly proportional to the number of active Gaussians. Since C3DGS prunes redundant Gaussians, rendering is faster than standard 3DGS. Memory Complexity: Storage is significantly reduced. C3DGS achieves ~15× reduced storage on average and up to 28× on the Deep Blending dataset compared to 3DGS. With post-processing (quantization and entropy coding), compression exceeds 25×. Measured Performance: On the Deep Blending dataset, C3DGS outperforms 3DGS in PSNR, with nearly 40% increase in rendering speed and over 28× storage efficiency enhancement. Strengths: High storage compression, faster rendering, maintains high visual fidelity. Limitations: Requires additional training complexity for mask optimization and grid/codebook learning. Performance may degrade in highly sparse scenes without the enhancements found in OMG. When to use: When storage and rendering speed are critical, and the scene has sufficient spatial redundancy in color and geometric similarity. When not to use: In highly sparse scenes where geometric diversity is high and spatial redundancy is low, unless using variants like OMG. C3DGS was proposed to address the critical memory and storage issues in 3DGS, which often require >1GB for large real-world scenes. It was introduced in the paper "Compact 3D Gaussian Representation for Radiance Field" (CVPR 2024). The method builds on the observation that standard 3DGS densification produces many redundant Gaussians and does not exploit spatial redundancy in attributes. It incorporates techniques from neural radiance fields (Instant-NGP) for color representation and vector quantization for geometry. name: Optimized Minimal 3D Gaussian Splatting (OMG)
body: Optimized Minimal 3D Gaussian Splatting (OMG) is a method for compact 3D Gaussian representation that retains per-Gaussian parameterization for geometry (scale and rotation) to handle sparsity, while using a small neural field and Sub-Vector Quantization (SVQ) for appearance features to exploit local continuity. It achieves state-of-the-art storage compression (e.g., >300× relative to 3DGS in the bicycle scene) while maintaining high visual fidelity, building on Compact 3D Gaussian Representation (C3DGS) by addressing the weakness of neural fields in sparse settings where neighboring Gaussians are further apart. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians initialized from training data. Output: A compressed representation consisting of quantized geometric attributes, quantized appearance features, and a set of pruned Gaussians, stored in a single file. Data Structures: 1. Gaussian Attributes: Center position: p \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}. Opacity: o \in [0, 1]^N. 3D Scale: s \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}. Rotation (Quaternion): r \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 4}. SH Coefficients (0-degree, static color): h^{(0)} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}. SH Coefficients (1-3 degrees, view-dependent color): h^{(1,2,3)} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 45}. 2. Learned Features: Static feature: T \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}. View-dependent feature: V \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}. D is the feature dimensionality. 3. SVQ Codebooks: For each sub-vector partition m \in \{1, \dots, M\}, a codebook C^{(m)} of size B \times L. M is the number of sub-vectors, L is the sub-vector length, B is the codebook size. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the Gaussian set using K-means clustering. 2. Feature Learning: Learn per-Gaussian static feature T and view-dependent feature V. 3. Space Feature Computation: For each Gaussian n, compute the space feature Fn based on its center position pn: Fn = \text{MLP}s(\gamma(pn)) where \gamma(\cdot) is positional encoding and \text{MLP}s(\cdot) is a neural network. 4. Appearance Generation: Compute static color, opacity, and view-dependent color using the learned features and space feature: h^{(0)}n = \text{MLP}t(\text{cat}(Tn, Fn)) on = \text{MLP}o(\text{cat}(Tn, Fn)) h^{(1,2,3)}n = \text{MLP}v(\text{cat}(Vn, Fn)) where \text{cat}(\cdot, \cdot) denotes concatenation, and \text{MLP}t, \text{MLP}o, \text{MLP}v are MLPs for static color, opacity, and view-dependent color, respectively. 5. Sub-Vector Quantization (SVQ) Application: Geometry: Apply SVQ to geometric attributes sn and rn to get quantized vectors \hat{s}n and \hat{r}n for rendering. Appearance: Concatenate appearance features Tn and Vn. Apply SVQ to the concatenated vector. Split the result back into quantized components \hat{T}n and \hat{V}n to replace Tn and Vn in Equations (3) and (4). SVQ Formulation: For a vector z \in \mathbb{R}^{ML}, split into M sub-vectors zm \in \mathbb{R}^L. The quantized vector \hat{z} is: \hat{z} = q(z; M) = \text{cat}(C^{(1)}[i1], \dots, C^{(M)}[iM]) where the index for sub-vector m is selected as: im = \arg \minj \|zm - C^{(m)}[j]\|2^2, \quad m \in \{1, \dots, M\}. 6. Training Strategy: Train using rendering loss. In the final 1,000 iterations, freeze the selected codebook indices and fine-tune only the codebook using the rendering loss. 7. Importance Scoring and Pruning: Base Importance Score (\bar{I}i): Determine if Gaussian i is the dominant contributor for at least one ray \rho. Let w{i,\rho} be the blending weight for ray \rho and NR be the total number of training rays: \bar{I}i = \begin{cases} \sum{\rho=1}^{NR} w{i,\rho} & \text{if } \exists \rho \in \{1, \dots, NR\} \text{ s.t. } w{i,\rho} = \maxj w{j,\rho} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}. Local Distinctiveness: Approximate neighbor selection by sorting Gaussians in Morton order and selecting adjacent indices as local neighbors. Compute the mean L1 distance to K-nearest neighbors Ni^K: \text{Distinctiveness}i = \frac{1}{D} \sum{j \in Ni^K} \|Ti - Tj\|1. Final Importance Score (Ii): Ii = \bar{I}i \left( \frac{1}{D} \sum{j \in Ni^K} \|Ti - Tj\|1 \right)^\lambda where \lambda is a scaling factor. Thresholding: Remove low-importance Gaussians using CDF-based thresholding with threshold \tau. 8. Post-processing and Storage: 1. Apply 16-bit quantization to position p and compress with G-PCC. 2. Huffman encode SVQ indices. 3. Store all components in a single file with LZMA compression. Rendering Equation: To render an image, Gaussians are depth-sorted. For a pixel coordinate x: C(x) = \sum{k=1}^{N(x)} ck \alphak(x) \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphaj(x)) where ck is color, \alphak(x) is 2D opacity, and N(x) is the number of Gaussians around x. The 2D opacity for Gaussian n is: \alphan(x) = on \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (x - p'n)^T \Sigma'n (x - p'n)\right) where p'n and \Sigma'n are the projected center and covariance. Parameters: Threshold \tau values for OMG variants: XS=0.96, X=0.98, M=0.99, L=0.999, XL=0.9999. K: Number of nearest neighbors for distinctiveness calculation. Not given in the sources. \lambda: Scaling factor for distinctiveness. Not given in the sources. D: Feature dimensionality. Not given in the sources. M, L, B: SVQ parameters (sub-vectors, length, codebook size). Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparsity: Neural fields assume local continuity, which weakens as Gaussians become sparser. OMG mitigates this by retaining per-Gaussian attributes for geometry and using SVQ for appearance. Redundancy: Naive thresholding based on blending weights can remove all similar Gaussians simultaneously or retain redundant ones. The local distinctiveness metric addresses this. Training Overhead: Updating indices and codes at every iteration increases training time. Freezing indices in the final 1K iterations reduces this overhead. Storage: On the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset, OMG-XS achieves nearly 50% reduction in storage compared to LocoGS-S while retaining PSNR and SSIM. In the bicycle scene, OMG-XS achieves over 300× compression relative to 3DGS. Performance: On the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset, OMG consistently shows the smallest storage requirements while maintaining high performance. Strengths: Effective in extreme compression scenarios; retains high visual fidelity despite reducing the number of Gaussians by an additional 20% compared to Mini-Splatting. Limitations: Requires post-processing steps (G-PCC, Huffman, LZMA) for final storage. OMG was proposed to address the challenges of representing minimal Gaussian primitives efficiently. It builds on the observation that existing neural field approaches weaken in sparse settings, while disregarding continuity leads to inefficient representation. The method was evaluated on real-world datasets including Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks&Temples, and Deep Blending. name: Monte Carlo Specular Energy Aggregator
head: MC Specular Energy Aggregator, Monte Carlo directional moments, Specular Energy Aggregator
body: The Monte Carlo Specular Energy Aggregator (MC-SEA) is a training-time compression technique that maps high-order (typically third-order) Spherical Harmonics (SH) radiance into a compact, low-order (typically first-order) subspace without requiring pre-training or teacher-student distillation. It solves the problem of high memory overhead and inference latency associated with high-order SH in mobile 3D Gaussian Splatting by extracting directional moments of the specular residual via Monte Carlo projection. Unlike Mobile-GS, which relies on computationally expensive distillation from a high-order teacher model, MC-SEA directly aggregates high-frequency energy into a latent space, preserving specular features while reducing storage costs. The method operates during the training phase of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It replaces the standard high-order SH storage with a compressed low-order representation, utilizing a neural network to recover lost details via an Attribute-Conditioned SH Enhancement module. Inputs: N: Number of 3D Gaussian primitives. Lo: Original SH degree (typically 3). Lt: Target lower SH degree (typically 1). c \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times (Lo+1)^2 \times 3}: The optimized third-order SH coefficient tensor after initial training. K: Number of Monte Carlo samples (default 2048). Outputs: c' \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times (Lt+1)^2 \times 3}: The compressed first-order SH coefficients. \Delta ci: View-independent residual offsets predicted by the enhancement MLP. Coefficient Tensor (c): Dimensions \mathbb{R}^{N \times (Lo+1)^2 \times 3}, where N is the number of Gaussians, Lo is the original SH degree, and 3 represents RGB channels. Reduced Coefficient Tensor (c'): Dimensions \mathbb{R}^{N \times (Lt+1)^2 \times 3}, where Lt is the target lower SH degree. Latents: E{mag}: Scalar specular energy magnitude per Gaussian. E{dir}: Vectorial directional energy per Gaussian. c{dc}: Base color SH (0-th order). 1. High-Order Optimization (Initial Phase): Optimize the 3D Gaussians using full third-order SH coefficients for the first 3,000 iterations (3k) to establish a high-frequency representation. 2. Uniform Spherical Sampling: Generate a set of directional vectors D = \{dk\}{k=1}^K by uniformly sampling K points on the unit sphere \mathbb{S}^2. For each sample k, draw independent random variables \phik \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 2\pi) and \xik \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1), then compute the colatitude \thetak = \arccos(1 - 2\xik). Convert to Cartesian coordinates: dk = [\sin \thetak \cos \phik, \sin \thetak \sin \phik, \cos \thetak]^T where \|dk\|2 = 1. 3. Photometric Residual Evaluation: For each Gaussian i and each direction dk, evaluate the photometric residual between the third-order SH radiance ci(dk) and the second-order SH radiance c^2i(dk): c{res}(dk) = ci(dk) - c^2i(dk) This residual captures the high-frequency information discarded by projecting to lower orders. 4. Monte Carlo Energy Aggregation: Compute the scalar specular energy magnitude E{mag} and the directional energy vector E{dir} using Monte Carlo integration over the K samples. The \max(0, \cdot) function ensures only positive energy contributions are aggregated, preserving the directionality of specular lobes: E{mag} = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} \max(0, c{res}(dk)) E{dir} = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} dk \otimes \max(0, c{res}(dk)) where \otimes denotes the outer product. 5. Neural Network Mapping (Compression): Map the aggregated latents to the first-order SH coefficients c' using a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) \Psi. The MLP takes E{mag}, E{dir}, and the normalized Gaussian position \hat{\mu} as input. The position is normalized using a clamping function f(\hat{\mu}) to handle spatial outliers: f(\hat{\mu}) = \begin{cases} \hat{\mu} & \text{if } \|\hat{\mu}\|2 \leq 1 \\ \left( 2 - \frac{1}{\|\hat{\mu}\|2} \right) \frac{\hat{\mu}}{\|\hat{\mu}\|2} & \text{if } \|\hat{\mu}\|2 > 1 \end{cases} The mapping is defined as: c' = \Psi(E{mag}, E{dir}, f(\hat{\mu})) The MLP \Psi is initialized with one hidden layer containing 64 neurons. 6. Attribute-Conditioned SH Enhancement (Refinement): To recover fine details lost during compression, predict a residual offset \Delta ci using a second MLP \Phi. This MLP concatenates normalized position \mu, normalized scale \hat{s}, rotation quaternion r, opacity o, and the normalized first-order SH \hat{c}': \Delta ci = \Phi([\mui, \hat{s}i, ri, oi, \hat{c}'i]) The final enhanced coefficients are: c^{out}i = c'i + \Delta ci The final linear layer of \Phi is strictly zero-initialized to ensure optimization stability, allowing the model to fall back to standard 3DGS at the start of the refinement phase. 7. Low-Order Optimization (Final Phase): Transition to first-order SH optimization for iterations greater than 3,000. The compression from third-order to first-order is executed only once. Subsequent updates maintain and optimize the lightweight first-order parameters and the enhancement offsets. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def montecarlospecularenergyaggregator(cthirdorder, K=2048): """ Compresses third-order SH coefficients to first-order using MC aggregation. Args: cthirdorder: Tensor of shape (N, 16, 3) representing 3rd-order SH (Lo=3). N is the number of Gaussians. K: Number of Monte Carlo samples. Returns: cfirstorder: Tensor of shape (N, 4, 3) representing 1st-order SH (Lt=1). """ N = cthirdorder.shape[0] # Step 2: Uniform Spherical Sampling # Generate K random directions phi = np.random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi, K) xi = np.random.uniform(0, 1, K) theta = np.arccos(1 - 2 xi) # Convert to Cartesian coordinates sintheta = np.sin(theta) costheta = np.cos(theta) cosphi = np.cos(phi) sinphi = np.sin(phi) # Directions D shape: (K, 3) D = np.stack([ sintheta cosphi, sintheta sinphi, costheta ], axis=-1) # Step 3 & 4: Energy Aggregation # Evaluate radiance for all Gaussians and all directions # Assuming a helper function evaluateshradiance exists that computes # c(d) given coefficients c and direction d. # cthirdorder shape: (N, 16, 3) # D shape: (K, 3) # radiance3rd shape: (N, K, 3) radiance3rd = evaluateshradiance(cthirdorder, D) # Evaluate second-order radiance (Lo=2, 9 coefficients) # Extract first 9 coefficients for 2nd order csecondorder = cthirdorder[:,:9,:] radiance2nd = evaluateshradiance(csecondorder, D) # Compute residual residual = radiance3rd - radiance2nd # Shape: (N, K, 3) # Apply max(0, residual) to capture positive energy positiveresidual = np.maximum(0, residual) # Shape: (N, K, 3) # Compute Emag: Mean of positive residual over K samples # Shape: (N, 3) Emag = np.mean(positiveresidual, axis=1) # Compute Edir: Mean of outer product of direction and positive residual # Outer product dk (3,) and residual (3,) results in (3, 3) # We sum over K and divide by K # Edir shape: (N, 3, 3) # Using einsum for efficiency: sum over k of D[k] (3) posres[k] (3) -> (3,3) Edir = np.einsum('nk, nkj -> nij', D, positiveresidual) / K # Step 5: Neural Network Mapping # This step requires the MLP Psi. In a real implementation, this would be # a PyTorch/TensorFlow module. Here we describe the logic. # Inputs to Psi: Emag (N,3), Edir (N,3,3), normalizedmu (N,3) # cfirstorder = Psi(Emag, Edir, normalizedmu) # For the purpose of this algorithmic description, we assume the mapping # produces the first-order coefficients. # Note: The actual implementation uses an MLP. The output shape is (N, 4, 3). cfirstorder = applymlpmapping(Emag, Edir) return cfirstorder def evaluateshradiance(csh, directions): """ Evaluates SH radiance for given coefficients and directions. csh: (N, numcoeffs, 3) directions: (K, 3) Returns: (N, K, 3) """ # This is a placeholder for the actual SH evaluation logic. # In practice, this involves computing SH basis functions Ylm for each direction # and dot-producting with coefficients. # Since the prompt requires self-contained valid Python without library internals, # and SH evaluation is complex, we note that this function implements the standard # SH basis evaluation. pass def applymlpmapping(Emag, Edir): """ Placeholder for the MLP Psi that maps latents to first-order SH. """ pass K: Number of spherical sample points. Default is 2048. Sensitivity analysis shows PSNR improves monotonically from K=64 to K=2048, then plateaus at K=4096. Lo: Original SH degree (e.g., 3). Lt: Target lower SH degree (e.g., 1). 3k: Initial training iterations for high-order optimization (3,000). Orthogonality Nullification: Naive aggregation of raw SH polynomials is futile because the integral of any purely high-order SH polynomial (l \ge 1) over the sphere evaluates to strictly zero due to orthogonality. The method avoids this by aggregating the residual energy magnitude and direction. Specular Representation: High-order SH polynomials are inefficient for sharp specular lobes due to ringing artifacts. MC-SEA addresses this by focusing on directional moments of the residual rather than absolute coefficients. Optimization Stability: The final linear layer of the enhancement MLP \Phi must be zero-initialized. This ensures the model starts with standard 3DGS parameters and smoothly learns residuals, preventing instability. Position Normalization: Gaussian positions must be normalized using the clamping function f(\hat{\mu}) to reduce the impact of spatial outliers and ensure convergence. Time Complexity: The aggregation step involves O(N \cdot K) operations for sampling and residual evaluation. The MLP mapping is O(N) per inference step. The training overhead is limited to the one-time aggregation at iteration 3,000. Memory Complexity: Reduces SH memory overhead from O(N \cdot (Lo+1)^2 \cdot 3) to O(N \cdot (Lt+1)^2 \cdot 3) plus the storage for latents E{mag} and E{dir}. For Lo=3, Lt=1, this is a significant reduction. Performance: On mobile hardware (e.g., Snapdragon 8 Gen 3), Flux-GS using MC-SEA achieves competitive PSNR (e.g., 30.31 vs 30.21 for 3DGS) with significantly higher FPS (151 vs 11) and lower storage (1.6 MB vs 4.2 MB for Mobile-GS). Strengths: No pre-training or distillation required; zero inference overhead for the enhancement module (offsets are baked); preserves high-frequency specular details. Limitations: Requires a training curriculum switch; relies on the quality of the initial 3k iterations. The Monte Carlo Specular Energy Aggregator was introduced in the Flux-GS paper by Du et al. (2026) as a method to enable real-time rendering on resource-constrained mobile devices. It was further applied in Mobile-4DGS for static and dynamic scenes. It addresses the limitations of Mobile-GS, which used distillation, by providing a direct, non-distillation-based compression method. name: Hardware and Computational Acceleration
head: Hardware Acceleration, Computational Optimization, GPU Acceleration for 3DGS
body: Hardware and Computational Acceleration encompasses the system-level and algorithmic optimizations required to render and train 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) efficiently on modern GPU architectures. It solves the bottlenecks of memory bandwidth, sorting latency, and GPU memory capacity that arise when processing scenes with tens of millions of primitives. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on system-level distribution (sharding across nodes), hardware-specific kernel design (Tensor Cores, Roofline optimization), and memory hierarchy management (CPU-GPU offloading) rather than just intra-GPU rasterization logic like tiling or sorting. All methods in this family operate on the set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N defined in Rendering Implementation and Acceleration. The core rendering operation involves projecting these 3D primitives to 2D screen space and performing alpha blending. Acceleration relies on the following shared mechanisms: 1. Tiling: Dividing the image plane into non-overlapping tiles (commonly 16 \times 16 pixels) to localize Gaussian processing and enable coalesced memory accesses. 2. Sorting: Sorting Gaussians within each tile by view-space depth (front-to-back) to enable correct alpha blending. 3. Culling: Discarding Gaussians that do not overlap with the camera frustum or specific tiles to reduce enumeration overhead. 4. Memory Hierarchy Management: Exploiting the distinction between global memory (VRAM), shared memory (on-chip), and host memory (CPU RAM) to minimize data movement. RoofGS is an end-to-end acceleration method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that optimizes the rendering pipeline based on stage-specific hardware constraints identified via the Roofline model. It addresses the inefficiency of generic optimization by applying bandwidth-reduction techniques to memory-bound front-end stages and instruction-level parallelism (ILP) enhancements to compute-bound rasterization stages. Unlike sibling methods that focus on memory management or distributed sharding, RoofGS restructures the core rendering kernel to minimize global memory traffic and arithmetic overhead simultaneously. It implements four core optimizations: front-end fusion, compact attribute storage, compressed radix-sort keys, and a reorganized rasterizer with dual-pixel ILP and fast exponential evaluation. The method operates on the standard 3D Gaussian primitive definition provided by the parent article Rendering Implementation and Acceleration. Data Structures: 1. Gaussian Attributes: Compressed to reduce memory footprint. Standard third-degree SHs require 192 bytes per Gaussian in single precision (3 \times (D{SH} + 1)^2 \times 4 bytes for D{SH}=3). RoofGS uses low-bit quantization with a single shared scale for all SH coefficients. 2. Depth Keys: Compressed dynamically to reduce sorting bandwidth. Algorithm Steps: 1. Front-End Fusion: Merge pre-processing stages to reduce intermediate data movement. 2. Compact Attribute Storage: Quantize SH coefficients using a shared scale to reduce global memory traffic. 3. Compressed Radix Sort: Sort Gaussians by view-space depth using compressed keys to enable correct alpha blending. 4. Rasterization with Dual-Pixel ILP: Evaluate and composite Gaussians per pixel with increased instruction-level parallelism. Formulas: The baseline rasterizer evaluates the Gaussian power p(x, y) for a pixel (x, y) as: p(x, y) = -\frac{1}{2} \left( a(x - w)^2 + b(x - u)(y - v) + c(y - v)^2 \right) where (u, v) is the projected 2D Gaussian center, and a, b, c are derived from the projected covariance matrix. The unclamped opacity contribution is then: \tilde{\alpha}(x, y) = o \exp(p(x, y)) where o is the Gaussian opacity. RoofGS optimizes the evaluation of this exponential term and the subsequent blending loop to increase ILP. Parameters: SH Degree: Typically D{SH}=3. Quantization Scale: Single shared scale for all SH coefficients. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Loss: Quantization of SH coefficients may introduce visual artifacts if the shared scale is not chosen carefully. Depth Key Compression: Aggressive compression may lead to sorting errors if key collisions are not handled. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def roofgsrender(gaussians, camera, imagewidth, imageheight): # Step 1: Front-end fusion and compact attribute storage # Quantize SH coefficients with a shared scale compressedgaussians = quantizesh(gaussians, sharedscale=True) # Step 2: Compressed radix sort # Compress depth keys and sort front-to-back sortedgaussians = compressedradixsort(compressedgaussians, camera) # Step 3: Rasterization with dual-pixel ILP image = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) alphaimage = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) for tile in tiles(imagewidth, imageheight, 16, 16): # Process tile for pixel in tilepixels(tile): # Evaluate Gaussian power # p(x,y) = -0.5 (a(x-w)^2 + b(x-u)(y-v) + c(y-v)^2) # Compute opacity: alpha = o exp(p) # Composite with ILP optimization color, alpha = rasterizepixel(pixel, sortedgaussians, camera) image[pixel] = color alphaimage[pixel] = alpha return image, alphaimage Note: The specific implementation of quantizesh, compressedradixsort, and rasterizepixel with ILP is detailed in the source. The pseudocode above represents the high-level structure. Tile-Based Comparison-Free Sorting restricts depth sorting operations to individual image tiles to avoid global synchronization, reduce hardware complexity, and achieve fixed latency per output. It solves the bottleneck of sorting millions of Gaussian points globally by leveraging the fact that alpha blending only requires correct depth ordering within the local tile. Unlike full-scene radix sort, which incurs high memory overhead and variable latency, this method provides deterministic, linear delay cycles suitable for low-power hardware. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of 3D Gaussians projected into screen space, each associated with a tile ID and a view-space depth value. Output: Gaussians ordered front-to-back within each tile, ready for alpha blending. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian primitive carries a tileid (identifying the 16 \times 16 tile it overlaps) and depth (view-space depth). Element Vector Table (EVT): A bit-vector of size N (where N is the number of Gaussians in the current tile/batch), initialized to all 1s to track unsorted elements. Algorithm Steps: The sorting process identifies the Largest Element (LE) iteratively until all elements are sorted. 1. Initialization: Initialize the EVT with all 1s. This indicates that all N elements are currently candidates for being the largest remaining element. 2. Iterative Selection: Repeat the following steps N times (once for each Gaussian to be sorted): a. Concurrent Phase: Process the N n-bit depth values using k parallel clusters. Each cluster handles a partition of the elements. Starting from the most significant bit (MSB), the clusters filter out smaller values through bitwise AND operations and multiplexer-based selection in cascaded blocks. b. Sequential Phase: Pass the outputs from the concurrent phase to a linear array of k cascaded blocks to further refine the selection and identify the single Largest Element (LE) among the candidates marked by the EVT. c. Conflict Resolution: If multiple elements have identical depth values, the EVT may return multiple candidates. Resolve this using bitwise inverter, bitwise AND, and an adder to compute the unique index of the first candidate: FO{NEW} = Fo \& (\sim Fo + 1'b1) where Fo is the output vector from the selection phase. d. Update EVT: Clear the bit corresponding to the identified LE in the EVT (set to 0). This removes the sorted element from future consideration. 3. Termination: The loop ends when the EVT contains all 0s, signaling that all N elements have been sorted. Parameters and Optimizations: Sorting Key: The primary key is \langle \text{tile-id}, \text{depth} \rangle. Sorting is performed independently per tile. Sign Bit Skipping: Since near-plane culling excludes points with depth < 0, the sign bit of the depth value is always 0. The algorithm skips operations on the sign bit to reduce computational overhead. Bit Width (n): Determined by the precision required for view-space depth. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Duplicate Depths: The conflict resolution logic (FO{NEW}) is critical to handle duplicate depth values correctly, ensuring deterministic ordering even when Gaussians share the same depth. Variable N: The number of Gaussians per tile varies significantly across scenes and views. The hardware must handle this variability without pipeline stalls. Distributed Training and Sharding refers to the family of methods that partition the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training and rendering pipeline across multiple GPUs to overcome single-device memory limits and accelerate large-scale reconstruction. It solves the problem of out-of-memory errors and slow training times when processing scenes with tens of millions of primitives or high-resolution scientific volume data. Unlike single-GPU baselines, these methods distribute Gaussian parameters, pixel blocks, or camera views across a GPU cluster, coordinating via communication primitives like all-to-all or all-reduce. What sets this family apart from its siblings is the focus on system-level distribution (sharding the model or data across nodes) rather than just intra-GPU optimization (like tiling or sorting) or inference-specific caching. All methods in this family operate on the standard 3D Gaussian primitive definition provided by the parent article Rendering Implementation and Acceleration. The core rendering operation involves projecting 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space and performing alpha blending. Acceleration strategies generally rely on the following shared mechanisms: 1. Tiling: Dividing the image plane into non-overlapping tiles (commonly 16 \times 16 pixels) to localize Gaussian processing and enable coalesced memory accesses. 2. Sorting: Sorting Gaussians within each tile by view-space depth (front-to-back) to enable correct alpha blending. 3. Culling: Discarding Gaussians that do not overlap with the camera frustum or specific tiles to reduce enumeration overhead. 4. Memory Hierarchy Management: Exploiting the distinction between global memory (VRAM), shared memory (on-chip), and host memory (CPU RAM) to minimize data movement. Cache-based Lazy Memory Management (CLM) is a memory offloading strategy that enables the training of large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes on a single consumer-grade GPU by exploiting the inherent sparsity of Gaussian memory access patterns. Unlike naive offloading approaches that load all Gaussians to the GPU or multi-GPU solutions that require complex synchronization, CLM keeps the majority of Gaussians in CPU memory and loads only the subset accessed by the current view, overlapping communication with computation to hide latency. CLM operates on the standard 3D Gaussian primitive definition provided by Rendering Implementation and Acceleration. The method manages the lifecycle of Gaussian parameters between CPU RAM and GPU VRAM to fit scenes exceeding GPU capacity. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of posed training images (views), the full list of N 3D Gaussians stored in CPU memory, and the current optimizer state. Output: Updated Gaussian parameters in CPU memory (and optionally GPU memory for the active subset) after a training iteration. Data Structures and Layout Each 3D Gaussian consists of 59 learnable parameters. These are divided into four attribute types: 1. 3D Position: 3 parameters. 2. Covariance (Scale + Rotation): 3 + 4 = 7 parameters. 3. Spherical Harmonics (Color): 48 parameters. 4. Opacity: 1 parameter. Total parameters per Gaussian: 59. During training, each parameter requires storage for: 1. The parameter value itself. 2. Its gradient. 3. Two additional versions for the Adam optimizer state. Each value is a 4-byte floating-point number. Thus, the memory required per parameter is 4 \times 4 = 16 bytes. The total memory required for N Gaussians is: \text{Memory} = N \times 59 \times 16 \text{ bytes} Or equivalently: \text{Memory} = N \times 59 \times 4 \times 4 \text{ bytes} Algorithm Steps The core strategy involves four key observations to minimize CPU-GPU communication overhead: 1. Ahead-of-Time Access Computation: Compute the set of Gaussians accessed by each view (training image) before the iteration begins. This allows the loading of Gaussians for the current iteration to overlap with the computation of the previous iteration. 2. Caching Overlapping Gaussians: Identify and cache Gaussians that are accessed by multiple different views. This reduces the volume of data transferred during each training iteration. 3. Spatial Locality Scheduling: Schedule training iterations such that views in the same spatial region are processed consecutively. Since views in the same region access similar Gaussians, this maximizes cache hits across successive iterations and minimizes overall communication volume. 4. Overlapping Gradient and Update: Exploit spatial locality to overlap the gradient computation phase with a substantial portion of the Gaussian parameter update phase. Pseudocode The following pseudocode implements the CLM offloading strategy. It assumes a standard 3DGS training loop where views is a list of training images, gaussians is the full dataset in CPU memory, and activegaussians is the subset accessed by a specific view. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainclm(views, gaussians, optimizerstate): """ Train 3DGS using Cache-based Lazy Memory Management. Args: views: List of training view objects, each containing camera pose and image. gaussians: Full list of N Gaussians stored in CPU memory. optimizerstate: Current state of the Adam optimizer (stored in CPU memory). Returns: Updated gaussians and optimizerstate in CPU memory. """ # Pre-compute access patterns for all views to enable ahead-of-time loading # This step determines which Gaussians are visible/active for each view. accesspatterns = computeaccesspatterns(views, gaussians) # Initialize a cache for Gaussians currently resident in GPU memory # The cache size is limited by available GPU memory (e.g., 24GB on RTX 4090) gpucache = Cache() # Initialize overlap pipeline: previous iteration's computation might still be running previtercomputetask = None for i, view in enumerate(views): # Step 1: Determine Gaussians needed for the current view currentgaussianindices = accesspatterns[i] # Step 2: Load necessary Gaussians from CPU to GPU # This operation is asynchronous and can overlap with previous computation loadtask = loadgaussianstogpu(gaussians, currentgaussianindices, gpucache) # Wait for load to complete if it hasn't started or if dependencies require it # In practice, this is managed by a pipeline to hide latency loadtask.wait() # Step 3: Perform GPU computation (Rasterization and Forward Pass) # This uses the Gaussians currently in the GPU cache renderedimage = rasterize(view, gpucache.getactivegaussians()) # Step 4: Compute Loss and Gradients on GPU loss = computeloss(renderedimage, view.gtimage) gradients = computegradients(loss, gpucache.getactivegaussians()) # Step 5: Transfer Gradients to CPU and Update Parameters # This overlaps with the next iteration's loading phase transfertask = transfergradientstocpu(gradients, optimizerstate, currentgaussianindices) # The actual parameter update (Adam step) happens on CPU # This can overlap with the loading of the NEXT iteration's Gaussians updatetask = updateoptimizer(optimizerstate, currentgaussianindices) # Manage pipeline overlap: # If the previous iteration's update is not done, wait for it to free up resources # or simply let the CPU handle it while GPU loads the next batch. if previtercomputetask: previtercomputetask.wait() # Schedule next iteration's load to start as soon as possible # The key insight is that loading for iteration i+1 can start while # iteration i's gradient update is happening on CPU. previtercomputetask = transfertask return gaussians, optimizerstate def computeaccesspatterns(views, gaussians): """ Compute which Gaussians are visible for each view. This is done ahead-of-time to enable overlap. """ patterns = [] for view in views: # Project Gaussians to screen space and check overlap with view frustum/tiles # Return indices of Gaussians that contribute to the render activeindices = getvisiblegaussians(view, gaussians) patterns.append(activeindices) return patterns def loadgaussianstogpu(cpugaussians, indices, gpucache): """ Load specific Gaussians from CPU to GPU, respecting cache limits. Evicts old Gaussians if cache is full. """ # Check which indices are already in GPU cache cachedindices = gpucache.getindices() neededindices = [idx for idx in indices if idx not in cachedindices] if neededindices: # Evict if necessary to make space gpucache.evictifneeded(len(neededindices)) # Transfer data gpudata = transfercputogpu(cpugaussians, neededindices) gpucache.add(gpudata, neededindices) return AsyncTask() # Placeholder for async transfer task def updateoptimizer(optimizerstate, indices): """ Run Adam optimizer step on CPU for the specified Gaussian indices. """ # Extract gradients and parameters for indices grads = getgradients(indices) params = getparameters(indices) # Update optimizer state (m, v) and parameters newparams, newstate = adamstep(params, grads, optimizerstate[indices]) # Write back to CPU memory updatecpumemory(indices, newparams, newstate) return AsyncTask() Parameters and Typical Values Gaussian Parameter Count: 59 per Gaussian. Memory per Parameter: 16 bytes (4 bytes for param, 4 for gradient, 8 for optimizer state). GPU Memory Capacity: The method is demonstrated on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 24GB VRAM. Scene Scale: Successfully trained scenes with 100 million to 102 million Gaussians on a single RTX 4090. Tile Size: Inherits the 16 \times 16 pixel tile size from the parent Rendering Implementation and Acceleration. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Naive Offloading Overhead: Naively offloading all Gaussians to the CPU and loading them per iteration incurs significant performance overhead due to CPU-GPU communication latency and the time required to run the Adam optimizer on the CPU. Memory Proportionality: Naive offloading fails to scale because it still requires GPU memory proportional to the total number of Gaussians if all are loaded simultaneously. Cache Thrashing: If the spatial locality is poor or the cache size is too small, frequent evictions and reloads can negate the benefits of offloading. Precision: The method relies on standard 32-bit floating-point arithmetic for parameters and gradients. Cache-Less Memory (CLM) is a system design that enables the training and rendering of large or highly detailed 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes on a single consumer-grade GPU by offloading Gaussian parameters and optimizer computation to the CPU. It solves the problem of GPU memory exhaustion in large-scene training by leveraging sparsity and spatial locality to minimize GPU-CPU communication overhead. Unlike sibling methods that focus on sorting or tiling acceleration, CLM specifically addresses memory capacity limits through attribute-wise offloading and microbatch pipelining. CLM operates by splitting Gaussian attributes based on their necessity for frustum culling, storing only selection-critical attributes on the GPU while keeping non-critical attributes and optimizer states on the CPU. The training loop is divided into microbatches (single images) to allow overlapping communication and computation. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of training images/views; 3D Gaussian primitives defined by position, rotation, scale, color (spherical harmonics), and opacity. Output: Updated Gaussian parameters and rendered images. Data Structures and Layout Gaussian attributes are split into two sets: 1. Selection-critical attributes: Position (3 floats), Rotation (4 floats), Scale (3 floats). These are stored in GPU memory for all Gaussians to enable frustum culling without loading all Gaussians. These constitute less than 20% (10 out of 59 floats) of a Gaussian's memory footprint. 2. Non-critical attributes: Color and Opacity. These are stored in CPU memory and loaded into GPU memory only when required. Steps 1. Attribute-Wise Offload: Store selection-critical attributes (position, rotation, scale) in GPU memory. Store non-critical attributes (color, opacity) in CPU memory. 2. Frustum Culling: Run frustum culling on the GPU using only the selection-critical attributes. A Gaussian is culled if it is outside 3 standard deviations (3\sigma) of its distribution. This determines the set of active Gaussians Si for microbatch i. 3. Precise Gaussian Caching: When preparing microbatch i+1, identify the intersection of active Gaussians from the previous microbatch Si and the current microbatch S{i+1}. Copy Gaussians in Si \cap S{i+1} from microbatch i's GPU tensors (already in GPU memory). Load Gaussians in S{i+1} \setminus Si from CPU memory. 4. Forward/Backward Pass: Perform forward and backward passes for microbatch i+1. 5. Gradient Caching: After microbatch i finishes: Transfer gradients only for Gaussians in Si \setminus S{i+1} to CPU. name: RoofGS
head: Roofline-Guided End-to-End Acceleration of 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: RoofGS is an end-to-end acceleration method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that optimizes the rendering pipeline based on stage-specific hardware constraints identified via the Roofline model. It addresses the inefficiency of generic optimization by applying bandwidth-reduction techniques to memory-bound front-end stages and instruction-level parallelism (ILP) enhancements to compute-bound rasterization stages. Unlike sibling methods that focus on memory management or distributed sharding, RoofGS restructures the core rendering kernel to minimize global memory traffic and arithmetic overhead simultaneously. RoofGS implements four core optimizations: front-end fusion, compact attribute storage, compressed radix-sort keys, and a reorganized rasterizer with dual-pixel ILP and fast exponential evaluation. The method operates on the standard 3D Gaussian primitive definition provided by the parent article Rendering Implementation and Acceleration. Inputs: 3D Gaussian primitives (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonic coefficients), camera parameters, image resolution. Outputs: Final composited color and opacity image. 1. Gaussian Attributes: Compressed to reduce memory footprint. Standard third-degree SHs require 192 bytes per Gaussian in single precision (3 \times (D{SH} + 1)^2 \times 4 bytes for D{SH}=3). RoofGS uses low-bit quantization with a single shared scale for all SH coefficients. 2. Depth Keys: Compressed dynamically to reduce sorting bandwidth. 1. Front-End Fusion: Merge pre-processing stages to reduce intermediate data movement. 2. Compact Attribute Storage: Quantize SH coefficients using a shared scale to reduce global memory traffic. 3. Compressed Radix Sort: Sort Gaussians by view-space depth using compressed keys to enable correct alpha blending. 4. Rasterization with Dual-Pixel ILP: Evaluate and composite Gaussians per pixel with increased instruction-level parallelism. The baseline rasterizer evaluates the Gaussian power p(x, y) for a pixel (x, y) as: p(x, y) = -\frac{1}{2} \left( a(x - w)^2 + b(x - u)(y - v) + c(y - v)^2 \right) where (u, v) is the projected 2D Gaussian center, and a, b, c are derived from the projected covariance matrix. The unclamped opacity contribution is then: \tilde{\alpha}(x, y) = o \exp(p(x, y)) where o is the Gaussian opacity. RoofGS optimizes the evaluation of this exponential term and the subsequent blending loop to increase ILP. SH Degree: Typically D{SH}=3. Quantization Scale: Single shared scale for all SH coefficients. Precision Loss: Quantization of SH coefficients may introduce visual artifacts if the shared scale is not chosen carefully. Depth Key Compression: Aggressive compression may lead to sorting errors if key collisions are not handled. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def roofgsrender(gaussians, camera, imagewidth, imageheight): # Step 1: Front-end fusion and compact attribute storage # Quantize SH coefficients with a shared scale compressedgaussians = quantizesh(gaussians, sharedscale=True) # Step 2: Compressed radix sort # Compress depth keys and sort front-to-back sortedgaussians = compressedradixsort(compressedgaussians, camera) # Step 3: Rasterization with dual-pixel ILP image = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) alphaimage = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) for tile in tiles(imagewidth, imageheight, 16, 16): # Process tile for pixel in tilepixels(tile): # Evaluate Gaussian power # p(x,y) = -0.5 (a(x-w)^2 + b(x-u)(y-v) + c(y-v)^2) # Compute opacity: alpha = o exp(p) # Composite with ILP optimization color, alpha = rasterizepixel(pixel, sortedgaussians, camera) image[pixel] = color alphaimage[pixel] = alpha return image, alphaimage Note: The specific implementation of quantizesh, compressedradixsort, and rasterizepixel with ILP is detailed in the source. The pseudocode above represents the high-level structure. A methodology that uses stage-wise performance characterization to match optimization strategies to the dominant hardware constraints of the baseline pipeline, by reducing intermediate data movement in the front end and reducing arithmetic overhead in rasterization. It solves the problem of uncoordinated software optimization in volume rendering contexts, where different stages of the rendering pipeline are bottlenecked by different hardware resources (memory bandwidth vs. compute throughput). It sets itself apart from generic optimization by explicitly using the Roofline model to identify the "knee" point and applying memory-centric optimizations to stages below it and compute-centric optimizations to stages near it. Time Complexity: Optimized for high throughput via ILP in rasterization and reduced memory traffic in front-end stages. Memory Complexity: Reduced global memory traffic through compact attribute storage and compressed depth keys. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: End-to-end acceleration targeting both memory and compute bottlenecks. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of quantization scales and compression ratios. When to use: When rendering 3D Gaussian Splatting on hardware where both memory bandwidth and compute throughput are critical constraints. When not to use: When memory bandwidth is not a bottleneck and compute is the sole constraint, or vice versa, simpler optimizations may suffice. RoofGS was introduced in the paper "RoofGS: Roofline-Guided End-to-End Acceleration of 3D Gaussian Splatting". It builds on prior roofline analyses that identified the rasterization stage of 3DGS as compute-bound and the front-end stages as memory-bound. The method applies stage-specific optimization principles to improve overall rendering performance.
