name: Roofline-guided stage-wise optimization
body: Roofline-guided stage-wise optimization is a methodology that uses stage-wise performance characterization to match optimization strategies to the dominant hardware constraints of the baseline pipeline, by reducing intermediate data movement in the front end and reducing arithmetic overhead in rasterization. It solves the problem of uncoordinated software optimization in volume rendering contexts, where different stages of the rendering pipeline are bottlenecked by different hardware resources (memory bandwidth vs. compute throughput). It sets itself apart from generic optimization by explicitly using the Roofline model to identify the "knee" point and applying memory-centric optimizations to stages below it and compute-centric optimizations to stages near it. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Baseline 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pipeline stages, hardware specifications (peak compute throughput P{\text{peak}}, memory bandwidth BW), and kernel execution traces. Output: An optimized pipeline where specific stages are modified to address their identified bottlenecks. Data Structures: Sorting Key: A dynamic 32-bit integer packing the tile index and quantized depth. Attributes: Compressed spherical harmonics (SH) and geometric attributes. Method Steps: 1. Roofline Characterization: For each stage in the rendering pipeline, calculate the arithmetic intensity I and the achievable performance P using the Roofline model. P = \min(P{\text{peak}}, BW \cdot I) \quad (1) Where: P{\text{peak}} is the peak compute throughput of the hardware. BW is the memory bandwidth of the hardware. I is the arithmetic intensity, defined as operations divided by data movement (I = F/B). 2. Identify Bottleneck Regime: Compare the stage's arithmetic intensity I to the hardware's balance point (knee) I{\text{knee}}. I{\text{knee}} = \frac{P{\text{peak}}}{BW} \quad (2) If I \ll I{\text{knee}}, the stage is bandwidth-bound (memory traffic sensitive). If I \approx I{\text{knee}}, the stage is compute-bound (arithmetic overhead sensitive). 3. Apply Front-End Optimizations (Bandwidth-Limited Stages): For stages identified as bandwidth-bound (typically preprocessing and sorting): Compress SH and geometric attributes to reduce memory footprint. Pack tile index and quantized depth into a single dynamic 32-bit sorting key to reduce intermediate data movement. Fuse preprocessing, tile duplication, and key generation into a single kernel to minimize global memory traffic. 4. Apply Rasterization Optimizations (Compute-Limited Stages): For stages identified as compute-bound (typically rasterization): Evaluate two adjacent pixels simultaneously to increase instruction-level parallelism (ILP). Replace standard exponential operations with a bit-level approximation tailored to alpha-thresholded blending to reduce arithmetic overhead. Parameters: Hardware Balance Point (I{\text{knee}}): On an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, P{\text{peak}} = 82.6 \text{ TFLOPS} and BW = 1008 \text{ GB/s}, resulting in I{\text{knee}} \approx 81.9 \text{ FLOPS/Byte}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The bit-level approximation in rasterization must be carefully calibrated to maintain visual fidelity while reducing arithmetic cost. Kernel Fusion: Fusing too many stages may exceed register limits or warp occupancy thresholds, potentially degrading performance. Workload Scaling: Optimizations tuned for a specific Gaussian count may not scale linearly; the total-frame speedup can be non-monotonic due to auxiliary overheads not eliminated by the primary optimization path. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rooflineguidedoptimization(stages, Ppeak, BW): """ Applies Roofline-guided optimizations to a rendering pipeline. Args: stages: List of stage objects with 'name', 'flops', 'bytes' attributes. Ppeak: Peak compute throughput (TFLOPS). BW: Memory bandwidth (GB/s). Returns: optimizedstages: List of optimized stage configurations. """ Iknee = Ppeak / BW optimizedstages = [] for stage in stages: # Calculate arithmetic intensity Istage = stage.flops / stage.bytes if Istage < Iknee: # Bandwidth-bound: Optimize for memory traffic reduction stage.attrs = compressshandgeometry(stage.attrs) stage.sortkey = packtileindexanddepth(stage.tileidx, stage.quantdepth) stage.kernel = fusepreprocesstiledupkey(stage) else: # Compute-bound: Optimize for arithmetic intensity/ILP stage.pixelproc = evaltwoadjacentpixels(stage.pixelproc) stage.blendop = bitlevelalphaapprox(stage.blendop) optimizedstages.append(stage) return optimizedstages def compressshandgeometry(attrs): """Compress spherical harmonics and geometric attributes to reduce memory footprint.""" return quantizeandpack(attrs, bits=16) def packtileindexanddepth(tileidx, quantdepth): """Pack tile index and quantized depth into a single dynamic 32-bit sorting key.""" return (tileidx << 16) | (quantdepth & 0xFFFF) def fusepreprocesstiledupkey(stage): """Fuse preprocessing, tile duplication, and key generation into a single kernel.""" return stage.mergekernels(['preprocess', 'tiledup', 'keygen']) def evaltwoadjacentpixels(proc): """Evaluate two adjacent pixels simultaneously to increase instruction-level parallelism.""" return proc.processwarppair() def bitlevelalphaapprox(blend): """Replace standard exponential operation with a bit-level approximation tailored to alpha-thresholded blending.""" return blend.replaceexpwithbitwiseapprox() A diagnostic method to isolate how sort/reordering and raster stages behave as Gaussian workload increases, using a fixed high-workload view from the bicycle scene. It synthetically scales the workload from 5M to 30M Gaussians and measures median-of-5 timings under a locked RTX 4090 timing-only protocol. At 30M emitted entries, the sort stage improves by 1.71x and the raster stage by 1.42x compared to the baseline. At 5M points, Base Sort is 1.051ms, TileGS Sort is 0.387ms (2.72x speedup); Base Raster is 2.277ms, TileGS Raster is 1.554ms (1.46x speedup). At 30M points, Base Sort is 5.709ms, TileGS Sort is 3.340ms (1.71x speedup); Base Raster is 7.980ms, TileGS Raster is 5.603ms (1.42x speedup). The total-frame speedup is smaller and not monotonic because the diagnostic includes non-raster and auxiliary overheads not eliminated by the binned raster path. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory usage is reduced in the front end due to attribute compression and key packing. Measured Performance: On an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, the FP32-DRAM balance point is approximately 81.9 FLOPS/Byte. In the Synthetic Scale-Up Stress Diagnostic, TileGS showed consistent improvements in sort and raster stages as workload increased. Scaling: The absolute timing gaps between optimized and baseline stages widen with scale. The total-frame speedup is not monotonic and is smaller than individual stage speedups due to auxiliary overheads. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Tailors optimizations to specific hardware bottlenecks, leading to significant speedups in critical stages. Limitations: The total-frame speedup may be limited by non-optimized auxiliary overheads. The method requires detailed hardware-specific knowledge (e.g., P{\text{peak}}, BW). When to use it: When optimizing a rendering pipeline for a specific hardware target where different stages have distinct bottlenecks. When memory bandwidth is a significant constraint in the front end. When not to use it: When the pipeline is uniformly compute-bound or memory-bound across all stages, as the stage-wise differentiation offers less benefit. When hardware specifications are unknown or highly variable. Roofline-guided stage-wise optimization is part of the RoofGS framework, presented in "RoofGS: Roofline-Guided End-to-End Acceleration of 3D Gaussian Splatting". It builds on the Roofline model to identify dominant bottlenecks in the 3DGS rendering pipeline. The method addresses the limited attention to coordinated software optimization across the whole rendering pipeline in prior work. It is used in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering acceleration. name: Tile-Based Comparison-Free Sorting
head: Comparison-Free Depth Sorting, Tile-Local Sorting
body: Tile-Based Comparison-Free Sorting restricts depth sorting operations to individual image tiles to avoid global synchronization, reduce hardware complexity, and achieve fixed latency per output. It solves the bottleneck of sorting millions of Gaussian points globally by leveraging the fact that alpha blending only requires correct depth ordering within the local tile. Unlike full-scene radix sort, which incurs high memory overhead and variable latency, this method provides deterministic, linear delay cycles suitable for low-power hardware. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of 3D Gaussians projected into screen space, each associated with a tile ID and a view-space depth value. Output: Gaussians ordered front-to-back within each tile, ready for alpha blending. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian primitive carries a tileid (identifying the 16 \times 16 tile it overlaps) and depth (view-space depth). Element Vector Table (EVT): A bit-vector of size N (where N is the number of Gaussians in the current tile/batch), initialized to all 1s to track unsorted elements. Algorithm Steps: The sorting process identifies the Largest Element (LE) iteratively until all elements are sorted. 1. Initialization: Initialize the EVT with all 1s. This indicates that all N elements are currently candidates for being the largest remaining element. 2. Iterative Selection: Repeat the following steps N times (once for each Gaussian to be sorted): a. Concurrent Phase: Process the N n-bit depth values using k parallel clusters. Each cluster handles a partition of the elements. Starting from the most significant bit (MSB), the clusters filter out smaller values through bitwise AND operations and multiplexer-based selection in cascaded blocks. b. Sequential Phase: Pass the outputs from the concurrent phase to a linear array of k cascaded blocks to further refine the selection and identify the single Largest Element (LE) among the candidates marked by the EVT. c. Conflict Resolution: If multiple elements have identical depth values, the EVT may return multiple candidates. Resolve this using bitwise inverter, bitwise AND, and an adder to compute the unique index of the first candidate: FO{NEW} = Fo \& (\sim Fo + 1'b1) where Fo is the output vector from the selection phase. d. Update EVT: Clear the bit corresponding to the identified LE in the EVT (set to 0). This removes the sorted element from future consideration. 3. Termination: The loop ends when the EVT contains all 0s, signaling that all N elements have been sorted. Parameters and Optimizations: Sorting Key: The primary key is \langle \text{tile-id}, \text{depth} \rangle. Sorting is performed independently per tile. Sign Bit Skipping: Since near-plane culling excludes points with depth < 0, the sign bit of the depth value is always 0. The algorithm skips operations on the sign bit to reduce computational overhead. Bit Width (n): Determined by the precision required for view-space depth. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Duplicate Depths: The conflict resolution logic (FO{NEW}) is critical to handle duplicate depth values correctly, ensuring deterministic ordering even when Gaussians share the same depth. Variable N: The number of Gaussians per tile varies significantly across scenes and views. The hardware must handle this variability without pipeline stalls. A tile-based, comparison-free sorting algorithm for Gaussian points that uses an Element Vector Table (EVT) to identify the largest element in O(N) deterministic cycles, avoiding the high memory overhead of radix sort. It employs concurrent and sequential phases to filter elements based on bit significance, optimized by skipping the sign bit and resolving data conflicts via bitwise operations. Time Complexity: O(N) deterministic cycles for sorting N elements. Hardware Complexity: Low gate count compared to radix sort, as it uses simple logic gates (AND, OR, MUX) rather than complex parallel scans or prefix sums. Latency: Fixed, predictable latency per output, avoiding the latency spikes associated with global synchronization in full-scene sorting. Performance: Achieved 129 FPS at Full HD resolution on the described hardware accelerator, offering 3× higher throughput and 5.98× smaller area compared to prior 3DGS accelerators (e.g., GSCore). Strengths: Ideal for low-power AR/VR hardware and predictable scheduling; avoids excess traffic from global resorting. Limitations: Requires hardware implementation to realize the deterministic cycle benefits; software emulation may not match the efficiency gains. Originating from hardware accelerator designs for 3D Gaussian Splatting, this method addresses the computational bottleneck of sorting millions of Gaussian points. Traditional global sorting is resource-intensive and unsuitable for real-time rendering on constrained hardware. The approach builds on parallel comparison-free sorting algorithms [21, 22] (cited in) but introduces optimizations specific to 3DGS, such as sign bit skipping and conflict resolution for duplicate depths. It was implemented in a hardware accelerator achieving real-time Full HD rendering. name: Distributed Training and Sharding
head: Multi-GPU 3D Gaussian Splatting, Distributed 3DGS
body: Distributed Training and Sharding refers to the family of methods that partition the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training and rendering pipeline across multiple GPUs to overcome single-device memory limits and accelerate large-scale reconstruction. It solves the problem of out-of-memory errors and slow training times when processing scenes with tens of millions of primitives or high-resolution scientific volume data. Unlike single-GPU baselines, these methods distribute Gaussian parameters, pixel blocks, or camera views across a GPU cluster, coordinating via communication primitives like all-to-all or all-reduce. What sets this family apart from its siblings is the focus on system-level distribution (sharding the model or data across nodes) rather than just intra-GPU optimization (like tiling or sorting) or inference-specific caching. All methods in this family operate on the standard 3D Gaussian primitive definition provided by the parent article Rendering Implementation and Acceleration. The core rendering operation involves projecting 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space and performing alpha blending. Acceleration strategies generally rely on the following shared mechanisms: 1. Tiling: Dividing the image plane into non-overlapping tiles (commonly 16 \times 16 pixels) to localize Gaussian processing and enable coalesced memory accesses. 2. Sorting: Sorting Gaussians within each tile by view-space depth (front-to-back) to enable correct alpha blending. 3. Culling: Discarding Gaussians that do not overlap with the camera frustum or specific tiles to reduce enumeration overhead. 4. Memory Hierarchy Management: Exploiting the distinction between global memory (VRAM), shared memory (on-chip), and host memory (CPU RAM) to minimize data movement. BlitzGS is a distributed 3DGS framework designed to accelerate city-scale reconstruction by reducing the active Gaussian workload at system, model, and view levels. Unlike spatial block partitioning which suffers from cross-block redundancy and imbalanced shards, BlitzGS shards Gaussians across GPUs by index parity and applies importance-based filtering to prune redundant primitives and gate spawns. It achieves nearly an order-of-magnitude faster training time compared to baselines like Momen.GS and CityGS-X while maintaining high reconstruction quality. GS-Cache is a holistic rendering framework designed to support real-time rendering of large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models, specifically targeting city-level scenes. It achieves an average frame rate exceeding 72 FPS at binocular 2K resolution by employing a cache-centric de-redundancy pipeline and elastic parallel scheduling. Unlike native 3DGS or unstructured methods, GS-Cache specifically targets "Structured Gaussian derivation methods" (such as Scaffold-GS and Octree-GS) that use anchors to derive neural Gaussians, addressing the computational bottleneck of the "Gaussian Derivation Stage" which dominates processing time. It sets itself apart from siblings like BlitzGS and Grendel by focusing on inter-frame redundancy elimination in the anchor decoding phase rather than just rasterization acceleration or distributed sharding. Distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting is a multi-GPU extension of the 3D-GS pipeline designed for scientific visualization, enabling the scalable processing of large datasets that exceed single-GPU memory capacity. It differs from single-GPU baselines by distributing the global point cloud and Gaussian parameters across multiple GPUs, allowing for the reconstruction of scenes with tens of millions of primitives. Unlike BlitzGS which focuses on inference acceleration, this method specifically addresses the training scalability for high-fidelity isosurface reconstruction from scientific volume data. A distributed rendering pipeline that processes camera views in batches, dividing the workload across multiple GPUs to enable high-resolution and large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training and inference that exceeds single-GPU memory limits. It differs from single-GPU rendering by introducing a dynamic strategy phase that maps camera views to GPU tasks, followed by sparse all-to-all communication to distribute Gaussian primitives to the GPUs responsible for rendering specific pixel regions. Unlike methods that process one view at a time, this loop supports batched training using multiple views, improving GPU utilization and scaling rendering quality by increasing the total quantity of Gaussians. Online Image Rendering Placement is a distributed training optimization method that dynamically assigns image patches to GPUs at each training iteration to minimize inter-node communication and balance computational load. It distinguishes itself from static partitioning methods by solving an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) problem online using a fast heuristic solver, allowing it to adapt to the random batch selection inherent in differentiable rendering training. Grendel is a distributed training system for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that partitions parameters and parallelizes computation across multiple GPUs to overcome single-GPU memory constraints in high-resolution and large-scale reconstruction. It distinguishes itself by exploiting mixed parallelism (Gaussian-wise and pixel-wise) and spatial locality to handle dynamic, unbalanced workloads, while supporting batched training with multiple camera views to improve GPU utilization. Unlike systems that rely on dense weight sharding or divide-and-conquer cell partitioning, Grendel uses sparse all-to-all communication to transfer only relevant Gaussians and employs dynamic load balancing to maintain efficiency. Definition: A hardware architecture co-designed with the LS-Gaussian algorithm to support workload-aware mapping, featuring a streaming pipeline that allows continuous processing across hardware modules without requiring global synchronization. Step: The accelerator predicts the workload for each tile based on viewpoint transformation to enable more balanced parallel computation. Comparison: Unlike naive assignment of tiles to rendering blocks which fails to achieve balanced load distribution, this architecture uses workload prediction to mitigate inter-block idling and intra-block bubbles. Definition: Divides the scene into fixed world-space spatial blocks (e.g., uniform grid). Each GPU is bound to a specific block and trains its Gaussians independently. Step: Construct a uniform grid (e.g., 4×5 or 5×6). Assign each block a boundary halo of neighboring Gaussians for cross-block consistency. Train blocks independently across GPUs. During rendering, cameras near block boundaries trigger cross-block visibility overlap and boundary reassignment. Perform a final single-GPU merge to assemble the full scene. Pitfall: Overlapping blocks re-optimize the same surfaces, wasting computation. In a 20-block split, 23.5M Gaussians are optimized but only 5.37M survive merge (77% discarded). Finer partitions increase redundancy and training time with negligible quality gain (<0.2 dB). Number: On Building (1,920 cameras, 4 GPUs), 86.8% of cameras fall in ≥2 blocks for 20-block partition, and 95.5% for 30-block partition. Wall-clock time for split/make-span/merge reaches 115.6–169.8 min vs 39 min for sharding. Definition: Distributes a single global Gaussian model across multiple GPUs by assigning Gaussians to ranks based on index parity. Each GPU holds a balanced, scene-wide slice of the model. Step: Assign each Gaussian primitive to a GPU rank using index parity. During rendering, distribute each step through balanced tile allocation across GPUs. Route projected Gaussians to tile owners via all-to-all communication. Train using a single global camera stream. Each camera enters training once per iteration with no cross-block duplication. Only distributed cost is the all-to-all exchange inside each render step. Number: On a 4-GPU setup (Building scene, 1,920 cameras), communication cost for routing projected Gaussians to tile owners is 3–5 ms per iteration, staying under 7% of total iteration time. Comparison: Unlike spatial block partitioning, it eliminates boundary reassignment, cross-block visibility overlap, and the final single-GPU merge step. Storage and per-step rendering remain evenly distributed as GPU count grows. Definition: A CPU offloading strategy for 3DGS training that transfers all Gaussian attributes to CPU memory before rendering, using pinned memory and CPU Adam. Step: Adopts pre-rendering frustum culling for efficient kernel computation. Trains each batch one image at a time with gradient accumulation to reduce activation memory usage. The need for distributed training in 3D Gaussian Splatting arises from the quadratic growth of memory requirements with scene complexity and resolution. Early 3DGS implementations were limited to single-GPU capacities, typically handling scenes with up to ~10-20 million Gaussians depending on resolution. As applications expanded to city-scale reconstruction and scientific volume visualization, methods like BlitzGS and Distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged to shard the model across multiple GPUs. Concurrently, systems like Grendel and Distributed Batched Rendering Loop focused on optimizing the communication overhead and load balancing inherent in distributed rasterization. The shift from spatial block partitioning to index-parity sharding was driven by the observation that spatial boundaries cause significant redundancy and imbalance in training workloads. name: BlitzGS
head: BlitzGS: City-Scale Gaussian Splatting at Lightning Speed
body: BlitzGS is a distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework designed to accelerate city-scale reconstruction by reducing the active Gaussian workload at system, model, and view levels. It addresses the high computational cost of training large-scale scenes by avoiding the redundancy and imbalance inherent in spatial block partitioning, achieving nearly an order-of-magnitude faster training times compared to baselines like Momen.GS and CityGS-X while maintaining high reconstruction quality. BlitzGS operates on the standard 3DGS primitive definition [21069-rendering-implementation-and-acceleration.md]. It reduces the number of Gaussians processed per iteration through three coupled mechanisms: system-level sharding, model-level population control, and view-level filtering. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, a set of C camera views, and M GPUs. Outputs: Rendered images for the camera views and optimized Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients). Global Gaussian Set \mathcal{G}: The complete set of Gaussians. Shard \mathcal{G}^{(m)}: The subset of Gaussians assigned to GPU m, where m \in \{0, \dots, M-1\}. Tile Ownership: The image plane is divided into tiles. Each tile is assigned to a specific GPU. 1. System-Level Sharding (Index Parity): Instead of partitioning Gaussians by spatial location, BlitzGS shards the global set \mathcal{G} across M GPUs based on index parity (even/odd indices). GPU m stores \mathcal{G}^{(m)} \approx |\mathcal{G}|/M Gaussians and their optimizer states. This avoids cross-block visibility waste and imbalanced shards associated with spatial partitioning. 2. Model-Level Population Control: Importance Scoring: A scoring pass evaluates the importance of each Gaussian. This signal is used to prune redundant Gaussians and reweight density control gradients. Spawn Gating: A lightweight gate predicts whether a candidate Gaussian (from densification) will survive. Candidates predicted not to survive are withheld before spawning, limiting peak population. 3. View-Level Filtering: Distance-based LOD Gate: Gaussians that are too fine-grained for the current camera distance are dropped. Importance Mask: Gaussians with negligible cross-view contribution are skipped, trimming the active set for each camera. 4. Distributed Rendering Loop: Projection: Each GPU m projects its local shard \mathcal{G}^{(m)} to screen space. Tiling and Routing: The image is tiled. Each tile is owned by a specific GPU. An all-to-all communication step routes every projected Gaussian to the GPUs owning the tiles it covers. Rasterization: Each GPU composites pixels for its owned tiles using the received Gaussians. Exchange: A single cross-GPU exchange ensures each device holds the necessary data for its assigned tiles. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def blitzgstraining(gaussians, cameras, numgpus): # 1. System-Level Sharding by Index Parity # Split global Gaussian list into M shards based on index parity shards = [g[i::numgpus] for i in range(numgpus)] # Assign tiles to GPUs (load balancers ensure balanced assignment) tileowners = assigntilestogpus(numgpus) for iteration in range(maxiterations): # 2. Model-Level Population Control # Compute importance scores for current Gaussians importancescores = computeimportance(gaussians) # Prune redundant Gaussians based on importance gaussians = prunegaussians(gaussians, importancescores) # Spawn gating: predict survival of new candidates # (Implementation detail: specific neural network or heuristic for prediction) candidates = densifygaussians(gaussians) survivingcandidates = spawngate(candidates, importancescores) gaussians = merge(gaussians, survivingcandidates) # Reweight density control gradients using importance signal # (Implementation detail: gradient modification step) # 3. View-Level Filtering activegaussians = [] for cam in cameras: # Distance-based LOD gate lodfiltered = filterbydistance(gaussians, cam) # Importance-based mask viewfiltered = filterbyimportance(lodfiltered, cam, importancescores) activegaussians.append(viewfiltered) # 4. Distributed Rendering # Each GPU projects its shard projectedshards = [project(g, cam) for g, cam in zip(shards, cameras)] # All-to-all exchange: route projected Gaussians to tile owners # Each GPU sends its projected Gaussians to GPUs owning the tiles they cover receivedgaussians = alltoallexchange(projectedshards, tileowners) # Rasterize tiles owned by each GPU for gpuid in range(numgpus): tiles = gettilesforgpu(gpuid, tileowners) rendertiles(tiles, receivedgaussians[gpuid]) # Backpropagation and optimization step computelossandupdate(gaussians, shards) Hardware: 4x NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. Sharding Factor: M (number of GPUs). Imbalanced Shards: Index parity sharding is chosen specifically to avoid the imbalanced shards common in spatial partitioning. Cross-Block Redundancy: By sharding by index rather than space, cross-block visibility waste is avoided. Merge Step: Unlike spatial partitioning, BlitzGS does not require a final merge step. Training Time: BlitzGS trains city-scale scenes in tens of minutes. For the Residence scene, it takes 38 minutes (PSNR 24.66 dB). For the Rubble scene, it takes 39 minutes (PSNR 33.79 dB). Comparison: It trains nearly an order of magnitude faster than baselines like Momen.GS (5h 03min, PSNR 31.81) and CityGS-X (4h 45min, PSNR 20.12). Quality: Matches recent baselines in rendering quality on large-scale benchmarks (Mill-19, UrbanScene3D, MatrixCity). Scalability: Storage and per-step compute scale with the GPU count M. Strengths: Significant speedup, no merge step, balanced shards. Limitations: Requires distributed infrastructure; relies on importance scoring and spawn gating which may have overhead if not lightweight. BlitzGS was introduced by Zhongtao Wang, Huishan Au, Yisong Chen, Meng Gai, Yilong Li, Fei Zhu, Mai Su, Haojie Jin, and Guoping Wang in the paper "BlitzGS: City-Scale Gaussian Splatting at Lightning Speed" (arXiv:2605.13794, 2026). It addresses the challenge of city-scale 3D reconstruction, which requires building scenes quickly, using multiple GPUs efficiently, and rendering high-quality free-viewpoint novel views from thousands of calibrated images. The method builds on insights from prior work on distributed 3DGS. name: GS-Cache Inference Framework
head: GS-Cache
body: GS-Cache is a holistic rendering framework designed to support real-time rendering of large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models at the city level, achieving >72 FPS at binocular 2K resolution by using a cache-centric de-redundancy pipeline and elastic parallel scheduling. It specifically targets 'Structured Gaussian derivation methods' (like Scaffold-GS and Octree-GS) which use anchors to derive neural Gaussians, addressing the bottleneck of the 'Gaussian Derivation Stage' (decoding anchor features) which dominates computation time. Unlike native 3DGS or unstructured methods, GS-Cache separates the pipeline into an anchor decoding part (where slight perspective changes cause little color difference, allowing cache optimization) and a rasterizer part (where slight perspective changes significantly affect occlusion, so it cannot be accelerated by cache to maintain quality). Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera parameters (view/projection matrices), current frame index, previous frame cache state, structured 3DGS model (anchors and MLP weights). Output: Rendered image (binocular 2K), updated cache state. Data Structures: Cache: Stores derived Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) for anchors. The cache is indexed by anchor indices mapped from the model. Anchor Set (X): The total set of anchors required for decoding in the current frame. Newly Decoded Anchors (Xk'): The subset of anchors from the previous k frames that were newly decoded (not present in the cache or expired). Numbered Steps: 1. Anchor Indexing: Compute anchor indices from the camera input. These indices filter which anchors need to be decoded and locate existing anchors in the cache. 2. Index Mapping: Translate anchor indices to cache indices. 3. Cache Scheduling: The cache scheduler performs scheduling based on the filtered anchors, loading necessary model parameters for the decoding stage. 4. Dynamic Depth Calculation: Calculate the expected reuse depth using the heuristic function H and the update rate: \text{depth} = H\left(\frac{|Xk'|}{|X|}\right) Where: |Xk'| is the number of newly decoded anchors from the previous k frames. |X| is the total anchor set for decoding in the current frame. H is the guiding function of the heuristic strategy. 5. Decoding and Caching: Gaussian parameters not included in the cache are decoded simultaneously using the AnchorDecoder (typically an MLP). Results from previous frames (cached parameters) are reused for anchors within the cache depth limit. The cache is updated with newly decoded results. The cache depth is adjusted dynamically to balance performance and quality. 6. Rasterization: Perform standard Gaussian rasterization (splatting) using the decoded/cached Gaussian parameters. This stage is not cached to preserve visual quality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gscacherender(camera, model, cache, k, Hfunc): """ Render a single frame using the GS-Cache framework. Args: camera: Camera parameters (view, projection). model: Structured 3DGS model (anchors, MLP weights). cache: Current cache state {anchorindex: gaussianparams}. k: Number of previous frames considered for update rate. Hfunc: Heuristic function for cache depth scheduling. Returns: image: Rendered image. cache: Updated cache state. """ # Step 1: Determine required anchors for current view requiredanchors = getrequiredanchors(camera, model) totalanchors = len(requiredanchors) # Step 2: Identify anchors already in cache cachedanchors = [a for a in requiredanchors if a in cache] uncachedanchors = [a for a in requiredanchors if a not in cache] # Step 3: Calculate update rate and dynamic cache depth # Note: |Xk'| needs to be tracked from previous frames. # For simplicity, assume we have a count of newly decoded anchors in recent history. # In practice, this requires maintaining a history of decoded anchors. newlydecodedcount = getnewlydecodedcountfromhistory(k) updaterate = newlydecodedcount / totalanchors if totalanchors > 0 else 0 # Calculate expected reuse depth reusedepth = Hfunc(updaterate) # Step 4: Decode uncached anchors decodedgaussians = {} for anchor in uncachedanchors: # Decode anchor features using MLP gaussianparams = model.anchordecoder(anchor.features) decodedgaussians[anchor.index] = gaussianparams # Step 5: Merge cached and decoded parameters # Apply reuse depth logic: if an anchor is in cache and its age <= reusedepth, reuse it. # Otherwise, it might need re-decoding or eviction. # For this simplified version, we assume cache hits are valid if within reusedepth. finalgaussians = {} for anchor in requiredanchors: if anchor.index in decodedgaussians: finalgaussians[anchor.index] = decodedgaussians[anchor.index] elif anchor.index in cache: # Check cache age/validity based on reusedepth if iscachevalid(anchor.index, cache, reusedepth): finalgaussians[anchor.index] = cache[anchor.index] else: # Evict and decode gaussianparams = model.anchordecoder(anchor.features) finalgaussians[anchor.index] = gaussianparams else: # Should not happen if logic is correct, but decode if missing gaussianparams = model.anchordecoder(anchor.features) finalgaussians[anchor.index] = gaussianparams # Step 6: Update cache # Add newly decoded/validated parameters to cache for index, params in finalgaussians.items(): if index not in cache or not iscachevalid(index, cache, reusedepth): cache[index] = params # Step 7: Rasterize image = rasterize(finalgaussians, camera) return image, cache def iscachevalid(anchorindex, cache, reusedepth): """ Check if a cached anchor is still valid based on reuse depth. This is a placeholder for the specific validity logic defined by Hfunc and cache management. """ # Implementation detail: Typically involves tracking frame count or timestamp # when the anchor was last updated/decoded. return True # Placeholder Parameters: k: The number of previous frames from which newly decoded anchors (Xk') are considered for the update rate calculation. H: The guiding function of the heuristic cache reuse depth scheduling strategy. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cache Flush: If the same Gaussian appearance parameters are maintained in the cache for too long, it can cause significant rendering errors (e.g., when moving around a centered target). The cache needs to be flushed in time to avoid this. Rapid Appearance Changes: Static cache reuse depth can cause rapid changes in scene appearance when the cache is flushed. Dynamic scheduling helps suppress this. Quality vs. Speed: Inter-frame reuse of derivation stage results must be restrained by conditions to ensure correctness within an acceptable range. Performance: Achieves an average frame rate exceeding 72 FPS at binocular 2K resolution for large-scale city-level scenes. Complexity: The framework reduces computational redundancy in the Gaussian Derivation Stage, which is a bottleneck for structured Gaussian methods. The rasterization stage remains computationally intensive but is not cached. Scalability: Designed for large-scale 3D scenes (city level) and VR applications. Strengths: Significant speedup for structured Gaussian derivation methods by caching decoded anchor features. Maintains visual quality by not caching the rasterization stage. Limitations: Requires structured Gaussian representations (anchors + MLP). Performance depends on the effectiveness of the cache reuse strategy and the heuristic function H. GS-Cache was introduced in the paper "A GS-Cache Inference Framework for Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting Models". It addresses the challenges of real-time photo-realistic rendering of large-scale 3DGS models, particularly for VR applications where binocular stereo rendering is required. The framework builds on the patterns of structured Gaussian derivation methods, which use anchors to derive neural Gaussians, and aims to optimize the computationally intensive Gaussian Derivation Stage. name: Distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: Distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting for Scientific Visualization, Distributed 3D-GS, Multi-GPU 3D-GS
body: Distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting is a multi-GPU extension of the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) pipeline designed for scientific visualization, enabling the scalable processing of large datasets that exceed the memory capacity of a single GPU. It differs from single-GPU baselines by distributing the global point cloud and Gaussian parameters across multiple workers, allowing for the reconstruction of scenes with tens of millions of primitives. Unlike BlitzGS which focuses on inference acceleration, this method addresses the fundamental memory bottleneck during the optimization phase. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scientific volume data (e.g., VTK, HDF5), number of GPUs (N{GPU}), image resolution (R \times R), number of synthetic views (N{views}). Output: Optimized set of 3D Gaussian primitives (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) distributed across the GPU cluster. Data Structures: The method relies on the standard 3D Gaussian primitive definition provided by Rendering Implementation and Acceleration. The global state consists of: 1. Point Cloud: A set of 3D points extracted from the isosurface. 2. Gaussian Parameters: For each Gaussian i: mean \mui, covariance matrix \Sigmai (or rotation Ri and scale Si), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients c{i,lm}. Sharding Strategy: The global point cloud and associated Gaussian parameters are partitioned into shards. Each GPU k holds a subset of the Gaussians \mathcal{G}k such that \bigcupk \mathcal{G}k constitutes the full scene. The training data (synthetic views) is also distributed across workers. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Extract isosurface point clouds directly from scientific volume data using ParaView. Initialize Gaussian primitives at these locations. This bypasses image-based reconstruction methods. 2. View Generation: Generate a set of synthetic camera views in a structured orbit. The number of views is set to 448 to support data complexity, an increase from the 250 views used in prior work. 3. Distribution: Distribute the shards of the global point cloud and Gaussian parameters to each GPU. Distribute the corresponding training views to the workers. 4. Forward Pass (Per GPU): Each GPU renders its assigned shard of Gaussians for its assigned views. This involves projecting 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space and performing alpha blending, utilizing the tiling, sorting, and culling mechanisms described in Rendering Implementation and Acceleration. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the reconstruction loss (e.g., L1 loss, D-SSIM) between the rendered images and the ground truth synthetic views for the assigned views. 6. Gradient Synchronization: Synchronize gradients across all GPUs via a fused all-reduce scheme. This ensures that the optimization updates are consistent across the distributed shards. 7. Parameter Update: Update the Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, SH coefficients) using an optimizer (typically Adam) based on the synchronized gradients. 8. Iteration: Repeat steps 4-7 until convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def distributed3dgstraining(volumedata, numgpus, resolution, numviews=448): # 1. Initialization # Extract isosurface point cloud using ParaView (external tool) globalpointcloud = extractisosurfacepointcloud(volumedata) # Initialize Gaussian parameters for all points # Positions, Scales, Rotations, Opacities, SH Coefficients globalgaussians = initializegaussians(globalpointcloud) # 2. Distribution # Shard the global data across GPUs # Each GPU gets a subset of Gaussians and a subset of views localgaussians = sharddata(globalgaussians, rank, numgpus) localviews = generateorbitviews(numviews, rank, numgpus) # 3. Training Loop for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Forward Pass: Render local shard renderedimages = [] for view in localviews: # Project local Gaussians to 2D # Sort by depth, cull, and alpha blend # This uses the acceleration primitives from parent article image = rendergaussians(localgaussians, view.cameraparams) renderedimages.append(image) # Compute Loss # Compare rendered images with ground truth synthetic views loss = computeloss(renderedimages, localviews.groundtruth) # Backward Pass gradients = computegradients(loss, localgaussians) # Synchronize Gradients via All-Reduce # Fused all-reduce scheme to aggregate gradients from all GPUs syncedgradients = allreduce(gradients, op='sum') # Update Parameters # Apply optimizer step (e.g., Adam) localgaussians = updateparameters(localgaussians, syncedgradients) return localgaussians Parameters: Number of synthetic camera views: 448. Image resolutions: 512x512, 1024x1024, 2048x2048. Hardware: NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Limits: A single A100 GPU supports up to approximately 11.2M Gaussians. Datasets larger than this (e.g., Miranda with ~18M Gaussians) are infeasible on a single GPU due to memory exhaustion. Data Complexity: Insufficient number of views (e.g., 250) may fail to capture the complexity of scientific data, necessitating an increase to 448 views. Time Complexity: Training time scales with the number of Gaussians, views, and resolution. The method demonstrates near-linear speedup with the number of GPUs. For the Kingsnake dataset (4M Gaussians) at 2048x2048 resolution, 4 GPUs provide a 5.6x speedup compared to 1 GPU (8.50 min vs 48.00 min). Memory Complexity: Memory usage is distributed. The total memory required is proportional to the number of Gaussians divided by the number of GPUs. This allows training on datasets exceeding single-GPU VRAM (e.g., 18M Gaussians on 4 A100s). Strengths: Enables high-resolution reconstruction of large-scale scientific data that cannot fit on a single GPU. Improves training throughput significantly. Limitations: Requires a multi-GPU setup and network bandwidth for gradient synchronization. Performance is limited by the slowest GPU and communication overhead. When to use: When the number of Gaussian primitives exceeds the memory capacity of a single GPU (e.g., >11.2M on A100) or when high-resolution training on large datasets is required. When not to use: For small datasets that fit comfortably on a single GPU, where the overhead of distributed training may not be justified. Origin: The method was presented by Mateevitsi, Papka, Petruzza, and Sizzi in 2025. History: It builds on previous work by Sewell et al. [4] which demonstrated high-fidelity isosurface reconstruction using Gaussian primitives from scientific volume data. It adapts the distributed training design from Grendel-GS [6] to the 3D-GS pipeline. Usage: Designed for HPC-based scientific workflows, enabling real-time post hoc and in situ visualization of complex simulations. Toward Distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting for High-Resolution Isosurface Visualization, https://doi.org/10.1109/escience65000.2025.00056, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Distributed Batched Rendering Loop
head: Distributed 3DGS Rendering Loop
body: A distributed rendering pipeline that processes camera views in batches, divides workload across multiple GPUs, preprocesses 3D Gaussian Splatting data, performs all-to-all communication, renders, and aggregates results across ranks. It enables high-resolution and large-scale 3D reconstruction by overcoming single-GPU memory limits through parallel computation and increased batch sizes. Unlike systems that process one camera view at a time, this method supports batched training using multiple views to better utilize distributed GPU resources. Inputs: A dataset of camera poses and intrinsics. 3D Gaussian primitives (positions, covariances, opacities, spherical harmonics coefficients). Pipeline configuration (projection matrices, background color). Distributed training parameters (args.bsz, args.samplefreq, args.generatenum). Outputs: Rendered images for the batched cameras. Aggregated gradients (implicit in training context, though the loop description focuses on rendering/evaluation steps). Data Structures: batchedcameras: List of camera parameters for the current batch. batchedstrategies: Mapping of camera views to GPU tasks. gpuid2tasks: Dictionary mapping GPU IDs to specific rendering tasks/cameras. batchedscreenspacepkg: Data structure holding preprocessed 3DGS data and screenspace packages for distributed rendering. strategyhistory: History of previous scheduling decisions (used for load balancing). Steps: 1. Batch Iteration: Iterate over the total number of cameras in steps of args.bsz. 2. Camera Fetch: Retrieve the next batch of cameras. If the remaining cameras are fewer than args.bsz, fetch only the remaining ones. 3. Strategy Calculation: Compute the workload division and GPU-to-task mapping based on the current batch and strategyhistory. This determines which GPU handles which camera view. 4. Data Transfer: Transfer camera data from CPU memory to all GPUs according to the calculated strategy. 5. Preprocessing and Communication: Preprocess the 3DGS data for the batch and execute an all-to-all communication step across GPUs. This distributes the relevant Gaussian primitives to the GPUs responsible for rendering the specific camera views in the batch. 6. Rendering: Execute the rendering kernel for each GPU on its assigned portion of the batch. 7. Aggregation: If distributed across multiple ranks, aggregate the rendered images using a sum reduction operation. 8. Post-processing: Clamp pixel values to the valid range [0.0, 1.0] and save the images if the sampling frequency condition is met. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: dataset: Dataset object providing camera poses. gaussians: 3D Gaussian primitive data. pipeline: Rendering pipeline configuration. background: Background color tensor. args: Argument namespace containing bsz, samplefreq, generatenum. utils: Utility module containing DEFAULTGROUP. """ numcameras = len(dataset) strategyhistory = [] # Initialize history for load balancing # Limit generation if generatenum is specified maxiterations = (args.generatenum + args.bsz - 1) // args.bsz if args.generatenum > 0 else (numcameras + args.bsz - 1) // args.bsz for idx in range(1, numcameras + 1, args.bsz): # Calculate number of cameras to load in this batch numcameratoload = min(args.bsz, numcameras - idx + 1) # Fetch batched cameras batchedcameras = dataset.getbatchedcameras(numcameratoload) # Compute workload division and GPU-to-task mapping # This function likely uses strategyhistory to balance load batchedstrategies, gpuid2tasks = startstrategyfinal(batchedcameras, strategyhistory) # Transfer camera data from CPU to all GPUs loadcamerafromcputoallgpuforeval(batchedcameras, batchedstrategies, gpuid2tasks) # Preprocess 3DGS data and execute all-to-all communication # Distributes Gaussians to GPUs based on which cameras they affect batchedscreenspacepkg = distributedpreprocess3dgsandall2allfinal( batchedcameras, gaussians, pipeline, background, batchedstrategies=batchedstrategies, mode="test") # Render the batched images batchedimage, = renderfinal(batchedscreenspacepkg, batchedstrategies) # Aggregate rendered images across distributed ranks using sum reduction if utils.DEFAULTGROUP.size() > 1: # Note: In a training loop, this would typically be backward pass aggregation. # In an evaluation/inference loop, sum reduction might be used for specific metrics # or if overlapping tiles are rendered. For standard independent camera rendering, # this step might be conditional or used for gradient accumulation in training. # Based on source, it is explicitly present. torch.distributed.allreduce(batchedimage, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM, group=utils.DEFAULTGROUP) # Clamp pixel values to valid range image = torch.clamp(batchedimage, 0.0, 1.0) # Save images if sampling frequency allows if args.samplefreq != -1 and (idx % args.samplefreq == 0 or idx == numcameras): torchvision.utils.saveimage(image, f"render{idx}.png") # Update strategy history for next iteration (implementation detail inferred from source context) strategyhistory.append(batchedstrategies) def startstrategyfinal(batchedcameras, strategyhistory): """ Computes the distribution strategy for the current batch. Returns: batchedstrategies: Mapping of cameras to GPUs. gpuid2tasks: Mapping of GPU IDs to tasks. """ # Implementation details depend on the specific load balancing algorithm. # Typically involves analyzing camera frustums and Gaussian distribution. # Placeholder for specific load balancing logic not fully detailed in source. pass def loadcamerafromcputoallgpuforeval(batchedcameras, batchedstrategies, gpuid2tasks): """ Transfers camera parameters to the appropriate GPUs. """ # Implementation involves torch.cuda.setdevice and tensor copying. pass def distributedpreprocess3dgsandall2allfinal(batchedcameras, gaussians, pipeline, background, batchedstrategies, mode): """ Preprocesses Gaussians and performs all-to-all communication. """ # Implementation involves computing bounding boxes, sorting, and # torch.distributed.alltoallsingle calls. pass def renderfinal(batchedscreenspacepkg, batchedstrategies): """ Executes the rendering kernel. """ # Implementation involves the standard 3DGS rasterization pipeline. pass Parameters: args.bsz: Batch size for camera processing. Controls how many views are processed per iteration. Typical values depend on GPU memory and scene complexity. args.samplefreq: Sampling frequency for saving renders. If != -1, only saves every args.samplefreq-th image. args.generatenum: Maximum number of images to generate before breaking the loop. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Limits: The primary motivation is overcoming single-GPU memory limits. If args.bsz is too large for the collective memory bandwidth or communication overhead, performance may degrade. Load Imbalance: Uneven distribution of Gaussians across camera views can lead to stragglers. The startstrategyfinal function attempts to mitigate this using strategyhistory. Communication Overhead: The all-to-all communication step can become a bottleneck if the number of Gaussians is very large or the network bandwidth is limited. A load balancing strategy for distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting training that groups pixels into 16x16 blocks to reduce scheduler overhead while maintaining workload balance across GPUs. Instead of scheduling individual pixels, it organizes all pixels from all images in a batch into a single row, divides this row into 16x16 pixel blocks, and allocates these blocks to GPUs. This trades off scheduler overhead against uneven workloads due to additional blocks. After scheduling, a 2D boolean array computelocally[i][j] is generated, indicating whether the pixel block at the i-th row and j-th column should be computed by the local GPU. Rendering is then performed only for pixels within blocks where computelocally is true. The block size is fixed at 16x16 pixels. Time Complexity: Dominated by the preprocessing, all-to-all communication, and rendering steps. The communication cost scales with the number of Gaussians and the number of GPUs. The rendering cost scales with the number of pixels and the number of Gaussians per pixel. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of Gaussians and the batch size. By distributing Gaussians and pixels, it allows for larger scenes than a single GPU can handle. Measured Performance: On the "Rubble" dataset, distributing 40.4 million Gaussians across 16 GPUs achieved a test PSNR of 27.28, compared to 26.28 PSNR with 11.2 million Gaussians on a single GPU. Strengths: Enables training on high-resolution and large-scale scenes that exceed single-GPU memory capacity. Supports batched training for better GPU utilization. Limitations: Communication overhead can be significant. Load balancing is non-trivial due to the sparse and dynamic nature of Gaussian visibility. When to Use: Large-scale 3D reconstruction tasks requiring high resolution and large numbers of Gaussians. When Not to Use: Small scenes that fit comfortably on a single GPU, where the overhead of distributed communication may outweigh the benefits. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023, offering real-time radiance field rendering with superior visual quality. However, initial implementations were limited to single-GPU training, restricting the scale of reconstructable scenes. Grendel, introduced by the NYU Systems group, addresses this by partitioning 3DGS parameters and parallelizing computation across multiple GPUs. It relies on sparse all-to-all communication and dynamic load balancing to handle the changing subset of pixels affected by each Gaussian. The method explores learning rate scaling strategies, identifying a simple sqrt(batch size) rule as effective. name: Online Image Rendering Placement
head: Image patch placement, Online placement of image rendering
body:
Online Image Rendering Placement is a per-iteration optimization step in distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting training that assigns image patches to GPUs to minimize inter-node communication and balance computational load. Unlike offline graph partitioning which clusters both points and images for the entire dataset, this method dynamically determines rendering assignments for a small, randomly selected batch of images at each training step. It distinguishes itself by operating at the granularity of image patches rather than whole images, enabling finer-grained load balancing and reduced communication overhead in large-scale multi-GPU setups. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A batch of B image patches (derived from B training images), the current 3D Gaussian point cloud partitioned across N GPUs, and configuration coefficients \alpha,  eta, \gamma, \delta. Outputs: A placement vector W where Wj is the GPU ID assigned to render image patch j. Data Structures: Access Pattern Matrix A: A B 	imes N matrix where A{j,k} is the number of 3D Gaussian points required from GPU k to render image patch j. This is determined by frustum culling on each GPU. Placement Vector W: An array of length B, where each element is an integer in \{0, \dots, N-1\}. Steps: 1. Frustum Culling: Each GPU k receives the entire batch of B image patches. It performs frustum culling against its locally stored 3D Gaussians to determine which points are visible for each patch. 2. Exchange Access Patterns: All GPUs exchange their culling results to construct the global access pattern matrix A, where A{j,k} represents the count of points needed from GPU k for patch j. 3. Initial Placement via Linear Sum Assignment (LSA): Solve a Linear Sum Assignment problem to minimize total communication volume. The objective is to minimize \sum{j=1}^{B} \sum{k 
eq Wj} A{j,k}, subject to the constraint that each GPU is assigned exactly B/N patches. This yields an initial placement W{init}. 4. Local Search Refinement: Iteratively refine W{init} to balance load. In each step, swap the GPU assignments of two image patches if it reduces the relaxed objective function. Continue until convergence or a time budget is exhausted. 5. Hierarchical Assignment (Optional): If nodes contain multiple GPUs, first assign patches across machines, then assign a machine's patches among its local GPUs. For intra-node assignment, set \alpha=0 to de-prioritize communication. Formulas: The ILP formulation aims to minimize: \alpha \cdot \sum{j=1}^{B} \sum{k 
eq Wj} A{j,k} +  eta \cdot \maxk (	ext{send}k) + \gamma \cdot \maxk (	ext{recv}k) + \delta \cdot \maxk (	ext{comp}k) Subject to: \sum{j=1}^{B} [Wj = k] =  rac{B}{N}, \quad  orall k \in \{1, \dots, N\} Where the loads for GPU k are: 	ext{send}k = \sum{j=1}^{B} [Wj 
eq k] \cdot A{j,k} 	ext{recv}k = \sum{j=1}^{B} [Wj = k] \cdot \left( \sum{i=1}^{N} A{j,i} - A{j,k} ight) 	ext{comp}k = \sum{j=1}^{B} [Wj = k] \cdot \sum{i=1}^{N} A{j,i} To avoid plateaus in local search, the max terms are replaced with p-norms in the relaxed objective:  eta \cdot \|	ext{send}\|p + \gamma \cdot \|	ext{recv}\|p + \delta \cdot \|	ext{comp}\|p where \|	ext{send}\|p = \left( \sum{k} 	ext{send}k^p ight)^{1/p}. Parameters: B: Batch size of training images. Typical value: 16–64. N: Number of GPUs. p: Power for the p-norm relaxation. Not given in the sources. \alpha,  eta, \gamma, \delta: Configurable coefficients. \alpha weights communication,  eta send imbalance, \gamma receive imbalance, \delta compute imbalance. p{grid}: Grid subdivision factor. Each H 	imes W image is divided into p{grid}^2 patches. Typical p{grid}: 2–8. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def onlineimagerenderingplacement(batchpatches, pointclouds, numgpus, alpha, beta, gamma, delta, pnorm=2, timebudget=1.0): """ batchpatches: List of B image patches. pointclouds: List of N point clouds, one per GPU. numgpus: N. Returns: W, list of GPU IDs for each patch. """ B = len(batchpatches) # Step 1 & 2: Frustum Culling and Access Matrix Construction # Each GPU k determines which points from its local cloud are needed for each patch # A[j, k] = number of points from GPU k needed for patch j A = zeros((B, numgpus)) for k in range(numgpus): for j in range(B): # Perform frustum culling for patch j against pointclouds[k] visiblepoints = frustumcull(batchpatches[j], pointclouds[k]) A[j, k] = len(visiblepoints) # Step 3: Linear Sum Assignment for initial placement # Minimize total communication: sum over j of sum over k!=W[j] of A[j,k] # Constraint: Each GPU gets exactly B/N patches # This is a standard LSA problem. We construct a cost matrix C where C[j, k] = A[j, k] # But we want to minimize communication, which is sum{k != W[j]} A[j,k]. # Note: sum{k != W[j]} A[j,k] = (sum{all k} A[j,k]) - A[j, W[j]] # Minimizing sum{j} (TotalA[j] - A[j, W[j]]) is equivalent to Maximizing sum{j} A[j, W[j]] # So we maximize the diagonal elements in the assignment. # Construct cost matrix for LSA (maximization problem converted to minimization) # Cost[j, k] = -A[j, k] costmatrix = -A # Solve LSA using Hungarian algorithm # Returns rowindices, colindices where colindices[j] is the GPU assigned to patch j rowindices, colindices = hungarianalgorithm(costmatrix) Winit = colindices # Step 4: Local Search Refinement W = Winit.copy() starttime = time.time() while time.time() - starttime < timebudget: improved = False # Try swapping assignments of two patches for i in range(B): for j in range(i + 1, B): # Calculate current objective currentobj = computerelaxedobjective(W, A, numgpus, beta, gamma, delta, pnorm) # Try swap W[i], W[j] = W[j], W[i] newobj = computerelaxedobjective(W, A, numgpus, beta, gamma, delta, pnorm) if newobj < currentobj: improved = True # Keep the swap else: # Revert swap W[i], W[j] = W[j], W[i] if not improved: break return W def computerelaxedobjective(W, A, numgpus, beta, gamma, delta, pnorm): B = len(W) send = zeros(numgpus) recv = zeros(numgpus) comp = zeros(numgpus) for k in range(numgpus): for j in range(B): if W[j] != k: send[k] += A[j, k] if W[j] == k: totalpointsforpatch = sum(A[j,:]) recv[k] += (totalpointsforpatch - A[j, k]) comp[k] += totalpointsforpatch # Compute p-norms sendnorm = (sum(spnorm for s in send))(1/pnorm) recvnorm = (sum(rpnorm for r in recv))(1/pnorm) compnorm = (sum(cpnorm for c in comp))(1/pnorm) return beta sendnorm + gamma recvnorm + delta compnorm Edge Cases and Pitfalls: ILP Solver Performance: Standard ILP solvers like Gurobi are too slow and unpredictable for online optimization within a training iteration. The heuristic LSA+local search approach is necessary. Granularity: Using whole images for placement severely limits scalability when the number of GPUs is large, as the batch size B is small (16–64). Patching allows finer-grained assignment. Intra-node Communication: For GPUs within the same node, communication bandwidth is high. Setting \alpha=0 for intra-node assignment de-prioritizes communication volume, focusing on load balancing. Time Complexity: The LSA step using the Hungarian method has a time complexity of O(B^3). The local search step's complexity depends on the number of swaps performed and the time budget, but is generally kept small to fit within the training iteration time. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the access pattern matrix A of size B 	imes N and the placement vector W of size B. This is negligible compared to the point cloud data. Strengths: Reduces inter-node communication by co-locating rendering with data access. Balances computational load across GPUs. Works online, adapting to the random batch selection in each training step. Limitations: The heuristic may not find the global optimum. The local search requires a time budget, which adds latency to each training iteration if not carefully tuned. When to Use: Large-scale distributed training of 3D Gaussian Splatting with many GPUs and limited inter-node bandwidth. When Not to Use: Small-scale setups with few GPUs where communication overhead is minimal, or when the overhead of the placement algorithm exceeds the communication savings. Online Image Rendering Placement was introduced in the Gaian system for scaling point-based differentiable rendering for large-scale reconstruction. It addresses the limitations of offline graph partitioning, which is static and does not adapt to the dynamic nature of training batches. The method leverages Linear Sum Assignment and local search to provide a fast, effective solution for dynamic resource allocation in distributed rendering.
