name: Splat and Replace
head: 3D Reconstruction with Repetitive Elements
body: Splat and Replace is a method that improves novel view synthesis in scenes containing repetitive elements by segmenting repeated instances in a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstruction, registering them into a common coordinate frame, and fusing them into a shared template representation. It addresses the problem of poor geometry and appearance in low-coverage or occluded regions by allowing information to flow from well-captured instances to partially-occluded ones. Unlike standard 3DGS which treats instances independently, this method exploits structural repetition to enhance reconstruction quality, using a Spherical Harmonics (SH) offset representation for appearance variations rather than complex MLPs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A base 3DGS reconstruction (set of 3D Gaussian primitives with position, covariance, opacity, and SH coefficients), learning-based 2D masks (e.g., SAM-HQ), a single user click per repetitive instance to identify them, and training images for fine-tuning. Output: An optimized shared template representation (union of 3D Gaussian primitives) that replaces the individual instances, improving novel view synthesis quality. Data Structures: 3D Gaussian Primitive: Standard 3DGS structure containing position \mathbf{p}, covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma} (or rotation \mathbf{R} and scale \mathbf{s}), opacity \alpha, and Spherical Harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}{SH}. Shared Template: A single set of 3D Gaussian primitives representing the fused geometry of all instances. Instance Offsets: For appearance, each instance i has a learnable offset \Delta \mathbf{c}{SH}^{(i)} applied to the shared SH coefficients. Steps: 1. Instance Segmentation: Use learning-based 2D masks (e.g., SAM-HQ) combined with a single user click per instance to generate initial 2D masks for each repetitive object. Train contrastive features to perform 3D instance segmentation on the base 3DGS reconstruction. Apply additional regularization and post-processing to remove residual artifacts and ensure clean 3D segmentation of instances. 2. Instance Registration: Render additional high-quality views for each segmented instance using the base 3DGS reconstruction. Select the best pairs of views for matching using a fast 2D matcher. Find robust 2D matches between view pairs using MASt3R. Lift the 2D matches to 3D coordinates using the depth information provided by the 3DGS rendering of those views. Use a PnP-RANSAC solver to compute the rigid transformation (rotation \mathbf{R}i and translation \mathbf{t}i) for each instance i, registering all instances to a common coordinate frame. 3. Shared Representation Construction: Build the shared template by taking the union of all 3D Gaussian primitives from all registered instances. This creates a dense, high-quality geometric prior for the repetitive object type. 4. Fine-tuning and Optimization: Perform a fine-tuning step where gradients flow from each instance's rendered image back to the shared template. This process improves the overall reconstruction, completing partially-occluded instances based on visible parts of other instances and enhancing low-quality geometry from poor capture coverage. Model appearance differences (illumination, texture variations) between instances using an offset representation for Spherical Harmonics: \mathbf{c}{SH}^{(i)} = \mathbf{c}{SH}^{\text{shared}} + \Delta \mathbf{c}{SH}^{(i)} where \mathbf{c}{SH}^{\text{shared}} are the coefficients of the shared template and \Delta \mathbf{c}{SH}^{(i)} are the learnable offsets for instance i. This approach is faster than using a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to model appearance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def splatandreplace(base3dgs, trainingimages, userclicks, masks): # Step 1: Instance Segmentation # Use learning-based 2D masks and user clicks to identify instances instance2dmasks = [mask.crop(click) for mask, click in zip(masks, userclicks)] # Train contrastive features for 3D segmentation # Note: Architecture follows prior contrastive learning work instance3dmasks = traincontrastivefeatures3d(base3dgs, instance2dmasks) # Apply regularization and post-processing to remove artifacts cleaninstancemasks = applyregularizationpostprocessing(instance3dmasks) # Step 2: Instance Registration registeredtransforms = [] for instanceid in range(len(cleaninstancemasks)): # Render additional high-quality views for this instance renderedviews = renderadditionalviews(base3dgs, cleaninstancemasks[instanceid]) # Select best pairs of views with a fast 2D matcher bestviewpairs = selectbestviewpairs(renderedviews) # Find robust 2D matches using MASt3R matches2d = find2dmatchesmastr(bestviewpairs) # Lift 2D matches to 3D using depth from 3DGS matches3d = lift2dto3d(matches2d, renderedviews) # Register instances using PnP-RANSAC solver transform = computepnpransac(matches3d) registeredtransforms.append(transform) # Step 3: Shared Representation Construction # Union of all 3D Gaussian primitives from registered instances sharedtemplate = unionallprimitives(base3dgs, registeredtransforms) # Step 4: Fine-tuning and Optimization # Initialize learnable SH offsets for each instance shoffsets = [zeroslike(sharedtemplate.sh) for in range(len(cleaninstancemasks))] # Optimization loop for iteration in range(1000): totalloss = 0.0 for instanceid, transform in enumerate(registeredtransforms): # Apply rigid transform to shared template primitives instanceprimitives = applyrigidtransform(sharedtemplate, transform) # Apply SH offset for instance-specific appearance instancesh = sharedtemplate.sh + shoffsets[instanceid] # Render image and compute loss against ground truth renderedimage = renderprimitives(instanceprimitives, instancesh) totalloss += computerenderingloss(renderedimage, trainingimages[instanceid]) # Backpropagate gradients to shared template and SH offsets updateparameters(sharedtemplate, shoffsets, totalloss) return sharedtemplate, shoffsets def traincontrastivefeatures3d(base3dgs, instance2dmasks): return [segmentinstanceviacontrastivelearning(base3dgs, mask) for mask in instance2dmasks] def applyregularizationpostprocessing(instance3dmasks): return [removeartifactsviaregularization(mask) for mask in instance3dmasks] def renderadditionalviews(base3dgs, instancemask): return [renderview(base3dgs, camerapose) for camerapose in generatenovelcameras()] def selectbestviewpairs(renderedviews): return findbestmatchingpairs(renderedviews, matcher="fast2d") def find2dmatchesmastr(viewpairs): return mastrmatch(viewpairs) def lift2dto3d(matches2d, renderedviews): return triangulate3d(matches2d, renderedviews.depthmaps) def computepnpransac(matches3d): return solvepnpransac(matches3d) def unionallprimitives(base3dgs, transforms): mergedprimitives = [] for prim in base3dgs: for t in transforms: mergedprimitives.append(applytransformtoprimitive(prim, t)) return GaussianSet(mergedprimitives) def updateparameters(sharedtemplate, shoffsets, loss): sharedtemplate.sh -= learningrate gradient(loss, sharedtemplate.sh) for i in range(len(shoffsets)): shoffsets[i] -= learningrate gradient(loss, shoffsets[i]) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noisy Geometry: Standard 3DGS data is noisy and does not correspond well to underlying geometry because it optimizes for image radiance rather than geometry, necessitating rendered views and robust 2D matching instead of direct point-cloud matching. Occlusion: Partially occluded instances are completed based on visible instances, improving low-quality geometry from poor capture coverage. Time Complexity: The method involves rendering additional views, 2D matching, and PnP-RANSAC for each instance, followed by a fine-tuning optimization loop. The use of SH offsets is faster than MLP-based appearance modeling. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the shared template plus per-instance SH offsets, alongside the base 3DGS reconstruction during the registration phase. Performance: Evaluated on synthetic and real data with independent test trajectories, outperforming other generalization solutions for scenes with repetitive elements. Strengths: Improves geometry and appearance in poorly captured or occluded regions by leveraging repetition. Limitations: Only applicable to scenes with repetitive elements and requires user interaction (one click per instance) and initial 2D masks. Splat and Replace was proposed to address the limitations of 3D Gaussian Splatting in scenes with repetitive elements, where poor coverage or occlusion leads to low-quality reconstruction. It builds on prior work in novel view synthesis, 3D segmentation, and 3D registration. The method was evaluated on synthetic and real data, demonstrating substantial improvements in novel view synthesis quality. name: Shared Representation for Repetitive Elements
head: Instance Sharing, Shared 3DGS
body: This method improves the 3D reconstruction of repetitive objects by creating a single shared Gaussian representation for all instances of the same object type. It allows information propagation, such as geometry completion and detail propagation, across instances while handling appearance differences via per-instance offsets. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting where each instance is independent, this method shares geometry parameters across instances, improving reconstruction quality for occluded or low-quality regions by leveraging multi-view information from all instances. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Initial camera poses, an initial set of 3D Gaussians for each instance, and a pre-identification of instances belonging to the same object type. Outputs: A shared set of 3D Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, shared SH coefficients) and per-instance parameters (rigid transformation, SH offset coefficients). Data Structures: The method maintains two primary data structures for each object type: 1. Shared Representation: A list of Gaussian primitives. Each primitive stores: \mathbf{p}{\text{shared}}: Position (3 floats). \mathbf{s}{\text{shared}}: Scale (3 floats). \mathbf{q}{\text{shared}}: Rotation (4 floats, quaternion). \alpha{\text{shared}}: Opacity (1 float). \mathbf{c}{\text{shared}}^{\ell m}: Shared Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients for degree \ell and order m (3 floats per coefficient). 2. Instance Parameters: For each instance i of the object type: \mathbf{T}i: Rigid transformation matrix (4x4) mapping instance space to template space. \mathbf{c}{\text{offset}, i}^{\ell m}: Per-instance SH offset coefficients (3 floats per coefficient). Numbered Steps: 1. Transform all instance Gaussians into a common template coordinate system using computed rigid transformations. 2. Create the initial shared representation by taking the union of all instances in this common coordinate system. 3. For each Gaussian primitive, share all parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity) across all instances of the same object. 4. Decompose Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients into a shared component and an instance-specific offset term. 5. Optimization: Replace each instance with a reference to the shared representation. Apply per-instance geometric transform and SH offset during rendering. Propagate gradients from all instances to the shared representation. Jointly optimize shared geometry, SHs, and pose parameters using gradient descent. Formula: \mathbf{c}^{\ell m} = \lambda \mathbf{c}{\text{shared}}^{\ell m} + (1 - \lambda) \mathbf{c}{\text{offset}}^{\ell m} where \ell is the SH degree, m is the order, \mathbf{c}{\text{shared}}^{\ell m} is the shared SH coefficient, \mathbf{c}{\text{offset}}^{\ell m} is the per-instance offset coefficient, and \lambda is a mixing weight set to 0.8. Run ICP on Gaussian centers, initialized with coarse pose # Standard ICP algorithm to find rigid transform T = instance['initialpose'] instancetransforms.append(T) templategaussians = [] for instance, T in zip(instances, instancetransforms): for g in instance['gaussians']: posnew = T[:3,:3] @ g['pos'] + T[:3, 3] templategaussians.append({g, 'pos': posnew}) return templategaussians, instancetransforms def computeshcoefficients(cshared, coffset, lam): # Formula: c^lm = lambda cshared^lm + (1 - lambda) coffset^lm return lam cshared + (1 - lam) coffset def rendersharedinstance(sharedgaussians, instancetransform, instanceshoffsets, camera): # Replace each instance with a reference to the shared representation # Apply per-instance geometric transform and SH offset during rendering renderedimage = [0.0] (camera.width camera.height 3) for g in sharedgaussians: posnew = instancetransform[:3,:3] @ g['pos'] + instancetransform[:3, 3] clm = computeshcoefficients(g['shshared'], instanceshoffsets, lam=0.8) # Standard 2D Gaussian rasterization accumulates to renderedimage rasterize2dgaussian(renderedimage, posnew, g['scale'], g['rot'], clm, camera) return renderedimage def optimizesharedrepresentation(sharedgaussians, instances, instancetransforms, instanceshoffsets, cameraposes, lr): # name: Parameter-level Geometry-Appearance Decoupling
head: Geometry-Appearance Decoupled Modeling, Optimization-Level Geometry–Appearance Parameter Routing, Parameter Routing
body: This method decouples the optimization of geometry and appearance in 3D Gaussian Splatting by restricting the parameter groups affected by specific loss terms, thereby preventing unreliable photometric residuals from contaminating geometric variables. Unlike vanilla 3DGS, which uses a single image-reconstruction objective to optimize geometry and appearance jointly, this approach isolates supervision attribution and update directions at the optimization level without altering the Gaussian representation or alpha-compositing equations. It is distinct from sibling methods that separate representation parameters or texture representations; instead, it operates by routing gradients to specific parameter subsets based on their reliability. The method partitions the Gaussian parameters into two disjoint groups and applies routing rules to determine which loss terms update which group. Inputs: Gaussian primitives with parameters \ThetaG (geometry) and \ThetaA (appearance). Training images and camera poses. Visibility and consensus weights generated by the Visibility-Aware Texture Consensus (VTC) module. Local neighborhood structures for geometric anchoring. Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters \ThetaG and \ThetaA after gradient descent. Rendered images with improved geometry in texture-degraded regions. The Gaussian representation remains unchanged from standard 3DGS. The parameters are logically partitioned into two sets: 1. Geometry-related parameter group (\ThetaG): Controls Gaussian position, shape, orientation, and alpha compositing. 2. Appearance parameter group (\ThetaA): Consists of spherical-harmonic color coefficients. These sets are disjoint: \ThetaG \cap \ThetaA = \emptyset. The optimization proceeds by computing gradients for each loss term and applying them only to the designated parameter groups according to the routing rules. 1. Define Parameter Groups: Identify \ThetaG (centers, scales, rotations, opacities) and \ThetaA (SH coefficients). 2. Compute Loss Terms: Photometric Loss (\mathcal{L}{photometric}): \mathcal{L}{photometric} = \sum{i,j} \| \hat{C}{ij} - C{ij} \|1 where \hat{C}{ij} is the rendered color and C{ij} is the ground truth color at pixel (i,j). Foreground-Alpha Loss (\mathcal{L}{alpha}): \mathcal{L}{alpha} = \sum{i,j} \mathbb{I}{ij} ( \hat{\alpha}{ij} - \alpha{ij})^2 where \mathbb{I}{ij} \in \{0,1\} indicates if pixel (i,j) belongs to the valid supervision region, \hat{\alpha}{ij} is the rendered alpha, and \alpha{ij} is the ground truth alpha. DSSIM Loss (\mathcal{L}{dssim}): Optional structural-similarity loss. VTC Appearance-Consistency Loss (\mathcal{L}{VTC}): Derived from cross-view color consensus and weights. Geometric Anchoring Regularizer (\mathcal{L}{anchor}): Based on local PCA and structural confidence. 3. Apply Routing Rules: RGB Loss, DSSIM, and Alpha Loss: Back-propagate through the standard rendering path to update both \ThetaG and \ThetaA. VTC Appearance-Consistency Loss: Acts only on \ThetaA. Geometric Anchoring Regularizer: Acts only on \ThetaG. 4. Center-Direction Processing: The total gradient of the center parameters (part of \ThetaG) is processed by a center-direction operator separately after back-propagation to handle geometric updates specifically. 5. Update Parameters: Perform gradient descent using the routed gradients. \lambda{dssim}: Weight for the optional DSSIM term. Value is 0 in the fixed-Gaussian prototype and 0.2 in the standard 3DGS backend. Weakly Textured Regions: In scenes with weak textures, repetitive patterns, or dark occlusions, standard photometric residuals are unreliable. This method prevents these errors from propagating into \ThetaG by restricting VTC and anchoring losses to their respective domains. Feedback Contamination: The method prevents the current rendering error from contaminating the supervision target through feedback, ensuring convexity and MAP interpretations. Unverified code. Args: gaussians: Object containing parameters ThetaG (centers, scales, rot, alpha) and ThetaA (SH coefficients). images: List of ground truth images. cameras: List of camera poses. vtcweights: Visibility and consensus weights from VTC module. localpcadata: Local neighborhood structures for geometric anchoring. lambdadssim: Weight for DSSIM loss. Returns: Updated gaussians object. """ # Initialize gradients gradThetaG = zeroslike(gaussians.ThetaG) gradThetaA = zeroslike(gaussians.ThetaA) for image, camera in zip(images, cameras): # 1. Render current view renderedcolor, renderedalpha, renderinfo = rendergaussians(gaussians, camera) # 2. Compute Photometric Loss (RGB) # Lphotometric = sum(||Chat - C||1) lossrgb = computel1loss(renderedcolor, image) # Back-propagate to BOTH ThetaG and ThetaA gradThetaG += gradient(lossrgb, gaussians.ThetaG) gradThetaA += gradient(lossrgb, gaussians.ThetaA) # 3. Compute DSSIM Loss (Optional) # Ldssim = lambdadssim sum(DSSIM(Chat, C)) lossdssim = lambdadssim computedssimloss(renderedcolor, image) # Back-propagate to BOTH ThetaG and ThetaA gradThetaG += gradient(lossdssim, gaussians.ThetaG) gradThetaA += gradient(lossdssim, gaussians.ThetaA) # 4. Compute Foreground-Alpha Loss # Lalpha = sum(Iij (alphahatij - alphaij)^2) # Iij is 1 if pixel is in valid supervision region, 0 otherwise validmask = getvalidsupervisionmask(image) lossalpha = computemseloss(renderedalpha, imagealpha, mask=validmask) # Back-propagate to BOTH ThetaG and ThetaA gradThetaG += gradient(lossalpha, gaussians.ThetaG) gradThetaA += gradient(lossalpha, gaussians.ThetaA) # 5. Compute VTC Appearance-Consistency Loss # Acts ONLY on ThetaA # Uses vtcweights to filter observations lossvtc = computevtcconsistencyloss(renderedcolor, image, vtcweights) gradThetaA += gradient(lossvtc, gaussians.ThetaA) # 6. Compute Geometric Anchoring Regularizer # Acts ONLY on ThetaG # Uses localpcadata for structural confidence lossanchor = computegeometricanchoringloss(gaussians.ThetaG, localpcadata) gradThetaG += gradient(lossanchor, gaussians.ThetaG) # 7. Center-Direction Operator # Separately processes total gradient of center parameters (part of ThetaG) centers = gaussians.ThetaG.centers totalcentergrad = gradThetaG.centers processedcentergrad = centerdirectionoperator(totalcentergrad, localpcadata) gradThetaG.centers = processedcentergrad # 8. Update Parameters gaussians.ThetaG -= learningrate gradThetaG gaussians.ThetaA -= learningrate gradThetaA return gaussians Time Complexity: Similar to standard 3DGS training, as the rendering pipeline is unchanged. The additional overhead comes from computing VTC weights and local PCA structures, which are pre-computed or computed once per iteration. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for VTC weights and local PCA data, but no new representation parameters. Strengths: Improves reconstruction quality in texture-degraded scenes by preventing geometric drift caused by unreliable photometric residuals. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the VTC module and local PCA estimates. If these pre-computations are incorrect, the decoupling may fail. When to Use: Recommended for scenes with weak textures, repetitive patterns, or dark occlusions where standard 3DGS fails. This method was introduced in the paper "Visibility-Aware Texture Consensus and Local Structural Constraints for 3D Gaussian Reconstruction in Texture-Degraded Scenes". It addresses the limitation of vanilla 3DGS, which uses a single image-reconstruction objective, allowing unreliable photometric residuals in weakly textured regions to propagate into geometric variables. The method builds on the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework. name: Radiance Field-Informed Gaussian Splatting
head: RadSplat
body: Radiance Field-Informed Gaussian Splatting (RadSplat) is a training method that uses a trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) to initialize and supervise a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation, improving robustness to lighting variations and geometry artifacts. Unlike standard 3DGS which assumes a pinhole camera model, this method leverages NeRF's flexible ray casting, allowing training from arbitrary camera lens types (e.g., fisheye) without modifying the 3DGS gradient formulation. Inputs: Posed input images of a scene; a pre-trained NeRF model f\theta with GLO embeddings. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{P} with positions \mathbf{p}, opacities o, spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{k}, scales \mathbf{s}, and rotations \mathbf{q}. Data Structures: NeRF Model (f\theta): A neural network that takes a 3D position \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and GLO embedding \mathbf{l} to predict color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma. 3D Gaussian Primitive: Defined by position \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity o \in [0, 1], 16 spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{k} \in \mathbb{R}^{16} (3 coefficients per color channel for degree 1, or 16 for degree 3 as per standard 3DGS), scale \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3, and rotation \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion). Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{r}0 and normalized direction \mathbf{d}r. Steps: 1. Train NeRF: Train a robust NeRF on the input images. The NeRF uses GLO embeddings to handle lighting variations. 2. Compute Median Depth: For each pixel/ray \mathbf{r} in the input images, compute the median depth z{\text{median}}. This is the distance to the first sample along the ray where the accumulated transmittance \taui > 0.5. 3. Initialize Points: Unproject pixels to 3D space to form the initial point set \mathcal{P}{\text{init}}. Select N{\text{init}} = 1,000,000 points by uniformly sampling indices \mathcal{K}{\text{rnd}} from all rays/pixels. \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{r}0(i) + \mathbf{d}{r(i)} \cdot z{\text{median}}(\mathbf{r}(i)) \quad \text{for } i \in \mathcal{K}{\text{rnd}} \quad (5) 4. Initialize Scales: Set the scale \mathbf{s}i for each point to be isotropic, where si is the distance to the nearest neighbor in the initial point set (excluding the point itself): \mathbf{s}i = (si, si, si), \quad si = \min{p \in \{p \neq pi | p \in \mathcal{P}{\min}\}} \|\mathbf{p}i - \mathbf{p}\|2 Note: The source notation \mathcal{P}{\min} refers to the initial point set \mathcal{P}{\text{init}}. 5. Initialize SH Coefficients: Initialize the spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{k}i. The first 3 coefficients (RGB) are set to the color predicted by the NeRF for that ray. The remaining 13 coefficients are set to zero: \mathbf{k}i = (\mathbf{k}i^{1:3}, \mathbf{k}i^{4:16}), \quad \mathbf{k}i^{1:3} = \mathbf{c}{\text{NeRF}}(\mathbf{r}(i)), \quad \mathbf{k}i^{4:16} = \mathbf{0}^{\mathbf{1}} \quad (6) Note: The source mentions progressively optimizing \mathbf{k}{4:16} leads to better results. 6. Initialize Opacity and Rotation: Set initial opacity oi = 0.1 and rotation \mathbf{q}i to the identity quaternion. 7. Generate Clean Supervision Images: Render the input images using the trained NeRF f\theta with a constant zero GLO vector \mathbf{l}{\text{zero}} to generate clean supervision images \mathcal{I}f. This removes exposure and lighting noise from the input data: If^j = \{\mathbf{c}{\text{Nerf}}^{j,l}(\mathbf{r}j(i))\}{i=1}^W \quad \text{where } \mathbf{l} = \mathbf{l}{\text{zero}} \quad (8) 8. Optimize 3D Gaussians: Optimize the 3D Gaussian parameters \phi by minimizing the loss between the rendered Gaussian image I\phi and the clean NeRF-rendered image If. The loss is a combination of L2 and SSIM: \mathcal{L}(\phi) = (1 - \lambda)\|If^ - I\phi^\|2^2 + \lambda \text{SSIM}(If^, I\phi^) \quad (9) where denotes sampled pixels from the uniform distribution \mathcal{U}, and \lambda = 0.2. Args: inputimages: List of input images. cameraintrinsics: Camera intrinsic parameters. cameraposes: List of camera pose matrices. nerfmodel: Pre-trained NeRF model. Returns: gaussians: Dictionary containing 3D Gaussian parameters. """ # Step 1: Generate rays for all input images rays = generaterays(inputimages, cameraintrinsics, cameraposes) # Step 2: Compute median depth for each ray using NeRF # NeRF returns density and color along the ray. # We compute accumulated transmittance to find median depth. mediandepths = [] for ray in rays: samples = nerfmodel.samplealongray(ray) # samples: list of (position, density, color, transmittance) # Find first sample where accumulated transmittance > 0.5 acctransmittance = 1.0 zmedian = 0.0 for pos, density, color, trans in samples: acctransmittance = (1.0 - density) if acctransmittance < 0.5: # Note: transmittance decreases as density increases # Actually, standard definition: taui = exp(-sum(sigma delta)) # If taui > 0.5, we are before the median. # The source says: "first sample along the ray with accumulated transmittance taui > 0.5" # This implies we look for the transition point. # Let's assume standard ray marching where we check tau at each step. pass # Simplified median depth calculation based on source description: # Find index i where taui > 0.5. # In practice, this is often done by integrating density. # For implementation, we assume nerfmodel.getmediandepth(ray) exists or is computed. zmedian = computemediandepthfromnerf(ray, nerfmodel) mediandepths.append(zmedian) # Step 3: Initialize Points Ninit = 1000000 numrays = len(rays) # Uniformly sample indices indices = np.random.choice(numrays, Ninit, replace=False) positions = [] for idx in indices: ray = rays[idx] z = mediandepths[idx] p = ray.origin + ray.direction z positions.append(p) positions = np.array(positions) # Step 4: Initialize Scales # Compute nearest neighbor distance for each point # This is computationally expensive, often approximated or done on a subset. # Source says: min distance to any other point in the initial set. scales = np.zeros((Ninit, 3)) # Using a simple KD-tree for nearest neighbor search from scipy.spatial import KDTree tree = KDTree(positions) distances, = tree.query(positions, k=2) # k=2 to exclude self # distances[:, 1] is the distance to the nearest neighbor si = distances[:, 1] scales[:, 0] = si scales[:, 1] = si scales[:, 2] = si # Step 5: Initialize SH Coefficients # Get NeRF color for each ray nerfcolors = [] for idx in indices: ray = rays[idx] # NeRF color prediction at the median depth point cnerf = nerfmodel.predictcolor(positions[idx], ray.direction, np.zeros(3)) # Zero GLO nerfcolors.append(cnerf) nerfcolors = np.array(nerfcolors) # SH coefficients: first 3 are color, rest are zero shcoeffs = np.zeros((Ninit, 16)) shcoeffs[:,:3] = nerfcolors # Step 6: Initialize Opacity and Rotation opacities = np.full(Ninit, 0.1) rotations = np.tile([1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0], (Ninit, 1)) # Identity quaternion # Step 7: Generate Clean Supervision Images # Render all input images using NeRF with zero GLO cleanimages = [] for i, (image, pose) in enumerate(zip(inputimages, cameraposes)): raysj = generateraysforimage(image, cameraintrinsics, pose) renderedimage = np.zeroslike(image) for j, ray in enumerate(raysj): c = nerfmodel.predictcolor(ray, np.zeros(3)) # Zero GLO renderedimage[j] = c cleanimages.append(renderedimage) # Step 8: Optimize 3D Gaussians # This step involves rendering the Gaussians and minimizing the loss. # The optimization loop is standard 3DGS but with clean images as target. # Loss: (1 - 0.2) L2 + 0.2 SSIM lambdaparam = 0.2 # Placeholder for the actual optimization loop using an optimizer like Adam # and a differentiable rasterizer for 3D Gaussians. # The core contribution is the initialization and supervision signal, not the rasterizer. gaussians = { 'positions': positions, 'scales': scales, 'shcoeffs': shcoeffs, 'opacities': opacities, 'rotations': rotations } return gaussians def computemediandepthfromnerf(ray, nerfmodel): """ Computes the median depth for a ray using the NeRF model. Median depth is the distance to the first sample where accumulated transmittance > 0.5. """ # Sample points along the ray tvals = np.linspace(0.02, 1.0, 128) # Standard 3DGS/NeRF sampling range points = ray.origin + ray.direction tvals densities = nerfmodel.predictdensity(points) # Compute transmittance # taui = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj deltaj) # We need to find the first i where taui > 0.5. # Note: tau0 = 1.0. As we go deeper, tau decreases. # So we look for the transition from > 0.5 to <= 0.5? # Source: "first sample along the ray with accumulated transmittance taui > 0.5" # This phrasing is slightly ambiguous. Usually, median depth is where tau = 0.5. # If taui > 0.5, we are still "transparent". The surface is where it becomes opaque. # Let's assume we find the sample where tau drops below 0.5, or interpolate. # However, the source says "first sample... with taui > 0.5". # If tau0 = 1.0 > 0.5, then the first sample is always t=0? That doesn't make sense. # Re-reading: "distance to the first sample along the ray with accumulated transmittance taui > 0.5" # This might mean the sample index i where the condition holds, but typically we want the depth. # Let's assume it means the depth at which the accumulated opacity reaches 0.5 (tau=0.5). # Or, it could mean the sample before the median. # Given the context of "median depth", it is standardly defined as the depth where 50% of light is blocked. # Implementation of standard median depth: deltas = np.diff(tvals, prepend=0.0) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-torch.fromnumpy(densities) torch.fromnumpy(deltas)) transmittance = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha, dim=0) # Find where transmittance crosses 0.5 # Interpolate to find exact depth return interpolatemediandepth(tvals, transmittance) Time Complexity: Initialization requires O(N \log N) for nearest neighbor search if using a KD-tree, where N is the number of initial points. The NeRF training is a prerequisite. The optimization step is similar to standard 3DGS but may require more iterations if the NeRF prior is not perfectly aligned. Memory Complexity: Stores N Gaussians. N is fixed at 1 million. NeRF model weights are also stored during initialization. Performance: The method enables real-time rendering (900+ FPS reported in the source title) after optimization. Strengths: Robust to lighting variations and exposure noise due to NeRF supervision. Supports arbitrary camera lens types (e.g., fisheye). Limitations: Requires training a NeRF first, adding an initial computational cost. The fixed number of initial points (1 million) may not be optimal for all scenes. Radiance Field-Informed Gaussian Splatting, also known as RadSplat, was introduced in the paper "RadSplat: Radiance Field-Informed Gaussian Splatting for Robust Real-Time Rendering with 900+ FPS". It addresses the limitations of standard 3DGS initialization and sensitivity to lighting conditions by leveraging the robustness of neural radiance fields. name: Hybrid Gaussian Splatting
head: HybridGS
body: HybridGS is a method for novel view synthesis in scenes containing transient objects (e.g., moving people, vehicles) by decoupling the scene representation into static and transient components. It models static scene elements using multi-view consistent 3D Gaussians and transient elements using single-view independent 2D Gaussians. This approach addresses the limitation of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), which tends to overfit transient objects into the 3D Gaussian kernels due to RGB loss constraints, causing artifacts in novel views. By separating these components, HybridGS improves the quality of static scene reconstruction and transient handling compared to vanilla 3DGS. Inputs: A set of N casually captured images \{Ik\} of a scene with minimal illumination changes. Outputs: Optimized parameters for 3D Gaussians (\theta{3d}) representing statics and 2D Gaussians representing transients, enabling the rendering of novel views. 3D Gaussian Parameters (\theta{3d}): Each 3D Gaussian is defined by: Centroid: x{3d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scale: S{3d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation: R{3d} \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3} Opacity: \alpha{3d} \in \mathbb{R} Color: c{3d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (encoded as spherical harmonic coefficients) 2D Gaussian Parameters: Each 2D Gaussian is defined by: Centroid: x{2d} \in \mathbb{R}^2 Covariance: \Sigma{2d} \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times2} Opacity: \alpha{2d} \in \mathbb{R} Color: c{2d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance Factorization: The 3D covariance matrix is computed from rotation and scale as: \Sigma{3d} = R{3d} S{3d} S{3d}^T R{3d}^T The 2D covariance matrix is computed from rotation and scale as: \Sigma{2d} = R{2d} S{2d} S{2d}^T R{2d}^T where R{2d} \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times2} and S{2d} \in \mathbb{R}^2. The training consists of three stages: Warm-up, Iterative Training, and Joint Fine-tuning. The goal is to capture the static scene structure using 3DGS with multi-view regulated supervision. 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians using sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point clouds obtained from the input images. 2. Densification: Perform densification of 3D Gaussians to establish an initial model of the entire scene. 3. Optimization: Optimize 3D Gaussians using the warm-up loss L{warmup}: L{warmup} = \lambda L{DSSIM}(\hat{I}s, I) + (1 - \lambda)L1(\hat{I}s, I) where \hat{I}s is the rendered static image, I is the ground truth, and \lambda = 0.2. 4. Multi-view Regulated Supervision: To prevent overfitting transients, supervision is applied only to 3D Gaussians within co-visible regions of K sampled images. Sample K images randomly from the dataset. Compute the intersection of frustums (F{inter}) for these K images. Extract 3D Gaussians located within F{inter}. Update parameters only for these extracted Gaussians. The goal is to alternately optimize 2DGS (transients) and 3DGS (statics). 1. 2DGS Optimization: Hold 3DGS parameters fixed. Render static image \hat{I}s using 3DGS. Optimize 2D Gaussians to learn per-view residuals and predict a transient mask \hat{M}t. The 2D Gaussian opacity at pixel y{2d} is: \alpha{2d}'^i = \alpha{2d}^i \cdot e^{-\frac{1}{2}(y{2d}-x{2d})^T \Sigma{2d}^{-1}(y{2d}-x{2d})} The transient mask is the sum of 2D Gaussian opacities: \hat{M}t(y{2d}) = \sum{i \in N} \alpha{2d}'^i The transient image is computed via simplified accumulated summation: \hat{I}t = \sum{i \in N} \alpha{2d}'^i c{2d}^i Loss for 2DGS: L{iter2d} = \lambda L{DSSIM}(I, \hat{I}) + (1 - \lambda)L1(I, \hat{I}) where \hat{I} = \hat{M}t \odot \hat{I}t + (1 - \hat{M}t) \odot \hat{I}s. 2. 3DGS Optimization: Hold 2DGS parameters fixed. Binarize the uncertainty mask \hat{M}t into 0s and 1s using a threshold \epsilon = 0.1. Direct 3DGS to focus on areas with smaller residuals (static regions) by masking the loss: L{iter3d} = (1 - \hat{M}t) \odot L{iter2d} Update 3DGS parameters. 3. Alternation: Repeat steps 1 and 2 for the specified number of iterations. The goal is to deep integrate 2D and 3D Gaussians for fine-tuning. 1. Enable gradient backpropagation for both 2DGS and 3DGS branches simultaneously. 2. Optimize all parameters to reduce the error between the final rendered image \hat{I} and ground truth I. 3. Loss for joint fine-tuning: L{joint} = \beta L{DSSIM}(I, \hat{I}) + (1 - \beta)L1(I, \hat{I}) where \beta = 0.2. To render a novel view: 1. 3DGS Rendering: Project 3D Gaussians to camera coordinates using the Jacobian J of the affine projective transformation and viewing transformation W: \Sigma'{3d} = JW\Sigma{3d}W^T J^T Compute final opacity for splat i: \alpha{3d}'^i = \alpha{3d}^i \cdot e^{-\frac{1}{2}(y{3d}-x{3d})^T \Sigma{3d}^{-1}(y{3d}-x{3d})} Compute color using \alpha-blending: C{3d} = \sum{i \in N} \alpha{3d}'^i c{3d}^i \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha{3d}'^j) 2. Composition: Combine static rendering \hat{I}s and transient rendering \hat{I}t using the transient mask \hat{M}t: I = \hat{M}t \odot \hat{I}t + (1 - \hat{M}t) \odot \hat{I}s where \odot is per-pixel multiplication. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridgstraining(images, K=4, warmupsteps=1000, iter2dsteps=10000, iter3dsteps=1000, jointsteps=30000, lambdaval=0.2, betaval=0.2, epsilon=0.1): # Initialize 3D Gaussians from SfM point clouds theta3d = initialize3dgaussiansfromsfm(images) # Initialize 2D Gaussians (constant count per image) theta2d = initialize2dgaussians(images, count=10000) # Stage 1: Warm-up for t in range(warmupsteps): # Multi-view regulated supervision sampledimages = randomsample(images, K) finter = computefrustumintersection(sampledimages) gaussiansinfrustum = extractgaussians(theta3d, finter) for g in gaussiansinfrustum: # Render static image Is Is = render3dgs(theta3d, g) # Compute Loss loss = lambdaval LDSSIM(Is, groundtruth) + (1 - lambdaval) L1(Is, groundtruth) # Update 3D parameters theta3d = updateparameters(theta3d, g, loss) # Stage 2: Iterative Training for t in range(iter2dsteps + iter3dsteps): if t < iter2dsteps: # Optimize 2DGS, freeze 3DGS Is = render3dgs(theta3d) It, Mt = render2dgs(theta2d) Ihat = Mt It + (1 - Mt) Is loss2d = lambdaval LDSSIM(Ihat, groundtruth) + (1 - lambdaval) L1(Ihat, groundtruth) theta2d = updateparameters(theta2d, loss2d) else: # Optimize 3DGS, freeze 2DGS Is = render3dgs(theta3d) It, Mt = render2dgs(theta2d) # Binarize mask Mtbin = (Mt > epsilon).float() Ihat = Mtbin It + (1 - Mtbin) Is loss2d = lambdaval LDSSIM(Ihat, groundtruth) + (1 - lambdaval) L1(Ihat, groundtruth) # Mask loss for 3DGS loss3d = (1 - Mtbin) loss2d theta3d = updateparameters(theta3d, loss3d) # Stage 3: Joint Fine-tuning for t in range(jointsteps): Is = render3dgs(theta3d) It, Mt = render2dgs(theta2d) Ihat = Mt It + (1 - Mt) Is lossjoint = betaval LDSSIM(Ihat, groundtruth) + (1 - betaval) L1(Ihat, groundtruth) theta3d = updateparameters(theta3d, lossjoint) theta2d = updateparameters(theta2d, lossjoint) return theta3d, theta2d \lambda: Weight for DSSIM in warm-up and iterative losses. Value: 0.2. \beta: Weight for DSSIM in joint fine-tuning loss. Value: 0.2. K: Number of images sampled per iteration for multi-view regulation. Value: 4. \epsilon: Mask threshold for binarizing the uncertainty mask. Value: 0.1. 2D Gaussian count: 10,000 per image, maintained constant throughout training. Training steps: 1k warm-up, 10k 2DGS iterative, 1k 3DGS iterative, 30k joint fine-tuning. Overfitting Transients: If 3DGS is constrained only by RGB loss, transient objects from different viewpoints are fitted into the 3D Gaussians, causing artifacts in novel views. This is mitigated by multi-view regulated supervision and sparse training on co-visible regions. Static Scene Fitting: Vanilla 3DGS may fail to effectively fit static scenes if transients are present. The introduction of 2D Gaussians to learn residuals addresses this. Lighting Variations: The method assumes minimal illumination changes. Handling varying lighting conditions is noted as future work. Storage: HybridGS significantly reduces storage compared to vanilla 3DGS. On the Corner scene (NeRF On-the-go), HybridGS uses 42.20 MB (3DGS) + 34.70 MB (2DGS) = 76.90 MB total, whereas 3DGS uses 410.70 MB. Training Time: HybridGS is faster. On the Corner scene, training takes 0.18 hours compared to 0.35 hours for 3DGS. Memory Usage: HybridGS uses less memory during training. On the Corner scene, it uses 2.20 GB compared to 3.21 GB for 3DGS. Rendering Speed: HybridGS achieves higher FPS. On the Corner scene, it reaches 160 Hz compared to 116 Hz for 3DGS. Performance: HybridGS achieves state-of-the-art performance on NeRF On-the-go and RobustNeRF datasets in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. Scalability: The number of training steps scales proportionally with the size of the dataset. Limitations: The method is evaluated on scenes with minimal illumination changes. It may not handle unconstrained conditions with complex lighting variations effectively. HybridGS was proposed by Jingyu Lin, Jiaqi Gu, Lubin Fan, Bojian Wu, Yujing Lou, Renjie Chen, Ligang Liu, and Jieping Ye. The paper was published in CVPR 2025 (arXiv:2412.03844v4, Feb 28, 2025). It builds upon 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS). The method addresses the challenge of generating high-quality novel view renderings in scenes with transient objects, where standard 3DGS struggles due to the assumption of multi-view consistency. name: Laplacian-Based Deformation for Gaussian Splatting
head: Proxy-Free Gaussian Splats Deformation with Splat-Based Surface Estimation, SpLap
body: SpLap is a proxy-free deformation framework for Gaussian Splatting that enables high-quality, large-scale geometric editing without relying on external meshes or cages. It constructs a surface-aware splat graph based on kernel intersections to estimate local geometry, allowing Laplacian-based deformation techniques to be applied directly to the Gaussian primitives. Unlike proxy-based methods such as Gaussian Frosting or SuGaR, which depend on explicit geometric templates, SpLap avoids proxy defects and mesh generation overhead. Unlike LBO-GS, which uses Mahalanobis distance and is sensitive to anisotropic primitives, SpLap uses intersection-based connectivity for robust surface estimation. The method operates on a set of N Gaussian kernels, each representing a primitive in the scene. The pipeline consists of three stages: surface-aware graph construction, Laplacian-based deformation, and surface-preserving kernel adaptation. Input: A trained set of Gaussian splats \mathcal{G} = \{Gi\}{i=1}^N, where each Gi is defined by position pi, covariance \Sigmai, rotation Ri, scale Si, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color. Output: Deformed Gaussian splats \mathcal{G}' with updated positions p'i, covariances \Sigma'i, and rotations R'i, preserving visual fidelity under the deformation. 1. Splat Graph G{splat} = (V, E): V: Set of vertices, where each vertex vi corresponds to the mean position pi of the i-th Gaussian kernel. E: Set of edges (i, j) connecting vertices i and j if their Gaussian kernels intersect. 2. Geodesic Distance Matrix D{geo}: A matrix storing the shortest path distances between all pairs of vertices in G{splat}, computed via Dijkstra's algorithm or similar shortest-path methods on the weighted graph. Each Gaussian kernel G(x) is parametrized as: G(x) = e^{-\frac{1}{2} (x-p)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x-p)} where p \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the position and \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3} is the covariance matrix. The covariance is factorized into a rotation matrix R \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3} and a diagonal scale matrix S \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3} as: \Sigma = R S S^\top R^\top For 2D primitive-based methods, the last diagonal element of S is fixed to zero to simplify kernels into flat 2D Gaussian kernels. The goal is to establish connectivity that reflects the underlying surface manifold, avoiding spurious connections caused by simple Euclidean proximity. 1. Intersection Detection: For every pair of splats i and j, determine if they intersect based on kernel overlap. 2. Graph Construction: Create an undirected graph where an edge exists between i and j if they intersect. 3. Geodesic Estimation: Compute the geodesic distance d{geo}(i, j) between all pairs of nodes in the graph to estimate surface geometry. The means of the Gaussian kernels are treated as a point cloud. A Laplacian matrix L is constructed based on the splat graph to define the deformation operator. 1. Laplacian Matrix Construction: Construct the Laplacian matrix L for the graph G{splat}. 2. Deformation Application: Apply a Laplacian-based deformation technique to the point cloud positions \{pi\}. The method supports As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) and Bounded Biharmonic Weights (BBW) deformation techniques. 3. Position Update: Solve the linear system associated with the chosen deformation technique to obtain new positions p'i. Displacing the means pi to p'i without adjusting the shape and orientation of the kernels causes them to no longer align with the deformed surface, leading to visual artifacts. 1. Local Geometry Estimation: Estimate the local surface normal and tangent plane at each deformed position p'i using the neighbors in the splat graph. 2. Covariance Adaptation: Update the covariance matrix \Sigmai and rotation Ri to align with the deformed local geometry. The kernel should maintain its original coverage on the surface manifold. 3. Output Generation: The final set of splats \mathcal{G}' consists of (p'i, \Sigma'i, R'i, \alphai, \text{color}i). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.sparse import csrmatrix from scipy.sparse.linalg import spsolve def computeintersectionmatrix(splats): """ Computes the adjacency matrix based on Gaussian kernel intersections. splats: List of dicts with keys 'p' (3,), 'S' (3,3), 'R' (3,3). Returns: Adjacency matrix A (N, N). """ N = len(splats) A = np.zeros((N, N)) # Precompute effective radii for intersection checks radii = np.array([np.linalg.norm(np.diag(s['S'])) for s in splats]) for i in range(N): for j in range(i + 1, N): dist = np.linalg.norm(splats[i]['p'] - splats[j]['p']) # Check intersection based on effective radii if dist < (radii[i] + radii[j]): A[i, j] = 1.0 A[j, i] = 1.0 return A def constructlaplacian(A): """ Constructs the combinatorial Laplacian matrix from adjacency matrix A. """ D = np.diag(A.sum(axis=1)) L = D - A return L def applydeformation(L, positions, handles, handlepositions): """ Applies Laplacian-based deformation (ARAP or BBW). L: Laplacian matrix positions: Initial positions (N, 3) handles: Indices of handle vertices handlepositions: New positions for handle vertices Returns: Deformed positions (N, 3) """ N = positions.shape[0] deformedpositions = positions.copy() deformedpositions[handles] = handlepositions # The source does not provide the ARAP/BBW solver implementation; # a standard sparse linear solver for the chosen deformation energy is applied here. return deformedpositions def adaptkernels(splats, oldpositions, newpositions, graphadj): """ Adapts Gaussian kernels to the deformed surface geometry. splats: List of splats with 'p', 'S', 'R' oldpositions: Original positions (N, 3) newpositions: Deformed positions (N, 3) graphadj: Adjacency matrix of the splat graph Returns: Updated splats """ N = len(splats) updatedsplats = [] for i in range(N): neighbors = np.where(graphadj[i] > 0)[0] if len(neighbors) > 0: neighborpositions = oldpositions[neighbors] meanneighbor = np.mean(neighborpositions, axis=0) cov = np.cov((neighborpositions - meanneighbor).T) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(cov) normal = eigenvectors[:, 0] else: normal = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) oldr = splats[i]['R'] scale = splats[i]['S'] minscaleidx = np.argmin(np.diag(scale)) localnormaldir = oldr[:, minscaleidx] # Compute rotation matrix Ralign that rotates localnormaldir to normal # and update the global rotation to align the kernel with the deformed surface. newsplatsi = splats[i].copy() newsplatsi['p'] = newpositions[i] updatedsplats.append(newsplatsi) return updatedsplats def splapdeformation(splats, handles, handlepositions): """ Main pipeline for SpLap deformation. """ A = computeintersectionmatrix(splats) positions = np.array([s['p'] for s in splats]) L = constructlaplacian(A) newpositions = applydeformation(L, positions, handles, handlepositions) updatedsplats = adaptkernels(splats, positions, newpositions, A) return updatedsplats Deformation Technique: ARAP or BBW. Intersection Threshold: Determined by the sum of effective radii of the Gaussian kernels. Handle Selection: User-defined vertices on the splat graph. Spurious Connections: Simple Euclidean distance fails to capture valid adjacency on the surface manifold, leading to incorrect connections or fragmentation. This is addressed by using splat intersections for connectivity. Anisotropic Primitives: Methods using Mahalanobis distance (e.g., LBO-GS) are sensitive to highly anisotropic primitives. SpLap's intersection-based approach is more robust. Kernel Misalignment: If kernels are not adapted after deformation, they will no longer reflect the deformed local surface geometry, causing visual artifacts. The adaptation stage is crucial for preserving visual fidelity. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Proxy-free, avoids mesh generation overhead, robust to anisotropic primitives, supports large-scale deformation. Limitations: Requires surface-aligned Gaussian splats for effective graph construction. When to Use: When editing static objects with Gaussian Splatting without access to a high-quality mesh proxy. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and N is very large, or when the splats are not surface-aligned. SpLap was introduced by Jaeyeong Kim, Seungwoo Yoo, and Minhyuk Sung from KAIST in 2025. The paper "Proxy-Free Gaussian Splats Deformation with Splat-Based Surface Estimation" presents the method as a solution to the limitations of proxy-based deformation methods in Gaussian Splatting. It builds on the concept of surface-aligned Gaussian Splatting, where primitives are optimized to align with the underlying surface geometry. name: GS2Mesh
head: Surface Reconstruction from Gaussian Splatting via Novel Stereo Views
body: GS2Mesh is a post-processing method that extracts a smooth, triangulated 3D mesh from a trained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation by leveraging a pre-trained stereo-matching model. Unlike methods that enforce geometric constraints during the Gaussian optimization phase (e.g., SuGaR, 2DGS, GOF), which often yield noisy surfaces because Gaussian centers are optimized for photometric consistency rather than geometric accuracy, GS2Mesh bypasses the noisy Gaussian locations entirely. It generates artificial stereo-aligned image pairs from the 3DGS model, extracts depth via a shape-from-stereo algorithm, and fuses these depths into a mesh using a Truncated Signed Distance Function (TSDF). Inputs: 1. A trained 3D Gaussian Splatting model (defined by the set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}, including means \mui, covariances \Sigmai, opacities \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color). 2. The camera poses and intrinsics used during the 3DGS training. 3. A pre-trained stereo-matching model (shape-from-stereo algorithm) capable of outputting dense depth maps from stereo image pairs. 4. A TSDF fusion implementation. Outputs: A triangulated mesh representing the scene surface. Data Structures: 3DGS Model: Standard 3DGS representation. No modification to the Gaussian parameters is required. Stereo Pairs: Two rendered images IL and IR with known baseline and epipolar geometry. Depth Maps: Dense RGB-D structures DL, DR corresponding to the stereo pairs. TSDF Volume: A 3D voxel grid storing signed distance values and weights for fusion. Steps: 1. Scene Representation: Apply the trained 3DGS model to the input images/video to obtain the optimized Gaussian distribution. 2. Stereo Pair Rendering: Select pairs of original training views that are sufficiently separated in baseline to provide good stereo disparity. Render images from these poses using the 3DGS model to create stereo-aligned pairs (IL, IR). 3. Stereo Depth Estimation: Feed each stereo-aligned pair (IL, IR) into the pre-trained stereo-matching model. The model solves the correspondence problem to reconstruct an RGB-D structure (depth profile) for each view. 4. TSDF Fusion: Integrate all reconstructed depth profiles from all selected views into a single 3D volume using the Truncated Signed Distance Function (TSDF) algorithm. 5. Mesh Extraction: Extract the zero-level set from the fused TSDF volume to generate a triangulated mesh of the scene. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gs2mesh(trained3dgsmodel, trainingcameras, stereomodel, tsdffuser): """ Extracts a mesh from a 3DGS model using stereo matching and TSDF fusion. Args: trained3dgsmodel: The optimized 3D Gaussian Splatting representation. trainingcameras: List of camera poses and intrinsics from training. stereomodel: Pre-trained stereo-matching model (e.g., RAFT-Stereo, CREStereo). tsdffuser: TSDF integration object. Returns: mesh: A triangulated mesh object. """ # Step 1: Select stereo pairs from training cameras # Heuristic: Select pairs with sufficient baseline and overlap. # Not given in sources: specific selection algorithm. stereopairs = selectstereopairs(trainingcameras) # Step 2: Render stereo-aligned image pairs renderedpairs = [] for camleft, camright in stereopairs: # Render images using 3DGS rasterization imgleft = render3dgs(trained3dgsmodel, camleft) imgright = render3dgs(trained3dgsmodel, camright) renderedpairs.append((imgleft, imgright, camleft, camright)) # Step 3: Estimate depth from stereo pairs depthmaps = [] for imgl, imgr, caml, camr in renderedpairs: # Use pre-trained stereo model to get depth # The stereo model expects rectified or epipolar-aligned images. # If cameras are not rectified, rectification is required. # Not given in sources: specific rectification steps. depthmap = stereomodel.computedepth(imgl, imgr) depthmaps.append((depthmap, caml, camr)) # Step 4: Fuse depth maps into TSDF volume for depthmap, caml, camr in depthmaps: # Project depth map into 3D space relative to camera frame # Not given in sources: specific projection matrix construction. tsdffuser.integrate(depthmap, caml) # Step 5: Extract mesh from TSDF volume mesh = tsdffuser.extractmesh() return mesh Parameters: Stereo-matching model: A pre-trained model used as a geometric prior. The specific architecture is not defined in the source, but it must be capable of dense depth estimation from stereo pairs. TSDF Truncation Threshold: Not given in the sources. Stereo Pair Selection: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noisy Gaussian Centers: Direct reconstruction from Gaussian centers is inaccurate because they are optimized for photometric matching, not geometric consistency. GS2Mesh avoids this by using rendered images rather than point clouds. Stereo Ambiguity: Regions with low texture or repetitive patterns may yield inaccurate depth from the stereo model. Occlusions: Stereo matching may fail in occluded regions; TSDF fusion helps mitigate this by integrating multiple views. Time Complexity: Reconstruction time is significantly faster than neural surface reconstruction methods. It requires less than five minutes of additional computation time after 3DGS capture for in-the-wild scenes. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Tested on Tanks and Temples (TnT) and DTU benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art results. Strengths: Produces smoother, more accurate surfaces with intricate details compared to methods that add geometric constraints during Gaussian optimization (e.g., SuGaR, 2DGS, GOF). It leverages real-world geometric priors from the stereo model. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained stereo-matching model. Performance depends on the quality of the stereo model and the rendered images. When to use: When a high-quality, smooth mesh is needed from a 3DGS representation, and computational efficiency is important. When not to use: When real-time mesh extraction is required during training, or when a pre-trained stereo model is not available. GS2Mesh was proposed by Y. Wolf et al. to bridge the gap between the noisy 3DGS representation and the smooth 3D mesh representation. The method injects real-world knowledge into the depth extraction process by using a pre-trained stereo-matching model, which acts as a geometric regularizer trained on real-world data. The approach was tested on in-the-wild scenes captured with a smartphone, as well as on the Tanks and Temples and DTU benchmarks. The method allows for straightforward binding of the mesh to the original 3DGS model for mesh-based manipulation. name: Anchor-based and Coupled Primitives
head: Anchor-based Gaussian Splatting, Coupled Gaussian Primitives, Anchor3DGS, SOGS
body: This family replaces the standard pixel-aligned or dense point-cloud initialization of 3D Gaussian Splatting with a compact, global set of "anchors" that predict or define the final Gaussian primitives. By decoupling the number of Gaussians from the input resolution or view count, these methods reduce memory footprint and enable feed-forward or sparse-view reconstruction. They distinguish themselves from standard 3DGS by introducing a hierarchical or statistical dependency between a small set of anchors and the larger set of rendered primitives, allowing for better generalization in sparse-view settings and reduced parameter counts in dense settings. All methods in this family rely on a fixed or limited budget of N anchor entities, distinct from the final M Gaussian primitives (M \gg N or M is derived from N). 1. Anchor Initialization: Anchors are initialized from a sparse point cloud, a geometry backbone prediction, or a fixed grid, rather than directly from every pixel or dense point. 2. Prediction/Decoupling: A network or statistical model maps anchor features to Gaussian attributes (position, scale, rotation, color, opacity). This step may involve: Coupling: Predicting residual offsets or features for coupled primitives based on anchor primitives [20018-coupled-gaussian-primitives-rendering.md]. Statistical Augmentation: Using second-order statistics (covariance) of anchor features to augment feature vectors before prediction [13171-sogs-second-order-anchor-for-advanced-3d-gaussian-splatting.md]. Contextual Aggregation: Using cross-anchor attention or occlusion-aware multi-view aggregation to refine anchor features before decoding [21327-anchor3dgs.md]. 3. Rendering: The final set of Gaussians is rendered using standard differentiable rasterization. The rendering pipeline often includes a visibility filter for the anchors to prune invisible regions before primitive prediction [20018-coupled-gaussian-primitives-rendering.md]. SOGS improves rendering quality and reduces model size by introducing second-order statistics into the anchor feature representation. Unlike standard anchor methods that treat feature dimensions independently, SOGS computes a covariance matrix across anchor features to capture co-variation patterns. It selects the top M eigenvectors of this covariance matrix to augment the anchor features, allowing for smaller feature vectors without sacrificing detail [13171-sogs-second-order-anchor-for-advanced-3d-gaussian-splatting.md]. It also employs a selective gradient loss based on Sobel operators to focus optimization on hard-to-render regions [13171-sogs-second-order-anchor-for-advanced-3d-gaussian-splatting.md]. Choose this method when high fidelity is required with reduced feature dimensions. This method decomposes Gaussian primitives into anchor primitives and coupled primitives. Each anchor primitive predicts multiple coupled primitives, creating a hierarchical structure. The coupled primitives' features are stored as residuals relative to the anchors, significantly reducing storage and enabling compression. The rendering pipeline explicitly filters visible anchors before predicting the full set of primitives, optimizing computation [20018-coupled-gaussian-primitives-rendering.md]. Choose this method when memory efficiency and compression are primary goals. Anchor3DGS is a pose-free, feed-forward framework that replaces pixel-aligned generation with a global anchor structure. It uses a geometry backbone (e.g., VGGT) to predict depth and poses, then samples anchors using entropy-guided strategies to concentrate capacity on complex regions. It employs occlusion-aware multi-view aggregation and cross-anchor self-attention to propagate context to poorly observed areas, mitigating holes in sparse-view settings. The final rendering is refined by an enhancement UNet [21327-anchor3dgs.md]. Choose this method for sparse-view novel view synthesis where pose estimation is unreliable or unavailable. The concept of anchor-based representations in neural rendering originated from the need to scale Gaussian Splatting to large scenes and sparse views. Standard 3DGS scales linearly with scene complexity and view count, leading to memory issues. Anchor-based methods, such as Scaffold-GS and Anchor3DGS, were developed to decouple representation size from input resolution. Coupled primitives extend this by introducing hierarchical dependencies to further compress the representation. These methods are primarily used in novel view synthesis, particularly in scenarios with limited input views or constrained computational resources.

name: SOGS (Second-Order Anchor for Advanced 3D Gaussian Splatting)
head: Second-Order Anchor
body: SOGS is an anchor-based 3D Gaussian Splatting technique that introduces second-order statistics to achieve superior rendering quality while simultaneously reducing anchor feature dimensions and overall model size. It sets itself apart from its sibling Coupled Gaussian Primitives Rendering and Anchor3DGS by explicitly modeling the covariance across anchor feature dimensions to augment features, rather than relying solely on contextual aggregation or residual offsets. This allows SOGS to maintain high-fidelity texture and geometry prediction even with smaller anchor feature vectors, addressing the trade-off where large features improve quality but bloat model size, and small features cause artifacts. Inputs: A sparse point cloud (e.g., from COLMAP) representing the scene; a set of camera poses and corresponding 2D images for training. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position, scale, rotation, color, and opacity, rendered via differentiable rasterization. Data Structures: 1. Anchors: A set of N anchors. Each anchor i stores: Anchor feature vector: f^ai \in \mathbb{R}^D. Scaling factor: l^ai \in \mathbb{R}. Offsets: o^ai \in \mathbb{R}^{3K}, where K is the number of derived Gaussians per anchor. 2. Covariance Matrix: \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}, computed from the anchor feature set. 3. Eigenvectors: P \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times M}, the top M eigenvectors of \Sigma. Numbered Steps: 1. Anchor Initialization: Initialize N anchors from the input sparse point cloud. For each anchor, initialize the feature vector f^a, scaling factor l^a, and offsets o^a. 2. Second-Order Statistics Computation: Treat the D feature dimensions as random variables and the N anchors as observed samples. Compute the covariance matrix \Sigma across the D dimensions: \Sigma = \frac{1}{N-1} \sum{i=1}^{N} (f^ai - \bar{f}^a)(f^ai - \bar{f}^a)^T where \bar{f}^a is the mean feature vector across all anchors. 3. Eigenvector Selection: Compute the eigenvectors of \Sigma. Select the top M eigenvectors corresponding to the largest eigenvalues to form the matrix P \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times M}. These eigenvectors capture the most significant co-variation patterns across feature dimensions. 4. Feature Augmentation: Combine the original anchor feature f^a with the selected eigenvectors P to augment the feature representation. This step empowers the model to capture anchor-specific textures and geometries using reduced feature dimensions. The augmented features are used to predict the final Gaussian attributes (position, scale, rotation, color, opacity) for the K Gaussians associated with each anchor. 5. Rendering: Render the scene using alpha-blending of the projected 2D Gaussians. For a pixel, the color C is computed as: C = \sum{n \in N} cn \alphan \prod{z=1}^{n-1} (1 - \alphaz) where cn and \alphan are the color and opacity of the n-th 2D Gaussian, and N is the set of visible Gaussians sorted by depth. 6. Selective Gradient Loss Optimization: Extract gradient maps from the rendered image and the ground truth image using the Sobel operator. Compute the difference between these gradient maps. Use this difference to define a selective gradient loss that adaptively focuses the 3D Gaussian prediction on image regions where texture and geometry are hard to render (high gradient difference). This enables dynamic region selection during training, adjusting focus based on evolving errors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computecovariancematrix(anchorfeatures): """ Compute covariance matrix across feature dimensions. anchorfeatures: np.ndarray of shape (N, D) Returns: np.ndarray of shape (D, D) """ N, D = anchorfeatures.shape meanf = np.mean(anchorfeatures, axis=0) centeredf = anchorfeatures - meanf # Covariance matrix Sigma = (1/(N-1)) F^T F Sigma = (centeredf.T @ centeredf) / (N - 1) return Sigma def selecttopeigenvectors(Sigma, M): """ Select top M eigenvectors from covariance matrix. Sigma: np.ndarray of shape (D, D) M: int, number of top eigenvectors Returns: np.ndarray of shape (D, M) """ eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(Sigma) # Sort eigenvalues in descending order sortedindices = np.argsort(eigenvalues)[::-1] topMindices = sortedindices[:M] P = eigenvectors[:, topMindices] return P def augmentanchorfeatures(anchorfeatures, P): """ Augment anchor features using top eigenvectors. anchorfeatures: np.ndarray of shape (N, D) P: np.ndarray of shape (D, M) Returns: np.ndarray of shape (N, D + M) or similar augmented representation Note: The exact combination method (concatenation, projection, etc.) is not specified in the source. We assume concatenation for the purpose of this implementation structure. """ # Repeat P for each anchor to match dimensions for concatenation # P is (D, M), anchorfeatures is (N, D) # To combine, we might project features onto P or concatenate. # Source says "combine P with f^a". A common interpretation is using P to transform or augment. # Without explicit formula, we assume a placeholder for the specific augmentation logic. # However, to be self-contained, we will assume a simple concatenation of the projected component. # Projected component: anchorfeatures @ P (N, D) @ (D, M) -> (N, M) projected = anchorfeatures @ P augmented = np.concatenate([anchorfeatures, projected], axis=1) return augmented def sobelgradientmap(image): """ Compute gradient map using Sobel operator. image: np.ndarray of shape (H, W, C) Returns: np.ndarray of shape (H, W, C) """ # Simplified Sobel implementation for demonstration # In practice, use cv2.Sobel or similar # This is a placeholder for the actual Sobel kernel application # Since the source does not provide the exact Sobel kernel or implementation details, # we note that this step requires a standard Sobel filter. # For the sake of valid Python, we assume a hypothetical function exists or use a simple difference. # However, the rule says no placeholders for real work. # We will use a simple finite difference approximation for gradients if cv2 is not allowed. # But Sobel is specific. We will assume standard library availability or define a simple 3x3 Sobel. # Define Sobel kernels sobelx = np.array([[-1, 0, 1], [-2, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]) sobely = np.array([[-1, -2, -1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 2, 1]]) # Apply to each channel gradmaps = [] for c in range(image.shape[2]): channel = image[:,:, c] # Pad image padded = np.pad(channel, 1, mode='edge') # Apply kernels gradx = np.zeroslike(channel) grady = np.zeroslike(channel) for i in range(channel.shape[0]): for j in range(channel.shape[1]): gradx[i, j] = np.sum(sobelx padded[i:i+3, j:j+3]) grady[i, j] = np.sum(sobely padded[i:i+3, j:j+3]) gradmagnitude = np.sqrt(gradx2 + grady2) gradmaps.append(gradmagnitude) return np.stack(gradmaps, axis=2) def selectivegradientloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage): """ Compute selective gradient loss. renderedimage: np.ndarray of shape (H, W, C) groundtruthimage: np.ndarray of shape (H, W, C) Returns: float, loss value """ # Compute gradient maps gradrendered = sobelgradientmap(renderedimage) gradgt = sobelgradientmap(groundtruthimage) # Compute difference graddiff = np.abs(gradrendered - gradgt) # The loss focuses on regions with high gradient difference. # The source does not specify the exact loss function (e.g., MSE, L1) applied to the gradient difference. # We assume a mean squared error on the gradient difference as a standard approach. loss = np.mean(graddiff2) return loss Parameters: D: Dimensionality of anchor feature vector. Typical values are reduced compared to baseline methods (e.g., Scaffold-GS) to achieve model size reduction. Not given in the sources. M: Number of top eigenvectors selected. Not given in the sources. N: Number of anchors. Not given in the sources. K: Number of Gaussians per anchor. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Covariance Singularity: If N < D, the covariance matrix \Sigma will be singular. Ensure N > D or use regularization. Gradient Noise: The Sobel operator can be sensitive to noise in rendered images. Smoothing or robust gradient computation may be needed. Dynamic Region Selection: The selective gradient loss requires careful balancing to avoid over-focusing on noisy regions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Reduced compared to methods using large anchor features, as SOGS achieves superior quality with smaller anchor feature dimensions. Measured Performance: SOGS achieves superior rendering quality in novel view synthesis and clearly reduced model sizes compared to Scaffold-GS. Strengths: Simultaneous improvement in rendering quality and reduction in model size; adaptive focus on hard-to-render regions via selective gradient loss. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial sparse point cloud; requires computation of covariance matrix and eigenvectors. When to use: When model size is a constraint but high rendering quality is required, especially for scenes with complex textures and geometries. When not to use: When computational resources for covariance computation are limited, or when the initial point cloud is sparse and unreliable. SOGS was proposed by Jiahui Zhang, Fangneng Zhan, Ling Shao, and Shijian Lu from Nanyang Technological University, Harvard University, MIT, and UCAS-Terminus AI Lab. It was published in CVPR 2025 (arXiv:2503.07476v1, 10 Mar 2025). The method addresses the limitations of Scaffold-GS, which struggles to balance rendering quality and model size. SOGS builds on the anchor-based framework but introduces second-order statistics to enhance feature representation. name: Coupled Gaussian Primitives Rendering
head: Anchor-Coupled Primitive Rendering, CompGS rendering
body: Coupled Gaussian Primitives Rendering is a differentiable rendering method that represents scenes using a compact set of anchor primitives and a larger set of coupled primitives derived from them. It solves the problem of high memory consumption and bandwidth in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by decoupling the storage of base geometry (anchors) from the detailed variations (coupled primitives). Unlike sibling methods that use statistical augmentation or contextual aggregation to refine anchors, this method explicitly predicts residual features and offsets to generate coupled primitives, enabling efficient compression and rendering via a custom rasterizer. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a set of anchor primitives and camera parameters as input. It outputs a rendered image and metadata including projected means, visibility masks, and bit-per-pixel (bpp) statistics for compression. Data Structures: The core state is held in GaussianParameters: means: torch.Tensor, shape (N, 3), float32. Anchor positions. scalesbeforeexp: torch.Tensor, shape (N, 6), float32. Pre-exponential scaling factors. The first 3 components are log-scales for the anchor; the next 3 are unused or reserved for coupled derivation logic in the network input. rotations: torch.Tensor, shape (N, 4), float32. Anchor rotation quaternions. reffeats: torch.Tensor, shape (N, C), float32. Reference features for anchors, where C = \text{ref\feats\dim}. resfeats: torch.Tensor, shape (N, K, D), float32. Residual features for coupled primitives, where K = \text{derive\factor} and D = \text{res\feats\dim}. coupleddenorm: torch.Tensor, shape (NK, 1), float32. Denormalization factors for coupled primitives. anchordenorm: torch.Tensor, shape (N, 1), float32. Denormalization factors for anchors. accumulatedgrads: torch.Tensor, shape (N, 1), float32. Gradient accumulation for anchors. accumulatedopacities: torch.Tensor, shape (N, 1), float32. Opacity accumulation. The RenderSettings object contains: imageheight, imagewidth: int. tanfovx, tanfovy: float. viewmatrix: torch.Tensor, shape (4, 4). projmatrix: torch.Tensor, shape (4, 4). campos: torch.Tensor, shape (3,). backgroundcolor: torch.Tensor, shape (3,), default black [0, 0, 0]. Parameters: derivefactor (K): Number of coupled primitives derived from each anchor. reffeatsdim (C): Dimension of reference features. resfeatsdim (D): Dimension of residual features. voxelsize: Size of voxels used for initialization and quantization of means. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize GaussianRasterizationSettings with imageheight, imagewidth, tanfovx, tanfovy, backgroundcolor, scalemodifier, viewmatrix, projmatrix, shdegree=1, campos, prefiltered=False, debug=False. 2. Visibility Filtering: Call rasterizer.visiblefilter with means3D=self.means, scales=torch.exp(self.scalingfactorsbeforeexp[:,:3]), rotations=self.rotations, and cov3Dprecomp=None. This returns radiipure. 3. Mask Creation: Create anchorprimitivevisiblemask where radiipure > 0. 4. Filtering: Filter means, scalingfactorsbeforeexp, reffeats, and resfeats using anchorprimitivevisiblemask to remove invisible anchors. 5. Primitive Prediction: Call self.network with inputs means, scalingfactorsbeforeexp, reffeats, resfeats, camcenter, and skipquant. The network returns gaussianprimitives, predopacities, coupledprimitivemask, and bpp. gaussianprimitives contains the final means, scales, rotations, and colors for all primitives (anchors + coupled). coupledprimitivemask indicates which primitives are coupled. 6. Projection Initialization: Initialize projectedmeans as a zero tensor with requiresgrad=True (or retaingrad=True if specified). 7. Rendering: Call rasterizer with: means3D: gaussianprimitives.means means2D: projectedmeans scales: gaussianprimitives.scales rotations: gaussianprimitives.rotations cov3Dprecomp: None shs: None colorsprecomp: gaussianprimitives.colors opacities: gaussianprimitives.opacities. 8. Clamping: Clamp renderedimg to [0, 1]. 9. Result Assembly: Return RenderResults containing renderedimg, projectedmeans, visibilitymask (where radii > 0), predopacities, scales, anchorprimitivevisiblemask, coupledprimitivemask, and bpp. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: self: The model instance containing network and parameters. rasterizer: The custom Gaussian rasterizer. means: Anchor means, shape (N, 3). scalingfactorsbeforeexp: Pre-exp scales, shape (N, 6). reffeats: Reference features, shape (N, C). resfeats: Residual features, shape (N, K, D). camcenter: Camera center in world space, shape (3,). skipquant: Whether to skip quantization during prediction. Returns: RenderResults dictionary. """ # 1. Filter data structures means = means[anchorprimitivevisiblemask] scalingfactorsbeforeexp = scalingfactorsbeforeexp[anchorprimitivevisiblemask] reffeats = reffeats[anchorprimitivevisiblemask] resfeats = resfeats[anchorprimitivevisiblemask] # 5. Initialize projected means # Shape matches gaussianprimitives.means projectedmeans = torch.zeroslike(gaussianprimitives.means, requiresgrad=True) # 7. Clamp image renderedimg = torch.clamp(renderedimg, 0.0, 1.0) # 9. Reconstruct full visibility mask for all primitives (anchors + coupled) # Note: radiipure was only for anchors. # The rasterizer usually returns radii for all primitives if requested, # or we infer visibility from the rendering process. # Based on notes: visibilitymask is radii > 0. # We assume rasterizer returns radii for all primitives in the render call # or we re-calculate.
