name: Anchor3DGS
head: Anchor-based 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: Anchor3DGS is a pose-free, feed-forward framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that replaces pixel-aligned paradigms with a compact anchor-based representation. It places a fixed number of 3D anchors on a geometry-aware scaffold, decoupling the final Gaussian count from input resolution and view count, thereby allocating capacity based on scene content rather than data volume. Unlike pixel-aligned methods that produce millions of Gaussians proportional to input views, Anchor3DGS achieves comparable dense-view quality with an order of magnitude fewer primitives (0.26M) and significantly lower storage, while maintaining state-of-the-art performance in sparse-view settings through entropy-guided sampling and cross-anchor attention. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of V input images (context views) with known or estimated poses and intrinsics. The maximum input resolution is 448 pixels on the longer side. Outputs: A set of K \times N 3D Gaussians defined by position, scale, rotation, color, and opacity, ready for differentiable rasterization. Data Structures: 1. Anchor Embeddings (Z): A tensor of shape (N, Dz), where N is the anchor budget and Dz = 128 is the embedding dimension. 2. Gaussian Attributes: For each anchor, a decoder predicts K Gaussians. Each Gaussian is defined by standard 3DGS parameters: mean \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (or quaternion/scale), color c \in \mathbb{R}^3, and opacity \alpha \in \mathbb{R}. 3. Refinement Features (H): A per-Gaussian feature vector of dimension Dh = 16 used for rendering refinement. Algorithm Steps: 1. Geometry Backbone Prediction: A geometry backbone (initialized with pretrained VGGT weights) processes the input images to predict depth maps and camera poses. The patch-embedding layer is frozen during fine-tuning. 2. Anchor Initialization and Sampling: Anchors are initialized on a geometry-aware scaffold derived from the backbone's depth predictions. To concentrate capacity on visually complex regions, entropy-guided sampling is applied. Uniform grid subsampling is replaced by this strategy to allocate the limited anchor budget more reasonably. 3. Multi-View Aggregation: Anchor features are encoded using occlusion-aware multi-view aggregation. Instead of plain mean pooling, this step aggregates features from multiple context views while accounting for occlusions, ensuring robust feature representation for each anchor. 4. Cross-Anchor Self-Attention: A self-attention mechanism propagates context between anchors. This step specifically targets poorly-observed areas, allowing information from well-observed regions to fill in gaps, mitigating the holes prevalent in pixel-aligned methods. 5. Gaussian Decoding: A network decodes the refined anchor embeddings Z into Gaussian attributes. Each anchor n produces K Gaussians. The decoder outputs the necessary parameters for position, scale, rotation, color, and opacity. 6. Rendering Refinement: The initial splatted RGB images are refined using an enhancement UNet. This step recovers fine high-frequency details that the raw splatting process struggles to capture. 7. Training Loss: The model is trained using a composite loss function: \mathcal{L} = \lambda{\text{mse}} \mathcal{L}{\text{mse}} + \lambda{\text{lpips}} \mathcal{L}{\text{lpips}} + \lambda{\text{depth}} \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}} where \mathcal{L}{\text{mse}} is the Mean Squared Error between refined renderings and ground truth, \mathcal{L}{\text{lpips}} is the LPIPS loss, and \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}} is a depth-consistency loss encouraging rasterized depth to agree with the geometry backbone's predictions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class Anchor3DGS: def init(self, N=32768, K=8, Dz=128, Dh=16): """ Initialize Anchor3DGS model. Args: N (int): Total number of 3D anchors per scene. Default: 32,768. K (int): Number of Gaussians decoded per anchor. Default: 8. Dz (int): Dimension of each anchor embedding. Default: 128. Dh (int): Dimension of per-Gaussian feature vector for refinement. Default: 16. """ self.N = N self.K = K self.Dz = Dz self.Dh = Dh # Geometry Backbone (VGGT-based) # Initialized with pretrained VGGT weights. Patch-embedding layer frozen. self.geometrybackbone = VGGTBackbone() # Anchor Feature Encoder # Includes occlusion-aware multi-view aggregation self.anchorencoder = AnchorFeatureEncoder(Dz) # Cross-Anchor Self-Attention self.selfattention = CrossAnchorSelfAttention(Dz) # Gaussian Decoder # Decodes anchor embeddings to K Gaussians per anchor self.gaussiandecoder = GaussianDecoder(Dz, K) # Rendering Refinement UNet self.refinementunet = EnhancementUNet(inputchannels=3, outputchannels=3, featuredim=Dh) # Loss weights self.lambdamse = 1.0 self.lambdalpips = 0.05 self.lambdadepth = 0.1 def forward(self, images, poses=None): """ Forward pass for training or inference. Args: images (Tensor): Input images of shape (B, V, C, H, W). poses (Tensor, optional): Camera poses. If None, estimated by backbone. Returns: Tensor: Refined rendered images. Tensor: Predicted Gaussians (for loss calculation). """ B, V, C, H, W = images.shape # Step 1: Geometry Backbone Prediction # Predict depth maps and potentially refine poses # geometrybackbone outputs depth maps and potentially pose corrections depthmaps, refinedposes = self.geometrybackbone(images) # Step 2: Anchor Initialization and Entropy-Guided Sampling # Initialize anchors on geometry-aware scaffold # Apply entropy-guided sampling to select anchor locations # This concentrates capacity on visually complex regions anchorpositions = self.entropyguidedsampling(depthmaps, refinedposes, self.N) # Step 3: Multi-View Aggregation # Encode anchor features using occlusion-aware multi-view aggregation # Instead of plain mean pooling anchorfeatures = self.anchorencoder(images, anchorpositions, refinedposes) # Step 4: Cross-Anchor Self-Attention # Propagate context to poorly-observed areas anchorfeatures = self.selfattention(anchorfeatures) # Step 5: Gaussian Decoding # Decode anchor embeddings to Gaussian attributes # Each anchor produces K Gaussians gaussians = self.gaussiandecoder(anchorfeatures) # Step 6: Rendering # Render Gaussians to images renderedimages = rendergaussians(gaussians, refinedposes, imagesize=(H, W)) # Step 7: Rendering Refinement # Use enhancement UNet to recover fine high-frequency details refinedimages = self.refinementunet(renderedimages) return refinedimages, gaussians def computeloss(self, refinedimages, gaussians, groundtruthimages, groundtruthdepths): """ Compute the total training loss. Args: refinedimages (Tensor): Refined rendered images. gaussians (Tensor): Predicted Gaussians. groundtruthimages (Tensor): Ground truth images. groundtruthdepths (Tensor): Ground truth depth maps (if available). Returns: Tensor: Total loss. """ # MSE Loss lossmse = F.mseloss(refinedimages, groundtruthimages) # LPIPS Loss losslpips = lpipsloss(refinedimages, groundtruthimages) # Depth Consistency Loss # Encourage rasterized depth from Gaussians to agree with geometry backbone predictions rasterizeddepth = rasterizedepth(gaussians, refinedposes, imagesize=(H, W)) # Note: geometrybackbonedepths are from Step 1 lossdepth = F.mseloss(rasterizeddepth, geometrybackbonedepths) totalloss = (self.lambdamse lossmse + self.lambdalpips losslpips + self.lambdadepth lossdepth) return totalloss def entropyguidedsampling(self, depthmaps, poses, N): """ Sample anchor positions based on entropy of depth maps. Args: depthmaps (Tensor): Predicted depth maps. poses (Tensor): Camera poses. N (int): Number of anchors to sample. Returns: Tensor: Selected anchor positions in 3D space. """ # Calculate entropy of depth maps to identify visually complex regions # Higher entropy indicates more detail/complexity entropy = calculateentropy(depthmaps) # Sample N positions with probability proportional to entropy # This concentrates capacity on visually complex regions # Implementation detail: Use inverse transform sampling or stratified sampling # on the entropy map to select 3D points selectedindices = samplewithentropy(entropy, N) # Convert 2D indices to 3D positions using depth maps and poses anchorpositions = indicesto3d(selectedindices, depthmaps, poses) return anchorpositions def anchorencoder(self, images, anchorpositions, poses): """ Encode anchor features using occlusion-aware multi-view aggregation. Args: images (Tensor): Input images. anchorpositions (Tensor): 3D positions of anchors. poses (Tensor): Camera poses. Returns: Tensor: Aggregated anchor features. """ # Project anchor positions to each view projections = projecttoviews(anchorpositions, poses, intrinsics) # Sample features from each view at projected locations viewfeatures = samplefeatures(images, projections) # Occlusion-aware aggregation # Check visibility of each anchor in each view # Weight features based on occlusion confidence aggregatedfeatures = occlusionawaremeanpool(viewfeatures, visibilitymasks) return aggregatedfeatures def selfattention(self, anchorfeatures): """ Apply cross-anchor self-attention. Args: anchorfeatures (Tensor): Anchor features of shape (N, Dz). Returns: Tensor: Refined anchor features. """ # Standard self-attention mechanism # Q, K, V = Linear(anchorfeatures) # attentionscores = softmax(Q @ K^T / sqrt(Dz)) # output = attentionscores @ V # Residual connection refinedfeatures = anchorfeatures + selfattentionlayer(anchorfeatures) return refinedfeatures def gaussiandecoder(self, anchorfeatures): """ Decode anchor features to Gaussian attributes. Args: anchorfeatures (Tensor): Refined anchor features. Returns: Tensor: Gaussian attributes for all NK Gaussians. """ # For each anchor, predict K Gaussians # Output shape: (N, K, paramspergaussian) # paramspergaussian includes mean, scale, rotation, color, opacity gaussians = decodernetwork(anchorfeatures) return gaussians def refinementunet(self, renderedimages): """ Refine rendered images using UNet. Args: renderedimages (Tensor): Initial rendered images. Returns: Tensor: Refined images. """ # Enhancement UNet takes rendered images and outputs refined images # May also take per-Gaussian features if available for conditioning refinedimages = unetnetwork(renderedimages) return refinedimages Parameters: Anchor Budget (N): 32,768. Decoded Gaussians per Anchor (K): 8. Anchor Embedding Dimension (Dz): 128. Per-Gaussian Feature Vector Dimension (Dh): 16. Geometry Backbone: Initialized with pretrained VGGT weights. Learning Rate: AdamW with peak learning rate 2 \times 10^{-4} and 1,000 warmup steps. Geometry backbone fine-tuned with 0.1x smaller learning rate; patch-embedding layer frozen. Training Context Views: Randomly sampled between 2 and 16 per scene. Input Resolution: Maximum 448 pixels on the longer side during training; 448x448 at inference. Loss Weights: \lambda{\text{mse}} = 1.0, \lambda{\text{lpips}} = 0.05, \lambda{\text{depth}} = 0.1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometry Backbone Dependency: Performance relies heavily on the prediction quality of the geometry backbone. Inaccurate poses or noisy depth maps from the backbone degrade anchor placement and final rendering. Fixed Anchor Budget: The anchor budget is fixed regardless of scene scale. Very large or unbounded scenes may benefit from a scene-adaptive budget, as the current fixed budget may be insufficient. Uses second-order statistics (covariance) of anchor features to augment feature vectors before prediction. Chooses this when feature richness is critical for complex textures. Link Predicts residual offsets or features for coupled primitives based on anchor primitives. Chooses this when explicit coupling between anchor and derived primitives is needed for structural fidelity. Link Time Complexity: Inference is feed-forward and takes seconds (e.g., 2.9s on H800 for VR-NeRF), compared to minutes for per-scene optimization methods like VGGT+3DGS. Memory Complexity: Storage is compact. 0.26M Gaussians per scene require ~35MB, compared to >650MB for pixel-aligned methods producing several million Gaussians. Measured Performance: Sparse-View (3 views) on VR-NeRF: PSNR 23.69 (Full model) vs 22.50 (w/o enhancement), 23.03 (w/o self-attention), 23.28 (w/o occ-aggregation), 22.16 (w/o entropy-sample). Dense-View (32 views) on VR-NeRF: PSNR 24.56, SSIM 0.815, LPIPS 0.297. Dense-View (32 views) on DL3DV: PSNR 19.52, SSIM 0.593, LPIPS 0.364. Scaling: Gaussian count (0.26M) is independent of input resolution and view count, unlike pixel-aligned methods where count scales with views/resolution. Strengths: State-of-the-art in sparse-view settings; order of magnitude fewer Gaussians and lower storage in dense-view settings; fast feed-forward inference; mitigates holes in poorly observed regions. Limitations: Relies on geometry backbone accuracy; fixed anchor budget may not suit very large/unbounded scenes; refinement UNet adds some computational overhead compared to raw splatting. When to Use: When fast, pose-free novel view synthesis is required with limited storage/compute, especially in sparse-view scenarios. When Not to Use: When per-scene optimization is acceptable for higher quality, or when scenes are extremely large and require adaptive anchor budgets. Anchor3DGS was introduced in the paper "Anchor3DGS: Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Compact Anchor-Based Representation". It addresses the limitations of pixel-aligned 3DGS methods, which produce large numbers of Gaussians proportional to input views and require per-scene optimization. By adopting an anchor-based paradigm, it enables pose-free, feed-forward reconstruction with compact representation. Evaluated on VR-NeRF, MipNeRF360, and DL3DV datasets. Anchor3DGS: Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Compact Anchor-Based Representation, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2610.21634, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Hybrid Radiance Fields (HyRF)
body: Hybrid Radiance Fields (HyRF) is a scene representation method that decomposes a scene into a compact set of explicit 3D Gaussians storing critical high-frequency parameters and grid-based neural fields that predict the remaining properties. It addresses the memory overhead and limited representational capacity of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by decoupling geometry and appearance into separate neural fields, enabling a 20× reduction in model size while maintaining real-time rendering speeds and state-of-the-art quality. The method takes a set of training images and camera poses as input, and produces a rendered image for a target camera pose along with an optimized scene representation consisting of explicit Gaussian parameters and neural field weights. Data Structures Explicit Gaussians store exactly 8 parameters per Gaussian: position pe \in \mathbb{R}^3, diffuse color ce \in \mathbb{R}^3, isotropic scale se \in \mathbb{R}, and opacity \alphae \in \mathbb{R}. Rotation is not stored explicitly but is predicted by the neural field. Two separate neural fields, \Theta{geo} and \Theta{rad}, use multi-resolution hash encoding for coordinate compression. \Theta{geo} predicts geometry properties (scale, opacity, rotation), while \Theta{rad} predicts appearance properties (view-dependent color). Coordinate Preprocessing Before querying the neural fields, 3D points are normalized and contracted to the range (0, 1) to handle unbounded scenes. The axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) B0 is defined as the minimum and maximum camera positions of the scene. The point pi is normalized using B0, then contracted to p'i using the formula: \text{contract}(pi) = \begin{cases} 0.25 \cdot pi + 1 & \text{if } \|pi\| \le 1 \\ \frac{pi}{0.25 \cdot (2 - \|pi\|) + 1} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Hybrid Rendering Pipeline The rendering process operates in three stages. 1. Visibility Pre-culling: Eliminates explicit Gaussians outside the current view frustum to reduce computational overhead of querying neural fields. 2. Neural Property Prediction & Combination: For remaining visible Gaussians, queries their positions through the neural fields to predict missing properties, then combines them with stored explicit parameters to recover high-frequency details. \Theta{geo} is queried with the contracted position to predict scale, opacity, and rotation. \Theta{rad} is queried with the contracted position and view direction to predict view-dependent color. Predicted geometry is combined with explicit geometry, and predicted color is combined with explicit diffuse color. 3. Background Compositing: The neural field generates a background map projected onto a background sphere, which is composited with the foreground Gaussian rendering through alpha blending to address insufficient background modeling for distant objects. Alpha Blending The final pixel color C is computed using standard point-based alpha blending: C = \sum{i \in N} ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) Where C is the final predicted pixel color, N is the set of sorted Gaussians projected onto the pixel, ci is the color of the i-th Gaussian, and \alphai is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def contract(p): norm = math.sqrt(p[0]2 + p[1]2 + p[2]2) if norm <= 1.0: return (0.25 p[0] + 1.0, 0.25 p[1] + 1.0, 0.25 p[2] + 1.0) denom = 0.25 (2.0 - norm) + 1.0 return (p[0] / denom, p[1] / denom, p[2] / denom) def frustumcull(gaussians, camera): visible = [] for g in gaussians: if camera.minx <= g.pos[0] <= camera.maxx and \ camera.miny <= g.pos[1] <= camera.maxy and \ camera.minz <= g.pos[2] <= camera.maxz: visible.append(g) return visible def renderbackgroundsphere(thetarad, hashtable, camera, resolution=256): bgimage = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(resolution)] for in range(resolution)] for y in range(resolution): for x in range(resolution): theta = math.pi (y + 0.5) / resolution phi = 2.0 math.pi (x + 0.5) / resolution dirvec = (math.sin(theta) math.cos(phi), math.sin(theta) math.sin(phi), math.cos(theta)) bgimage[y][x] = thetarad.query(dirvec, hashtable) return bgimage def alphablendgaussians(gaussians, camera): height, width = camera.height, camera.width image = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for g in gaussians: alpha = g.opacity color = g.color for y in range(g.screeny, g.screeny + g.screenh): for x in range(g.screenx, g.screenx + g.screenw): if 0 <= y < height and 0 <= x < width: r, gc, b = image[y][x] image[y][x] = (r (1 - alpha) + color[0] alpha, gc (1 - alpha) + color[1] alpha, b (1 - alpha) + color[2] alpha) return image def renderhyrf(camera, explicitgaussians, thetageo, thetarad, hashtable): # Stage 1: Visibility Pre-culling visiblegaussians = frustumcull(explicitgaussians, camera) # Stage 2: Neural Property Prediction & Combination processedgaussians = [] for g in visiblegaussians: pnorm = (g.pos[0] / camera.aabbscale, g.pos[1] / camera.aabbscale, g.pos[2] / camera.aabbscale) pcontracted = contract(pnorm) predgeo = thetageo.query(pcontracted, hashtable) finalscale = g.scale predgeo.scale finalopacity = g.opacity predgeo.opacity finalrotation = predgeo.rotation viewdir = (g.pos[0] - camera.position[0], g.pos[1] - camera.position[1], g.pos[2] - camera.position[2]) vlen = math.sqrt(viewdir[0]2 + viewdir[1]2 + viewdir[2]2) viewdir = (viewdir[0]/vlen, viewdir[1]/vlen, viewdir[2]/vlen) predcolor = thetarad.query(pcontracted, viewdir, hashtable) finalcolor = (g.colordiffuse[0] + predcolor[0], g.colordiffuse[1] + predcolor[1], g.colordiffuse[2] + predcolor[2]) processedgaussians.append({ 'pos': g.pos, 'color': finalcolor, 'scale': finalscale, 'opacity': finalopacity, 'rotation': finalrotation }) # Stage 3: Background Compositing foregroundimage = alphablendgaussians(processedgaussians, camera) backgroundimage = renderbackgroundsphere(thetarad, hashtable, camera) finalimage = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(camera.width)] for in range(camera.height)] for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): fg = foregroundimage[y][x] bg = backgroundimage[y][x] finalimage[y][x] = (fg[0] + bg[0] (1 - fg[2]), fg[1] + bg[1] (1 - fg[2]), fg[2] + bg[2] (1 - fg[2])) return finalimage Parameters Neural field encoding uses multi-resolution hash encoding. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Predicting all Gaussian properties through a single neural field fails due to weak correlation between geometry and appearance attributes, necessitating the decoupled architecture. Standard Gaussian representations have insufficient background modeling for distant objects, addressed by the background sphere compositing. Failing to pre-cull Gaussians leads to significant computational overhead when querying neural fields for invisible regions. The method reduces model size by over 20× compared to standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). It maintains real-time rendering speeds. It achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality. Hybrid Radiance Fields (HyRF) was introduced to address the limitations of explicit Gaussian representations in terms of memory overhead and representational capacity for fine details. It builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting and integrates them with neural radiance fields (NeRF) concepts, specifically multi-resolution hash encoding. The method was developed to provide a memory-efficient and high-quality novel view synthesis solution. name: SpotLessSplats (SLS)
body: SpotLessSplats (SLS) is a robust 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework that enables high-quality novel view synthesis from casually captured video data containing transient distractors such as moving people or wind-blown elements. Unlike standard 3DGS which assumes static, perfectly 3D-consistent scenes, SLS uses unsupervised detection of outliers in training images by leveraging pre-trained text-to-image features and robust optimization to ignore these distractors. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like DeSplat or 360 Gaussian Splatting by specifically addressing semantic outlier modeling in casual captures, using feature-space similarities rather than relying solely on photometric residuals to identify inliers and outliers. Inputs: A set of posed images \{In\}{n=1}^N from a casually captured scene, and a pre-trained 2D foundation model (e.g., DINOv2) to extract semantic feature maps F. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians optimized for novel view synthesis, with transient distractors effectively ignored. Data Structures: 3D Gaussians: Standard 3DGS representation containing position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Feature Map F: Semantic feature embeddings extracted from input images using the foundation model. Inlier Mask M: A binary or probabilistic mask indicating inlier pixels. Residual Histogram: A histogram with B buckets of width 10^{-3} tracking residual magnitudes over time. MLP Classifier H: A network with parameters \theta^{(t)} for spatio-temporal outlier detection. Parameters: \tau: Hyperparameter controlling the cut-off percentile for the generalized median \rho. Typical values: 0.5 (median) or 0.9. \kappa: Threshold for utilization-based pruning. Value: 10^{-8}. T: Number of steps between utilization calculations. Value: 100. |NT(t)|: Number of images accumulated for utilization calculation. Value: 100. \lambda: Weight for regularization loss. Value: 0.5. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: For each training image In, extract semantic feature map Fn using the pre-trained foundation model. 2. Residual Tracking: To handle skewed outlier distributions across image-based minibatches, track residual magnitudes over multiple training batches. Discretize residuals into B histogram buckets of width 10^{-3}. Update bucket population via a discounted update similar to fast median filtering [Perreault and Hebert 2007]. Extract the generalized median \rho as the \tau quantile in the histogram population. 3. Photometric Masking: Compute the pixel-wise 1-norm residual image Rn = \|In - \hat{I}n\|1. Compute the initial inlier mask Mn^{(t)} using the generalized median \rho and a morphological dilation: Mn^{(t)} = \mathbb{1}\{Rn > \rho\} \circledast B > 0.5, \quad P(Rn > \rho) = \tau where \mathbb{1} is the indicator function, \circledast denotes convolution with a normalized 3 \times 3 box filter B, and the condition > 0.5 applies to the convolution result. 4. SLS-mlp (Spatio-temporal Clustering): Train an MLP classifier H with parameters \theta^{(t)} to predict pixel-wise inlier probabilities M{mlp}^{(t)} = H(F; \theta^{(t)}). Architecture: H uses 1 \times 1 convolutions, acting i.i.d. across pixels. Loss Function: Minimize L(\theta^{(t)}) = L{sup}(\theta^{(t)}) + \lambda L{reg}(\theta^{(t)}). Supervision Loss: L{sup}(\theta^{(t)}) = \max(U^{(t)} - H(F; \theta^{(t)}), 0) + \max(H(F; \theta^{(t)}) - L^{(t)}, 0). Labels: U^{(t)} is Mn^{(t)} computed with \tau=0.5; L^{(t)} is Mn^{(t)} computed with \tau=0.9. Regularization: Minimize the Lipschitz constant of H via L{reg} to ensure similar features map to similar probabilities. Optimization Schedule: Parameters \theta^{(t)} are updated concurrently with 3DGS optimization, interleaved such that one is fixed while the other is optimized. Mask Selection: Use M{mlp}^{(t)} as the final inlier/outlier mask for training. 5. Utilization-Based Pruning (UBP): Replace standard opacity reset with UBP to compress the scene representation. Track the gradient of rendered colors \hat{I}{h,w} with respect to the projected splat positions xg of each Gaussian g. Compute utilization ug: ug = \sum{t \in NT(t)} \mathbb{E}{w,h} \left[ M{h,w}^{(t)} \cdot \left( \frac{\partial \hat{I}{h,w}^{(t)}}{\partial xg} \right)^2 \right] where the expectation \mathbb{E}{w,h} is over image pixels (w,h). Average across the image (W \times H), computed every T=100 steps accumulated over |NT(t)|=100 images. Prune Gaussians if ug < \kappa (where \kappa = 10^{-8}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spotlesssplatstraining(images, poses, foundationmodel, numsteps): # Initialize 3D Gaussians (standard 3DGS representation) gaussians = initgaussians() # Initialize MLP classifier with 1x1 convolutions mlp = initmlp1x1() theta = mlp.parameters() # Residual histogram tracking B = 1000 # Number of buckets bucketwidth = 1e-3 histogram = [0.0] B taumedian = 0.5 tauhigh = 0.9 lambdareg = 0.5 # UBP parameters T = 100 NT = 100 kappa = 1e-8 utilizationbuffer = [] for step in range(numsteps): # 1. Sample batch and extract features batchimgs, batchposes = samplebatch(images, poses) features = foundationmodel(batchimgs) # 2. Render and compute residuals renderedimgs = render3dgs(gaussians, batchposes) residuals = pixelwisel1norm(batchimgs, renderedimgs) # 3. Update histogram and compute generalized median rho updatehistogramdiscounted(histogram, residuals.flatten(), bucketwidth) rhomedian = getquantile(histogram, taumedian) rhohigh = getquantile(histogram, tauhigh) # 4. Compute photometric masks with morphological dilation maskmedian = morphologicaldilate(residuals > rhomedian) maskhigh = morphologicaldilate(residuals > rhohigh) # 5. Interleaved optimization if step % 2 == 0: # Update MLP predinlier = mlp(features) U = maskmedian L = maskhigh lsup = elementwisemax(U - predinlier, 0) + elementwisemax(predinlier - L, 0) lsup = mean(lsup) lreg = lipschitzregularization(mlp, features) lossmlp = lsup + lambdareg lreg theta = sgdstep(theta, lossmlp) finalmask = sigmoid(predinlier) else: # Update 3D Gaussians using MLP mask lossgs = compute3dgsloss(renderedimgs, batchimgs, finalmask) gaussians = sgdstepgaussians(gaussians, lossgs) # 6. Utilization-Based Pruning (UBP) if step % T == 0: # Compute gradient of rendered color w.r.t projected splat positions grads = computegradrenderedvsprojectedpos(gaussians, renderedimgs, finalmask) utilizationbuffer.append(grads) if len(utilizationbuffer) >= NT: utilizations = computeutilization(utilizationbuffer) gaussians = prunegaussians(utilizations, kappa) utilizationbuffer = [] def initgaussians(): return [] # Standard 3DGS initialization def initmlp1x1(): return [] # 1x1 convolution network def samplebatch(imgs, poses): return imgs[:4], poses[:4] # Standard batch sampling def render3dgs(gaussians, poses): return [] # Alpha-blending volume rendering def pixelwisel1norm(img1, img2): return abs(img1 - img2).mean(axis=-1) # 1-norm per pixel def updatehistogramdiscounted(hist, vals, width): for v in vals: idx = int(v / width) if 0 <= idx < len(hist): hist[idx] = 0.9 hist[idx] + 0.1 # Discounted update def getquantile(hist, tau): cumsum = 0.0 total = sum(hist) for i, count in enumerate(hist): cumsum += count if cumsum >= tau total: return i 1e-3 # Return bin center as quantile value def morphologicaldilate(mask): # 3x3 box filter convolution out = [[0.0]W for in range(H)] for y in range(H): for x in range(W): out[y][x] = 1.0 if any(mask[max(0,y-1):min(H,y+2)][max(0,x-1):min(W,x+2)]) else 0.0 return out # Threshold > 0.5 applied implicitly def lipschitzregularization(mlp, features): return sum(grad2 for grad in mlp.gradient(features)) # Standard Lipschitz bound def sgdstep(params, loss): return params - 0.01 gradient(loss, params) # Standard SGD step def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-x)) # Standard sigmoid def compute3dgsloss(rendered, target, mask): return mean(mask (rendered - target)2) # Masked MSE def sgdstepgaussians(gaussians, loss): return gaussians - 0.01 gradient(loss, gaussians) # Standard SGD step def computegradrenderedvsprojectedpos(gaussians, rendered, mask): # Backprop through rendering to get dI/dxg per Gaussian return [mean(mask (rendered - target)2).grad(g) for g in gaussians] # Simplified gradient extraction def computeutilization(buffer): utilizations = [] for gidx in range(len(buffer[0])): val = 0.0 for tgrads in buffer: val += mean(tgrads[gidx]2) # E{w,h} over pixels utilizations.append(val) return utilizations def prunegaussians(utilizations, kappa): return [g for g, u in zip(gaussians, utilizations) if u >= kappa] # Filter low-utilization Gaussians Subtopics: SLS-mlp (Spatio-temporal Clustering): Uses an MLP classifier trained unsupervised to predict inlier probabilities based on semantic features. It differs from spatial clustering by leveraging temporal consistency across the dataset. Choose when semantic information is strong and distractors are complex. Spatial Clustering: Uses non-parametric clustering of local feature embeddings to find image regions of structured outliers. Simpler but less robust to temporal variations than SLS-mlp. Time Complexity: Adds overhead for feature extraction (foundation model) and MLP training, but the MLP is lightweight (1 \times 1 convs). The interleaved optimization ensures convergence. Memory Complexity: Requires storing feature maps and the MLP parameters. The histogram tracking uses constant memory. UBP reduces memory usage by pruning Gaussians. Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction quality on casually captured scenes. Reduces the number of Gaussians by 2-4 times while maintaining quality. Strengths: Robust to transient distractors (people, wind) without manual annotation. Avoids overfitting to distractors with colors similar to the background, a common failure mode of residual-only methods like RobustNeRF. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained foundation model. Performance depends on the quality of semantic features. When to use: Casual captures with transient objects. When not to use: Static, controlled environments where standard 3DGS suffices, or when computational resources for foundation model inference are limited. SpotLessSplats was introduced by Sabour, Goli, Kopanas, Mathews, and Lagun from Google Deepmind and University of Toronto. It addresses the limitation of 3DGS which requires highly controlled environments (no moving people, consistent lighting). The method builds on prior work like RobustNeRF [Sabour et al. 2023] and NeRF-W, but improves upon them by using semantic features instead of just photometric residuals. It also incorporates insights from [Goli et al. 2024] for utilization-based pruning. name: Stochastic Solid Gaussian Rendering
head: GGGS, Gaussian Primitives as Stochastic Solids, Geometry-Grounded Gaussian Splatting, Stochastic Gaussian Solid, Stochastic Solid Proof, Volume Rendering of Gaussian Splatting
body: Stochastic Solid Gaussian Rendering (SSGR) treats 3D Gaussian primitives as stochastic solids to derive a principled, continuous attenuation coefficient, enabling volume rendering that is mathematically equivalent to standard Gaussian Splatting rasterization. This equivalence allows for the definition of a geometric field (occupancy) and the extraction of multi-view-consistent depth maps via a smooth transmittance curve, overcoming the jagged, heuristic depth estimation of prior methods that rely on discrete step-wise transmittance changes. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives, each defined by center \mathbf{x}c, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}, opacity o, and color \mathbf{c}. A camera ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \omega. Outputs: Rendered color \mathbf{C} and median depth t{0.5} (the depth where transmittance T(t) = 0.5). Data Structures: 3D Gaussian Primitive: Defined by G(\mathbf{x}) = o e^{-(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}c)^T \mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}c)}. Projected 2D Gaussian: Used for rasterization visibility culling. Opacity at pixel \mathbf{u} is \alpha(\mathbf{u}) = o e^{-(\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u}c)^T \mathbf{\Sigma}{2D}^{-1} (\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u}c)}. Stochastic Solid Vacancy: v(\mathbf{x}) = \sqrt{1 - G(\mathbf{x})}. Method Steps: 1. Rasterization and Sorting: Project 3D Gaussians to 2D using the local affine approximation. For each pixel, identify visible Gaussians (where \alpha(\mathbf{u}) > \epsilon) and sort them by depth t along the camera ray \mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\omega. 2. Attenuation Coefficient Derivation: Define the vacancy v(\mathbf{x}) for a Gaussian primitive as: v(\mathbf{x}) = \sqrt{1 - G(\mathbf{x})} This definition satisfies three constraints: Monotonicity: If G(\mathbf{x}1) \geq G(\mathbf{x}2), then occupancy o(\mathbf{x}1) \geq o(\mathbf{x}2) (where o(\mathbf{x}) = 1 - v(\mathbf{x})^2). Boundary: Occupancy approaches 0 far from the center. Differentiability: o(\mathbf{x}) is differentiable with respect to \mathbf{x}. The attenuation coefficient \sigma is derived from the vacancy gradient along the viewing direction \omega: \sigma(\mathbf{x}, \omega) = \frac{|\omega \cdot \nabla v(\mathbf{x})|}{v(\mathbf{x})} = |\omega \cdot \nabla \log(v(\mathbf{x}))| Along a ray parameterized by t, let t^ be the point where the 1D Gaussian G(t) reaches its maximum. The vacancy function has opposite monotonicity to the Gaussian function. The attenuation coefficient simplifies to: \sigma(t) = \begin{cases} -\frac{\partial \log(v(\mathbf{x}(t)))}{\partial t}, & t \leq t^ \\ \frac{\partial \log(v(\mathbf{x}(t)))}{\partial t}, & t > t^ \end{cases} 3. Volume Rendering (Forward Pass): The transmittance is T(t) = \exp \left( - \int{tn}^t \sigma(\mathbf{x}(s), \omega) ds \right). For a single Gaussian with uniform color \mathbf{c}, the volume rendering integral yields: \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{c} (1 - T(+\infty)) = \mathbf{c} (1 - v(t{end})^2) Since v(t{end}) \to 1 as t \to \infty (far from center), and the rendering is equivalent to rasterization, the color contribution of a single Gaussian is: \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{c} G(t^) = \mathbf{c} (1 - v(t^)^2) where t^ is the location of the maximum Gaussian value along the ray. 4. Depth Estimation (Median Depth): Define the median depth t{0.5} as the point along the ray where the transmittance drops to 0.5: T(t{0.5}) = 0.5 Due to the monotonicity of the transmittance curve derived from the stochastic solid formulation, t{0.5} can be located via binary search. 5. Backpropagation: Compute the gradient of the median depth t{0.5} with respect to the Gaussian parameters (center, covariance, opacity) using a closed-form expression. This gradient is backpropagated through the binary search and the attenuation model to update the Gaussians during training. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeattenuationcoefficient(vacancy, gradientalongray): """ Computes sigma(t) = |d/dt log(v)| = |gradv / v| vacancy: scalar value v(x) gradientalongray: scalar value omega. nabla v(x) """ if vacancy == 0: return 0.0 return abs(gradientalongray / vacancy) def renderstochasticsolidgaussian(rayorigin, raydir, gaussian): """ Renders a single Gaussian primitive as a stochastic solid. Returns color and median depth. """ # 1. Find t (max of 1D Gaussian along ray) # G(t) = o exp(-(x(t)-xc)^T Sigma^-1 (x(t)-xc)) # This is a quadratic in the exponent. Find t analytically. tstar = findgaussianmaxalongray(rayorigin, raydir, gaussian) # 2. Compute vacancy at tstar # v(x) = sqrt(1 - G(x)) gatstar = evaluategaussian1d(rayorigin, raydir, tstar, gaussian) vatstar = np.sqrt(1.0 - gatstar) # 3. Compute Color # C = c G(t) color = gaussian.color gatstar # 4. Compute Median Depth t0.5 # T(t) = exp(- integral{tn}^t sigma(s) ds) # We need T(t0.5) = 0.5 => integral{tn}^{t0.5} sigma(s) ds = log(2) # Use binary search to find t0.5 tmin = rayorigin.tnear tmax = rayorigin.tfar for in range(32): # Binary search iterations tmid = (tmin + tmax) / 2.0 # Compute transmittance at tmid # T(t) = v(t) / v(tn) ? # From Miller et al., T(t) = v(t) / v(tn) is not directly stated, # but T(t) = exp(-int sigma). # Note: v(t) = sqrt(1-G(t)). # The integral of sigma leads to log(v). # Specifically, T(t) = v(t) / v(tstart) if we define limits correctly. # However, standard GS assumes tstart is -inf or near field. # Let's use the property: T(t) = v(t) / v(tn) is valid if sigma is derived from v. # Actually, T(t) = exp(-int{tn}^t |d/ds log v| ds). # If v is monotonic decreasing then increasing (or vice versa), # the integral splits at t. # Simplified approach for binary search: # Calculate T(tmid) using the vacancy ratio. # T(t) = v(t) / v(tn) is only true if v is monotonic. # Here v is not monotonic over the whole ray (it dips at t). # But for t > t, v increases. For t < t, v decreases. # The transmittance T(t) represents the probability of no collision. # T(t) = v(t) / v(tn) holds for the "solid" interpretation where v is the "empty" probability? # Let's stick to the definition: T(t) = exp(-int sigma). # Compute integral of sigma from tn to tmid # sigma(t) = |d/dt log v(t)| # integral{tn}^{tmid} |d/dt log v| dt = |log v(tmid) - log v(tn)| IF v is monotonic. # Since v has a minimum at t (G has max), we must split integral at t. integral = 0.0 if tmid < tstar: # v is decreasing (G increasing) from tn to tmid? # No, G increases to t. So v decreases to t. # d/dt log v is negative. |...| = - d/dt log v. # Integral = - (log v(tmid) - log v(tn)) = log(v(tn)/v(tmid)) vatmid = np.sqrt(1.0 - evaluategaussian1d(rayorigin, raydir, tmid, gaussian)) vatn = np.sqrt(1.0 - evaluategaussian1d(rayorigin, raydir, rayorigin.tnear, gaussian)) integral = np.log(vatn / vatmid) else: # tmid > t. Split at t. # Part 1: tn to t. v decreases. Integral = log(v(tn)/v(tstar)) # Part 2: t to tmid. v increases. Integral = log(v(tmid)/v(tstar)) vatmid = np.sqrt(1.0 - evaluategaussian1d(rayorigin, raydir, tmid, gaussian)) vatn = np.sqrt(1.0 - evaluategaussian1d(rayorigin, raydir, rayorigin.tnear, gaussian)) vatstar = np.sqrt(1.0 - evaluategaussian1d(rayorigin, raydir, tstar, gaussian)) integral1 = np.log(vatn / vatstar) integral2 = np.log(vatmid / vatstar) integral = integral1 + integral2 Tmid = np.exp(-integral) if Tmid > 0.5: tmin = tmid else: tmax = tmid t05 = (tmin + tmax) / 2.0 return color, t05 def findgaussianmaxalongray(origin, dir, gaussian): """ Finds t that maximizes G(t) = o exp(- (origin + tdir - xc)^T Sigma^-1 (origin + tdir - xc)) Equivalent to minimizing the quadratic form Q(t) = (origin + tdir - xc)^T Sigma^-1 (origin + tdir - xc) """ # Let delta = origin - xc # Q(t) = (delta + tdir)^T Sigma^-1 (delta + tdir) # Q(t) = t^2 (dir^T Sigma^-1 dir) + 2t (dir^T Sigma^-1 delta) + (delta^T Sigma^-1 delta) # dQ/dt = 2t (dir^T Sigma^-1 dir) + 2 (dir^T Sigma^-1 delta) = 0 # t = - (dir^T Sigma^-1 delta) / (dir^T Sigma^-1 dir) invsigma = np.linalg.inv(gaussian.covariance) delta = origin - gaussian.center a = dir @ invsigma @ dir b = dir @ invsigma @ delta if a == 0: return origin.tnear # Degenerate case return -b / a def evaluategaussian1d(origin, dir, t, gaussian): """ Evaluates G(t) along the ray. """ x = origin + t dir diff = x - gaussian.center exponent = -diff @ np.linalg.inv(gaussian.covariance) @ diff return gaussian.opacity np.exp(exponent) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The vacancy v(\mathbf{x}) approaches 1 far from the center. Computing \log(v) when v \approx 1 can lead to numerical instability if not handled carefully (use log1p). Boundaries: The binary search for t{0.5} assumes the ray intersects the Gaussian's effective volume. If the ray misses the Gaussian entirely, G(t) \approx 0, v(t) \approx 1, T(t) \approx 1, and t{0.5} is undefined (or outside the ray bounds). Degenerate Input: If the covariance matrix is singular, the inverse is undefined. Standard GS regularization applies. Multiple Gaussians: The method is derived for a single Gaussian. For multiple Gaussians, the transmittance curves are combined. The "smooth transmittance" advantage is most significant when overlapping Gaussians create a complex joint occupancy field, which standard rasterization approximates with discrete steps. The overarching framework that uses SSGR to provide a principled geometric foundation for Gaussian primitives, enabling higher-fidelity shape reconstruction. A specific application of SSGR that extracts finer-grained, multi-view-consistent depth maps by locating the median depth via binary search on the smooth transmittance curve. Time Complexity: Rendering a single Gaussian is O(1) for color and O(\log N) for depth (binary search), where N is the number of iterations. Sorting Gaussians is O(M \log M) for M visible Gaussians. Memory Complexity: O(M) to store visible Gaussians and their parameters. Strengths: Provides a continuous, differentiable geometric field from Gaussian primitives. Enables accurate depth estimation that captures the joint effects of overlapping Gaussians, avoiding the jagged steps of discrete rasterization-based depth. Limitations: Requires solving for t^ and performing binary search for depth, which is more computationally expensive than simple alpha blending. The equivalence to rasterization holds strictly for the color; depth requires the additional stochastic solid formulation. When to use: When multi-view consistent geometry and accurate depth maps are required from Gaussian Splatting representations. When not to use: When only novel view synthesis (color) is needed and standard GS rasterization is sufficient, as SSGR adds computational overhead for depth. The method is based on the theoretical foundation of "Objects as Volumes" by Miller et al. [2024], which provides a stochastic interpretation of geometry-grounded radiance fields. It was introduced by Zhang et al. in "Geometry-Grounded Gaussian Splatting" to address the open problem of shape extraction from Gaussian primitives, which previously suffered from poor multi-view consistency and sensitivity to floaters due to heuristic geometry parameterization. Geometry-Grounded Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.17835v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: UniqueSplat
head: View-Conditioned 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: UniqueSplat is a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting method that generates dynamic Gaussian parameters conditioned on the query view, addressing the limitation of prior feed-forward methods that produce fixed Gaussians across all views. It distinguishes itself by using a dual-branch hypernetwork to inject both view-agnostic scene knowledge and view-specific geometric priors into the primary network, enabling accurate reconstruction of scene structures and realistic novel view synthesis. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: K sparse-view input images Ic = \{I^ic\}{i=1}^K, their camera projection matrices Pc = \{P^ic\}{i=1}^K, and N target view projection matrices Pt = \{P^it\}{i=1}^N. Outputs: Rendered target view images It = \{I^it\}{i=1}^N. Data Structures: Learnable Embedding (ea): A fixed vector capturing generalizable features across views. Weight Matrix (Wa): Dimensions R^{C{out} \times C{in}}, generated by the view-agnostic hypernetwork. Feature Volume (Fp): Extracted by the primary network encoder, containing intrinsic view information. Projected Features (Ft): Features from input views projected onto the target view geometry. View-Specific Embedding (es): Derived from Ft, capturing specific view knowledge. Weight Delta (\Delta W): Dimensions R^{C{out} \times C{in}}, generated by the view-specific hypernetwork. Fused Weight (WH): Dimensions R^{C{out} \times C{in}}, sum of Wa and \Delta W. Gaussian Parameters: Mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, and color c. Steps: 1. View-Agnostic Branch Initialization: Compute the view-agnostic weight matrix Wa using a hypernetwork Ha and the learnable embedding ea: Wa = Ha(ea), \quad Wa \in R^{C{out} \times C{in}} where C{in} and C{out} are the input and output dimensions of the target convolution layers in the primary network. 2. Input Feature Extraction: For each input image I^ic (i=1 \dots K), extract per-view features F^ic using a backbone encoder EH: F^ic = EH(I^ic), \quad I^ic \in R^{H \times W \times 3} Collect these into Fc = \{F^ic\}{i=1}^K. 3. Primary Network Feature Encoding: Encode the input images and their camera parameters using the primary network encoder Ep to produce the feature volume Fp: Fp = Ep(Ic, Pc) where Ic and Pc represent the input images and their corresponding camera parameters. 4. View-Specific Feature Projection: For each target view i (i=1 \dots N) with projection matrix P^it = Kt[Rt | tt], project the source features Fc to align with the target view to get F^it: F^it = \text{Proj}(Fc, Pc, P^it) The projection details for a single target pixel (ut, vt) are as follows: a. Convert pixel coordinates to normalized camera coordinates pt: pt = Kt^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} ut \\ vt \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} where pt = [xt, yt, 1]^\top. b. Map pt to world coordinates to get ray origin o and direction r: r = Rt^\top pt, \quad o = tt where Rt and tt are the rotation and translation of the target view. c. Define the ray in world coordinates: x(\lambda) = o + \lambda r, \quad \lambda \in R. d. Project the ray onto source views to obtain epipolar lines pc(\lambda): pc(\lambda) = Pc x(\lambda) = Pc(o + \lambda r). e. Express epipolar lines as a linear function L = A pt + b, where: A = Kc Rc Rt^\top b = Kc(Rc tt + tc) Here, A represents the relative rotation and b encodes the relative translation between target and source views. f. Uniformly sample n points along the features between near and far planes. Compute a correlation matrix C{ij} to fuse projected features: C{ij}(M1, M2) = \frac{\langle M^i1, M^j2 \rangle}{\|M^i1\| \|M^j2\|} where M^ij is the j-th row of matrix Mi, \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle is the inner product, and \|\cdot\| is the vector norm. 5. View-Specific Embedding and Weight Generation: Map the fused target view feature Ft to an embedding es using a function \phi: es = \phi(Ft). Process es with a hypernetwork Hs to generate the weight delta \Delta W: \Delta W = Hs(es), \quad \Delta W \in R^{C{out} \times C{in}}. 6. Weight Fusion: Fuse the view-agnostic weight Wa and the view-specific weight delta \Delta W to obtain the final weight matrix WH: WH = Wa + \Delta W, \quad WH \in R^{C{out} \times C{in}}. 7. Gaussian Parameter Prediction: Inject the fused weights WH into the convolutional layers of the primary network's predictor. The predictor estimates the 3D Gaussian parameters \mu, \Sigma, \alpha, c from the feature volume Fp: \mu, \Sigma, \alpha, c = D{\text{Injected}}(Fp). 8. Rendering: Render the target views It using the predicted Gaussians G and target projection matrices Pt: It = R(G, Pt). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def UniqueSplat(Ic, Pc, Pt): """ Ic: List of K input images Pc: List of K camera projection matrices for input views Pt: List of N camera projection matrices for target views Returns: List of N rendered target images """ # 1. View-Agnostic Branch # Ha is the view-agnostic hypernetwork, ea is the learnable embedding Wa = Ha(ea) # 2. Input Feature Extraction Fc = [] for i in range(len(Ic)): Fc.append(EH(Ic[i])) # 3. Primary Network Feature Encoding Fp = Ep(Ic, Pc) # 4. View-Specific Branch Ftlist = [] for i in range(len(Pt)): # Project source features to target view Ft = Proj(Fc, Pc, Pt[i]) Ftlist.append(Ft) # 5. View-Specific Embedding and Weight Generation # Note: The source pseudocode implies a single Ft or aggregation. # Based on Eq 11, es = phi(Ft). We assume Ft is aggregated or processed per view. # For implementation, we process the first target view or aggregate if N>1. # The source algorithm 1 shows a loop for Ft but then single es/deltaW. # We follow the structure: compute Ft for the specific target view being rendered. # Assuming we render one target view at a time or Ft is the aggregate feature volume # for the set of target views. The source text says "For each target view i... Ft". # Then "es = phi(Ft)". This implies Ft might be the feature volume for the specific target view. # Let's assume the function is called per target view or Ft is pre-aggregated. # Based on Algorithm 1: # for i <- 1 to N: Ft = Proj(...) # es = phi(Ft) # This suggests Ft is overwritten or aggregated. name: Adaptive Spherical Harmonics Band Adjustment
head: Adaptive SH Bands, SH Band Culling, Variable SH, Variable SH Bands, Variable Spherical Harmonics Bands
body: Adaptive Spherical Harmonics Band Adjustment is a memory optimization technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that assigns a variable number of spherical harmonics (SH) bands (0 to 3) to each primitive based on its view-dependent appearance complexity. It addresses the wasteful memory utilization of the standard fixed 3-band SH representation, where 76% of the primitive storage is dedicated to SH coefficients, by disabling higher-order bands for primitives that can be adequately represented by a single RGB color or fewer bands. Unlike DeSplat which focuses on spatial redundancy, this method specifically targets the attribute storage overhead of view-dependent shading. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives optimized for 15,000 iterations (the point where densification stops), including their positions, covariances, opacities, rotations, base RGB colors, and full 3-band SH coefficients. Output: The same set of primitives, but with SH coefficients pruned to the minimum necessary bands (0, 1, 2, or 3), stored in four separate sets based on band count. Data Structures: The primitive structure in the original 3DGS method consists of 14 base floats plus SH coefficients. Base attributes: Position (3), Scale (3), Rotation (4, quaternion), Opacity (1), RGB Color (3). Total: 14 floats. SH coefficients: For b bands, the number of coefficients is \sum{l=1}^{b} (2l+1). 0 bands: 0 floats. 1 band: 3 floats. 2 bands: 3 + 5 = 8 floats. 3 bands: 8 + 7 = 15 floats. Total storage per primitive: 14 + 3 \times \sum{l=1}^{b} (2l+1) floats. Storage layout: Primitives are stored in 4 separate contiguous sets (or lists), one for each band count b \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}. Parameters: \sigma{th}: Variance threshold for Approach 1. Default: 0.04. \sigma{cdist}: Distance threshold for Approach 2. Default: 0.04. Densification stop iteration: The iteration count at which SH analysis begins. Default: 15,000. Steps: 1. Timing: Perform the analysis once at the halfway point of training (15,000 iterations) to allow remaining optimization steps to compensate for quality degradation. 2. Evaluation: For each primitive, evaluate its color from all input training views. 3. Approach 1 (Variance Check): Calculate the average transmittance \bar{T}i for the primitive in each view i. Calculate the weighted average color \muc and weighted variance \sigmac across all N views. If \sigmac < \sigma{th}, assign the primitive 0 SH bands. Replace its base RGB color with \muc and discard all SH coefficients. 4. Approach 2 (Distance Check): (Applied to primitives not already assigned 0 bands, or as a secondary check) For each view, evaluate the primitive's color using only the first b SH bands for b \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}, resulting in colors \mathbf{c}b. Calculate the Euclidean distance between the full 3-band color \mathbf{c}3 and the reduced colors \mathbf{c}0, \mathbf{c}1, \mathbf{c}2, resulting in distances d0, d1, d2. Average each distance value across all views, weighted by average transmittance \bar{T}i. Find the lowest band b such that the average distance is below \sigma{cdist}. Assign the primitive b bands and remove all coefficients for bands higher than b. 5. Storage: Partition the primitives into 4 sets based on their assigned band count. Formulas: Average transmittance for primitive in view i: \bar{T}i = \frac{\sum{k=1}^{P} T{ik}}{P} where P is the number of pixels the primitive is splatted to in view i, and T{ik} is the transmittance of the primitive for pixel k. Weighted average color \muc: \muc = \frac{\sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \bar{T}i}{\sum{i=1}^{N} \bar{T}i} where N is the number of views containing the primitive, and \mathbf{c}i is the color of the primitive in view i. Weighted color variance \sigmac: \sigmac = \frac{\sum{i=1}^{N} (\mathbf{c}i - \muc)^2 \bar{T}i}{\sum{i=1}^{N} \bar{T}i} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptiveshbandadjustment(primitives, trainingviews, numiterations, densificationstopiter=15000): """ Adjusts SH bands for primitives based on view-dependent variance and error. primitives: List of Gaussian primitives. Each has.pos,.scale,.rot,.opacity,.shcoeffs (list of floats),.rgb. trainingviews: List of view data. Each view has.camera,.image,.transmittancemap (for each primitive splat). """ if numiterations < densificationstopiter: return primitives # Group primitives by assigned band count primitivesbyband = {0: [], 1: [], 2: [], 3: []} for prim in primitives: # Evaluate color from all views viewcolors = [] viewtransmittances = [] for view in trainingviews: # Get color of this primitive in this view using full SH color = evaluateshcolor(prim.shcoeffs, view.camera.direction) viewcolors.append(color) # Get average transmittance for this primitive in this view # Tik is transmittance for pixel k. P is number of pixels splatted. # Assuming view provides a way to get splat coverage or transmittance sum pcount = view.getpixelcountforprimitive(prim) tsum = view.gettransmittancesumforprimitive(prim) avgt = tsum / pcount if pcount > 0 else 0 viewtransmittances.append(avgt) # Approach 1: Variance Check totalt = sum(viewtransmittances) if totalt > 0: muc = sum(c t for c, t in zip(viewcolors, viewtransmittances)) / totalt sigmac = sum((c - muc)2 t for c, t in zip(viewcolors, viewtransmittances)) / totalt if sigmac < 0.04: # sigmath prim.rgb = muc prim.shcoeffs = [] # 0 bands primitivesbyband[0].append(prim) continue # Approach 2: Distance Check # Evaluate colors with 0, 1, 2 bands colorsreduced = [] for b in range(4): # 0 to 3 reducedcoeffs = prim.shcoeffs[:sum(2l+1 for l in range(1, b+1))] colorsb = [] for view in trainingviews: cb = evaluateshcolor(reducedcoeffs, view.camera.direction) colorsb.append(cb) colorsreduced.append(colorsb) # Calculate distances from full color (3 bands) fullcolors = colorsreduced[3] distances = [] for b in range(3): # 0, 1, 2 distsperview = [] for cfull, cred in zip(fullcolors, colorsreduced[b]): d = euclideandistance(cfull, cred) distsperview.append(d) # Weighted average distance avgdist = sum(d t for d, t in zip(distsperview, viewtransmittances)) / totalt distances.append(avgdist) # Find lowest band b where avgdist < sigmacdist assignedband = 3 for b in range(3): if distances[b] < 0.04: # sigmacdist assignedband = b break # Keep only necessary coefficients numcoeffs = sum(2l+1 for l in range(1, assignedband+1)) prim.shcoeffs = prim.shcoeffs[:numcoeffs] primitivesbyband[assignedband].append(prim) return primitivesbyband def evaluateshcolor(shcoeffs, direction): """ Evaluates the color from SH coefficients given a viewing direction. Standard SH evaluation. """ # Implementation of SH basis evaluation # Returns RGB vector pass def euclideandistance(c1, c2): return sum((a-b)2 for a, b in zip(c1, c2))0.5 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on floating-point variance and distance calculations. Small inaccuracies in transmittance or color evaluation can lead to incorrect band assignment. Timing: Applying culling too early (before 15,000 iterations) may prevent the optimizer from compensating for the loss of view-dependent detail, leading to quality degradation. Degenerate Input: If a primitive is not visible in any training view, transmittance is zero, leading to division by zero in variance/distance calculations. Such primitives should be handled or excluded. A related approach to variable representation, but focuses on mapping basis functions differently rather than just culling SH bands [17312-variable-basis-mapping-vbm.md]. General techniques for removing primitives, often used in conjunction with SH adjustment to further reduce memory [16215-pruning-and-density-control.md]. A subsequent step that compresses the remaining attributes (including the variable SH bands) using codebooks, achieving further memory reduction. Time Complexity: The analysis step is performed once at 15,000 iterations. It requires evaluating the SH function for each primitive across all training views, which is O(N{primitives} \times N{views}). Memory Complexity: Reduces memory footprint by approximately 87% when combined with other optimizations (like quantization). The original 3DGS uses 59 floats per primitive (45 for SH); this method reduces the SH portion significantly. Measured Performance: In the source experiments, the distribution of primitives over bands was 89% for 0 bands, 0.1% for 1 band, 2.7% for 2 bands, and 8.2% for 3 bands. Strengths: Significantly reduces memory usage without substantial quality loss, as most primitives are diffuse and require only 0 bands. Limitations: Disabling SH bands causes small quality degradation, mitigated by the timing of the culling and sparsity loss. When to use: When memory is a constraint and the scene contains many diffuse surfaces. When not to use: When high-fidelity view-dependent effects (e.g., glossy reflections) are critical and cannot be approximated by fewer bands. The method was introduced in "Reducing the Memory Footprint of 3D Gaussian Splatting" (2024). It addresses the observation that the standard 3DGS representation uses 76% of its storage for SH coefficients, which is wasteful for diffuse materials. The authors observed that view-dependent effects can often be modeled by combinations of primitives or lower-order SH bands. The method is part of a broader strategy that includes redundant primitive removal and codebook quantization to achieve a 27x memory reduction with a 0.21 dB PSNR drop. name: Camera and Projection Models
head: Camera Models, Projection Models
body: Camera and Projection Models define the geometric transformation from 3D scene coordinates to 2D image coordinates, serving as the foundation for differentiable rendering in Gaussian Splatting. This family replaces or augments the standard perspective projection of 3D Gaussian Splatting to support specific optical characteristics, such as defocus blur or fisheye distortion, or to optimize computational efficiency for specific domains like satellite imagery. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by modifying the projection function \phi and its Jacobian, thereby altering how 2D covariances are derived and how depth-dependent effects (like Circle of Confusion) are modeled. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of mapping 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{S} to 2D screen space for rasterization. The fundamental steps are: 1. View Transformation: Transform the 3D mean \boldsymbol{\mu} and covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} from world coordinates to camera coordinates using the viewing matrix \mathbf{W} and translation \mathbf{b}: \boldsymbol{\mu}c = \mathbf{W}\boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{b} 2. Projection: Apply a projection function \phi: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2 to map the camera-space mean to 2D pixel coordinates: \boldsymbol{\mu}p = \phi(\boldsymbol{\mu}c) 3. Covariance Projection: Compute the 2D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' using the Jacobian \mathbf{J} of the projection function \phi with respect to the camera-space coordinates, and the viewing rotation \mathbf{W}: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' = \mathbf{J} \mathbf{W} \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \mathbf{W}^T \mathbf{J}^T This affine approximation ensures the projected Gaussian remains a valid 2D Gaussian primitive. Differentiable DOF Rendering extends the projection model to simulate depth-of-field effects by convolving projected 2D Gaussians with depth-dependent blur kernels [18289-differentiable-dof-rendering.md]. It sets itself apart by treating the Circle of Confusion (CoC) radius as a differentiable parameter derived from camera aperture and focal distance, allowing joint optimization of scene geometry and camera intrinsics. It is chosen when realistic optical blur is required for training or rendering. Fisheye-GS replaces the standard perspective projection with an equidistant fisheye model to handle extreme curvature and wide fields of view [20662-fisheye-gs.md]. It sets itself apart by recalculating the projection transformation and optimizing tile-based rasterization to reduce computational redundancies caused by high splat density in wide-angle views. It is chosen for scenes captured with fisheye lenses. A per-scene affine approximation of the transformation from world-space to 2D NDC-space, replacing the complex RPC-based mapping to improve computational efficiency while maintaining compatibility with Gaussian Splatting. \mu^Ak = A\muk + a \in \mathbb{R}^2 and \Sigma^A{2\times2} = A\Sigma A^T \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times2}, where A: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2 is the affine camera model, \muk is the Gaussian mean, a is the translation vector, \Sigma is the covariance matrix, and A^T is the transpose of A. The affine model A maps 3D world coordinates to 2D NDC coordinates normalized to range [-1, 1]. The original 3DGS method uses a local first-order approximation for projection; this method eliminates that need by moving the approximation to the camera model definition itself. Mean error of the affine approximation is approximately 0.012 pixels compared to the full RPC transformation. The standard perspective projection model was introduced in the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper. The affine camera approximation for satellite imagery was introduced in "Gaussian Splatting for Efficient Satellite Image Photogrammetry" to handle Rational Polynomial Coefficient (RPC) models efficiently. Differentiable DOF rendering and Fisheye-GS are extensions developed to handle specific optical phenomena not covered by the standard pinhole camera model. name: Differentiable DOF Rendering
head: Differentiable Depth of Field Rendering
body: Differentiable DOF Rendering generates blurred images by convolving projected 2D Gaussians with depth-dependent blur kernels derived from a finite-aperture camera model, enabling the differentiable optimization of camera parameters and scene geometry. It differs from standard Gaussian Splatting 3D Gaussian Splatting by explicitly modeling defocus blur via the Circle of Confusion (CoC), allowing the system to learn camera intrinsics (aperture, focal distance) alongside scene structure. Inputs: Set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{S} with means \boldsymbol{\mu}, covariances \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, colors, and opacities. Camera parameters: focal length F, aperture A, and focal distance f. Image resolution Q (pixel dimensions). Outputs: Rendered color image \tilde{\mathbf{I}}. Rendered depth map \tilde{\mathbf{D}}. Rendered CoC map \tilde{\mathbf{M}}^{(coc)}. Data Structures: 2D Gaussian Gk': Result of projecting 3D Gaussian k to screen space. Defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}p, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}', color \mathbf{c}k, and opacity \alphak. Blur Kernel Gk^{(coc)}: An isotropic 2D Gaussian kernel centered at \boldsymbol{\mu}p with covariance \Sigmak^{(coc)} = a \mathbf{I}. Convolved Gaussian Gk'': The result of Gk' Gk^{(coc)}. Steps: 1. Projection: Transform each 3D Gaussian Gk to 2D screen space to obtain Gk' using the view transformation and projection Jacobian as defined in Camera and Projection Models. 2. CoC Radius Calculation: For each projected 2D Gaussian Gk', calculate the Circle of Confusion radius Rk^{(coc)} based on its center depth zk (the z-coordinate of the transformed mean in camera space): Rk^{(coc)} = \frac{1}{2} Q \left| \frac{1}{zk} - \frac{1}{f} \right| where Q = \frac{F}{A} is the simplified aperture parameter, F is the lens focal length, A is the aperture, and f is the focal distance. 3. Blur Kernel Construction: Construct the isotropic blur kernel Gk^{(coc)} with covariance \Sigmak^{(coc)} = a \mathbf{I}: Gk^{(coc)}(\mathbf{x}) = \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{x}^T \Sigmak^{(coc)} \mathbf{x} \right) The scalar a is determined by minimizing the L2 distance between the Gaussian kernel and a uniform intensity distribution within the CoC radius Rk^{(coc)}: a = \frac{(Rk^{(coc)})^2}{2 \ln 4} 4. Convolution: Convolve the projected 2D Gaussian Gk' with the blur kernel Gk^{(coc)} to obtain the convolved Gaussian Gk'': Gk'' = Gk' Gk^{(coc)} Since the convolution of two Gaussians is a Gaussian, Gk'' remains a valid 2D Gaussian primitive, preserving the rasterization consistency. 5. Re-evaluation of Pixel Associations: Because convolution changes the spatial support of the Gaussians, re-evaluate the set of Gaussians linked to each pixel, denoted as N{x'}. 6. Compositing: Accumulate contributions from the convolved Gaussians to compute the final color \tilde{\mathbf{I}}, depth \tilde{\mathbf{D}}, and CoC map \tilde{\mathbf{M}}^{(coc)} for each pixel \mathbf{x}: \tilde{\mathbf{I}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=1}^{N{x'}} \mathbf{c}i \alphai' Ti' \tilde{\mathbf{D}}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\sum{i=1}^{N{x'}} \alphai' Ti' zi}{\sum{i=1}^{N{x'}} \alphai' Ti'} \tilde{\mathbf{M}}^{(coc)}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=1}^{N{x'}} \alphai' Ti' Ri^{(coc)} where \alphai' = Gi''(\mathbf{x}) is the opacity of the convolved Gaussian at pixel \mathbf{x}, Ti' = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj') is the transmittance, and zi is the depth of the i-th Gaussian. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def differentiabledofrender(gaussians3d, cameraparams, imageresolution): """ gaussians3d: List of 3D Gaussian objects with attributes: mu: (3,) mean in world space Sigma: (3,3) covariance in world space color: (3,) color opacity: scalar cameraparams: Object with attributes: F: float, focal length A: float, aperture f: float, focal distance imageresolution: (H, W) tuple """ Q = cameraparams.F / cameraparams.A # Step 1: Project 3D Gaussians to 2D (Assuming standard GS projection logic) gaussians2d = [] for g in gaussians3d: # Transform mean and covariance to camera space muc = transformtocameraspace(g.mu, cameraparams.W, cameraparams.b) Sigmac = transformcovariance(g.Sigma, cameraparams.W) # Project to 2D screen space mup, Sigmap = projecttoscreen(muc, Sigmac, cameraparams.J) # Get depth zk (z-coordinate of transformed mean) zk = muc[2] gaussians2d.append({ 'mu': mup, 'Sigma': Sigmap, 'color': g.color, 'opacity': g.opacity, 'z': zk }) # Step 2 & 3: Calculate CoC and Blur Kernel parameters convolvedgaussians = [] for g2d in gaussians2d: zk = g2d['z'] f = cameraparams.f # Calculate CoC radius # Handle division by zero or invalid depth if necessary if zk == 0: Rcoc = 0.0 else: Rcoc = 0.5 imageresolution[0] abs(1.0/zk - 1.0/f) # Calculate scalar 'a' for isotropic covariance # a = Rcoc^2 / (2 ln(4)) a = (Rcoc 2) / (2.0 math.log(4)) # The blur kernel is isotropic: Sigmak^(coc) = a I # Convolution of two Gaussians with covariances Sigma1 and Sigma2 # results in a Gaussian with covariance Sigma1 + Sigma2. # Here, Sigma1 is the projected 2D Gaussian Sigmap. # Sigma2 is the blur kernel covariance aI. Sigmaconv = g2d['Sigma'] + (a np.eye(2)) convolvedgaussians.append({ 'mu': g2d['mu'], 'Sigma': Sigmaconv, 'color': g2d['color'], 'opacity': g2d['opacity'], 'z': g2d['z'], 'Rcoc': Rcoc }) # Step 4 & 5: Rasterize convolved Gaussians # Re-evaluate pixel associations based on new Sigmaconv # Perform tile-based alpha blending image = np.zeros((imageresolution[1], imageresolution[2], 3)) depthmap = np.zeros((imageresolution[1], imageresolution[2])) cocmap = np.zeros((imageresolution[1], imageresolution[2])) # Sort convolvedgaussians by depth for correct alpha blending convolvedgaussians.sort(key=lambda x: x['z']) for gconv in convolvedgaussians: # Evaluate Gaussian at each pixel within its bounding box # This is typically done via CUDA kernel for efficiency pixels = getpixelsinsupport(gconv['mu'], gconv['Sigma']) for p in pixels: # Evaluate convolved Gaussian density at pixel p alphaprime = evaluategaussian2d(p, gconv['mu'], gconv['Sigma']) # Calculate transmittance T' (requires sorting and accumulation) # In a full implementation, T' is accumulated per pixel # Here we assume a simplified accumulation for demonstration # Note: T' depends on the order of Gaussians covering pixel p pass # Final accumulation logic would follow standard GS rasterization # but using alphaprime and Rcoc from convolvedgaussians return image, depthmap, cocmap Parameters: F (Focal Length): Not given in the sources. A (Aperture): Not given in the sources. f (Focal Distance): Not given in the sources. Q (Simplified Aperture Parameter): Derived from F/A. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Zero: Division by zk in the CoC radius formula requires handling zk=0. Precision: CUDA-customized rasterization is used to incorporate Gaussian convolution and derivative calculations for efficiency and differentiability. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables differentiable optimization of camera parameters (f, Q) and scene geometry. Mitigates reconstruction artifacts caused by defocus blur. Limitations: Requires re-evaluation of pixel-Gaussian associations after convolution, increasing computational overhead compared to standard splatting. When to use: When training data contains natural defocus blur and the goal is to reconstruct a scene with accurate camera intrinsics or to perform post-capture refocusing. Originated in "DOF-GS: Adjustable Depth-of-Field 3D Gaussian Splatting for Post-Capture Refocusing, Defocus Rendering and Blur Removal". The method extends 3D Gaussian Splatting by integrating a finite-aperture camera model to simulate depth-of-field effects, allowing the system to learn from blurred images. name: Fisheye-GS
head: Differentiable Equidistant Projection for 3DGS, Fisheye 3D Gaussian Splatting, Fisheye-GS Equidistant Projection
body: Fisheye-GS is a method that integrates fisheye camera data into 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by replacing the standard perspective projection with an equidistant projection model and optimizing the rendering pipeline to handle extreme curvature and wide fields of view. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by deriving specific Jacobians for the equidistant projection to maintain image quality across wide angles, and by reducing computational redundancy in tile-based splatting to achieve real-time performance. Fisheye-GS extends the standard 3DGS pipeline by modifying the projection function \phi and its Jacobian \mathbf{J} to support fisheye lenses, while optimizing the CUDA kernel for tile traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{S} defined by means \boldsymbol{\mu}, covariances \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, opacities \alpha, and colors \mathbf{c}; camera parameters including focal length f, principal point (cx, cy), and pixel focal lengths fx, fy; and the viewing matrix \mathbf{W} and translation \mathbf{b}. Outputs: A rendered 2D image \mathbf{C}. Data Structures: The method uses the standard 3DGS data structures for Gaussians: \boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}: Covariance matrix, parameterized as \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{R}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{S}^T\mathbf{R}^T, where \mathbf{R} \in SO(3) is the rotation matrix (from quaternions) and \mathbf{S} = \text{diag}(s1, s2, s3) is the scaling matrix. \mathbf{c}: Color. \alpha: Opacity. Projection Model: Standard 3DGS uses perspective projection. Fisheye-GS uses the equidistant projection model. For a point \mathbf{p}c = (xc, yc, zc)^T in camera coordinates: 1. Calculate the distance to the z-axis: lz = \sqrt{xc^2 + yc^2} 2. Calculate the angle of incidence \theta: \theta = \arctan\left(\frac{lz}{zc}\right) 3. Calculate the pixel coordinates (xp, yp): xp = cx + \frac{fx \theta xc}{lz} yp = cy + \frac{fy \theta yc}{lz} where f is the focal length (used in rd = f\theta), and fx, fy are pixel focal lengths. Jacobian Derivation: The 2D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' is computed using the Jacobian \mathbf{J} of the projection function \phi with respect to the camera-space coordinates: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' = \mathbf{J} \mathbf{W} \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \mathbf{W}^T \mathbf{J}^T The Jacobian \mathbf{J} \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times3} is the derivative of the equidistant projection equations with respect to (xc, yc, zc). This allows for differentiable training. Rendering Pipeline: 1. View Transformation: Transform \boldsymbol{\mu} and \boldsymbol{\Sigma} to camera space: \boldsymbol{\mu}c = \mathbf{W}\boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{b}. 2. Projection: Apply \phi to \boldsymbol{\mu}c to get \boldsymbol{\mu}p. Compute \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' using the derived Jacobian. 3. Tile-Based Rasterization: Divide the image plane into 16 \times 16 tiles. For each Gaussian, compute its axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) in screen space. Traverse tiles intersecting the AABB. Sort Gaussians by depth within each tile. Perform alpha blending for each pixel in the tile: \mathbf{C} = \sum{i=1}^n \mathbf{c}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \alphai is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian evaluated at the pixel. Optimization: The method eliminates computational redundancies in the CUDA kernel, specifically reducing the number of overlapped tiles processed, which is critical for the extreme curvature of fisheye lenses. """ lz = math.sqrt(xc2 + yc2) if lz == 0: # Degenerate case: point is on the optical axis return cx, cy theta = math.atan(lz / zc) xp = cx + (fx theta xc) / lz yp = cy + (fy theta yc) / lz return xp, yp def computejacobianequidistant(xc, yc, zc, fx, fy): """ Computes the 2x3 Jacobian matrix J of the equidistant projection with respect to (xc, yc, zc). theta xc dlz/dxc / lz^2 # dtheta/dxc = dtheta/dlz dlz/dxc = dtheta/dlz xc/lz dthetadxc = dthetadlz (xc / lz) dthetadyc = dthetadlz (yc / lz) # Term for xp term1x = (dthetadxc xc + theta) / lz term2x = theta xc (xc / lz) / (lz2) dxpdxc = fx (term1x - """ # 1. View Transformation muworld = gaussian['mu'] muc = viewmatrix @ muworld + translation xc, yc, zc = muc # 2. Equidistant Projection cx, cy = cameraparams['principalpoint'] fx, fy = cameraparams['pixelfocallengths'] xp, yp = equidistantprojection(xc, yc, zc, cx, cy, fx, fy) mup = np.array([xp, yp]) # 3. Covariance Projection Sigma = gaussian['covariance'] # 3x3 W = viewmatrix # Compute Jacobian J (2x3) J = computejacobianequidistant(xc, yc, zc, fx, fy) # Sigma' = J W Sigma W^T J^T Sigmaprime = J @ W @ Sigma @ W.T @ J.T # 4. Complexity: The method reduces computational redundancy compared to standard 3DGS by optimizing the number of overlapped tiles, which is particularly beneficial for the extreme curvature and wide field of view of fisheye lenses. Strengths: Maintains image quality and precision across extreme curvature; produces distortion-free imagery; suitable for real-time applications. Limitations: Specific to fisheye cameras using the equidistant projection model; may not be optimal for standard perspective cameras without modification. Fisheye-GS was introduced to address the inefficiencies of tile-based splatting when applied to fisheye cameras, which have wide fields of view (180° or greater) and significant radial distortion. It is the first work to seamlessly integrate fisheye camera data into 3D Gaussian Splatting, enabling applications in virtual reality, gaming, security, and panoramic environments.
