name: RaDe-GS Rasterized Depth and Normal Computation
head: RaDe-GS
body: RaDe-GS is a method for deriving rasterized depth and normal maps directly from 3D Gaussian splats by exploiting the planar property of intersection points in ray space, allowing direct integration into existing Gaussian Splatting pipelines. It differs from NeRF-based implicit methods that use Signed Distance Fields (SDF) to represent the scene and transform SDF to opacity for ray-tracing by utilizing explicit rasterized depth and normal maps from Gaussian splats. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians (centers, covariances, opacities, spherical harmonics coefficients) initialized from a sparse point cloud (e.g., via COLMAP). Training images with known camera poses. Outputs: Rasterized depth map, rasterized normal map, and optimized 3D Gaussian parameters. Data Structures: 3D Gaussian: Defined by center \mathbf{u}c = (uc, vc, tc)^\top in ray space, covariance matrix, opacity, and color. Ray Space Coordinates: The local affine transformation \mathbf{J} maps camera space to ray space. CUDA Kernels: Customized kernels are used for rasterized depth, normal map computations, and regularization terms, built upon the public code of 3D Gaussian Splatting. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Generate a sparse point cloud for each scene using COLMAP given the camera poses. Initialize 3D Gaussians from this point cloud. 2. Photometric Training: Train the 3D Gaussians using only rendering losses (photometric loss \mathcal{L}c) for 15,000 iterations. 3. Geometry-Aware Training: Optimize the result further with depth and normal constraints for another 15,000 iterations. During this phase, detach the gradient propagation of the blending weight \omega when calculating the depth distortion loss. Set weight parameters wd = 100 and wn = 5. 4. Mesh Extraction: Render depth maps for all training views. Construct a Truncated Signed Distance Field (TSDF). Extract the mesh using the Marching Cubes algorithm. Formulas and Definitions: Ray Space Plane Equation: The intersection points between a Gaussian splat and a bundle of light rays lie on a plane in ray space. Let \mathbf{u}c = (uc, vc, tc)^\top be the Gaussian center. Let \mathbf{p} contain the first two components of \hat{\mathbf{p}}. Define \mathbf{q} as: \mathbf{q} = \frac{tc}{zc} \mathbf{p} where \mathbf{q} is a 2D vector derived from the Gaussian center and projection parameters. The plane equation for all intersection points is: (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}c) = \begin{pmatrix} -\Delta u \\ -\Delta v \\ (\Delta u - \Delta v) \mathbf{q}^\top \end{pmatrix} where \mathbf{u} is a point on the plane in ray space. Ray Space Normal: The vector \mathbf{q} - \mathbf{1} is normal to the plane formed by all intersection points, where \mathbf{1} is a vector of ones. The normal pointing toward the image plane is: \mathbf{n}' = -(\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{1})^T Here, \mathbf{n}' is a 3 \times 1 vector since \mathbf{q} is a 1 \times 2 vector. Camera Space Normal: Transform the ray-space normal \mathbf{n}' to camera-space normal \mathbf{n} using the local affine matrix \mathbf{J}: \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{J}^\top \mathbf{n}' After transformation, the vector \mathbf{n} is normalized to unit length. Loss Functions: Depth Distortion Loss: Minimizes disparity between depths of different Gaussian splats on a ray. \mathcal{L}d = \sum{i,j} \omegai \omegaj (di - dj)^2 where \omegai is the blending weight of the i-th Gaussian and di is its depth. Normal Consistency Loss: Ensures Gaussian splats align with the surface. \mathcal{L}n = \sumi \omegai (1 - \mathbf{n}i^\top \tilde{\mathbf{n}}) where \mathbf{n}i is the Gaussian normal, and \tilde{\mathbf{n}} is the surface normal obtained by applying finite-difference on the depth map. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}c + wd \mathcal{L}d + wn \mathcal{L}n where \mathcal{L}c is the photometric loss. Parameters: wd = 100. wn = 5. Iterations: 15k for photometric training, 15k for geometry-aware training. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient propagation of the blending weight \omega must be detached when calculating depth distortion loss to ensure stability. The method assumes the local affine transformation assumption, which is standard in Gaussian Splatting. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computerayspacenormal(gaussiancenter, projectionparams): """ Computes the ray-space normal n' for a Gaussian splat. Args: gaussiancenter: tuple (uc, vc, tc) projectionparams: object containing zc and p (first two components of phat) Returns: nprime: 3x1 vector in ray space """ uc, vc, tc = gaussiancenter zc = projectionparams.zc p = projectionparams.p # 2D vector # Compute q # q = (tc / zc) p q = (tc / zc) p # q is 1x2 vector. 1 is vector of ones [1, 1] # n' = -(q - 1)^T # q - 1 is element-wise subtraction # Result is 1x2. Transpose makes it 2x1? # Note: Source says n' is 3x1. # Equation 21: n' = -(q - 1)^T. # If q is 1x2, q-1 is 1x2. (q-1)^T is 2x1. # However, source says "n' is a 3x1 vector since q is a 1x2 vector". # This implies n' might be padded or the definition implies a specific embedding. # Looking at Eq 20: (q 1)(u - uc) = 0. # The normal to the plane in 3D ray space (u, v, t) is derived from coefficients of u, v, t. # Plane eq: -qu u - qv v + 1 t +... = 0 ? # Let's stick to the vector definition provided: n' = -(q - 1)^T. # If q = [qu, qv], then q - 1 = [qu - 1, qv - 1]. # Transpose is column vector [[qu - 1], [qv - 1]]. # To make it 3x1, we likely append a component or the source implies a specific basis. # Given the ambiguity in "3x1" vs "2x1" from the formula, we implement the formula as written. # However, Eq 22 uses J^T n'. J is 3x3 (local affine). So n' must be 3x1. # The plane equation is (u - uc) =... # The normal to the plane defined by (u - uc) dot n' = 0? # Eq 20: (q 1) (u - uc) = 0. # Let n'ray = [qu, qv, -1]? Or [qu, qv, 1]? # If (q 1) is a row vector [qu, qv, 1] acting on (u-uc)? # No, (q 1) is likely [qu, qv] concatenated with 1? # Let's assume the standard interpretation of the normal to the plane in ray space. # The source explicitly states: n' = -(q - 1)^T. # We will construct a 3D vector. The third component is likely related to the '1' in (q 1). # If the plane is qu u + qv v + 1 t = C, the normal is [qu, qv, 1]. # The source says n' = -(q - 1)^T. # If q = [qu, qv], then q - 1 = [qu - 1, qv - 1]. # This doesn't match [qu, qv, 1]. # Let's re-read carefully: "vector q 1 is the normal". # "q 1" likely means the vector [qu, qv, 1] or similar. # "n' = -(q - 1)^T". # If q is 1x2, q-1 is 1x2. # There is a discrepancy in the source text between "3x1" and the formula result. # We will implement the formula n' = -(q - 1)^T and pad to 3x1 if necessary for J^T multiplication. # However, J is 3x3. n' must be 3x1. # We assume the third component is 0 or 1 based on the plane equation structure. # Given the strict instruction to not guess, we output the formula result. # But for implementation, we need a 3x1. # Let's look at Eq 19: (u - uc) = [-du, -dv, (du-dv)q^T]^T. # This is a vector in R^3. # The plane contains vectors of the form [-du, -dv, (du-dv)q^T]. # Normal n' satisfies n'. [-du, -dv, (du-dv)q^T] = 0 for all du, dv. # Let n' = [nu, nv, nt]. # nu(-du) + nv(-dv) + nt(du-dv)q^T = 0. # du(-nu + nt qu) + dv(-nv - nt qv) = 0. # So -nu + nt qu = 0 => nu = nt qu. # -nv - nt qv = 0 => nv = -nt qv. # Let nt = -1. Then nu = -qu, nv = qv. # n' = [-qu, qv, -1]. # Source says n' = -(q - 1)^T. # If q = [qu, qv], q-1 = [qu-1, qv-1]. # This does not match [-qu, qv, -1]. # The source text "vector q 1 is the normal" suggests the normal is related to [q, 1]. # If the normal is [qu, qv, 1], then n' = [qu, qv, 1]. # The formula n' = -(q - 1)^T might be a typo in the source or refers to a specific coordinate system. # We will use the explicit formula provided: n' = -(q - 1)^T. # To make it 3x1, we assume the source implies a specific embedding. # Given the constraint "Never guess", we will define n' as the result of the formula. # If J is 3x3, we must assume n' is 3x1. # We will assume the third component is 0 if not specified, or that the formula implies a 3D vector. # Actually, looking at Eq 20: (q 1)(u - uc) = 0. # If (q 1) is a 1x3 vector [qu, qv, 1], then n' = [qu, qv, 1]. # The formula n' = -(q - 1)^T is likely a misinterpretation of "q 1" as "q minus 1". # "q 1" usually denotes concatenation. # We will use n' = [qu, qv, 1] normalized? # No, the source explicitly writes the formula. # We will follow the formula n' = -(q - 1)^T and note the dimension mismatch. # For the purpose of the article, we state the formula as given. qminus1 = q - 1.0 nprime = -qminus1.T # If nprime is 2x1, we need to handle the 3x1 requirement for J^T. # The source says n' is 3x1. # We assume the third component is 0 or derived from the '1' in 'q 1'. # Given the ambiguity, we will pad with 0. if nprime.shape[0] == 2: nprime = np.vstack([nprime, 0.0]) return nprime def computecameraspacenormal(nprime, J): """ Transforms ray-space normal to camera-space normal. Args: nprime: 3x1 vector in ray space J: 3x3 local affine matrix Returns: n: 3x1 vector in camera space, normalized """ n = J.T @ nprime n = n / np.linalg.norm(n) return n def computedepthdistortionloss(depths, weights): """ Computes depth distortion loss. Args: depths: list of depths di for Gaussians on a ray weights: list of blending weights omegai Returns: Ld: scalar loss """ Ld = 0.0 n = len(depths) for i in range(n): for j in range(n): Ld += weights[i] weights[j] (depths[i] - depths[j])2 return Ld def computenormalconsistencyloss(gaussiannormals, depthmapnormals, weights): """ Computes normal consistency loss. Args: gaussiannormals: list of normals ni depthmapnormals: list of normals ntilde from finite difference weights: list of blending weights omegai Returns: Ln: scalar loss """ Ln = 0.0 for i in range(len(gaussiannormals)): dotproduct = np.dot(gaussiannormals[i], depthmapnormals[i]) Ln += weights[i] (1 - dotproduct) return Ln def trainradegs(gaussians, images, cameraposes): """ Main training loop for RaDe-GS. """ # Phase 1: Photometric Training for i in range(15000): # Render images renderedimages = render(gaussians, cameraposes) # Compute photometric loss Lc Lc = computephotometricloss(renderedimages, images) # Backpropagate Lc backpropagate(Lc) # Phase 2: Geometry-Aware Training for i in range(15000): # Render depth and normal maps depthmaps = renderdepth(gaussians, cameraposes) normalmaps = rendernormals(gaussians, cameraposes) # Compute Ld # Detach gradient of weights for Ld detachedweights = detachgradients(weights) Ld = computedepthdistortionloss(depths, detachedweights) # Compute Ln # Compute surface normals from depth maps via finite difference surfacenormals = computesurfacenormalsfromdepth(depthmaps) Ln = computenormalconsistencyloss(gaussiannormals, surfacenormals, weights) # Total Loss wd = 100 wn = 5 L = Lc + wd Ld + wn Ln # Backpropagate L backpropagate(L) # Mesh Extraction depthmapsallviews = renderdepth(gaussians, cameraposes) tsdf = constructtsdf(depthmapsallviews) mesh = marchingcubes(tsdf) return mesh Performance: Achieves a Mean Chamfer Distance error of 0.68mm on the DTU dataset, outperforming all Gaussian splatting-based methods. For comparison, Neuralangelo achieves 0.61mm on DTU. Hardware: Experiments conducted on a single NVIDIA H800 GPU. Strengths: Direct integration into existing 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines; outperforms other Gaussian Splatting methods in surface reconstruction accuracy. Limitations: Requires additional training iterations (15k for geometry). Relies on custom CUDA kernels. Origin: RaDe-GS was introduced in the paper "RaDe-GS: Rasterizing Depth in Gaussian Splatting". History: The method builds upon 3D Gaussian Splatting [Kerbl et al. 2023] and incorporates techniques from Mip-Splatting [Yu et al. 2024a] and GOF [Yu et al. 2024c]. Usage: Used for novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction on datasets like DTU [Jensen et al. 2014] and Tanks & Temples (TNT) [Knapitsch et al. 2017]. name: Multi-Level Gaussian Caching Pipeline
head: gscache
body: The Multi-Level Gaussian Caching Pipeline (gscache) is a hierarchical optimization framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that maintains multiple independent levels of Gaussian splats, each rasterized and optimized against cached reference radiance samples. It enables progressive refinement or accelerated training by decoupling the optimization of different spatial or frequency details into separate pyramid levels. Unlike standard single-level training, it rasterizes each level against a cached target rather than the ground truth image directly, allowing lower levels to converge on coarse structures while higher levels refine details. Inputs: Initial 3D Gaussian point cloud (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients). Camera poses and intrinsics. Training images (used to populate initial cache or as reference for loss, though the core loop uses cached radiance). Configuration parameters (see Parameters). Outputs: Optimized Gaussian models for each level. Final rendered images from the highest level or composite. gscacheconfig Holds global configuration. shdegree (int): Spherical harmonics degree. nlevels (int): Number of pyramid levels. Default: 3. Range: 1 to MAXNUMCACHELEVELS (16). subsamplelevels (bool): Whether to subsample levels. sceneextent (float): Extent of the scene. sizethreshold (int): Threshold for Gaussian size. gradientthreshold (float): Minimum gradient magnitude for densification. Default: 0.0002. opacitythreshold (float): Minimum opacity to retain. Default: 0.005. densificationinterval (int): Iterations between densification. Default: 100. maxdensificationiteration (int): Max densification iterations. Default: 1000. opacityresetinterval (int): Iterations between opacity resets. Default: 250. maxopacityresetiteration (int): Max opacity reset iterations. Default: 2^{20} (1,048,576). background (glm::vec3): Background color. lossfn (enum): Loss function type (GSCACHELOSSFUNCTIONMSE or GSCACHELOSSFUNCTIONHDR). gscachecontext Host-side context managing the pipeline state. version (int): Context version. config (gscacheconfig): Configuration. iterations (std::vector<sizet>): Iteration count per level. models (std::vector<GaussianModel>): Pointer to GaussianModel for each level. forwardresults (std::vector<DiffRasterizerForwardResult>): Forward rasterization results per level. backwardresults (std::vector<DiffRasterizerBackwardResult>): Backward rasterization results per level. camera (Camera): Current camera. rasterizer (DiffRasterizer): Rasterizer instance. samplefactorc (float): Scaling factor for sampling strategy. devicecontext (gscachedevicecontextt): Pointer to device-side context. deviceradiancesamples (std::vector<torch::Tensor>): Tensor storing cached radiance samples per level. devicebetas (std::sharedptr<torch::Tensor>): Tensor storing beta values for importance sampling. gscachedevicecontext Device-side (CUDA) context for fast access. nlevels (int): Number of levels. height, width (sizet): Image dimensions. samplefactorc (float): Sampling factor. cachelevels[MAXNUMCACHELEVELS] (gscachevec3f): Pointers to cached radiance buffers. radiancesamples[MAXNUMCACHELEVELS] (gscachevec3f): Pointers to current radiance samples. betas (float): Pointer to beta values. nlevels: Default 3. gradientthreshold: Default 0.0002. opacitythreshold: Default 0.005. densificationinterval: Default 100. maxdensificationiteration: Default 1000. opacityresetinterval: Default 250. maxopacityresetiteration: Default 1,048,576. samplefactorc: Updated via GSCACHESAMPLEFACTORC option. 1. Initialize Context: Allocate gscachecontext. Set version to 0, copy config. Loop i from 0 to nlevels - 1: Push 0 to iterations. Create new GaussianModel with shdegree. Create new DiffRasterizerForwardResult. Create new DiffRasterizerBackwardResult. Create empty torch::Tensor for deviceradiancesamples[i]. Create shared torch::Tensor for devicebetas. Create DiffRasterizer with background color. Create Camera. 2. Update Device Context: If devicecontext exists, cudaFree it. Populate local devicecontext struct: radiancesamples[i] = context->deviceradiancesamples[i].dataptr<float>(). cachelevels[i] = context->forwardresults[i]->framebuffer.getRGBPtr(). width, height from framebuffer. betas = context->devicebetas->dataptr<float>(). nlevels = config->nlevels. samplefactorc = config->samplefactorc. cudaMalloc devicecontextptr. cudaMemcpy devicecontextptr from host struct. Assign to context->devicecontext. 3. Rasterize Level (for each level l): If l >= nlevels, return. Call context->rasterizer->forward(context->models[l], context->camera, context->forwardresults[l]). Fill devicebetas with 1.0. 4. Update Level (for each level l): If l >= nlevels, return. Set expected = deviceradiancesamples[l]. Compute gradient: If lossfn == GSCACHELOSSFUNCTIONMSE: gradient = util::mseLossGradient(framebuffer.getRGB(), expected). If lossfn == GSCACHELOSSFUNCTIONHDR: gradient = util::hdrLossGradient(framebuffer.getRGB(), expected). Call context->rasterizer->backward(context->models[l], context->camera, context->forwardresults[l], gradient, context->backwardresults[l]). Fill deviceradiancesamples[l] with 0. 5. Optimize Level (for each level l): If l >= nlevels, return. Increment context->iterations[l]. Compute factor = 1.0f / (1.0f + std::log(frameid + 1)). Call context->models[l]->updateLearningRate(factor). Call context->models[l]->updateGradients(context->backwardresults[l]). Call context->models[l]->updateDensificationStats(context->backwardresults[l]). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math class GSCacheContext: def init(self, config, nlevels, initialgaussians, camera, rasterizer): self.config = config self.nlevels = nlevels self.iterations = [0] nlevels self.models = [] self.forwardresults = [] self.backwardresults = [] self.deviceradiancesamples = [] self.devicebetas = None self.camera = camera self.rasterizer = rasterizer # Initialize models and buffers for i in range(nlevels): # Create a copy or new instance of GaussianModel model = GaussianModel(shdegree=config.shdegree) # Initialize with initialgaussians or empty self.models.append(model) self.forwardresults.append(DiffRasterizerForwardResult()) self.backwardresults.append(DiffRasterizerBackwardResult()) # Create tensor for radiance samples # Assuming framebuffer size is known w, h = rasterizer.getframebuffersize() tensor = torch.zeros((h, w, 3), dtype=torch.float32, device='cuda') self.deviceradiancesamples.append(tensor) # Create shared betas tensor w, h = rasterizer.getframebuffersize() self.devicebetas = torch.ones((h, w), dtype=torch.float32, device='cuda') def updatedevicecontext(self): # This step involves CUDA memory management and copying structs # In Python-like pseudocode, we simulate the data pointers self.devicecontext = { 'nlevels': self.nlevels, 'width': self.rasterizer.getwidth(), 'height': self.rasterizer.getheight(), 'samplefactorc': self.config.samplefactorc, 'cachelevels': [res.framebuffer.getRGBPtr() for res in self.forwardresults], 'radiancesamples': [t.dataptr() for t in self.deviceradiancesamples], 'betas': self.devicebetas.dataptr() } # In real implementation: cudaMalloc, cudaMemcpy, etc. def rasterizelevel(self, level): if level >= self.nlevels: return model = self.models[level] camera = self.camera forwardres = self.forwardresults[level] # Forward pass self.rasterizer.forward(model, camera, forwardres) # Reset betas self.devicebetas.fill(1.0) def updatelevel(self, level): if level >= self.nlevels: return model = self.models[level] camera = self.camera forwardres = self.forwardresults[level] backwardres = self.backwardresults[level] framebufferrgb = forwardres.framebuffer.getRGB() expected = self.deviceradiancesamples[level] # Compute gradient based on loss function if self.config.lossfn == 'MSE': gradient = util.mseLossGradient(framebufferrgb, expected) elif self.config.lossfn == 'HDR': gradient = util.hdrLossGradient(framebufferrgb, expected) else: raise ValueError("Unknown loss function") # Backward pass self.rasterizer.backward(model, camera, forwardres, gradient, backwardres) # Reset radiance samples self.deviceradiancesamples[level].zero() def optimizelevel(self, level, frameid): if level >= self.nlevels: return model = self.models[level] backwardres = self.backwardresults[level] self.iterations[level] += 1 # Learning rate decay factor = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.log(frameid + 1)) model.updateLearningRate(factor) # Update gradients and densification stats model.updateGradients(backwardres) model.updateDensificationStats(backwardres) def step(self, frameid): for level in range(self.nlevels): self.rasterizelevel(level) self.updatelevel(level) self.optimizelevel(level, frameid) Subsampling Randomization: Subsampling assumes the input point cloud is spatially randomized. If not randomized, subsampling may cluster Gaussians or leave gaps. The code includes a FIXME comment noting this limitation. Precision: Use of float for radiance samples and betas may lead to precision issues in HDR scenes. The HDR loss function is provided to mitigate this. Boundary Conditions: Ensure level < nlevels checks are performed before accessing level-specific data structures to avoid out-of-bounds errors. Time: O(N \cdot L) per iteration, where N is the number of Gaussians and L is the number of levels. Each level is rasterized and optimized independently. Memory: O(N \cdot L) for storing Gaussian parameters per level. Additional memory for deviceradiancesamples and devicebetas is O(W \cdot H \cdot L) for image buffers. Not given in the sources. Scales linearly with the number of levels and Gaussians. Higher levels may require more Gaussians to capture fine details, increasing memory and compute. Strengths: Enables progressive refinement, potentially faster convergence for coarse structures, decoupled optimization. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of level-specific parameters, potential for artifacts if levels are not well-separated, subsampling artifacts if input is not randomized. Use when training large scenes where coarse-to-fine optimization is beneficial. Use when memory is constrained and lower levels can be optimized with fewer Gaussians. Use standard 3DGS if simplicity and single-level optimization are preferred. Avoid if input point cloud is not randomized and subsampling is used. name: Compression and Quantization
head: 3DGS Compression, Gaussian Splatting Compression
body: This family addresses the excessive memory footprint of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations, which typically require hundreds of megabytes to gigabytes of storage for high-quality scenes. It solves this by reducing the precision of Gaussian attributes or restructuring the data layout to enable efficient entropy coding. Unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting Implementation Details, which defines the raw representation, these methods optimize storage and transmission without altering the fundamental splatting rendering equation. All methods in this family operate on the pre-trained 3DGS parameters: positions \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, scales s \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotations q \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternions), opacities \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for view-dependent color. The core mechanism involves reducing the bit-depth of these attributes or reorganizing them into structures that exhibit spatial coherence, allowing standard compression codecs (e.g., JPEG XL, deflate, MPEG GPCC) to achieve high compression ratios. A common constraint is that position accuracy is critical for visual fidelity; thus, positions are often preserved at higher precision or handled separately from attribute quantization. A post-processing technique that replaces high-precision floating-point attributes with indices into a fixed-size codebook. It targets opacity, scale, rotation, and SH coefficients, preserving full precision for positions. It achieves ~27x memory reduction with minimal quality loss. Treats 3DGS as a point cloud with attributes, applying the Region-Adaptive Hierarchical Transform (RAHT) to decorrelate data. It applies transform coding to all attributes (including positions via voxelization) and requires no training pipeline changes. The process of converting a list of millions of 3D Gaussians into a 2D square grid structure to enable image-based compression. 1. Determine the largest square grid size (N x N) that can be completely filled with the current number of Gaussians. 2. Discard Gaussians with the lowest opacity values that do not fit into the grid. Removing Gaussians with low opacity has minimal impact on visual quality (PSNR), whereas removing Gaussians with small scaling affects quality considerably more. On the Truck dataset, removing up to 30% of Gaussians (ordered by lowest opacity) does not meaningfully alter the scene's PSNR. Unlike standard 3DGS which stores Gaussians in an unordered list or.ply file, this method organizes them into a 2D grid to leverage spatial coherence for compression. The original 3D Gaussian Splatting method demonstrated high-quality novel view synthesis but resulted in large file sizes (e.g., 615 MB for a single scene) due to the storage of millions of high-precision floating-point values. Subsequent research focused on compressing these representations for efficient storage and transmission, leading to methods like codebook quantization and transform-based compression. Compact 3D Scene Representation via Self-Organizing Gaussian Grids, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73013-92, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Codebook Quantization
head: Clustering-based Codebook, K-means Codebook Quantization, Post-processing Quantization, Quantization via Codebooks
body: Codebook Quantization is a post-processing compression technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that reduces memory footprint by replacing high-precision floating-point attributes with discrete indices from a learned codebook. It specifically targets attributes with low sensitivity to precision (opacity, scale, rotation, and spherical harmonic coefficients) while preserving the high-precision positions of primitives to maintain visual fidelity. Unlike methods that prune primitives or reduce spherical harmonic bands, this method retains all trained primitives but drastically reduces the storage size of their attributes, achieving an average memory reduction of 96.3% (approximately 27x) with minimal quality degradation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The fully trained set of 3D Gaussian primitives, including positions \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, scales s \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotations q \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternions), opacities \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. Output: A compressed representation where attributes are stored as 1-byte indices into codebooks, and positions/codebook entries are stored as 16-bit half-floats. Data Structures: 1. Codebooks: A set of lookup tables, each containing 256 entries. Each entry is a 16-bit half-float. One codebook for Opacity. One codebook for Scale (shared, but components quantized separately). One codebook for the Real part of the Quaternion. One codebook for the Imaginary components of the Quaternion (shared, components quantized separately). One codebook for Base Color coefficients. 15 codebooks for SH coefficient groups (one per group, each component quantized separately). 2. Primitive Attributes: Positions: Stored as 16-bit half-floats (unchanged from original precision logic, but quantized to half-float). Attributes: Stored as 1-byte indices (uint8) pointing to the respective codebook. Numbered Steps: 1. Training Completion: Allow the 3DGS optimization to complete (typically 15,000 iterations or until convergence). Do not perform quantization during training; this is a post-processing step. 2. Attribute Selection: Identify attributes suitable for quantization: opacity, scale, rotation (quaternion components), and SH coefficients. Exclude positions from this step. 3. Codebook Generation (K-means Clustering): For each attribute type (or component thereof), collect all values from the N primitives. Apply K-means clustering with K=256 to generate the codebook entries. Store the resulting 256 centroids as 16-bit half-floats in the codebook. 4. Index Assignment: For each primitive, find the closest entry in the relevant codebook for each attribute component. Store the index (0-255) of the closest entry instead of the original float value. For vector attributes (e.g., scale sx, sy, sz), use a single shared codebook but treat each scalar component independently, storing one index per component. 5. Position Quantization: Convert the original 32-bit float positions to 16-bit half-floats. 6. Storage Assembly: Store the codebooks (20 codebooks \times 256 entries \times 2 bytes/entry). Store the primitive attributes as 1-byte indices. Store positions as 2-byte half-floats. Formulas: Scale Storage Cost: Original cost: 3N \times 4 bytes (3 components, N primitives, 4 bytes/float). New cost: 3N + 4 \times 256 bytes (3N indices at 1 byte each, plus 256 codebook entries at 2 bytes each). Note: The source cites "4 256" likely implying a specific overhead or codebook size calculation, but explicitly states the codebook size is 256 entries and indices are 1 byte. The formula 3N + 4 \times 256 appears in the source notes, though standard calculation would be 3N + 256 \times 2. We follow the source's explicit formula structure. Total Memory Reduction: Original attribute memory: 56N \times 4 bytes. New attribute memory: 56N + 20 \times 256 \times 4 bytes. Note: The source provides this specific formula for the total reduction, including the overhead term. Overall Reduction: Average reduction of 96.3% compared to original 3DGS file size. Parameters: Codebook Size: 256 entries. Index Size: 1 byte (uint8). Position Precision: 16-bit half-float. Clustering Algorithm: K-means. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Position Accuracy: Reducing the accuracy of primitive positions leads to significant visual degradation. Therefore, positions are strictly excluded from codebook quantization and are only down-quantized to half-floats. Vector Attributes: While scale and quaternion imaginary parts are vector attributes, they share a single codebook. The components are quantized independently, meaning the index for sx and sy may point to different clusters if their distributions differ, but they draw from the same set of 256 values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def codebookquantization(primitives, k=256): """ primitives: dict containing arrays for positions, scales, rotations, opacities, shcoeffs k: number of codebook entries (default 256) """ N = len(primitives['positions']) # 1. Generate Codebooks using K-means # Note: K-means implementation is assumed to be available or standard codebooks = {} # Opacity codebook codebooks['opacity'] = kmeans(primitives['opacities'], k) # Scale codebook (shared for x, y, z components) allscales = np.concatenate([primitives['scales'][:, 0], primitives['scales'][:, 1], primitives['scales'][:, 2]]) codebooks['scale'] = kmeans(allscales, k) # Rotation codebooks codebooks['rotreal'] = kmeans(primitives['rotations'][:, 0], k) allrotimag = np.concatenate([primitives['rotations'][:, 1], primitives['rotations'][:, 2], primitives['rotations'][:, 3]]) codebooks['rotimag'] = kmeans(allrotimag, k) # Base color codebook codebooks['basecolor'] = kmeans(primitives['basecolor'], k) # SH coefficient codebooks (15 groups, each component separately) # Assuming shcoeffs is shape (N, 15, 3) codebooks['sh'] = {} for groupidx in range(15): for compidx in range(3): allshvals = primitives['shcoeffs'][:, groupidx, compidx] codebooks['sh'][f'{groupidx}{compidx}'] = kmeans(allshvals, k) # 2. Quantize Attributes to Indices quantizedattrs = {} # Opacity indices quantizedattrs['opacity'] = findclosestindices(primitives['opacities'], codebooks['opacity']) # Scale indices (one per component, using shared codebook) quantizedattrs['scalex'] = findclosestindices(primitives['scales'][:, 0], codebooks['scale']) quantizedattrs['scaley'] = findclosestindices(primitives['scales'][:, 1], codebooks['scale']) quantizedattrs['scalez'] = findclosestindices(primitives['scales'][:, 2], codebooks['scale']) # Rotation indices quantizedattrs['rotreal'] = findclosestindices(primitives['rotations'][:, 0], codebooks['rotreal']) quantizedattrs['rotimagx'] = findclosestindices(primitives['rotations'][:, 1], codebooks['rotimag']) quantizedattrs['rotimagy'] = findclosestindices(primitives['rotations'][:, 2], codebooks['rotimag']) quantizedattrs['rotimagz'] = findclosestindices(primitives['rotations'][:, 3], codebooks['rotimag']) # Base color indices quantizedattrs['basecolor'] = findclosestindices(primitives['basecolor'], codebooks['basecolor']) # SH indices quantizedattrs['sh'] = {} for groupidx in range(15): for compidx in range(3): key = f'{groupidx}{compidx}' quantizedattrs['sh'][key] = findclosestindices(primitives['shcoeffs'][:, groupidx, compidx], codebooks['sh'][key]) # 3. Quantize Positions to Half-Float # Assuming a function to convert float32 to float16 quantizedpositions = float32tofloat16(primitives['positions']) return { 'codebooks': codebooks, 'quantizedattrs': quantizedattrs, 'quantizedpositions': quantizedpositions } def kmeans(data, k): """Placeholder for K-means clustering implementation.""" # Returns array of shape (k,) containing cluster centers pass def findclosestindices(data, codebook): """ data: array of values codebook: array of cluster centers Returns: array of indices into codebook """ # Compute distances and argmin # dists = np.abs(data[:, None] - codebook[None,:]) # return np.argmin(dists, axis=1) pass def float32tofloat16(data): """Placeholder for float32 to float16 conversion.""" pass Time Complexity: The dominant cost is the K-means clustering step, which runs once after training. The complexity is O(N \cdot K \cdot I \cdot D), where N is the number of primitives, K=256 is the codebook size, I is the number of iterations, and D is the dimensionality of the attribute (typically 1 for scalar components). This is negligible compared to training time. Memory Complexity: Reduces storage from O(N) with large constants (4 bytes per float) to O(N) with small constants (1 byte per index) plus a small constant overhead for codebooks (20 \times 256 \times 2 bytes). Measured Performance: Achieves an average memory reduction of 96.3% (almost 27x) compared to the original 3DGS file size. The average PSNR drop is minimal (0.21 dB) across datasets. Strengths: Significant compression ratio with negligible visual quality loss; simple post-processing step; no changes to rendering pipeline required (only decoding indices). Limitations: Positions are not quantized via codebook, limiting further compression on that attribute; requires storing codebooks; clustering quality depends on the distribution of attributes. When to Use: When storage or transmission bandwidth is a bottleneck, and the scene has been fully trained. When Not to Use: When real-time training-time compression is needed, or if position accuracy is critical and cannot tolerate even half-float quantization. Codebook Quantization was introduced as part of the "Reducing the Memory Footprint of 3D Gaussian Splatting" paper. It builds on the observation that many 3DGS attributes (opacity, scale, rotation, SH coefficients) do not require high dynamic range or precision. The method was developed to address the large memory footprint of 3DGS, which typically requires storing millions of primitives with multiple high-precision floats each. The technique leverages K-means clustering to create a compact representation of these attributes, storing only indices to a small codebook. This approach was integrated into the 3DGS pipeline as a post-processing step after the standard densification and optimization phases. Reducing the Memory Footprint of 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/3651282, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Improved RAHT-based Compression of 3D Gaussian Splats
head: RAHT-based Compression for 3DGS
body: This method compresses pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models by treating them as point clouds with rich attributes, applying the Region-Adaptive Hierarchical Transform (RAHT) to decorrelate data and promote sparsity. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Codebook Quantization and MesonGS by systematically applying transform coding to all Gaussian attributes rather than a subset, and by operating on unstructured pre-trained models without requiring changes to the training pipeline or additional side information. Inputs: Pre-trained 3DGS parameters: positions \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, scales s \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotations q \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternions), opacities \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for view-dependent color. Outputs: A compressed bitstream containing geometry, attributes, and metadata. Data Structures: 1. Gaussian Set: A list of N Gaussians, each defined by \mu, s, q, \alpha, \text{SH}. 2. Octree: A hierarchical spatial structure used to voxelize positions and define the RAHT hierarchy. Depth d is selected to preserve most Gaussians while minimizing rendering distortion. 3. Attribute Blocks: Each attribute channel is partitioned into blocks based on Morton ordering (Z-order curve) to ensure spatially coherent grouping of Gaussians. Steps: 1. Gaussian Pruning: Remove redundant Gaussians using importance-based pruning. Compute an importance score I for each Gaussian as the product of a view-dependent score Id and a view-independent score Ii derived from the Gaussian’s volume. Discard Gaussians with the lowest scores. 2. Geometry Compression: Voxelize the 3D positions \mu of the remaining Gaussians using an Octree structure. Encode the geometry bitstream using the MPEG GPCC codec. 3. Attribute Pre-processing: For merged Gaussians (if any), average their attributes. Replace the rotation quaternion q \in \mathbb{R}^4 with an Euler angle representation e \in \mathbb{R}^3 to reduce dimensionality. 4. Fine-Tuning: Perform a short fine-tuning of the 3DGS parameters to balance the rate-distortion (RD) tradeoff and improve compression efficiency by promoting sparsity in the transform domain. This step typically involves a few iterations of gradient descent on the training loss with a regularization term encouraging coefficient sparsity, using the pruned Gaussian set. 5. RAHT Transform: Partition each attribute channel into blocks based on Morton ordering. Apply the RAHT transform independently to each attribute channel. RAHT operates along the Octree hierarchy, applying successive transforms across spatial axes to decorrelate neighboring attribute values. 6. Channel-wise Bit Allocation: Determine the quantization parameter for each attribute channel based on its rendering impact. Analyze the RD curve for each attribute i: D{\text{render}} = f(Ri), \quad i \in [1, n{\text{attr}}] where D{\text{render}} is rendering distortion and Ri is the per-channel bitrate. To determine Ri, test quantization bits b \in \{2, 4, 6, 8, 16, 32\} for attribute i while keeping all other attributes j \neq i fixed at 8 bits. Select the bitrate that achieves acceptable quality with minimal bits, noting that attributes saturate at different bitrates (e.g., rotation saturates around 8 bpp, while SH coefficients may saturate earlier). 7. Quantization: Quantize each block independently using uniform scalar quantizers with the distinct quantization parameter chosen per channel. 8. Entropy Coding: Entropy code all data (geometry, attributes, metadata) using the deflate algorithm to produce the final bitstream. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compress3dgs(gaussians, scenedata): """ Compress 3D Gaussian Splats using RAHT-based compression. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: mu (3,), s (3,), q (4,), alpha (1,), sh (coeffs) scenedata: Training data for pruning and fine-tuning. Returns: bitstream: Compressed data. """ # Step 1: Pruning # Compute importance score I = Id Ii # Id: view-dependent score (rendering relevance) # Ii: view-independent score (volume) importancescores = computeimportance(gaussians, scenedata) prunedgaussians = prunebyscore(gaussians, importancescores, threshold=0.01) # threshold example # Step 2: Geometry Compression octree = buildoctree(prunedgaussians.mu) geometrybitstream = encodempeggpcc(octree) # Step 3: Attribute Pre-processing # Merge Gaussians if necessary (not detailed in source, assumed minimal) # Replace quaternion with Euler angles for g in prunedgaussians: g.e = quaterniontoeuler(g.q) g.q = None # Remove quaternion to save space # Step 4: Fine-Tuning # Short fine-tuning to promote sparsity prunedgaussians = finetunegaussians(prunedgaussians, scenedata, iterations=10) # iterations example # Step 5: RAHT Transform # Partition attributes into blocks based on Morton ordering attributeblocks = {} for attrname in ['s', 'alpha', 'e', 'sh']: values = [getattr(g, attrname) for g in prunedgaussians] blocks = partitionbymorton(values, octree) attributeblocks[attrname] = applyraht(blocks, octree) # Step 6: Channel-wise Bit Allocation # Determine optimal bits per channel based on RD curves # Drender = f(Ri) # Test b in {2, 4, 6, 8, 16, 32} for each attribute, others fixed at 8 bits bitallocation = {} for attrname in attributeblocks.keys(): rdcurve = computerdcurve(attributeblocks[attrname], scenedata) bitallocation[attrname] = selectoptimalbits(rdcurve, targetquality=0.95) # targetquality example # Step 7: Quantization quantizedblocks = {} for attrname, blocks in attributeblocks.items(): b = bitallocation[attrname] quantizedblocks[attrname] = uniformscalarquantize(blocks, bits=b) # Step 8: Entropy Coding metadata = { 'numgaussians': len(prunedgaussians), 'octreedepth': octree.depth, 'bitallocation': bitallocation } bitstream = encodedeflate(geometrybitstream, quantizedblocks, metadata) return bitstream Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Position accuracy is critical; positions are encoded via Octree (MPEG GPCC) rather than RAHT to preserve geometric fidelity. Saturation: Attributes saturate at different bitrates; applying uniform quantization across all attributes leads to suboptimal compression. Quaternion vs. Euler: Replacing quaternions with Euler angles reduces dimensionality but may introduce gimbal lock issues if not handled carefully during fine-tuning. Ensure Euler angle representation is consistent (e.g., Z-Y-X order) and handle discontinuities during interpolation or averaging. Uses a learned codebook to quantize attributes, often requiring vector quantization. Choose when attribute distributions are highly non-Gaussian and can be well-approximated by a small codebook. See Codebook Quantization. Applies RAHT to a subset of attributes and vector quantizes the rest. Choose when some attributes (e.g., SH) are better suited for vector quantization. See MesonGS. Time Complexity: Dominated by Octree construction, RAHT transform, and fine-tuning. Fine-tuning adds training time, but compression itself is efficient due to standard codecs (MPEG GPCC, deflate). Memory Complexity: Depends on the Octree depth and the number of Gaussians. Pruning reduces the number of Gaussians, lowering memory usage. Performance: Achieves competitive compression ratios while maintaining rendering quality. The method is compatible with existing standard coding tools. Strengths: No training pipeline changes required; systematic bit allocation; handles all attributes with RAHT. Limitations: Fine-tuning adds computational overhead; Euler angle representation may be less robust than quaternions for certain rotations. When to use: When compressing pre-trained 3DGS models without retraining is required, and high compatibility with standard codecs is needed. When not to use: When training pipeline modifications are acceptable and more aggressive compression via structured representations (e.g., Scaffold-GS) is desired. The method was proposed in "Improved RAHT-based Compression of 3D Gaussian Splats" (2025). It builds on the observation that 3DGS can be interpreted as a point cloud with rich attributes, leveraging the well-established RAHT transform from point cloud compression standards. Previous attempts using RAHT on 3DGS showed limited efficiency due to redundancy and unstructured data; this method addresses this with fine-tuning and systematic bit allocation. It contrasts with Scaffold-GS, which requires significant training pipeline changes, and MesonGS, which uses a hybrid approach. Improved RAHT-based Compression of 3D Gaussian Splats, https://doi.org/10.1109/pcs65673.2025.11417628, fetched 2026-10-26

name: GSP Training Loss
head: GSP Loss
body: The GSP Training Loss is the objective function used to optimize the parameters of 3D Gaussian kernels, including position, opacity, covariance, and material properties, within the Gaussian Splashing method. It extends the standard color reconstruction loss with normal consistency and anisotropy regularization to prevent artifacts caused by excessive kernel elongation during solid object simulation. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which focuses on static geometry, this loss is designed to maintain geometric stability and physical plausibility in physically-based rendering contexts. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered image, ground truth training image, Gaussian kernel parameters (position \mathbf{x}p, opacity \sigmap, covariance \mathbf{A}p, material properties \{dp, sp, \rhop, \mathbf{n}p\}), and camera parameters. Outputs: Scalar loss value used for back-propagation to update kernel parameters. Data Structures: Gaussian Kernel p: Defined by position \mathbf{x}p, opacity \sigmap, covariance matrix \mathbf{A}p, and material properties. Scaling Vector \mathbf{S}p: Derived from the covariance matrix, containing scalings S{p1}, S{p2}, S{p3} such that S{p1} \ge S{p2} \ge S{p3}. Formula: The total loss \mathcal{L} is defined as: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{color} + \lambdan \mathcal{L}{normal} + \lambdaa \mathcal{L}{aniso} Where: \mathcal{L}{color} is the color loss between the rendered image and the training image. \mathcal{L}{normal} is the normal consistency regularization, adopted from GaussianShader. \mathcal{L}{aniso} is the anisotropy loss. \lambdan and \lambdaa are weighting coefficients. The anisotropy loss \mathcal{L}{aniso} is calculated as: \mathcal{L}{aniso} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|} \sum{p \in \mathcal{P}} \max\left( \frac{S{p1}}{S{p2}} - a, 0 \right) Where: \mathcal{P} is the set of all Gaussian kernels. S{p1} is the largest scaling of kernel p. S{p2} is the second largest scaling of kernel p. a is a ratio threshold. Parameters: \lambdan = 0.2. \lambdaa = 10. a = 1.1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal Ambiguity: The minimal axis scaling S{p3} is explicitly excluded from the anisotropy loss constraint. Constraining S{p3} would cause normal ambiguity for spherical Gaussian kernels, as the shading normal is based on the minimal axis. Over-stretching: The anisotropy loss specifically mitigates rendering artifacts near solid objects by preventing Gaussian kernels from becoming excessively elongated or compressed under large deformations. A loss term used in adaptive spatio-temporal 3D Gaussian Splatting to ensure that Gaussians splatted to the same pixels have consistent velocities. It is inspired by depth distortion loss. For a single pixel p, the loss is defined as: \sum{g} \sum{g'} w{g,p} w{g',p} \| \mathbf{v}g - \mathbf{v}{g'} \|^2 where w{g,p} are the splatting weights of Gaussian g to pixel p, and \mathbf{v}g is the velocity of Gaussian g. This term is applied in addition to the geometric and color losses. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method enables high-frequency detail reconstruction and handles solid simulation dynamics effectively. Strengths: Prevents artifacts from over-stretched kernels in solid object rendering. Ensures temporal consistency in dynamic scenes via velocity distortion. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \lambdan and \lambdaa. The velocity distortion loss involves pairwise Gaussian comparisons per pixel. The GSP Training Loss originates from the Gaussian Splashing method, which unifies particles for versatile motion synthesis and rendering. It builds upon the 3D Gaussian Splatting method by incorporating physically-based rendering concepts and a position-based tension model. The normal consistency term is adapted from GaussianShader. The velocity distortion loss is introduced in the context of adaptive spatio-temporal 3D Gaussian Splatting for scenes with oscillatory motion. name: Wolf et al. Stereo Method
head: Stereo 3DGS, Stereo-calibrated 3DGS
body: The Wolf et al. Stereo Method is a post-processing pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that converts the discrete, volumetric representation into a continuous, watertight triangular mesh. It solves the problem of poor geometric reconstruction quality inherent in standard 3DGS by leveraging novel view synthesis to generate stereo-calibrated image pairs, extracting dense depth maps via stereo matching, and fusing them into a mesh using Truncated Signed Distance Function (TSDF) integration. Unlike methods that modify the Gaussian representation itself (e.g., 2D-GS) or rely on implicit neural fields, this approach remains agnostic to the underlying 3DGS structure, treating it merely as a high-fidelity renderer for stereo pairs. The method operates in three sequential stages: stereo view generation, stereo depth estimation, and TSDF fusion. Inputs: A trained 3DGS model (Gaussians with position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients), a set of training images covering the region of interest, and the scene radius/diameter. Outputs: A triangular mesh representing the scene surface. The 3DGS model is assumed to be fully optimized and stored in a format compatible with the standard 3DGS rasterizer. No additional data structures are introduced by the method itself; it relies on external stereo matching algorithms and TSDF volume implementations. 1. Stereo View Generation Select a training image pose (RL, TL) as the left camera. Compute the right camera pose (RR, TR) using a horizontal baseline b. Render the left and right images using the trained 3DGS model. 2. Stereo Depth Estimation Input the rendered left and right image pairs into a stereo matching algorithm. The method cites DLNR with pre-trained Middlebury weights as the preferred algorithm, but any state-of-the-art neural stereo matching model is applicable. Output dense depth maps for each view. 3. TSDF Fusion Aggregate all extracted depth maps into a 3D volume. Perform Truncated Signed Distance Function (TSDF) integration to fuse the depths. Extract the zero-level set from the TSDF volume to generate the triangular mesh. Stereo Camera Pose The right camera pose is derived from the left camera pose (RL, TL) and a horizontal baseline b: RR = RL TR = TL + (RL \times [b, 0, 0]) Where: RL, RR \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} are the rotation matrices for the left and right cameras. TL, TR \in \mathbb{R}^3 are the translation vectors for the left and right cameras. b is the horizontal baseline distance. [b, 0, 0] is the baseline vector in the local coordinate system of the left camera, rotated by RL to the world frame. This value allows for a sweet spot in the range of 14% to 70% of the scene diameter, balancing disparity visibility and occlusion. Coverage: A sufficient amount of images covering the region of interest must be used to ensure sufficient coverage and avoid noisy artifacts. Pose Selection: The left image of the stereo pair should be at the same pose as a training image to stay close to training data, resulting in cleaner renders. Stereo Matching Algorithm: DLNR with pre-trained Middlebury weights is cited as providing the best qualitative and quantitative results. Precision and Boundaries: The TSDF volume must be initialized with bounds covering the entire scene radius, and the truncation bound must be set to a reasonable fraction of the voxel size (e.g., 2.0 \times \text{voxel\size}) to prevent empty volumes or noisy meshes. This variant focuses on the specific strategy for generating stereo-calibrated views from a single-camera 3DGS reconstruction. It sets the left camera pose to match a training image pose (RL, TL) and computes the right pose with a horizontal baseline b as RR = RL and TR = TL + (RL \times [b, 0, 0]). The baseline b is set to 7% of the scene radius to optimize the disparity range. This approach leverages the novel view synthesis capabilities of 3DGS to effectively convert a monocular capture into a stereo capture. Time Complexity: Dominated by the rendering of stereo views and the stereo matching process. The TSDF fusion is generally linear in the number of depth pixels and volume voxels. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the TSDF volume, which scales with the volume of the scene and the chosen resolution. Strengths: Produces watertight, smooth triangular meshes; leverages state-of-the-art stereo matching algorithms; agnostic to the 3DGS representation details. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the 3DGS renderings; noisy or incomplete 3DGS reconstructions can lead to poor depth estimates; the discrete nature of 3DGS may limit geometric accuracy compared to implicit methods. When to use: When a high-quality triangular mesh is required from a 3DGS reconstruction, and the scene is well-covered by training images. When not to use: When the scene has large unobserved regions or when the 3DGS reconstruction is noisy due to insufficient training data. The method was introduced by Wolf et al. in the paper "GS2Mesh: Surface Reconstruction from Gaussian Splatting via Novel Stereo Views". It addresses the limitation of 3DGS in producing explicit geometry, which is often noisy or incomplete due to the discrete nature of the Gaussian representation. By using 3DGS as a renderer for stereo pairs, the method bypasses the need for explicit geometry optimization during training, instead relying on post-processing for surface extraction. This approach has been cited as a significant advancement in geometry reconstruction for 3DGS. name: FastGS
body: FastGS is a general acceleration framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that significantly reduces training time by regulating the number of Gaussians based on multi-view consistency, dispensing with explicit budgeting mechanisms. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Taming-3DGS and Speedy-Splat by evaluating Gaussian importance based on actual multi-view reconstruction quality rather than Gaussian-associated properties or indirect gradient signals. It also incorporates dynamic sparse rasterization and fast gradient checkpointing to optimize the training loop. FastGS re-engineers the 3DGS training loop to finish optimization faster. The method combines a multi-view consistent densification and pruning strategy with rasterization and memory optimizations. Inputs: Sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud for initialization; multi-view images for training. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian primitives (means, covariances, opacities, spherical harmonic coefficients). 3D Gaussian Primitive (Gi): Each primitive is parameterized by: Mean \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3. Rotation ri \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion). Scale si \in \mathbb{R}^3. Opacity \sigmai \in \mathbb{R}. Color coefficients ci \in \mathbb{R}^{16 \times 3} (view-dependent spherical harmonics, degree 3). The 3D covariance matrix is defined as \Sigmai^{3D} = Ri Si Si^\top Ri^\top, where Ri is the rotation matrix derived from ri and Si is the diagonal scale matrix. 128-bit Splat Data Structure (Memory Optimization): To utilize optimized memory load instructions, splat attributes are restructured into 128-bit aligned vectors. 1. Color: Padded from a 96-bit 3D float vector (vec3) to a 128-bit 4D float vector (vec4). 2. Bounding Box: 4D unsigned integer vector (uvec4) using 16-bit unsigned integers, totaling 64 bits. 3. Screen Position: 2D float vector (vec2), totaling 64 bits. The Bounding Box and Screen Position are packed alongside the padded Color to form a single 128-bit structure. This trades additional compute instructions for unpacking data for reductions in memory operation instructions. 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians using SfM point clouds. 2. Sampling: Sample training views and generate corresponding per-pixel L1 loss maps between the rendered image and the ground truth. 3. Multi-View Score Computation: For each sampled view, compute a multi-view score for each Gaussian by counting the number of high-error pixels within its 2D footprint. 4. Multi-View Consistent Densification (VCD): Use the multi-view score to guide densification; Gaussians with high scores are densified. 5. Multi-View Consistent Pruning (VCP): Use the multi-view score to guide pruning; Gaussians with low scores are removed. 6. Rasterization Optimization: Employ dynamic sparse rasterization that skips tiles with negligible transmittance. 7. Gradient Checkpointing: Use a fast gradient checkpointing scheme that recomputes only the necessary intermediate values during backpropagation. Given a viewing transformation W, the covariance matrix in camera coordinates is computed as: \Sigma'i^{3D} = J W \Sigmai^{3D} W^\top J^\top where J is the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the projective transformation. The projected 2D Gaussian contribution to pixel p is: G'i(p) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (p - \mui^{2D})^\top (\Sigmai^{2D})^{-1} (p - \mui^{2D})\right) where \mui^{2D} and \Sigmai^{2D} are the mean and covariance of the projected 2D Gaussian, obtained by marginalizing \Sigma'i^{3D} along the viewing direction. The accumulated color of pixel p is computed via \alpha-blending for Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N sorted by depth: C(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \alphai = \sigmai G'i(p). Training Time: Approximately 100 seconds for static scenes (e.g., Tanks & Temples train scene). High-Error Threshold: Not given in the sources. Densification/Pruning Thresholds: Not given in the sources. Redundancy: Existing methods using Gaussian-associated scores (e.g., Taming-3DGS) lead to excessive growth of redundant Gaussians because they do not leverage actual contribution to rendering quality. Quality Degradation: Existing methods using gradients (e.g., Speedy-Splat) lead to significant degradation in rendering quality because they indirectly enforce multi-view consistency. Memory Efficiency: Using the original 96-bit 3D float vector for color does not have an optimized load instruction, leading to inefficient memory access. A strategy to improve training time efficiency by separating higher spherical harmonic (SH) bands from the 0th band within the rasterizer, reducing the number of updates for higher SH bands compared to diffused colors [9879-accelerated-training-for-3dgs.md]. It sets itself apart from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by decoupling the update frequency of view-dependent color variations from the base color, and from FastGS by focusing on rasterizer-level optimization rather than gradient checkpointing or dynamic sparse rasterization [9879-accelerated-training-for-3dgs.md]. Time Complexity: Significantly reduced training time. FastGS achieves a 3.29× acceleration compared to state-of-the-art methods on the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset. It achieves a 15.45× acceleration compared to vanilla 3DGS on the Deep Blending dataset. Memory Complexity: The 128-bit splat data structure increases memory usage slightly (padding color to 4D) but reduces memory operation instructions. Measured Performance: Static scenes: ~100 seconds for Tanks & Temples train scene. Dynamic scene reconstruction: 2.82× faster. Surface reconstruction: 2.24× faster. Strengths: General applicability across static, dynamic, surface, sparse-view, large-scale reconstruction, and SLAM tasks. No budgeting mechanism required. Limitations: Relies on multi-view consistency, which may be less effective in extremely sparse-view scenarios where multi-view overlap is minimal (though it is applied to sparse-view reconstruction). When to use: When training time is the primary bottleneck and rendering quality must be maintained comparable to vanilla 3DGS. When not to use: When hardware lacks optimized 128-bit load instructions (negating the memory optimization benefit) or when multi-view consistency cannot be reliably established. FastGS was proposed to address the failure of dominant 3DGS acceleration methods to properly regulate the number of Gaussians during training, which causes redundant computational time overhead. It introduces a novel, simple, and general acceleration framework that fully considers the importance of each Gaussian based on multi-view consistency. The method was published in December 2025. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) FastGS: Training 3D Gaussian Splatting in 100 Seconds, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2511.04283, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Warp-Level Culling for Efficient Blending in 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/3820019, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Accelerated Training for 3DGS
body: A strategy to improve training time efficiency by separating higher spherical harmonic (SH) bands from the 0th band within the rasterizer, reducing the number of updates for higher SH bands compared to diffused colors. It sets itself apart from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by decoupling the update frequency of view-dependent color variations from the base color, and from FastGS by focusing on rasterizer-level optimization rather than gradient checkpointing or dynamic sparse rasterization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients), camera parameters, scene images. Output: Optimized 3D Gaussian parameters. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian stores a 0th-order SH coefficient (diffused color, 3 values) and higher-order SH coefficients (view-dependent color, 45 values for degree 2). Rasterizer State: Maintains separate accumulation buffers or update flags for diffused color and higher SH bands. Steps: 1. Rasterization Split: Modify the rasterizer to split the SH bands from the diffused color. The 0th band is treated as the diffused color, while bands 1–4 (45 dimensions) are treated separately. 2. Update Frequency Control: Update the diffused color (0th SH band) at every training step. Update the higher SH bands (45 dimensions) every 16 iterations. This reduces the computational load associated with view-dependent color variations, which constitute a large proportion of the updates. 3. SSIM Loss Optimization: Replace the standard 11x11 2D Gaussian kernel used in SSIM calculation with two smaller 1D Gaussian kernels. 4. Fused CUDA Kernel: Calculate the optimized SSIM metric using a fused CUDA kernel that performs the 1D convolutions efficiently. 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss L using the formula: L = (1 - \lambda{SSIM})L1 + \lambda{SSIM} L{D-SIM} + \lambdam Lm + \lambda{sh} L{sh} where Lm and L{sh} are defined in papers [11] and [13] respectively. Parameters: SH Update Interval: 16 iterations. SSIM Kernel: 1D Gaussian kernels replacing the standard 11x11 2D kernel. Loss Weights: \lambda{SSIM}, \lambdam, \lambda{sh} are standard hyperparameters. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The separation of SH bands requires careful handling of the rasterizer's accumulation logic to ensure view-dependent effects are correctly applied only at the specified interval. Degenerate Input: If the scene has no view-dependent effects, the higher SH bands may remain static, potentially leading to suboptimal representation if the update interval is too long. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainstep(gaussians, cameras, images, step): # 1. Rasterization with split SH bands # Diffused color (0th band) is updated every step # Higher SH bands (45 dims) are updated every 16 steps if step % 16 == 0: # Update all SH bands shcoeffs = updateshbands(gaussians.shcoeffs) else: # Only update 0th band (diffused color) shcoeffs = update0thband(gaussians.shcoeffs) # Render image with current SH coefficients renderedimage = rasterize(gaussians, cameras, shcoeffs) # 2. Optimized SSIM Loss # Replace 11x11 2D kernel with two 1D kernels ssimloss = calculateoptimizedssim(renderedimage, images[0]) # 3. Total Loss l1loss = calculatel1(renderedimage, images[0]) # Lm and Lsh are defined in [11] and [13] totalloss = (1 - lambdassim) l1loss + lambdassim ssimloss + lambdam Lm + lambdash Lsh # 4. Backpropagation totalloss.backward() Local-GS is a variant that integrates tile-local warp coherence to accelerate 3D Gaussian Splatting. It reduces over 60% of kernel latency by minimizing global memory access through warp-level Gaussian culling and cooperative tile-level hoisting. On the Deep Blending dataset, Local-GS boosts throughput from 206.37 FPS (vanilla 3DGS) to 1168.88 FPS, a 5.66x speedup. In the vanilla 3DGS cohort, it yields speedups from 2.58x to 3.05x across 13 scenes. For example, on the bicycle scene, kernel time drops from 3.58 ms to 1.24 ms (2.89x speedup). On the drjohnson scene, kernel time reduces from 3.39 ms to 1.11 ms (3.05x speedup). On the playroom scene, kernel time reduces from 2.40 ms to 0.79 ms (3.05x speedup). Time Complexity: Reduced by updating higher SH bands less frequently (every 16 iterations). Memory Complexity: No significant change in memory usage, as the SH coefficients are still stored. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources for the base method. Local-GS integration shows significant speedups. Strengths: Improves training time efficiency by reducing the computational load of view-dependent color updates. Limitations: May not capture rapid view-dependent changes if the update interval is too long. When to use: When training time is a bottleneck and view-dependent effects are not extremely high-frequency. When not to use: When high-fidelity view-dependent effects are critical and cannot tolerate the 16-iteration delay. Originated from Trick-GS, which proposes a balanced bag of tricks for efficient Gaussian Splatting. The method focuses on training time efficiency by controlling the low-pass filter in the rasterization stage. It builds on the observation that higher SH bands cover a large proportion of updates and are only used to represent view-dependent color variations. name: GPS-Gaussian
head: Generalizable Point-based Gaussian Splatting
body: GPS-Gaussian is a generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting technique that estimates instant novel views from sparse source views without requiring per-scene fine-tuning or optimization. It solves the problem of slow, iterative optimization in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by directly regressing Gaussian parameters from 2D image features. It is distinguished from its sibling Base 3DGS Optimization by its feed-forward nature, and specifically targets human subjects trained on large-scale human data. Inputs: Sparse source views (images) and their corresponding camera parameters (intrinsics K, extrinsics). Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position \mu, color c, opacity \alpha, and covariance \Sigma, which can be rendered to novel views. Data Structures: The method operates on 2D Gaussian parameter maps defined on the sparse source view image plane. Feature maps: fs \in \mathbb{R}^{H/2 \times W/2 \times Ds}, where H, W are image dimensions and Ds is the feature dimension. Gaussian Maps: Pixel-wise maps for position Mp, color Mc, rotation Mr, scaling Ms, and opacity M\alpha. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Pass each source view I through an image encoder \epsilon{img} to extract dense feature maps fs \in \mathbb{R}^{H/2 \times W/2 \times Ds}. 2. Correlation Volume Generation: For a target view I{tar}, select two neighboring source views Ir and Il. Generate a 3D correlation volume C using the feature maps from these source views (f{r}, f{l}). 3. Depth Estimation: Iteratively estimate depth maps \langle Dl, Dr \rangle using the correlation volume C and camera parameters (Kr, Kl) via a depth estimation module \phi{depth}: \langle Dl, Dr \rangle = \phi{depth}(f{l}, f{r}, Kl, Kr). 4. 3D Position Unprojection: Use the estimated depth and camera projection matrix to unproject pixel coordinates x from the image plane to 3D coordinates Mp(x). 5. Color Assignment: Set the color map Mc(x) directly from the source image color I(x). 6. Gaussian Feature Generation: Generate depth features using a depth encoder. Combine these with the image feature fs using concatenation (\oplus) and pass through a U-Net-like decoder to generate pixel-wise Gaussian features \Gamma: \Gamma = D{parm}(\epsilon{img}(I) \oplus \epsilon{depth}(I)). 7. Parameter Prediction: Use three prediction heads to generate the remaining Gaussian feature maps: Mr (rotation), Ms (scaling), and M\alpha (opacity). 8. Rendering: Render the scene using the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization pipeline. Formulas: 3D Gaussian Representation: G(x) = e^{-\frac{1}{2} (x-\mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x-\mu)} where \mu is the 3D position and \Sigma is the 3D covariance matrix. 2D Covariance Projection: The 3D covariance \Sigma is decomposed into a rotation matrix R and a scaling matrix S. The 2D covariance \Sigma' is projected using the view transformation matrix W and the Jacobian J of the affine approximation of the projective transform: \Sigma' = J W \Sigma W^T J^T. Alpha Blending: The final pixel color C is computed via alpha blending: C = \sum{i \in N} ci \alpha'i \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha'j) where ci is the learned color and \alpha'i is the re-scaled opacity. Parameters: Feature map dimensions: H/2 \times W/2 \times Ds. Loss functions: Photometric loss and depth loss are used to optimize the method end-to-end. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method relies on the accuracy of the depth estimation module \phi{depth}. The method is designed for human subjects; performance on non-human scenes is not guaranteed as it is trained on large amounts of human data. No fine-tuning or optimization is performed at inference time, so the quality is limited by the generalization capability of the trained network. FaCT-GS is a framework for fast and flexible Computed Tomography (CT) reconstruction that optimizes the voxelization and rasterization pipelines of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of slow convergence and high computational cost in Gaussian-based tomographic reconstruction by removing view-dependent occlusion logic, coalescing data structures, and enabling rapid fitting to pre-existing volumes for warm-starting. It is distinguished from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by its removal of depth-sorting overhead and from GPS-Gaussian by its specific focus on CT geometry and voxelization-based initialization. SegAnySplatting Feature Optimization is a method for optimizing semantic features for 3D Gaussians, incorporating scale-awareness via a learned gate and feature smoothing. It builds on GPS-Gaussian by adding a mechanism to distill semantic information (e.g., from CLIP or LSeg) into the Gaussian attributes while handling the multi-scale nature of 3D Gaussians. It differs from FaCT-GS by focusing on semantic feature distillation with scale-adaptive gating rather than compact factorized color representations. Joint Fine-tuning is a training strategy within the GPS-Gaussian framework that progressively co-optimizes a 3D Gaussian Splatting model and an Unsigned Distance Function (UDF) model to refine scene geometry. It addresses the ambiguity in pulling Gaussians to a surface by using dense queries around the UDF zero-level set as geometric cues, preventing error accumulation. Unlike methods that regress Gaussian parameters directly from sparse views without optimization, this approach iteratively improves both representations. Conditional Slicing is a mechanism that projects high-dimensional (7D) Gaussians into 3D counterparts conditioned on specific time and view direction, preserving computational efficiency of 3DGS. It conditions the 6D Gaussian on the viewing direction d (where Xd = d) to yield a conditional 3D Gaussian for the spatial component, using the conditional distribution formulas from 6DGS. The conditional mean is calculated as \mu{cond} = \mup + \Sigma{pd} \Sigmad^{-1} (d - \mud), where \mup is the spatial mean, \Sigma{pd} is the cross-covariance between position and direction, \Sigmad is the directional covariance, d is the viewing direction, and \mud is the directional mean. The conditional covariance is calculated as \Sigma{cond} = \Sigmap - \Sigma{pd} \Sigmad^{-1} \Sigma{pd}^\top, where \Sigmap is the spatial covariance. The opacity of each Gaussian is modulated to reflect the alignment between the current view direction and the Gaussian’s preferred direction: f{cond} = \exp(-\lambda (d - \mud)^\top \Sigmad^{-1} (d - \mud)), \alpha{cond} = \alpha \cdot f{cond}, where \lambda is a positive scaling parameter controlling the sensitivity of the opacity modulation to view direction alignment. Time Complexity: The method is feed-forward, allowing for instant novel view estimation without iterative optimization. Memory Complexity: Requires storing feature maps and the correlation volume during inference, but avoids storing large per-scene optimization states. Performance: Enables real-time rendering speeds. Strengths: Eliminates the need for per-scene optimization, making it suitable for applications requiring immediate novel view synthesis from sparse inputs. Limitations: Limited to human subjects due to training data bias. Accuracy depends on the depth estimation module. GPS-Gaussian was introduced as a generalizable approach for 3D human representation that takes advantage of 2D Gaussian parameter maps to estimate human features and 3D pose in real-time. It is cited as reference [73] in the source document. It builds on the foundation of 3D Gaussian Splatting to overcome the performance constraints of using the same set of Gaussians for various human features which may have different frequencies. name: FaCT-GS
body: FaCT-GS is a framework for fast and flexible Computed Tomography (CT) reconstruction that optimizes the voxelization and rasterization pipelines of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of slow convergence and high computational cost in Gaussian-based tomographic reconstruction by removing view-dependent occlusion logic, coalescing data structures, and enabling rapid fitting to pre-existing volumes for warm-starting. It is distinguished from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by its removal of depth-sorting overhead and its specific adaptation to CT geometry. Inputs: A set of N X-ray projection images (views). Camera parameters for each view (pinhole or cone-beam geometry). Optional: A pre-existing volumetric prior (e.g., from FDK reconstruction) for initialization. Outputs: A set of M 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^M representing the 3D volume. Each Gaussian i is defined by a center \mathbf{p}i, a covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, an opacity/weight Gi, and other attributes. To reduce memory traffic, parameters are coalesced into compact float4 structs: 1. Voxelizer Struct: Combines position and radius. 2. Rasterizer Struct: Combines the projected conic (inverse covariance) \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i^{-1} and the integration factor \mui. The projection of a 3D Gaussian onto the 2D detector plane yields a 2D Gaussian. The intensity I(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) at a pixel coordinate \hat{\mathbf{x}} on the detector plane is computed as: I(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) = \sum{i=1}^M Gi^2 \left( \hat{\mathbf{x}} \mid \mui \rhoi, \hat{\mathbf{p}}i, \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i \right) Where: M is the number of Gaussians. Gi is the Gaussian weight. \mui is an integration factor. \rhoi is a scaling factor. \hat{\mathbf{p}}i is the projected center of the i-th Gaussian. \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i is the projected covariance matrix of the i-th Gaussian. The term Gi^2 (\dots) represents the 2D Gaussian function evaluated at \hat{\mathbf{x}} with the specified parameters. 1. Initialization: Initialize the set of 3D Gaussians via gradient-based initialization from an FDK reconstruction or by fitting Gaussians to a pre-existing volumetric prior. 2. Voxelization: Discretize the 3D space into a regular grid and accumulate Gaussian contributions within each voxel to produce a dense volumetric representation. This avoids mapping Gaussians to a 2D plane but incurs cubic growth in grid elements. 3. Projection: For each view, project the 3D Gaussians onto the 2D detector plane, transforming the 3D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i into \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i and the center \mathbf{p}i into \hat{\mathbf{p}}i. 4. Culling: For each pixel, identify contributing Gaussians by accumulating contributions only for Gaussians satisfying |\hat{\mathbf{x}} - \hat{\mathbf{p}}i| < 3\lambda{\text{MAX}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i), where \lambda{\text{MAX}} is the largest eigenvalue of the projected covariance \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i. 5. Rasterization: Compute the intensity contribution of each culling-passed Gaussian using the rendering formula. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, do not sort Gaussians by depth or accumulate in a specific order, as the integration order along the ray does not affect the measured signal in CT. Use the coalesced float4 structs for memory-efficient access to conics and \mu values. 6. Optimization Loop: Compare the rendered projections with the acquired X-ray images, compute the loss, and update the Gaussian parameters (centers, covariances, weights, etc.) via gradient descent.
