Execution Time: Approximately 2 minutes per scan on 75 projections of 512^2 size; competitive results after 45 seconds. Scalability: Generates high-quality reconstructions in about 1 minute for 1k projections and 4 minutes for 2k projections. Occlusion Logic: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting accumulates splat contributions in a specific order to model view-dependent occlusion. In CT, integration order along the ray has no effect on the measured signal. Removing this ordering logic is critical to avoid unnecessary overhead. Memory Traffic: Failure to coalesce function parameters into compact float4 structs (combining position/radius in voxelizer, conics/\mu in rasterizer) leads to higher memory traffic and reduced performance. Voxelization Cost: Voxelization is computationally expensive due to the cubic growth in the number of grid elements. Care must be taken with grid resolution. Time Complexity: Significantly faster than State of the Art GS CT reconstruction. Over 4x faster on standard 512^2 projections and over 13x faster on 2k projections. Memory Complexity: Reduced by coalescing parameters into float4 structs. Voxelization incurs cubic growth in grid elements. Scalability: Scales well with projection and output volume size. Strengths: Fast execution, flexible initialization (including warm-starting from pre-existing volumes), and compression properties comparable to 2D JPEG stacks. Limitations: Voxelization can be computationally expensive for high-resolution grids. When to use: Sparse-view tomography, fast CT reconstruction, scenarios requiring warm-starting from prior volumes. When not to use: Standard 3D rendering with view-dependent occlusion is required. FaCT-GS was introduced to address the limitations of Gaussian Splatting-based CT reconstruction, specifically the slow convergence and high computational cost. It builds on the observation that projecting a 3D Gaussian yields a 2D Gaussian, allowing for simplified rendering equations. The method was developed to enable rapid fitting of Gaussians to pre-existing volumes, serving as a prior for warm-starting or as a compressed representation. It is related to R2-Gaussian, which also highlighted the irrelevance of integration order in CT, but FaCT-GS fully removes the ordering logic from the pipeline. name: SegAnySplatting Feature Optimization
head: Scale-Aware Semantic Features, SegAnyGS
body: SegAnySplatting Feature Optimization optimizes semantic features for 3D Gaussians by incorporating scale-awareness through a learned gate and feature smoothing. It differs from FaCT-GS by focusing on distilling semantic information (e.g., from CLIP or LSeg) into Gaussian attributes with scale-adaptive gating, rather than compact factorized color representations. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a frozen pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting model and a training dataset containing semantic masks or features as input, and outputs an optimized semantic feature tensor attached to each Gaussian. Data Structures: The semantic features are stored as a torch.nn.Parameter of shape (ngaussians, nfeaturedims) and initialized with torch.randn(...) 1e-2. The scale gate is implemented as an nn.Sequential module containing nn.Linear(1, nfeaturedims) followed by nn.Sigmoid(). The background color is stored as a torch.nn.Parameter of shape (nfeaturedims,), initialized to zeros, and marked as non-trainable. Parameters: The method uses nfeaturedims (int, default 32) for the number of semantic feature dimensions per Gaussian. It uses scaleawaredim (int) to control scale awareness, where values <=0 or >=32 trigger the adaptive scale gate. It uses smoothK (int, default 16) for the feature smoothing kernel size. It uses smoothdropout (float, default 0.5) for the feature smoothing dropout rate. It uses rfn (float, default 1.0) as the feature normalization factor. It uses downsamplefactor (int) to reduce the resolution of the rendered feature map and accelerate distillation. Steps: 1. Load the pre-trained Gaussian model and freeze its geometric and color parameters. 2. Gather all scale values from the training dataset to compute upperboundscale. 3. If scaleawaredim is not in the range [1, 31], initialize a quantile transformer (qtrans) with a uniform output distribution to normalize the scale values. 4. If scaleawaredim is in the range [1, 31], initialize a fixed scale gate tensor fixedscalegate of shape (scaleawaredim + 1, 32) where row i contains 1s in the first 32 - \text{scale\aware\dim} + i positions and 0s elsewhere. 5. Preprocess masks by sorting them by scale in descending order and sampling indices for the largest, smallest, and random intermediate scales. 6. Render semantic features from the Gaussians, downsample the feature map using downsamplefactor, compute the distillation loss against ground-truth semantic features, apply feature smoothing with kernel size smoothK and dropout smoothdropout, and update Semantic Features and Scale Gate via gradient descent. 7. After distillation, visualize the rendered feature map using the provided viewer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class SegAnySplattingFeatureOptimization: def init(self, ngaussians, nfeaturedims=32, scaleawaredim=0, smoothK=16, smoothdropout=0.5, rfn=1.0): self.ngaussians = ngaussians self.nfeaturedims = nfeaturedims self.scaleawaredim = scaleawaredim self.smoothK = smoothK self.smoothdropout = smoothdropout self.rfn = rfn # Semantic Features: (ngaussians, nfeaturedims) self.semanticfeatures = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(ngaussians, nfeaturedims) 1e-2) # Background Color: (nfeaturedims,), not trainable self.backgroundcolor = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(nfeaturedims), requiresgrad=False) # Scale Gate initialization if not (1 <= scaleawaredim <= 31): self.scalegate = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, nfeaturedims), nn.Sigmoid()) self.fixedscalegate = None else: self.fixedscalegate = torch.zeros(scaleawaredim + 1, 32) for i in range(scaleawaredim + 1): self.fixedscalegate[i,:32 - scaleawaredim + i] = 1.0 self.scalegate = None self.qtrans = None def quantilenormalize(self, scales): # Standard quantile normalization mapping to uniform distribution sortedscales, = torch.sort(scales) ranks = torch.searchsorted(sortedscales, scales) return ranks / len(scales) def preprocessscales(self, scales): upperboundscale = torch.max(scales) if self.scalegate is not None: self.qtrans = self.quantilenormalize(scales) return upperboundscale def preprocessmasks(self, masks, scales): sortedindices = torch.argsort(scales, descending=True) sortedmasks = [masks[i] for i in sortedindices] n = len(sortedmasks) indices = [0, n - 1] if n > 2: midindices = torch.randint(1, n - 1, (max(1, n // 4),)) indices.extend(midindices.tolist()) return [sortedmasks[i] for i in indices] def smoothfeatures(self, features): # Apply spatial smoothing via average pooling and dropout if self.smoothdropout > 0: features = F.dropout(features, p=self.smoothdropout, training=True) k = self.smoothK if features.dim() == 2: features = F.avgpool2d(features.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), kernelsize=k, stride=1).squeeze() return features def renderandoptimize(self, gaussians, semantictargets, optimizer): optimizer.zerograd() # Standard 3DGS rasterization accumulating semantic features renderedfeatures = self.renderfeatures(gaussians) # Downsample for speed renderedfeatures = F.avgpool2d(renderedfeatures, kernelsize=2, stride=2) # Loss loss = F.mseloss(renderedfeatures, semantictargets) # Smoothing smoothed = self.smoothfeatures(renderedfeatures) # Loss typically computed on smoothed or original features; here on original per standard distillation loss.backward() optimizer.step() def renderfeatures(self, gaussians): # Standard 3DGS projection and accumulation scales = gaussians.scales # (ngaussians, 3) scalarscales = torch.max(scales, dim=1).values if self.scalegate is not None: gate = self.scalegate(scalarscales.unsqueeze(1)) features = self.semanticfeatures gate else: # Map scalar scale to fixed gate row index scalenorm = scalarscales / (torch.max(scalarscales) + 1e-8) rowidx = torch.clamp((scalenorm self.scaleawaredim).long(), 0, self.scaleawaredim) gate = self.fixedscalegate[rowidx] features = self.semanticfeatures gate # Rasterize features to image space return features # Simplified return for pseudocode structure Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If scaleawaredim falls outside [1, 31], the adaptive gate is automatically selected. The downsamplefactor must be \ge 1 to prevent invalid tensor shapes during distillation. Degenerate scale values (e.g., all zeros) should be handled by the quantile transformer or clamped to a minimum positive value. Precision issues with the random initialization are mitigated by the 10^{-2} scaling factor. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Joint Fine-tuning
head: Progressive Joint Optimization
body: Joint Fine-tuning is a training strategy within the GPS-Gaussian framework that progressively co-optimizes a 3D Gaussian Splatting model and an Unsigned Distance Function (UDF) model to refine scene geometry. It addresses the ambiguity in pulling Gaussians to a surface by using dense queries around the UDF zero-level set as geometric cues, preventing error accumulation. Unlike methods that regress Gaussian parameters directly from sparse views without optimization, this approach iteratively improves both representations. Inputs: Sparse source views, initial 3D Gaussian distribution (positions, scales, rotations, opacities, colors), initial UDF field parameterized by a neural network, and camera poses. Outputs: Refined 3D Gaussian parameters and refined UDF field. Gaussian Model: Set of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian k has position \mathbf{p}k, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}k, opacity \alphak, and color \mathbf{c}k. UDF Model: Neural network f{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) predicting unsigned distance at point \mathbf{x}. Ray Vk: Ray passing through Gaussian k's center. 1. Initialization: Initialize the Gaussian model and UDF model. 2. Progressive Joint Optimization Loop: a. Ray Casting: For each Gaussian k, define ray Vk passing through its center. b. Depth Projection: Calculate dt, the depth of the projection point from Gaussian k onto Vk. c. UDF Query: Query the UDF at the Gaussian's position to obtain dn, the depth of the surface point \{qn\} along the ray direction. d. Loss Calculation: Compute a geometric consistency loss using the depth difference, applying the stop-gradient operation sg(\cdot) to the UDF prediction to stabilize training. e. Gradient Update: Update both the Gaussian parameters and the UDF network parameters \theta jointly via backpropagation. f. Iteration: Repeat steps 2a-2e for multiple epochs, progressively refining geometry over time. g. Joint Refinement Training: Train the backbone f\theta and refinement module h\phi jointly in an end-to-end manner by supervising the output of the final refinement iteration. h. Unrolled Gradients: Compute the total loss after all K refinement iterations, allowing gradients to propagate through the rasterizer and the entire unrolled sequence of updates. i. Per-Attribute Heads: Use three parallel MLPs for position, opacity, and color updates, with all output layers zero-initialized so refinement starts at \Delta = 0. The geometric loss leverages the depth difference between the Gaussian projection and the UDF surface. Let dt be the depth of the Gaussian's projection onto ray Vk and dn be the depth of the surface point \{qn\} predicted by the UDF. The update involves a stop-gradient operation sg(\cdot) on the UDF term: \mathcal{L}{\text{geo}} = \| dt - sg(dn) \|^2 The total training loss combines pixel-wise mean squared error with a perceptual loss over all rendered views: \mathcal{L} = \sum{i \in C \cup T} \| \hat{I}^{(K)}i - Ii \|2^2 + \lambda{\text{lp}} \text{LPIPS}(\hat{I}^{(K)}i, Ii) where \hat{I}^{(K)}i is the rendering of the final Gaussian set G^{(K)} at camera pi, \|\cdot\|2^2 denotes mean squared error over pixels, and \lambda{\text{lp}} is the perceptual loss weight. \lambda{\text{lp}} = 0.1 with a VGG backbone. K = 3 refinement iterations. Training runs for 50,000 steps with shared weights across iterations. Progressive Schedule: Not given in the sources. Learning Rate: Not given in the sources. Ambiguous Pulling Directions: Directly pulling Gaussians to the UDF zero-level set can cause error accumulation due to ambiguous directions. This method avoids this by using dense queries around the zero-level set. UDF Accuracy: The UDF is not perfectly accurate initially, but provides reliable optimization directions. Poor initial UDF quality may slow convergence. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def jointfinetuning(gaussians, udfnet, sourceviews, cameras, epochs=50000, K=3, lambdalp=0.1, learningrate=0.01): # Initialize parameter lists for optimization gaussparams = [g.position for g in gaussians] + [g.covariance for g in gaussians] + [g.opacity for g in gaussians] + [g.color for g in gaussians] udfparams = list(udfnet.parameters()) for step in range(epochs): for gaussian in gaussians: # 1. Define ray Vk through Gaussian center rayorigin = gaussian.position raydirection = normalize(gaussian.position - cameras.center) # 2. Compute depth dt of Gaussian projection onto Vk dt = gaussian.depthalongray(rayorigin, raydirection) # 3. Query UDF for surface depth dn dn = udfnet.querysurfacedepth(rayorigin, raydirection) # 4. Compute geometric loss with stop-gradient on UDF term loss = (dt - stopgradient(dn)) 2 # 5. Backpropagate to update both models loss.backward() # 6. Update parameters using gradient descent for p in gaussparams: p.data -= learningrate p.grad for p in udfparams: p.data -= learningrate p.grad # Clear gradients for p in gaussparams + udfparams: p.grad = None return gaussians, udfnet def stopgradient(tensor): return tensor.detach() def normalize(v): return v / magnitude(v) A method for compressing 3D Gaussian Splatting models. It focuses on reducing memory footprint through factorization, unlike Joint Fine-tuning which focuses on geometric refinement via UDFs. Optimizes features for segmentation-aware Gaussian Splatting. It targets semantic feature learning rather than geometric refinement through joint UDF optimization. Time Complexity: Higher than non-optimizing methods like the initial GPS-Gaussian regression because it involves iterative joint optimization of Gaussians and a UDF network. Memory Complexity: Requires storing both the Gaussian parameters and the UDF network parameters. Strengths: Prevents error accumulation from ambiguous pulling directions by using dense queries around the zero-level set. Continuously improves geometry over time. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to joint optimization. Relies on the UDF providing reliable directions despite not being perfectly accurate. When to Use: When high-fidelity geometry is required and sparse views are available, and computational resources allow for iterative optimization. When Not to Use: When real-time inference without fine-tuning is required, as this method is a training-time optimization. Joint Fine-tuning, also known as Progressive Joint Optimization, was introduced in the VRP-UDF paper. It builds on the GPS-Gaussian framework, which initially introduced Gaussian parameter maps on sparse source views to regress parameters jointly with a depth estimation module without fine-tuning. The Joint Fine-tuning method extends this by adding a progressive joint optimization step to refine the geometry further. It addresses limitations in existing methods that directly pull Gaussians to the UDF zero-level set. name: Mini-Splatting Pipeline
head: Mini-Splatting, Mini-Splatting-D, Mini-Splatting-C
body: The Mini-Splatting Pipeline is a training methodology for 3D Gaussian Splatting 3D Gaussian Splatting designed to reconstruct scenes using a constrained, minimal number of Gaussians. It solves the problem of excessive memory consumption and redundant Gaussian proliferation inherent in standard 3DGS by integrating densification, simplification, and depth-based reinitialization phases. It sets itself apart from the base training loop 3D Gaussian Splatting Training by explicitly managing the Gaussian count through iterative pruning and re-initialization, rather than relying solely on adaptive density control. The pipeline manages the lifecycle of 3D Gaussians through three distinct phases: densification, simplification, and depth reinitialization. It operates on a loop that continues until convergence, adjusting the Gaussian population based on geometric consistency and rendering error. Inputs: Sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points, a set of training images with known camera poses, and hyperparameters for iteration counts and sampling ratios. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians (centers, covariances, opacities, spherical harmonics coefficients) optimized to render the input views. The core data structure is a list of Gaussians. Each Gaussian gi contains: Center: \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance: \mathbf{\Sigma}i (represented via rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{s}i) Opacity: \alphai \in [0, 1] Spherical Harmonics (SH) Coefficients: \mathbf{c}{SH, i} In the Mini-Splatting-C variant, attributes are stored differently for compression: Centers are stored as float32. Scales and SH coefficients are processed using Region-adaptive Hierarchical Transform (RHT) [6] with depth level 16 and quantization step 0.02, then compressed via numpy.savezcompressed(). The training loop is summarized below. Let i be the current iteration counter. 1. Initialization: Initialize the set of Gaussians \mathcal{G} from SfM points. Set i = 0. 2. Loop: While not converged: 1. Densification: If i \le \text{DensificationIteration} (15K): Perform importance-weighted sampling to identify regions requiring more Gaussians. Clone and split Gaussians based on gradient magnitude or rendering error. Update \mathcal{G}. 2. Depth Reinitialization: If i \pmod{5000} == 0 (enabled every 5K iterations): For Gaussians with low opacity or high uncertainty, reinitialize their centers using depth information from the training views. Note: This strategy relies on accurate depth values. 3. Simplification: If i \ge \text{SimplificationIteration1} (15K) and i < \text{SimplificationIteration2} (20K): Remove redundant Gaussians using intersection-preserving sampling. Merge or prune Gaussians that contribute minimally to the final image. If i \ge \text{SimplificationIteration2} (20K): Perform final simplification passes to ensure minimal Gaussian count. 4. Optimization: Render images from current camera poses using the current \mathcal{G}. Compute loss (e.g., L1, SSIM) against ground truth images. Update Gaussian parameters (centers, scales, rotations, opacities, SH coefficients) using an optimizer (typically Adam). 5. Increment: i \leftarrow i + 1. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def minisplattingpipeline(sfmpoints, trainingimages, hyperparams): """ Implements the Mini-Splatting training loop. Args: sfmpoints: List of 3D points from SfM. trainingimages: List of (image, camerapose) tuples. hyperparams: Dict containing DensificationIteration, SimplificationIteration1, SimplificationIteration2, reinitinterval, samplingratio. Returns: optimizedgaussians: List of Gaussian objects. """ # Initialize Gaussians from SfM points gaussians = initializefromsfm(sfmpoints) i = 0 while not converged(gaussians, trainingimages): # 1. Densification Phase if i <= hyperparams['DensificationIteration']: # Identify regions with high error or low coverage importantregions = importanceweightedsampling(gaussians, trainingimages) # Clone and split Gaussians in important regions gaussians = densify(gaussians, importantregions) # 2. Depth Reinitialization Phase # Enabled every 5K iterations if i % 5000 == 0: gaussians = depthreinitialize(gaussians, trainingimages) # 3. Simplification Phase if i >= hyperparams['SimplificationIteration1']: # Remove redundant Gaussians gaussians = simplify(gaussians, trainingimages) if i >= hyperparams['SimplificationIteration2']: # Final simplification gaussians = finalsimplify(gaussians, trainingimages) # 4. Optimization Step # Render current view renderedimages = render(gaussians, trainingimages) # Compute loss loss = computeloss(renderedimages, trainingimages) # Update parameters gaussians = optimize(gaussians, loss) i += 1 return gaussians def initializefromsfm(sfmpoints): """Create Gaussian primitives from SfM points.""" gaussians = [] for point in sfmpoints: g = Gaussian() g.center = point.xyz g.scale = defaultscale g.rotation = identityrotation g.opacity = defaultopacity g.shcoeffs = defaultsh gaussians.append(g) return gaussians def importanceweightedsampling(gaussians, images): """ Select regions for densification based on rendering error or gradient magnitude. Returns a list of regions (e.g., bounding boxes or pixel masks). """ # Implementation detail: Typically involves backprojecting gradients to 3D # and selecting top-k regions. pass def densify(gaussians, regions): """ Clone and split Gaussians in the specified regions. """ newgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: if g in regions: # Clone gclone = clone(g) # Split gsplit = split(g) newgaussians.extend([gclone, gsplit]) else: newgaussians.append(g) return newgaussians def depthreinitialize(gaussians, images): """ Reinitialize Gaussians using depth information. Fails in areas without depth (e.g., sky). """ for g in gaussians: if needsreinitialization(g): # Use depth from closest view depth = getdepth(g.center, images) if depth is not None: g.center = reprojectto3d(depth, g.camerapose) return gaussians def simplify(gaussians, images): """ Remove redundant Gaussians. """ # Implementation detail: Typically involves pruning low-opacity Gaussians # or merging nearby Gaussians. pass def finalsimplify(gaussians, images): """ Final pruning to minimize Gaussian count. """ # Implementation detail: Aggressive pruning based on contribution to loss. pass def render(gaussians, images): """ Render images using 2D Gaussian splatting. """ # Standard 3DGS rasterization pass def computeloss(rendered, groundtruth): """ Compute L1 and SSIM loss. """ l1 = l1loss(rendered, groundtruth) ssim = ssimloss(rendered, groundtruth) return l1 + ssim def optimize(gaussians, loss): """ Update Gaussian parameters using Adam optimizer. """ # Standard Adam update step pass DensificationIteration: 15,000 iterations. Densification occurs up to this point. SimplificationIteration1: 15,000 iterations. Simplification begins here. SimplificationIteration2: 20,000 iterations. Final simplification phase begins here. Depth Reinitialization Interval: Every 5,000 iterations. Sampling Ratio: Manually controlled to limit Gaussian count. A high ratio can lead to background distortion. Depth Reinitialization Failure: The depth-based reinitialization strategy fails in areas without reliable depth values, such as the sky or transparent objects. Background Distortion: A high sampling ratio (too few Gaussians) leads to distortion in the background. Manual Tuning: The number of Gaussians is manually controlled by the sampling ratio, which requires careful tuning to balance quality and memory. A variant of Mini-Splatting where the simplification process is simply disabled. It retains densification and depth reinitialization but does not prune Gaussians after the densification phase. This results in a higher Gaussian count compared to the standard Mini-Splatting but may preserve more detail in complex regions. A variant focused on memory efficiency and storage compression. It is based on the standard Mini-Splatting pipeline but applies specific compression techniques to the Gaussian attributes. Gaussian centers are stored as float32, while scales and SH coefficients are processed using Region-adaptive Hierarchical Transform (RHT) with a depth level of 16 and a quantization step of 0.02. The transformed coefficients are then losslessly compressed using numpy.savezcompressed(). This variant is suitable for scenarios where storage size is a critical constraint. Memory Usage: Significantly lower than standard 3DGS due to the constrained number of Gaussians. The exact reduction depends on the sampling ratio and simplification aggressiveness. Training Time: Comparable to or slightly longer than standard 3DGS due to the additional simplification and reinitialization steps. Rendering Speed: Faster than standard 3DGS due to fewer Gaussians to rasterize. Quality: On the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset, Mini-Splatting achieves competitive results: SSIM: 0.772 (bicycle), 0.626 (flowers), 0.847 (garden), 0.806 (stump), 0.654 (treehill), 0.921 (room), 0.904 (counter), 0.926 (kitchen), 0.940 (bonsai), 0.874 (truck), 0.796 (train), 0.904 (johnson), 0.912 (playroom). PSNR: 25.15 (bicycle), 21.58 (flowers), 26.84 (garden), 27.26 (stump), 22.72 (treehill), 31.39 (room), 28.41 (counter), 31.17 (kitchen), 31.57 (bonsai), 25.09 (truck), 21.28 (train), 29.47 (johnson), 30.49 (playroom). LPIPS: 0.225 (bicycle), 0.327 (flowers), 0.150 (garden), 0.199 (stump), 0.312 (treehill), 0.211 (room), 0.199 (counter), 0.130 (kitchen), 0.199 (bonsai), 0.159 (truck), 0.245 (train), 0.257 (johnson), 0.250 (playroom). Strengths: Reduced memory footprint, faster rendering, competitive image quality. Limitations: Requires manual tuning of sampling ratio, depth reinitialization fails in sky/transparent areas, potential background distortion if too few Gaussians are used. Mini-Splatting was introduced to address the memory and computational overhead of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting. It builds on the 3DGS rendering pipeline but introduces explicit mechanisms to control the number of Gaussians. The method was proposed in "Mini-Splatting: Representing Scenes with a Constrained Number of Gaussians". name: Dynamic and Temporal Modeling
head: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting, Dynamic Neural Rendering, On-the-Fly Training
body: Dynamic and Temporal Modeling extends static volumetric representations to handle non-rigid motion and time-varying scenes by parameterizing attributes as functions of time or modeling temporal deformation fields. It solves the limitation of static radiance fields and fixed Gaussian sets, which cannot represent evolving geometry or appearance. It sets itself apart from static methods by introducing explicit temporal dependencies, either through canonical space deformation Deformation Field Modeling or direct time-conditioned attribute prediction Temporal Input Conditioning, and distinguishes itself from offline 4D reconstruction methods by supporting on-the-fly or incremental training strategies On-the-Fly Dynamic NeRF Training and 3DGStream. The family shares the following core mechanisms for handling temporal dynamics: 1. Temporal Parameterization: Attributes that vary with time, such as position \mathbf{c}, rotation \mathbf{q}, opacity \alpha, density \sigma, or color \mathbf{c}, are expressed as functions of time t. Common functional forms include: Polynomial/Linear: \mathbf{q}(t) = \mathbf{q}0 + \mathbf{m}t. Fourier Series: \mathbf{c}(t) = \mathbf{c}0 + \sum{k=0}^{K} (\mathbf{a}k \cos(k \omega t) + \mathbf{b}k \sin(k \omega t)). Neural Deformation: A neural network \Psit(x, t) predicts a displacement \Delta x to warp dynamic coordinates to a canonical space. Implicit Fields: Time-dependent NeRFs map (x, d, t) to density and color, often using local neighborhoods of frames. 2. Canonical Space Mapping: Many methods (e.g., D-NeRF, Nerfies) introduce a canonical configuration, typically at t=0, where the scene is static. A deformation network maps dynamic coordinates x at time t to canonical coordinates x': x' = x + \Psit(x, t) The radiance field is then queried in the canonical space: [\sigma, c] = \Psix(x', d). 3. Rendering with Dynamics: The rendering process integrates time-dependent attributes. For Gaussian-based methods, position and rotation are computed for the specific time t of the camera ray before rasterization. For NeRF-based methods, density \sigma and color c are queried at the deformed or time-conditioned point. 4. Loss Functions: Optimization typically minimizes photometric loss (L1 or LPIPS) between rendered and ground truth images. Additional constraints often include: Temporal Smoothness: Penalizing abrupt changes in attributes between adjacent frames. Rigid/Flow Constraints: Using optical flow or KNN rigid loss to guide deformation. Regularization: Elastic or background regularization to prevent overfitting in deformation fields. An on-the-fly training method that replaces temporal deformation fields with a NeRF model conditioned on multi-view projected colors. It leverages the invariance of projected color for corresponding 3D points across consecutive frames to implicitly track correspondence, allowing it to utilize radiance fields from previous frames to render the current frame with minimal optimization iterations. Unlike sibling methods that use explicit temporal inputs or deformation networks which extrapolate poorly to unseen times, OD-NeRF requires the minimum number of optimization iterations per new frame. Choose this method when streaming dynamic scenes with minimal per-frame optimization latency is required and specular/occlusion artifacts are manageable. A method for training dynamic Neural Radiance Fields concurrently with the acquisition of training frames, enabling the streaming of dynamic scenes as they unfold. It estimates the radiance field for the current time step tk using only the images up to tk and the radiance field from the previous step t{k-1}. It is distinguished by its application of a first-order Markov assumption to decouple current estimation from the entire history, allowing for minimal optimization iterations per frame and interactive-speed streaming. Choose this method for real-time dynamic scene reconstruction where scalability to long sequences is critical. A method for online training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) in dynamic scene reconstruction. It models the transformation between frames as a neural transformation cache and adaptively adds 3D Gaussians to handle emerging objects. It is distinguished from static 3DGS by its ability to incrementally update the scene representation as new video frames arrive, rather than requiring offline batch optimization of a fixed set of Gaussians. Choose this method when explicit Gaussian representation is preferred over neural fields for dynamic scenes, especially with emerging geometry. This family addresses the limitations of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) when applied to dynamic scenes, non-line-of-sight (NLOS) imaging, and real-world captures with optical artifacts. It extends the static Gaussian representation to handle temporal dynamics, transient occluders, and blur effects. It differs from sibling NeRF-based methods (e.g., D-NeRF) by maintaining a unified, explicit Gaussian representation rather than a neural field, which yields efficiency and state-of-the-art results on diverse photo scenes without requiring explicit transient labels. Choose this method when handling complex optical artifacts or transient objects in dynamic scenes. Deformation Field Modeling addresses the problem of reconstructing and rendering dynamic scenes from static image or video sequences by explicitly modeling the temporal evolution of geometry and appearance. It solves the limitation of static radiance fields by mapping dynamic, time-varying coordinates to a static canonical space where the radiance field is defined. What sets this approach apart from siblings like Dynamic Object Embedding in Static Scenes (which isolates motion to specific objects) or Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting (which uses explicit parametric functions) is its reliance on a learned implicit function (typically an MLP) to predict continuous displacement vectors or feature transformations, allowing for complex, non-rigid, and global deformations without assuming a specific motion prior. Choose this method for complex non-rigid deformations where explicit parametric motion models are insufficient. 4D-GS extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to dynamic scenes by parameterizing Gaussian attributes as functions of time, enabling the reconstruction and rendering of non-rigidly deforming objects. It distinguishes itself from sibling NeRF-based dynamic methods by retaining the efficient splatting rasterization pipeline while replacing static positional encoding with multi-resolution hexplane voxels to capture spatiotemporal correlations. Choose this method when high-fidelity dynamic reconstruction is needed with the efficiency of Gaussian splatting, particularly for scenes with complex spatiotemporal correlations. Temporal Input Conditioning is a family of techniques that parameterize scene attributes—such as position, rotation, opacity, density, or color—as explicit functions of time t to enable the synthesis of novel views for dynamic scenes. It solves the problem of representing non-rigid motion and temporal evolution in volumetric data without requiring ground-truth geometry or multi-view stereo data at every instant. It sets itself apart from naive time-extended NeRFs by decomposing the representation into a static canonical space and a learned deformation field, thereby exploiting temporal redundancy that direct 6D mappings fail to capture. Unlike DaReNeRF, which focuses on specific direction-aware wavelet decompositions, this family establishes the foundational canonical-space paradigm for dynamic neural rendering. Choose this method as a general-purpose approach for dynamic scene representation using canonical space and deformation fields. A method that introduces a temporal radial basis function to represent temporal opacity, modeling emerging or vanishing content. Polynomial functions model motion and rotation. Spherical harmonics are replaced with features consisting of base color, view-related feature, and time-related feature. The latter two are translated into residual color through an MLP added to the base color. During optimization, new 3D Gaussians are sampled at under-optimized positions based on training error and coarse depth. A procedure coupled with the two-step DynART/P-DVC algorithm to handle large displacement amplitudes by resolving large-scale features first and progressively enriching with finer details. Resolve large-scale features of both microstructure and motion. Progressively enrich the description with finer details. An explicit deformation modeling method using parametric functions to ensure temporal continuity and robustness, where the number of parameters is independent of time. 1. Use a Fourier series to fit changes in the Gaussian’s position. 2. Approximate rotation by a linear function. 3. Keep other attributes unchanged over time. 4. Use dynamic optimization to optimize the parameters of the Fourier series and the linear function. Introduce a bidirectional optical flow loss in addition to image losses. Dynamic and Temporal Modeling in volumetric rendering originated from the need to extend static Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting to 4D scenes. Early works like D-NeRF introduced canonical space deformation for dynamic NeRFs Deformation Field Modeling. The adaptation to 3D Gaussian Splatting followed, with methods like 4D-GS and 3DGStream introducing explicit temporal parameterization and neural transformation caches. On-the-fly training methods like On-the-Fly Dynamic NeRF Training further enabled real-time streaming by leveraging Markov assumptions. name: Projected Color-Guided Dynamic NeRF
head: OD-NeRF
body: Projected Color-Guided Dynamic NeRF (OD-NeRF) is an on-the-fly training method for dynamic scenes that replaces temporal deformation fields with a NeRF model conditioned on multi-view projected colors. By leveraging the invariance of projected color for corresponding 3D points across consecutive frames, the model implicitly tracks correspondence, allowing it to utilize radiance fields from previous frames to render the current frame with minimal optimization iterations. Unlike sibling methods that use explicit temporal inputs or deformation networks which extrapolate poorly to unseen times, OD-NeRF requires the minimum number of optimization iterations per new frame. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of multi-view images representing a dynamic scene. For synthetic datasets, the method builds upon the TiNeuVox architecture; for real-world datasets, it builds upon InstantNGP (via NerfAcc). Outputs: A radiance field representation that can render novel views for any frame in the sequence, updated incrementally frame-by-frame. Data Structures: 1. Occupancy Grid: A spatial structure used for efficient sampling, transited and updated from the previous frame in synthetic datasets. In real-world datasets, the hash voxel grid from InstantNGP serves this purpose. 2. NeRF MLP: A Multi-Layer Perceptron that maps concatenated spatial features and projected color statistics to density and color. 3. Spatial Feature: The feature vector queried from the voxel grid at a sampled point's location. Parameters: \sigma{\min}: Density threshold for rejection sampling. Not given in the sources. R: Fixed interval for rejection sampling. Not given in the sources. Warm-up Duration: 2 seconds for the first frame in synthetic datasets to compensate for slower convergence of hashed voxels compared to multi-scale voxels. Optimization Schedule: Intensity scaled from 1 (frame 1) to 0.05 (frame 10) for better convergence. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: For the first frame, initialize the radiance field. For synthetic datasets, apply a 2-second warm-up period. 2. Sampling: Sample points along rays. Synthetic: Use rejection sampling based on the transited occupancy grid from the previous frame. A sample xi is rejected if its occupancy value \sigma{\text{occ}}(xi) is below \sigma{\min} AND it is not on a fixed interval R: \text{reject } xi \text{ if } (\sigma{\text{occ}}(xi) < \sigma{\min}) \land \neg(i \mod R \equiv R//2) Real-world: Use the standard sampling strategy of InstantNGP. 3. Projected Color Computation: For each sampled point, compute the mean and variance of its projected colors from the training views. 4. Feature Concatenation: Concatenate the mean and variance of the projected colors with the spatial feature queried from the voxel grid at the point's location. 5. NeRF Query: Input the concatenated feature vector into the NeRF MLP to predict density and color. 6. Rendering: Render the image using standard volume rendering integration. 7. Optimization: Minimize the photometric loss between the rendered image and the ground truth image. Real-world Specific: Add a depth smoothness regularization loss L{\text{depth}} calculated over any 3 \times 3 patch of rays: L{\text{depth}} = \frac{\text{std}(d{\text{far}} / d{3 \times 3})}{\text{std}(c{3 \times 3})} where d{\text{far}} is the depth of the farthest sample, d{3 \times 3} is the mean depth of the 3 \times 3 patch, and c{3 \times 3} is the mean color of the patch. 8. Transition and Update: Update the occupancy grid for the next frame based on the current frame's results to guide sampling for the subsequent frame. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def trainodnerfframebyframe(videosequence, config): # Initialize NeRF MLP and occupancy grid model = NeRFMLP() if config['datasettype'] == 'synthetic': occupancygrid = OccupancyGrid() if config.get('warmupduration', 2.0) > 0: time.sleep(config['warmupduration']) else: occupancygrid = HashVoxelGrid() for frameidx, framedata in enumerate(videosequence): # Optimization schedule: scale from 1.0 (frame 1) to 0.05 (frame 10) optscale = max(0.05, 1.0 - (frameidx / 10.0) 0.95) for camera in framedata.cameras: rays = createrays(camera) renderedcolors = [] for ray in rays: samples = [] # Step 2: Sampling if config['datasettype'] == 'synthetic': uniformsamples = sampleuniformalongray(ray) for i, xi in enumerate(uniformsamples): sigmaocc = occupancygrid.query(xi) # Rejection sampling condition if not (sigmaocc < config['sigmamin'] and not (i % config['R'] == config['R'] // 2)): samples.append(xi) else: samples = sampleinstantngp(ray, occupancygrid) # Step 3: Projected Color Computation projectedcolors = computeprojectedcolors(samples, videosequence[:frameidx]) meancolor = np.mean(projectedcolors, axis=0) varcolor = np.var(projectedcolors, axis=0) # Step 4: Feature Concatenation spatialfeature = occupancygrid.queryspatialfeatures(samples) inputfeature = np.concatenate([spatialfeature, meancolor, varcolor], axis=-1) # Step 5: NeRF Query density, color = model.forward(inputfeature) # Step 6: Rendering (Standard volume rendering integration) T = 1.0 renderedcolor = np.zeros(3) for j in range(len(samples)): dist = np.linalg.norm(samples[j] - samples[j-1]) if j > 0 else 1.0 alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-density[j] dist) renderedcolor += color[j] alpha T T = (1.0 - alpha) renderedcolors.append(renderedcolor) # Step 7: Optimization gtimages = framedata.gtimages loss = np.mean(np.abs(np.array(renderedcolors) - np.array(gtimages))) optscale # Real-world specific depth regularization if config['datasettype'] == 'real': depthloss = computedepthsmoothness(renderedcolors, samples) loss += depthloss model.backward(loss) # Step 8: Transition and Update updateoccupancygridfromrender(occupancygrid, samples, density) def NeRFMLP(): pass def OccupancyGrid(): pass def HashVoxelGrid(): pass def createrays(camera): pass def sampleuniformalongray(ray): pass def sampleinstantngp(ray, grid): pass def computeprojectedcolors(samples, prevframes): pass def updateoccupancygridfromrender(grid, samples, density): pass def computedepthsmoothness(renderedcolors, samples): pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Specular Surfaces: Specular highlights violate the assumption of projected color invariance, leading to artifacts. Occlusions: Occluded points also violate relative invariance, causing artifacts. Filtering these outliers may incur significant computational costs. Convergence Speed: Hashed voxels converge slower than multi-scale voxels, necessitating the warm-up period for synthetic datasets. Planar Backgrounds: Real-world datasets with large planar backgrounds (e.g., walls, tables) may fail to converge well even for the first frame, requiring the depth smoothness regularization. Speed: Achieves an interactive speed of 6 FPS for both training and rendering on synthetic dynamic scenes on-the-fly. It provides a significant speed-up compared to state-of-the-art methods on real-world dynamic scenes. Optimization Efficiency: Requires the minimum number of optimization iterations for each new frame compared to models with temporal input dimensions or deformation fields. Extrapolation: Exhibits excellent temporal extrapolation capability, unlike deformation-based models that extrapolate poorly to unseen times. Memory: Uses hash voxel grids (InstantNGP) or multi-scale voxel grids (TiNeuVox), which are generally more memory-efficient than dense 3D grids. Limitations: Performance degrades on scenes with strong specularities or significant occlusions due to the reliance on projected color invariance. OD-NeRF was introduced in the paper "OD-NeRF: Efficient Training of On-the-Fly Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields". It addresses the challenge of efficient on-the-fly training, where the radiance field is trained and rendered frame-by-frame, effectively utilizing the radiance field estimated from previous frames. The method was implemented on top of TiNeuVox for synthetic datasets and InstantNGP (via NerfAcc) for real-world datasets. name: On-the-Fly Dynamic NeRF Training
head: OD-NeRF
body: On-the-fly Dynamic NeRF Training (OD-NeRF) is a method for training dynamic Neural Radiance Fields concurrently with the acquisition of training frames, enabling the streaming of dynamic scenes as they unfold. Unlike traditional dynamic NeRFs that require full video sequences for offline 4D reconstruction, this approach estimates the radiance field for the current time step tk using only the images up to tk and the radiance field from the previous step t{k-1}. It is distinguished by its application of a first-order Markov assumption to decouple current estimation from the entire history, allowing for minimal optimization iterations per frame and interactive-speed streaming. Inputs: C{0:k}: The set of multi-view images captured up to the current time step tk. F{k-1}: The radiance field function estimated at the previous time step t{k-1}. Outputs: Fk: The updated radiance field function at time tk, parameterized by spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}. The method relies on standard NeRF representations: 1. Radiance Field Fk: A neural network mapping (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \sigma \in \mathbb{R} is volume density and \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is RGB color. For dynamic scenes, this may implicitly or explicitly encode time via deformation fields or 4D expansion, but the core optimization target is the field state Fk. 2. Occupancy Grid Gk: A sparse data structure used for efficient ray sampling, which is updated via a transition function from G{k-1}. 1. Initialize: Start with an initial radiance field F0. The occupancy grid G0 is initialized to cover the scene volume. 2. Receive Data: At time step k, acquire the new set of images Ck. 3. Markov Simplification: Apply the first-order Markov assumption to simplify the probability model. Assume conditional independence such that the current radiance field Fk is independent of all previous images \{C{0:k-1}\} and fields \{F{0:k-2}\} given the current images Ck and previous field F{k-1}: Fk \perp\!\!\!\perp \{C{0:k-1}, F{0:k-2}\} \mid \{Ck, F{k-1}\} This reduces the estimation objective to: Fk = \arg\max{Fk} P(Fk \mid Ck, F{k-1}) 4. Define Loss: Minimize the rendering loss between the rendered image \hat{C}k(r) and the ground truth image Ck(r) for all rays r \in R: Fk = \arg\min{Fk} \sum{r \in R} ||\hat{C}k(r) - Ck(r)||^22 5. Volume Rendering: For each ray r, compute the rendered color \hat{C}k(r) by aggregating N points along the ray with intervals \deltai: \hat{C}k(r) = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci where the transmittance Ti is: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=0}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) Here, \sigmai and ci are the density and color queried from Fk at the i-th point on the ray. 6. Optimization: Update the parameters of Fk (and potentially Gk) using gradient descent to minimize the loss defined in Step 4. The optimization starts from the state F{k-1} to ensure continuity and minimize the number of iterations required. 7. Transition: Update the occupancy grid Gk from G{k-1} using a simple transition function to maintain efficient sampling. 8. Stream: Render novel views using Fk at time tk. Unverified code. name: Temporal 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: Li et al
body: Temporal 3D Gaussian Splatting extends static 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle dynamic scenes by parameterizing Gaussian attributes as functions of time. It solves the problem of modeling emerging, vanishing, or moving content that static splatting cannot represent. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by using explicit temporal radial basis functions for opacity and polynomial functions for motion/rotation, rather than neural deformation fields or canonical space mappings. Inputs: A sequence of training images with known camera poses and timestamps t. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians with time-dependent attributes. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i stores the following fields: Base color \mathbf{c}{base} (3 floats). View-related feature vector \mathbf{f}{view} (dimension Dv). Time-related feature vector \mathbf{f}{time} (dimension Dt). Position \mathbf{c}(t) and Rotation \mathbf{q}(t) defined by polynomial coefficients. Opacity \alpha and Scale \mathbf{s}. Temporal parameters for opacity modulation (e.g., center time t'i, width \sigmai, static/dynamic flag gi). Method Steps: 1. Temporal Opacity Modeling: A temporal radial basis function is applied to opacity to model content that emerges or vanishes over time. The exact functional form is not specified in the sources. 2. Motion and Rotation Parameterization: Motion and rotation are modeled using polynomial functions of time t. Position is computed as \mathbf{c}(t) = \sum{k=0}^{N} \mathbf{a}k t^k. Rotation \mathbf{q}(t) is similarly parameterized by polynomial coefficients. The exact polynomial degree N and coefficient initialization are not given in the sources. 3. Color Representation: Spherical harmonics are replaced by a feature-based approach. The final color is computed as \mathbf{c}(t, \mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{c}{base} + \text{MLP}([\mathbf{f}{view}, \mathbf{f}{time}]), where \mathbf{v} is the view direction. The MLP takes the concatenation of the view-related and time-related features as input. 4. Optimization and Initialization: Optimization iterates between static and dynamic phases. New 3D Gaussians are sampled at under-optimized positions based on training error and coarse depth. The loss function includes temporal smoothness loss and KNN rigid loss. Adaptive timestep scaling is applied during optimization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def concat(a, b): # Standard array/tensor concatenation return a + b def mlp(features): # MLP architecture and weights are not specified in the sources # Standard feedforward network implementation provided for completeness return features def temporalrbf(t, center, width): # Standard Gaussian RBF implementation return exp(-0.5 ((t - center) / width) 2) def computecolor(gaussian, viewdir, timet): fview = gaussian.viewfeature ftime = gaussian.timefeature combined = concat(fview, ftime) residual = mlp(combined) return gaussian.basecolor + residual def computeposition(gaussian, timet): pos = 0.0 for k, coeff in enumerate(gaussian.positioncoeffs): pos += coeff (timet k) return pos def computeopacity(gaussian, timet): # Temporal RBF formula is not specified in the sources return gaussian.baseopacity temporalrbf(timet, gaussian.tcenter, gaussian.twidth) A mechanism to assign a positive temporal duration to dynamic Gaussians so they smoothly appear and disappear, modeling visibility changes and occlusions. It defines a temporal weight wi(t) and effective opacity oi(t). The temporal weight is computed as wi(t) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{t - t'i}{\sigmai + \epsilon}\right)^2\right), where \epsilon prevents division by zero. The effective opacity is defined as oi(t) = -(1 - gi) + gi wi(t) oi, where gi=1 for dynamic Gaussians and gi=0 for static ones. During rendering, the original opacity oi is replaced with oi(t) in the standard alpha compositing process. The temporal duration parameter is stored as \sigmai = \text{clip}(\exp(\rhoi), \sigma{min}, \sigma{max}). This temporal window is differentiable with respect to \nui, ai, t'i, and \rhoi. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Explicitly models emerging and vanishing scene content. Replaces spherical harmonics with MLPs for a potentially more flexible color representation. Limitations: Relies on polynomial functions for motion, which may not capture complex non-linear dynamics as effectively as neural deformation fields. The specific implementation details of the temporal RBF and MLP are not fully specified in the provided notes. The method originated from Li et al. [78], as cited in. It is part of the broader effort to extend 3D Gaussian Splatting to dynamic scenes, following the shared family principles of temporal parameterization and rendering with dynamics. name: 3DGStream
body: 3DGStream is a method for online training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) in dynamic scene reconstruction. It models the transformation between frames as a neural transformation cache and adaptively adds 3D Gaussians to handle emerging objects. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of video frames with known camera poses, processed online. Output: A dynamic 3DGS representation where Gaussian attributes are transformed over time via the cache, with an adaptive Gaussian count. Input/Output Dimensions: Not given in the sources. Data Structures: 3D Gaussians: Initialized at the first frame with standard attributes (position, rotation, scale, opacity, color). Neural Transformation Cache (NTC): A shallow, fully fused multi-layer perceptron (MLP) utilizing multi-resolution hash encoding to predict transformations across frames. Steps: 1. Initialize 3D Gaussians at the first frame. 2. Construct the NTC to model transformations between frames. 3. For each new frame, query the NTC to transform canonical Gaussian attributes to the current time t. 4. Render the frame using the transformed Gaussians and optimize parameters online. 5. Apply an adaptive 3D Gaussian addition strategy to dynamically add new Gaussians for emerging objects while regulating their overall quantity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class NeuralTransformationCache: def init(self): # Shallow, fully fused MLP with multi-resolution hash encoding # Architecture details and dimensions are not given in the sources pass def transform(self, canonicalgaussians, timet): # Predicts transformation for time t # Returns transformed Gaussians # Implementation details are not given in the sources pass def initializegaussians(firstframe): # Initializes 3D Gaussians at the first frame # Implementation details are not given in the sources pass def rendergaussians(gaussians, camerapose): # Projects Gaussians onto image plane and rasterizes return rasterize(gaussians, camerapose) def computerenderingloss(rendered, groundtruth): # Computes photometric loss (e.g., L1 or LPIPS) return l1loss(rendered, groundtruth) def updateparameters(gaussians, cache, loss): # Backpropagates to update Gaussian attributes and cache weights return optimizestep(gaussians, cache, loss) def adaptiveaddgaussians(gaussians, rendered, groundtruth): # Dynamically adds new Gaussians for emerging objects while regulating quantity # Implementation details are not given in the sources return gaussians def trainonline(videoframes): gaussians = initializegaussians(videoframes[0]) cache = NeuralTransformationCache() for t, (image, pose) in enumerate(videoframes): transformedgaussians = cache.transform(gaussians, t) rendered = rendergaussians(transformedgaussians, pose) loss = computerenderingloss(rendered, image) gaussians, cache = updateparameters(gaussians, cache, loss) gaussians = adaptiveaddgaussians(gaussians, rendered, image) return gaussians, cache Parameters: Learning rates for Gaussians and Cache: Not given in the sources. Hash encoding resolutions and MLP depth: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Emerging Objects: The adaptive addition strategy must regulate the overall Gaussian quantity to prevent unbounded growth. Online Training: Incremental updates require stable optimization to avoid catastrophic forgetting of earlier frames. A per-frame training method that initializes 3D Gaussians at the first timestamp and conducts static reconstruction. Gaussians have fixed parameters except for position and rotation, enabling tracking of points across frames. Optimization is conducted by regularization without leveraging a neural network. Time Complexity: Online training implies per-frame processing time. The exact complexity is not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians and the size of the neural transformation cache. Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables online reconstruction of dynamic scenes; handles emerging objects; uses compact hash encoding for efficiency and adaptability. Limitations: Requires careful initialization; relies on an adaptive addition strategy that must be regulated to control Gaussian count. When to use: When reconstructing dynamic scenes from video in an online or incremental manner. 3DGStream was introduced as a method for online training of 3DGS in dynamic scene reconstruction. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting and extends it to handle temporal dynamics through a neural transformation cache and adaptive Gaussian addition. It is part of the broader family of dynamic 3DGS methods. name: Blur and Transient Modeling
head: Transient Gaussian Splatting, Neural Transient Field, Blur-Aware 3DGS
body: This family addresses the degradation of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) quality caused by temporal dynamics (transient occluders) and optical artifacts (blur) in real-world captures. While standard 3DGS assumes static, sharp scenes, this family introduces methods to explicitly model transient objects as separate Gaussian sets or to simulate and detect blur during optimization. It sets itself apart from sibling dynamic modeling methods (e.g., Deformation Field Modeling) by focusing on unposed or loosely posed casual captures where explicit camera poses or continuous deformation fields are unavailable or unreliable, instead relying on unsupervised transient Gaussian training or blur-aware loss weighting. The family shares the following core mechanisms for handling temporal dynamics: 1. Temporal Parameterization: Attributes that vary with time, such as position \mathbf{c}, rotation \mathbf{q}, opacity \alpha, density \sigma, or color \mathbf{c}, are expressed as functions of time t [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. Common functional forms include: Polynomial/Linear: \mathbf{q}(t) = \mathbf{q}0 + \mathbf{m}t [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. Fourier Series: \mathbf{c}(t) = \mathbf{c}0 + \sum{k=0}^{K} (\mathbf{a}k \cos(k \omega t) + \mathbf{b}k \sin(k \omega t)) [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. Neural Deformation: A neural network \Psit(x, t) predicts a displacement \Delta x to warp dynamic coordinates to a canonical space [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. Implicit Fields: Time-dependent NeRFs map (x, d, t) to density and color, often using local neighborhoods of frames [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. 2. Canonical Space Mapping: Many methods (e.g., D-NeRF, Nerfies) introduce a canonical configuration, typically at t=0, where the scene is static. A deformation network maps dynamic coordinates x at time t to canonical coordinates x': x' = x + \Psit(x, t) The radiance field is then queried in the canonical space: [\sigma, c] = \Psix(x', d) [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. 3. Rendering with Dynamics: The rendering process integrates time-dependent attributes. For Gaussian-based methods, position and rotation are computed for the specific time t of the camera ray before rasterization [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. For NeRF-based methods, density \sigma and color c are queried at the deformed or time-conditioned point [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. 4. Loss Functions: Optimization typically minimizes photometric loss (L1 or LPIPS) between rendered and ground truth images [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. Additional constraints often include: Temporal Smoothness: Penalizing abrupt changes in attributes between adjacent frames [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. Rigid/Flow Constraints: Using optical flow or KNN rigid loss to guide deformation [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. Regularization: Elastic or background regularization to prevent overfitting in deformation fields [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md][13852-deformation-field-modeling.md][17390-temporal-input-conditioning.md]. NeTF is a neural modeling framework for Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) imaging that recovers the 5D transient function (spatial location and direction) implicitly represented by a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Unlike NeRF, which parametrizes input training data along lines (rays), NeTF parametrizes input training data on spherical wavefronts. It sets itself apart from siblings like SWAG by explicitly modeling the transient field in NLOS contexts, handling sparse and unbalanced sampling via MCMC, and producing sharper edges in semi-occluded scenes compared to Phasor Field or DLCT. SWAG is a method for unsupervised transient modeling in 3D Gaussian Splatting that extends the standard representation by conditioning Gaussians on learned appearance embeddings. It solves the problem of transient occluders (e.g., pedestrians, moving vehicles) in casual photo captures by training dedicated transient Gaussians that are explicitly optimized to ignore occlusion, yielding state-of-the-art results on diverse photo scenes. It differs from sibling methods like Wild-GS, which aligns pixel appearance features from image triplanes to 3D Gaussians using depth regularization and visibility maps, by focusing on unsupervised transient Gaussian training rather than triplane alignment. Definition: Techniques to explicitly incorporate blur modeling during training to address real-world capture issues like motion blur and defocus blur. Steps: 1. Employ coarse-to-fine kernel optimization. 2. Employ photometric bundle adjustment. Definition: A strategy to mitigate the negative influence of blurry training data by simulating blur on rendered images and down-weighting blurry reference images during training. Steps: 1. Inject blur into the rendered image patch C to obtain blurred rendered image \hat{C}, mimicking real-world blurry effects. 2. Calculate rendering loss by comparing the blurred rendered image \hat{C} with the ground-truth image patch C{gt}. 3. Calculate blurriness scores for images using a content-aware blur detection approach. 4. Down-weight the importance of samples during training using pre-computed quality-aware weights \omega^tb. The challenge of reconstructing reflective, transparent, and transient objects in general scenes remains difficult for standard 3DGS. While 3DGS excels on carefully curated datasets, real-world captures often suffer from blurs such as motion blur and defocus blur. Recent approaches explicitly incorporated blur modeling during training, employing techniques such as coarse-to-fine kernel optimization [193] and photometric bundle adjustment [325] to address this challenge. Images captured in the wild inevitably contain artifacts, such as motion blur, which deteriorates the quality of rendered images. Accordingly, strategies to simulate blur effects on the rendered images to mitigate the negative influence of blurriness images and reduce their importance during training based on precomputed quality-aware weights have been proposed. name: Neural Transient Field (NeTF)
body: Neural Transient Field (NeTF) is a neural modeling framework for Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) imaging that recovers the 5D transient function in both spatial location and direction, implicitly represented by a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Unlike NeRF, which parametrizes input training data along lines (rays), NeTF parametrizes input training data on spherical wavefronts. The final reconstruction of the hidden scene corresponds to a 3D density volume implicitly represented by the MLP. NeTF is designed to handle sparse and unbalanced sampling inherent in NLOS setups, producing sharper edges in semi-occluded scenes and separating distinct mesh parts better than methods like DLCT. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Sparse set of detection spots on a relay wall, capturing transient responses (time-of-flight histograms) for various incident and exit angles. The data is parameterized on spherical wavefronts rather than Cartesian rays. Output: A 3D density volume representing the hidden scene, which can be converted to a mesh via thresholding and Marching Cubes. Data Structures: Neural Network: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). The specific architecture (number of layers, hidden units, activation functions) is not detailed in the provided sources [G: Standard MLP architecture for implicit fields, e.g., ReLU activations, is assumed]. Sampling Data: A set of (x, y, t) measurements from SPAD (Single-Photon Avalanche Diode) arrays, where x, y are spatial coordinates on the relay wall and t is time. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the MLP parameters. [G: Standard random initialization for MLP weights]. 2. Spherical Parameterization: For each training sample, map the NLOS measurement geometry to spherical coordinates. Unlike ray-based rendering, the input data is treated as originating from/arriving at spherical wavefronts. 3. Forward Pass: Query the MLP with the spherical coordinates and time information to predict the transient density/color values. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the loss between the predicted transients and the measured transients at every measuring spot on the relay wall. 5. Optimization with MCMC: Use Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to account for sparse and unbalanced sampling in the transient field. MCMC enables more reliable volume density estimation. [G: Specific MCMC implementation details (e.g., Metropolis-Hastings kernel, proposal distribution) are not provided in the sources]. 6. Two-Stage Training (Optional but recommended for sparse data): Stage 1: Train using all initial samples to obtain an initial reconstruction. Calculate Loss Map: Compute the loss function between predicted and measured transients at every measuring spot. Normalize to PDF: Normalize the calculated loss to form a Probability Density Function (PDF). Higher loss implies undersampling. Resample: Resample detection spots using the PDF. Higher loss corresponds to higher PDF and is more densely sampled. Stage 2: Build a new training dataset from the resampled spots and retrain the network to refine reconstruction. 7. Surface Extraction: Map the implicit volume to surfaces by thresholding the density values followed by Marching Cubes. Formulas: Spherical Parameterization: The input data is parameterized on spherical wavefronts. Specific mathematical formulation of the spherical coordinate transformation is not provided in the sources. Loss Normalization: The loss Li at spot i is normalized to form a PDF Pi: Pi = \frac{Li}{\sumj Lj} Parameters: Sampling Resolution: Tested on 256x256, 16x16, 8x8, and 4x4 spots on the relay wall. Thresholding: Not given in the sources. [G: A standard threshold (e.g., 0.5 or based on density distribution) is typically used for Marching Cubes]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Confocal vs. Non-Confocal: NeTF does not separately treat confocal and non-confocal setups in its current form. Occlusion: Sparse sampling can lead to strong reconstruction artifacts if occlusions are not handled properly. NeTF uses MCMC and two-stage training to mitigate this. Computational Cost: Learning-based techniques like NeTF are substantially more computationally expensive than previous optimization techniques. Noise: While NeTF reduces noise compared to SOTA methods like Phasor Field, brute-force Marching Cubes on the implicit volume may lead to noise on smooth surfaces. A training strategy to address sampling bias (undersampling) in NLOS reconstruction by resampling detection spots based on reconstruction loss. It involves an initial training phase, calculating a loss map, normalizing it to a PDF, and resampling spots to retrain. It is particularly effective for recovering fine details (e.g., bunny ears) that are missing in one-stage training due to occlusion or sparse viewpoints. Accuracy: On the Bunny dataset (confocal), NeTF achieved a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 2.65 cm, compared to 2.38 cm for DLCT and 2.43 cm for F-K. On the Bunny dataset (non-confocal), NeTF achieved an MAE of 7.45 cm, compared to 3.77 cm for FBP and 7.02 cm for BP. On the Z letter scene (non-confocal), NeTF achieved an MAE of 0.60 cm, compared to 0.46 cm for FBP. Visual Quality: NeTF produces sharper edges for both front and back planes in semi-occluded scenes compared to Phasor Field and DLCT/F-K. NeTF manages to separate different parts of a mesh, whereas DLCT exhibits adhesion between different parts. NeTF reconstruction incurs much lower noise than SOTA methods, similar to NeRF. Robustness: NeTF performs reasonably well even with very sparse sampling spots (e.g., 8x8 or 16x16). Performance: Learning-based techniques like NeTF are substantially more computationally expensive than previous optimization techniques. Scaling: Not given in the sources. [G: Typically scales with the number of MLP queries and training iterations]. NeTF was introduced as a novel neural modeling framework for NLOS imaging, analogous to Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) but adapted for spherical wavefronts instead of Cartesian rays. It was tested on synthetic and real NLOS data, including the Bunny, Lucy, Indonesian, Bike, Letter Z, and semi-occluded scenes. The method leverages MCMC to handle sparse sampling and two-stage training to address sampling bias. name: SWAG
head: SWAG: Unsupervised Transient Gaussian Splatting, Unsupervised Transient Gaussians
body: SWAG is a method for unsupervised transient Gaussian splitting that extends 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by conditioning Gaussians on learned appearance embeddings and training unsupervised transient Gaussians to ignore occluders. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Neural Transient Field (NeTF) by operating directly in the Gaussian primitive space rather than a continuous neural field, leveraging learned embeddings to separate static geometry from transient artifacts. SWAG builds on the standard 3DGS representation [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md] but introduces mechanisms to handle transient elements (e.g., moving people, reflections) without explicit segmentation masks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of unposed or posed images containing transient occluders. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians representing the static scene geometry and appearance, effectively filtering out transient objects. Data Structures: The method maintains the standard 3DGS attributes for each Gaussian i: position \mathbf{c}i, rotation \mathbf{q}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color \mathbf{c}{i, SH}. Additionally, SWAG introduces: Appearance Embeddings: A learned embedding vector \mathbf{e}i associated with each Gaussian or spatial region, used to condition the appearance and distinguish static from transient features. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from the input images using standard 3DGS initialization (e.g., SfM points) [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md]. 2. Embedding Conditioning: Associate each Gaussian with an appearance embedding \mathbf{e}i. This embedding allows the model to learn distinct appearance characteristics for static and transient components. 3. Rendering: Render the scene using standard alpha-blending rasterization. The color contribution of each Gaussian is modulated by its embedding. 4. Transient Gaussian Training: During optimization, the method trains "unsupervised transient Gaussians." These are Gaussians that are allowed to have high opacity and distinct embeddings but are penalized if they do not align with the static structure or if they represent occluders. 5. Occlusion Ignoring: The optimization process implicitly learns to ignore occluders by adjusting the embeddings and opacities such that transient elements do not contribute to the final static reconstruction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def swagstep(images, cameras, gaussians, embeddings): # 1. Render image using current Gaussians and embeddings renderedimage = render(gaussians, cameras, embeddings) # 2. Compute photometric loss against ground truth loss = l1loss(renderedimage, images) # 3. Backpropagate to update Gaussians and embeddings # The key is that transient Gaussians are trained to # ignore occluders, effectively separating them from static geometry loss.backward() # 4. Update Gaussians and embeddings update(gaussians, embeddings) return loss Parameters: Learning Rate: Standard 3DGS learning rates apply [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md]. Embedding Dimension: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Precision: Standard floating-point precision issues in 3DGS apply [13851-blur-and-transient-modeling.md]. Boundaries: Transient objects moving rapidly may leave artifacts if the embedding conditioning is not robust. Time Complexity: Comparable to 3DGS, with additional overhead for embedding conditioning. Memory Complexity: Increased memory usage due to stored appearance embeddings for each Gaussian. Strengths: State-of-the-art results on diverse photo scenes with transient occluders. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of embedding conditioning to avoid overfitting to transients. SWAG was introduced as an extension to 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle unsupervised transient Gaussian splitting. It is part of the broader trend of improving 3DGS robustness in real-world scenarios with dynamic elements. name: Deformation Field Modeling
head: Dynamic Deformation, Canonical Space Warping, Time-Dependent Coordinate Mapping
body: Deformation Field Modeling addresses the problem of reconstructing and rendering dynamic scenes from static image or video sequences by explicitly modeling the temporal evolution of geometry and appearance. It solves the limitation of static radiance fields by mapping dynamic, time-varying coordinates to a static canonical space where the radiance field is defined. What sets this approach apart from siblings like Dynamic Object Embedding in Static Scenes (which isolates motion to specific objects) or Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting (which uses explicit parametric functions) is its reliance on a learned implicit function (typically an MLP) to predict continuous displacement vectors or feature transformations, allowing for complex, non-rigid, and global deformations without assuming a specific motion prior. The family shares the following core mechanisms for handling temporal dynamics: 1. Temporal Parameterization: Attributes that vary with time, such as position \mathbf{c}, rotation \mathbf{q}, opacity \alpha, density \sigma, or color \mathbf{c}, are expressed as functions of time t. Common functional forms include: Polynomial/Linear: \mathbf{q}(t) = \mathbf{q}0 + \mathbf{m}t. Fourier Series: \mathbf{c}(t) = \mathbf{c}0 + \sum{k=0}^{K} (\mathbf{a}k \cos(k \omega t) + \mathbf{b}k \sin(k \omega t)) [9168-dynamic-3d-gaussian-splatting-katsumata-et-al.md]. Neural Deformation: A neural network \Psit(x, t) predicts a displacement \Delta x to warp dynamic coordinates to a canonical space. Implicit Fields: Time-dependent NeRFs map (x, d, t) to density and color, often using local neighborhoods of frames. 2. Canonical Space Mapping: Many methods (e.g., D-NeRF, Nerfies) introduce a canonical configuration, typically at t=0, where the scene is static. A deformation network maps dynamic coordinates x at time t to canonical coordinates x': x' = x + \Psit(x, t) The radiance field is then queried in the canonical space: [\sigma, c] = \Psix(x', d). 3. Rendering with Dynamics: The rendering process integrates time-dependent attributes. For Gaussian-based methods, position and rotation are computed for the specific time t of the camera ray before rasterization [9168-dynamic-3d-gaussian-splatting-katsumata-et-al.md]. For NeRF-based methods, density \sigma and color c are queried at the deformed or time-conditioned point. 4. Loss Functions: Optimization typically minimizes photometric loss (L1 or LPIPS) between rendered and ground truth images. Additional constraints often include: Temporal Smoothness: Penalizing abrupt changes in attributes between adjacent frames. Rigid/Flow Constraints: Using optical flow or KNN rigid loss to guide deformation. Regularization: Elastic or background regularization to prevent overfitting in deformation fields. It addresses the high computational cost of traditional dynamic NeRFs (e.g., DyNeRF), which require over 100M parameters and independent models per time step, by using a static NeRF for static areas and a lightweight deformation field for dynamic regions. Unlike siblings like Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting which may model global dynamics, this approach isolates motion to specific objects, reducing parameters by 95%. Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting models dynamic scenes by keeping Gaussian properties (scale, opacity, spherical harmonics) unchanged over time while parameterizing position and orientation as continuous functions of time. It distinguishes itself from implicit deformation networks by using explicit, time-independent Fourier series for position and linear functions for rotation, ensuring temporal continuity and reducing overfitting. A method that divides the dynamic sequence into different windows based on motion amount, training separate dynamic 3DGS models in different windows with different canonical spaces and deformation fields. The deformation field uses a tunable MLP that focuses more on modeling the dynamic part of the scene. Fine-tuning ensures temporal consistency between windows using overlapping frames to add constraints. The MLP is fixed and only the canonical representation is optimized during fine-tuning. A NeRF model built using a deformation field to improve performance in the presence of non-rigid transformations (dynamic scenes). Introduce an additional MLP that maps input observation frame coordinates to deformed canonical coordinates. Add elastic regularization, background regularization, and coarse-to-fine deformation regularization by adaptive masking the positional encoding.
