Rasterize renderedimage, radii, depth = rasterizer( means3D=means3D, means2D=None, shs=shs, colorsprecomp=None, opacities=opacity, scales=scales, rotations=rotationsemb, cov3Dprecomp=None) return { "render": renderedimage, "viewspacepoints": None, "visibilityfilter": radii > 0, "radii": radii, "depth": depth } The concept of deformation fields for dynamic scenes originated with the introduction of Nerfies by Park et al. in November 2020. Nerfies introduced an additional MLP to map input observation frame coordinates to deformed canonical coordinates, enabling the reconstruction of non-rigid transformations that baseline NeRFs failed to handle. This was followed by concurrent work like NerFace (December 2020) and subsequent extensions like HyperNeRF (June 2021). In the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting, methods like SWAGS have adapted these principles by dividing sequences into motion-based windows and using tunable MLPs for localized deformation. name: Dynamic Object Embedding in Static Scenes
head: Lightweight Dynamic NeRF Modeling via Local Deformation Field, Local deformation field model
body: This method integrates dynamic advertising objects into static NeRF scenes by ensuring perspective consistency through spatial alignment and joint rendering with alpha blending. It addresses the high computational cost of traditional dynamic NeRFs (e.g., DyNeRF), which require over 100M parameters and independent models per time step, by using a static NeRF for static areas and a lightweight deformation field for dynamic regions. Unlike siblings like Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting which may model global dynamics, this approach isolates motion to specific objects, reducing parameters by 95%. Inputs: 1. Sparse video frames of the static scene (exhibition stand + background). 2. Sparse video frames of the dynamic object (e.g., rotating watch). 3. Four corresponding marking points (e.g., corners) in both the static scene and dynamic object for alignment. Outputs: A rendered frame at time t combining the static scene and the dynamically deformed object. Data Structures: 1. Static NeRF Model (F{static}): A standard NeRF representation with fixed parameters, no time dimension, and no deformation field. 2. Deformation Field (\Delta): A 3-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Input: Spatial coordinate \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and time t \in \mathbb{R}. Hidden Layers: Two hidden layers, each with dimension 128. Output: Displacement vector \Delta(\mathbf{x}, t) \in \mathbb{R}^3. Parameters: Total 5 million parameters. Steps: 1. Static Scene Reconstruction: Generate a static NeRF model for the advertising scene using sparse input reconstruction. The model parameters are fixed and do not include a time dimension. 2. Dynamic Object Modeling: Train a local deformation field model on the dynamic object using sparse video acquisition (e.g., 25-30 frames). The model learns the displacement \Delta(\mathbf{x}, t) of spatial points over time. 3. Spatial Alignment: Select four marking points in both the static scene and the dynamic object. Use the RANSAC algorithm to align the coordinate system of the dynamic object with the static scene. This ensures perspective consistency with an alignment error of less than 1 pixel. 4. Joint Rendering: For a given time t: a. Calculate the deformation position of the dynamic object using the local deformation field: \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + \Delta(\mathbf{x}, t). b. Input the deformed coordinates \mathbf{x}' into the static NeRF model F{static} to obtain color and density. c. Fuse the dynamic object with the static scene using alpha blending with a blending factor of 0.95. Formulas: The dynamic radiation field is expressed as: F(\mathbf{x}, t) = F{static}(\mathbf{x} + \Delta(\mathbf{x}, t)) where F(\mathbf{x}, t) is the output radiance field at spatial coordinate \mathbf{x} and time t, F{static} is the static NeRF query function, and \Delta(\mathbf{x}, t) is the displacement predicted by the deformation field. Parameters: Deformation Field Architecture: 3-layer MLP. Hidden Layer Dimension: 128. Total Parameters: 5 million. Alpha Blending Factor: 0.95. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Alignment Error: Must be kept below 1 pixel to ensure perspective consistency. Sparse Input: The method is designed for sparse input reconstruction, which may affect reconstruction quality compared to dense inputs. Dynamic Region Size: The method is most effective when the dynamic region constitutes \le 20\% of the scene. Temporal Discontinuity: Visual discontinuities such as color jumps or sudden light/shadow changes can occur without temporal consistency constraints. Parameter Efficiency: Uses 5M parameters, which is 95% less than DyNeRF's 100M+ parameters. Performance: PSNR increased by 2.3 \pm 0.2 dB under sparse input (mean \pm std over 10 trials). Temporal Consistency: Achieves SSIM \ge 0.92. Suitability: Suitable for VR devices due to lower parameter count and computational load compared to traditional dynamic NeRFs. Limitations: Requires sparse input reconstruction and is constrained to dynamic regions comprising \le 20\% of the scene. This method was proposed to address the limitations of traditional dynamic NeRFs like DyNeRF, which require independent models for each time step and over 100M parameters, making them unsuitable for VR devices. It introduces a local deformation field model to efficiently model motion displacement in dynamic advertising objects embedded in static scenes. Efficient Sparse Input Scene Reconstruction and Real-Time Rendering for VR Advertising Using Optimized NeRF Framework, https://www.informatica.si/index.php/informatica/article/download/12804/6562, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting (Katsumata et al.)
head: Dynamic 3DGS, Fourier-based Dynamic 3DGS, Katsumata et al
body: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting models dynamic scenes by keeping Gaussian properties (scale, opacity, spherical harmonics) unchanged over time while parameterizing position and orientation as continuous functions of time. It distinguishes itself from implicit deformation networks by using explicit, time-independent Fourier series for position and linear functions for rotation, ensuring temporal continuity and reducing overfitting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians with static attributes and a sequence of training images with known camera poses and timestamps t. Output: Optimized Fourier series coefficients for position and linear coefficients for rotation, minimizing rendering and flow losses. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i stores: 1. Static Attributes: Base position \mathbf{c}0 \in \mathbb{R}^3, base rotation \mathbf{q}0 \in \mathbb{R}^4, scale \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, and spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}{SH}. 2. Dynamic Parameters: Position: Fourier series coefficients \{\mathbf{a}k, \mathbf{b}k\}{k=0}^{K} for each spatial dimension. Rotation: Linear coefficients \mathbf{m}q \in \mathbb{R}^4 representing the rate of change of quaternion components. The total number of dynamic parameters per Gaussian is independent of time. Formulas: The position \mathbf{c}(t) and rotation \mathbf{q}(t) at time t are computed as: \mathbf{c}(t) = \mathbf{c}0 + \sum{k=0}^{K} \left( \mathbf{a}k \cos(k \omega t) + \mathbf{b}k \sin(k \omega t) \right) \mathbf{q}(t) = \mathbf{q}0 + \mathbf{m}q t where \omega is the base frequency. Optimization Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from a static reconstruction. Set dynamic coefficients \mathbf{a}k, \mathbf{b}k, \mathbf{m}q to zero or small random values. 2. Forward Pass: For each training image at time t: Compute \mathbf{c}(t) and \mathbf{q}(t) using the formulas above. Rasterize the Gaussians using standard 3DGS rasterization with the time-dependent position and rotation. Render the image \hat{I}. 3. Loss Calculation: Image Loss: Compute image losses between the rendered image \hat{I} and the ground truth I{gt}. Optical Flow Loss: Compute bidirectional optical flow between rendered frames or between rendered and ground truth frames, and add L{flow} to penalize temporal inconsistencies. Total Loss: L = L{img} + \lambda{flow} L{flow}. 4. Backpropagation: Update Fourier coefficients and linear rotation parameters using gradient descent to minimize the total loss. Parameters: K: Number of Fourier harmonics. Not given in the sources. \omega: Base frequency. Not given in the sources. \lambda{flow}: Weight for optical flow loss. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Periodicity Assumption: The Fourier series assumes periodic motion, which aligns with the observation that human and articulated object motion often exhibits periodic characteristics. Non-periodic motions may require higher K or hybrid models. Temporal Continuity: The parametric functions are continuous with respect to time, which ensures temporal continuity and robustness for novel view synthesis. Time Complexity: Optimization time is independent of the number of time steps because the parameterization is time-independent. Rendering time per frame is comparable to static 3DGS. Memory Complexity: Storage increases by O(K) per Gaussian for Fourier coefficients and O(1) for linear rotation parameters. Strengths: Fast training due to explicit parameterization; temporal continuity ensured by continuous functions; robust against overfitting compared to implicit deformation fields. Limitations: Assumes smooth or periodic motion; may struggle with abrupt, non-periodic changes without high-frequency terms. Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting was proposed by Katsumata et al.. It was introduced as an explicit deformation method to address the overfitting and high parameter count associated with implicit deformation modeling in NeRF-based approaches. The method leverages the observation that human and articulated object motion often exhibits periodic characteristics, justifying the use of Fourier series for position modeling. name: Deformation Network (Dynamic)
body: The Deformation Network (Dynamic) models temporal dynamics in 3D Gaussian Splatting by predicting time-dependent deformations for Gaussian attributes. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Dynamic Object Embedding by applying explicit displacement fields to the Gaussian parameters rather than relying on static scene embeddings or separate dynamic object tracking. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray-point embeddings raysptsemb (containing 3D coordinates), pre-computed Gaussian attributes scalesemb, rotationsemb, opacityemb, and shsemb (Spherical Harmonics coefficients), and a scalar time value timeemb. Outputs: Deformed Gaussian attributes (means3Dfinal, scalesfinal, opacityfinal, shsfinal) ready for rasterization. Data Structures: raysptsemb: Tensor of shape [N, D{pts}], where N is the number of Gaussian points and D{pts} includes spatial coordinates and potentially other embeddings. scalesemb: Tensor of shape [N, 3]. rotationsemb: Tensor of shape [N, 4] (quaternions). opacityemb: Tensor of shape [N, 1]. shsemb: Tensor of shape [N, K, 3], where K is the number of SH bands (e.g., 16 for degree 2). timeemb: Scalar or tensor representing the normalized time t \in [0, 1]. Parameters: args.staticmlp: Boolean flag. If true, uses a static MLP to compute a mask. args.emptyvoxel: Boolean flag. If true, uses empty voxel queries for masking. args.nodx: Boolean flag. If false, predicts position deformation. args.nods: Boolean flag. If false, predicts scale deformation. args.nodo: Boolean flag. If false, predicts opacity deformation. args.nodshs: Boolean flag. If false, predicts SH deformation. Steps: 1. Query Time-Dependent Features: Compute a hidden representation by concatenating spatial, scale, rotation, and time embeddings and passing them through a time-query network \Psit. \text{hidden} = \Psit(\text{rays\pts\emb}, \text{scales\emb}, \text{rotations\emb}, \text{time\feature}, \text{time\emb}) 2. Compute Mask: Determine a mask m to distinguish static from dynamic regions or to handle empty space. If args.staticmlp is true: m = \text{StaticMLP}(\text{hidden}). Else if args.emptyvoxel is true: m = \text{EmptyVoxelQuery}(\text{rays\pts\emb}[:,:3]). Else: m = \mathbf{1} (all ones). 3. Deform Position: If args.nodx is false, predict displacement \Delta x and update means. \Delta x = \text{PosDeform}(\text{hidden}) \mathbf{c}{\text{new}} = \mathbf{c}{\text{old}} \cdot m + \Delta x 4. Deform Scale: If args.nods is false, predict scale change \Delta s and update scales. \Delta s = \text{ScalesDeform}(\text{hidden}) \mathbf{s}{\text{new}} = \mathbf{s}{\text{old}} \cdot m + \Delta s 5. Deform Opacity: If args.nodo is false, predict opacity change \Delta \alpha and update opacity. \Delta \alpha = \text{OpacityDeform}(\text{hidden}) \alpha{\text{new}} = \alpha{\text{old}} \cdot m + \Delta \alpha 6. Deform SH Coefficients: If args.nodshs is false, predict SH changes \Delta \text{SH} and update coefficients. \Delta \text{SH} = \text{SHSDeform}(\text{hidden}).\text{reshape}([N, 16, 3]) \text{SH}{\text{new}} = \text{SH}{\text{old}} \cdot m{\text{unsqueeze}} + \Delta \text{SH} 7. Rasterize: Pass the final deformed attributes to the rasterizer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def deformgaussians(raysptsemb, scalesemb, rotationsemb, opacityemb, shsemb, timeemb, args): # 1. Query time-dependent features hidden = querytime(raysptsemb, scalesemb, rotationsemb, timeemb) # 2. Compute mask for static vs dynamic regions if args.staticmlp: mask = staticmlp(hidden) elif args.emptyvoxel: mask = emptyvoxel(raysptsemb[:,:3]) else: mask = oneslike(opacityemb[:, 0]).unsqueeze(-1) # 3. Compute position deformation if not args.nodx: dx = posdeform(hidden) means3D = raysptsemb[:,:3] mask + dx else: means3D = raysptsemb[:,:3] # 4. Compute scale deformation if not args.nods: ds = scalesdeform(hidden) scales = scalesemb[:,:3] mask + ds else: scales = scalesemb[:,:3] # 5. Compute opacity deformation if not args.nodo: do = opacitydeform(hidden) opacity = opacityemb[:,:1] mask + do else: opacity = opacityemb[:,:1] # 6. Compute SHS deformation if not args.nodshs: dshs = shsdeform(hidden).reshape([shsemb.shape[0], 16, 3]) shs = shsemb mask.unsqueeze(-1) + dshs else: shs = shsemb # 7. Rasterize renderedimage, radii, depth = rasterizegaussians( means3D=means3D, shs=shs, opacities=opacity, scales=scales, rotations=rotationsemb) return { "render": renderedimage, "visibilityfilter": radii > 0, "radii": radii, "depth": depth } def querytime(pts, scales, rots, time): return hiddenstate def staticmlp(hidden): return maskvalues def emptyvoxel(pts): return maskvalues def posdeform(hidden): return dxvalues def scalesdeform(hidden): return dsvalues def opacitydeform(hidden): return dovalues def shsdeform(hidden): return dshsvalues def rasterizegaussians(means3D, shs, opacities, scales, rotations): return img, rad, dep def oneslike(tensor): return tensor 0 + 1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Masking Logic: The mask multiplication m applies to the base attributes. If m=0, the deformation is zeroed out, effectively keeping the attribute static or zeroed. SH Reshaping: The SH deformation output must be reshaped to match the input SH tensor dimensions before addition. Time Normalization: timeemb should be normalized to a consistent range (e.g., [0, 1]) across the dataset. A method for updating 3D Gaussian kernels after deformation to prevent "spike-like" artifacts by preserving surface coverage without geometric proxies. Choose when naive affine transformations fail to represent the occupancy region. A component of the Mesh-adsorbed Gaussian Splatting framework that refines dynamic mesh deformations by learning motion priors from video data. Choose when Gaussians need to roam on a mesh surface and adjust logical coordinates in response to mesh changes. A learnable non-rigid deformation field that warps the canonical CAD shape onto physical observations to correct shape discrepancies. Choose when anchoring 3D Gaussian primitives to a CAD mesh surface and jointly optimizing the deformation field with 3DGS parameters and camera registration. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussians N for the deformation network forward pass, plus the standard O(N) rasterization cost. The deformation network query is typically a small MLP. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the deformation network weights and the additional deformation fields for position, scale, opacity, and SH. This increases memory usage compared to static 3DGS. Strengths: Allows for continuous time interpolation and smooth animation of Gaussian attributes. Limitations: Performance depends on the capacity of the deformation network. When to use: When animating dynamic scenes with continuous motion is required. When not to use: For static scenes or when computational resources are severely limited. The Deformation Network (Dynamic) approach is implemented in the unofficial 4DGS repository by ElenaViewSynthesis. It builds on the principles of dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting, where time is treated as an additional input to predict attribute variations. name: Surface-Preserving Kernel Adaptation
head: Laplacian-Based Deformation Adaptation
body: Surface-Preserving Kernel Adaptation is a method for updating 3D Gaussian kernels after a deformation field has been applied to their means, ensuring that the kernels maintain their original surface coverage on the deformed geometry. It solves the problem of "spike-like" artifacts that arise when naive local affine transformations are estimated from partial neighborhoods, which fail to represent the transformation of the entire occupancy region. It sets itself apart from prior works that use geometric proxies like bounding scales or splitting by operating in a proxy-free scenario, directly adapting the kernel parameters to preserve the underlying surface manifold. Inputs: Deformed Gaussian means \{\phi\Delta(pi)\}{i=1}^N. Original Gaussian means \{pi\}{i=1}^N. Original Gaussian axes \{v{i,1}, v{i,2}\} representing the major and minor axes of the occupancy region \Omegai. Splat graph structure defining adjacency. Outputs: Adapted Gaussian kernels G{\phi\Delta, i} with updated parameters (position, scale, orientation) that preserve surface coverage. Data Structures: Splat Graph: An implicit or explicit graph where nodes are Gaussian kernels and edges connect adjacent kernels based on spatial proximity or splat overlap, with adjacency determined by graph distance. Inscribed Triangle Ti: A set of three vertices \{t{i,1}, t{i,2}, t{i,3}\} representing the occupancy region \Omegai of Gaussian Gi. Steps: 1. Define Inscribed Triangle Proxy: For each Gaussian kernel Gi with mean pi and axes v{i,1} (major) and v{i,2} (minor), define the inscribed triangle of maximum area Ti = \{t{i,k}\}{k=1}^3 as a proxy for its occupancy region \Omegai. The vertices are computed as: t{i,1} = pi + v{i,1} t{i,2} = pi - \frac{1}{2}v{i,1} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}v{i,2} t{i,3} = pi - \frac{1}{2}v{i,1} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}v{i,2} 2. Identify Adjacent Gaussians: For each triangle vertex t{i,k}, identify a set of adjacent Gaussians M(t{i,k}) from the splat graph. The selection is based on graph distance to ensure the adjacency of the surface. 3. Transfer Displacement to Vertices: The deformation map \phi\Delta is defined only on the Gaussian means. To find the deformed position of each triangle vertex t{i,k}, compute the displacement using inverse distance weighting from the adjacent Gaussians in M(t{i,k}). The deformed vertex t'{i,k} is: t'{i,k} = t{i,k} + \frac{\sum{j \in M(t{i,k})} w{ij} (\phi\Delta(pj) - pj)}{\sum{j \in M(t{i,k})} w{ij}} where the weight w{ij} is the inverse squared distance: w{ij} = \|t{i,k} - pj\|^{-2} 4. Recover Adapted Kernel Parameters: Compute the Steiner circumellipse of the deformed triangle T'i = \{t'{i,1}, t'{i,2}, t'{i,3}\}. The parameters of the adapted Gaussian kernel G{\phi\Delta, i} (position, scale, and orientation) are uniquely recovered from this ellipse to preserve the original surface coverage. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeinscribedtriangle(mean, majoraxis, minoraxis): """ Computes the vertices of the inscribed triangle of maximum area for a Gaussian kernel defined by its mean and axes. """ t1 = mean + majoraxis t2 = mean - 0.5 majoraxis + (np.sqrt(3) / 2) minoraxis t3 = mean - 0.5 majoraxis - (np.sqrt(3) / 2) minoraxis return np.array([t1, t2, t3]) def inversedistanceweighteddisplacement(vertex, adjacentmeans, deformedmeans): """ Computes the displaced position of a triangle vertex using inverse distance weighting from adjacent Gaussians. """ displacements = [np.array(pprime) - np.array(p) for p, pprime in zip(adjacentmeans, deformedmeans)] weights = [] for p in adjacentmeans: distsq = np.sum((vertex - p) 2) if distsq < 1e-8: distsq = 1e-8 weights.append(1.0 / distsq) weights = np.array(weights) weightssum = np.sum(weights) if weightssum == 0: return vertex weighteddisplacement = np.zeros(3) for w, disp in zip(weights, displacements): weighteddisplacement += w disp return vertex + weighteddisplacement / weightssum def steinercircumellipseparameters(vertices): """ Recovers Gaussian kernel parameters from the vertices of the Steiner circumellipse. The exact reconstruction algorithm is referenced as [47] in the source. Standard reconstruction: center is centroid, axes are eigenvectors of covariance matrix. """ newmean = np.mean(vertices, axis=0) centered = vertices - newmean cov = np.dot(centered.T, centered) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(cov) idx = eigenvalues.argsort()[::-1] eigenvalues = eigenvalues[idx] eigenvectors = eigenvectors[:, idx] scale1 = np.sqrt(eigenvalues[0]) scale2 = np.sqrt(eigenvalues[1]) scale1 = max(scale1, 1e-6) scale2 = max(scale2, 1e-6) return { 'mean': newmean, 'majoraxis': eigenvectors[:, 0] scale1, 'minoraxis': eigenvectors[:, 1] scale2 } def surfacepreservingkerneladaptation(gaussians, deformationmap, splatgraph): """ Main adaptation routine. """ adaptedgaussians = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): pi = g['mean'] v1 = g['majoraxis'] v2 = g['minoraxis'] triangle = computeinscribedtriangle(pi, v1, v2) deformedtriangle = np.zeroslike(triangle) for k in range(3): tk = triangle[k] # Adjacency query depends on splat graph implementation adjindices = splatgraph.getadjacentgaussians(tk, gaussians) if not adjindices: deformedtriangle[k] = tk continue adjmeans = [gaussians[j]['mean'] for j in adjindices] adjdeformedmeans = [deformationmap(gaussians[j]['mean']) for j in adjindices] deformedtriangle[k] = inversedistanceweighteddisplacement(tk, adjmeans, adjdeformedmeans) params = steinercircumellipseparameters(deformedtriangle) adaptedgaussians.append(params) return adaptedgaussians Parameters: M(t{i,k}): Set of adjacent Gaussians to vertex t{i,k}, chosen based on graph distance on the splat graph. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Naive Affine Estimation Failure: Estimating a local affine transformation from a neighborhood that only partially covers a subset of a Gaussian's occupancy region \Omega causes the kernel to deviate from the underlying surface, leading to spike-like artifacts. No Adjacent Neighbors: If a vertex has no adjacent Gaussians in the splat graph, the displacement cannot be computed via weighting, requiring an identity fallback. Precision: Inverse distance weighting involves division by squared distances; small distances can lead to numerical instability if not clamped. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Preserves geometric structure and visual fidelity by maintaining original surface coverage; avoids spike-like artifacts common in naive deformation approaches; works in a proxy-free scenario. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the splat graph for adjacency; requires the deformation map to be defined on means. When to Use: When deforming 3D Gaussian Splatting representations where preserving surface fidelity is critical and proxy-based methods (bounding scales, splitting) are not applicable or desired. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in "Proxy-Free Gaussian Splats Deformation with Splat-Based Surface Estimation". It addresses limitations in existing deformation techniques for 3D Gaussian Splatting, particularly the failure of naive local affine transformations to preserve surface coverage. The approach builds on the foundation of 2D Gaussian Splatting, which encourages each kernel to act as a local patch covering the underlying surface. It references Steiner circumellipse [47] and inverse distance weighting [48] as mathematical foundations. The method was evaluated using Laplacian-based deformation techniques such as As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) [1] and Bounded Biharmonic Weights (BBW) [2] on synthetic objects from ShapeNet, Objaverse, and Sketchfab. name: Relative Mesh Deformation Network
head: RMD-Net
body: The Relative Mesh Deformation Network (RMD-Net) refines dynamic mesh deformations by learning motion priors from video data. It predicts the relative displacement between a coarse guide mesh and a refined mesh, ensuring the underlying mesh structure accurately drives associated 3D Gaussians. Unlike rigid facet-anchoring methods, it operates within a system that allows Gaussians to roam on the mesh surface, adjusting their logical coordinates in response to mesh changes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: EM (global mesh embedding), E{Vi} (per-vertex embedding for vertex i). Outputs: A 5-tuple (\Delta v, \Delta q, \Delta s, \Delta \sigma, \Delta c)i per vertex. \Delta v is vertex displacement, \Delta q is vertex rotation. \Delta s, \Delta \sigma, \Delta c are parameters for Mesh-adsorbed Gaussian rendering, not direct mesh deformation geometry. Data Structures: The network outputs a fixed-size 5-tuple per vertex. The exact internal bit-packing or tensor layout of EM and E{Vi} is not specified. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute EM and E{Vi} for the guide mesh. 2. Pass embeddings to the network: (\Delta v, \Delta q, \Delta s, \Delta \sigma, \Delta c)i = \text{RMD}(EM, E{Vi}). 3. Apply \Delta v and \Delta q to refine the guide mesh deformation. Pass \Delta s, \Delta \sigma, \Delta c to the rendering pipeline. 4. Update Gaussians via interpolation: (w{\text{gaussians}} + \Delta w) \times (v{\text{mesh}} + \Delta v) \rightarrow \text{Final Deformed Gaussians}, where \times is the MaGS interpolation operation. Formulas: Deformation prediction: (\Delta v, \Delta q, \Delta s, \Delta \sigma, \Delta c)i = \text{RMD}(EM, E{Vi}). Gaussian update: (w{\text{gaussians}} + \Delta w) \times (v{\text{mesh}} + \Delta v) \rightarrow \text{Final Deformed Gaussians}. Loss: L = L{\text{L1}} \times (1 - \lambda{\text{ssim}}) + L{\text{SSIM}} \times \lambda{\text{ssim}}, where L{\text{L1}} is pixel-wise L1 difference and L{\text{SSIM}} is structural similarity loss. Parameters: \lambda{\text{ssim}}: Weight for the SSIM loss component. Typical value not given in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The pipeline relies on full differentiability for backpropagation through deformation and interpolation. Degenerate mesh topology or missing vertex embeddings will break the embedding extraction step. \Delta s, \Delta \sigma, \Delta c do not correspond directly to mesh deformation but are critical for the rendering step. Calculates changes in logical coordinates \Delta w during mesh deformation, allowing Gaussians to roam on the mesh surface rather than anchor to a facet. It takes EM, the vertex embeddings of the containing facet (E{V1}, E{V2}, E{V3}), and the Gaussian's current logical coordinate wi as input, outputting \Delta wi. Formula: \Delta wi = \text{RGD}(EM, E{V1}, E{V2}, E{V3}, wi). Choose this variant when Gaussian position drift relative to the mesh surface is required for accurate dynamic reconstruction. See also Deformation Network (Dynamic). Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enables joint optimization of mesh deformation and Gaussian properties via backpropagation on rendering errors. Allows flexible Gaussian roaming on deforming surfaces. Limitations: Computational cost is unspecified. When to Use: Use for dynamic 3D object reconstruction where mesh-guided deformation is preferred over point-based methods, particularly when physics simulation on the reconstructed mesh is needed. Introduced in "Reconstructing and Simulating Dynamic 3D Objects with Mesh-adsorbed Gaussian Splatting". It is part of the MaGS framework, combining mesh-based deformation with Gaussian Splatting for dynamic scene reconstruction and simulation. The method builds on Mesh-adsorbed Gaussians, where Gaussians associate with mesh facets but adjust positions relative to the mesh during deformation. name: 4D-GS
body: 4D-GS extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to dynamic scenes by parameterizing Gaussian attributes as functions of time, enabling the reconstruction and rendering of non-rigidly deforming objects from multi-view video. It distinguishes itself from other dynamic Gaussian methods by replacing standard positional encoding with multi-resolution hexplane voxels for spatiotemporal information and employing a two-stage optimization process that first stabilizes the static scene before learning the deformation field. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of multi-view images \{Iv\} with known camera poses and timestamps t. Outputs: A set of 4D Gaussians, where each Gaussian is defined by a base set of static attributes and a time-dependent deformation field. Data Structures: 1. Static Gaussians: Each Gaussian i stores base attributes: position \mathbf{c}i, rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}{i, SH}. 2. Hexplane Voxels: A multi-resolution structure encoding spatiotemporal information, replacing positional encoding. 3. Attribute MLPs: Compact Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) dedicated to predicting delta values for specific attributes based on inputs from the hexplane voxels and the query time t. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize a static 3D Gaussian point cloud using standard 3DGS initialization (e.g., from SfM points). 2. Stage 1: Static Optimization: Optimize the static Gaussian attributes (\mathbf{c}i, \mathbf{q}i, \mathbf{s}i, \alphai, \mathbf{c}{i, SH}) using standard 3DGS rendering and photometric loss until convergence. 3. Stage 2: Deformation Field Learning: Voxel Encoding: For each Gaussian i and query time t, encode its spatial position \mathbf{c}i and time t into the multi-resolution hexplane voxels. Temporal Smoothing: Add linearly decaying Gaussian noise to the encoded time vector to improve temporal smoothing without additional computational overhead. Delta Prediction: Pass the encoded spatiotemporal features through attribute-specific compact MLPs to predict delta values (\Delta \mathbf{c}, \Delta \mathbf{q}, \Delta \mathbf{s}, etc.). Attribute Update: Compute the dynamic attributes for time t by applying the predicted deltas to the base attributes. Rotation quaternions are normalized after delta application. Rendering: Render the scene using the time-dependent attributes \mathbf{c}i(t), \mathbf{q}i(t), \mathbf{s}i(t) for the camera timestamp t. Optimization: Minimize photometric loss (L1) between rendered and ground truth images while optimizing the MLP weights representing the deformation field. Formulas: The exact mathematical formulations for the hexplane voxel lookup and MLP forward pass are not provided in the sources. Attributes are updated as \mathbf{a}i(t) = \mathbf{a}i + \Delta \mathbf{a}i(t), where \Delta \mathbf{a}i(t) is predicted by the attribute-specific MLP. Parameters: Hexplane Resolution: Not given in the sources. MLP Architecture: Compact MLPs; specific layer sizes not given in the sources. Noise Schedule: Linearly decaying Gaussian noise on the time vector; decay rate not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Temporal Artifacts: Without noise injection, time interpolation can amplify artifacts. Optimization Stability: Jointly optimizing static and dynamic attributes from scratch can be unstable; the two-stage approach mitigates this. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. A probabilistic graphical model for 4D Gaussian Splatting that reformulates reconstruction as a Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) estimation problem, introducing structured dependencies among cameras, time, and components to handle uncertainty. Unlike deterministic 4DGS methods that minimize photometric error directly, GraphiXS uses stochastic priors and Bayesian inference to regularize dynamics and component visibility, making it robust to sparse views and missing frames. Complexity: Rendering complexity is similar to 3DGS, but training involves additional overhead from hexplane voxel lookups and MLP inference for each Gaussian at each time step. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Stable training via two-stage optimization; efficient spatiotemporal encoding via hexplanes; robust temporal smoothing via noise injection. Limitations: Requires a static baseline optimization phase. 4D-GS extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle dynamic scenes by replacing positional encoding with multi-resolution hexplane voxels for spatiotemporal information and utilizing compact MLPs for attribute deformation. name: GraphiXS
head: GraphiTS, Graphical X Splatting
body: GraphiXS is a probabilistic graphical model for 4D Gaussian Splatting that reformulates reconstruction as a Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) estimation problem, introducing structured dependencies among cameras, time, and components to handle uncertainty. Unlike deterministic 4DGS methods that minimize photometric error directly, GraphiXS uses stochastic priors and Bayesian inference to regularize dynamics and component visibility, making it robust to sparse views and missing frames. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 2D images I{ct} indexed by camera c and time t; camera poses C; time indices T. Outputs: A set of 4D Gaussian components parameterized by \theta, including mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, base opacity o, spherical harmonics color sh, appearance time g, duration u, velocity v, acceleration a, jerk j, and snap s. Data Structures: Each component p stores: \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix (symmetric positive definite). o \in \mathbb{R}: Base opacity. sh: Spherical harmonics coefficients for color. g \in \mathbb{R}: Appearance time. u \in \mathbb{R}: Duration of existence. v, a, j, s \in \mathbb{R}^3: Velocity, acceleration, jerk, and snap parameters for dynamics. Generative Process: The model defines a generative process with four steps: 1. Component Selection: Given mixture model F, camera c \sim C, and time t \sim T, sample a subset of components \{\alphai\} with L components for image I{ct}. 2. Ray Casting: For each pixel X{c,d}^t, cast a ray R{c,d}^t from camera c at time t. 3. Intersection: Identify the subset of components \{\betaj\} from \{\alphai\} that intersect with ray R{c,d}^t. 4. Rasterization: Generate the color for pixel X{c,d}^t based on \{\betaj\} and ray R{c,d}^t. Factorized Likelihood: The likelihood is factorized according to the graphical dependencies: P(X | \cdot) = P(X | \beta, R) P(\beta | \alpha, R) P(R | C, T) P(\alpha | \delta\theta, C, T) where X is the image, \beta are per-pixel components, R is the ray, \alpha are per-image components, and \delta\theta is the mixture model. Rendering (Rasterization): The rendering step P(X | \beta, R) is implemented as standard alpha blending: Ras(X; \beta, R) = \sum{i=1}^N \lambdai \beta{2D}^i(X) where \lambdai = si oi \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - oj \beta{2D}^j(X)) is the transmittance/weight, si is a scale/color factor, oi is opacity, and \beta{2D}^i(X) is the projected 2D Gaussian. Image Loss (Energy-based Likelihood): The baseline rendering loss is converted into an energy-based likelihood: P(I | \beta, R, \theta, C, T) \propto \exp \left( - \sum{t} \sum{c}^{M} L{img}(I{ct}) \right) where the image loss L{img} is: L{img} = (1 - \epsilonD^{-SSIM})L1 + \epsilonD^{-SSIM} L{D-SSIM} + \epsilono \sumi ||oi||1 + \epsilon\Sigma \sum{i,j} ||\lambda{i,j}||1 Here, L1 and L{D-SSIM} are L1 and Deep-SSIM losses, \lambda{i,j} are eigenvalues of covariance \Sigma, and \epsilon terms are hyperparameters. Priors: The prior P(\theta) regularizes the parameters to ensure well-behaved dynamics and structure: 1. Mean Dynamics (Brownian Motion): The mean \mu evolves via Brownian motion with a deterministic drift f(\mu, t): \frac{d\mu}{dt} = f(\mu, t) + \mathcal{N}(0, \epsilon^2 I) Discretized as: \mu(t) = \mu(t-1) + f(\mu, t)\Delta t + \mathcal{N}(0, \epsilon^2 I)\Delta t The drift function f(\mu, t)\Delta t uses higher-order derivatives: f(\mu, t)\Delta t = v(t-g) + \frac{1}{2}a(t-g)^2 + \frac{1}{6}j(t-g)^3 + \frac{1}{24}s(t-g)^4 where v, a, j, s are velocity, acceleration, jerk, and snap, and g is the appearance time. 2. Opacity Prior: P(o) \propto \frac{1}{N1} \sum{i=1}^N oi^2 \exp\left(-\frac{(t-g)^2}{2u^2}\right) \psi(\cdot) where u is the duration a component lasts, N1 is a normalization constant, and \psi(\cdot) is the splatting response. 3. Dynamics Prior: P(vp, ap, jp, sp) \propto \exp\left(-\lambdah \frac{1}{Nt} \sum{p} \frac{||vp||^2 + ||ap||^2 + ||jp||^2 + ||sp||^2}{|\det(\Sigmap)|^{1/2}}\right) This prefers slowly moving components, weighted by the volume proxy |\det(\Sigmap)|. 4. Covariance Prior: P(\Sigmap) \propto \exp\left(-\lambda\sigma \frac{1}{Nt} \sum{p} ||\Sigmap - \hat{\Sigma}t||F^2\right) where \hat{\Sigma}t is the mean covariance of components at time t. 5. Component Confidence: A metric to prefer components visible across all frames: P(\alpha | \delta\theta, C, T) = E\{P(r{c,d}^t | \alpha)\} \approx \frac{\sum{c,t,d} P(r{c,d}^t | \alpha)}{\sum{p,c,t,d} P(r{c,d}^t | \delta{\thetap})} The numerator is the soft visibility of component \alpha to all pixels; the denominator is the sum of soft visibility of all components. Full Prior: P(\theta(t)) = P(o) P(\mu(1)) \prod{t=2}^K \mathcal{N}(\mu(t-1) + f(\mu, t), \epsilon^2 I) \prod{t=1}^K P(v, a, j, s) P(\Sigma) [ S1 ] Optimization (MAP): The objective is to maximize the posterior: \arg\max\theta \log P(X | R, \beta, \alpha, C, T, \theta) P(\theta) Equivalent to minimizing: L{full} = -\log P(I | \cdot) - \log P(\alpha | \cdot) - \log P(\theta) L{full} = L{img} + L\alpha + L\theta [ S1 ] Algorithm: Optimization uses Stochastic Gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (SGHMC). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traingraphixs(images, cameras, times, initialcomponents, numiterations): # Initialize component parameters theta (mu, Sigma, o, sh, g, u, v, a, j, s) theta = {key: torch.zeroslike(param) for key, param in initialcomponents.items()} # SGHMC hyperparameters frictioncoeff = 120.0 noisescale = 1.0 burniniters = 7000 burninfriction = 5e5 browniannoisestd = 1e-4 # Loss weights lambdaalpha = 1e-3 temporalopacityweight = 0.01 lambdah = 1e-4 epsilono = 0.01 epsilonSigma = 0.01 # Learning rate annealing for dynamics parameters (v, a, j, s, u) lrstart = 1e-2 lrend = 1e-4 for iteration in range(numiterations): # 1. Sample batch of (camera, time) pairs batchcameras, batchtimes = samplebatch(cameras, times) # 2. Compute gradients of Lfull w.r.t. theta # Lfull = Limg + Lalpha + Ltheta grads = computegradients(theta, batchcameras, batchtimes, images, lambdaalpha, temporalopacityweight, lambdah, epsilono, epsilonSigma) # 3. Anneal learning rates for dynamics parameters progress = iteration / numiterations lrdynamics = lrend + (lrstart - lrend) (1 - progress) # 4. SGHMC update with burn-in phase if iteration < burniniters: currentfriction = burninfriction else: currentfriction = frictioncoeff # Add controlled stochasticity (SGHMC noise) noise = torch.randnlike(grads) noisescale currentfriction # Update parameters: theta <- theta - lr (grads + noise) for key in theta: theta[key] = theta[key] - lrdynamics (grads[key] + noise[key]) # 5. Component management (stochastic multinomial sampling or deterministic top-N) # Based on evidence: stochastic multinomial sampling for addition/recycling # or deterministic top-N selection in ablation theta = managecomponents(theta, images, batchcameras, batchtimes) return theta Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Methods relying on a canonical Gaussian set deformed via a neural field (e.g., HexPlane or MLP) cannot be upgraded directly; instead, GraphiXS priors must be applied to the displaced components at each sampled timestamp with gradients backpropagated through the deformation network. The deterministic variant replaces SGHMC with Adam, disables component confidence loss, removes Brownian motion noise, and uses deterministic top-N selection for densification. Time and Memory Complexity: The method involves millions of parameters, requiring significant memory for storing component states and gradients. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The total number of components is capped at 1.5 million in experiments. Strengths: Robust to sparse views and missing frames due to probabilistic modeling of uncertainty and component confidence. Handles arbitrary and potentially discontinuous motions via Brownian motion and higher-order derivatives. Limitations: Not directly applicable to implicit deformation-based methods without modification. When to use: When dealing with dynamic scenes with uncertainty, sparse views, or missing temporal data, and when using explicit 3D/4D Gaussians or similar primitives (e.g., FTGS, Ex4DGS, 4DGS-1). GraphiXS was introduced by Zhu et al. in 2025. It generalizes the unnormalized mixture model of 3D/4DGS by introducing structured dependencies among random variables to enable Bayesian inference and regularization. It builds on the framework of 4D Gaussian Splatting. Graphical X Splatting (GraphiXS): A Graphical Model for 4D Gaussian Splatting under Uncertainty, https://doi.org/10.1145/3799902.3811085, fetched 2026-11-05

name: Temporal Input Conditioning
head: Time-conditioned rendering, Dynamic scene parameterization
body: Temporal Input Conditioning parameterizes scene attributes—such as position, rotation, opacity, density, or color—as explicit functions of time t to enable novel view synthesis for dynamic scenes. It addresses the challenge of modeling non-rigid motion and temporal evolution from monocular or sparse multi-view inputs without requiring ground-truth geometry or dense multi-view stereo data at every instant. It sets itself apart from naive time-extended NeRFs by decomposing the representation into static canonical geometry and time-varying deformation fields, or by conditioning radiance fields directly on time, thereby exploiting temporal redundancy that direct 6D mappings fail to capture. Unlike DaReNeRF, which focuses on direction-aware wavelet decompositions, this family establishes the foundational canonical-space and time-conditioning paradigms for dynamic neural rendering. Builds on Dynamic and Temporal Modeling. D-NeRF synthesizes novel views at arbitrary time instances for dynamic scenes with complex non-rigid geometries, optimizing a deformable volumetric function from a sparse set of monocular input images. It sets itself apart from naive time-extended NeRFs by decomposing the representation into a static canonical space and a learned deformation field, thereby exploiting temporal redundancy that direct 6D mappings fail to capture. Unlike DaReNeRF, which focuses on specific deformation regularizations, D-NeRF establishes the foundational canonical-space paradigm for dynamic neural rendering. DaReNeRF is a method for novel view synthesis of dynamic scenes that employs a direction-aware representation to capture scene dynamics from six distinct orientations. It addresses the shift variance and direction ambiguity (checkerboard artifacts) inherent in traditional 2D Discrete Wavelet Transforms (DWT) by utilizing the Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Transform (DTCWT). Unlike standard plane-based decompositions, DaReNeRF models features from six different directions to eliminate ghosting artifacts around moving objects. A NeRF variant that represents scene geometry and appearance at each specific time step t, trained using neighboring frames around time t, to capture local scene geometry and motion. It represents scene appearance using a mapping function c = \phic(x, d) taking point x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and viewing direction d \in \mathbb{R}^2 to predict color c \in \mathbb{R}^3, and scene geometry via s = \phig(x) mapping a 3D point to a signed distance value s \in \mathbb{R}. For a camera ray r(h) = o + hd, it samples K 3D points and uses the time-dependent NeRF to compute SDF flows, which constrain the learning of continuous camera motion via the linear relationship between SDF flow and scene flow. Density is converted from signed distance si using \sigmai = \max((\Phi(si) - \Phi(s{i+1}))/\Phi(si), 0), where \Phi(s) = 1/(1+e^{1-\gamma s}) and \gamma is learnable. Pixel color is rendered via \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^K Li \sigmai ci, with Li = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \sigmaj). Extends ControlNet to the 3D generation task. It allows extra conditioning inputs like edge, depth, normal, and scribbles to be fed into existing multi-view generation models. The concept of temporal input conditioning in neural rendering originated with D-NeRF, which introduced the canonical space paradigm for dynamic scenes. This approach allows for the decomposition of dynamic scenes into static geometry and time-varying deformations, addressing the limitations of direct 6D mappings. Subsequent works like DaReNeRF have refined this by introducing direction-aware representations to mitigate artifacts such as shift variance and checkerboard effects. More recent developments, such as the time-dependent NeRF, integrate these concepts with continuous camera motion optimization, using local temporal neighborhoods to constrain SDF flows and improve pose estimation. name: D-NeRF
head: Deformable Neural Radiance Fields, Nerfies, Neural Radiance Fields for Dynamic Scenes
body: D-NeRF synthesizes novel views at arbitrary time instants for dynamic scenes with complex non-rigid geometries, optimizing a deformable volumetric function from a sparse set of monocular input images without ground-truth geometry or multi-view stereo data. It sets itself apart from naive extensions of NeRF (which map 6D coordinates directly to radiance) and T-NeRF (which uses a 6D input without canonical mapping) by decomposing the representation into a static canonical scene and a time-dependent deformation field, effectively exploiting temporal redundancy. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sparse set of T RGB images \{It\}{t=1}^T captured by a monocular camera, where each image It \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} is associated with a camera pose matrix Tt \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4} (SE(3)) at time t. The method assumes a single view per time instant. Outputs: A rendered RGB pixel color C'(p, t) for a pixel p at time t, given a camera ray defined by origin o and direction d. Data Structures: The model consists of two deep fully connected networks (MLPs) without convolutional layers: 1. Deformation Network (\Psit): Maps a 3D point x and time t to a displacement vector \Delta x. Architecture: 8-layer MLP with ReLU activations. Output: No non-linearity applied to \Delta x. 2. Canonical Network (\Psix): Maps a canonical 3D point x' and viewing direction d to volume density \sigma and emitted color c. Architecture: 8-layer MLP with ReLU activations. Output: Sigmoid non-linearity applied to c and \sigma. Positional Encoding: Raw coordinates are encoded into a higher-dimensional space using \gamma(p) = \langle (\sin(2^l \pi p), \cos(2^l \pi p)) \rangle{l=0}^{L-1}, applied independently to each coordinate component. For spatial coordinates x: L = 10. For viewing direction d and time t: L = 4. Numbered Steps: 1. Canonical Configuration Definition: Define the canonical scene as the scene state at time t=0. Enforce that the deformation displacement is zero at this time: \Psit(x, 0) = 0 \quad \text{for all } x For t \neq 0, \Psit(x, t) = \Delta x. 2. Ray Sampling: For a pixel p at time t, define the camera ray x(h) = o + h d, where o is the camera center and d is the viewing direction. Sample N points \{hn\}{n=1}^N along the ray interval [hn, hf] using stratified sampling from evenly-spaced bins. 3. Deformation Transform: For each sample point x(hn) at time t, compute the displacement \Delta x using the deformation network: \Delta x = \Psit(\gamma(x(hn)), \gamma(t)) Transform the point to the canonical space: p(hn, t) = x(hn) + \Delta x. 4. Canonical Query: Query the canonical network with the transformed point and viewing direction to obtain density and color: [c(p(hn, t), d), \sigma(p(hn, t))] = \Psix(\gamma(p(hn, t)), \gamma(d)). 5. Volume Rendering Approximation: Compute the accumulated transmittance and opacity for each sample. Let \deltan = h{n+1} - hn be the distance between quadrature points. Opacity: \alpha(hn, t, \deltan) = 1 - \exp(-\sigma(p(hn, t)) \deltan) Transmittance: T'(hn, t) = \exp\left(-\sum{m=1}^{n-1} \sigma(p(hm, t)) \deltam\right). 6. Pixel Color Computation: Approximate the pixel color C'(p, t) as the weighted sum of emitted colors: C'(p, t) = \sum{n=1}^{N} T'(hn, t) \alpha(hn, t, \deltan) c(p(hn, t), d). 7. Training Optimization: Minimize the mean squared error (MSE) between the rendered pixel C'(p, t) and the ground truth pixel \hat{C}(p, t): \text{Loss} = \frac{1}{Ns} \sum{i=1}^{Ns} \|\hat{C}(pi, t) - C'(pi, t)\|^2 where Ns is the batch size in rays. Parameters: Canonical Time: t=0. Positional Encoding Depth: L=10 for x, L=4 for d and t. Network Depth: 8 layers for both \Psit and \Psix. Training Resolution: 400 \times 400 images. Iterations: 800,000. Batch Size: Ns = 4096 rays. Samples per Ray: 64. Optimizer: Adam with learning rate 5 \times 10^{-4}, \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.999, decaying exponentially to 5 \times 10^{-5}. Curriculum Learning: Input images are sorted by timestamp and added incrementally to improve convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class PositionalEncoding(nn.Module): def init(self, L): super().init() self.L = L def forward(self, x): # x shape: (..., 3) or (..., 1) # Apply encoding independently to each dimension freqbands = 2.0 torch.linspace(0, self.L - 1, self.L).to(x.device) # Expand dimensions for broadcasting # x: (..., D) -> (..., D, 1) # freqbands: (L,) -> (1, 1, L) # result: (..., D, 2L) xexpanded = x.unsqueeze(-1) freqbands = freqbands.view(1, 1, -1) sines = torch.sin(xexpanded freqbands torch.pi) cosines = torch.cos(xexpanded freqbands torch.pi) return torch.cat([sines, cosines], dim=-1).view(x.shape[:-1], -1) class DeformationNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self, inputdim, hiddendim=256, numlayers=8): super().init() layers = [] for i in range(numlayers): layers.append(nn.Linear(inputdim if i == 0 else hiddendim, hiddendim)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) self.network = nn.Sequential(layers) def forward(self, xenc, tenc): # xenc: (..., 30) for L=10, tenc: (..., 8) for L=4 # Concatenate encoded spatial and temporal inputs inputvec = torch.cat([xenc, tenc], dim=-1) # Output displacement without non-linearity return self.network(inputvec) class CanonicalNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self, inputdim, hiddendim=256, numlayers=8): super().init() layers = [] for i in range(numlayers): layers.append(nn.Linear(inputdim if i == 0 else hiddendim, hiddendim)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) # Final layer outputs density and color layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim, 4)) # 1 for sigma, 3 for RGB self.network = nn.Sequential(layers) def forward(self, xenc, denc): # xenc: (..., 30), denc: (..., 8) inputvec = torch.cat([xenc, denc], dim=-1) out = self.network(inputvec) sigma = out[...,:1] rgb = out[..., 1:] # Apply sigmoid to sigma and rgb sigma = torch.sigmoid(sigma) rgb = torch.sigmoid(rgb) return sigma, rgb def renderray(rayso, raysd, near, far, Nsamples, deformnet, canonnet, posencx, posencd, posenct): """ Renders a single ray. rayso: (3,) raysd: (3,) near: float far: float t: float (time) """ # Stratified sampling tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., Nsamples + 1) tvals = tvals[:-1] # Add noise for stratified sampling noise = torch.rand(Nsamples) tvals = tvals + noise / Nsamples # Interpolate points along ray # x(h) = o + h d # We map tvals from [0,1] to [near, far] hvals = near + tvals (far - near) points = rayso.unsqueeze(0) + hvals.unsqueeze(1) raysd.unsqueeze(0) # (Nsamples, 3) # Encode inputs pointsenc = posencx(points) # (Nsamples, 30) denc = posencd(raysd) # (8,) tenc = posenct(torch.tensor([t])) # (8,) # Deformation deltax = deformnet(pointsenc, tenc) # (Nsamples, 3) # Canonical points canonicalpoints = points + deltax # (Nsamples, 3) canonicalpointsenc = posencx(canonicalpoints) # (Nsamples, 30) # Canonical Query sigma, rgb = canonnet(canonicalpointsenc, denc) # (Nsamples, 1), (Nsamples, 3) # Volume Rendering # Distances between samples dists = hvals[1:] - hvals[:-1] dists = torch.cat([dists, torch.tensor([1e10]).to(points.device)]) # Last sample distance doesn't matter much # Alpha and Transmittance alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma.squeeze(-1) dists) # (Nsamples,) transmittance = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([torch.ones(1).to(points.device), 1.0 - alpha + 1e-10]), dim=0)[:-1] # (Nsamples,) # Contribution contribution = transmittance alpha.unsqueeze(-1) rgb # (Nsamples, 3) # Final color color = torch.sum(contribution, dim=0) # (3,) return color def trainstep(batchrayso, batchraysd, batchcolors, batchtimes, near, far, deformnet, canonnet, optimizer): optimizer.zerograd() # batchrayso: (Ns, 3) # batchraysd: (Ns, 3) # batchcolors: (Ns, 3) # batchtimes: (Ns,) renderedcolors = [] for i in range(batchrayso.shape[0]): # Render one ray # Note: In practice, this is vectorized, but for clarity we loop # Assuming helper functions defined above are accessible # This loop is inefficient for implementation but clear for logic # A real implementation would vectorize the ray processing pass # Vectorized implementation logic: # 1. Sample points for all rays # 2. Encode all points, directions, and times # 3. Compute deformations # 4. Query canonical network # 5. Render # Simplified vectorized steps for pseudocode completeness: Nsamples = 64 Ns = batchrayso.shape[0] # Sample depths tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., Nsamples + 1).to(batchrayso.device) tvals = tvals[:-1] + torch.rand(Nsamples, 1).to(batchrayso.device) / Nsamples hvals = near + tvals (far - near) # (Ns, Nsamples) # Points raysoexp = batchrayso.unsqueeze(1) # (Ns, 1, 3) raysdexp = batchraysd.unsqueeze(1) # (Ns, 1, 3) points = raysoexp + hvals.unsqueeze(2) raysdexp # (Ns, Nsamples, 3) # Encodings pointsenc = posencx(points) # (Ns, Nsamples, 30) denc = posencd(batchraysd) # (Ns, 8) tenc = posenct(batchtimes) # (Ns, 8) # Deformation deltax = deformnet(pointsenc, tenc) # (Ns, Nsamples, 3) # Canonical Points canonicalpoints = points + deltax canonicalpointsenc = posencx(canonicalpoints) # Canonical Query # Repeat denc for each sample dencexp = denc.unsqueeze(1).repeat(1, Nsamples, 1) # (Ns, Nsamples, 8) sigma, rgb = canonnet(canonicalpointsenc, dencexp) # (Ns, Nsamples, 1), (Ns, Nsamples, 3) # Rendering dists = hvals[:, 1:] - hvals[:,:-1] # (Ns, Nsamples-1) dists = torch.cat([dists, torch.tensor([1e10]).to(points.device)].unsqueeze(0).repeat(Ns, 1), dim=1) # (Ns, Nsamples) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma.squeeze(-1) dists) # (Ns, Nsamples) transmittance = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([torch.ones(Ns, 1).to(points.device), 1.0 - alpha + 1e-10], dim=1)[:,:-1], dim=1) # (Ns, Nsamples) contribution = transmittance.unsqueeze(-1) alpha.unsqueeze(-1) rgb # (Ns, Nsamples, 3) renderedcolors = torch.sum(contribution, dim=1) # (Ns, 3) loss = F.mseloss(renderedcolors, batchcolors) loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss.item() Replaces explicit temporal coordinate t with multi-view projected color statistics to improve point correspondence estimation during on-the-fly training, mapping inputs to a "space-color" coordinate system. Complexity: Time and memory complexity are dominated by the two 8-layer MLPs and the ray sampling process. The method requires storing parameters for two networks. Performance: On the 'Hell Warrior' scene, D-NeRF achieves MSE 31 \times 10^{-4}, PSNR 23.19, SSIM 0.93, LPIPS 0.08, compared to NeRF's MSE 44 \times 10^{-3}, PSNR 13.52, SSIM 0.81, LPIPS 0.25. On the 'T-Rex' scene, D-NeRF achieves MSE 5 \times 10^{-4}, PSNR 32.80, SSIM 0.98, LPIPS 0.03, compared to NeRF's MSE 21 \times 10^{-3}, PSNR 18.19, SSIM 0.89, LPIPS 0.14. Scaling: Training uses 400x400 images, 800k iterations, batch size 4096 rays, sampled 64 times per ray, trained on a single Nvidia GTX 1080 for 2 days. Strengths: Can handle rigid, articulated, and non-rigid motions from a sparse set of monocular views without ground-truth geometry. Limitations: Deformation fields are difficult to learn when complex scene motions exist, leading to blurry results similar to Neural Volumes. It cannot easily handle topology changes because the deformation field must be continuous. D-NeRF was proposed by Pumarola et al. in November 2020. It extends NeRF to handle dynamic scenes by introducing time as an additional input and splitting the representation into a deformation network and a canonical radiance network. It is compared against Neural Volumes (NV), Scene Representation Networks (SRN), and T-NeRF. T-NeRF represents the scene with a 6D input (x,y,z,\theta,\phi,t) directly without canonical mapping, which D-NeRF improves upon by using an intermediate canonical configuration. name: Dynamic NeRF Guided by Projected Colors
head: Projected Color Conditioning, Space-Color Dynamic NeRF
body: This method is a dynamic Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) variant that replaces the explicit temporal coordinate t with multi-view projected color statistics to improve point correspondence estimation during on-the-fly training. Unlike standard space-time dynamic NeRFs that optimize irregular temporal deformation fields, this approach maps inputs to a "space-color" coordinate system where correspondence is easier to track due to color invariance under motion. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Spatial coordinates x \in \mathbb{R}^3, viewing direction d \in \mathbb{R}^3, projected color mean \bar{c}p(x, k), and projected color variance Var(cp(x, k)) at frame k. Outputs: Density \sigma \in \mathbb{R} and color c \in \mathbb{R}^3. Data Structures The model input vector consists of: 1. x: 3D spatial position. 2. d: Normalized viewing direction. 3. \bar{c}p(x, k): Scalar mean of projected colors. 4. Var(cp(x, k)): Scalar variance of projected colors. Projected Color Calculation For a 3D point x at frame k, the set of projected colors cp(x, k) is derived from all training cameras M. Let C{k, cam} be the pixel color at the projection of x in camera cam's image at frame k, and P{cam} be the camera projection matrix: cp(x, k) = \{ C{k, cam}(P{cam} \cdot x) \mid cam \in M \} The scalar inputs are the mean and variance of this set: \bar{c}p(x, k) = \text{mean}(cp(x, k)) Var(cp(x, k)) = \text{variance}(cp(x, k)) Algorithm Steps 1. Precompute Projections: For each 3D point x sampled during training and each frame k, project x into the image plane of every camera cam \in M using P{cam}. 2. Sample Colors: Retrieve the pixel colors C{k, cam} at the projected coordinates. Handle out-of-bounds projections by excluding them or using a default value. 3. Compute Statistics: Calculate the mean \bar{c}p(x, k) and variance Var(cp(x, k)) of the collected colors. 4. Model Forward Pass: Construct the input vector [x, d, \bar{c}p(x, k), Var(cp(x, k))]. Pass this through the neural network Fk to predict density \sigma and color c: Fk: (x, d, \bar{c}p(x, k), Var(cp(x, k))) \mapsto (\sigma, c) 5. Render and Optimize: Use volume rendering to synthesize images and optimize network parameters using gradient descent. Pitfalls Color Invariance Assumption: Projected colors are not perfectly invariant due to reflections, lighting changes, and occlusions. However, they remain largely similar across consecutive frames. Projection Errors: Incorrect camera matrices P{cam} or misaligned frames will corrupt the projected color statistics. Complexity: Reduces optimization time compared to space-time dynamic NeRFs by avoiding the need to learn irregular temporal deformation fields. Strengths: Better point correspondence estimation on-the-fly; easier extrapolation to untrained frames. Limitations: Relies on multi-view consistency; performance degrades if lighting or reflections vary significantly between frames. This method was introduced in OD-NeRF. It addresses the difficulty of estimating point correspondence in dynamic scenes where temporal trajectories are irregular. By shifting from a space-time to a space-color coordinate system, it leverages the invariance of point color under motion to simplify the learning task. name: DaReNeRF
head: DaReNeRF architecture, Direction-Aware Representation, Direction-aware Representation for Dynamic Scenes
body: DaReNeRF is a method for novel view synthesis of dynamic scenes that extends plane-based 4D volume decomposition with a direction-aware representation to capture scene dynamics from six distinct directions. It addresses the shift variance and direction ambiguity (checkerboard artifacts) inherent in traditional 2D Discrete Wavelet Transforms (DWT) by utilizing the Inverse Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Transform (DTCWT). Unlike D-NeRF, which models dynamic scenes using a static MLP with time as an input, DaReNeRF decomposes the 4D spatiotemporal volume into low-rank plane-based components enhanced by directional wavelet coefficients, offering improved efficiency and artifact reduction for complex motions. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of posed 2D images with timestamps. The scene is represented in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC). Outputs: Rendered RGB images for arbitrary camera poses and time steps via differentiable volumetric rendering. Data Structures The core data structure is the Direction-Aware Representation, which decomposes the 4D spatiotemporal volume D into three terms, each consisting of the Hadamard product of two 2D plane-based representations and a learned vector. 1. Plane-based Representations (M): Learned 2D tensors M{rAB} \in \mathbb{R}^{A \times B} where (A, B) \in \{X, Y, Z, T\}^2 and A \neq B. These are not stored directly but are reconstructed from wavelet coefficients. 2. Learned Vectors (v): Vectors v{ri} \in \mathbb{R}^F along the feature axes, where F=3 for RGB colors. 3. Wavelet Coefficients: For each plane M{rAB}, the representation is defined by: One approximation coefficient: W^{AB}{a,r} \in \mathbb{R}^{m/2 \times n/2}. Six real direction-aware wavelet coefficients: \{R\{W^{AB}{i,r}\}\}{i=1}^6. Six imaginary direction-aware wavelet coefficients: \{I\{W^{AB}{i,r}\}\}{i=1}^6. Here, m, n are the spatial dimensions of the plane, and l is the DTCWT transformation level. 4. Masks (M^{AB}): Learnable scalar masks used to enforce sparsity. 5. Voxel Grid: A small 3D voxel representation indicating emptiness, used to skip points in empty regions. Formulas The 4D volume D is represented as the sum of three components: D = \sum{r=1}^{R1} M{rXY} \circ M{rZT} \circ v{r1} + \sum{r=1}^{R2} M{rXZ} \circ M{rYT} \circ v{r2} + \sum{r=1}^{R3} M{rYZ} \circ M{rXT} \circ v{r3} where R1, R2, R3 are the number of low-rank components, and R = R1 + R2 + R3 \ll N (spatial resolution). The plane-based representation M^{AB}r is recovered from the wavelet coefficients using the Inverse Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Transform (IDTCWT): M^{AB}r = \text{IDTCWT}\left([W^{AB}{a,r}, \{R\{W^{AB}{i,r}\}\}{i=1}^6, \{I\{W^{AB}{i,r}\}\}{i=1}^6]\right) To handle storage and sparsity, wavelet coefficients are masked: \tilde{W}^{AB} = \text{sg}\left(H(M^{AB}) - \text{sigmoid}(M^{AB})\right) \odot W^{AB} where \text{sg} is the stop-gradient operator, H is the Heaviside step function, and M^{AB} are the learned masks. For static scenes, the decomposition simplifies to a TensorRF-like form: D = \sum{r=1}^{R1} M^{XY}r \circ v^rZ \circ v^{r1} + \sum{r=1}^{R2} M^{XZ}r \circ v^rY \circ v^{r2} + \sum{r=1}^{R3} M^{YZ}r \circ v^rX \circ v^{r3} Numbered Steps 1. Decomposition: Decompose the 4D spatiotemporal volume D into the sum of three terms as defined in the volume formula above. 2. Reconstruction: For each pair of planes (e.g., XY and ZT), reconstruct the plane-based representation M^{AB}r from the approximation and directional wavelet coefficients using IDTCWT. 3. Feature Extraction: Extract feature vectors from the paired planes. Multiply these feature vectors element-wise. 4. Concatenation: Concatenate the multiplied results from all three terms into a single vector. 5. Feature Projection: Multiply the concatenated vector by V{RF}, a 2D tensor stacking all v{ri}, to compute density and appearance features. 6. Opacity Query: Query point opacities directly from the computed density features. 7. Color Regression: Regress RGB color values using a compact Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). The inputs to the MLP are the appearance features and the view directions. 8. Rendering: Synthesize final images via differentiable volumetric rendering along rays. 9. Optimization: Minimize the total loss function, which includes photometric loss, total variation regularization, and mask sparsity loss. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def darenerfforward(xyzt, viewdirs, params): """ Forward pass for DaReNeRF. xyzt: (N, 4) tensor of space-time coordinates [x, y, z, t] in NDC. viewdirs: (N, 3) tensor of view directions. params: Dictionary containing wavelet coefficients, vectors, masks, and MLP weights. """ # 1. Reconstruct planes from wavelet coefficients # For each term r in {1, 2, 3} and plane pairs (AB, CD) planes = {} for r in range(3): for pair in [('XY', 'ZT'), ('XZ', 'YT'), ('YZ', 'XT')]: planeabname, planecdname = pair # Apply mask to wavelet coefficients Wab = applymask(params['W' + planeabname + '' + str(r)], params['M' + planeabname]) Wcd = applymask(params['W' + planecdname + '' + str(r)], params['M' + planecdname]) # Reconstruct plane using IDTCWT Mab = idtcwt(Wab) Mcd = idtcwt(Wcd) planes[(r, planeabname)] = Mab planes[(r, planecdname)] = Mcd # 2. Compute features for each point densityfeatures = [] appearancefeatures = [] for r in range(3): # Get feature vectors for the two planes # Note: In implementation, this involves sampling Mab and Mcd at xyzt projections featab = sampleplane(planes[(r, 'AB')], xyzt[:,:2]) # Example: XY plane featcd = sampleplane(planes[(r, 'CD')], xyzt[:, 2:]) # Example: ZT plane # Element-wise multiplication prod = featab featcd # Concatenate results from all 3 terms # (Assuming prod is reshaped appropriately) densityfeatures.append(prod[:,:DENSITYDIM]) appearancefeatures.append(prod[:, APPEARANCESTART:APPEARANCEEND]) # Concatenate all terms alldensity = torch.cat(densityfeatures, dim=1) allappearance = torch.cat(appearancefeatures, dim=1) # Multiply by VRF (stacked vectors) # VRF shape: (TotalR FeatureSize, FeatureOut) finaldensity = torch.matmul(alldensity, params['VRFdensity']) finalappearance = torch.matmul(allappearance, params['VRFappearance']) # 3. Query Opacity opacity = sigmoid(finaldensity) # 4. Regress Color # MLP takes appearance features and view directions color = colormlp(finalappearance, viewdirs) return opacity, color def applymask(W, M): """Apply trainable mask to wavelet coefficients.""" # sg: stop-gradient, H: Heaviside, sigmoid: sigmoid function maskval = stopgradient(heaviside(M) - sigmoid(M)) return maskval W def idtcwt(coeffs): """Inverse Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Transform.""" # coeffs: [approx, realcoeffs6, imagcoeffs6] # Returns 2D plane representation pass Parameters F: Feature size, typically 3 (RGB). R: Total number of low-rank components (R = R1 + R2 + R3), where R \ll N. Spatial Grid Size: 512. Temporal Grid Size: 300. Batch Size: 4,096. Loss Weights: \lambda{reg} for total variation loss, \lambdam for mask sparsity loss. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Shift Variance: Traditional 2D DWT suffers from shift variance, where small shifts in input signal disrupt wavelet oscillation patterns, causing poor results in dynamic regions with motion or camera movement. DaReNeRF uses DTCWT to ensure shift invariance. Direction Ambiguity: Traditional 2D DWT has poor direction selectivity, producing a checkerboard pattern that blends representations from \pm 45^\circ, leading to ghosting artifacts around moving objects. DaReNeRF uses 6 real and 6 imaginary coefficients aligned to specific directions to eliminate this. Empty Regions: Large empty regions in dynamic scenes waste computation. DaReNeRF uses a small 3D voxel representation indicating emptiness by aggregating maximum opacities across time steps to skip these points. Memory Complexity: Reduced from O(N^3 T F) for direct 4D volume modeling to O(R N^2 T F) using the plane-based decomposition. Training Time: Achieves a twofold reduction in training time compared to prior work. Hardware: Trained on a single A100 GPU. Strengths: Eliminates checkerboard artifacts and shift variance issues of DWT; efficient memory usage for high-resolution dynamic scenes; handles complex motions well. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of mask sparsity; DTCWT implementation is more complex than standard DWT. When to Use: Novel view synthesis of dynamic scenes with complex motion where high fidelity and artifact reduction are critical. When Not to Use: Static scenes (simpler methods like TensorRF may suffice); real-time applications requiring extremely low latency without pre-training. DaReNeRF was introduced in the paper "DaReNeRF: Direction-aware Representation for Dynamic Scenes". It builds upon plane-based 4D volume decomposition methods and addresses limitations of 2D DWT-based representations. The method is used in DaReNeRF and DaReNeRF-S (sparse variant) for novel view synthesis on Plenoptic Video and D-NeRF datasets.
