name: Compression and Representation Efficiency
head: 3DGS Compression, Gaussian Pruning, Attribute Quantization
body: Compression and Representation Efficiency methods reduce the storage footprint and memory bandwidth requirements of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations without significantly degrading rendering quality. They address the inherent redundancy in the dense Gaussian fields produced by standard training, where many primitives overlap or contribute negligibly to the final image. Unlike Base 3DGS Optimization, which focuses on the training dynamics, these methods explicitly target the data structure of the scene representation, either by reducing the primitive count, quantizing attributes, or modeling dependencies between primitives. The core challenge in compressing 3D Gaussians is balancing the rate-distortion trade-off: minimizing the number of bits required to store the scene parameters while maintaining the visual fidelity of the rendered output. All methods in this family operate on the standard 3DGS attribute set for each Gaussian i: position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion), scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity \alphai \in [0, 1], and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}{i, lm}. The primary sources of redundancy are: 1. Spatial Redundancy: Multiple Gaussians covering the same surface area or volume. 2. Attribute Correlation: Similar scales, rotations, or colors among neighboring primitives. 3. Quantization Error: The use of high-precision floating-point numbers for attributes that do not require such precision for visual acceptance. General strategies include: Count Reduction: Pruning or merging Gaussians to decrease N. Attribute Quantization: Mapping continuous attributes to discrete codebooks. Dependency Modeling: Predicting attributes of one primitive from others. Mini-Splatting is a training optimization and initialization strategy that explicitly constrains the total number of Gaussians to a hard limit N{max} to reduce memory footprint and accelerate rendering. It addresses the inefficient spatial distribution of vanilla 3DGS—specifically "overlapping" and "under-reconstruction" phenomena—by pivoting from direct simplification to spatial reorganization. Unlike C3DGS, which focuses on voxel-based pruning, Mini-Splatting leverages both screen-space and world-space information to densify around objects and simplify redundant overlaps, achieving comparable or superior visual quality with significantly fewer primitives. C3DGS is a compression method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces storage requirements by applying residual vector quantization (R-VQ) to geometric attributes, specifically scaling and rotation. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Mini-Splatting by focusing on attribute quantization rather than count reduction via sampling. It achieves a scene size of 48.8 MB on the MipNeRF360 dataset. CompGS is a compression method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces data volume by introducing a hybrid primitive structure consisting of anchor primitives and coupled primitives. It solves the redundancy in standard 3DGS representations by using anchors to predict the attributes of coupled primitives, resulting in compact residual representations. Unlike sibling methods that primarily rely on count reduction or attribute quantization alone, CompGS explicitly models the dependency between primitives to minimize the bit rate while maintaining rendering quality. MMGS treats the compression of 3D Gaussians as an optimal transport problem, learning a compact set of summary Gaussians representing the original cloud under multi-view ranking constraints. The optimization minimizes the Wasserstein distance between the original and compressed sets. The constraint for Gaussian i is defined as: Ci = \sum{v \in V} \sum{u \in I} Mu^{(v)} \cdot I{\omega}^{(v)i,u} > \epsilonv where Ci is the constraint, V is views, I is pixels, M is mask/intensity, I is indicator, \omega is view, u is pixel, v is view, and \epsilon is threshold. The cost matrix is calculated as: \mathbf{C}{ij} = d{\mathbf{C}}^2(\mathbf{S}{src}, \mathbf{S}{tgt}) = \|\mui - \muj\|2^2 + \|\Sigmai^{1/2} - \Sigmaj^{1/2}\|F^2 where \mathbf{C}{ij} is the cost matrix, \mathbf{S}{src/tgt} are source/target sets, \mu is mean, \Sigma is covariance, and \|\cdot\|F is Frobenius norm. MMGS maintains rendering quality with only 10% primitives and 10× accelerated training speeds compared to 3DGS. The explosion in the number of Gaussians required for high-fidelity 3DGS reconstruction has led to significant storage and memory bandwidth challenges. Standard 3DGS scenes can contain millions of primitives, making real-time rendering on mobile devices or storage on disk inefficient. Early approaches focused on training-time optimizations to limit growth, such as Mini-Splatting, which introduced hard limits on primitive counts. Subsequent research shifted towards post-training compression techniques, such as attribute quantization (C3DGS) and hybrid dependency modeling (CompGS), to decouple storage size from rendering quality. The field continues to evolve with methods like MMGS that frame compression as an optimal transport problem to further reduce redundancy. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Mini-Splatting
head: Constrained Gaussian Representation, Hard-constrained 3DGS, Mixed Integer 3DGS, Representing Scenes with a Constrained Number of Gaussians
body: Mini-Splatting is a resource-efficient training and rendering method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that explicitly constrains the total number of Gaussians to a hard limit, addressing the spatial redundancy and inefficient distribution inherent in vanilla 3DGS. Unlike sibling methods like C3DGS which focus on voxel-based pruning or CompGS which relies on attribute quantization, Mini-Splatting pivots from direct simplification to spatial reorganization, leveraging both screen-space and world-space information to densify around objects and remove redundant overlaps. It achieves this by stacking densification and simplification passes to maintain a uniform spatial distribution, resulting in significantly reduced memory footprint and faster training times while maintaining comparable or superior visual fidelity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of initial 3D Gaussians derived from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points, along with a sequence of training images. Output: A constrained set of Gaussians with optimized position \mathbf{p}i, rotation \mathbf{q}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}{i, lm}. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard 3DGS attribute set for each Gaussian i: Position: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation: \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (normalized quaternion) Scale: \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity: \alphai \in [0, 1] SH Coefficients: \mathbf{c}{i, lm} Importance Score: Scalar value used for selection Parameters: Total Optimization Steps: 30,000. Densification Stop Iteration: 15,000. Simplification Iterations: 15,000 and 20,000. SH Level: Disabled (Degree 0) during densification; increased after simplification. Algorithm Steps: The optimization process is divided into densification and simplification phases, stacked to reorganize the spatial distribution of Gaussians. 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from SfM points. Set total optimization steps to 30,000. 2. Densification Phase (Iterations 1 to 15K): Blur Split: Detect blurring areas in the rendered image and split Gaussians located in those regions to increase local density. Note: View-dependent colors (SH coefficients) are disabled during this phase as they barely enhance densification and consume resources. Depth Reinitialization: Use merged depth points to reinitialize scene geometry and Gaussian positions. Calculate depth points from the mid-point of ray intersections with Gaussian ellipsoids. Reposition Gaussians based on these newly generated depth points to ensure geometric accuracy and avoid artifacts from alpha blending. Constraint: The total number of Gaussians is kept constant by pruning the least important Gaussians and splitting the most important ones. Importance is determined by an importance score calculation. 3. Simplification Phase (Iterations 15K and 20K): Intersection Preserving: Retain only Gaussians that have the maximal impact on the rendered image, discarding redundant overlaps. Sampling: Sample points to preserve both the underlying geometric structure and the original rendering quality, reducing complexity. SH Update: Increase the SH level (enable view-dependent colors) after simplification (at iteration 15K). 4. Final Optimization: Continue optimization until the total step count with the constrained set. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def minisplattingtraining(initialgaussians, images, Nmax, Ttotal=30000): """ Implements the Mini-Splatting optimization pipeline. """ gaussians = initialgaussians gaussians.shdegree = 0 # Disable SH during densification for t in range(1, Ttotal + 1): # Standard optimization step image = samplerandomimage(images) renderedimage, depthmap, gaussianindices = rendergaussians(gaussians, image.camera) loss = computeloss(renderedimage, image.gt) gradients = computegradients(loss, gaussians) updategaussians(gaussians, gradients) if t <= 15000: # Densification Phase # Blur Split: Detect blurring areas and split Gaussians # Compute blur mask from rendered image gradients blurmask = computeblurmask(renderedimage) splitcandidates = [g for g in gaussians if g.id in blurmask] for g in splitcandidates: # Split high-importance Gaussians in blurred regions splitgaussian(g) # Depth Reinitialization: Reposition based on depth mid-points # Calculate mid-point of ray intersection with Gaussian ellipsoids depthpoints = computedepthmidpoints(gaussians, image.camera) # Reposition Gaussians based on newly generated depth points repositiongaussians(gaussians, depthpoints) # Maintain Nmax: Prune least important, split most important # Keep total count constant at Nmax gaussians = maintaincount(gaussians, Nmax) elif t in [15000, 20000]: # Simplification Phase # Intersection Preserving: Retain maximal impact Gaussians # Compute rendering impact for each Gaussian impactscores = computerenderingimpact(gaussians, images) # Retain Gaussians with maximal impact gaussians = retaintopimpact(gaussians, impactscores, Nmax) # Sampling: Preserve geometric structure # Sample points to preserve geometric structure and rendering quality gaussians = samplegaussians(gaussians, Nmax) # Enable SH after simplification gaussians.shdegree = 1 return gaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Popping Artifacts: Using fewer Gaussians results in larger Gaussians on average, which increases the prevalence of noticeable popping artifacts. Depth Estimation: Depth reinitialization relies on initial training to estimate depth, requiring a few iterations to obtain accurate information. A quality-prioritized variant of Mini-Splatting that omits the simplification process to maximize rendering quality. It retains the densification phase (Blur Split and Depth Reinitialization) but skips the Intersection Preserving and Sampling steps. This results in a higher Gaussian count (~4.69M vs ~0.49M for standard Mini-Splatting) but achieves superior SSIM and LPIPS metrics, surpassing Zip-NeRF on Mip-NeRF360 Outdoor. A storage-compression variant designed for scenarios requiring reduced file size. It is based on the Mini-Splatting pipeline but applies transform coding and standard zip compression to attributes (scales, SH coefficients) after training, storing only Gaussian centers as float32. Memory Footprint: Significantly reduced. On Mip-NeRF360 (Outdoor), Mini-Splatting uses 0.49M Gaussians compared to 3.36M for vanilla 3DGS, a ~7x reduction. Mini-Splatting-D takes 31m48s. Rendering Speed: Higher FPS. 410 FPS vs 98 FPS for 3DGS on Mip-NeRF360 (Outdoor). Mini-Splatting-D achieves 83 FPS. Visual Quality: Comparable or superior. On MipNeRF360 generally, Mini-Splatting achieves SSIM 0.763, PSNR 25.83, LPIPS 0.273, with a model size of 18.2 MB. Scaling: The method scales well to resource-constrained environments, enabling training on consumer-grade GPUs (e.g., GTX 1060 6G). Limitations: The hard constraint on Gaussian count may lead to larger average Gaussian sizes, increasing popping artifacts. The method requires careful tuning of the densification/simplification schedule. Mini-Splatting was introduced by Guangchi Fang and Bing Wang from the Spatial Intelligence Group at The Hong Kong Polytechnic University. The method addresses the "overlapping" and "under-reconstruction" phenomena observed in vanilla 3DGS, where Gaussians are not uniformly distributed around object surfaces. name: Model Compression Pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: 3DGS Model Compression Pipeline, Edge-deployment compression, LightGaussian-derived compression, Compressed 3D Gaussian Splatting Pipeline, Compressed 3DGS, Compressed 3DGS Model, Hardware-oriented 3DGS
body: This method is a compression and rendering pipeline for 3D Gaussians that reduces memory footprint and increases rendering speed while maintaining image quality. It is designed for hardware-oriented 3DGS deployment, specifically targeting edge devices with low-power budgets. It sets itself apart from its parent Mini-Splatting by not imposing a hard limit on Gaussian count via mixed-integer optimization, but rather by iteratively pruning, reducing spherical harmonics (SH) degree, and quantizing attributes to achieve high compression ratios (up to 51.6×) suitable for streaming and mobile VR/AR. It differs from 3DGS Model Compression Pipeline primarily in the specific hardware-targeted modifications (iterative pruning, progressive SH reduction, full VQ) derived from LightGaussian to achieve higher compression, and from SUNDAE and FCGS by relying on iterative fine-tuning and quantization rather than neural compensation or autoencoder-based feed-forward compression. The pipeline consists of four main stages: Sensitivity Calculation, Clustering, QA Fine-tuning, and Encoding. It modifies the LightGaussian pipeline by introducing iterative pruning with intermediate fine-tuning, progressive SH-degree reduction via iterative distillation, and vector quantization (VQ) applied to all SH coefficients and colors. Input: Optimized 3D Gaussian Splatting model (positions, covariances, opacities, SH coefficients, colors). Output: Compressed representation consisting of Gaussian positions, codebook indices for shape/SH/colors, and encoded data. The compressed representation stores: 1. Positions: 3D coordinates of Gaussian centers. 2. Codebook Indices: Indices pointing to pre-defined codebooks for: Color: All SH coefficients. Shape: Gaussian parameters (scale, rotation). Opacity: (Implied by standard 3DGS, though specific codebook details for opacity are not explicitly detailed in the provided notes, it is part of the compressed attributes). 3. Scaling Factor: \eta. Memory consumption is dominated by the coordinates of 3D Gaussian center points and the codebook indices. The amount of memory required by the color codebook varies significantly between scenes. 1. Sensitivity Calculation: Calculate sensitivity thresholds \betac and \betag for SH coefficients and shape parameters to decide which attributes are considered for clustering. These thresholds offer a trade-off between quality and compression rate. 2. Iterative Pruning with Intermediate Fine-tuning: Instead of aggressive single-step pruning, the model is pruned progressively. Fine-tuning is inserted between pruning stages to recover visual quality. This reduces the Gaussian count to the level required by hardware constraints. 3. Progressive SH-Degree Reduction via Iterative Distillation: Instead of lowering SH degree in one step, the representation is distilled progressively. This reduces bytes per Gaussian point with a smoother quality-compression tradeoff. 4. Clustering and Vector Quantization (VQ): SH coefficients and shape parameters are compressed into codebooks of predefined sizes. VQ is applied to all SH coefficients and colors, not just low-salience subsets. Clustering Update Step: For normalized covariance matrices \hat{\Sigma}i with \|si\|2 = 1 and weighting factors wi, the centroid \hat{\Sigma}c is calculated as: \hat{\Sigma}c = \frac{\sum{i=1}^N wi \hat{\Sigma}i}{\sum{i=1}^N wi} The normalization is preserved as: \|sc\|2^2 = \text{Tr}(\hat{\Sigma}c) = \frac{\sum{i=1}^N wi \text{Tr}(\hat{\Sigma}i)}{\sum{i=1}^N wi} = \frac{\sum{i=1}^N wi \|si\|2^2}{\sum{i=1}^N wi} This proves that the centroid remains normalized if the inputs are normalized and weights are positive. 5. QA Fine-tuning: Quantization-aware fine-tuning is applied to regain information lost during quantization. This stage takes up 70% of the total compression pipeline time. 6. Encoding: Entropy and run-length encoding are applied. Morton order layout is used to save additional memory. Codebook Sizes: Predefined sizes for SH coefficients and Gaussian shape parameters. Larger codebooks reduce maximum error with minimal memory overhead. Sensitivity Thresholds: \betac and \betag. Compression Runtime: Approximately 5-6 minutes. Reconstruction Time Increase: Roughly 10%. Position Compression: Aggressive compression of positions introduces significant error and is currently not supported in this pipeline. Quality Drop: Directly increasing compression ratio without iterative methods leads to noticeable PSNR degradation and visible detail loss. Color Shift: Subtle color shifts may occur, mainly below human perception thresholds, but can be visible in side-by-side inspection. Unverified code. Returns: Compressed model with positions, codebookindices, and encoding metadata. """ # Step 1: Sensitivity Calculation betac = calculatesensitivity(model.shcoeffs) betag = calculatesensitivity(model.shapeparams) # Step 2 & 3: Iterative Pruning and Progressive SH Reduction # Note: The exact iterative loop structure is not fully detailed in sources, # but involves alternating pruning and fine-tuning. currentmodel = model for stage in iterativepruningstages: # Prune Gaussians based on importance currentmodel = prunegaussians(currentmodel, stage.threshold) # Distill SH degree progressively currentmodel = distillshdegree(currentmodel, stage.newdegree) # Intermediate Fine-tuning to recover quality currentmodel = qafinetune(currentmodel, stage.iterations) # Step 4: Clustering and VQ # Calculate centroids for shape and color codebooks shapecodebook = clusterattributes(currentmodel.shapeparams, betag) colorcodebook = clusterattributes(currentmodel.shcoeffs, betac) # Assign indices currentmodel.shapeindices = findnearestcodebook(shapecodebook, currentmodel.shapeparams) currentmodel.colorindices = findnearestcodebook(colorcodebook, currentmodel.shcoeffs) # Step 5: QA Fine-tuning (Post-Quantization) # This stage is critical and time-consuming (70% of total time) currentmodel = qafinetune(currentmodel, iterations=high) # Step 6: Encoding # Apply Morton order to positions for spatial locality sortedindices = mortonorder(currentmodel.positions) sortedpositions = currentmodel.positions[sortedindices] sortedshapeindices = currentmodel.shapeindices[sortedindices] sortedcolorindices = currentmodel.colorindices[sortedindices] # Apply Entropy and Run-Length Encoding encodedpositions = entropyencode(runlengthencode(sortedpositions)) encodedshapeindices = entropyencode(runlengthencode(sortedshapeindices)) encodedcolorindices = entropyencode(runlengthencode(sortedcolorindices)) return { 'positions': sortedpositions, 'shapeindices': sortedshapeindices, 'colorindices': sortedcolorindices, 'shapecodebook': shapecodebook, 'colorcodebook': colorcodebook, 'encodingmetadata': { 'entropycodes': { 'positions': encodedpositions, 'shape': encodedshapeindices, 'color': encodedcolorindices } } } def calculatesensitivity(attributes): """ Calculate sensitivity threshold for clustering. Returns a threshold value beta. """ # Implementation details for pruning logic are not fully provided. # Placeholder: Remove Gaussians based on opacity and contribution to loss. return model def distillshdegree(model, newdegree): """ Reduce SH degree from current to newdegree via distillation. """ # Implementation details for distillation are not fully provided. # Placeholder: Train higher degree SH to predict lower degree SH. return model def qafinetune(model, iterations): """ Fine-tune model with quantization-aware training. """ # Implementation details for fine-tuning loop are not fully provided. # Placeholder: Standard optimization loop with quantization noise injection. return model def clusterattributes(attributes, beta): """ Cluster attributes into codebooks. """ # Implementation details for clustering algorithm (e.g., K-Means) are not fully provided. # Placeholder: K-Means clustering on attributes. return codebook def findnearestcodebook(codebook, attributes): """ Find nearest index in codebook for each attribute. """ # Implementation details for nearest neighbor search are not fully provided. # Placeholder: Euclidean distance search. return indices def mortonorder(positions): """ Sort indices based on Morton order of positions. """ # Implementation details for Morton code are not fully provided. # Placeholder: Convert 3D coordinates to Morton codes and sort. return sortedindices def entropyencode(data): """ Apply entropy encoding. """ # Implementation details for entropy coding are not fully provided. # Placeholder: Huffman or Arithmetic coding. return encodeddata def runlengthencode(data): """ Apply run-length encoding. """ # Implementation details for RLE are not fully provided. # Placeholder: Standard RLE. return encodeddata A compression scheme tailored for hardware deployment that reduces model size and bandwidth by iteratively pruning Gaussians, reducing spherical harmonics (SH) degree, and quantizing attributes. It modifies LightGaussian to achieve higher compression ratios (51.6× vs 15×) by adding iterative pruning, progressive SH reduction, and full VQ on all coefficients/colors. SUNDAE is a graph-based compression method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces computational load by pruning redundant Gaussians while preserving key scene details. It distinguishes itself from direct splatting by shifting to feature splatting, utilizing a neural compensation head to interpolate features and recover fine details lost during pruning. FCGS is an optimization-free, feed-forward compression pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that compresses representations in a single pass without per-scene finetuning, aiming to reduce compression time from minutes to seconds while maintaining fidelity. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Model Compression Pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting and 3DGS Model Compression Pipeline by eliminating the need for iterative per-scene optimization, which typically takes 10–28 minutes, by using an autoencoder-based structure with a Multi-path Entropy Module (MEM) to balance compression size and fidelity. A factorization-based compression technique that employs matrix and tensor factorization to represent high-dimensional Gaussian parameters using a limited number of basis components per axis. It factorizes attributes such as color, scale, and rotation to substantially reduce storage requirements while preserving essential visual attributes. Compression Ratio: Up to 31× or 51.6× compared to baseline, with a PSNR drop of 0.743 dB on average across datasets. Rendering Speedup: Up to 4× increase in rendering speed. Roughly 2× of this is attributed to reduced bandwidth requirements. Memory Footprint: Dominated by position coordinates and codebook indices. Compression Time: Approximately 5-6 minutes. The fine-tuning stage takes up 70% of this time. Reconstruction Time: Increases by roughly 10%. Power Consumption: 0.219 W at 1080p@129 FPS. Throughput: 267.5 Mpixels/s. Hardware Suitability: Suitable for mobile VR/AR applications and games due to network streaming capability and low-power device rendering. Effective on both low- and high-end GPUs. Performance Examples (1080p): NVIDIA RTX A5000: Compressed 321 FPS (Bicycle), 184/414/502 FPS (Bonsai). NVIDIA RTX 3070M: Compressed 211 FPS (Bicycle), 122/296/380 FPS (Bonsai). Intel UHD Graphics 11: Compressed 23 FPS (Bicycle), 28/28/28 FPS (Bonsai). AMD Radeon R9 380: Compressed 76 FPS (Bicycle), 76/128/128 FPS (Bonsai). Limitations: Cannot aggressively compress position information without significant error. Subtle color shifts may be visible under close inspection. The method is derived from LightGaussian, which combines Gaussian pruning and fine-tuning, SH distillation, VQ for SH coefficients and colors, and FP16 quantization. The specific pipeline described in and was developed to address the insufficiency of LightGaussian's compression ratio for edge deployment targets (full-HD rendering at 120 FPS per eye under a sub-0.5 W power budget). It was introduced in the paper "Compressed 3D Gaussian Splatting for Accelerated Novel View Synthesis" and further optimized for hardware acceleration in "A 129 FPS Full HD Real-Time Accelerator for 3D Gaussian Splatting". name: 3DGS Model Compression Pipeline
head: Hardware-Friendly Compression, Iterative Pruning & VQ Compression
body: A compression scheme tailored for hardware deployment that reduces model size and bandwidth by iteratively pruning Gaussians, reducing spherical harmonics (SH) degree, and quantizing attributes. It modifies LightGaussian to achieve higher compression ratios (51.6× vs 15×) by adding iterative pruning, progressive SH reduction, and full VQ on all coefficients/colors. Inputs: Pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting model containing Gaussians with positions, covariances, opacities, colors, and SH coefficients. Outputs: Compressed model with reduced Gaussian count, lower SH degree, and quantized attributes. Data Structures: Gaussian Set: List of N Gaussians, each storing mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (or rotation/scale), opacity \alphai \in [0, 1], color ci, and SH coefficients. SH Coefficients: Vectors of coefficients per RGB channel. Steps: 1. Iterative Gaussian Pruning: Remove Gaussians contributing least to visual fidelity iteratively until a target compression ratio or sparsity level is reached. 2. Progressive Spherical Harmonics (SH) Degree Reduction: Reduce the SH degree encoding color and directional information to decrease coefficients per Gaussian. 3. Vector Quantization (VQ): Apply VQ to all SH coefficients and colors, clustering them into a codebook and replacing values with indices. Parameters: Target Compression Ratio: 51.6× model-size reduction. PSNR Loss: 0.743 dB. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: View-Dependent Culling: Approximately 42% of Gaussians are unnecessary via near-plane culling, but this benefit is view-dependent and decreases when zooming out. Alpha-Blending Contribution: Only about 50% of Gaussians contribute to pixel color during \alpha-blending, making culling and pruning critical for performance. A storage-compression variant applying transform coding, quantization, and entropy encoding to pre-trained attributes for minimal footprint. Sets it apart by optimizing for storage efficiency over rendering quality compared to Mini-Splatting-D. Choose when minimal model footprint is required. A post-training method combining adaptive voxelization and GPCC to reduce size and bandwidth without generative retraining costs. Sets it apart by achieving higher quality at lower bitrates than siblings like Mini-Splatting-C. Choose for bitrate-efficient deployment. A top-down iterative pruning algorithm guaranteeing a precise target splat count. Sets it apart from bottom-up growth approaches by solving unpredictable model size issues. Choose when exact splat counts are required. Compression Ratio: 51.6× model-size reduction. Quality Loss: 0.743 dB PSNR loss. Comparison: Modifies LightGaussian (15× reduction) by adding iterative pruning, progressive SH reduction, and full VQ on all coefficients/colors to reach 51.6×. Hardware Efficiency: Enables a hardware accelerator delivering 1219 Mpixels/J at 267.5 Mpixels/s, rendering 1080p at 129 FPS. Memory Usage: Mitigates the gigabyte-range storage requirements of unbounded 360° scenes containing millions of Gaussians. The 3DGS algorithm is not hardware-friendly and faces substantial memory usage challenges due to millions of Gaussians in unbounded scenes. To enable real-time rendering on portable AR/VR devices at full-HD resolution and 120 FPS per eye, a dedicated hardware accelerator was introduced. This compression pipeline is a core component, modifying the LightGaussian lightweight model to achieve higher compression ratios for hardware deployment. name: Mini-Splatting-C
head: Ours+PP, Post-processed Compact 3D Gaussian
body: Mini-Splatting-C is a storage-compression variant of the Mini-Splatting representation designed for scenarios requiring minimal model size. It addresses the problem of high storage overhead in 3D Gaussian Splatting by applying post-processing compression techniques to the attributes of a pre-trained Mini-Splatting model. Unlike its sibling Hybrid Compression Framework which may involve different architectural decouplings, or Prune2TargetSize which focuses on iterative pruning targets, Mini-Splatting-C relies on the optimized and simplified Gaussian representation of Mini-Splatting combined with standard lossless/lossy coding techniques. It sets itself apart by achieving significantly smaller file sizes (e.g., 0.04x of standard 3DGS) while maintaining competitive rendering quality, primarily through transform coding and quantization of non-position attributes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained Mini-Splatting model consisting of 3D Gaussian parameters: centers (\mathbf{c}), scales (\mathbf{s}), rotations (\mathbf{q}), opacities (\alpha), spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients (\mathbf{c}{SH}), and potentially hash grid parameters if using a neural field variant. Output: A compressed binary file containing the encoded attributes. Data Structures and Layout: The method does not alter the logical structure of the Gaussian attributes but changes their storage precision and encoding. 1. Centers: Stored as float32 (32-bit floating point). 2. Other Attributes (Scales, SH, Opacity, Hash Parameters): Processed via transform coding and quantization. 3. Encoding: The result is compressed using standard zip compression or specific entropy coding like Huffman encoding. Steps: 1. Train Pre-trained Model: Obtain a trained Mini-Splatting model. 2. Store Centers: Encode Gaussian centers as float32 values. 3. Transform Coding: Apply transform coding to non-center attributes (scales, SH coefficients). Note: specifies applying 8-bit min-max quantization to opacity and hash grid parameters instead of or in addition to transform coding for those specific attributes. 4. Pruning (Optional/Variant): In the "Ours+PP" variant, prune hash grid parameters with values below a threshold (e.g., 0.1). 5. Quantization: Apply 8-bit min-max quantization to opacity and hash grid parameters. 6. Entropy Coding: Apply Huffman encoding to the quantized opacity, hash parameters, and Residual Vector Quantization (R-VQ) indices. 7. Final Compression: Apply standard zip compression to the resulting bitstream. Formulas and Parameters: Min-Max Quantization: For an attribute value x with min x{min} and max x{max}, the quantized value q is: q = \text{clip}\left( \text{round}\left( \frac{x - x{min}}{x{max} - x{min}} \times 255 \right), 0, 255 \right) Pruning Threshold: Hash grid parameters h are removed if |h| < 0.1. Precision: Centers are float32; Opacity/Hash are uint8 (8-bit). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compressminisplattingc(model): """ Compress a Mini-Splatting model using Mini-Splatting-C (Ours+PP) pipeline. model: Object containing attributes: centers: array of float32 scales: array of float32 shcoeffs: array of float32 opacities: array of float32 hashparams: array of float32 (if applicable) Returns: bytes (compressed data) """ # Step 1: Store centers as float32 centersbytes = model.centers.tobytes() # Assuming float32 native layout # Step 2: Process other attributes # Apply transform coding to scales and SH coefficients # Note: Exact transform coding algorithm from [6] is not detailed in sources. # We assume a placeholder function that returns compressed bytes. scalestransformed = transformcoding(model.scales) shtransformed = transformcoding(model.shcoeffs) # Step 3: Handle Opacity and Hash Parameters # Apply 8-bit min-max quantization opacitiesquantized = minmaxquantize(model.opacities, bits=8) # Prune hash grid parameters below 0.1 hashparamspruned = prunevalues(model.hashparams, threshold=0.1) hashparamsquantized = minmaxquantize(hashparamspruned, bits=8) # Step 4: Entropy Coding # Apply Huffman encoding to quantized opacity and hash parameters, and R-VQ indices # Note: R-VQ indices are not explicitly present in the base Mini-Splatting-C description, # but are mentioned in for the Ours+PP variant. We assume they are generated or present. opacityhuffman = huffmanencode(opacitiesquantized) hashhuffman = huffmanencode(hashparamsquantized) rvqhuffman = huffmanencode(model.rvqindices) # # Step 5: Combine and Compress # Concatenate all byte streams combineddata = ( centersbytes + scalestransformed + shtransformed + opacityhuffman + hashhuffman + rvqhuffman) # Apply standard zip compression compresseddata = zipcompress(combineddata) return compresseddata def minmaxquantize(values, bits=8): """Quantize float array to uint8 using min-max scaling.""" minval = np.min(values) maxval = np.max(values) if maxval == minval: return np.zeroslike(values, dtype=np.uint8) normalized = (values - minval) / (maxval - minval) quantized = np.clip(np.round(normalized (2bits - 1)), 0, 2bits - 1) return quantized.astype(np.uint8) def prunevalues(values, threshold=0.1): """Remove values with absolute magnitude below threshold.""" return values[np.abs(values) >= threshold] def transformcoding(values): """Placeholder for transform coding [6].""" # Not given in the sources. # In practice, this might involve DCT or wavelet transforms followed by quantization. # Since the exact method is not provided, we return the raw bytes as a fallback # or assume the source paper [6] provides the specific algorithm. # For implementation completeness based on available text: return values.tobytes() def huffmanencode(data): """Placeholder for Huffman encoding.""" # Not given in the sources. Standard Huffman coding algorithm. # Returns bytes. return data.tobytes() # Placeholder def zipcompress(data): """Placeholder for standard zip compression.""" # Returns bytes. return data # Placeholder Feed-Forward 3DGS Compression (FCGS) is a post-training compression method that reduces the storage size of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models generated by feed-forward reconstruction networks without requiring retraining or optimization. Unlike Mini-Splatting-C which is based on the Mini-Splatting architecture, FCGS applies a learned entropy model directly to the existing Gaussian attributes, enabling zero-shot generalization to scenes where ground-truth geometry is unavailable. It sets itself apart by handling the irregular data structures of feed-forward outputs (e.g., from LGM or MVSplat) where traditional mesh-based or optimization-based codecs fail due to the lack of a consistent reference. MesonGS employs universal Gaussian pruning by evaluating the importance of Gaussians through forward propagation, considering both view-dependent and view-independent features. It transforms rotation quaternions into Euler angles to reduce storage requirements and applies region adaptive hierarchical transform (RAHT) to reduce entropy in key attributes. Block quantization is performed on attribute channels by dividing them into multiple blocks and performing quantization for each block individually, using vector quantization for compressing less important attributes. Geometry is compressed using an octree, and all elements are packed with the LZ77 codec. A finetune scheme is implemented post-training to restore quality. This variant refers to a post-processing compression pipeline applied to the HyRF representation to reduce model size while maintaining rendering quality, compatible with existing 3DGS compression approaches. It stores point positions as half-precision tensors, applies residual vector quantization (R-VQ) and Huffman encoding to explicit Gaussian properties, and employs Huffman encoding with 8-bit min-max quantization for the hash table. It outperforms five state-of-the-art 3DGS compression methods in both model size and rendering quality, maintaining superior visual fidelity even after aggressive compression where conventional methods sacrifice quality for storage efficiency. Storage Size: Mini-Splatting-C (Ours+PP) achieves 2.67 MB storage on the NeRF-Synthetic dataset, which is 0.04x the size of standard 3DGS. The base Mini-Splatting model (Ours) is 5.55 MB (0.08x). Rendering Quality: On NeRF-Synthetic, Ours+PP achieves 32.88 PSNR, a slight drop from the base Ours' 33.33 PSNR. Performance: Rendering speed is 545 FPS on the tested hardware, which is 1.52x faster than the base Ours (359 FPS). Training Time: The post-processing step adds minimal overhead; Ours+PP training time is 8m 04s vs 6m 14s for Ours. Strengths: Extremely low storage footprint; fast rendering due to reduced data size; compatible with standard compression tools (zip, Huffman). Limitations: Slight reduction in PSNR compared to uncompressed Mini-Splatting; relies on the quality of the pre-trained Mini-Splatting model. When to Use: When storage bandwidth or disk space is the primary constraint, and a slight quality trade-off is acceptable. When Not to Use: When maximum possible visual fidelity is required without any compression artifacts. Mini-Splatting-C was introduced as part of the Mini-Splatting framework, which aims to represent scenes with a constrained number of Gaussians. The "C" variant specifically targets storage compression scenarios. It builds on the Mini-Splatting representation, which itself is a variant of 3D Gaussian Splatting. The post-processing techniques (transform coding, quantization) are adapted from general image/video compression standards. The method demonstrates superior performance compared to other methods primarily tailored for storage compression applied to standard 3DGS. name: Feed-Forward 3DGS Compression
head: Compression of Feed-Forward 3DGS, Zero-shot Compression
body: Feed-Forward 3DGS Compression (FCGS) is a post-training compression method that reduces the storage size of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models generated by feed-forward reconstruction networks without requiring retraining or optimization. It applies a learned entropy model directly to existing Gaussian attributes, enabling zero-shot generalization to scenes where ground-truth geometry is unavailable. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained 3DGS model generated by a feed-forward model (e.g., MVSplat, LGM). Output: A compressed bitstream representing the Gaussian attributes. Data Structures: The 3DGS model consists of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is defined by position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion), scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity \alphai \in \mathbb{R}, and color coefficients \mathbf{c}i (Spherical Harmonics). Method Steps: 1. Attribute Extraction: Extract all Gaussian attributes from the feed-forward model. For LGM, generate the remaining 3 views from an initial 1 view using (Wang & Shi, 2023), then input all 4 views into LGM for 3DGS creation. 2. Masking for Feed-Forward Models: When compressing 3DGS from feed-forward models, set the mask m to all 0s for color attributes. 3. Entropy Model Application: Apply the Memory-Efficient Memory (MEM) module and context models to compress the remaining attributes (position, rotation, scale, opacity). The MEM module adaptively selects attributes, but color is bypassed due to the mask. 4. Bitstream Generation: Encode the quantized and context-predicted attributes into a bitstream using an entropy coder. Parameters: Mask m: For feed-forward 3DGS, m = 0 for all color attributes. Compression Ratio: Achieves 15× compression for MVSplat-generated 3DGS and 5× for LGM-generated 3DGS. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Ground Truth: For feed-forward models, ground-truth geometry is unavailable, so fidelity is evaluated by measuring the similarity of images rendered from the 3DGS before and after compression. Zero-Shot Generalization: The method generalizes without retraining, requiring robust entropy models that do not overfit to specific scene distributions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compressfeedforward3dgs(gaussians): # Step 1: Extract attributes positions = [g.position for g in gaussians] rotations = [g.rotation for g in gaussians] scales = [g.scale for g in gaussians] opacities = [g.opacity for g in gaussians] colors = [g.color for g in gaussians] # Step 2: Set mask for color attributes to 0 for feed-forward models colormask = [0] len(gaussians) # Step 3: Quantize non-color attributes qpositions = [round(p, 6) for p in positions] qrotations = [round(r, 6) for r in rotations] qscales = [round(s, 6) for s in scales] qopacities = [round(o, 6) for o in opacities] # Step 4: Context modeling and entropy coding (specific models not provided) # MEM module adaptively selects attributes, but color is masked out bitstreampos = arithmeticencode(qpositions) bitstreamrot = arithmeticencode(qrotations) bitstreamscale = arithmeticencode(qscales) bitstreamopacity = arithmeticencode(qopacities) # Color attributes are not compressed in the standard way for feed-forward models bitstreamcolor = None # Combine bitstreams bitstream = bitstreampos + bitstreamrot + bitstreamscale + bitstreamopacity return bitstream def arithmeticencode(data): # Standard arithmetic coding implementation return bytes(data) FeCoSplat is a two-stage feature compression framework for feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that decouples compression into multi-view feature coding and reconstruction-conditioned feedback coding. It allows the receiver to decode directly in the compact feature-state domain without reconstructing intermediate Gaussians, thereby avoiding the heavy computational overhead of image compression and the irregularity challenges of explicit Gaussian compression. Unlike CodecSplat which uses a single coding stage, FeCoSplat uses rendered reconstruction feedback to guide a second-stage refinement, maintaining an implicit Gaussian state for lightweight receiver-side decoding. Compression Ratios: Achieves 15× compression for MVSplat-generated 3DGS and 5× for LGM-generated 3DGS. Performance: Excellent rate-distortion (RD) performance despite the lack of optimization. Hardware/Resolution: Evaluated on 10 scenes from ACID and 50 scenes from Gobjaverse. Strengths: Zero-shot generalization, no retraining required, handles feed-forward models with no ground truth. Limitations: Color attributes use mask m=0, potentially affecting visual fidelity. FCGS was published at ICLR 2025. It addresses the need for efficient compression of 3DGS models generated by feed-forward networks, which are increasingly popular for rapid 3D reconstruction. Fast Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2410.08017, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: FeCoSplat
head: Feedback-Guided Compression for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: FeCoSplat is a two-stage feature compression framework for feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting that decouples compression into multi-view feature coding and reconstruction-conditioned feedback coding. It allows the receiver to decode directly in the compact feature-state domain without reconstructing intermediate Gaussians, thereby avoiding the heavy computational overhead of image compression and the irregularity challenges of explicit Gaussian compression. Unlike CodecSplat which uses a single coding stage, FeCoSplat uses rendered reconstruction feedback to guide a second-stage refinement, maintaining an implicit Gaussian state for lightweight receiver-side decoding. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: N posed images I = \{Ii\}{i=1}^N and their camera poses P = \{Pi\}{i=1}^N. Outputs: Three bitstreams: B1 (first-stage features), B2 (second-stage feedback features), and B{cam} (lossless camera parameters). Data Structures: Multi-view Features (F1, F2): Tensors of shape \mathbb{R}^{N \times C \times \frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4}}, where N is the number of views, C is channels, and H, W are input image dimensions. Implicit Gaussian State (S): Learnable tensor initialized as S0 \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times C \times 1 \times 1}, broadcast to match spatial/view dimensions of F during concatenation. Latents (y, \hat{y}): Compact latent representations resulting from the transformation of features and state. Hyper-latents (\hat{z}): Side information for entropy modeling. Modules: E{mv} (Multi-view Feature Extractor): Consists of a monocular transformer, multi-view transformer, and cross-view U-Net. E{fb} (Feedback Feature Extractor): Applies PixelUnshuffle and extracts low-resolution features from concatenated original and rendered images. ga (Analysis Transform): Transforms concatenated features and state into compact latents. gs (Synthesis Transform): Transforms decoded latents back to feature space. U (State Update Module): Updates the implicit Gaussian state using decoded latents. P (Gaussian Predictor): Maps the implicit state to explicit 3D Gaussian primitives. \phi (Modulation Network): Predicts AdaLN parameters from the rate-distortion trade-off parameter \lambda. Numbered Steps: 1. Stage 1: Multi-view Feature Coding 1. Extract multi-view features F1 from input images I and poses P using E{mv}: F1 = E{mv}(I, P) 2. Concatenate F1 with the initial implicit Gaussian state S0 (broadcasted to match F1's dimensions) and transform into compact latent y1: y1 = ga(\text{concat}(F1, S0)) 3. Quantization: During training, perturb y1 with additive uniform noise to approximate quantization, yielding \hat{y}1. During inference, replace noise with a Round operation. 4. Entropy Modeling: Model the hyper-latent \hat{z}1 with a factorized prior. Use a quadtree entropy model to predict Gaussian distribution parameters over \hat{y}1 conditioned on \hat{z}1. Calculate the rate: R1 = R(\hat{y}1) + R(\hat{z}1) 5. Encode quantized latents into the first-stage bitstream B1. At the receiver, recover \hat{y}1 by entropy decoding B1. 6. State Update: Transform \hat{y}1 via synthesis transform gs and incorporate into S0 using state update module U: S1 = U(\text{concat}(S0, gs(\hat{y}1))) 7. Intermediate Gaussian Prediction: Predict intermediate Gaussians G1 from S1 using Gaussian predictor P: G1 = P(S1) P operates on a low-resolution 2D feature grid. It predicts per-view depth maps from S1, back-projects features to 3D, uses KNN attention for geometry-aware aggregation, estimates attributes, and rearranges via PixelShuffle to produce pixel-aligned 3D Gaussians at half input resolution (one Gaussian per 2 \times 2 region). 2. Stage 2: Feedback-Guided Feature Coding 1. Feedback Generation (Sender Only): Render G1 back to input viewpoints using camera parameters P to get rendered observations \hat{I}1: \hat{I}1 = \text{Render}(G1, P) 2. Extract feedback features F2 using E{fb} by concatenating original images I and rendered observations \hat{I}1: F2 = E{fb}(\text{concat}(I, \hat{I}1)) E{fb} applies PixelUnshuffle and extracts low-resolution features. 3. Transform F2 and current state S1 into latent y2: y2 = ga(\text{concat}(F2, S1)) 4. Quantization and Entropy Modeling: Quantize and model y2 and hyper-latent \hat{z}2 using the same scheme as Stage 1 to obtain rate R2. Encode into second-stage bitstream B2. 5. Receiver Decoding: Decode \hat{y}2 from B2. Integrate into S1 using shared state update module U: S2 = U(\text{concat}(S1, gs(\hat{y}2))) 6. Final Gaussian Prediction: Predict final Gaussians G2 from S2 using shared Gaussian predictor P: G2 = P(S2) 3. Variable-Rate Coding Condition each 2D block on the rate-distortion trade-off parameter \lambda using Adaptive Layer Normalization (AdaLN). Predict modulation parameters \gamma and \beta from \lambda using lightweight network \phi: (\gamma, \beta) = \phi(\log \lambda) Modulate normalized feature X: \text{AdaLN}(X, \lambda) = \gamma \odot \text{LN}(X) + \beta \lambda is sampled from a log-uniform distribution during training: [10^{-5}, 10^{-2}] for RealEstate10K and [10^{-5}, 10^{-3}] for DL3DV. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class MultiViewFeatureExtractor(nn.Module): def forward(self, I, P): # Monocular transformer, multi-view transformer, cross-view U-Net # Output shape: [N, C, H/4, W/4] return torch.zeros(I.shape[0], I.shape[1], I.shape[2]//4, I.shape[3]//4) class FeedbackFeatureExtractor(nn.Module): def forward(self, X): # PixelUnshuffle + feature extraction return F.pixelunshuffle(X, downscalefactor=2) class AnalysisTransform(nn.Module): def forward(self, x): return x class SynthesisTransform(nn.Module): def forward(self, x): return x class StateUpdateModule(nn.Module): def forward(self, x): return x class GaussianPredictor(nn.Module): def forward(self, S): # Low-res 2D grid -> depth -> back-project -> KNN attention -> attributes -> PixelShuffle # Output: pixel-aligned 3D Gaussians at half input resolution return torch.zeros(S.shape[0], 1, S.shape[2]2, S.shape[3]2) class ModulationNetwork(nn.Module): def forward(self, loglambda): # Lightweight network predicting gamma, beta return torch.zeroslike(loglambda), torch.zeroslike(loglambda) class FeCoSplat: def init(self, numviews, channels, height, width): self.numviews = numviews self.channels = channels self.height = height self.width = width self.Emv = MultiViewFeatureExtractor() self.Efb = FeedbackFeatureExtractor() self.ga = AnalysisTransform() self.gs = SynthesisTransform() self.U = StateUpdateModule() self.P = GaussianPredictor() self.phi = ModulationNetwork() self.S0 = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(1, channels, 1, 1)) self.beta = 0.05 def stage1encode(self, I, P, lambdaval): F1 = self.Emv(I, P) S0broadcast = self.S0.expandas(F1) y1 = self.ga(torch.cat([F1, S0broadcast], dim=1)) if self.training: y1quant = y1 + torch.randlike(y1) 0.5 else: y1quant = torch.round(y1) # Entropy coding uses ANS and quadtree prior as per. # Returns bitstream B1 and rate R1 B1, R1 = b'', 0.0 y1decoded = y1quant y1synthesized = self.gs(y1decoded) S1 = self.U(torch.cat([self.S0.expandas(y1synthesized), y1synthesized], dim=1)) G1 = self.P(S1) return G1, S1, B1, R1 def stage2encode(self, I, P, G1, S1, lambdaval): Ihat1 = self.render(G1, P) F2 = self.Efb(torch.cat([I, Ihat1], dim=1)) y2 = self.ga(torch.cat([F2, S1], dim=1)) if self.training: y2quant = y2 + torch.randlike(y2) 0.5 else: y2quant = torch.round(y2) # Entropy coding uses ANS and quadtree prior as per. B2, R2 = b'', 0.0 y2decoded = y2quant y2synthesized = self.gs(y2decoded) S2 = self.U(torch.cat(, dim=1)) G2 = self.P(S2) return G2, S2, B2, R2 def decode(self, B1, B2, P): y1decoded = torch.randn(1, self.channels, self.height//4, self.width//4) y1synthesized = self.gs(y1decoded) S1 = self.U(torch.cat([self.S0.expandas(y1synthesized), y1synthesized], dim=1)) y2decoded = torch.randn(1, self.channels, self.height//4, self.width//4) y2synthesized = self.gs(y2decoded) S2 = self.U(torch.cat(, dim=1)) G2 = self.P(S2) return G2 def render(self, G, P): # Differentiable rasterization of 3D Gaussians G with poses P return torch.randnlike(G) def computeloss(self, Itgt, G, P): Ihat = self.render(G, P) lossmse = torch.mean((Itgt - Ihat) 2) losslpips = torch.mean((Itgt - Ihat) 2) # Placeholder for LPIPS metric totalloss = lossmse + self.beta losslpips return totalloss Parameters: \beta (LPIPS weight): 0.05. \lambda (Rate-distortion trade-off): Sampled from log-uniform distribution. RealEstate10K: [10^{-5}, 10^{-2}]. DL3DV: [10^{-5}, 10^{-3}]. Receiver Parameters: 3.45M. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Receiver Efficiency: The receiver does not need to reconstruct G1 or render \hat{I}1. Decoding is causal and efficient, relying only on bitstreams B1, B2 and B{cam}. Precision: Quantization-aware training uses additive uniform noise to approximate quantization. During inference, this is replaced by Round. Resolution: The Gaussian predictor produces Gaussians at half the input resolution (one Gaussian per 2 \times 2 region). Time Complexity: Sender-side computation is heavy, involving multi-view feature extraction, two-stage coding, and intermediate rendering. Receiver-side complexity is low, requiring only progressive state updates and a final lightweight conversion. Memory Complexity: Peak GPU memory (Sender): 1.316 GiB. Peak GPU memory (Receiver): Not explicitly listed, but implied to be low given the 0.117s latency and 3.45M parameters. Performance: Receiver latency: 0.117s. FeCoSplat achieves favorable rate-distortion performance, particularly at low bitrates. Strengths: Balances rate-distortion performance and receiver-side complexity. Avoids challenges of heterogeneous attributes and irregular spatial organization found in explicit Gaussian compression. Avoids execution of the entire feed-forward 3DGS pipeline at the receiver, preventing compression distortion propagation. Limitations: Sender-side computation is significant due to intermediate rendering and two-stage coding. When to Use: Compression of feed-forward 3DGS representations (e.g., from MVSplat, LGM) where low receiver-side complexity and good low-bitrate performance are required. When Not to Use: When sender-side computational resources are severely constrained, or when real-time bidirectional interaction requiring immediate intermediate state access is needed (though FeCoSplat is designed for one-way transmission). FeCoSplat was proposed to address the limitations of existing feed-forward 3DGS compression methods. Image compression incurs high receiver-side computation and error propagation, while Gaussian compression is challenged by heterogeneous attributes and irregular primitives. Feature compression, as seen in CodecSplat, offers a middle ground but lacks reconstruction-aware refinement. FeCoSplat introduces a feedback-guided two-stage coding strategy to improve rate-distortion performance, particularly at low bitrates, while maintaining a lightweight receiver. The method builds on Feed-Forward 3DGS Compression by applying FCGS to compress 3DGS generated by feed-forward models without retraining. name: Hybrid Compression Framework
head: Adaptive Voxelization and GPCC Compression for 3DGS
body: The Hybrid Compression Framework is a post-training compression method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that reduces model size and bandwidth by combining adaptive voxelization with Generalized Prediction Context Coding (GPCC). It addresses the impracticality of generative compression, which requires retraining distinct models for each bitrate, and the quality degradation of standard post-training methods due to parameter distortion. By quantizing mean positions to voxel centers and fine-tuning remaining attributes, it achieves higher quality at lower bitrates compared to sibling methods like Mini-Splatting-C. Inputs: Pre-trained 3DGS model G = \{\mui, \Sigmai, Ci, \alphai\}{i=1}^N, where \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 are means, \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3} are covariances, Ci are spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, and \alphai \in [0,1] are opacities. Training images \{\tilde{I}i\}{i=1}^k and camera views \{\tilde{\theta}i\}{i=1}^k. Outputs: Compressed bitstream containing GPCC-coded positions, covariances, SH coefficients, and opacities. Data Structures: 1. Voxelized Model \tilde{G}: A set of M Gaussians (M < N) with quantized means \{\hat{\mu}i\}{i=1}^M, fine-tuned covariances \{\tilde{\Sigma}i\}{i=1}^M, fine-tuned SH coefficients \{\tilde{C}i\}{i=1}^M, and fine-tuned opacities \{\tilde{\alpha}i\}{i=1}^M. 2. GPCC Context: Octree structure for position coding; transform coding context for attributes. Parameters: Q{dc}: Quantization parameter for low-frequency SH coefficients (DC/base color). Q{ac}: Quantization parameter for high-frequency SH coefficients (AC). Q{op}: Quantization parameter for opacity. J: Number of octree partitioning levels (resolution). Steps: 1. Adaptive Voxelization: Partition the 3D space into an octree up to level J, where only occupied voxels are subdivided. Quantize each Gaussian mean \mui to the center of its containing voxel \hat{\mu}i. Merge Gaussians falling into the same voxel to obtain unique voxel centers \{\hat{\mu}i\}{i=1}^M. 2. Attribute Initialization: For each unique voxel center \hat{\mu}i, initialize the remaining attributes \Sigmai, Ci, \alphai by averaging the attributes of all original Gaussians mapped to that voxel. 3. Fine-Tuning: Keep the quantized mean positions \{\hat{\mu}i\}{i=1}^M fixed. Optimize the remaining attributes \{\tilde{\Sigma}i, \tilde{C}i, \tilde{\alpha}i\}{i=1}^M by minimizing the training loss L{train} until the rendering quality matches the input model G. The training loss is defined as: L{train} = \frac{1}{k} \sum{i=1}^k \frac{1}{2} \| R{\tilde{\theta}i}(\tilde{G}) - \tilde{I}i \|F where R{\theta} is the rendering function for view \theta, and \| \cdot \|F is the Frobenius norm. 4. Compression: Losslessly compress the voxelized positions \{\hat{\mu}i\}{i=1}^M using GPCC (octree coding followed by an octree-designed entropy coder). Compress covariances \{\tilde{\Sigma}i\}{i=1}^M using vector quantization. Compress SH coefficients \{\tilde{C}i\}{i=1}^M and opacities \{\tilde{\alpha}i\}{i=1}^M using transform coding with quantization parameters Q{dc}, Q{ac}, and Q{op} via GPCC. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridcompression(model, trainimgs, trainviews, Qdc, Qac, Qop, maxdepth): # 1. Adaptive Voxelization voxelmap = {} for g in model: voxelid = quantizetovoxel(g.mean, maxdepth) # standard octree quantization voxelmap.setdefault(voxelid, []).append(g) voxelized = [] for voxelid, group in voxelmap.items(): mean = getvoxelcenter(voxelid) # center of the voxel cube # Initialize attributes by averaging merged Gaussians cov = sum(g.cov for g in group) / len(group) sh = sum(g.sh for g in group) / len(group) alpha = sum(g.alpha for g in group) / len(group) voxelized.append({'mean': mean, 'cov': cov, 'sh': sh, 'alpha': alpha}) # 2. Fine-Tuning # Keep quantized means fixed, optimize attributes to minimize Ltrain for g in voxelized: g.mean = g.mean # Fixed # Minimize Ltrain = (1/k) sum{i=1}^k (1/2) ||Rthetai(G) - Ii||F voxelized = gradientdescentoptimize(voxelized, trainimgs, trainviews) # [Comment: Sources do not specify the exact optimizer or convergence criteria] # 3. Compression # Positions: lossless GPCC (octree coding + entropy coder) posstream = gpccoctreeencode([g['mean'] for g in voxelized]) # [Comment: Standard GPCC implementation] # Covariances: vector quantization covstream = vectorquantizeencode([g['cov'] for g in voxelized]) # [Comment: Standard vector quantization] # SH and Opacity: transform coding with quantization parameters shstream = gpcctransformencode([g['sh'] for g in voxelized], Qdc, Qac) alphastream = gpcctransformencode([g['alpha'] for g in voxelized], Qop) return posstream + covstream + shstream + alphastream Time Complexity: Requires a fine-tuning phase after voxelization, which incurs retraining costs proportional to the number of voxels and training iterations. Memory/Bandwidth: Significantly reduces model size compared to the original 3DGS by merging Gaussians and compressing attributes. Quality: Achieves higher quality at equivalent bitrates compared to standard post-training PCC methods by mitigating distortion through fine-tuning. Strengths: No need to retrain the entire model from scratch for different bitrates (unlike generative compression). Limitations: The fine-tuning step adds computational overhead during compression. The method was proposed in "Adaptive Voxelization for Transform Coding of 3D Gaussian Splatting Data" (2025). It builds on the observation that 3DGS data can be viewed as a 3D point cloud (3DPC). Previous post-training methods relied on point cloud compression (PCC) but suffered from quality loss due to parameter distortion. Generative compression methods, while efficient, require retraining for each rate-distortion point, making them impractical for multi-rate applications. This framework combines adaptive voxelization with GPCC to balance compression efficiency and rendering quality. name: Prune2TargetSize
head: Top-down pruning and recovery
body: Prune2TargetSize is an algorithm designed to reduce a pretrained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model to a precise target number of splats while maintaining visual quality. It solves the problem of unpredictable model size in standard 3DGS training, where hyperparameters like cloning thresholds and densification intervals interact in complex, scene-dependent ways, making it impossible to guarantee a specific final splat count. Unlike bottom-up approaches that grow splats to a target, this method uses a top-down strategy of iterative pruning and recovery, which has been found to perform better in practice. Inputs: G: A pretrained 3DGS model. d: The target number of splats for the output layer. r: The maximum pruning ratio per iteration (hyperparameter). I: Training view images. P: Camera poses associated with images I. Outputs: GL: A list of d splats, sorted in descending order of global significance score. Data Structures: The 3DGS model G consists of a set of splats Gi. Each splat typically includes position, scale, rotation, opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients, though the internal layout is inherited from the base 3DGS implementation [15] cited in. Global significance score S is a scalar value for each splat, computed by CalGS. The exact formula for CalGS is not provided in the source text, but it references external work [10] for the calculation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize G^ \leftarrow G. 2. Compute current splat count n = \text{NumOfGS}(G^). 3. While n > d: a. Compute global significance scores S for all splats in G^ using I and P via CalGS. b. If n \times (1 - r) > d: i. Prune the bottom r fraction of splats (those with the lowest S) from G^. ii. Run Recovery training on the pruned G^ with IsRefinementIteration=True. This allows cloning, splitting, and pruning. iii. Update n = \text{NumOfGS}(G^). c. Else (if n \times (1 - r) \le d): i. Prune G^ to remove exactly n - d splats (lowest S). ii. Run Finetune training on G^ with IsRefinementIteration=False. This disables cloning, splitting, and pruning. iii. Update n = \text{NumOfGS}(G^). 4. Compute final global significance scores S for the pruned model G^. 5. Sort splats in G^ in descending order of S to produce GL. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def Prune2TargetSize(Gpretrained, targetsized, maxpruningratior, imagesI, posesP): """ Reduces a pretrained 3DGS model to a precise target number of splats. Args: Gpretrained: Pretrained 3DGS model. targetsized: Target number of splats. maxpruningratior: Max fraction of splats to prune in one step. imagesI: List of training images. posesP: List of camera poses. Returns: GL: List of splats sorted by significance. """ # Initialize Gstar = Gpretrained n = len(Gstar) while n > targetsized: # Compute global significance scores scores = CalGS(Gstar, imagesI, posesP) # Determine pruning strategy if n (1 - maxpruningratior) > targetsized: # Prune a fraction r numtoprune = int(n maxpruningratior) # Identify indices of splats with lowest scores sortedindices = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: scores[i]) pruneindices = set(sortedindices[:numtoprune]) # Prune splats Gstar = [s for i, s in enumerate(Gstar) if i not in pruneindices] # Recovery training: allows cloning, splitting, pruning Gstar = RecoveryTraining(Gstar, imagesI, posesP, isrefinement=True) # Update count n = len(Gstar) else: # Prune to exact target numtoprune = n - targetsized sortedindices = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: scores[i]) pruneindices = set(sortedindices[:numtoprune]) # Prune splats Gstar = [s for i, s in enumerate(Gstar) if i not in pruneindices] # Finetune training: disables cloning, splitting, pruning Gstar = FinetuneTraining(Gstar, imagesI, posesP, isrefinement=False) # Update count n = len(Gstar) # Final sorting finalscores = CalGS(Gstar, imagesI, posesP) sortedindices = sorted(range(len(Gstar)), key=lambda i: finalscores[i], reverse=True) GL = [Gstar[i] for i in sortedindices] return GL def CalGS(model, images, poses): # Computes global significance score for each splat # Exact formula is in external reference [10] return [0.0] len(model) def RecoveryTraining(model, images, poses, isrefinement): # Training step allowing cloning, splitting, and pruning return model def FinetuneTraining(model, images, poses, isrefinement): # Training step disabling cloning, splitting, and pruning return model Parameters: r: Max pruning ratio. Typical values are not specified in the sources. d: Target number of splats. Scene-dependent. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Standard 3DGS hyperparameters (e.g., \taup for cloning/splitting, densification interval) do not allow precise control over the total splat count because their interactions are complex and scene-dependent. The mapping between hyperparameter settings and total splat count is unclear and can change across different 3D scenes. The algorithm assumes CalGS can compute a consistent global significance score for all splats. A sibling compression method. A sibling compression method. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides precise control over the final model size (number of splats). The top-down approach (prune then grow) is preferred over bottom-up approaches because it worked better in practice. Limitations: Requires a pretrained model as a starting point. When to use: When hardware deployment requires a strict upper bound on model size or bandwidth, and visual quality must be preserved as much as possible. When not to use: When computational resources for iterative training are limited, or when an approximate size is acceptable. Prune2TargetSize was introduced in the paper "L3GS: Layered 3D Gaussian Splats for Efficient 3D Scene Delivery" published at ACM MOBICOM ’25 in November 2025. It is part of the L3GS pipeline, which aims to create layered 3DGS models for efficient scene delivery. The method addresses the lack of precise control over model size in standard 3DGS training. name: SUNDAE
head: Spectrally Pruned Gaussian Fields with Neural Compensation
body: SUNDAE is a graph-based compression method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces computational load by pruning redundant Gaussians while preserving key scene details. It distinguishes itself from direct splatting by shifting to feature splatting, utilizing a neural compensation head to interpolate features and recover fine details lost during pruning. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} with attributes (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients, color). Output: A pruned subset of Gaussians and a trained neural network model for feature reconstruction. Data Structures: Gaussian Graph: Nodes represent Gaussians, and edges encode spatial relationships or proximity between them. Neural Compensation Head: A lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) used for feature interpolation. Steps: 1. Graph Construction: Construct a graph where nodes are the 3D Gaussians and edges capture their spatial relationships. 2. Spectral Pruning: Apply a band-limited graph filter to the constructed graph to selectively down-sample (prune) the Gaussians, removing redundant ones while preserving key scene details. 3. Feature Splatting Setup: Shift from direct Gaussian attribute rendering to feature splatting, where the pruned Gaussians carry reduced or interpolated features. 4. Neural Compensation: Employ the lightweight neural network-based feature interpolation head to recover fine details potentially lost during the pruning process, compensating for information loss from down-sampling. name: Fast Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting (FCGS)
head: Fast Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression
body: FCGS is an optimization-free, feed-forward compression pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that compresses representations in a single pass without per-scene finetuning, aiming to reduce compression time from minutes to seconds while maintaining fidelity. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Model Compression Pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting and 3DGS Model Compression Pipeline by eliminating the need for iterative per-scene optimization, which typically takes 10–28 minutes, by using an autoencoder-based structure with a Multi-path Entropy Module (MEM) to balance compression size and fidelity. Inputs and outputs: Input: A trained 3DGS representation consisting of unstructured Gaussian blobs with attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color, spherical harmonics coefficients). Output: A compressed bitstream representing the latent space of the Gaussian attributes. Data structures: The method treats Gaussian attributes as a set of unstructured blobs. The core data structure is the latent vector \mathbf{z} derived from the analysis transform. Attributes \mathbf{x}: The raw Gaussian parameters. Latent \mathbf{y}: The output of the analysis transform ga(\mathbf{x}). Hyperprior \mathbf{z}: The output of the hyperanalysis transform, used to model the entropy of \mathbf{y}. Quantized Latent \hat{\mathbf{y}}: The discretized latent representation. Method steps: 1. Analysis Transform: Map input Gaussian attributes \mathbf{x} into a latent space \mathbf{y} using an analysis transform network ga. This step is inspired by image compression autoencoders. 2. Multi-path Entropy Module (MEM): Determine the processing path for each attribute group based on sensitivity to balance compression size and fidelity. Geometry attributes (position, scale, rotation) bypass the autoencoder and are directly quantized: \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}. Color attributes (opacity, SH coefficients) pass through the autoencoder: \mathbf{y} = ga(\mathbf{x}). This prevents model collapse caused by geometry deviations that would break rasterization. 3. Quantization: Quantize the latent variables \mathbf{y} to obtain \hat{\mathbf{y}}. 4. Context Modeling: Eliminate redundancies among parameters using customized context models. Inter-Gaussian Context: Models dependencies between different Gaussians. Intra-Gaussian Context: Models dependencies within the parameters of a single Gaussian. These context models are lightweight and efficient. 5. Hyperprior Encoding: Encode the quantized latent \hat{\mathbf{y}} into a hyperprior \mathbf{z} using a hyperanalysis transform to estimate the probability distribution for entropy coding. 6. Entropy Coding: Encode the quantized latents and hyperprior using the estimated probabilities to produce the final bitstream. 7. Decoding (Reverse): Decode the bitstream to recover \hat{\mathbf{y}} and \hat{\mathbf{z}}. Use the hyperprior \hat{\mathbf{z}} to predict the distribution of \hat{\mathbf{y}}. Apply the synthesis transform gs (if applicable for color attributes) to reconstruct the attributes. Directly use the quantized geometry attributes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Placeholder for learned transform def hyperanalysistransform(x): """Learned neural network mapping quantized latents to hyperprior.""" return x # Placeholder for learned transform def synthesistransform(y, z): """Learned neural network mapping latent and hyperprior back to attributes.""" return y # Placeholder for learned transform def getcontextmodels(): """Returns inter- and intra-Gaussian context models.""" return {"inter": None, "intra": None} def entropyencode(data, contextmodels, hyperprior): """Arithmetic coding using estimated probabilities from context and hyperprior.""" return b"" # Placeholder for entropy coder output def entropydecode(bitstream, contextmodels, hyperprior): """Arithmetic decoding to recover quantized data.""" return bitstream # Placeholder for decoded data def fcgcompress(gaussians): """Compress 3DGS using FCGS.""" # Geometry attributes bypass autoencoder and are directly quantized posq = quantize(gaussians["pos"]) scaleq = quantize(gaussians["scale"]) rotq = quantize(gaussians["rot"]) # Color attributes pass through the autoencoder colorinput = (gaussians["opacity"], gaussians["shcoeffs"]) colorlatent = analysistransform(colorinput) colorlatentq = quantize(colorlatent) # Hyperprior branch for entropy modeling hyperprior = hyperanalysistransform(colorlatentq) hyperpriorq = quantize(hyperprior) # Context models condition probability distributions contextmodels = getcontextmodels() bitstream = entropyencode( {"pos": posq, "scale": scaleq, "rot": rotq, "color": colorlatentq}, contextmodels, hyperpriorq) return bitstream def fcgdecompress(bitstream): """Decompress 3DGS using FCGS.""" contextmodels = getcontextmodels() data = entropydecode(bitstream, contextmodels, None) # Geometry attributes are directly dequantized pos = dequantize(data["pos"]) scale = dequantize(data["scale"]) rot = dequantize(data["rot"]) # Color attributes pass through synthesis transform colorlatentq = data["color"] opacity, shcoeffs = synthesistransform(colorlatentq, None) return { "pos": pos, "scale": scale, "rot": rot, "opacity": opacity, "shcoeffs": shcoeffs } Parameters: Compression Ratio: Over 20×. Compression Time: Seconds (compared to 10-28 minutes for optimization-based methods). Edge cases and pitfalls: Geometry Sensitivity: Directly quantizing geometry attributes is critical; processing them through the autoencoder leads to model collapse because rasterization fails due to deviations. Color Attributes: Allowing all color attributes to be processed by the autoencoder without fixing geometry can lead to densification issues and suboptimal fidelity. A technique to boost compression performance by applying FCGS to 3DGS that have been pruned using techniques like Trimming or Mini-Splatting. When combined with pruning (e.g., Mini+Ours on Deep Blending dataset), FCGS achieves a compression ratio of 100× over vanilla 3DGS. The size of compressed 3DGS using FCGS (at the highest rate) is only 40% that of MSC (Model Compression Pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting) with the same fidelity. Time Complexity: O(1) per scene in terms of optimization iterations, as it is a single feed-forward pass. Compression time is reduced from minutes to seconds. Memory Complexity: Depends on the autoencoder and context model sizes, but described as lightweight and efficient. Measured Performance: Achieves a compression ratio of over 20× while maintaining fidelity, surpassing most SOTA per-scene optimization-based methods. When combined with pruning, it achieves 100× compression ratio. Strengths: Fast, optimization-free, high compression ratio, compatible with pruning techniques. Limitations: May have lower fidelity than optimization-based methods if not carefully tuned, though it surpasses most SOTA methods. When to use: When rapid compression is required, or when per-scene optimization is computationally prohibitive. When not to use: When maximum possible fidelity is required and optimization time is not a constraint. FCGS was introduced in 2024 by Yihang Chen et al. as a solution to the storage challenges posed by the vast number of Gaussians in 3DGS. It is inspired by image compression methods, specifically autoencoder-based structures like those proposed by Ballé et al. (2018). The method addresses the limitation of previous compression techniques that required per-scene optimization, making them sluggish and slow.
