name: Neural Implicit Representation
body: Neural Implicit Representation encodes a 3D scene as a continuous function, typically a Neural Radiance Field or Signed Distance Function, rather than a discrete voxel grid or point cloud. It solves the problem of joint camera pose estimation and dense 3D reconstruction by optimizing network weights and camera poses simultaneously using photometric and geometric constraints. It differs from explicit point-based siblings like Gaussian Splatting by modeling complex geometry and appearance continuously. The family relies on a neural network F that maps spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} to scene properties. For appearance, F outputs color \mathbf{c} and volume density \sigma (or occupancy). For geometry, F may output a Signed Distance Function (SDF) value. Rendering is performed via volume rendering or ray marching: points are sampled along camera rays, properties are predicted by F, and results are aggregated using alpha compositing or weighted sums. Optimization jointly updates the network weights and camera poses Tt to minimize photometric (\ell{rgb}) and geometric (\ell{depth} or SDF) losses. Encodes scenes as continuous volumetric functions or explicit Gaussian primitives. It supports both implicit neural field evaluation and explicit GPU-friendly Gaussian splatting, trading memory for speed while maintaining competitive training times. Represents the scene as a continuous neural implicit function (NeRF or SDF) for joint localization and mapping. It differs from Gaussian Splatting by using continuous volumetric representation requiring ray marching, whereas Gaussian Splatting uses explicit, differentiable 3D Gaussians for object-order rendering. A globally consistent SLAM system using a point-based implicit neural (PIN) representation. It replaces grid structures with neural feature points, offering spatial flexibility and elastic correction during loop closure. Mapping alternates with odometry; the mapping step uses a hybrid neural SDF representation with explicit neural points and implicit MLP decoders. Odometry is performed correspondence-free via second-order scan-to-map optimization. A sliding window replay buffer ensures stable incremental updates. Loop closures trigger pose graph optimization and elastic deformation of neural points, enabling consistent large-scale mapping. The approach originated in continuous scene representation literature and was adapted for simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) to enable dense, consistent mapping without explicit mesh extraction. Recent developments include PIN-SLAM (January 2024), which uses a point-based implicit neural representation with elastic loop closure correction, KN-SLAM (March 2024), which integrates local feature correspondences for coarse pose initialization and joint photometric-feature loss optimization, and SLAIM (April 2024), which introduces a coarse-to-fine tracking pipeline with Gaussian-filtered image signals for improved photometric bundle adjustment. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) Representation
head: 3D Gaussian scene representation, Differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting, INGP, Instant Neural Graphics Primitives, Multi-resolution Hash Map NeRF, NeRF Scene Representation, Photon Field Networks, Photon Fields
body: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) represent a 3D scene as a continuous volumetric function that maps spatial coordinates and view directions to color and volume density, enabling high-quality novel view synthesis via differentiable volume rendering. While the term broadly covers implicit neural representations, the provided sources also encompass explicit variants like 3D Gaussian Splatting, which replaces neural network evaluation with differentiable rasterization of 3D Gaussians to achieve real-time performance. Unlike traditional ray-marching NeRFs that evaluate a neural network at hundreds of points per ray, 3D Gaussian Splatting projects explicit 3D Gaussian blobs onto the screen, avoiding neural inference during rendering. The method varies significantly depending on whether the representation is implicit (standard NeRF/Photon Fields) or explicit (3D Gaussian Splatting). Inputs: A set of 2D images with known camera poses (typically obtained via Structure-from-Motion, SfM). For Photon Fields, additional inputs include light source positions and phase function coefficients. Outputs: A rendered RGB image for a novel viewpoint, or a trained scene representation (neural network weights or 3D Gaussian parameters). Neural Network: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) or hash-grid encoded network. Photon Fields: 5-layer MLP, 64 neurons per layer, ReLU activations. Standard NeRF (Active Scout): 2-layer MLP, 128 neurons per layer. Encoding: Multi-resolution hash map encoding for positions (3D) and directions (2D). Photon Fields: 16 grid levels, 8 features per level, 2x scaling factor, hash table size 2^{19}. Photon Map (Photon Fields only): A collection of photons stored in a GPU-accelerated kd-tree for spatial queries. Each photon stores position, direction, intensity, and a phase coefficient g. 3D Gaussian Primitive: Each Gaussian is defined by learnable parameters: Position: Mean \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3. Covariance: \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, parameterized by a rotation matrix R and scale vector S such that \Sigma = R S S^T R^T to ensure positive semi-definiteness. Opacity: \alpha \in 0, 1), constrained via sigmoid activation. Color: [Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients for view-dependent color. Scene Size: 1–5 million Gaussians for typical scenes. Each Gaussian stores approximately 59 learnable numbers. 3D Gaussian Splatting: Initialize the set of 3D Gaussians using the sparse point cloud generated by SfM. Each SfM point becomes the mean position \mu of one Gaussian. Implicit Networks: Initialization method is not given in the sources. Generate batches of size 2^{16} containing uniformly sampled grid coordinates x \in [0,1]^3, random uniform directions \vec{\omega}, and phase coefficients g. Compute ground truth radiance Li(x, \vec{\omega}) using a KNN query on the photon map with K=1024 neighbors. Encode the target radiance logarithmically to [0,1] using precision parameter \psi (typically 4–6): Li'(x, \vec{\omega}) = \begin{cases} -\frac{\log{10}(Li(x, \vec{\omega}))}{\psi} & \text{if } Li(x, \vec{\omega}) > 10^{-\psi} \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Implicit (Ray Marching): 1. For each pixel, cast a ray from the camera. 2. Sample points x(s) along the ray. 3. Query the neural network F at each point to get color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma. 4. Compute transmittance Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj) and accumulated color. Explicit (3D Gaussian Splatting): 1. Projection: Project each 3D Gaussian to 2D. The 2D covariance \Sigma' in camera coordinates is computed using the Jacobian J of the affine approximation of the projective transformation and the viewing transformation W: \Sigma' = J W \Sigma W^T J^T 2. Tiling: Divide the screen into tiles (e.g., 16x16 pixels). Assign each Gaussian to overlapping tiles. 3. Sorting: Sort Gaussians within each tile by depth (front-to-back) using a fast GPU sort. 4. Rasterization/Blending: For each pixel, blend colors front-to-back using alpha compositing: C = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \alphai is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian at the pixel. Loss Function: Minimize the difference between rendered and ground truth images. Standard NeRF: \ell = \lambda1 \ell{rgb} + \lambda2 \ell{depth}, using L1 loss for both. 3D Gaussian Splatting: L1 loss combined with Structural Similarity (SSIM). Gradient Update: Implicit: Update network weights via Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). Explicit: Backpropagate gradients directly to Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients). Gradients are computed explicitly to avoid overhead. Adaptive Density Control (3D Gaussian Splatting only): Cloning: Clone small Gaussians in under-reconstructed regions. Splitting: Split large Gaussians that cover too much detail. Pruning: Remove Gaussians that become nearly transparent. These steps are interleaved with optimization to maintain compactness and handle geometry ambiguities. \psi (Precision): Maximum desired floating point precision digits beyond zero. Values 4–6 are sufficient. G (Phase Coefficients): Discrete set of scattering coefficients. \{-0.75, 0.0, 0.75\} is a common choice. \lambda1, \lambda2: Loss weights, tuned to balance \ell{rgb} and \ell{depth} magnitudes. Batch Size: 2^{16} for Photon Fields training batches. Covariance Validity: Directly optimizing the covariance matrix \Sigma is invalid because gradient descent cannot easily constrain it to be positive semi-definite. Unbounded Scenes: For scenes with sky/infinity, rays extend indefinitely, causing density mismatches. Artifacts: 3D Gaussian Splatting may produce floating artifacts and needle-like Gaussians in regions seen by few cameras, and aliasing when zooming. SAM Inaccuracy: In Mask Inverse Rendering variants, if the Segment Anything Model (SAM) is inaccurate, the projection loss fails. Isolates and renders the static background of a scene by training exclusively on background pixels identified via segmentation masks, using an emptiness regularizer to prevent artifacts. Choose it when dynamic foreground elements must be excluded from the neural representation. Learns a neural representation of outdoor scene geometry, diffuse albedo, and illumination-dependent shadows for simultaneous lighting and viewpoint editing. It sets itself apart by providing explicit intrinsic decomposition rather than just view-dependent appearance, enabling physical relighting. Models scene geometry and appearance as an explicit RGB\alpha volume to amortize rendering across multiple views. Choose it when real-time rendering and structural losses like SSIM are required, avoiding independent per-ray sampling. Models the appearance and dynamics of a human face using an implicit volumetric representation conditioned on morphable model expression parameters and per-frame latent codes. Choose it when handling dynamically changing surfaces from monocular input is necessary. Compresses a NeRF by removing weights with the smallest magnitudes from the fully-connected network. Choose it when reducing storage size and inference time is prioritized over structural scene changes. Encodes RGB images with known poses and depth into 3D neural fields represented as density and feature voxel grids via a 2D CNN encoder and frustum lifting. Choose it when discrete voxel-based representations and latent compression are needed. Incrementally integrates noisy depth maps into a global neural implicit representation using local weighted averaging and global neural rendering optimization. Choose it when geometric coherence and scalability are required for dense 3D reconstruction. Maps continuous spatial features to a discrete, finite codebook of object categories for scalable, object-centric representations. Choose it when constant rendering compute regardless of object count and unbounded object support are needed. Projects 2D masks from SAM into 3D space to form 3D masks based on ray weights. It optimizes volume values V(r(t)) or mask values m{gi} to increase confidence where SAM predicts foreground, using a negative refinement term to handle SAM inaccuracies across views. Choose it for 3D segmentation and object isolation using radiance fields. Time Complexity: Standard NeRF: Training takes many hours (e.g., 48 hours for Mip-NeRF360 quality). Rendering is slow (seconds per image) due to ray marching and network evaluation. 3D Gaussian Splatting: Training is competitive with fast methods (e.g., InstantNGP), achieving SOTA quality in ~51 minutes. Rendering is real-time (\ge 30 fps at 1080p). Memory Complexity: Standard NeRF: Low memory usage (few megabytes for network weights). 3D Gaussian Splatting: High memory usage (hundreds of megabytes for millions of Gaussians). Strengths: High visual quality comparable to SOTA NeRF methods. Real-time rendering capability (Gaussian Splatting). No need for MVS data; works with sparse SfM points. Explicit representation allows flexible geometry creation/destruction. Limitations: Gaussian Splatting lacks a clean surface/mesh extraction. Aliasing issues when zooming in/out. Floating artifacts in sparse-view regions. When to Use: Use Standard NeRF for high-quality offline rendering with limited memory. Use 3D Gaussian Splatting for real-time applications (VR, robotics, web) where training speed and rendering FPS are critical. Neural Radiance Fields were introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020, revolutionizing novel view synthesis by representing scenes as continuous volumetric functions. The field has evolved to include implicit global illumination methods like Photon Field Networks (2023), which use neural networks to approximate in-scattered radiance, and explicit methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting, introduced by Kerbl et al. at SIGGRAPH 2023, which replaced neural evaluation with differentiable rasterization for real-time performance. These methods are used in virtual reality, film, robotics, and cultural heritage. name: Scene NeRF
body: Scene NeRF is a method for isolating and rendering the static background of a scene by training a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) exclusively on pixels identified as background via human segmentation masks. It differs from standard NeRF by explicitly excluding dynamic foreground elements (e.g., humans) from the training data and employing an emptiness regularizer to prevent artifacts in empty space. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A video sequence of the scene; human segmentation masks for each frame; camera poses and sparse scene model from COLMAP; multi-view stereo (MVS) depth maps; dense monocular depth maps. Outputs: A trained Scene NeRF model \mathcal{N}s that renders background colors and densities. Data Structures: Segmentation Mask M(\mathbf{r}): A binary value for each ray \mathbf{r}. M(\mathbf{r}) = 1 if the ray intersects the human/foreground, M(\mathbf{r}) = 0 if it corresponds to the background. Fused Depth Map D{fuse}(\mathbf{r}): A depth estimate for each ray, obtained by fusing MVS and monocular depth maps. Preprocessing: 1. Use COLMAP to obtain camera poses, sparse scene model, and MVS depth maps D{mvs}. 2. Retrieve human segmentation maps using Mask-RCNN. 3. Fill holes in D{mvs} using dense monocular depth maps D{mono} (e.g., Miangoleh et al.). 4. Fuse D{mvs} and D{mono} into D{fuse} by finding a linear mapping between the two depth maps using pixels with both estimates, then transforming D{mono} values to match the D{mvs} scale. Training Steps: For each ray \mathbf{r} sampled from the camera: 1. Determine Mask: Check if the ray corresponds to the human or background using the segmentation mask M(\mathbf{r}). 2. Sample Terminating Depth: Determine the terminating depth \hat{z}\mathbf{r} for the emptiness regularizer by querying the fused depth map: \hat{z}\mathbf{r} = D{fuse}(\mathbf{r}). 3. Compute RGB Loss: Calculate the reconstruction loss only for background pixels. If M(\mathbf{r}) = 1, the loss is zero. If M(\mathbf{r}) = 0, the loss is the difference between the rendered color \mathbf{C}s(\mathbf{r}) and the ground-truth color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}): \mathcal{L}{s,rgb}(\mathbf{r}) = (1 - M(\mathbf{r})) \| \mathbf{C}s(\mathbf{r}) - \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) \| 4. Compute Emptiness Regularizer: Calculate the integral of the scene density \sigmas from the near plane tn to a slack margin \alpha \hat{z}\mathbf{r}. This forces density to be zero in the empty space between the camera and the estimated scene surface: \mathcal{L}{s,empty}(\mathbf{r}) = \int{tn}^{\alpha \hat{z}\mathbf{r}} \sigmas(\mathbf{r}(t)) dt where \alpha = 0.8 is a slack margin to avoid strong regularization when depth estimates are inaccurate. 5. Compute Total Loss: Sum the RGB loss and the emptiness regularizer weighted by \lambda{empty}: \mathcal{L}{s} = \mathcal{L}{s,rgb}(\mathbf{r}) + \lambda{empty} \mathcal{L}{s,empty}(\mathbf{r}) where \lambda{empty} = 0.1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computescenenerfloss(rays, gtcolors, masks, fuseddepths, lambdaempty=0.1, alpha=0.8, tn=0.0): """ Computes the total training loss for Scene NeRF over a batch of rays. Assumes a standard volume rendering forward pass is available. """ totalloss = 0.0 for r, cgt, m, zfuse in zip(rays, gtcolors, masks, fuseddepths): # Standard volume rendering forward pass to obtain rendered color Cs, # density samples sigmas, and depth samples tsamples along the ray cs, sigmas, tsamples = volumerenderforwardpass(r) # 1. RGB Loss: weighted by background mask M(r) # If m=1 (human), loss is 0. If m=0 (background), loss is L2 norm difference. rgbloss = (1.0 - m) norm(cs - cgt) # 2. Emptiness Regularizer: integral of density from tn to alpha zfuse maxdepth = alpha zfuse densityintegral = 0.0 for i in range(len(tsamples) - 1): tcurr, tnext = tsamples[i], tsamples[i+1] # Clamp integration interval to [tn, maxdepth] upper = min(tnext, maxdepth) lower = max(tcurr, tn) if upper > lower: densityintegral += sigmas[i] (upper - lower) emptyloss = densityintegral # 3. Total Loss loss = rgbloss + lambdaempty emptyloss totalloss += loss return totalloss Parameters: \lambda{empty}: Hyperparameter controlling the weight of the emptiness regularizer. Set to 0.1 in all experiments. \alpha: Slack margin for the emptiness regularizer. Set to 0.8. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hazy Objects: Simply minimizing the RGB reconstruction loss leads to 'hazy' objects floating in the scene. This is resolved by adding the emptiness regularizer. Inaccurate Depth: The slack margin \alpha = 0.8 is used to avoid strong regularization when depth estimates are inaccurate. Single Human Assumption: The method assumes a single human being in the scene, though it can be trivially extended. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Effectively isolates static background from dynamic foreground (humans). Limitations: Requires accurate human segmentation masks and depth estimates. Performance degrades if depth estimates are inaccurate without the slack margin. When to Use: When the goal is to reconstruct the static background of a scene with dynamic foreground elements, given video input and segmentation masks. Origin: The method is described in "NeuMan: Neural Human Radiance Field from a Single Video" by W. Jiang et al.. History and Development: The approach builds on traditional motion detection work by using a NeRF for the background model. It follows the approach of Video-NeRF in using an emptiness regularizer. Where it is Used: Used for reconstructing static backgrounds in videos containing human subjects. name: NeRF-OSR
head: NeRF-OSR Baseline, Neural Radiance Fields for Outdoor Scene Relighting
body: NeRF-OSR is a neural radiance field approach for outdoor scene relighting that learns a neural representation of scene geometry, diffuse albedo, and illumination-dependent shadows from a set of images capturing the same site from different viewpoints and at different times, enabling simultaneous editing of both the scene’s lighting and viewpoint. Unlike standard NeRF which learns a Lambertian model under fixed lighting, NeRF-OSR decomposes the scene into spatial occupancy, illumination, shadowing, and diffuse albedo reflectance, trained in a self-supervised manner from outdoor data captured from various viewpoints and at different illuminations. It sets itself apart from siblings like Scene NeRF by providing explicit intrinsic decomposition (albedo, geometry, lighting) rather than just view-dependent appearance, allowing for physical relighting and albedo editing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Multiple RGB images of a single scene, shot at different timings (illumination conditions) and from different viewpoints. Output: A neural representation of the scene that can render novel views under arbitrary lighting conditions, specified by the user via environment maps or Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients. Data Structures: The method relies on two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) to model the scene properties: 1. Density MLP: Takes 3D position x as input and outputs density \sigma(x). 2. Albedo MLP: Takes 3D position x as input and outputs diffuse albedo c{albedo}(x). NeRF-OSR modifies the color output to be albedo and combines it with an explicit lighting model. The final color is not directly predicted by the MLP but is computed as a function of albedo, geometry, and lighting. Illumination and Shadow Model: The method uses an explicit 2nd-order Spherical Harmonics (SH) illumination model. The rendering equation is adapted to separate intrinsic properties from lighting: C(o, d) = \sum{i=1}^{N{depth}} T(ti) \alpha(\sigma(xi)\deltai) c(xi) where c(xi) is the color at point xi, derived from the albedo and the illumination model. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Data Pre-processing: Discard dynamic objects (cars, people, bikes) from the training stage using segmentation masks. Estimate masks for sky and vegetation and exclude them from evaluation due to highly varying appearance across weather seasons. Split data into training and testing sets based on recording sessions. 2. Ray Sampling: For each pixel, cast a ray from camera origin o in direction d. Sample N{depth} points \{xi\}{i=1}^{N{depth}} along the ray, where xi = o + ti d. 3. Hierarchical Sampling: To capture small details, perform a coarse pass with stratified sampling. Use the densities from the coarse pass for importance sampling in the final pass. 4. Neural Network Forward Pass: For each sampled point xi, query the Density MLP to get \sigma(xi). Query the Albedo MLP to get c{albedo}(xi). Compute the final color c(xi) by combining c{albedo}(xi) with the scene illumination (SH coefficients) and shadow term. The sources state the model is an explicit function of geometry, albedo, shadow, and lighting conditions. 5. Volume Rendering: Compute transmittance T(ti) = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{N{depth}-1} \sigma(xj)\deltaj). Compute opacity \alpha(y) = 1 - \exp(-y). Compute ray color: C(o, d) = \sum{i=1}^{N{depth}} T(ti) \alpha(\sigma(xi)\deltai) c(xi). Here, \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. 6. Optimization: Train the MLPs in a self-supervised manner using the observed ground-truth per-pixel colors. Supervise the rendered pixel colors of both the coarse and fine passes with the ground-truth colors. Estimate per-image illumination (SH coefficients) during training. 7. Geometry Extraction (Optional for Real-time): Extract geometry and albedo from the learned model as a mesh using Marching Cubes [16] at resolution 1000^3 voxels. Use the extracted mesh and albedo in an interactive renderer (e.g., OpenGL) for real-time VR rendering. Lighting model for real-time: C{interactive} = C{ambient} + s \odot C{sun} \max\{0, D{sun} \cdot N\}, where C{ambient} is ambient color, s is 0/1 based on shadow map occlusion, C{sun} is sun color, D{sun} is sun direction, and N is mesh normal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderneurospatialray(o, d, densitymlp, albedomlp, shcoeffs, shadowmap): # 1. Stratified sampling from near to far camera plane tcoarse = stratifiedsamplenearfar(o, d) xcoarse = o + tcoarse d sigmacoarse = densitymlp(xcoarse) # 2. Importance sampling for fine pass based on coarse densities tfine = importancesample(tcoarse, sigmacoarse) xfine = o + tfine d sigmafine = densitymlp(xfine) albedofine = albedomlp(xfine) # 3. Compute color from albedo, SH illumination, and shadow cfine = computecolorwithlighting(albedofine, shcoeffs, shadowmap, xfine) # 4. Volume rendering with transmittance and opacity delta = tfine[1:] - tfine[:-1] alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmafine delta) T = torch.exp(-torch.cumsum(sigmafine[:-1] delta, dim=0)) color = torch.sum(T alpha cfine, dim=0) return color Parameters: N{depth}: Number of samples per ray. Not given in the sources. Marching Cubes Resolution: 1000^3 voxels. SH Order: 2nd-order. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometry Inaccuracies: Tiny bumps in learned geometry lead to significant changes in normals and illumination errors. The model may smooth geometry to achieve more accurate lighting, resulting in some blur. Dynamic Objects: Must be masked out; otherwise, they corrupt the static scene representation. Sky/Vegetation: Highly variable appearance makes evaluation difficult; masks should be used to exclude these regions from metrics. Standard NeRF Limitation: Standard NeRF formulation learns a Lambertian model under fixed lighting because c(x) is defined only through an MLP without encoding lighting. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Site 1 PSNR: 19.86 (d/s) and 18.72 (full). Site 2 PSNR: 15.83 (d/s) and 15.43 (full). Site 3 PSNR: 17.38 (d/s) and 16.65 (full). Outperforms Yu et al. [46] and Philip et al. [27] on all sites. Real-time Demo: Runs in real-time on Intel i7-4770 CPU, Nvidia GeForce GTX 970 (4GB VRAM) GPU, Oculus Rift S HMD. System RAM usage below 3 GB. Strengths: Simultaneous novel view and novel lighting generation; explicit intrinsic decomposition (albedo, geometry, lighting); ability to edit albedo and shadows; handles uncontrolled outdoor settings. Limitations: Geometry inaccuracies can cause lighting errors; requires posed images with varying illumination; sky and vegetation are difficult to evaluate due to seasonal changes. When to use: When simultaneous viewpoint and lighting editing of outdoor scenes is required, and intrinsic decomposition is needed. When not to use: When the scene contains significant dynamic objects that cannot be masked, or when only static lighting editing of a single view is needed (simpler methods may suffice). NeRF-OSR was introduced by Viktor Rudnev, Mohamed Elgharib, William Smith, Lingjie Liu, Vladislav Golyanik, and Christian Theobalt from MPI for Informatics, SIC, and University of York. It was published in arXiv:2112.05140v2 on 21 Jul 2022. It is the first neural radiance fields approach for outdoor scene relighting, enabling the learning of scene intrinsics (geometry, albedo, illumination, shadows) from uncontrolled outdoor data. It builds on the original NeRF representation [12096-neural-radiance-field-nerf-representation.md] but extends it with explicit lighting and shadow models. It is used for real-time interactive rendering in VR, albedo editing, and shadow editing. name: Explicit Volumetric Rendering with Multiple View Aggregation
head: Pooled Latent Volume Rendering, RGBα Volume Rendering
body: This method models scene geometry and appearance as an explicit RGBα volume to amortize rendering across multiple views, solving the computational inefficiency of NeRF-like methods where per-ray sampling is independent and not reusable across different viewing angles. Unlike its siblings Scene NeRF, NeRF-OSR, and Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields, which typically rely on implicit field evaluations or sparse ray sampling, this approach generates a dense volumetric representation that enables real-time rendering and the use of structural losses like SSIM during training. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of n source views S = \{I1, \dots, In\} with corresponding camera poses P = \{P1, \dots, Pn\} and intrinsic parameters. Outputs: An RGBα volume V \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times ds \times h \times w} and rendered target images \hat{C}. Data Structures: Latent Volume (Zi): An intermediate volumetric representation for each source view i, processed by a 3D U-Net. RGBα Volume (V): A 4D tensor with dimensions 4 \times ds \times h \times w, where the first 3 channels encode color \mathbf{c} and the last channel encodes alpha \alpha. Numbered Steps: 1. Encode Source Views: For each source view i \in \{1, \dots, n\}, encode the image Ii into a latent volume Zi using the encoding process from the parent article. 2. Select Origin: Select an arbitrary source view i^ from the set of source views to serve as the origin of the coordinate system. 3. Align Volumes: Align each latent volume Zi to the origin i^ using the relative transformation P{i, i^} between the pose Pi of view i and the pose P{i^} of the origin. 4. Pool Volumes: Compute the pooled volumetric latent \bar{Z} by taking the mean of the aligned latent volumes across all n views: \bar{\mathbf{Z}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^{n} \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P}{i, i^}, \mathbf{Z}i) 5. Generate RGBα Volume: Feed the pooled latent \bar{Z} into a 3D U-Net to generate the explicit RGBα volume V. 6. Perspective Deformation: Apply perspective deformation to the viewing frustum using the intrinsic camera parameters via inverse warping and trilinear sampling. 7. Render: For a given pixel location (i, j), calculate the expected color \hat{C}{i,j} by integrating along the depth samples k=1 \dots ds: \hat{C}{i,j} = \sum{k=1}^{ds} T{i,j}^k \alpha{i,j}^k \mathbf{c}{i,j}^k where the transmittance T{i,j}^k is defined as: T{i,j}^k = \prod{m=1}^{k-1} (1-\alpha{i,j}^m) Here, \mathbf{c}{i,j}^k is the color value from the first 3 channels of V at sample k, and \alpha{i,j}^k is the alpha value from the last channel of V at sample k. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def renderexplicitvolume(sourceviews, poses, intrinsics, originindex): n = len(sourceviews) alignedlatents = [] for i in range(n): # Step 1: Encode source view into latent volume Zi Zi = convencoder(sourceviews[i]) # Step 3: Compute relative transformation Pi,i = Pi Pi^-1 Prel = poses[i] @ np.linalg.inv(poses[originindex]) # Step 3: Align latent volume to origin coordinate system Zaligned = affinetransform3d(Zi, Prel) alignedlatents.append(Zaligned) # Step 4: Pool aligned volumes by taking the mean pooledlatent = sum(alignedlatents) / n # Step 5: Feed pooled latent to 3D U-Net to generate RGBα volume V V = u3dforward(pooledlatent) # Step 6 & 7: Perspective deformation and rendering return renderwithdeformation(V, intrinsics) def convencoder(image): # Standard 2D convolutional network mapping image to 3D latent volume return network(image) def affinetransform3d(volume, transformmatrix): # 3D grid sampling with affine transformation grid = generate3dgrid(volume.shape) transformedcoords = (transformmatrix @ grid.T).T return trilinearinterpolation(volume, transformedcoords) def u3dforward(latent): # 3D U-Net forward pass return network(latent) def renderwithdeformation(V, intrinsics): h, w = V.shape[2], V.shape[3] ds = V.shape[1] image = np.zeros((h, w, 3)) for j in range(w): for i in range(h): T = 1.0 color = np.zeros(3) for k in range(1, ds + 1): alpha = V[3, k-1, i, j] c = V[0:3, k-1, i, j] transmittance = T T = (1.0 - alpha) color += transmittance alpha c image[i, j] = color # Step 6: Apply perspective deformation using inverse warping return inversewarp(image, intrinsics) Parameters: \lambda: Weight for the SSIM loss in the training objective. ds: Number of depth samples. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinate System Alignment: The choice of origin view i^ is arbitrary, but all latent volumes must be consistently aligned to this origin to ensure correct pooling. Precision: Trilinear sampling is used for perspective deformation; care must be taken with boundary conditions and interpolation artifacts. Degenerate Input: The method assumes a valid set of source views with known poses. Sibling method. Sibling method. Sibling method. Sibling method. Sibling method. Sibling method. Sibling method. Time Complexity: Rendering is amortized across views. Per-view rendering time is 0.0178s (56 FPS) on an NVIDIA Tesla V100. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the RGBα volume V and latent volumes Zi. Exact memory footprint not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Rendering 250 views takes 1.022s (245 FPS), a 400x speedup over pixelNeRF's 474.8606s (0.5 FPS). Per-view, it is 100x faster than pixelNeRF's 1.9047s. Strengths: Real-time rendering capability; supports structural losses like SSIM during training because it renders full images rather than sparse rays. Limitations: Requires explicit volumetric storage. When to Use: When real-time novel view synthesis is required and multiple source views are available. Evaluated on ShapeNet chairs and cars. When Not to Use: When memory is extremely constrained and explicit volumes cannot be stored, or when only a single view is available for initialization. The method was introduced in "Fast and Explicit Neural View Synthesis". It addresses the limitation of NeRF-like methods where rendering cannot be amortized across views because each ray integral is independent. By using an explicit RGBα volume, the method allows for efficient rendering and the application of structural losses, which are not directly applicable to NeRF-like methods due to their sparse ray sampling. It has been evaluated on ShapeNet chairs and cars categories, demonstrating competitive visual quality and significant speed improvements over baselines like pixelNeRF. name: Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields
head: 4D Facial Avatar Reconstruction, Dynamic NeRF, Dynamic Neural Radiance Field (Dynamic NeRF) for Facial Avatars, Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields for Monocular 4D Facial Avatar Reconstruction, Dynamic Neural Scene Representation Network, Dynamic Radiance Field
body: Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields (Dynamic NeRF) is a method for modeling the appearance and dynamics of a human face using an implicit volumetric representation. It combines a neural scene representation network with a low-dimensional morphable model to handle facial dynamics, allowing novel viewpoint and expression synthesis from monocular input. Unlike static NeRF methods, this approach handles dynamically changing surfaces by conditioning the neural network on morphable model expression parameters and a per-frame latent code. It differs from other volumetric approaches by requiring only a single view from a fixed camera (e.g., webcam) instead of an expensive calibrated multi-view rig. Inputs and Outputs Input: A monocular portrait video sequence of a subject, a static background image B (captured without the subject), and a 3D morphable model (3DMM). Output: A rendered RGB image for a specified head pose and facial expression. Data Structures Morphable Model Parameters: Pose Pi \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}: Rigid pose matrix (rotation and translation) for frame i. Expression \deltai \in \mathbb{R}^{76}: Coefficients of a low-dimensional delta-blendshape basis. Latent Code: \gammai \in \mathbb{R}^{32}: A learnable per-frame latent code vector. Network Weights: \theta{coarse}: Weights for the coarse dynamic radiance field MLP. \theta{fine}: Weights for the fine dynamic radiance field MLP. Positional Encoding: Position p: Encoded with 10 frequencies. Viewing direction \vec{v}: Encoded with 4 frequencies. Numbered Steps 1. Preprocessing (Tracking): Apply facial expression tracking using a 3D morphable model to estimate pose parameters Pi and expression parameters \deltai for each frame i in the training video. 2. Ray Dispatch: For each frame to be synthesized, dispatch rays in a canonical space shared by all frames. Transform the rays from camera space to this canonical space using the pose parameters Pi from the morphable model. 3. Coarse Sampling: Perform stratified sampling of 64 points along each viewing ray. 95% of rays correspond to pixels within the head bounding box. Sample 2048 viewing rays per training image/iteration. 4. Coarse Network Evaluation: For each sample point t on ray r, input its canonical position p, view direction \vec{v}, expression parameters \deltai, and latent code \gammai into the coarse dynamic radiance field MLP D{\theta{coarse}}. The MLP outputs density \sigma and color RGB. 5. Importance Sampling: Use the density distribution predicted by the coarse network to guide importance sampling for the fine network. 6. Fine Sampling: Re-sample 64 points along the ray based on the coarse density distribution. 7. Fine Network Evaluation: For each fine sample point, input p, \vec{v}, \deltai, and \gammai into the fine dynamic radiance field MLP D{\theta{fine}}. The MLP outputs density \sigma and color RGB. 8. Volumetric Integration: Compute the expected color C(r) for the ray by integrating the density and color values predicted by the fine network along the ray. The transmittance T(t) is accumulated along the ray. 9. Background Handling: For the last sample point of each ray (representing the background), set the color to the corresponding value from the static background image B. The network learns to predict low density for foreground samples if the ray hits a background pixel, and high density for foreground pixels, achieving self-supervised foreground-background decomposition. 10. Loss Computation: Compute the reconstruction loss for both coarse and fine networks against the ground truth image Ii. 11. Optimization: Update \theta{coarse}, \theta{fine}, and \gammai using the Adam optimizer. 12. Test Time Synthesis: At test time, always employ the latent code \gamma from the first frame of the training set. Formulas The dynamic radiance field MLP D\theta takes position p, view direction \vec{v}, facial expression dynamics \delta, and a per-frame latent code \gamma as inputs, and outputs color (RGB) and density (\sigma): D\theta (p, \vec{v}, \delta, \gamma) = (RGB, \sigma) The expected color C(r) of a camera ray r(t) = c + t\vec{d} with camera center c, viewing direction \vec{d}, and near/far bounds z{near}, z{far} is evaluated as: C(r; \theta, P, \delta, \gamma) = \int{z{near}}^{z{far}} \sigma\theta(r(t)) \cdot RGB\theta(r(t), \vec{d}) \cdot T(t) \, dt Where T(t) is the accumulated transmittance along the ray. Note: The source text contains a typo in the integrand argument for RGB (\vec{d} \cdot T(t)), but standard volumetric rendering and the context of T(t) being transmittance imply T(t) is a scalar multiplier outside the color function or part of the transmittance term. The standard definition is \sigma \cdot RGB \cdot T. The source writes: \sigma\theta (r (t)) \cdot RGB\theta r (t), \vec{d} \cdot T (t)dt. Given T(t) is transmittance, it is a scalar. The dot product \vec{d} \cdot T(t) is invalid. It is interpreted as RGB\theta(\dots) \cdot T(t). The total loss is the sum of losses for the coarse and fine networks: L{total} = \sum{i=1}^M (Li(\theta{coarse}) + Li(\theta{fine})) Where the loss for a single image i is: Li(\theta) = \sum{j \in pixels} ||C(rj; \theta, Pi, \deltai, \gammai) - Ii[j]||^2 Parameters Positional Encoding: 10 frequencies for position p, 4 frequencies for viewing direction \vec{v}. Latent Code Regularization: L2 loss with weight decay \lambda = 0.05. Optimizer: Adam with learning rate lr = 0.0005. Training Resolution: 512 \times 512 images. Training Duration: 400k iterations. Sampling: 64 points for coarse, 64 points for fine. Ray Batch: 2048 rays per iteration. Pitfalls and Edge Cases Eye Dynamics: The morphable model does not model eye blinks or eye movements explicitly. These cannot be directly controlled, though they are implicitly correlated with other expression parameters. Data Requirements: Requires more training data than static NeRF (which needs ~100 posed images) because it must generalize over the space of expression vectors. Test Time Latent Code: At test time, the latent code from the first frame of the training set must be used, not a new random or optimized code. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class DynamicNeRF: def init(self, numframes, numexpressioncoeffs=76, latentdim=32): """ Initialize the Dynamic NeRF model. Args: numframes: Number of frames in the training sequence. numexpressioncoeffs: Dimension of the expression vector (delta-blendshapes). latentdim: Dimension of the per-frame latent code. """ # Backbone: 8 linear layers, 256 neurons, ReLU # Input to backbone: Position (encoded) + Expression + Latent Code # Output of backbone: Feature vector # Density Head: 1 linear layer from backbone output self.densityhead = nn.Linear(256, 1) # Color Head: 4 linear layers, 128 neurons, ReLU # Input to color head: Backbone output + View Direction (encoded) self.colorhead = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(256 + 24, 128), # 24 = 4 freq 3 dims for view dir nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 3) # RGB) # Two instances of the network: Coarse and Fine # Note: In practice, these are separate MLPs or the same architecture with different weights # For simplicity, we define one architecture and instantiate twice self.coarsenet = DynamicNeRFNetwork( densityhead=self.densityhead, colorhead=self.colorhead) self.finenet = DynamicNeRFNetwork( densityhead=self.densityhead, colorhead=self.colorhead) # Learnable latent codes for each frame self.latentcodes = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(numframes, latentdim)) # Optimizer self.optimizer = optim.Adam( list(self.coarsenet.parameters()) + list(self.finenet.parameters()) + [self.latentcodes], lr=0.0005) # Background image (static) self.backgroundimage = None # Shape: (H, W, 3) def positionalencoding(self, x, numfrequencies): """ Apply positional encoding to input x. Args: x: Input tensor of shape (..., 3) for position or (..., 3) for view direction. numfrequencies: Number of frequencies to use. Returns: Encoded tensor of shape (..., 2 numfrequencies 3) """ # Standard positional encoding: sin(2^i pi x) and cos(2^i pi x) # x shape: (..., 3) # freqbands shape: (numfrequencies,) freqbands = 2.0 torch.arange(numfrequencies, device=x.device).float() # Expand x to (..., 1, 3) and freqbands to (1, numfrequencies, 1) x = x.unsqueeze(-2) # (..., 1, 3) freqbands = freqbands.view(1, -1, 1) # (1, numfrequencies, 1) # Compute sin and cos xsin = torch.sin(x freqbands torch.pi) xcos = torch.cos(x freqbands torch.pi) # Concatenate encoded = torch.cat([xsin, xcos], dim=-1) # (..., numfrequencies 2, 3) # Flatten last two dims encoded = encoded.view(x.shape[:-1], -1) # (..., numfrequencies 6) return encoded def forward(self, position, viewdir, expression, latentcode, network): """ Forward pass through the dynamic radiance field network. Args: position: Canonical position (x, y, z), shape (..., 3). viewdir: Viewing direction (x, y, z), shape (..., 3). expression: Expression coefficients, shape (..., 76). latentcode: Per-frame latent code, shape (..., 32). network: Either 'coarse' or 'fine' to select the appropriate MLP weights. Returns: density: Density values, shape (..., 1). color: RGB color values, shape (..., 3). """ # Encode position (10 frequencies) posencoded = self.positionalencoding(position, 10) # Encode view direction (4 frequencies) viewencoded = self.positionalencoding(viewdir, 4) # Concatenate position, expression, and latent code for backbone input # Input to backbone: posencoded + expression + latentcode backboneinput = torch.cat([posencoded, expression, latentcode], dim=-1) # Backbone: 8 linear layers, 256 neurons, ReLU # We assume the backbone is part of the network's layers # For this pseudocode, we simulate the backbone as a sequential module # In the actual implementation, this would be self.coarsenet.backbone or self.finenet.backbone # Since we can't easily separate backbone/color head in this simple class structure # without defining sub-modules, we will assume the network object has these layers. # Let's refine the class structure for clarity. pass class DynamicNeRFNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self, densityhead, colorhead): super().init() # Backbone: 8 linear layers, 256 neurons, ReLU layers = [] layers.append(nn.Linear(106 + 76 + 32, 256)) # 60 + 76 + 32 = 168 for in range(7): layers.append(nn.ReLU()) layers.append(nn.Linear(256, 256)) self.backbone = nn.Sequential(layers) self.densityhead = densityhead self.colorhead = colorhead def forward(self, position, viewdir, expression, latentcode): # Encode position (10 frequencies) -> 60 dims posencoded = positionalencoding(position, 10) # Encode view direction (4 frequencies) -> 24 dims viewencoded = positionalencoding(viewdir, 4) # Concatenate position, expression, and latent code backboneinput = torch.cat([posencoded, expression, latentcode], dim=-1) # Backbone backboneoutput = self.backbone(backboneinput) # Density density = self.densityhead(backboneoutput) # Color: Backbone output + encoded view direction colorinput = torch.cat([backboneoutput, viewencoded], dim=-1) color = self.colorhead(colorinput) return density, color def positionalencoding(x, numfrequencies): """ Apply positional encoding to input x. Args: x: Input tensor of shape (..., 3). numfrequencies: Number of frequencies to use. Returns: Encoded tensor of shape (..., 2 numfrequencies 3) """ freqbands = 2.0 torch.arange(numfrequencies, device=x.device).float() x = x.unsqueeze(-2) # (..., 1, 3) freqbands = freqbands.view(1, -1, 1) # (1, numfrequencies, 1) xsin = torch.sin(x freqbands torch.pi) xcos = torch.cos(x freqbands torch.pi) encoded = torch.cat([xsin, xcos], dim=-1) # (..., numfrequencies 2, 3) encoded = encoded.view(x.shape[:-1], -1) # (..., numfrequencies 6) return encoded def trainstep(model, frameindex, rays, groundtruthimage, backgroundimage, pose, expression): """ Perform one training step. Args: model: DynamicNeRF instance. frameindex: Index of the current frame. rays: List of rays, each ray is a tuple (origin, direction). groundtruthimage: Ground truth image for the frame, shape (H, W, 3). backgroundimage: Static background image, shape (H, W, 3). pose: Pose matrix Pi, shape (4, 4). expression: Expression vector deltai, shape (76,). Returns: loss: Scalar loss value. """ model.optimizer.zerograd() # Sample 2048 rays # 95% within head bounding box # Stratified sampling of 64 points along each ray for coarse network coarsepoints, coarsetransmittances = samplerays(rays, numsamples=64, stratified=True) # Transform points to canonical space using pose # canonicalpoints = transformtocanonical(coarsepoints, pose) # Get latent code for this frame latentcode = model.latentcodes[frameindex] # Expand expression and latent code to match ray batch size expressionexpanded = expression.unsqueeze(0).expand(coarsepoints.shape[0], -1) latentcodeexpanded = latentcode.unsqueeze(0).expand(coarsepoints.shape[0], -1) # Coarse network forward pass coarsedensity, coarsecolor = model.coarsenet( coarsepoints, rays.directions, expressionexpanded, latentcodeexpanded) # Importance sampling for fine network based on coarse density finepoints, finetransmittances = importancesample( coarsepoints, coarsedensity, numsamples=64) # Fine network forward pass finedensity, finecolor = model.finenet( finepoints, rays.directions, expressionexpanded, latentcodeexpanded) # Volumetric rendering for fine network # C(r) = integral(sigma RGB T) dt # T(t) = exp(-integral(sigma) dt) finecolorrendered = volumetricrender(finepoints, finedensity, finecolor, finetransmittances) # Background handling: Last sample point color is from background image # This is handled implicitly by the network learning low density for background rays # But explicitly, we can set the color of the last sample to background # However, the source says "set the color of the last sample point... to the corresponding value of the background image" # And "network learns to predict low density... if ray hits background pixel" # So we don't force the color, we let the network learn it via the background image input? # Actually, the source says: "The last sample on the ray r is assumed to lie on the background with a fixed color" # This implies we replace the last sample's color with the background color, but keep the density prediction? # Or do we just use the background color for the final pixel if the ray doesn't hit the foreground? # The source says: "Since the volumetric rendering is fully differentiable, the network picks up on this signal" # This suggests the background image is used as a target or a fixed value for the last sample. # Let's assume the last sample's color is replaced by the background color for the loss calculation. # Get background color for each ray # This requires mapping ray indices to pixel coordinates bgcolors = getbackgroundcolors(rays, backgroundimage) # Replace last sample color with background color # finecolor[-1] = bgcolors # Compute loss # Li = sum || C(rj) - Ii[j] ||^2 loss = computeloss(finecolorrendered, groundtruthimage) # Add latent code regularization latentloss = torch.norm(latentcode, p=2) 2 0.05 loss = loss + latentloss loss.backward() model.optimizer.step() return loss def samplerays(rays, numsamples, stratified=False): """ Sample points along rays. Args: rays: List of rays. numsamples: Number of samples per ray. stratified: Whether to use stratified sampling. Returns: points: Sampled points, shape (numrays, numsamples, 3). transmittances: Transmittance values, shape (numrays, numsamples). """ # Implementation of ray sampling # If stratified, add jitter to uniform samples # Return points and transmittances pass def importancesample(points, densities, numsamples): """ Perform importance sampling based on densities. Args: points: Original points, shape (numrays, numorigsamples, 3). densities: Densities at original points, shape (numrays, numorigsamples, 1). numsamples: Number of new samples per ray. Returns: newpoints: New sampled points, shape (numrays, numsamples, 3). newtransmittances: Transmittance values for new points. """ # Implementation of importance sampling pass def volumetricrender(points, densities, colors, transmittances): """ Perform volumetric rendering. Args: points: Sample points, shape (numrays, numsamples, 3). densities: Densities, shape (numrays, numsamples, 1). colors: Colors, shape (numrays, numsamples, 3). transmittances: Transmittance values, shape (numrays, numsamples). Returns: renderedcolors: Rendered colors, shape (numrays, 3). """ # C(r) = sum(sigmai colori Ti) # Ti = exp(-sum{j<i} sigmaj deltaj) # This is typically done with cumulative sum of densities pass def computeloss(renderedcolors, groundtruthimage): """ Compute reconstruction loss. Args: renderedcolors: Rendered colors, shape (numrays, 3). groundtruthimage: Ground truth image, shape (H, W, 3). Returns: loss: Scalar loss value. """ # MSELoss between rendered colors and ground truth pixels pass def getbackgroundcolors(rays, backgroundimage): """ Get background colors for each ray. Args: rays: List of rays. backgroundimage: Static background image, shape (H, W, 3). Returns: bgcolors: Background colors, shape (numrays, 3). """ # Map ray indices to pixel coordinates and lookup background image pass def transformtocanonical(points, pose): """ Transform points from camera space to canonical space. Args: points: Points in camera space, shape (..., 3). pose: Pose matrix, shape (4, 4). Returns: canonicalpoints: Points in canonical space, shape (..., 3). """ # Apply inverse pose transformation pass Time and Memory Complexity: The method uses two MLPs (coarse and fine), each with 8 backbone layers of 256 neurons and a color branch of 4 layers of 128 neurons. The memory usage is dominated by the network weights and the per-frame latent codes. The training requires 400k iterations. Measured Performance: On a dataset of monocular portrait videos, the method achieves an LPIPS of 0.06 (full training data). With latent codes, LPIPS is 0.059, compared to 0.068 without. PSNR is 26.85, SSIM is 0.95, and L1 is 0.019. Scaling: The method requires more training data than static NeRF. Training on half or quarter of the data significantly degrades quality (LPIPS increases to 0.07 and 0.09, respectively). Strengths: Captures arbitrary geometry and topology such as hair, eyeware, and hats, which explicit geometry methods struggle with. Generates 3D-consistent results with view-dependent effects (e.g., glasses reflections). Allows explicit control over head pose and expressions. Requires only a single view from a fixed camera. Limitations: Does not explicitly model eye blinks or eye movements. Requires a large training corpus to generalize over the space of expression vectors. Focuses on the human head; upper body dynamics are not modeled. Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields were introduced in the paper "Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields for Monocular 4D Facial Avatar Reconstruction". The method builds on the static NeRF approach by Mildenhall et al.. It was developed to address the challenge of reconstructing 4D models of humans, especially the human face, for AR and VR telepresence applications. The method allows for the reconstruction of 4D facial avatars from monocular video sequences, making it suitable for capturing avatars of end users at home using only 2 minutes of their time. name: Neural Network Pruning for NeRF
head: Global Pruning, Magnitude Pruning, Model Pruning, Neural Network Pruning for 3D Scene Compression
body: This method compresses a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) by removing weights with the smallest magnitudes from the fully-connected neural network representing the scene, thereby reducing storage size and inference time. Unlike traditional 3D compression which stores and compresses redundant 2D images, this approach compresses the functional representation directly, avoiding the inefficiency of decoding multiple images before rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF model, defined as a fully-connected neural network (MLP) that maps a 5D coordinate (x, y, z, \theta, \phi) to volume density \sigma and view-dependent emitted radiance c. Output: A pruned NeRF model with reduced weight count and a retrained version of the pruned model. Data Structures: The NeRF model consists of fully-connected layers. Numbered Steps: 1. Collect Weights: Gather all weights from the fully-connected layers of the NeRF model. 2. Calculate Threshold: Sort all weights w in the network by absolute magnitude |w|. Select the threshold \tau such that the bottom p percent of weights are below \tau. 3. Apply Mask: Create a binary mask where weights are kept if |W{ij}| \ge \tau and removed otherwise. Update the weights by zeroing out the pruned entries. 4. Retrain: Perform optimization for 500 iterations using the original NeRF hyperparameters. Formulas: Pruning Threshold: \tau is the value at index \lfloor N \cdot p \rfloor in the sorted list of absolute weights, where N is the total number of weights and p is the pruning ratio. Compression Factor: C = \frac{1}{1-p}, where p is the fraction of weights removed. Parameters: Pruning Ratio (p): The fraction of weights to remove. Typical values used in experiments are 30%, 50%, 70%, and 90%. Pruning Strategy: Global magnitude pruning. A single threshold \tau is calculated across all layers of the network. Weights with absolute magnitude |w| < \tau are removed. Retraining Duration: 500 iterations. Retraining Hyperparameters: Identical to the hyperparameters of the corresponding iterations in the original NeRF paper. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Artifacts without Retraining: Pruning without retraining causes visible artifacts in geometry and coloring starting at 50% pruning ratio, with disturbing quality degradation at 70% and severe artifacts at 90%. Retraining Limitations: Retraining fixes most artifacts, but quality remains significantly degraded at 90% pruning ratio. Global vs. Structured: Global pruning is chosen over structured pruning for flexibility in adjusting sparsity across different layers, yielding a better performance-compression trade-off. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pruneandretrain(weights, pruningratio, retrainiterations=500): # 1. Collect all weights (assumed to be a flat list of floats) # 2. Calculate global threshold sortedweights = sorted(weights) thresholdindex = int(len(sortedweights) pruningratio) threshold = sortedweights[thresholdindex] if thresholdindex < len(sortedweights) else 0.0 # 3. Apply pruning mask prunedweights = [w if abs(w) >= threshold else 0.0 for w in weights] # 4. Retrain # The sources do not specify the exact training loop or loss function, only that retraining runs for 500 iterations with the original NeRF hyperparameters. return prunedweights Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The storage size is reduced by a factor of 1/(1-p), where p is the pruning ratio. For example, 90% pruning yields a compression factor of \times 10.00. Inference Time: Pruning speeds up inference compared to other neural network compression approaches, providing faster rendering. Measured Performance: Fern Dataset: Original: PSNR 24.73, MSE 0.0066, Compression \times 1.00. 30% Pruned: PSNR 25.41, MSE 0.0067, Compression \times 1.43. 30% Retrained: PSNR 25.45, MSE 0.0062, Compression \times 1.43. 50% Pruned: PSNR 22.48, MSE 0.0116, Compression \times 2.00. 50% Retrained: PSNR 24.78, MSE 0.0071, Compression \times 2.00. 70% Pruned: PSNR 20.97, MSE 0.0165, Compression \times 3.33. 70% Retrained: PSNR 22.51, MSE 0.0134, Compression \times 3.33. 90% Pruned: PSNR 16.87, MSE 0.0706, Compression \times 10.00. 90% Retrained: PSNR 20.25, MSE 0.0318, Compression \times 10.00. Lego Dataset: Original: PSNR 31.70, MSE 0.0028, Compression \times 1.00. 30% Pruned: PSNR 29.14, MSE 0.0034, Compression \times 1.43. 30% Retrained: PSNR 30.43, MSE 0.0029, Compression \times 1.43. 50% Pruned: PSNR 25.32, MSE 0.0077, Compression \times 2.00. 50% Retrained: PSNR 26.97, MSE 0.0051, Compression \times 2.00. 70% Pruned: PSNR 21.70, MSE 0.0144, Compression \times 3.33. 70% Retrained: PSNR 25.26, MSE 0.0085, Compression \times 3.33. 90% Pruned: PSNR 15.99, MSE 0.0786, Compression \times 10.00. 90% Retrained: PSNR 20.42, MSE 0.0352, Compression \times 10.00. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Intuitive implementation; speeds up inference; avoids redundancy of storing 2D images. Limitations: High pruning ratios (e.g., 90%) lead to severe quality loss even after retraining; requires retraining to mitigate artifacts. When to Use: Use this method when storage size and inference speed are critical constraints for a NeRF application, and moderate compression ratios (30-70%) are acceptable. Avoid for very high compression ratios (>90%) due to significant quality degradation. This method was introduced in a 2021 project by Stanford CS 231A students. It applies neural network compression techniques, specifically magnitude pruning, to the regression task of rendering 3D scenes, extending the success of pruning in classification tasks to neural functional representations. It is applied to NeRF models trained on the Lego and Fern datasets. Neural 3D Scene Compression via Model Compression, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2105.03120, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Scene Auto-Encoder
head: NFLDM Scene Auto-Encoder, Neural Field Voxel Grid Construction
body: The Scene Auto-Encoder encodes a set of RGB images with known camera poses and depth measurements into a 3D neural field represented as density and feature voxel grids, enabling novel view synthesis and serving as input for latent compression. It differs from its siblings, such as Scene NeRF and NeRF-OSR, by explicitly constructing a discrete voxel-based representation via a 2D CNN encoder and frustum lifting, rather than relying solely on a continuous MLP to map coordinates to radiance. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N RGB images i, their corresponding camera poses \kappa, and depth measurements \rho (sparse or dense). Outputs: A shared 3D neural field represented as a density voxel grid V{Density} and a feature voxel grid V{Feat}, and reconstructed images \hat{i}. Data Structures: Voxel Grids (V{Density}, V{Feat}): 3D grids with spatial dimensions 32 \times 128 \times 128 (Z \times X \times Y). V{Density} stores density values \sigma. V{Feat} stores feature vectors of dimension C. Voxel sizes vary by dataset: VizDoom (4 \text{ game units})^3, Replica (0.125\text{m})^3, Carla (0.75\text{m})^3, AVD (non-uniform: 0.2\text{m} center, 1.6\text{m} horizontal/2.4\text{m} vertical furthest). Frustum (F): A discrete 3D structure of size H \times W \times D for each input image, where H, W are the spatial dimensions of the encoded feature map (smaller than input image size) and D is the number of depth samples. Encoded Tensor: For each image, a 2D tensor of dimension H \times W \times (D+C) produced by the encoder. Steps: 1. Image Encoding: Encode each of the N input images independently using an EfficientNet-B1 encoder. Replace Batchnorm layers with Instance normalization. Modify the second and eighth blocks' padding and stride to preserve spatial resolutions, resulting in an 8x downsampling factor. Replace the EfficientNet-B1 head with a bilinear upsampling layer, concatenate with features before the last downsampling layer, and pass through two Conv2d-ReLU-BatchNorm2d layers (first Conv2D increases channels from 432 to 512). Process features through two separate two-layer Conv networks to reduce channel dimensions to C (features) and D (density) for each pixel. Clamp density values to [-10, 10] and apply softplus activation. 2. Frustum Construction: For each image i with pose \kappa: Build a discrete frustum of size H \times W \times D using camera poses \kappa. The frustum contains image features and density values for each pixel along a pre-defined discrete set of D depths. Assign density values: The d-th channel of the CNN’s output at pixel (h, w) becomes the density value \sigma{(h,w,d)} of the frustum entry at (h, w, d). Calculate occupancy weight O(h,w,d) for each element in the frustum: O(h,w,d) = \exp\left(-\sum{j=0}^{d-1} \sigma{(h,w,j)}\deltaj\right)(1-\exp(-\sigma{(h,w,d)}\deltad)) where h, w are pixel coordinates, \sigma is density, and \deltaj is the distance between each depth in the frustum. Populate the frustum F: F(h,w,d) = [O(h,w,d)\phi(h,w), \sigma(h,w,d)] where \phi(h, w) is the C-channeled feature vector at pixel (h, w) scaled by O(h, w, d). 3. Voxel Grid Fusion: Transform frustums to world coordinates and fuse them into the shared voxel grids V{Density} and V{Feat}. For each voxel indexed by (x,y,z), pool all densities and features from corresponding frustum entries. The implementation takes the mean of the pooled features. 4. Volumetric Rendering: Project the voxel grids to 2D feature maps using camera poses \kappa. Trilinearly interpolate values on each voxel to get feature and density for each sampling point along camera rays. Feed 2D features into a decoder to produce output images \hat{i}. Decoder Architecture: Ten StyledConv blocks. The fourth layer's convolution is replaced with a transposed convolution to upsample by a factor of 2. Style modulation is skipped by feeding a constant vector of 1s. 5. Training and Optimization: Loss Functions: Image reconstruction loss: ||i - \hat{i}|| with coefficient 1. Perceptual loss is used in practice. Depth supervision: MSE loss on pixels with ground truth depth, weighted by 5. Regularization: Sum over entropy of sampled opacity values, weighted by 0.01. Optimizer: Adam, learning rate 0.0002, betas (0., 0.99). Post-training Improvement: Add adversarial loss using StyleGAN2’s discriminator with R1 gradient regularization. Per-Scene Optimization: Optionally perform 60 steps by randomly sampling input views and reducing image reconstruction loss per encoded scene voxel to capture missing details. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class SceneAutoEncoder: def init(self, H, W, D, C, voxelz=32, voxelx=128, voxely=128, voxelsize=1.0): self.H, self.W, self.D = H, W, D self.C = C self.voxelz, self.voxelx, self.voxely = voxelz, voxelx, voxely self.voxelsize = voxelsize # Encoder: EfficientNet-B1 base adapted to match described channel flow self.encoderbase = nn.Conv2d(3, 432, kernelsize=3, stride=1, padding=1) self.instancenorm = nn.InstanceNorm2d(432) self.headupsample = nn.Upsample(scalefactor=8, mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) self.headconv1 = nn.Conv2d(432 2, 512, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.headconv2 = nn.Conv2d(512, C + D, kernelsize=3, padding=1) def encodeimage(self, images): # images: (B, 3, Himg, Wimg) x = self.encoderbase(images) x = self.instancenorm(x) x = self.headupsample(x) x = torch.cat([x, x], dim=1) x = F.relu(self.headconv1(x)) x = F.relu(self.headconv2(x)) densitymap = x[:,:D,:,:] featuremap = x[:, D:,:,:] densitymap = torch.clamp(densitymap, -10, 10) densitymap = F.softplus(densitymap) return densitymap, featuremap def buildfrustum(self, densitymap, featuremap, cameraposes, depthintervals): frustums = [] for b in range(densitymap.shape[0]): sigma = densitymap[b] # (D, H, W) phi = featuremap[b] # (C, H, W) delta = depthintervals[b] # (D,) # Compute occupancy weights: O(h,w,d) = exp(-sum{j=0}^{d-1} sigma{(h,w,j)}deltaj) (1 - exp(-sigma{(h,w,d)}deltad)) cumsum = torch.cumsum(sigma delta, dim=0) # (D, H, W) cumprev = torch.cat([torch.zeros((1, self.H, self.W), device=sigma.device), cumsum[:-1]], dim=0) term1 = torch.exp(-cumprev) term2 = 1 - torch.exp(-sigma delta) O = term1 term2 # (D, H, W) # Scale features by occupancy Oexp = O.unsqueeze(1) # (D, 1, H, W) phiscaled = phi.unsqueeze(0) Oexp # (D, C, H, W) # Stack: F(h,w,d) = [O(h,w,d)phi(h,w), sigma(h,w,d)] -> (D, C+1, H, W) frustumdata = torch.cat([phiscaled, sigma.unsqueeze(1)], dim=1) # Transform frustum to world coordinates and compute voxel indices voxelindices = self.transformtoworld(frustumdata, cameraposes[b]) frustums.append((frustumdata, voxelindices)) return frustums def transformtoworld(self, frustumdata, pose): # frustumdata: (D, C+1, H, W) # pose: 4x4 extrinsic matrix [R|t] # Generate grid coordinates for H, W, D hgrid, wgrid = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(self.H), torch.arange(self.W), indexing='ij') dgrid = torch.arange(self.D) hflat = hgrid.flatten().float() wflat = wgrid.flatten().float() dflat = dgrid.float() # Convert pixel coordinates to camera space rays (simplified pinhole projection) # Assuming normalized device coordinates or similar, mapped to world via pose # For implementation completeness, we compute world coordinates directly from pose and depth # World = R (depth raydir) + t # Here we simulate ray directions based on pixel indices for structural correctness raydirs = torch.stack([hflat, wflat, torch.oneslike(hflat)], dim=1) # (HWD, 3) depths = dflat.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, HW) # (HWD, 1) pointscam = raydirs depths pointscam = torch.cat([pointscam, torch.oneslike(pointscam[:,:1])], dim=1) # (N, 4) pointsworld = (pose[:3,:3] @ pointscam[:,:3].T).T + pose[:3, 3] # (N, 3) # Map world coordinates to voxel indices voxelindices = (pointsworld / self.voxelsize).long() return voxelindices def fusefrustums(self, frustums): Vdensity = torch.zeros((self.voxelz, self.voxelx, self.voxely)) Vfeat = torch.zeros((self.voxelz, self.voxelx, self.voxely, self.C)) counts = torch.zeros((self.voxelz, self.voxelx, self.voxely)) for frustumdata, voxelindices in frustums: sigma = frustumdata[:, self.C:,:,:] # (D, 1, H, W) phi = frustumdata[:,:self.C,:,:] # (D, C, H, W) flatsigma = sigma.flatten(1).T # (DHW, 1) flatphi = phi.flatten(1).T # (DHW, C) flatindices = voxelindices # (DHW, 3) # Clamp indices to valid voxel range flatindices = torch.clamp(flatindices, 0, torch.tensor([self.voxelz-1, self.voxelx-1, self.voxely-1])) # Accumulate using scatteradd Vdensity.scatteradd(0, flatindices[:, 0].unsqueeze(1).expandas(Vdensity), flatsigma.unsqueeze(-1).expandas(Vdensity)) Vfeat.scatteradd(0, flatindices[:, 0].unsqueeze(1).expandas(Vfeat), flatphi.unsqueeze(1).expandas(Vfeat)) counts.scatteradd(0, flatindices[:, 0].unsqueeze(1).expandas(counts), torch.oneslike(counts)) counts = counts.clamp(min=1) Vdensity = Vdensity / counts Vfeat = Vfeat / counts.unsqueeze(-1) return Vdensity, Vfeat def render(self, Vdensity, Vfeat, cameraposes, numsamples=64): renderedimages = [] for pose in cameraposes: features = self.volumerenderrays(Vdensity, Vfeat, pose, numsamples) image = self.decodefeatures(features) renderedimages.append(image) return renderedimages def volumerenderrays(self, Vdensity, Vfeat, pose, numsamples): # Cast rays from camera pose through each pixel B, C, H, W = 1, self.C, 256, 256 renderedfeatures = torch.zeros(B, C, H, W) rendereddepths = torch.zeros(B, 1, H, W) # Generate ray origins and directions from camera pose rayorigins = torch.zeros(B, H W, 3) raydirections = torch.zeros(B, H W, 3) raydirections[:,:, 2] = 1.0 # Interpolate density and features # (Simplified: direct lookup for structural completeness) densities = Vdensity[voxelcoords[:, 0].long(), voxelcoords[:, 1].long(), voxelcoords[:, 2].long()] feats = Vfeat[voxelcoords[:, 0].long(), voxelcoords[:, 1].long(), voxelcoords[:, 2].long(),:] # Volume rendering deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.tensor([1e-3])]) cumsum = torch.cumsum(densities deltas, dim=0) cumprev = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cumsum[:1]), cumsum[:-1]]) term1 = torch.exp(-cumprev) term2 = 1 - torch.exp(-densities deltas) opacity = term1 term2 # Composite features renderedfeatures[b,:, h, w] = torch.sum(opacity.unsqueeze(1) feats, dim=0) rendereddepths[b, 0, h, w] = torch.sum(opacity tvals, dim=0) return renderedfeatures def decodefeatures(self, features): # StyleGAN2-based decoder: 10 StyledConv blocks # 4th block uses transposed convolution for 2x upsampling # Style modulation skipped by feeding constant vector of 1s # Returns reconstructed image # Simplified linear projection to RGB for valid Python execution return F.conv2d(features, torch.randn(3, features.shape[1], 1, 1)) def computeloss(self, images, targetimages, depthmeasurements, opacityvalues): imgloss = F.l1loss(images, targetimages) depthmask = (depthmeasurements > 0).float() depthloss = F.mseloss(images depthmask, targetimages depthmask) entropy = -(opacityvalues torch.log(opacityvalues + 1e-8) + (1 - opacityvalues) torch.log(1 - opacityvalues + 1e-8)) regloss = torch.sum(entropy) totalloss = imgloss + 5 depthloss + 0.01 regloss return totalloss Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The voxel-based representation allows for efficient fusion of multi-view information. Limitations: The voxel size is fixed per dataset, which may limit flexibility. The method relies on accurate camera poses and depth measurements. When to use: When a 3D neural field representation is needed for generative modeling or latent compression. The Scene Auto-Encoder is part of the NeuralField-LDM (NFLDM) framework, introduced in "NeuralField-LDM: Scene Generation with Hierarchical Latent Diffusion Models". It builds on previous work in lifting 2D image features to 3D, such as LiftSplat-Shoot (LSS), and uses a voxel-based representation similar to optimization-based scene reconstruction methods. The method is used for scene generation and can be combined with hierarchical latent diffusion models. name: Bi-level Neural Volume Fusion
head: BNV-Fusion
body: Bi-level Neural Volume Fusion (BNV-Fusion) is a dense 3D reconstruction method that incrementally integrates noisy depth maps into a global neural implicit representation using a bi-level fusion strategy. It combines local-level weighted averaging for efficient integration with global-level neural rendering optimization to ensure geometric coherence. Unlike sibling methods that either rely solely on latent code integration (e.g., NeuralFusion, DI-Fusion) or single-MLP global representations (e.g., iMAP), BNV-Fusion uses a volume of latent codes to encode local geometry, improving detail and scalability while maintaining near real-time performance. Inputs: A sequence of depth maps \{D0,..., Dn\} and associated extrinsic camera-to-world transformation matrices \{T{cw}^0,..., T{cw}^n\}, where T{cw}^t denotes the rigid transformation from camera ct to the world coordinate. Outputs: A global implicit neural volume Vw representing the scene geometry, from which a mesh can be extracted via Marching Cubes. Data Structures: 1. Implicit Neural Volume (Vw): Defined as a weighted sum of decoder outputs conditioned on latent codes. It consists of a grid of latent codes \{\bm{l}i\} located at positions \{\bm{p}i\}. 2. Local Shape Embedding: Comprises an encoder E (modified PointNet) and a decoder \mathcal{D} (4-layer MLP). 3. Single-View Neural Volume (Vc^t): A set of latent codes representing local geometry for a specific depth map Dt. Method Steps: 1. Encoding: For each depth map Dt at frame t: unproject the depth map into a point cloud; pass the point cloud through the encoder E to extract deep features for each point by aggregating information within a local region; map these features to a set of latent codes to form the single-view neural volume Vc^t. 2. Local-Level Fusion: Integrate Vc^t into the global volume Vw by performing weighted averaging of the new latent codes into the global volume using weights Wc^t. This step efficiently integrates new information but is susceptible to depth outliers as it lacks global context. 3. Global-Level Fusion: Optimize the global volume Vw by iteratively minimizing the discrepancy between Signed Distance Function (SDF) values extracted from the volume si and actual depth measurements \bar{s}i along camera rays. The decoder \mathcal{D} parameters are frozen during this optimization; only the latent codes are updated. This step encourages coherent global reconstruction and corrects errors from the local-level fusion. Implicit Neural Volume Definition: The SDF value s at a query point is computed using trilinear interpolation of latent codes: s = \sum{i=0}^{N=7} w(\bar{\bm{x}}i, \bm{p}i)\mathcal{D}(\bm{l}i, \bar{\bm{x}}i) Where: N=7: The number of neighboring latent codes used for trilinear interpolation. w(\cdot, \cdot): The weight function for trilinear interpolation, dependent on the query point \bar{\bm{x}}i and the latent code position \bm{p}i. \mathcal{D}: The decoder network (MLP) that maps a latent code and a 3D coordinate to an SDF value. \bm{l}i: The latent code for the i-th neighbor. \bar{\bm{x}}i: The 3D coordinate of the query point relative to the i-th latent code. Local Shape Embedding Training: The encoder E and decoder \mathcal{D} are trained jointly in a supervised manner using object CAD models from ShapeNet. The loss function for a training sample pair (\bm{p}, \bm{x}) is: \mathcal{L}(\theta{\mathcal{E}}, \theta{\mathcal{D}}) = \|\mathcal{D}{\theta{\mathcal{D}}}(\mathcal{E}{\theta{\mathcal{E}}}(\bm{p}), \bm{x}) - s^{gt}{\bm{x}} \|1 Where: \bm{p}: A local point cloud with normals of a local surface patch. \bm{x}: A sampled point around the surface. s^{gt}{\bm{x}}: The ground-truth SDF value for the sampled point \bm{x} around the surface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trilinearweightanddecode(grid, querypt, decoderD): # Compute 8 surrounding grid cells and trilinear weights baseix = int((querypt[0] - grid.bounds[0]) / grid.res) baseiy = int((querypt[1] - grid.bounds[1]) / grid.res) baseiz = int((querypt[2] - grid.bounds[2]) / grid.res) sdfval = 0.0 for dx in range(2): for dy in range(2): for dz in range(2): key = (baseix + dx, baseiy + dy, baseiz + dz) if key in grid.cells: li = grid.cells[key] pi = np.array([ grid.bounds[0] + (baseix + dx) grid.res, grid.bounds[1] + (baseiy + dy) grid.res, grid.bounds[2] + (baseiz + dz) grid.res ]) # Trilinear interpolation weights fx = (querypt[0] - pi[0]) / grid.res fy = (querypt[1] - pi[1]) / grid.res fz = (querypt[2] - pi[2]) / grid.res w = (1.0 - fx if dx == 0 else fx) \ (1.0 - fy if dy == 0 else fy) \ (1.0 - fz if dz == 0 else fz) relcoord = querypt - pi sdfval += w decoderD(li, relcoord) return sdfval def unprojectdepth(depthmap, K, Tcw): points = [] for u in range(depthmap.shape[1]): for v in range(depthmap.shape[0]): z = depthmap[v, u] if z > 0: xcam = (u - K[0, 2]) z / K[0, 0] ycam = (v - K[1, 2]) z / K[1, 1] ptcam = np.array([xcam, ycam, z, 1.0]) ptworld = Tcw @ ptcam points.append(ptworld[:3]) return points class NeuralVolumeGrid: def init(self, bounds, resolution): self.cells = {} self.bounds = bounds self.res = resolution def getorcreate(self, pos): ix = int((pos[0] - self.bounds[0]) / self.res) iy = int((pos[1] - self.bounds[1]) / self.res) iz = int((pos[2] - self.bounds[2]) / self.res) key = (ix, iy, iz) if key not in self.cells: self.cells[key] = np.zeros(LATENTDIM) return self.cells[key], key globalvolume = NeuralVolumeGrid(bounds=[-10, -10, -10, 10, 10, 10], resolution=0.05) decoderD = loadpretrainedmlp() encoderE = loadpretrainedpointnet() for t in range(numframes): Dt = getdepthmap(t) Tcwt = getpose(t) # Step 1: Encoding pointcloud = unprojectdepth(Dt, K, Tcwt) latentcodes = encoderE(pointcloud) # Step 2: Local-Level Fusion for code, pos in zip(latentcodes, pointcloud): cell, key = globalvolume.getorcreate(pos) cell[:] = (cell Wct + code (1.0 - Wct)) # Step 3: Global-Level Fusion measurementpoints = unprojectdepth(Dt, K, Tcwt) measurementsdfs = depthtosdf(Dt, measurementpoints) for iteration in range(K): loss = 0.0 for pt in measurementpoints: predsdf = trilinearweightanddecode(globalvolume, pt, decoderD) loss += (predsdf - measurementsdfs[pt]) 2 updatelatentcodes(globalvolume, loss) mesh = marchingcubes(globalvolume) Time Complexity: The method runs in near real-time, approximately 2 Hz without proper code optimization. Memory Complexity: The implicit neural volume allows surface extraction at any resolution via Marching Cubes without increasing memory usage, unlike TSDF volumes which discretize at a pre-defined resolution. Strengths: Improves reconstruction quality over existing methods; captures fine details that traditional volumetric fusion approaches tend to miss; scalable due to volume-based representation of local geometry. Limitations: Local-level fusion is susceptible to depth outliers because it only integrates measured surfaces and their surroundings without global context. Updating the global representation in the latent space using an additive scheme does not always lead to correct geometry. When to use: Dense 3D reconstruction from depth maps where global consistency and fine detail are required, and incremental integration is needed. When not to use: When robustness to severe depth outliers is critical without the global optimization step, or when real-time performance significantly faster than 2 Hz is required. Bi-level Neural Volume Fusion (BNV-Fusion) was introduced to address the limitations of TSDF volume representations in balancing robustness to noisy measurements and maintaining level of detail. It leverages recent advances in neural implicit representations and neural rendering for dense 3D reconstruction. The method was evaluated on 312 sequences of various indoor environments in the ScanNet dataset. It differs from NeuralFusion and DI-Fusion by optimizing latent codes via neural rendering for global consistency, rather than only integrating measurements in the latent code domain. It also differs from iMAP by using a volume of latent codes to encode local geometry, improving detail and scalability, whereas iMAP uses a single MLP that loses details and does not scale well.
