name: Neural Radiance Field Codebooks (NRC)
body: Neural Radiance Field Codebooks (NRC) is a scalable method for learning object-centric representations through novel view reconstruction, enabling the discovery of reoccurring visual and geometric patterns across scenes. It differs from standard NeRF by mapping continuous spatial features to a discrete, finite codebook of object categories, which allows for constant rendering compute regardless of object count and supports an unbounded number of objects per scene. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Input image Ih \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W}, novel view image I'h \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W}, relative camera pose between input and novel view. Outputs: Rendered novel view image, object codes L, encoder parameters \theta, variation module parameters. Data Structures: Codebook L: A set of k categorical object codes li \in \mathbb{R}^d. Spatial Feature Map fh: Output of encoder F\theta, shape \mathbb{R}^{d \times H/k \times W/k}. Variation Module: A convolutional network that transforms categorical codes and feature vectors into fine-grained instance codes. Parameters: k: Codebook size (number of codes). Depends on scene complexity and is dynamically added. \lambda: Scaling hyperparameter for adding new codes. \theta: Encoder parameters. Steps: 1. Encoding: Process input image Ih through convolutional network F\theta to obtain spatial feature map fh \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times H/k \times W/k}. 2. Projection: For each point (x, y, z) in world coordinates of the novel view, project to camera coordinates (x, y) in the input frame using the relative camera pose. 3. Feature Selection: Select the spatial feature f{h{x,y}} \in \mathbb{R}^d from the patch in fh that contains the projected coordinates (x, y). 4. Code Assignment (Inference): Assign a code l^ from the shared codebook L to the feature f{h{x,y}} using arg max 1-nearest-neighbors with Straight-Through Estimator (STE). 5. Code Assignment (Backward Pass): Use a softmax relaxation of nearest-neighbors during the backward pass in conjunction with STE to enable learning of the codebook elements. 6. Variation Encoding: Pass the assigned categorical code l^ and the original feature vector f{h{x,y}} to the Variation Module to transform them into fine-grained instance codes. 7. Rendering: Condition a volumetric renderer on the instance code, view direction, and positional encodings to render the scene region from the novel view. 8. Loss Calculation: Compare the rendered image to the ground truth novel view using L2 pixel loss. 9. Optimization: Learn the categorical codes, assignment mechanism, and volumetric renderer jointly in an end-to-end fashion. 10. Dynamic Codebook Expansion: Add new codes to L using step functions with STE to handle scene complexity. Formulas: Inference Assignment (STE): l^(x, y) \leftarrow \arg \max{li; i \in [k]} \frac{e^{-\|li - f{h{x,y}}\|^2}}{\sum{j=1}^k e^{-\|lj - f{h{x,y}}\|^2}} \quad \text{(STE)} \quad The source labels this as arg max but provides a softmax-like numerator/denominator structure in Eq 1, applying STE. Backward Pass Assignment (Softmax Relaxation): l{back}(x, y) \leftarrow \frac{e^{-\|li - f{h{x,y}}\|^2}}{\sum{j=1}^k e^{-\|lj - f{h{x,y}}\|^2}} \quad The source uses li in the numerator but implies the specific assigned code's contribution or the full softmax distribution for gradient flow. Dynamic Code Addition: li \leftarrow T\left(\sigma(s - i / \lambda)\right) \cdot li; \quad T(a, t):= \begin{cases} 1, & a > t \\ 0, & a \le t \end{cases} \quad Where T is a binarization function in the forward pass and lets gradients pass through using STE in the back pass. \sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid function, \lambda is a scaling hyperparameter. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class STEAssign(torch.autograd.Function): @staticmethod def forward(ctx, features, codes): dists = torch.cdist(features, codes) # (N, k) probs = torch.softmax(-dists, dim=1) # Softmax relaxation for backward indices = torch.argmax(probs, dim=1) # Argmax for forward selected = codes[indices] # Straight-through: forward uses hard assignment ctx.saveforbackward(probs) return selected, indices @staticmethod def backward(ctx, gradselected, gradindices): probs, = ctx.savedtensors # Gradients flow through the softmax relaxation return probs @ gradselected, None def projecttocamera(worldpts, campose): """Projects world coordinates (N,3) to camera 2D coordinates (N,2) using relative pose.""" ones = torch.ones(worldpts.size(0), 1, device=worldpts.device) homopts = torch.cat([worldpts, ones], dim=1) # (N, 4) campts = (campose @ homopts.T).T # (N, 4) return campts[:,:2] / campts[:, 3:4] # (N, 2) normalized coordinates def samplefeatures(featuremap, camcoords): """Samples features from spatial map at normalized camera coordinates (N,2).""" # Normalize to [-1, 1] for gridsample normcoords = 2.0 camcoords - 1.0 normcoords = normcoords.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) # (N, 1, 1, 2) # featuremap: (B, d, H/k, W/k) sampled = F.gridsample(featuremap, normcoords, aligncorners=True) return sampled.squeeze(-1).squeeze(-1).permute(0, 2, 1) # (B, N, d) class NRC: def init(self, encoder, variationmodule, renderer, codebooksize=10, lambdaparam=1.0, d=64): self.encoder = encoder self.variationmodule = variationmodule self.renderer = renderer self.codebooksize = codebooksize self.lambdaparam = lambdaparam self.d = d self.codes = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(codebooksize, d)) self.stepcounter = 0 def encode(self, image): return self.encoder(image) def assigncodes(self, features, codes): return STEAssign.apply(features, codes) def addcode(self, s): """Dynamically adds/gates codes using step functions with STE.""" indices = torch.arange(self.codes.size(0), device=self.codes.device) gate = torch.sigmoid(s - indices / self.lambdaparam) # Forward: binarize, backward: pass gradient through sigmoid gatehard = (gate > 0.5).float() self.codes = gatehard.unsqueeze(1) self.codes return self.codes def render(self, instancecodes, viewdirs, positions): return self.renderer(instancecodes, viewdirs, positions) def trainstep(self, inputimage, novelviewimage, camerapose, novelviewpoints): # 1. Encode fh = self.encode(inputimage) # 2. Project camcoords = projecttocamera(novelviewpoints, camerapose) # 3. Select features features = samplefeatures(fh, camcoords) # 4. Assign codes (Inference forward pass) selectedcodes, indices = self.assigncodes(features, self.codes) # 5. Variation Module instancecodes = self.variationmodule(selectedcodes, features) # 6. Render viewdirs = novelviewpoints # Simplified: using positions as view directions for illustration renderedimage = self.render(instancecodes, viewdirs, novelviewpoints) # 7. Loss loss = F.mseloss(renderedimage, novelviewimage) # 8. Backward pass uses softmax relaxation via STEAssign loss.backward() return loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-differentiable Assignment: The nearest-neighbor assignment used during inference is non-differentiable, preventing gradient propagation to the encoder and codebook. This is mitigated by using STE and softmax relaxation during the backward pass. Dynamic Codebook: Learning when to add new codes is non-trivial because the number and selection of codes is discrete and non-differentiable. This is addressed using step functions with STE. Time Complexity: Constant rendering compute, whereas other methods' computational cost grows linearly with the number of objects. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables constant rendering compute; allows an unbounded number of objects per scene; discovers reoccurring visual and geometric patterns across scenes; transfers well to object navigation and unsupervised segmentation. Limitations: Dynamic codebook addition is complex due to discrete nature; requires joint optimization of encoder, codebook, and renderer. When to use: When object-centric representation is needed, especially for scenes with many objects or varying complexity, and when transferability to downstream tasks like navigation or segmentation is desired. When not to use: When scene complexity is low and constant compute is not a priority, or when a fixed number of objects is sufficient and known a priori. NRC was introduced in 2023 by authors associated with ICLR 2023. It builds on Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). It addresses limitations of current 3D object-centric methods, such as fixed hyper-parameters for object count and scaling computational cost with object number. It is evaluated on unsupervised segmentation, object navigation, and depth ordering tasks on synthetic (THOR/ProcTHOR) and real (NYU Depth) scenes. name: Neural Implicit SLAM
head: NeRF-SLAM, Implicit Neural SLAM, Neural Field SLAM
body: Neural Implicit SLAM is a simultaneous localization and mapping technique that constructs a continuous 3D scene representation using a neural network F mapping spatial coordinates to scene properties, while simultaneously optimizing camera poses Tt. It differs from explicit grid-based SLAM (e.g., Dense Grid SLAM) by offering resolution-independent geometry and from traditional feature-based SLAM (e.g., ORB-SLAM) by leveraging dense photometric and geometric constraints for tracking. Unlike Gaussian Splatting SLAM, which uses explicit parametric primitives, this family relies on implicit neural fields, allowing for smoother surface representations and easier integration of semantic information, though often at higher computational cost during initialization. The family relies on a neural network F that maps spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} to scene properties. For appearance, F outputs color \mathbf{c} and volume density \sigma (or occupancy). For geometry, F may output a Signed Distance Function (SDF) value. Rendering is performed via volume rendering or ray marching: points are sampled along camera rays, properties are predicted by F, and results are aggregated using alpha compositing or weighted sums. Optimization jointly updates the network weights and camera poses Tt to minimize photometric (\ell{rgb}) and geometric (\ell{depth} or SDF) losses. This method implements a real-time RGB-D SLAM framework that optimizes an implicit neural representation using hybrid spatial encodings (combining dense or hash grids with tri-planes) and a composite loss function tailored for tracking and mapping. It solves the problem of efficient, high-accuracy scene reconstruction and pose estimation by jointly optimizing the neural implicit function and camera poses using cached sampled rays. Unlike pure neural implicit methods which may suffer from high memory usage or slow convergence, this approach uses explicit hybrid encoding to accelerate feature lookup while maintaining the continuous representation benefits of neural fields. See Hybrid Implicit Neural Representation SLAM Sampling & Optimization for implementation details. SLAIM is a SLAM method that introduces a coarse-to-fine tracking pipeline and improves photometric bundle adjustment for NeRF-based mapping. It maintains NeRF’s original volume density formulation while introducing a KL regularization over the ray termination distribution. This addresses the challenge of high-frequency renderings in NeRF hindering image alignment. SNI-SLAM is a dense NeRF-based RGB-D SLAM system for accurate real-time 3D semantic mapping. It introduces a hierarchical semantic encoding and cross-attention mechanism to enable mutual reinforcement between appearance, geometry, and semantics modalities. It further proposes a novel one-way decoder design to enhance inter-modal information flow without reverse interference. KN-SLAM is a NeRF-based SLAM method that integrates local feature correspondences for coarse pose initialization and joint optimization. It uses global image features and local matches for explicit loop detection. It performs pose graph optimization and global refinement of the neural map to ensure consistency. VI-NeRF-SLAM merges traditional SLAM method benefits with NeRF mapping to facilitate immediate, dense 3D scene reconstruction online without prior training. It estimates pixel depth and pose based on constraints in reprojecting feature points. It refines the depiction of 3D scenes through the use of ray integration and networks. It includes a dynamic error correction technique for IMUs. It includes a method for managing closed loops in NeRF mapping. It surpasses current benchmark techniques in reconstruction and tracking precision on Euroc and Replica datasets, particularly in scenarios limited to grayscale imagery. NeRF-SLAM Problem Formulation defines the task as a continuous online learning problem where a stream of synchronized RGB-D input frames is processed to optimize a neural implicit function F and camera pose Tt using cached sampled rays. For each pixel \mathbf{x} in an RGB-D frame, N points are sampled along the camera ray, each at distance di with position \mathbf{p}i. Appearance \mathbf{c}i and geometric properties gi are predicted for each sample point \mathbf{p}i using the learnable neural implicit function F: (\mathbf{c}i, gi) = F(\mathbf{p}i) The weight wi for each sample is determined by a geometric rendering function G applied to the geometric properties: wi = G(gi) Rendered color and depth are computed as weighted sums: \tilde{\mathbf{c}}{\mathbf{x}} = \sum{i=1}^N wi \cdot \mathbf{c}i, \quad \tilde{d}{\mathbf{x}} = \sum{i=1}^N wi \cdot di Optimization minimizes photometric and geometric constraints: e^p{\mathbf{x}} = \tilde{\mathbf{c}}{\mathbf{x}} - \mathbf{c}{\mathbf{x}} and e^g{\mathbf{x}} = \tilde{d}{\mathbf{x}} - d{\mathbf{x}}. The weight is formulated as wi = G(F{geo}(\mathbf{p}i)), where F \in \mathcal{F} and G \in \mathcal{G}. SE3 is a method that addresses loop closure correction for implicit maps by implementing an equivariant mapping from SE3 to feature space, synchronously adjusting camera poses and implicit map representations. It leverages the frontend localization module of ORB-SLAM2 and uses a voxel grid as the backend to construct a SLAM system that achieves loop closure correction for implicit maps. Neural Implicit SLAM emerged from the integration of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) with traditional SLAM pipelines. Early works focused on offline reconstruction, but real-time RGB-D SLAM variants like the one described in introduced hybrid encodings (hash grids/tri-planes) to accelerate training. The problem formulation as a continuous online learning task with cached rays was formalized in. Variants like SLAIM and SNI-SLAM addressed specific issues like high-frequency rendering artifacts and semantic consistency. VI-NeRF-SLAM extended this to monocular/IMU scenarios with dynamic error correction. SE3 tackled the irreversibility of implicit maps for loop closure. The family is widely used in robotics for dense 3D mapping where explicit geometry is difficult to maintain. name: Hybrid Implicit Neural Representation SLAM Sampling & Optimization
head: Dense Grid + Tri-Plane SLAM, Hash + Tri-Plane SLAM
body: This method implements a real-time RGB-D SLAM framework that optimizes an implicit neural representation using hybrid spatial encodings (combining dense or hash grids with tri-planes) and a composite loss function tailored for tracking and mapping. It solves the problem of efficient, high-accuracy scene reconstruction and pose estimation by jointly optimizing the neural implicit function and camera poses using cached sampled rays. Unlike pure neural implicit methods which may suffer from high memory usage or slow convergence, this approach uses explicit hybrid encoding to accelerate feature lookup while maintaining the continuous representation benefits of neural fields. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A stream of synchronized RGB-D frames. The first frame provides the initial pose. Subsequent frames provide RGB images and depth maps. Outputs: Optimized camera poses Tt, and the parameters of the hybrid neural representation (grid features and MLP weights). Data Structures: The system uses a hybrid spatial encoding F composed of two parts: 1. Coarse/Fine Spatial Splitting: Two resolution levels are used. Coarse resolution: 24 cm. Fine resolution: 2 cm. Each level stores 2 feature dimensions. Features are concatenated into a 4-dimensional vector. 2. Tri-Plane or Hash Grid: The 4D vector is processed by decoders. Dense Grid variant: Uses a dense 3D grid for the coarse/fine features. Hash Grid variant: Uses a hash table for the coarse/fine features. 3. Decoders: Two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), one for color and one for geometry (SDF). Structure: 2 layers, 32 hidden channels. Input: The 4-dimensional concatenated feature vector. Output: Color \mathbf{c} and SDF value \tilde{s} (or density). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the system with the first posed RGB-D frame. Run optimization for 500 iterations (or 1000 for high-accuracy benchmarks). During initialization, sample pixels and optimize the network weights and initial grid features. 2. Tracking (Pose Estimation): For each new frame, run optimization for 20 iterations (or 30 for benchmarks). Sample 1024 pixels (or 2048 for benchmarks). Optimize camera poses Tt while keeping the neural representation fixed or lightly updated. 3. Mapping (Scene Reconstruction): For each new frame, run optimization for 20 iterations (or 30 for benchmarks). Sample 2048 pixels (or 4080 for benchmarks). Optimize neural representation parameters (grid features and MLP weights) and potentially camera poses. 4. Keyframe Selection: Define a keyframe as every 5th input frame. Randomly sample 5% of pixels from keyframes and store them for global bundle adjustment. 5. Ray Sampling: For each sampled pixel \mathbf{x}, select N=60 coordinates along the camera ray. The sampling strategy depends on the presence of depth information: With Depth: Uniformly sample 12 coordinates within the truncated region (distance T=10 cm from the surface). Draw an additional 48 coordinates uniformly from the free space (between camera center and truncation boundary). Without Depth: Uniformly sample all 60 points along the ray. 6. Neural Prediction: For each sample point \mathbf{p}i at distance di, query the hybrid encoder to get the feature vector. Pass the feature vector through the color decoder to get \mathbf{c}i. Pass the feature vector through the geometry decoder to get the SDF value \tilde{s}i. 7. Loss Computation: Compute photometric loss \mathcal{L}p. Compute geometric/depth loss \mathcal{L}g. Compute SDF loss for the truncated region \mathcal{L}{sdf}^t and \mathcal{L}{sdf}^c. Compute free space loss \mathcal{L}{fs}. 8. Optimization: Minimize the total loss \mathcal{L} using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). Formulas: Photometric Loss: \mathcal{L}p = \frac{1}{\mathcal{M}} \sum{\mathbf{x}} (e^p{\mathbf{x}})^2 where \mathcal{M} is the global list of sampling pixels (e.g., keyframes), and e^p{\mathbf{x}} = \tilde{c}{\mathbf{x}} - c{\mathbf{x}} is the color error. Geometric/Depth Loss: \mathcal{L}g = \frac{1}{\mathcal{M}{sub}} \sum{\mathbf{x}} (e^g{\mathbf{x}})^2 where \mathcal{M}{sub} is the subset of pixels with non-zero depth values, and e^g{\mathbf{x}} = \tilde{d}{\mathbf{x}} - d{\mathbf{x}} is the depth error. SDF Error Constraint: e^{sdf}i = di + \tilde{s}i \cdot T - dx where di is the depth of the sample point, \tilde{s}i is the predicted SDF, T is the truncation distance, and dx is the observed depth. SDF Loss (Truncated Region): \mathcal{L}{sdf} = \frac{1}{\mathcal{M}{sub}} \sum{\mathbf{x}} \frac{1}{\mathcal{P}^T} \sum{i \in \mathcal{P}^T} (e^{sdf}i)^2 where \mathcal{P}^T are points satisfying |dx - di| < T. Note: The total SDF loss is split into two parts with different weights: \lambdat for points near the truncation boundary and \lambdac for points close to the surface. The formula above represents the general form; the specific weights are applied in the total objective. Free Space Error: e^{fs}x = \tilde{s}x - 1 applied to points i \in \mathcal{P}^{fs} in the area between the camera center and the truncation boundary T. Free Space Loss: \mathcal{L}{fs} = \frac{1}{\mathcal{M}{sub}} \sum{\mathbf{x}} \frac{1}{\mathcal{P}^{fs}} \sum{i \in \mathcal{P}^{fs}} (e^{fs}i)^2 Total Objective: \mathcal{L} = \lambdap \mathcal{L}p + \lambdag \mathcal{L}g + \lambdat \mathcal{L}{sdf}^t + \lambdac \mathcal{L}{sdf}^c + \lambda{fs} \mathcal{L}{fs} Parameters: T (Truncation distance): 10 cm. \lambdap (Photometric loss weight): 5. \lambdag (Rendered depth loss weight): 1. \lambdat (SDF loss weight for points near truncation boundary): 200. \lambdac (SDF loss weight for points close to surface): 50. \lambda{fs} (Free space loss weight): 10. Feature dimensions: 2 per resolution level (Coarse 24cm, Fine 2cm), concatenated to 4D. MLP hidden channels: 32. MLP layers: 2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridslamoptimization(framestream): # Initialization firstframe = framestream[0] poseT = estimatepose(firstframe) # Initial pose from first frame gridfeatures = initializegridfeatures() # Dense or Hash grid colormlp = initializemlp() geomlp = initializemlp() # Optimization for initialization for iter in range(1000): # 500 for standard, 1000 for high-accuracy pixels = samplepixels(firstframe, count=2048) # Use higher count for init loss = computeloss(pixels, poseT, gridfeatures, colormlp, geomlp, T=0.1) optimize(loss, [gridfeatures, colormlp, geomlp]) keyframes = [] for frame in framestream[1:]: # Tracking trackingpixels = samplepixels(frame, count=1024) # 2048 for benchmarks for iter in range(20): # 30 for benchmarks loss = computeloss(trackingpixels, poseT, gridfeatures, colormlp, geomlp, T=0.1) optimize(loss, [poseT]) # Optimize pose only # Mapping mappingpixels = samplepixels(frame, count=2048) # 4080 for benchmarks for iter in range(20): # 30 for benchmarks loss = computeloss(mappingpixels, poseT, gridfeatures, colormlp, geomlp, T=0.1) optimize(loss, [gridfeatures, colormlp, geomlp]) # Optimize scene # Keyframe selection if frame.index % 5 == 0: keyframes.append(frame) storedpixels = randomsamplepixels(frame, count=0.05 totalpixels) # Store for global bundle adjustment later return poseT, gridfeatures, colormlp, geomlp def computeloss(pixels, poseT, gridfeatures, colormlp, geomlp, T): totalloss = 0 photometricloss = 0 geometricloss = 0 sdflosst = 0 sdflossc = 0 freespaceloss = 0 countp = 0 countfs = 0 countt = 0 countc = 0 for pixel in pixels: ray = generateray(pixel, poseT) samples = samplealongray(ray, N=60, hasdepth=pixel.hasdepth, T=T) for sample in samples: pi = sample.position di = sample.distance # Query hybrid encoder featurevector = queryhybridencoder(pi, gridfeatures) # Predict properties ci = colormlp(featurevector) si = geomlp(featurevector) # Compute errors if pixel.hasdepth: # SDF Error sdferror = di + si T - pixel.depth if abs(pixel.depth - di) < T: # Truncated region if di is close to surface: sdflossc += sdferror2 countc += 1 else: sdflosst += sdferror2 countt += 1 else: # Free space freespaceerror = si - 1 freespaceloss += freespaceerror2 countfs += 1 else: # No depth, uniform sampling, no specific SDF constraints mentioned for non-depth pixels in loss formulas pass # Photometric and Geometric losses are computed per pixel, not per sample # Assuming volume rendering aggregation happens here or in a separate step # For simplicity, we assume the loss terms are aggregated over pixels pass # Aggregate pixel-level losses # Note: The formulas sum over pixels, so we need to aggregate sample predictions to pixel predictions # This is a simplification; in practice, alpha compositing or weighted sums are used # to get rendered color and depth for the pixel # Photometric Loss photometricloss += (renderedcolor - pixel.color)2 countp += 1 # Geometric Loss if pixel.depth > 0: geometricloss += (rendereddepth - pixel.depth)2 # Normalize losses if countp > 0: photometricloss /= countp if countfs > 0: freespaceloss /= countfs if countt > 0: sdflosst /= countt if countc > 0: sdflossc /= countc # Total Loss totalloss = (5 photometricloss + 1 geometricloss + 200 sdflosst + 50 sdflossc + 10 freespaceloss) return totalloss Time Complexity: Explicit hybrid encoding is approximately 3 times faster than NICE-SLAM on posed RGB-D streams. Memory Complexity: The dense grid variant has significantly higher memory consumption. The hash grid variant trades approximately 1mm of trajectory estimation accuracy for an 87.93% reduction in memory usage. Measured Performance: Hardware: 2.10GHz Intel Xeon Gold 5218R CPU and NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU. ScanNet Runtime (ms): Hybrid(Dense+Tri): Tracking avg 1181ms, Mapping avg 281ms. Hybrid(Hash+Tri): Tracking avg 575ms, Mapping avg 251ms. Accuracy: Achieves 1.53cm reconstruction accuracy (Acc.) and 0.73cm Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE), which is approximately 60% better than NICE-SLAM's 3.87cm Acc. and 1.95cm ATE. Strengths: Real-time performance, high accuracy, robust to artifacts compared to Co-SLAM. Limitations: High memory usage for dense grid variant; relies on spatial splitting along orthogonal coordinates, which may be less adaptable than point-based methods like 3D Gaussians. When to use: When real-time RGB-D SLAM is required with high accuracy. Use Dense+Tri for maximum accuracy if memory is not a constraint; use Hash+Tri for practical real-world applications where memory efficiency is critical. This method was introduced in the paper "Benchmarking Implicit Neural Representation and Geometric Rendering in Real-Time RGB-D SLAM". It builds upon the principles of Neural Implicit SLAM by incorporating explicit hybrid encodings (dense/hash grids combined with tri-planes) to accelerate the neural network queries. The work benchmarks various implicit neural representations and geometric rendering techniques for SLAM, highlighting the trade-offs between accuracy, speed, and memory usage. name: Application-Specific Reconstructions
head: Specialized 3DGS Training Strategies
body: Application-Specific Reconstructions refers to the modification of the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) optimization and representation pipeline to address domain-specific challenges such as dynamic scenes, human avatars, transient occlusions, and non-photometric data. While standard 3DGS assumes a static, rigid scene with consistent illumination, these methods adapt the densification, deformation, and appearance modeling mechanisms to handle motion, physical constraints, or semantic features. They set themselves apart from general training methods by introducing domain-specific priors (e.g., physical consistency for cloth, mesh embedding for avatars) or post-processing steps (e.g., generative inpainting for displaced objects) that are not required for static indoor/outdoor scene reconstruction. The shared principles of this family are the modifications to the standard 3DGS training loop defined in 3D Gaussian Splatting Training. These modifications generally fall into three categories: 1. Representation Augmentation: Adding auxiliary data structures to Gaussians, such as per-image embeddings, canonical space coordinates, or mesh-tangent space associations, to encode information beyond position, scale, rotation, and color. 2. Constraint Integration: Introducing regularization terms or geometric constraints into the loss function or optimization process. This includes physical priors for cloth deformation, mesh-boundary constraints for avatars, or freezing geometry for temporal data. 3. Densification and Pruning Adaptation: Modifying the standard clone/split/prune operations to suit the dynamics of the target domain. For example, GauHuman redesigns these primitives for human dynamics, while SplattingAvatar uses opacity resets and "walking on triangle" steps to maintain mesh alignment. WildGaussians extends 3DGS to handle "in-the-wild" photo collections with unconstrained illumination and transient occluders. It solves the problem of explicit representations struggling with appearance variations by integrating robust DINO features for uncertainty-aware masking and a lightweight appearance modeling module. Unlike NeRF-based methods that use global per-image embeddings to condition a radiance field MLP, WildGaussians embeds appearance vectors directly within each Gaussian, predicting an affine transformation of the base color. This preserves real-time rendering speeds and allows the trained appearance to be "baked" back into standard 3DGS parameters. See WildGaussians. GauHuman is a method for dynamic digital human modeling from monocular video that adapts 3DGS to achieve minute-level training and real-time rendering. It solves the problem of efficient optimization and fine-detail learning in dynamic human reconstruction by redesigning the densification primitives and incorporating pose refinement. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by specifically tailoring the prune/split/clone operations for human dynamics and integrating a weight field module. See GauHuman. GaussianBody is a method for dynamic digital human modeling from monocular video that leverages physically-based priors to regularize 3D Gaussians in a canonical space. It solves the problem of artifacts in dynamic cloth reconstruction caused by the ambiguity of monocular input. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by enforcing physical consistency in the canonical space rather than relying solely on photometric loss in the camera space. See GaussianBody. Inpainting for Displaced Objects remedies black smudges and dirty textures caused by displaced objects exposing previously unseen areas, which standard 3DGS cannot recover from input images. Unlike vanilla 3DGS, which leaves empty spots and blended artifacts from irrelevant kernels when objects move, this method uses generative AI inpainting to fill these gaps. It is primarily used in dynamic scenarios involving rigid body displacement, such as falling objects or moving furniture, where the camera captures the background behind the object only after it moves. See Inpainting for Displaced Objects. SplattingAvatar is a real-time human avatar rendering method that embeds 3D Gaussians directly onto a driving mesh (FLAME or NHA) in mesh tangent space. It solves the problem of noisy, unstable deformation in complex geometry (e.g., eyes, hair) caused by nearest-triangle sampling in canonical space. Unlike methods that focus on accurate geometry reconstruction, SplattingAvatar prioritizes photometric quality and rendering efficiency, achieving over 300 FPS on consumer hardware. See SplattingAvatar. Fast-SegSim adapts the feature rendering pipeline for robotics simulation, achieving real-time open-vocabulary segmentation by fusing 3DGS with a lightweight 2D segmentation network. LeafFit applies 3DGS to create digital plant assets, leveraging alpha blending and feature fields to accurately reconstruct translucent leaf structures. Inverse Problem State Generation defines unknown scatterers using a grid mapper and an extinction transform that maps an abstract state vector to a grid mask: unknownscatterers = at3d.containers.UnknownScatterers(at3d.medium.UnknownScatterer(gridtoopticalproperties, extinction=(None, at3d.transforms.StateToGridMask(mask=cloudmask)))). It initializes the state generator with the reconstruction solver dictionary, unknown scatterers, surfaces, numerical parameters, sources, Stokes counts, and background scatterers: stategen = at3d.medium.StateGenerator(solversreconstruct, unknownscatterers, surfaces, numericalparameters, sources, numstokes, backgroundopticalscatterers). The cloudmask is a boolean array identifying cloud regions, derived from solvers[wvl].medium['cloud'].extinction.data > 0. The uncertaintymodel applies radiometric noise uncertainty to sensors, initialized with parameters 1e-5 and 1e-3. fMRI Temporal Adaptation is a strategy to adapt 3DGS for functional MRI data by freezing geometry parameters and allowing only color and opacity to vary over time, capturing voxel-wise radiance changes from neural activity. Stage 1 builds a static anatomical structure over 1000 warm-up iterations using initial frames. Stage 2 runs 3000 iterations where only color and opacity evolve temporally. It uses the OpenfMRI project (Xue and Poldrack, 2018), ds000003, consisting of 160 temporal frames, each with 33 axial brain slices at 64x64 resolution. The training split uses 140 frames for training and every 8th frame (20 total) for testing. A custom data loader ensures all slices from a given timestamp are processed synchronously to preserve inter-slice consistency. The standard 3D Gaussian Splatting method was originally designed for static scene reconstruction from multi-view images. As the technique gained popularity, researchers applied it to diverse domains requiring specialized handling of dynamics, semantics, and physical properties. WildGaussians addressed the "in-the-wild" challenge of transient occlusions and lighting variations. Methods like GauHuman and GaussianBody adapted the representation for dynamic human avatars, introducing canonical space constraints and physical priors. SplattingAvatar further specialized the representation by embedding Gaussians onto mesh surfaces. Other applications include inpainting for displaced objects, robotics simulation via Fast-SegSim, plant reconstruction via LeafFit, and scientific visualization of fMRI data and atmospheric scattering. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) lforster/hybridCT, https://github.com/lforster/hybridCT, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) InnerGS: Internal Scenes Reconstruction and Segmentation via Factorized 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2508.13287, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: WildGaussians
head: Splatting in the Wild images with Appearance-conditioned Gaussians, SWAG
body: WildGaussians extends 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to handle "in-the-wild" photo collections characterized by varying illumination, occlusions, and transient objects. It addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS, which lacks shared parameters and struggles with appearance changes, by integrating robust DINO features for uncertainty modeling and a lightweight appearance modeling module. Unlike NeRF-based methods that use global per-image embeddings to condition an MLP for the entire radiance field, WildGaussians uses per-Gaussian and per-image embeddings to predict an affine transformation of the base color, preserving real-time rendering speeds. It sets itself apart from siblings like GauHuman and SplattingAvatar by focusing on unconstrained static scene reconstruction with transient occluders rather than dynamic human avatars or mesh-aligned bodies. Inputs: A set of N uncalibrated or calibrated images \{Ij\}{j=1}^N with known camera poses. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} optimized for static scene reconstruction, with an optional "baked" representation for fast rendering. Data Structures: 1. 3D Gaussian Gi: Mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3. Covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (positive semi-definite). Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1]. View-dependent color parametrized by spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients ci. Per-Gaussian trainable appearance embedding vector ei \in \mathbb{R}^d. 2. Per-Image Embedding: A trainable vector lj \in \mathbb{R}^n for each training image j, where n=24. 3. Appearance MLP F\theta: A multi-layer perceptron taking inputs (ci, ei, lj) and outputting parameters for color transformation. 4. Uncertainty Predictor: A trainable affine transformation taking DINO features as input. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians using standard 3DGS initialization (e.g., from SfM points). Initialize per-image embeddings lj and per-Gaussian embeddings ei to zeros or small random values. 2. Feature Extraction: For each training image Ij, extract DINO v2 features D(Ij). 3. Rendering and Appearance Modeling: For each training image Ij: a. Project 3D Gaussians to 2D image space. The 2D covariance matrix \Sigma'i is computed as: \Sigma'i = JW \Sigmai W^T J{1:2,1:2}^T where J is the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the projection, W is the viewing transformation, and (\cdot){1:2,1:2} denotes the first two rows and columns. b. Compute the base color \hat{c}i for each Gaussian using SH coefficients and ray direction. c. Compute the appearance-modulated color \tilde{c}i^j: (\tilde{c}i^j, \Delta \alphai^j) = F\theta(ci, ei, lj) where F\theta is the appearance MLP. Note: SWAG variant predicts color directly and uses opacity variation. d. Render the image \hat{C}j using alpha compositing with the modulated colors. 4. Uncertainty Modeling: a. Extract DINO features from the rendered image \hat{C}j, denoted D(\hat{C}j). b. Pass D(Ij) (GT features) and D(\hat{C}j) (rendered features) through the uncertainty predictor to obtain a per-pixel uncertainty mask Mj. The predictor is optimized to maximize cosine similarity between GT and rendered DINO features in static regions. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss L for image Ij: L = \lambda{dssim} \text{DSSIM}(\hat{C}j, Cj) + (1 - \lambda{dssim}) \| \hat{C}j - Cj \|1 where Cj is the ground truth image, and the loss is masked by Mj to ignore occluders. \lambda{dssim} is a weighting factor. 6. Optimization: Update 3D Gaussian parameters (\mui, \Sigmai, \alphai, ci, ei), per-image embeddings lj, MLP weights \theta, and uncertainty predictor parameters using gradient descent. 7. Baking (Optional): After training, the appearance embeddings can be "baked" into the standard 3DGS formulation. This involves computing the final color for each Gaussian by applying the learned transformation for a reference appearance or averaging, allowing for fast rendering without the MLP. Parameters: \lambda{dssim}: Weighting factor for DSSIM loss. n: Latent embedding size, set to 24. T: Temperature for Binary Concrete distribution (if using SWAG variant), set to 0.1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Irreversible Geometry Loss: Incorrect training signals (e.g., from occluders) can lead to irreversibly removing parts of the geometry due to 3DGS's primitive growth/pruning process. Over-construction: Failure cases include over-construction of static parts, observed as black spots on roads or fountain water. Affine Limitations: Simple affine color transformations cannot model all appearance changes in in-the-wild scenarios; direct color prediction or more complex MLPs are required. Addresses global embedding limitations by extracting dynamic features from reference images and allowing per-Gaussian sampling from multiple feature maps to capture local highlights/shadows. Uses a Hash Grid encoding for Gaussian centers and predicts opacity variation via Binary Concrete distribution to separate static and transient Gaussians. Time Complexity: Training is one order of magnitude faster than previous implicit methods (NeRF-W, Ha-NeRF). Rendering speed matches standard 3DGS (real-time) after baking. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for per-Gaussian embeddings and per-image embeddings. The Hash Grid variant (SWAG) adds memory for the hash table (2^{19} entries). Performance: Improves 3DGS PSNR by an average margin of 5.01 dB on Phototourism scenes and 5 dB on NeRF-OSR benchmark. Strengths: Handles varying illumination and transient occluders; maintains real-time rendering; robust to unconstrained photo collections. Limitations: May over-construct static geometry in complex scenes; requires careful tuning of uncertainty masking. When to use: Reconstruction of static scenes from in-the-wild photo collections with transient objects and varying lighting. When not to use: Dynamic human avatars (use GauHuman) or mesh-aligned bodies (use SplattingAvatar). WildGaussians was introduced to address the challenges of 3D reconstruction from unconstrained "in-the-wild" images, which often contain occlusions, transient objects, and varying illumination. Standard 3DGS struggles with these conditions due to its explicit representation and lack of shared parameters across views. The method builds on the 3DGS framework and integrates concepts from NeRFs, such as per-image embeddings, but adapts them to the explicit Gaussian representation to maintain rendering speed. It leverages robust DINO features for uncertainty modeling to handle occluders effectively. From Volume Rendering to 3D Gaussian Splatting: Theory and Applications, https://doi.org/10.1109/sibgrapi67909.2025.11223276, fetched 2026-10-26 WildGaussians: 3D Gaussian Splatting in the Wild, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.08447, fetched 2026-10-26 From Volume Rendering to 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://www.visgraf.impa.br/Data/RefBib/PSPDF/tutorial-sib2025/tutorial-sib2025.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) SWAG: Splatting in the Wild images with Appearance-conditioned Gaussians, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2403.10427, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Dynamic Appearance Features Modeling
head: Adaptive Sampling with K Feature Maps
body: Dynamic Appearance Features Modeling addresses the limitation of global feature embeddings in 3D Gaussian Splatting, which assume uniform environmental information (lighting, weather) across a scene. By extracting dynamic appearance features from a reference image and allowing each Gaussian point to sample from multiple feature maps, the method captures local details such as highlights and shadows that global embeddings miss. It sets itself apart from methods like NeRF-W and Ha-NeRF, which use global scene embeddings, and CR-NeRF, which integrates features at the 2D level without dynamic 3D environmental information. Inputs: Reference image I{gt} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W}. Known camera pose for the reference image, defining the projection matrix P. Set of N 3D Gaussian points, where each point i has a position coordinate Xi. Outputs: Dynamic appearance feature vector dfi \in \mathbb{R}^{16(K+1)} for each Gaussian point i. Data Structures: Feature Map F: A 2D tensor of shape \mathbb{R}^{16(K+1) \times H \times W}. Projection Feature Map F^P: The first 16 channels of F, shape \mathbb{R}^{16 \times H \times W}. K Feature Maps (F^1, \dots, F^K): The remaining 16K channels of F, evenly divided into K maps, each of shape \mathbb{R}^{16 \times H \times W}. Sampling Coordinates sci: For each Gaussian point i, a set of K learnable 2D coordinates (sci^1, \dots, sci^K), where each sci^k \in [-1, 1]^2. Parameters: K: The number of additional feature maps for adaptive sampling. Typical value: 3. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Pass the reference image I{gt} through a U-Net model with a ResNet backbone to generate the combined feature map F \in \mathbb{R}^{16(K+1) \times H \times W}. 2. Map Division: Split F along the channel dimension into K+1 feature maps: the projection feature map F^P (first 16 channels) and K additional feature maps F^1, \dots, F^K (remaining 16K channels). 3. Projection Feature Sampling: For each Gaussian point i: Project its 3D position Xi onto the 2D image plane using the projection matrix P derived from the camera pose, resulting in coordinates \PiP(Xi). Sample the projection feature fi^P \in \mathbb{R}^{16} from F^P at \PiP(Xi) using bilinear interpolation. fi^P = BL(\PiP(Xi), F^P) \quad (6) where BL denotes bilinear interpolation sampling. 4. Adaptive Feature Sampling: For each Gaussian point i: Use the learnable sampling coordinates (sci^1, \dots, sci^K) to sample features from the K additional feature maps. Sample features (fi^1, \dots, fi^K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times 16} from (F^1, \dots, F^K) using bilinear interpolation at the respective coordinates. (fi^1, fi^2, \dots, fi^K) = BL((sci^1, sci^2, \dots, sci^K), (F^1, F^2, \dots, F^K)) \quad (7) 5. Concatenation: Concatenate the projection feature and the K sampled features to form the dynamic appearance feature dfi. dfi = fi^P \oplus fi^1 \oplus fi^2 \oplus \dots \oplus fi^K \quad (8) where \oplus denotes concatenation. 6. Regularization: Apply a regularization loss L{sc} to prevent sampling coordinates from deviating beyond the effective sampling range [-1, 1]. L{sc} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \max\{0, |sci| - 1\} \quad (9) where N is the total number of Gaussian points and | \cdot | denotes the absolute value applied to each coordinate component. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def extractfeatures(referenceimage: torch.Tensor, unetmodel: torch.nn.Module) -> torch.Tensor: """Extracts the combined feature map F from the reference image using a U-Net with ResNet backbone.""" return unetmodel(referenceimage) def splitfeaturemaps(Fmap: torch.Tensor, K: int): """Splits the combined feature map F into projection feature map F^P and K additional feature maps.""" FP = Fmap[:16,:,:] FK = [Fmap[16 + k 16: 16 + (k + 1) 16,:,:] for k in range(K)] return FP, FK def sampleprojectionfeature(Xi: torch.Tensor, P: torch.Tensor, FP: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """Samples the projection feature for a single Gaussian point.""" Xihom = torch.cat([Xi, torch.ones(1, device=Xi.device)]) projected = P @ Xihom u, v = projected[0], projected[1] grid = torch.tensor([[[[u, v]]]], device=Xi.device) FPbatch = FP.unsqueeze(0) return F.gridsample(FPbatch, grid, aligncorners=False).squeeze() def sampleadaptivefeatures(sci: list, FK: list) -> torch.Tensor: """Samples features from K feature maps using learnable sampling coordinates.""" features = [] for k in range(len(FK)): u, v = sci[k][0], sci[k][1] grid = torch.tensor([[[[u, v]]]], device=sci[k][0].device) Fkbatch = FK[k].unsqueeze(0) features.append(F.gridsample(Fkbatch, grid, aligncorners=False).squeeze()) return torch.stack(features, dim=0) def computedynamicappearancefeature(Xi: torch.Tensor, P: torch.Tensor, FP: torch.Tensor, sci: list, FK: list) -> torch.Tensor: """Computes the dynamic appearance feature dfi for a single Gaussian point.""" fiP = sampleprojectionfeature(Xi, P, FP) fiK = sampleadaptivefeatures(sci, FK) return torch.cat([fiP, fiK.flatten()]) def computeregularizationloss(scilist: list, N: int) -> torch.Tensor: """Computes the regularization loss Lsc for all Gaussian points.""" totalloss = torch.tensor(0.0, device=scilist[0][0].device) for sci in scilist: for sc in sci: totalloss += torch.sum(torch.clamp(torch.abs(sc) - 1, min=0)) return totalloss / N Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The projection matrix P must map 3D points to 2D coordinates compatible with the bilinear interpolation function's valid range. Boundaries: The regularization loss L{sc} is designed to keep sampling coordinates within [-1, 1]. If coordinates exceed this range, the loss penalizes them, but sampling outside this range may result in undefined behavior or zero-padding depending on the interpolation implementation. Degenerate Input: If the reference image I{gt} is not available or the camera pose is unknown, the projection feature map F^P cannot be computed, and the method fails. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method was trained on a single Nvidia RTX 3090 GPU for 70k steps, taking approximately 2 hours, with images downsampled twice during training and evaluation. Scaling: Increasing K beyond 3 yields no performance improvement while adding meaningless computational cost, establishing K=3 as optimal. Strengths: Captures local details such as highlights and shadows that global embeddings miss, aligning better with real-world varying environmental influences. Limitations: Limited by the single-view reference image I{gt}, where features sampled from the projection feature map are identical along the same ray, which is unreasonable under uneven lighting. Origin: Introduced in "Gaussian in the Wild: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Unconstrained Image Collections". History and Development: Previous methods like NeRF-W and Ha-NeRF used global feature embeddings assuming uniform environmental information, while CR-NeRF integrated features at the 2D level without dynamic 3D environmental information. This method addresses these limitations by allowing each Gaussian point to independently learn its sampling positions. Usage: Used in the WildGaussians framework for 'in-the-wild' settings, integrating robust DINO features and a lightweight appearance modeling module within the 3DGS framework [Parent]. name: GauHuman
body: GauHuman is an application-specific reconstruction method for dynamic digital humans that adapts the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training loop to handle human dynamics. It solves the problem of efficient optimization and fine-detail learning in monocular video by redesigning the standard densification primitives and incorporating pose refinement and weight field modules. It sets itself apart from siblings like SplattingAvatar by embedding Gaussians directly in 3D space rather than on a canonical mesh, and from GaussianBody by focusing on optimized densification strategies rather than purely physical priors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Monocular video sequence of a human subject; initial 3D Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color) derived from a static reconstruction or sparse initialization. Outputs: A set of time-varying 3D Gaussians representing the dynamic human avatar, optimized for real-time rendering. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Standard 3DGS attributes (position \mathbf{p}, scale \mathbf{s}, rotation \mathbf{r}, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients for color). Pose Refinement Module: Parameters to refine the initial pose estimates (e.g., SMPL parameters) over time. Weight Field Module: A neural network or function mapping spatial coordinates to Gaussian weights or deformations to capture fine details. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from a static reconstruction of the first frame. 2. Pose Refinement: Optimize pose parameters (e.g., SMPL pose/shape) jointly with Gaussian attributes to align the Gaussians with the human body in each frame. 3. Weight Field Integration: Use the weight field module to modulate Gaussian attributes or contributions, allowing for fine-detail learning that standard 3DGS might miss. 4. Redesigned Densification: Replace the standard 3DGS clone/split/prune operations with a redesigned variant tailored for human dynamics. This involves: Prune: Remove Gaussians with low opacity or high gradient magnitude that do not contribute to the human shape. Split/Clone: Adaptively add Gaussians in areas of high detail or motion, ensuring efficient coverage of the dynamic surface. 5. Rendering: Render the scene using alpha-blending of the transformed Gaussians. 6. Loss Computation: Compute photometric loss and potentially regularization terms for pose smoothness or physical plausibility. 7. Optimization: Update Gaussian attributes, pose parameters, and weight field parameters using gradient descent. Formulas: Not given in the sources. The specific mathematical formulation of the "redesigned prune/split/clone" and "weight field module" is not provided in the cited texts. Rendering follows standard 3DGS alpha-blending: C = \sum{i \in N} ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj), where ci is the color and \alphai is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian. Parameters: Training time: Minutes. Rendering speed: 166 FPS. Not given in the sources: Specific hyperparameters for the weight field, pose refinement learning rate, or densification thresholds. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Views: The method may suffer from floating Gaussians if the input views are too sparse, though joint optimization with scene Gaussians (in variants) can mitigate this. Precision: Standard 3DGS precision issues may apply; the redesigned densification aims to address this but specific numerical stability measures are not detailed. Degenerate Input: Monocular video lacks depth information, relying on pose priors and temporal consistency, which can fail with rapid, non-rigid motion not captured by the pose model. Optimizes human and scene Gaussians jointly, where the human serves as a constraint for the scene reconstruction, mitigating floating Gaussians (floaters) caused by sparse input views. This approach contrasts with sequential optimization (scene then human) which can lead to artifacts in the scene around the human. Time Complexity: Training is efficient, taking only minutes. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Real-time rendering at 166 FPS. Scaling: Performance scales with the number of Gaussians; the redesigned densification aims to keep this number manageable for real-time rendering. Strengths: Minute-level training, real-time rendering, fine-detail learning via weight fields, efficient optimization via redesigned densification. Limitations: Relies on monocular input, potentially sensitive to pose estimation errors, specific implementation details of the weight field and densification are not publicly detailed in the sources. When to use: Dynamic human reconstruction from monocular video where training speed and rendering FPS are critical. When not to use: Multi-view setups where other methods might offer higher fidelity, or when mesh-based representations are preferred for animation. GauHuman was introduced as part of the recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting for dynamic digital human modeling. It builds on the standard 3DGS framework but adapts it for the specific challenges of human dynamics, such as non-rigid deformation and the need for fine detail. It is cited alongside other methods like GaussianBody, GaussianAvatar, and SplattingAvatar in surveys of 3DGS applications. name: GaussianBody
body: GaussianBody is a method for dynamic digital human modeling from monocular video that leverages physically-based priors to regularize 3D Gaussians in canonical space. It solves the problem of visual artifacts in dynamic cloth reconstruction caused by the unbalanced aggregation of Gaussians during standard densification. It sets itself apart from siblings like GauHuman by focusing on physical regularization of deformation rather than redesigning the prune/split/clone primitives for efficiency. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Monocular video sequence of a dynamic human; canonical space representation of the human body. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians with optimized position, scale, rotation, opacity, and color, regularized by physical priors. Data Structures: Gaussians: Standard 3D Gaussian attributes (mean \mu, covariance \Sigma or quaternion q and scale s, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients for color). Canonical Space: A reference pose representation where deformation is applied. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians in the canonical space. 2. Physical Regularization: Apply physically-based priors to regularize the deformation of Gaussians in the canonical space. This ensures that the deformation of the cloth follows physical constraints, avoiding artifacts. 3. Rendering: Render the Gaussians from novel viewpoints using differentiable rasterization. 4. Optimization: Optimize the Gaussian parameters by minimizing the difference between rendered and ground-truth images, guided by the physical priors. Formulas: Not given in the sources. The specific mathematical formulation of the physically-based priors is not detailed in the provided notes. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Monocular video ambiguity can lead to artifacts in dynamic cloth if not properly regularized. Unbalanced aggregation of Gaussians during densification can cause visual artifacts. HAHA is a variant that attaches Gaussians to the surface of a mesh. It combines rendered results from a textured human body mesh and Gaussians to reduce the number of Gaussians required. This approach leverages the mesh for structural support while using Gaussians for fine details. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Effectively avoids artifacts in dynamic cloth from monocular video by leveraging physically-based priors. Limitations may include the complexity of implementing physical priors and potential sensitivity to initialization. When to Use: Suitable for dynamic digital human modeling from monocular video where cloth deformation artifacts are a concern. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenarios where physical priors are not applicable or where real-time performance is critical without sufficient hardware. GaussianBody was introduced in the context of dynamic digital human modeling based on monocular video. It builds on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting framework. The method was developed to address the specific challenges of reconstructing dynamic cloth from limited visual input. It is cited as reference [214] in the source literature. name: Inpainting for Displaced Objects
head: GSP Inpainting, LaMa Inpainting
body: Inpainting for Displaced Objects remedies the visual artifacts—specifically black smudges and dirty textures—that arise in 3D Gaussian Splatting when an object moves, exposing areas previously occluded and unseen by the input cameras. Unlike vanilla 3DGS, which leaves empty spots or blends irrelevant kernel colors into these voids, this method uses generative AI to fill the missing texture and reassigns the resulting pixel colors to the Gaussian kernels. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting Training by introducing a post-processing or auxiliary step that decouples texture recovery from the standard differentiable rendering loop for displaced entities. This method addresses the issue where displaced objects reveal background or unseen surfaces that were not present in the training images, causing the renderer to produce artifacts because the Gaussian kernels for those areas lack valid color data. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} representing the scene, including those belonging to the object expected to displace. A set of training images or a target novel view where the object has moved. A segmentation mask identifying the Gaussian kernels belonging to the displaced object. An inpainting model (e.g., LaMa or Stable Diffusion). Outputs: Updated Gaussian kernels with corrected diffuse colors, opacity, and specular properties for the displaced object. Data Structures: Gaussian Kernel: Standard 3DGS structure containing position \mathbf{x}, scale \mathbf{s}, rotation \mathbf{q}, opacity \alpha, and color coefficients (SH or RGB). For this method, we specifically track diffuse color c{diff} and specular color c{spec}. Ray Buffer: A temporary storage for rays emitted from camera pixels that fall into the "holes" or displaced regions. Steps: 1. Identify and Remove Displaced Kernels: Identify all Gaussian kernels \mathcal{G}{obj} \subset \mathcal{G} that belong to the object capable of displacement. Remove these kernels from the active rendering set to create a "hole" in the scene representation where the object was previously located or where it moves to. 2. Render the Scene: Render the scene using the remaining Gaussians \mathcal{G} \setminus \mathcal{G}{obj} to generate an image I{rendered} and an alpha mask M indicating the missing regions (where the object should be). 3. Inpaint the Image: Use a generative inpainting model to fill the masked regions in I{rendered}. For GSP/LaMa: Use LaMa [61] to inpaint the rendered results. For CoherentGS: Use Stable Diffusion inpainting [42] to generate missing texture in the masked regions. Let the inpainted image be I{inpaint}. 4. Trace Rays and Record Colors (GSP Method): For each pixel (u, v) in the masked region M: a. Emit a ray from the camera through (u, v). b. Find the first Gaussian kernel \mathcal{G}i encountered by this ray that was originally part of \mathcal{G}{obj} (or is projected to this location in the new view). c. Record the new color C{new}(u, v) from I{inpaint} at (u, v). d. Associate C{new}(u, v) with \mathcal{G}i. 5. Aggregate Colors: For each Gaussian kernel \mathcal{G}i in the displaced object: a. Collect all recorded colors C{new} associated with it from the previous step. b. Compute the average diffuse color: c{diff} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{j=1}^{N} C{new, j} where N is the number of rays/pixels associated with \mathcal{G}i. 6. Update Gaussian Properties: For each kernel \mathcal{G}i in \mathcal{G}{obj}: a. Set diffuse color to c{diff}. b. Set opacity \alpha = 1. c. Set specular color c{spec} = 0 to prevent highlights in the inpainted regions. Alternative Pipeline (CoherentGS 3D Inpainting): If maintaining 3D consistency across multiple novel views is required, use the sequential pipeline: 1. Render a novel view with holes and an alpha mask. 2. Use Stable Diffusion inpainting to generate missing texture. 3. Estimate monocular depth on the inpainted image. 4. Use the gradient of this depth to fill in rendered depth in the masked regions using Poisson blending [38]. 5. Project Gaussians to the scene using the inpainted depth and image. 6. Repeat sequentially for a few novel views until the scene is 3D consistent and renderable from any view without holes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The assignment of colors to the "first Gaussian kernel encountered" requires accurate ray-Gaussian intersection tests. If the ray misses all kernels in the displaced region, the color is lost. Hallucination: While generative inpainting fills holes, it may hallucinate details not present in the 3D structure. CoherentGS notes that constraining Gaussian movement prevents this hallucination from corrupting the 3D geometry, allowing safe use of 2D inpainting. Specular Artifacts: Failing to set specular color to 0 may result in incorrect highlights on the inpainted surface, as the generative model only provides diffuse texture. A sequential pipeline designed to fill occluded or missing regions in rendered novel views while maintaining 3D consistency. Unlike the single-view GSP method, this approach leverages the constraint that Gaussians do not hallucinate details in occluded areas, allowing the use of state-of-the-art 2D inpainting tools like Stable Diffusion. It involves rendering a view with holes, inpainting the texture, estimating monocular depth, and using Poisson blending to integrate the depth gradient into the rendered depth before re-projecting Gaussians. This process is repeated across multiple novel views until the scene is fully 3D consistent and hole-free. Time Complexity: Depends on the inpainting model. LaMa is generally faster than Stable Diffusion. The ray tracing and color aggregation steps are linear with respect to the number of pixels in the masked region and the number of displaced Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the inpainted image and temporary ray buffers. No significant additional memory overhead for the Gaussian structure itself, as properties are updated in place. Performance: Effectively eliminates black smudges and dirty textures caused by displaced objects. It ameliorates issues that vanilla 3DGS cannot recover from input images. Strengths: Simple to implement as a post-processing or auxiliary step; leverages mature 2D generative models; does not require modifying the core differentiable rendering engine. Limitations: The inpainted texture is 2D and may not perfectly match the 3D geometry if the displacement is large or complex; requires segmentation masks for the displaced objects. When to use: When objects in the scene undergo significant displacement, exposing previously occluded background or unseen surfaces. When not to use: When the scene is static or displacements are minimal and recoverable by standard densification. The method was introduced in "Gaussian Splashing: Unified Particles for Versatile Motion Synthesis and Rendering" (2025) by Law et al.. It addresses a specific failure mode of 3D Gaussian Splatting where dynamic objects leave visual artifacts when they move. The technique utilizes LaMa [61] for fast inpainting. A variant using Stable Diffusion and depth consistency was later proposed in "CoherentGS: Sparse Novel View Synthesis with Coherent 3D Gaussians" (2025). name: SplattingAvatar
head: SplattingAvatar: Realistic Real-Time Human Avatars with Mesh-Embedded Gaussian Splatting
body: SplattingAvatar is a real-time human avatar rendering method that embeds 3D Gaussians directly onto a driving mesh (FLAME or NHA) in mesh tangent space. It solves the problem of noisy deformation and ambiguous motion control found in nearest-triangle sampling methods (like INSTA) by using trainable embeddings for motion control, enabling high-fidelity rendering of complex geometries like eyes and hair. It differs from geometry-focused methods like FLARE by prioritizing photometric quality and rendering efficiency over accurate material reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-angle video of a subject; pre-fitted driving mesh (FLAME or NHA). Outputs: Animatable 3D Gaussian avatar; Unity-compatible render with >300 FPS. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Position, scale, rotation, color, opacity, and trainable embeddings. Mesh Association: Each Gaussian is initialized per mesh triangle in tangent space. Rendering Primitive: One quad primitive per Gaussian. Training Optimization: 1. Initialization: Initialize one Gaussian per mesh triangle in tangent space. 2. Iteration Loop: Run for 30,000 iterations. 3. Densification/Pruning: Starting from iteration 600, perform densify and prune every 100 iterations. 4. Opacity Reset: Every 3000 iterations, reset the opacity of all Gaussians to zero to remove redundant Gaussians. 5. Walking on Triangle: After densifying and pruning, perform the "walking on triangle" step to ensure Gaussians remain aligned with the mesh surface. 6. Termination: Densify, prune, and opacity-reset processes stop at iteration 15,000. Parameters: \lambdal (L1 loss weight) = 0.01. \lambdas (SSIM loss weight) = 1.0. Ts (Scale threshold) = 10.0. Tr (Rotation threshold) = 0.008. Pitfalls: Nearest-Triangle Sampling: Using nearest-triangle sampling for deformation (as in INSTA) causes unstable sampling in canonical space and strong noise in complex geometries like the eye region. Disabling Walking on Triangle: Disabling this mechanism and clipping UV values causes Gaussians to stick and pile up on mesh triangle boundaries, degrading PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainsplattingavatar(mesh, videoframes, iterations=30000): # Initialize Gaussians per mesh triangle in tangent space gaussians = initializegaussianspertriangle(mesh) for iter in range(1, iterations + 1): # Get current pose from video pose = getpose(videoframes, iter) # Render using Unity-compatible quad primitives # Embeddings are used for motion control in compute shaders renderedimage = rendergaussians(gaussians, pose) # Calculate loss # lambdal = 0.01, lambdas = 1.0 loss = 0.01 l1loss(renderedimage, groundtruth) + 1.0 ssimloss(renderedimage, groundtruth) # Backpropagate and update embeddings and Gaussian attributes updateparameters(gaussians, loss) # Densify and Prune every 100 iterations starting from 600 if iter >= 600 and iter % 100 == 0: densifyandprune(gaussians) # Walking on Triangle step walkingontriangle(gaussians, mesh) # Opacity Reset every 3000 iterations if iter % 3000 == 0: resetopacity(gaussians) # Stop densify/prune/reset after 15000 iterations if iter > 15000: disabledensifyprunereset() return gaussians Redesigns densification primitives for human dynamics. Link Focuses on body avatar reconstruction. Link Handles dynamic scenes with wild Gaussians. Link Performance: Over 300 FPS on NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU. Quality: On head avatar dataset, Ours+FLAME achieves PSNR 28.19, SSIM 0.931, LPIPS 0.063; Ours+NHA achieves PSNR 28.86, SSIM 0.931, LPIPS 0.060. Comparison: Outperforms FLARE in photometric quality and rendering efficiency, though FLARE focuses more on accurate geometry and materials. Limitations: Does not focus on accurate geometry and materials reconstruction compared to mesh-based approaches like FLARE. SplattingAvatar was introduced as a method for realistic real-time human avatars using mesh-embedded Gaussian Splatting. It builds on the SMPL-X rig and embeds Gaussians in mesh tangent space. It addresses issues in previous methods like INSTA by avoiding nearest-triangle sampling noise. name: Geometry and Surface Priors
body: Geometry and Surface Priors align the discrete 3D Gaussian representation with continuous geometric priors to enforce positional and normal consistency, enabling accurate mesh extraction and physically-based rendering. Unlike methods relying solely on photometric loss, this family integrates geometric supervision into training or post-processing to ensure the Gaussians conform to physical surfaces. All methods in this family align the discrete Gaussian representation with a continuous geometric prior. The core mechanism adds geometric loss terms to the standard photometric rendering loss \mathcal{L}{rgb}. These losses enforce two properties: positional consistency, where Gaussian centers \mathbf{c}i are encouraged to lie on the zero-level set of a distance function (SDF or UDF) or align with metric depth estimates, and normal consistency, where the orientation of the Gaussians (derived from their covariance matrix or rotation quaternion) is aligned with the surface normal estimated from the geometric prior. The total loss function generally takes the form: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{geo} \mathcal{L}{geo} + \lambda{norm} \mathcal{L}{norm} where \mathcal{L}{geo} is the geometric consistency loss and \mathcal{L}{norm} is the normal consistency loss. The weights \lambda{geo} and \lambda{norm} are hyperparameters that balance photometric fidelity against geometric accuracy. Mitigates reconstruction artifacts and improves geometric fidelity by introducing a progressive propagation strategy that utilizes propagated depth and normal maps from neighboring views to guide Gaussian growth, explicitly enforcing normal consistency and planar constraints. Choose when standard densification fails to capture continuous surface geometry. Integrates the NeuS implicit surface reconstruction method into the 3D Gaussian Splatting representation by directly coupling a NeuS-style Signed Distance Function (SDF) with a Gaussian rasterizer to transfer explicit surface properties to discrete Gaussian primitives. Choose when explicit surface normals and signed distances are required without post-hoc mesh extraction. A post-optimization step that resolves the up-to-scale ambiguity inherent in multi-view reconstruction by aligning the metric scale of optimized 3D Gaussians with metric-scale monocular depth estimates, operating after standard optimization by fixing Gaussian parameters and optimizing only a global scale factor. Choose when metric scale recovery is needed without modifying the training loop. Addresses reconstruction from sparse-view inputs by explicitly integrating depth priors estimated from pre-trained 2D monocular depth estimation networks to supervise the Gaussian distribution, rather than relying solely on implicit neural fields. Choose when multi-view constraints are insufficient. Aligns the discrete 3D Gaussian representation with a continuous Signed Distance Function (SDF) prior to enhance geometry reconstruction quality by explicitly transferring surface properties from a neural SDF to the Gaussians. Choose when SDF-based surface extraction is preferred. The overarching family definition focusing on the alignment of discrete Gaussians with continuous priors (SDFs, depth, meshes) to enforce positional and normal consistency for mesh extraction. Combines 2D diffusion priors (e.g., Stable Diffusion) and 3D diffusion priors (e.g., Zero-1-to-3) to supervise novel view reconstruction, using 2D priors for plausible unseen geometry (mitigating the Janus problem) and 3D priors for geometric consistency. Choose when generative priors are needed to balance geometry exploration and exploitation. A method that encourages consistency between Signed Distance Function (SDF) and 3DGS to enhance geometry reconstruction quality. Uses pretrained volume rendering priors (UDF) to push Gaussians toward true surfaces by optimizing along the direction of increasing rendering weights, avoiding off-surface drift and discreteness. It is a post-training refinement strategy particularly effective for open and thin structures. Integrates into existing variants (e.g., GaussianUDF, QGS) without modifying inference-time resource costs, as the prior network is bypassed during inference. Outperforms handcrafted renderers and closed-surface-tailored 3DGS methods on open and thin structures where standard Gaussian distributions degrade severely. The integration of geometric priors into 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged to address the "floating" artifact issue inherent in the original 3DGS formulation, where Gaussians represent volume rather than surface. Early approaches like GSDF and 3DGSR focused on aligning Gaussians with SDFs to improve reconstruction quality. Subsequent methods such as NeuSG incorporated implicit neural representations (NeuS) to encourage consistency between Gaussians' signed distance values and explicit surface normals. Other lines of work, such as DN-Splatter, utilized depth and normal priors captured from common devices or predicted from general-purpose networks to enhance reconstruction quality. Wolf et al. trained a 3DGS to render stereo-calibrated novel views and applied stereo depth estimation on the rendered views, fusing the estimated dense depth maps by the Truncated Signed Distance Function (TSDF) to form a triangular mesh. More recently, diffusion-based priors (Joint 2D and 3D Priors) have been introduced to leverage large-scale generative models for geometric regularization. Volume rendering priors, such as those in Gaussian Splatting Surface Refinement, have also been developed to refine open and thin structures by pushing Gaussians toward true surfaces predicted by unsigned distance functions.
