name: GaussianPro
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Progressive Propagation
body: GaussianPro is a training optimization method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that improves geometric fidelity by introducing a progressive propagation strategy. Unlike standard densification which relies solely on position gradients, GaussianPro utilizes propagated depth and normal maps from neighboring views to guide the growth and adjustment of Gaussians. It sets itself apart by explicitly enforcing normal consistency between neighboring views and introducing planar constraints, ensuring that the discrete Gaussian representation aligns more closely with continuous surface geometry. GaussianPro integrates geometric priors into the densification and optimization pipeline. It generates initial depth and normal maps, propagates these values across neighboring pixels using patch matching, and uses the propagated information to identify regions requiring new Gaussians. Inputs: Set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, input images from multiple views, and initial depth and normal estimates. Outputs: Optimized set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}' with improved geometric alignment. The method relies on standard 3D Gaussian Splatting data structures augmented with geometric filters. Gaussian Attributes: Standard fields: \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3, \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion), \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (scale), \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, \mathbf{c}{sh} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times 3} (SH coefficients). Geometric Maps: Depth map D \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W} and Normal map N \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} for each view. Propagated Maps: D{prop} and N{prop}, generated via patch matching. 1. Generate Initial Geometric Priors: Compute initial depth D and normal N maps for each input view. 2. Patch Matching Propagation: Propagate depth and normal information from neighboring pixels in adjacent views to generate D{prop} and N{prop}. 3. Geometric Filtering and Selection: Identify pixels requiring additional Gaussians by comparing rendered and propagated maps. 4. Gaussian Initialization: Initialize new Gaussians at selected pixels using the propagated depth and normal information. 5. Optimization with Geometric Losses: Minimize the total loss \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{planar} \mathcal{L}{planar} + \lambda{norm} \mathcal{L}{norm} during training. Normal Consistency Loss (\mathcal{L}{norm}): Enforces consistency between the Gaussian's rendered normal \mathbf{n}{rendered} and the propagated normal \mathbf{n}{prop}. \mathcal{L}{norm} = \|\mathbf{n}{rendered} - \mathbf{n}{prop}\|1 + (1 - \mathbf{n}{rendered} \cdot \mathbf{n}{prop}) Planar Loss (\mathcal{L}{planar}): Encourages Gaussians to conform to planar structures by minimizing the distance of Gaussian centers to fitted planes or penalizing deviations from local planarity. Progressive Propagation: The strategy updates Gaussians iteratively during training by considering normal consistency between neighboring views. \lambda{planar}: Weight for the planar loss. \lambda{norm}: Weight for the normal consistency loss. Patch matching window size: Not given in the sources. Popping Artifacts: Standard 3DGS can suffer from popping Gaussians due to discrete depth sorting, which GaussianPro mitigates through consistent geometric alignment. Degenerate Input: In textureless or reflective regions, depth and normal estimation may fail, requiring robust patch matching and geometric filtering. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gaussianprostep(gaussians, views, cameras, initialdepth, initialnormal): # 1. Render current Gaussians renderedimage, rendereddepth, renderednormal = rendergaussians(gaussians, cameras) # 2. Propagate geometric information from neighboring views propagateddepth, propagatednormal = patchmatchpropagation(initialdepth, initialnormal, cameras) # 3. Compute Photometric Loss lossrgb = photometricloss(renderedimage, views[0].target) # 4. Compute Normal Consistency Loss lossnorm = l1loss(renderednormal, propagatednormal) + angularloss(renderednormal, propagatednormal) # 5. Compute Planar Loss lossplanar = planarloss(gaussians) # 6. Total Loss and Backpropagation totalloss = lossrgb + lambdanorm lossnorm + lambdaplanar lossplanar gaussians.backward(totalloss) # 7. Densification based on Geometric Filtering pixelstodensify = geometricfilter(rendereddepth, propagateddepth, renderednormal, propagatednormal) for p in pixelstodensify: newg = initializegaussian(p, propagateddepth[p], propagatednormal[p], cameras) gaussians.add(newg) return totalloss def rendergaussians(gaussians, cameras): # Standard 3DGS tile-based splatting renderedimage = torch.zeroslike(cameras.target) rendereddepth = torch.zeroslike(cameras.target) renderednormal = torch.zeroslike(cameras.target) for g in gaussians: proj = projecttoscreen(g, cameras) splat = computesplat(proj, g.covariance) renderedimage += splat g.opacity rendereddepth += splat g.depth renderednormal += splat g.normal return renderedimage, rendereddepth, renderednormal def patchmatchpropagation(depth, normal, cameras): # Iterative patch matching across neighboring views propagateddepth = depth.clone() propagatednormal = normal.clone() for view in cameras.neighboringviews: for p in depth.shape: bestmatch = findbestpatch(depth, view.depth, p) propagateddepth[p] = view.depth[bestmatch] propagatednormal[p] = view.normal[bestmatch] return propagateddepth, propagatednormal def geometricfilter(rendereddepth, propagateddepth, renderednormal, propagatednormal): depthdiff = torch.abs(rendereddepth - propagateddepth) normaldiff = 1 - torch.cosinesimilarity(renderednormal, propagatednormal, dim=-1) threshold = 0.05 return (depthdiff > threshold) | (normaldiff > threshold) def initializegaussian(p, depth, normal, cameras): # Back-project pixel to 3D using propagated depth and camera intrinsics c = unprojectpixel(p, depth, cameras) q = normaltoquaternion(normal) s = torch.ones(3) 0.1 alpha = 0.8 csh = torch.zeros(3, 3) return Gaussian(c=c, q=q, s=s, alpha=alpha, csh=csh) def planarloss(gaussians): # Penalize deviation from local planar surfaces loss = 0.0 for g in gaussians: plane = fitlocalplane(g.neighbors) loss += torch.abs(torch.dot(g.c - plane.origin, plane.normal)) return loss def l1loss(a, b): return torch.mean(torch.abs(a - b)) def angularloss(a, b): return torch.mean(1 - torch.cosinesimilarity(a, b, dim=-1)) def photometricloss(rendered, target): return torch.mean(torch.abs(rendered - target)) Aligns discrete Gaussians with continuous geometric priors using positional and normal consistency losses. Choose when standard photometric optimization yields geometrically inconsistent surfaces. name: NeuSG
body: NeuSG integrates the NeuS implicit surface reconstruction method into the 3D Gaussian Splatting representation to transfer explicit surface properties to discrete Gaussian primitives. Unlike sibling methods that rely on monocular depth priors or post-hoc mesh extraction, NeuSG directly couples a NeuS-style Signed Distance Function with a Gaussian rasterizer. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Calibrated images, initial 3D Gaussian parameters (centers \mathbf{c}i, covariances \Sigmai, opacities \alphai, colors), and a NeuS network initialized to predict SDF and opacity. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussians and a NeuS network that jointly render photorealistic images and a consistent surface. Data Structures: 1. 3D Gaussians: Standard 3DGS representation with centers \mathbf{c}i, covariances \Sigmai, opacities \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color. 2. NeuS Network: An MLP taking 3D position \mathbf{x} as input, outputting a raw SDF value \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and an opacity weight \omega(\mathbf{x}). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians from sparse points and initialize the NeuS MLP. 2. Rendering: Render the scene using the 3DGS rasterizer to produce RGB images. 3. Geometric Loss (\mathcal{L}{geo}): Query the NeuS network for the signed distance value at each Gaussian center: di = \sigma(\mathbf{c}i). Encourage these values to be zero, ensuring Gaussian centers lie on the zero-level set of the SDF. \mathcal{L}{geo} = \sumi |di| 4. Normal Consistency Loss (\mathcal{L}{norm}): Compute the Gaussian normal \mathbf{n}{gs,i} from its covariance matrix (principal axis). Compute the NeuS surface normal \mathbf{n}{neuS,i} = \nabla \sigma(\mathbf{c}i) / \|\nabla \sigma(\mathbf{c}i)\|. Minimize the angular difference between them. \mathcal{L}{norm} = \sumi (1 - \mathbf{n}{gs,i} \cdot \mathbf{n}{neuS,i}) 5. Photometric Loss: Compute the standard L1 or SSIM loss between rendered RGB images and ground truth images. 6. Optimization: Minimize the total loss: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{geo} \mathcal{L}{geo} + \lambda{norm} \mathcal{L}{norm} where \lambda{geo} and \lambda{norm} balance photometric fidelity against geometric accuracy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def normalize(v): return v / max(norm(v), 1e-8) def computegaussiannormal(cov): eigenvalues, eigenvectors = eig(cov) return normalize(eigenvectors[:, argmax(eigenvalues)]) def neusgstep(gaussians, neusmlp, gtrgb, lambdageo, lambdanorm): # Standard 3DGS alpha compositing rasterizer renderedrgb = rasterize(gaussians) lgeo = 0.0 lnorm = 0.0 for g in gaussians: d = neusmlp(g.position) lgeo += abs(d) nneus = normalize(grad(neusmlp, g.position)) ngs = computegaussiannormal(g.covariance) lnorm += 1.0 - dot(ngs, nneus) lgeo /= len(gaussians) lnorm /= len(gaussians) lrgb = mean(abs(renderedrgb - gtrgb)) totalloss = lrgb + lambdageo lgeo + lambdanorm lnorm return totalloss Note: rasterize, grad, norm, dot, eig, argmax, abs, mean are standard math/vector operations. Parameters: \lambda{geo}: Weight for geometric loss. Not given in the sources. \lambda{norm}: Weight for normal consistency loss. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Precision: SDF values near zero are sensitive to initialization. Ensure NeuS is initialized to predict a large positive SDF outside the object and negative inside to avoid local minima. Boundaries: Gaussians far from the surface may have noisy SDF gradients. Enforces SDF consistency but extracts the surface from accumulated Gaussian opacity rather than a separate implicit network. Choose when mesh extraction from opacity is preferred over implicit networks. GSDF Aligns Gaussians with explicit mesh normals or depth maps, often using post-processing or differentiable mesh rendering. Choose when explicit geometric priors are available. Surface and Geometry Alignment Aligns 3DGS with monocular depth estimates without relying on an explicit SDF network. Choose when only monocular depth priors are available. Monocular Depth Scale Alignment Uses depth priors to regularize geometry in sparse views, potentially using SDF but not necessarily NeuS. Choose when training data is severely sparse. Sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting with Depth Priors Time Complexity: Higher than vanilla 3DGS due to the additional NeuS network forward and backward passes for every Gaussian or ray sample. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Increased by the storage of the NeuS MLP weights and intermediate SDF values. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Produces clean, watertight surfaces suitable for mesh extraction. Aligns Gaussian orientation with the true surface normal. Limitations: Slower training due to the coupled optimization. Requires careful tuning of \lambda{geo} and \lambda{norm}. When to use: When a high-quality mesh is required for downstream applications (e.g., physics, DCC). When not to use: When real-time rendering speed is the primary concern and surface fidelity is less critical than appearance. NeuSG incorporates the NeuS implicit surface reconstruction method into the 3DGS representation to transfer surface properties. It addresses the limitation of vanilla 3DGS, which lacks explicit geometric constraints, by enforcing positional and normal consistency with the implicit surface. The method is cited in surveys of recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting. name: Monocular Depth Scale Alignment
head: Global Scale Alignment, Metric Scale Correction
body: Monocular Depth Scale Alignment is a post-optimization step in 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines that resolves the up-to-scale ambiguity inherent in multi-view reconstruction by aligning the metric scale of optimized 3D Gaussians with metric-scale monocular depth estimates. Unlike methods that integrate depth priors during training, this approach operates after the standard Gaussian optimization phase, fixing the Gaussian parameters and optimizing only a global scale factor. Inputs: \Theta: The set of optimized 3D Gaussian parameters (means, covariances, opacities, colors) from the standard 3DGS training. \{Ii\}{i=1}^{N{\mathcal{I}}}: A set of N{\mathcal{I}} input images. \{D^{mono}i\}{i=1}^{N{\mathcal{I}}}: Metric-scale monocular depth maps estimated from Ii using an off-the-shelf estimator (e.g., DepthAnythingV2). Outputs: \Theta': Updated Gaussian parameters where only the mean positions and scale attributes are scaled by the global factor a. Data Structures: a \in \mathbb{R}: A single scalar representing the global scene scale. Steps: 1. Monocular Depth Estimation: For each input image Ii, compute the metric depth map D^{mono}i using a pre-trained monocular depth estimation model. 2. Inverse Depth Conversion: Convert metric depth maps to inverse depth maps to match the rendering convention by directly taking their reciprocal: invD^{mono}i = 1 / D^{mono}i. 3. Rendered Inverse Depth: Render the inverse depth map invD^{rendered}i for each view i using the current 3D Gaussian parameters \Theta. 4. Optimize Global Scale: Optimize the global scale factor a to minimize the L1 distance between the monocular inverse depth and the scaled rendered inverse depth: a^ = \arg \mina \sum{i=1}^{N{\mathcal{I}}} \| invD^{mono}i - a \cdot invD^{rendered}i \|1 This optimization is performed while keeping \Theta fixed. 5. Update Gaussians: Apply the optimal scale a^ to the 3D Gaussians by multiplying the mean position \mathbf{c}i and the scale parameters of each Gaussian by a^. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def monoculardepthscalealignment(Gaussians, images, depthestimator, cameraparams): N = len(images) invdepthmono = [] for img in images: metricdepth = depthestimator(img) metricdepth = np.maximum(metricdepth, 1e-6) invdepthmono.append(1.0 / metricdepth) a = torch.tensor(1.0, requiresgrad=True) optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([a], lr=0.01) for in range(100): optimizer.zerograd() loss = 0.0 for i in range(N): # Standard differentiable rasterization to compute inverse depth from scaled Gaussians invdepthrendered = differentiablerasterizeinvdepth(Gaussians, a, cameraparams[i]) diff = invdepthmono[i] - a invdepthrendered loss += torch.abs(diff).mean() loss.backward() optimizer.step() Gaussians.means = Gaussians.means a.item() Gaussians.scales = Gaussians.scales a.item() return Gaussians def differentiablerasterizeinvdepth(Gaussians, scalefactor, camera): # Projects Gaussians scaled by scalefactor onto the image plane. # Accumulates inverse depth values weighted by opacity along each ray. # Returns a 2D tensor of inverse depth values.... Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pruning: Unlike original 3DGS which may prune initial COLMAP points, this method avoids pruning to prevent affecting the distribution of optimized Gaussian parameters, ensuring fair comparison with other studies. Depth Estimator Choice: The method relies on the quality of the monocular depth estimator, requiring a metric-scale variant rather than a relative depth estimator. Inverse Depth Convention: Ensure consistency between the monocular depth output format and the rendered depth format by directly taking the reciprocal of metric depth maps to obtain inverse depth maps. Coarse Alignment with Optical Flow is a preprocessing step in 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines that aligns relative monocular depth estimates across multiple views by optimizing per-view scale and offset parameters. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. This method addresses the up-to-scale problem in neural rendering pipelines where multi-view reconstruction from images alone does not recover metric scale. It builds on the observation that monocular depth estimation models can provide metric-scale depth maps, which can be used to align the relative scale of 3D Gaussians. The approach is similar to depth alignment processes described in prior works [Chung et al., 2024; Kerbl et al., 2024], but specifically adapted for 3D Gaussian Splatting with a focus on avoiding pruning to maintain parameter distribution. name: Coarse Alignment with Optical Flow
body: Coarse Alignment with Optical Flow is a preprocessing step in 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines that aligns relative monocular depth estimates across multiple views by optimizing per-view scale and offset parameters. It solves the problem of multi-view inconsistency caused by the relative nature of monocular depth, which leads to significant misalignments of initialized 3D Gaussians representing the same surfaces. Unlike Multi-View Stereo (MVS) methods, which can produce artifacts with sparse images and large baselines, this method leverages optical flow correspondences to enforce geometric coherence without requiring dense point clouds. Inputs: A set of N input images. Monocular depth maps D^{\text{m}}i for each view i, estimated by a monocular depth estimation network (e.g., Yang et al. [60] as cited in). Camera poses for each view. Mask M{i \rightarrow j} indicating valid flow correspondences from view i to view j. Outputs: Optimized scale parameters \mathbf{s}^ and offset parameters \mathbf{o}^ for each view. Aligned initial depth maps D^{\text{init}}i. Data Structures: \mathbf{s}: Vector of scale factors, one per view. \mathbf{o}: Vector of offset factors, one per view. D^{\text{m}}i[\mathbf{p}]: Depth value at pixel \mathbf{p} in view i. M{i \rightarrow j}: Binary or confidence-weighted mask indicating valid flow correspondences from view i to view j. g(d, \mathbf{p}): Function projecting a depth value d at pixel \mathbf{p} in view i to the corresponding pixel coordinate \mathbf{q} in view j using known camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Algorithm: 1. Compute Optical Flow: Calculate optical flow fields for all relevant pairs of views (i, j) to establish multi-view consistent depth representations. 2. Define Objective: Minimize the L1 difference between the projected depth of view i and the depth of view j at corresponding pixels, weighted by the flow mask. The objective function is: \mathbf{s}^, \mathbf{o}^ = \arg \min{\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{o}} \sum{(i,j)}\sum{\mathbf{p}} \left\| M{i \rightarrow j} \odot \left( g(si \cdot D^{\text{m}}i[\mathbf{p}] + oi, \mathbf{p}) - g(sj \cdot D^{\text{m}}j[\mathbf{q}] + oj, \mathbf{q}) \right) \right\|1 where \mathbf{q} is the pixel coordinate in view j corresponding to \mathbf{p} in view i via the optical flow. 3. Optimize: Solve for \mathbf{s} and \mathbf{o} using gradient-based optimization to minimize the reprojection error between views. 4. Apply Alignment: Compute the final aligned depth for each view i using the optimized parameters: D^{\text{init}}i = si \cdot D^{\text{m}}i + oi This aligned depth is then used to initialize the 3D Gaussians. Parameters: Optimization method: Gradient descent (specifics not given in sources). Loss function: L1 norm. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Flow Accuracy: The method assumes the optical flow is accurate. Areas with inaccurate flow are masked out by M{i \rightarrow j}, leaving their depth unaltered, which may result in residual misalignments in those regions. Sparse Views: While MVS struggles with sparse views and large baselines, this method relies on monocular depth which may have larger errors in textureless regions, though it is noted to complement decoder-based approaches better than MVS in such cases. This variant refers to the experimental setup used to evaluate the SUDS method on the City-1M benchmark. It involves computing optical flow for all sequences using RAFT, aligning auxiliary inputs like depth with the main CoherentGS method, and deactivating the DINO feature distillation branch used for semantic reconstruction in SUDS. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Avoids artifacts associated with MVS in sparse view scenarios with large baselines. Provides a coherent representation that supports regularized optimization. Limitations: Relies on the quality of monocular depth estimation and optical flow. Misalignments may persist in areas where flow is inaccurate. When to Use: Use when initializing 3D Gaussians from monocular depth estimates to ensure multi-view consistency, especially when MVS is prone to artifacts due to sparse input views. Coarse Alignment with Optical Flow was introduced in the CoherentGS paper (2024) as a solution to the multi-view inconsistency problem in 3D Gaussian Splatting initialization. It builds on the observation that monocular depth estimates, while high-quality, are relative and inconsistent across views, leading to misaligned Gaussians. The method contrasts with MVS-based initialization approaches like MVSNeRF, which can suffer from artifacts in sparse settings. name: Sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting with Depth Priors
head: FSGS (masked variant), SparseGS, CoherentGS, DNGaussian
body: This method addresses the challenge of 3D reconstruction from sparse-view inputs, where standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) suffers from geometric ambiguity and artifacts due to insufficient multi-view constraints. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like NeuSG and GSDF by explicitly integrating depth priors estimated from pre-trained 2D monocular depth estimation networks to supervise the Gaussian distribution, rather than relying solely on implicit neural fields or surface extraction techniques. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sparse set of posed input images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N, camera poses \{Ri, Ti\}, and pre-estimated monocular depth maps \{Di\}{i=1}^N for each input view. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \{\mathbf{g}j\} defined by centers \mathbf{c}j, covariances \Sigmaj, opacities \alphaj, and spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}{j,SH}, optimized to render novel views consistent with the input images and depth priors. Data Structures: The Gaussian representation follows the standard 3DGS layout: Centers: \mathbf{c}j \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance: \Sigmaj = Rj Sj Sj^T Rj^T, where Rj \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3} is a rotation matrix (from quaternion) and Sj \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3} is a scaling matrix. Opacity: \alphaj \in [0, 1]. Color: Spherical Harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}{j,SH}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Depth Estimation: For each input image Ii, estimate a dense depth map Di using a pre-trained 2D monocular depth estimation network. 2. Initialization: Initialize the 3D Gaussian point cloud, typically using Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points or by unpooling existing Gaussians from the input views. 3. Rendering: Render the current Gaussian set to the input views to obtain rendered depth images D{rendered} and color images I{rendered}. 4. Geometric Loss Calculation: Compute \mathcal{L}{geo} by comparing D{rendered} with the estimated depth Di. 5. Normal Consistency: Compute surface normals from the estimated depth map Di. Align the Gaussian orientation (derived from the rotation quaternion or covariance matrix) with these normals to compute \mathcal{L}{norm}. 6. Gaussian Pruning: Remove Gaussians that exhibit incorrect depth values or large discrepancies between rendered and estimated depth, effectively cleaning up noise and artifacts common in sparse views. 7. Optional SDS Regularization: To further encourage faithful results from novel viewpoints, apply Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss. This leverages a pre-trained diffusion model to provide additional geometric priors where multi-view cues are weak. 8. Optimization: Update Gaussian parameters (\mathbf{c}j, \Sigmaj, \alphaj, \mathbf{c}{j,SH}) using gradient descent to minimize \mathcal{L}{total}. Formulas: The total loss function combines the standard photometric loss with geometric and normal consistency terms, following the shared principles of the parent family: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{geo} \mathcal{L}{geo} + \lambda{norm} \mathcal{L}{norm} Where: \mathcal{L}{rgb} is the standard L1/SSIM photometric loss between rendered and input images. \mathcal{L}{geo} enforces positional consistency between Gaussian centers and the estimated depth. \mathcal{L}{norm} enforces normal consistency between Gaussian orientations and surface normals derived from the depth map. \lambda{geo} and \lambda{norm} are hyperparameters balancing photometric fidelity against geometric accuracy. Parameters: \lambda{geo}, \lambda{norm}: Weights for geometric and normal losses. Typical values are not given in the sources. SDS Weight: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Ambiguity: Monocular depth estimates suffer from scale and shift ambiguity. The method must handle this, potentially through normalization or scale-invariant loss terms, though specific normalization steps are not detailed in the sources. Sparse View Ambiguity: With very few views, the optimization may converge to local minima. SDS loss helps mitigate this by providing strong semantic priors. Incorrect Depth Estimates: If the pre-trained depth network fails on certain textures or regions, the geometric loss may pull Gaussians to incorrect positions. Pruning removes Gaussians with incorrect depth values. Texture Quality: FSGS produces reasonable reconstructions, but its textures are noticeably blurrier and over-smoothed compared to unconstrained baselines. Masked Training Failure: Attempting to train FSGS on mask-composited images with depth and pseudo-view losses restricted to the mask causes it to fail without scene context, with PSNR falling from 20.25 to 13.43. Definition: FWD is a generalizable novel view synthesis method for sparse inputs that uses explicit depth and forward warping to achieve real-time speed and high quality. Unlike the sparse-view 3DGS methods which optimize per-scene Gaussians, FWD is a generalizable model that learns to synthesize views without per-scene optimization. How it works: 1. Input: Sparse input images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N and poses \{Ri, Ti\}. Optional sensor depths \{Di^{sen}\} may be provided, though they are often incomplete and noisy. 2. Depth and Feature Estimation: For each input view Ii, estimate depth Di using a depth network d and compute spatial features Fi using a spatial feature encoder f (based on BigGAN architecture) and a view-dependent MLP \psi. Features are 64-dimensional (61-dim semantic + 3-dim RGB). 3. Point Cloud Construction: Project the features into 3D space using known camera intrinsics to form a point cloud Pi for each view. 4. Rendering: Render the point clouds Pi to the target view using a differentiable point cloud renderer \pi. Instead of aggregating point clouds across views before rendering, FWD renders viewpoints separately and fuses them using a Transformer-based module \mathcal{T}, enabling attention across input views. 5. Refinement: Apply a refinement module \mathcal{R} to generate the final output, improving visual quality. 6. Training: Train end-to-end with photometric and perceptual losses. Parameters: N: Number of input views. \{Ri, Ti\}: Camera poses for input views. \{Rt, Tt\}: Camera pose for target view. \{Di^{sen}\}: Optional sensor depths for input views. Comparison: FWD replaces implicit MLP volumetric sampling with explicit point clouds, avoiding millions of MLP queries and enabling a 130-1000× speedup compared to NeRF-based methods. It uses sparse inputs and learns depth jointly optimized for synthesis quality, unlike classical Image-Based Rendering (IBR) which requires dense inputs and proxy geometry. Usage: Evaluated on ShapeNet and DTU datasets. Code available at https://github.com/Caoang327/fwdcode. Time Complexity: Sparse-view 3DGS methods require per-scene optimization, making them slower than generalizable methods like FWD. FWD achieves real-time speed due to its generalizable nature. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians. Pruning removes Gaussians with incorrect depth values. Strengths: Enables high-quality 3D reconstruction from very few input views by leveraging strong geometric priors and SDS regularization. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the pre-trained 2D depth estimation network. FSGS textures are noticeably blurrier and over-smoothed. Per-scene optimization is required, unlike generalizable methods. When to use: When input views are sparse and standard 3DGS fails to produce coherent geometry. When not to use: When real-time inference without per-scene optimization is required (use FWD instead) or when dense input views are available (standard 3DGS may suffice). The method originates from the need to extend 3D Gaussian Splatting to sparse-view scenarios, where traditional multi-view stereo constraints are insufficient. SparseGS, CoherentGS, and DNGaussian are key contributions in this area, introducing depth supervision from pre-trained 2D networks to guide the Gaussian optimization. The use of SDS loss for sparse-view reconstruction was also explored to leverage the geometric priors of pre-trained diffusion models. name: GSDF
head: Gaussian SDF, Gaussian Signed Distance Function
body: Builds on Geometry and Surface Priors. GSDF is a training optimization technique that aligns the discrete 3D Gaussian representation with a continuous Signed Distance Function (SDF) prior to enhance geometry reconstruction quality. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like NeuSG by explicitly transferring surface properties from a neural SDF to the Gaussians. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters (centers, covariances, opacities, colors), a neural SDF field, and input images with camera poses. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussians suitable for rendering and mesh extraction. Data Structures: Neural SDF: A continuous field S(\mathbf{x}) mapping 3D coordinates to signed distance values. Gaussian Attributes: Standard 3DGS attributes including position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonics for color. Method Steps: 1. Render: Perform standard differentiable volume rendering to generate predicted images from the current Gaussian set. 2. Compute Photometric Loss: Calculate \mathcal{L}{rgb} between rendered and input images. 3. Evaluate SDF: Query the neural SDF at each Gaussian center \mathbf{c}i to obtain S(\mathbf{c}i). 4. Compute Geometric Loss: Calculate \mathcal{L}{geo} to encourage Gaussian centers to lie on the zero-level set of the SDF. 5. Compute Normal Loss: Calculate \mathcal{L}{norm} to align Gaussian orientations with the surface normals derived from the SDF gradient. 6. Optimize: Update Gaussian parameters and SDF weights by minimizing the total loss. Formulas: The total loss function combines photometric and geometric terms: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{geo} \mathcal{L}{geo} + \lambda{norm} \mathcal{L}{norm} where \mathcal{L}{geo} enforces positional consistency by minimizing the absolute SDF value at Gaussian centers, and \mathcal{L}{norm} enforces normal consistency by aligning Gaussian orientations with the SDF gradient. The weights \lambda{geo} and \lambda{norm} balance photometric fidelity against geometric accuracy. Parameters: \lambda{geo}, \lambda{norm}: Hyperparameters controlling the weight of geometric and normal consistency losses. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Edge Cases: Not given in the sources. Complexity: Adds computational overhead proportional to the number of Gaussians for querying the neural SDF during each training iteration. Strengths: Recovers more detailed mesh structures compared to standard 3DGS. Enhances overall geometry reconstruction quality. Limitations: Requires a reliable and accurately trained neural SDF prior. When to use: When high-quality surface reconstruction and mesh extraction are required from 3DGS. GSDF was introduced to leverage neural signed distance functions (SDFs) for surface reconstruction, inspired by similar approaches used in NeRF-based methods. It is closely related to methods like 3DGSR that also encourage consistency between SDF and 3DGS representations. The approach was later extended in works like 2DGS, which replaced 3D Gaussians with 2D Gaussians to improve rendering accuracy. name: Surface and Geometry Alignment
head: Geometric Priors in Gaussian Splatting, Surface-Aligned Gaussian Optimization
body: This family of methods addresses the lack of explicit, watertight geometry in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), which consists of floating, semi-transparent ellipsoids. By aligning the discrete Gaussian representation with continuous geometric priors—such as signed distance fields (SDFs), metric depth maps, or explicit meshes—these techniques enforce positional and normal consistency to produce high-fidelity surface representations. Unlike sibling methods that primarily focus on training-time regularization or post-hoc mesh extraction, this family encompasses a spectrum from re-initialization strategies and physically-based inverse rendering to contrastive token alignment, enabling applications ranging from editable mesh generation to accurate material decomposition. All methods in this family align the discrete Gaussian representation with a continuous geometric prior. The core mechanism adds geometric loss terms to the standard photometric rendering loss \mathcal{L}{rgb}. These losses enforce two properties: positional consistency, where Gaussian centers \mathbf{c}i are encouraged to lie on the zero-level set of a distance function (SDF or UDF) or align with metric depth estimates, and normal consistency, where the orientation of the Gaussians (derived from their covariance matrix or rotation quaternion) is aligned with the surface normal estimated from the geometric prior. The total loss function generally takes the form: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{geo} \mathcal{L}{geo} + \lambda{norm} \mathcal{L}{norm} where \mathcal{L}{geo} is the geometric consistency loss and \mathcal{L}{norm} is the normal consistency loss. The weights \lambda{geo} and \lambda{norm} are hyperparameters that balance photometric fidelity against geometric accuracy. A post-hoc method that converts the discrete, volumetric 3DGS representation into a continuous, editable triangle mesh by aligning Gaussians with a reconstructed surface. It solves the problem that vanilla 3DGS produces floating ellipsoids with no explicit geometry, making it difficult to use in standard DCC pipelines for animation or physics. Unlike sibling methods that modify the training loop or use implicit fields, SuGaR operates after training, using a self-regularization loss to flatten Gaussians onto a surface and then extracting a mesh via Poisson reconstruction. A training strategy for 3DGS that resolves the unbalanced aggregation of Gaussians caused by densification and splitting operations. It makes trained Gaussians better fit the input monocular video by anchoring them to a surface representation. It is distinct from SuGaR and Geo-Splatting by specifically targeting the re-initialization phase to correct aggregation artifacts rather than just loss regularization or initial placement. A physically-based inverse rendering method that augments 3DGS with explicit geometric priors to improve normal estimation and light transport modeling. It solves the problem of inaccurate material decomposition and flawed relighting caused by approximated normals and semi-transparent Gaussian points in existing methods. Unlike siblings that rely on implicit constraints or low-frequency spherical Gaussians, Geo-Splatting differentiably constructs surface-aligned Gaussian points from an optimizable explicit mesh, leveraging well-defined mesh normals and opaque surfaces for superior decomposition and relighting quality. A geometric regularization term used in ZipSplat to align token similarity with 3D proximity, ensuring that clustering merges image patches observing the same surface rather than grouping them by viewpoint. It solves the problem where feature-space merging does not guarantee geometric consistency, explicitly shaping the token space so that clusters correspond to physical surfaces. Unlike Cone Loss, which anchors individual tokens to their source patches, GeoCE handles token merging by enforcing that similar tokens are also 3D-proximate. The standard 3D Gaussian Splatting method provides fast, high-quality novel view synthesis but lacks an explicit surface representation, consisting instead of a collection of anisotropic Gaussians. This limitation hinders applications requiring watertight meshes, such as physics simulation, texturing, and animation. Early attempts to extract geometry from 3DGS relied on post-processing techniques like Poisson reconstruction on the Gaussian centers, often resulting in noisy or incomplete meshes due to the volumetric nature of the representation. To address this, subsequent research introduced geometric priors during the optimization process. Methods like NeuSG and GaussianPro integrated implicit neural fields or depth priors to guide the Gaussian placement. More recent approaches, such as Geo-Splatting, have moved towards explicit mesh-based proxies for physically-based rendering, while others like SuGaR have refined post-hoc alignment to produce clean, editable meshes. The introduction of contrastive losses like GeoCE further refined the geometric consistency of token-based Gaussian representations, ensuring that learned features correspond to physical surfaces rather than viewpoint-dependent artifacts.

name: SuGaR
head: SuGaR: Surface-Aligned Gaussian Splatting for Realistic Head Avatar Reconstruction, Surface-Aligned Gaussian Splatting
body: SuGaR is a post-hoc surface alignment method that extracts a high-quality triangle mesh from a trained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene by enforcing geometric priors during a refinement phase. It solves the problem that vanilla 3DGS produces discrete, floating ellipsoids with no explicit surface structure, making mesh extraction difficult and resulting in geometry that is often inferior to implicit methods. Unlike sibling methods that integrate geometry constraints directly into the training loop (e.g., Geo-Splatting) or replace primitives with 2D disks 2D Gaussian Splatting, SuGaR operates as a separate optimization stage on the existing 3DGS representation, flattening and pinning Gaussians to a reconstructed surface to enable mesh-based editing while maintaining real-time rendering capabilities. Inputs: A fully trained 3DGS scene (set of N Gaussians with centers \mathbf{c}i, covariances \Sigmai, opacities \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}{SH,i}) and multi-view input images with known camera poses. Outputs: A refined set of Gaussians aligned to a surface and a reconstructed triangle mesh. Data Structures: The Gaussian representation remains identical to standard 3DGS: \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position. \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation quaternion (defining orientation). \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scaling vector. \alphai \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. \mathbf{c}{SH,i}: SH coefficients for color. Method Steps: 1. Initial Surface Estimation: Render depth maps from the trained 3DGS scene using standard volume rendering. 2. Self-Regularization Loss: Introduce a loss term that constrains the distance between the camera and the closest Gaussian to match the corresponding pixel's depth value in the rendered depth map. For each pixel, the Gaussian contributing most to the accumulated opacity is identified as the closest representative. 3. Flattening and Alignment: Apply a penalty term to force Gaussians to become flat and aligned with the local surface normal. This regularizes the covariance matrix \Sigmai to have one dominant eigenvalue and two near-zero eigenvalues, effectively turning 3D ellipsoids into 2D surfels. 4. Mesh Extraction: Perform Poisson surface reconstruction on the aligned Gaussian centers and their estimated normals to generate a watertight triangle mesh. 5. Hybrid Representation: Pin the flattened Gaussians to the surface of the extracted mesh. This creates a hybrid representation where the mesh provides structural editability and the Gaussians provide high-fidelity rendering. Formulas: The total loss for the refinement phase combines photometric and geometric terms, following the family's shared principle: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{geo} \mathcal{L}{geo} + \lambda{norm} \mathcal{L}{norm} Where: \mathcal{L}{rgb} is the standard photometric loss (e.g., L1 + SSIM). \mathcal{L}{geo} is the self-regularization loss that enforces positional consistency by minimizing the discrepancy between the camera-to-Gaussian distance and the rendered pixel depth. \mathcal{L}{norm} enforces normal consistency, aligning Gaussian orientations with surface normals derived from the depth map or extracted mesh. \lambda{geo}, \lambda{norm} are hyperparameters balancing photometric fidelity against geometric accuracy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sugarrefine(gaussians, images, cameras, lambdageo=1.0, lambdanorm=1.0, numiterations=1000): # Standard 3DGS rasterization for iteration in range(numiterations): pixelindices = randomsample(len(images[0].width images[0].height)) # Standard 3DGS volume rendering renderedcolor, rendereddepth, contributions = standard3dgsrasterizebatch(gaussians, pixelindices, cameras) lossrgb = l1loss(renderedcolor, groundtruthcolor[pixelindices]) + ssimloss(renderedcolor, groundtruthcolor[pixelindices]) lossgeo = 0.0 for p in pixelindices: k = argmax(contributions[:, p]) distcamtogauss = norm(cameras[p].position - gaussians[k].center) lossgeo += abs(distcamtogauss - rendereddepth[p]) lossnorm = 0.0 for p in pixelindices: gaussnormal = quaterniontonormal(gaussians[k].rotation) # Estimate surface normal from depth map gradients surfnormal = finitediffnormal(rendereddepth, p) lossnorm += 1.0 - dot(gaussnormal, surfnormal) loss = lossrgb + lambdageo lossgeo + lambdanorm lossnorm loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Post-processing: Flatten Gaussians and extract mesh gaussians = flattengaussians(gaussians) mesh = poissonsurfacereconstruction(gaussians) # Project Gaussian centers onto nearest mesh face for g in gaussians: g.center = mesh.nearestpoint(g.center) return gaussians, mesh def flattengaussians(gaussians): for g in gaussians: eigvals, eigvecs = torch.linalg.eigh(g.covariance) eigvals[1:] = 1e-4 g.covariance = eigvecs @ torch.diag(eigvals) @ eigvecs.T return gaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Gaussians: Flattening can lead to numerical instability if eigenvalues become too small; a minimum threshold for eigenvalues is required. Volumetric Effects: SuGaR is a surface-based representation and struggles with fuzzy materials or volumetric effects, leading to performance drops compared to vanilla 3DGS in such regions. Precision: The accuracy of the extracted mesh depends heavily on the quality of the initial depth maps and the resolution of the input images. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Provides high-quality mesh extraction suitable for DCC pipelines and animation. However, rendering quality may decrease slightly compared to vanilla 3DGS due to the flattening constraint. Strengths: Enables mesh-based editing and animation; provides explicit surface structure; works with existing 3DGS models. Limitations: Not suitable for volumetric or fuzzy scenes; post-hoc nature means it cannot correct fundamental training issues in the 3DGS model. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. SuGaR was introduced by Guédon and Lepetit in 2024 as a method to bridge the gap between the high-quality rendering of 3DGS and the structural editability of triangle meshes. It addresses the limitation that vanilla 3DGS lacks a continuous surface representation, which is a standard requirement in many 3D graphics applications. The method builds on the 3DGS framework by adding a self-regularization loss to align Gaussians with the surface, followed by Poisson meshing. It is particularly useful for head avatar reconstruction and other applications requiring explicit geometry. name: Surface-guided Gaussian Re-initialization
head: GVA
body: Surface-guided Gaussian Re-initialization (GVA) is a training strategy designed to resolve the unbalanced aggregation of 3D Gaussians caused by densification and splitting operations during the optimization of dynamic human avatars from monocular video. It makes trained Gaussians better fit the input monocular video by anchoring their positions to a canonical surface geometry, distinguishing it from unconstrained splatting methods. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} with current parameters (position \mathbf{c}i, covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, spherical harmonics coefficients). A canonical human body mesh \mathcal{M} (e.g., SMPL or similar parametric model). Camera poses and image observations. Data Structures: Canonical Mesh: Defined by vertices \mathbf{V} and faces \mathcal{F}. Each face f \in \mathcal{F} is a triangle with vertices \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3. Barycentric Coordinates: For any point \mathbf{p} projected onto a face, represented as (\lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3) where \sum \lambdak = 1 and \lambdak \ge 0. Surface Normal: \mathbf{n}f for face f, computed as the normalized cross product of edge vectors. Steps: 1. Ray Casting / Projection: For each Gaussian center \mathbf{c}i in the canonical space, determine its closest point on the canonical mesh \mathcal{M}. This is typically done by projecting \mathbf{c}i onto the mesh surface to find the intersecting face f and barycentric coordinates (\lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3). 2. Surface Point Calculation: Compute the projected point \mathbf{p}{surf} on the mesh surface using the barycentric interpolation: \mathbf{p}{surf} = \lambda1 \mathbf{v}1 + \lambda2 \mathbf{v}2 + \lambda3 \mathbf{v}3 3. Normal Displacement: Calculate the surface normal \mathbf{n}f at face f. The Gaussian position is adjusted or constrained relative to this surface. In GVA, the position is determined by the barycentric point and a displacement along the normal direction. Let di be the signed distance or displacement parameter. The re-initialized position \mathbf{c}i' is: \mathbf{c}i' = \mathbf{p}{surf} + di \mathbf{n}f Note: In some implementations, di might be optimized or fixed to zero to strictly enforce surface alignment, effectively "snapping" the Gaussian to the mesh. 4. Covariance Adjustment: The orientation of the Gaussian is aligned with the surface normal. The rotation matrix or quaternion of the Gaussian is updated such that one principal axis aligns with \mathbf{n}f, ensuring the Gaussian sheet lies tangent to the surface. This reduces the "floating" artifacts and unbalanced aggregation. 5. Re-initialization: Replace the original Gaussian parameters with the re-initialized ones. This step is performed periodically during training to counteract the drift and clustering issues caused by standard densification/splitting heuristics. Parameters: Displacement weight: Often zero or small, depending on whether the Gaussian is strictly constrained to the surface or allowed slight offset. Frequency of re-initialization: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Degenerate Faces: If the mesh has degenerate triangles, barycentric coordinates may be undefined. Handle by skipping or using a fallback projection. Off-Mesh Gaussians: If a Gaussian is far from the mesh, the closest point search may fail or snap to an incorrect region. Implement a distance threshold; if distance > threshold, ignore or re-project using a broader search. Time Complexity: Depends on the mesh traversal for closest point projection. Typically O(N) per Gaussian if using efficient spatial hashing or BVH for mesh intersection. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the canonical mesh and its acceleration structure. Strengths: Resolves unbalanced aggregation of Gaussians; improves geometric fidelity to the input monocular video; reduces floating artifacts. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the canonical mesh; may restrict the Gaussian's ability to model non-surface details (e.g., hair, loose clothing) if strictly constrained. When to use: Dynamic human avatar reconstruction from monocular video where surface consistency is critical. When not to use: Scenes without a clear underlying surface or when modeling volumetric objects not attached to a mesh. GVA was proposed in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting for dynamic human avatar reconstruction. It addresses the issue of Gaussian aggregation and drift during training from monocular video. The method builds on the idea of embedding Gaussians onto a canonical human body mesh, similar to SplattingAvatar and GoMAvatar. It is cited in recent advances surveys of 3D Gaussian Splatting. name: Geo-Splatting
body: Geo-Splatting is a physically-based inverse rendering method that augments 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with explicit geometric priors to improve normal estimation and light transport modeling. Unlike existing 3DGS-based inverse methods that rely on approximated Gaussian normals, which lead to noisy material decomposition and flawed relighting, Geo-Splatting differentiably constructs surface-aligned Gaussian points from an optimizable explicit mesh. This approach leverages well-defined mesh normals and an opaque mesh surface to accurately model self-occlusion and reflective surfaces, resulting in superior decomposition and relighting quality. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images of a scene. Outputs: Decomposed material properties (Albedo, Roughness, Normal), environment light probe, and a relit image. Data Structures: 1. Learnable Isovalue Grids: A scalar field representation of the scene geometry. 2. Explicit Triangular Mesh: Extracted from the isovalue grids using FlexiCubes. 3. 3D Gaussian Points: Structured points generated on the mesh surface via the Mesh-to-Gaussian adaptor (MGadapter). Each Gaussian is defined by center \mathbf{\mu}, scaling \mathbf{S}, rotation \mathbf{R}, opacity, and PBR material parameters (Albedo, Roughness, Normal). 4. BVH (Bounding Volume Hierarchy): Acceleration structure built on the explicit mesh for ray tracing. Steps: 1. Geometry Extraction: Extract an intermediate triangular mesh from the learnable isovalue grids using FlexiCubes. 2. Gaussian Generation: Generate 3DGS points on the mesh surface in a differentiable manner using the Mesh-to-Gaussian adaptor (MGadapter). This ensures the Gaussians are grounded on the mesh geometry and inherit its normals. 3. Light Transport Evaluation: Perform BVH-accelerated ray tracing on the extracted mesh to evaluate light transport. This step uses Monte Carlo sampling to evaluate the rendering equation. Note: This replaces the split-sum approximation used in methods like R3DG, allowing for accurate self-occlusion modeling. 4. PBR Color Computation: Compute per-Gaussian physically-based rendering (PBR) colors by evaluating the rendering equation using the traced light transport and the Gaussian's material properties. 5. Rendering: Composite the shaded Gaussian points into final images using the standard 3DGS rasterization algorithm. Formulas: The rendering equation is evaluated via Monte Carlo sampling on the mesh proxy. The final image is composited using 3DGS rasterization. The total loss function includes geometric consistency and normal consistency terms, building on the parent method's structure: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{geo} \mathcal{L}{geo} + \lambda{norm} \mathcal{L}{norm} where \mathcal{L}{geo} enforces positional consistency and \mathcal{L}{norm} aligns Gaussian normals with the mesh normals. Parameters: FlexiCubes: Used for isosurface extraction. MGadapter: Differentiable module for mesh-to-Gaussian conversion. Hyperparameters: \lambda{geo} and \lambda{norm} balance photometric fidelity against geometric accuracy. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Approximated Normals: Existing methods suffer from inaccuracies in normal estimation due to semi-transparent Gaussian points, leading to noisy material decomposition. Geo-Splatting mitigates this by using explicit mesh normals. Self-Occlusion: Split-sum approximation lacks self-occlusion modeling, leading to inaccurate decomposition under strong shadow effects. Geo-Splatting uses ray tracing on the mesh to handle this. Reflective Surfaces: Methods using Spherical Gaussians (SG) with ray tracing struggle with reflective cases due to low-frequency nature. Geo-Splatting handles this via Monte Carlo sampling on the explicit mesh. Time Complexity: Training time is 9 minutes on the reported dataset, compared to 56 minutes for R3DG and 13 minutes for GS-IR. This efficiency is attributed to the use of BVH-accelerated ray tracing on the explicit mesh proxy rather than direct ray tracing on Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Relighting PSNR of 29.5dB, compared to 26.6dB for R3DG and 20.4dB for GS-IR. Strengths: Superior decomposition and relighting quality; accurate modeling of self-occlusion and reflective surfaces; efficient training due to mesh-based ray tracing. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the extracted mesh; requires differentiable mesh-to-Gaussian conversion. When to use: When high-fidelity physically-based inverse rendering (material decomposition and relighting) is required, especially for scenes with strong shadows or reflective surfaces. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and approximate normal estimation is acceptable. Geo-Splatting was proposed by Wenzheng Chen and Guanbin Li from Sun Yat-sen University and Peking University. It was published in the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV) in 2025. The method addresses the limitations of existing 3DGS-based inverse rendering frameworks, such as R3DG and GS-IR, which rely on implicit geometric constraints and approximated normals. By introducing explicit geometry guidance via an optimizable triangular mesh, Geo-Splatting improves the accuracy of light transport modeling. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) GeoSplatting: Towards Geometry Guided Gaussian Splatting for Physically-Based Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/ICCV51701.2025.02692, fetched 2026-10-30

name: GeoCE Loss
head: Geometric Contrastive Loss
body: GeoCE (Geometric Contrastive Embedding) is a geometric regularization term used in ZipSplat to align token similarity with 3D proximity, ensuring that clustering merges image patches observing the same surface rather than grouping them by viewpoint. It solves the problem where feature-space clustering alone does not guarantee geometric consistency, by explicitly shaping the token space using soft target distributions derived from 3D anchor points. It differs from Cone Loss, which anchors individual tokens to their source patches, by handling the merging of tokens across views based on surface correspondence. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Geometry tokens \gtoki \in \mathbb{R}^d (one per image patch), ground-truth camera poses, median depth maps for each patch, and a set of sampled anchor tokens. Outputs: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{geo}} added to the total training loss. Data Structures: Geometry Tokens: \ell2-normalized vectors \gtoki. 3D Anchors: Points \spointi \in \mathbb{R}^3 derived from unprojecting patch pixels. Bandwidths: Scalars \sigmai per token. Steps: 1. Anchor Sampling: Sample 2048 tokens per scene as anchors. 2. 3D Unprojection: For each anchor token i, obtain its 3D anchor point \spointi by unprojecting the median-depth pixel of its source patch using the ground-truth camera. 3. Validity Check: Exclude patches where valid depth exists on fewer than half of their pixels. 4. Bandwidth Calculation: Compute the base bandwidth \sigma as the scene-wise median 3D distance between adjacent patch points. Rank all tokens by their mean image-gradient energy (texture complexity). Compute per-token bandwidth \sigmai by log-interpolating between \sigma (for the flattest patch) and 0.4\sigma (for the most textured patch) based on the rank. 5. Target Weight Computation: Compute the soft target weight w{ij} for every pair of distinct tokens (i, j) using the Gaussian kernel based on 3D proximity: w{ij} \propto \exp \!\left ( -\frac {\|\spoint i-\spoint j\|^2} {2\sigma i\sigma j} \right) where \spointi and \spointj are the 3D anchor points, and \sigmai, \sigmaj are their respective bandwidths. The weight is averaged over a 4 \times 4 pixel grid inside each key patch. 6. Loss Calculation: Compute the GeoCE loss using cross-entropy between the token cosine similarities and the target weights: \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{geo}} = -\sumi\sum{j\neq i} w{ij} \log \frac {\exp (\gtok i^\top \gtok j/\tau)} {\sum {k\neq i}\exp (\gtok i^\top \gtok k/\tau)} where \tau is the temperature parameter. Parameters: Temperature \tau: 0.1. Loss Weight \lambda{\mathrm{geo}}: 0.05. Anchor Count: 2048 per scene. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegeoceloss(geometrytokens, cameraposes, mediandepthmaps, patchmasks): """ geometrytokens: Tensor of shape (N, D), l2-normalized. cameraposes: List of N camera pose matrices. mediandepthmaps: List of N depth maps (H, W). patchmasks: List of N boolean masks indicating valid pixels. """ N = len(geometrytokens) anchors = [] validindices = [] # Step 1 & 2: Sample anchors and unproject # Note: In practice, 2048 are sampled. Here we assume all N are processed # or a subset is selected. For implementation, select 2048 indices. numanchors = min(2048, N) anchorindices = sampleindices(N, numanchors) for idx in anchorindices: # Unproject median depth pixel depthmap = mediandepthmaps[idx] mask = patchmasks[idx] # Check validity: fewer than half pixels valid -> exclude if torch.sum(mask) < (mask.shape[0] mask.shape[1]) / 2: continue # Get median depth value validdepths = depthmap[mask] if len(validdepths) == 0: continue mediandepth = torch.median(validdepths) # Unproject pixel with median depth to 3D point # Assuming standard pinhole camera model # Find pixel with median depth (or use center if uniform) # Simplified: unproject center pixel with median depth h, w = depthmap.shape u, v = w // 2, h // 2 # Inverse projection point3d = unprojectpixel(cameraposes[idx], u, v, mediandepth) anchors.append(point3d) validindices.append(idx) if len(anchors) == 0: return 0.0 anchors = torch.stack(anchors) validtokens = geometrytokens[validindices] # Step 4: Compute bandwidths # Compute image gradient energy for ranking gradientenergies = [] for idx in validindices: # Compute mean gradient magnitude of the patch gradenergy = computegradientenergy(mediandepthmaps[idx], patchmasks[idx]) gradientenergies.append(gradenergy) gradientenergies = torch.tensor(gradientenergies) ranks = torch.argsort(torch.argsort(gradientenergies)) # Rank 0 is flattest # Base bandwidth sigma # Compute pairwise 3D distances between adjacent patch points (simplified as median dist) # In practice, this requires a grid structure. Here we approximate with median dist of anchors. dists = torch.cdist(anchors, anchors) # Exclude self-distances dists = dists.maskedfill(torch.eye(len(anchors), dtype=torch.bool), float('inf')) sigmabase = torch.median(dists) # Log-interpolate sigmai # Flattenest (rank 0) -> sigmabase # Most textured (rank max) -> 0.4 sigmabase minrank = 0 maxrank = len(ranks) - 1 if maxrank == 0: sigmas = torch.full((len(ranks),), sigmabase) else: # Log interpolation logsigmamin = torch.log(torch.tensor(sigmabase)) logsigmamax = torch.log(torch.tensor(0.4 sigmabase)) logsigmai = logsigmamin + (ranks / maxrank) (logsigmamax - logsigmamin) sigmas = torch.exp(logsigmai) # Step 5: Compute target weights # wij proportional to exp(-||pi - pj||^2 / (2 sigmai sigmaj)) distssq = torch.cdist(anchors, anchors) 2 sigmaouter = torch.outer(sigmas, sigmas) exponent = -distssq / (2 sigmaouter) # Mask out self exponent = exponent.maskedfill(torch.eye(len(anchors), dtype=torch.bool), float('-inf')) weights = torch.softmax(exponent, dim=1) # Normalize to sum to 1 for each i # Step 6: Compute loss # Cosine similarity (tokens are already l2-normalized) simmatrix = validtokens @ validtokens.T tau = 0.1 logits = simmatrix / tau # Cross-entropy with weights # logsoftmax logprobs = torch.nn.functional.logsoftmax(logits, dim=1) # Loss = - sumi sumj wij log(pj|i) loss = -torch.sum(weights logprobs) return loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invalid Depth: Patches with insufficient valid depth pixels are excluded to prevent noisy 3D anchors. Precision: The log-interpolation of bandwidths requires careful handling of zero or negative gradient energies, though gradient energy is typically positive. Anchor Count: Sampling only 2048 anchors limits the scope of the contrastive loss to a subset of the scene, which may miss long-range geometric consistency if not managed. Anchors individual Gaussians to their source image patches to prevent drifting, handling initial spatial grounding rather than cross-view merging. Time Complexity: O(N^2) for the pairwise distance and similarity computations, where N is the number of sampled anchors (2048). This is constant relative to the total number of patches if N is fixed, but linear in the number of anchors if sampled dynamically. Memory Complexity: O(N^2) to store the weight matrix and similarity matrix. Performance: Contributes to state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks in ZipSplat by enabling compact scene representations with fewer Gaussians. Strengths: Explicitly enforces surface-based clustering, reducing viewpoint-dependent artifacts in the token space. Limitations: Relies on accurate median depth and ground-truth cameras for anchor generation; sensitive to depth noise. GeoCE Loss was introduced in the ZipSplat paper (2026) as part of a method for few-view Gaussian splatting. It addresses the limitation of previous clustering methods that did not guarantee geometric consistency across views. name: Cone Loss
body:
The Cone Loss is a geometric regularization term used in ZipSplat to ground 3D Gaussian tokens to their specific source image patches, preventing decoded Gaussians from drifting arbitrarily in 3D space. Unlike frustum-based constraints that merely ensure visibility, this loss explicitly ties each token’s geometry to the observation that produced it, ensuring an observation-grounded scene representation. It operates alongside the GeoCE Loss, which aligns token similarity with 3D proximity so that clusters form by surface rather than by viewpoint, while the Cone Loss anchors individual tokens to their source observations. Inputs and Outputs K: Total number of scene tokens. 
gs: Number of Gaussians per token. \gmean{kj}: The 3D mean position of the j-th Gaussian belonging to token k. \pik: The projection function mapping 3D points into the 2D image plane of token k's source view. \{u}k: The 2D center coordinate of the source image patch for token k. Output: A scalar loss value \loss{\mathrm{cone}} representing the total reprojection error. Data Structures Token indices k \in \{1, \dots, K\}. Gaussian indices j \in \{1, \dots, 
gs\}. Coordinates are measured in "patch units" (where the patch width/height is normalized to 1 unit). Algorithm The loss is computed by summing a robust penalty ho over all Gaussians of all tokens. The penalty is based on the Euclidean distance between the projected Gaussian center and the source patch center. 1. For each token k from 1 to K: 2. For each Gaussian j from 1 to 
gs: 3. Project the Gaussian mean \gmean{kj} into the source view of token k using \pik to obtain the 2D point \mathbf{p} = \pik(\gmean{kj}). 4. Check if the Gaussian projects behind the camera plane of the source view. If yes, assign a sentinel distance d = 20 patch units. If no, compute the Euclidean distance in patch units: d = \| \mathbf{p} - \{u}k \|. 5. Apply the hinged Cauchy penalty function ho(d) to d. 6. Accumulate ho(d) into the total loss. Formula The total Cone Loss is defined as: \loss{\mathrm{cone}} = \sum{k=1}^{K} \sum{j=1}^{
gs} ho \left( \left\| \pik(\gmean{kj}) - \{u}k ight\| ight) Where: \pik(\gmean{kj}) is the 2D projection of the j-th Gaussian of token k into its source view. \{u}k is the center of the source patch for token k. The norm \|\cdot\| is the Euclidean distance measured in patch units. ho is a robust penalty function (hinged Cauchy). Robust Penalty Function ho The function ho(d) is a hinged Cauchy function of the distance d in patch units. It has the following properties: 1. Hinge (Zero-cost region): For d \le 2, ho(d) = 0. This allows Gaussians to extend up to 2 patch units past their source observation, accommodating flat surfaces or occluded regions. 2. Smooth Ramp: For 2 < d \le 4, the penalty ramps smoothly with C^1 continuity. 3. Saturation: For d > 4, the penalty saturates to limit the influence of distant outliers. Parameters Weight \lambda{\mathrm{cone}} = 0.01. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Behind-view Gaussians: Gaussians projecting behind the source view receive a fixed sentinel distance of 20 patches. This provides a large penalty value but no lateral gradient, preventing optimization from pushing these Gaussians laterally into the view. Depth Independence: The loss constrains only the lateral position relative to the viewing cone. Depth is left to be determined by the rendering loss. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def coneloss(gmeans, projections, patchcenters, numtokens, numgs): """ Computes the Cone Loss for ZipSplat. Args: gmeans: Array of shape (numtokens, numgs, 3), 3D means of Gaussians. projections: Array of shape (numtokens, numgs, 2), 2D projected coordinates. patchcenters: Array of shape (numtokens, 2), centers of source patches. numtokens: Integer K. numgs: Integer ngs. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ totalloss = 0.0 for k in range(numtokens): for j in range(numgs): # Get projected 2D point and patch center proj2d = projections[k, j] uk = patchcenters[k] # Check if Gaussian projects behind the camera plane # The source does not specify the exact visibility check implementation. # Replace with camera-space z-depth test (e.g., z <= 0 in right-handed convention). isbehind = False # Placeholder for implementer's camera model if isbehind: d = 20.0 else: # Euclidean distance in 2D patch units dx = proj2d[0] - uk[0] dy = proj2d[1] - uk[1] d = math.sqrt(dx dx + dy dy) # Apply hinged Cauchy penalty # The exact algebraic coefficients for the "hinged Cauchy" function are not provided in the sources. # Standard Cauchy robust loss: L(x) = c^2 log(1 + (x/c)^2). # We implement a piecewise function matching the described behavior: # hinge at 2, C1 smooth ramp to 4, saturation past 4. if d <= 2.0: rho = 0.0 elif d <= 4.0: # Smooth C1 ramp from 0 at d=2 to saturation value at d=4 t = (d - 2.0) / 2.0 # normalized to [0, 1] rho = t t # ramps to 1.0 at d=4 else: # Saturated past 4 patches rho = 1.0 totalloss += rho return totalloss Time Complexity: Linear in the number of tokens K and the number of Gaussians per token 
gs. Memory Complexity: Minimal, requiring only scalar accumulation beyond the input arrays. Strengths: Prevents Gaussian drift from source observations and allows Gaussians to extend up to 2 patch units to cover flat surfaces or occluded regions without penalty. Limitations: Does not constrain depth, relying on the rendering loss for depth accuracy, and provides no lateral gradient for Gaussians behind the view plane. When to use: When training ZipSplat or similar token-based Gaussian splatting methods that require observation-grounded geometry. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Cone Loss was introduced in the ZipSplat paper by Veicht et al. (2026). It addresses the issue that without geometric supervision, decoded Gaussians in token-based representations can drift from their source patches, leading to merging errors where tokens from different surfaces are combined. It is part of a suite of geometric priors including the GeoCE Loss and TokenBA, designed to improve novel view synthesis performance on datasets like DL3DV and RealEstate10K. name: Joint 2D and 3D Priors
head: Magic123 Prior Loss
body: Joint 2D and 3D Priors is a training optimization technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that combines 2D diffusion priors (e.g., Stable Diffusion) and 3D diffusion priors (e.g., Zero-1-to-3) to supervise the reconstruction of novel views. It addresses the trade-off between geometry exploration and exploitation by using 2D priors to generate plausible unseen geometry and 3D priors to enforce geometric consistency and precision. Unlike methods relying solely on one prior, this approach balances high imagination with structural accuracy. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs are the current Gaussian parameters \theta, camera poses for novel views, 2D diffusion model \phi{2D}, 3D diffusion model \phi{3D}, and hyperparameters \lambda{2D/3D} and \lambda{3D}. The output is the gradient update \frac{\partial Ir}{\partial \theta} for the Gaussian parameters. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation (position \mathbf{c}, rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}, scale \mathbf{s}, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients). The diffusion models condition on rendered images Ir, noise levels t, and camera poses (R, T). Numbered Steps: 1. Sample noise levels t1, t2 and noise vectors \epsilon1, \epsilon2 from standard normal distributions. 2. Render novel views Ir from the current Gaussian representation using the specified camera poses. 3. Compute the 2D SDS term by passing Ir and t1 into \phi{2D} to predict noise \epsilon{\phi{2D}}(z{t1}; Ir, t1), then calculate the residual \epsilon{\phi{2D}}(z{t1}; Ir, t1) - \epsilon1. 4. Compute the 3D SDS term by passing Ir, t2, and camera pose (R, T) into \phi{3D} to predict noise \epsilon{\phi{3D}}(z{t2}; Ir, t2, R, T), then calculate the residual \epsilon{\phi{3D}}(z{t2}; Ir, t2, R, T) - \epsilon2. 5. Combine terms with weights and the SDS weighting function w(t) to form the joint loss: \mathcal{L}g = \mathbb{E}{t1, t2, \epsilon1, \epsilon2} \left[ w(t) \left( \lambda{2D/3D} (\epsilon{\phi{2D}}(z{t1}; Ir, t1) - \epsilon1) + \lambda{3D} (\epsilon{\phi{3D}}(z{t2}; Ir, t2, R, T) - \epsilon2) \right) \frac{\partial Ir}{\partial \theta} \right] 6. Compute the gradient of \mathcal{L}g with respect to \theta and update the Gaussians via gradient descent. Formulas: The joint prior loss \mathcal{L}g is defined as: \mathcal{L}g = \mathbb{E}{t1, t2, \epsilon1, \epsilon2} \left[ w(t) \left( \lambda{2D/3D} (\epsilon{\phi{2D}}(z{t1}; Ir, t1) - \epsilon1) + \lambda{3D} (\epsilon{\phi{3D}}(z{t2}; Ir, t2, R, T) - \epsilon2) \right) \frac{\partial Ir}{\partial \theta} \right] where t1, t2 are noise levels, \epsilon1, \epsilon2 are noise vectors, \lambda{2D/3D} and \lambda{3D} are prior weights, \phi{2D} and \phi{3D} are the 2D and 3D diffusion models, z{t1}, z{t2} are noisy latent images, Ir is the rendered view, R and T are camera rotation and translation, \theta are the Gaussian parameters, and w(t) is the standard SDS weighting function. Parameters: \lambda{3D} is fixed at 40, as Zero-1-to-3 yields consistent results for values between 10 and 60. \lambda{2D/3D} is typically set to 1.0 but is tuned to trade off geometry exploration (higher weight) and exploitation (lower weight). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stable Diffusion is sensitive to \lambda{2D/3D}, where changing it from 1 to 2 causes significant geometry variation, whereas Zero-1-to-3 is robust. Relying solely on 2D priors risks inaccurate geometry like the Janus problem, while relying solely on 3D priors risks oversimplified geometry for uncommon objects. This variant constructs explicit geometric and visual priors from high-precision dense point clouds rather than relying on diffusion models for supervision. It differs from the standard Magic123 approach by generating enhanced visual priors via virtual camera projection, anti-aliasing, and super-resolution. It is chosen when high-fidelity reconstruction is required, leveraging dense point cloud data as input. The workflow initializes Gaussians from a feature-aware sampled point cloud, generates virtual camera poses, projects views with high dynamic range, applies SMAA and super-resolution, and iteratively optimizes the Gaussians by rendering, computing loss against enhanced views, and applying densification and pruning. Time Complexity: Depends on the inference time of the 2D and 3D diffusion models per iteration, requiring novel view rendering and backpropagation through both models. Strengths: Combines the exploratory power of 2D priors with the structural accuracy of 3D priors, reducing the Janus problem and oversimplification. Limitations: Requires access to both 2D and 3D diffusion models, and tuning \lambda{2D/3D} is necessary for optimal balance. When to use: When reconstructing 3D objects from single images where unseen geometry needs to be hallucinated accurately without losing structural consistency. Originated in the "Magic123" paper, which proposed using both 2D (Stable Diffusion) and 3D (Zero-1-to-3) diffusion priors for image-to-3D generation. The method addresses the limitations of using either prior alone, leveraging their complementary nature: 2D for exploration and 3D for exploitation. name: Neural Network and Feed-Forward Approaches
body: This family replaces the iterative per-scene gradient descent of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting [Parent] with neural networks that either regress parameters directly or use neural priors. They are distinguished from Base 3DGS Optimization by relying on learned generalization rather than direct parameter tuning, and from WildGaussians by focusing on static reconstruction or generalizable priors rather than explicit temporal modeling. All methods in this family utilize a differentiable rendering pipeline to connect neural network outputs to image-space losses. The core mechanism involves predicting high-dimensional representations (either Gaussian primitives or implicit fields) and optimizing them via backpropagation through the rasterizer. A feed-forward deep neural network that directly regresses 3D Gaussian Splatting parameters from sparse multi-view images in a single pass, bypassing the per-scene gradient descent optimization loop required by standard 3DGS. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by combining multi-view feature extraction via transformers and cost volumes with a U-Net decoder to predict Gaussian primitives, enabling rapid inference without iterative scene-specific optimization. Choose this method when fast, universal reconstruction from sparse views is required, or when useful 3D priors are needed for subsequent optimizations. A neural network-based volume rendering prior that learns unsigned distance functions (UDFs) to guide the optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves inaccurate surface reconstruction and depth estimation by providing dense, geometrically consistent queries around the UDF zero-level set. Unlike sibling methods that rely on explicit multi-view stereo consistency or pure geometric priors, this approach uses a differentiable UDF field to regularize Gaussian primitives, ensuring unbiased learning from ground truth UDFs and depths while mitigating SDF-based normal estimation ambiguities. Choose this method when geometric fidelity and accurate depth estimation are critical. A feedforward neural network architecture that predicts pixel-aligned 3D Gaussians from unposed images by separating the representation of geometry and appearance into distinct branches. Unlike single-network baselines that predict all Gaussian parameters simultaneously, this decoupled approach prevents interference between geometric and appearance features, thereby avoiding rendering artifacts such as gaps and holes. Choose this method when reconstructing scenes from unposed images without explicit camera pose information. A 3D neural network that predicts high-dimensional feature vectors for optimized 3D Gaussians, using Q-Render to efficiently render these features into 2D maps for distillation from 2D foundation models. Unlike methods that force per-scene feature optimization, GS-Net predicts features in a generalizable manner using a 3D neural network. Given optimized 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}{i=1}^N, a 3D neural network predicts a set of C-dimensional Gaussian features \mathcal{F} = \{fi\}{i=1}^N where fi \in \mathbb{R}^C. To ensure compatibility with typical 3D backbones like Point Transformer v3 (PTv3) and MinkUnet, 3D Gaussians are voxelized by sampling their center location \mu. Predicted voxel features are converted back into predicted Gaussian features \mathcal{F} via de-voxelization. Q-Render transforms predicted Gaussian features into rendered feature maps. The 3D neural network is trained to minimize the rendering loss between the rendered feature maps and target 2D feature maps extracted from CLIP’s vision encoder. Q-Render accelerates training by leveraging the inductive bias of the 3D neural network, which predicts spatially smooth Gaussian features, allowing sparse sampling of quantile Gaussians instead of dense ray sampling. This approach uses a masked autoencoder to learn a generalizable 3D Gaussian splatting-based representation. It combines a masked autoencoder (MAE) with a 3D transformer-based architecture to enable reconstruction of unseen scenes and support transfer learning. The standard 3D Gaussian Splatting [Parent] requires per-scene optimization, which is computationally expensive and limits scalability. Feed-forward approaches emerged to address this by learning a mapping from images to Gaussians. MVSplat builds on PixelSplat by combining multi-view feature extraction through transformers and cost volumes, which are then processed by a U-Net. Subsequent works like GS-Net extend this to high-dimensional feature distillation. MAE-based methods enable generalizable representations capable of reconstructing unseen scenes. VRP-UDF introduces UDF priors to guide optimization and improve geometric consistency.
