name: MVSplat
head: Amortized 3D Reconstruction, Feed-forward 3DGS, Feedforward 3D Reconstruction, Single-pass 3DGS
body: MVSplat is a feed-forward deep neural network that directly regresses 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) parameters from sparse multi-view images in a single pass, bypassing the per-scene gradient descent optimization loop required by standard 3DGS. It builds upon PixelSplat by combining multi-view feature extraction through transformers and cost volumes, which are then processed by a U-Net. Unlike iterative methods that optimize primitives for a specific scene, MVSplat provides a universal reconstruction model trained on all CO3Dv2 categories, offering useful 3D priors for subsequent 3D optimizations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: K sparse-view images I^i \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} and their corresponding camera projection matrices P^i = Ki [Ri | ti]. Output: A set of H \times W \times K 3D Gaussian primitives, each defined by position \muj, opacity \alphaj, covariance \Sigmaj, and color cj (represented as spherical harmonics). Data Structures: The core intermediate structure is a per-view cost volume that stores cross-view feature similarities for all potential depth candidates, providing geometry cues for depth estimation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Extract multi-view image features using a Transformer backbone. 2. Construct per-view cost volumes using plane sweeping to store cross-view feature similarities for potential depth candidates. 3. Concatenate Transformer features and cost volumes as input to a 2D U-Net with cross-view attention. 4. Refine the cost volume and predict per-view depth maps using the 2D U-Net. 5. Unproject the per-view depth maps to 3D space using camera intrinsics and poses. 6. Combine unprojected depths using a deterministic union operation to form the 3D Gaussian centers. 7. Predict opacity, covariance, and color Gaussian parameters jointly with the depth maps in parallel. 8. Render novel views from the predicted 3D Gaussians using the differentiable splatting rasterization operation. Formulas: Cost volume construction: Ci(u, dk) = \text{Agg}{m,i} \langle Fi(u), W{m\to i}(Fm; dk) \rangle, where Ci is the cost volume, u is the pixel coordinate, dk is a depth hypothesis, Fi and Fm are features from view i and reference view m, and W is a warping function. Depth prediction: \hat{d}i = \sumk \text{softmax}(Ci)k dk, where \hat{d}i is the predicted depth and dk are depth hypotheses. Gaussian center unprojection: \mui(u) = \pi^{-1}(u, \hat{d}i(u); Ki, Ti), where \mui is the Gaussian mean, \pi^{-1} is the unprojection function, Ki is the camera intrinsic matrix, and Ti is the camera pose. Parameters: Training Setup: 20 source images are used as inputs during training, with MSE losses calculated on 5 novel views. Finetuning Setup: 80 views are used as inputs to the feed-forward model for initialization in the finetuning regime. Loss Function: The model is trained end-to-end purely with photometric loss between rendered and ground truth images. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Single-View Ambiguity: Single-view reconstruction is ill-posed and ambiguous for general scenes; MVSplat avoids this by requiring multi-view inputs. Feature-to-Depth Mapping: Predicting probabilistic depth distributions solely from image features is ambiguous and unreliable, leading to noisy geometry artifacts; MVSplat mitigates this by using a cost volume for feature matching. Addresses reconstructing 3D scenes from a limited number of input views (sparse views) or even a single image, bypassing the iterative per-scene optimization required by standard 3D Gaussian Splatting. It achieves this by employing learned priors within a feed-forward deep neural network that directly regresses 3D Gaussian parameters from input images in a single pass. This approach favors inference speed and cross-scene generalization over the high geometric fidelity typically achieved by regularization-based methods that rely on per-scene gradient descent. VolSplat is a feed-forward deep neural network that directly regresses 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) parameters from sparse multi-view images in a single pass, bypassing the per-scene gradient descent optimization required by standard 3DGS Parent. It distinguishes itself by lifting 2D features into a sparse 3D voxel grid via plane-sweep depth prediction and predicting one Gaussian primitive per occupied voxel, ensuring scene-adaptive primitive allocation while maintaining stable sparse 3D decoding. Time Complexity: The method performs inference in a single forward pass, achieving 22 fps on RealEstate10K and ACID benchmarks. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is determined by the neural network's parameter count and intermediate feature maps, requiring 1.18 GiB GPU memory on RealEstate10K. Measured Performance: Model-stage latency is 37.63 ms with a throughput of 26.57 scenes/s, yielding 871.21 rFPS for decoder-only rendering. The model uses 10× fewer parameters and infers more than 2× faster than pixelSplat, while providing higher appearance and geometry quality. Strengths: Bypasses per-scene gradient descent; provides useful 3D priors for subsequent 3D optimizations; works on a variety of object types. Limitations: As a feed-forward model, it may not achieve the same level of geometric fidelity as iterative methods that overfit to a specific scene's data, particularly in areas with limited viewpoint coverage. MVSplat was introduced to combine multi-view feature extraction through transformers and cost volumes, processed by a U-Net, building upon the foundations of PixelSplat. It is part of a broader trend towards amortized 3D reconstruction, where a neural network is trained to generalize across scenes rather than optimizing for a single instance. The model was trained on all CO3Dv2 categories to create a universal reconstruction model capable of handling various object types. Unlike typical MVS methods that require ground truth depth supervision, MVSplat is fully differentiable and trained from RGB images alone using only photometric loss. name: Sparse Input Reconstruction via Generalizability
head: Feed-Forward Gaussian Models, Learned Prior 3D GS
body: Sparse Input Reconstruction via Generalizability refers to methods that leverage learned priors to reconstruct 3D scenes, enabling reconstruction from a single input image or a very sparse set of views after training on multiple views. Unlike regularization-based methods that rely on strong constraints and per-scene optimization to favor geometric quality, these generalizability-based methods use learned priors for fast feed-forward inference, prioritizing speed and cross-scene generalization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: One or more calibrated input images. Output: A set of N 3D Gaussian parameters representing the scene. Each Gaussian i comprises mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (parameterized by rotation Ri and scale Si), opacity \alphai \in [0, 1], and spherical harmonics coefficients c{i, l} for color. Steps: 1. Training: Train a feed-forward neural network on a dataset of scenes with multiple views to learn the mapping from 2D image features to 3D Gaussian parameters. 2. Inference: Pass one or more input images through the trained network to directly generate the properties of a set of 3D Gaussians in a single forward pass. Variants: PixelSplat: Samples Gaussians from dense probability distributions. Splatter Image: Uses a 2D image-to-image network to map an input image to a 3D Gaussian per pixel. Pitfalls: Generative Augmentation Cost: Synthesizing additional views through generative models to augment input data is computationally intensive and bounded by the capabilities of the generative model. Uniform Distribution: In pixel-aligned approaches like Splatter Image, generated pixel-aligned Gaussians are distributed nearly evenly in space, struggling to represent high-frequency details and smoother regions with an appropriate number of Gaussians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generalizablereconstruction(inputimages): # inputimages: Tensor of shape (B, C, H, W) # Step 1: Extract multi-scale features using a backbone network (e.g., CNN or Transformer) features = extractfeatures(inputimages) # Step 2: Predict Gaussian parameters directly from features # Sources do not specify the exact network architecture for this mapping. gaussians = predictgaussianparameters(features) return gaussians def extractfeatures(images): # Standard backbone feature extraction (e.g., ResNet or ViT forward pass) return images def predictgaussianparameters(features): # Standard prediction head outputting position, covariance, opacity, and SH coefficients return features Sparse View Input Scalability is the capability of generalizable neural rendering methods to process an arbitrary number of input views, with reconstruction quality progressively improving as more views are added. It leverages cost volume representations as input to attribute prediction networks for Gaussians, enabling direct inference from sparse calibrated inputs without per-scene optimization. Speed: Inference is a single forward pass, providing fast feed-forward inference compared to iterative optimization methods. Generalization: Excels at cross-scene generalization due to learned priors. Geometric Fidelity: Sometimes at the expense of geometric fidelity compared to regularization-based methods. Memory: Memory usage depends on the number of Gaussians predicted; pixel-aligned methods may use more Gaussians than necessary for smooth regions. Limitations: Performance is bounded by the training data distribution. Not given in the sources. The challenge of 3D Gaussian Splatting for sparse inputs centers on how priors are modeled, whether through depth information, generative models, or feed-forward Gaussian models. Traditional regularization-based methods rely on strong constraints and per-scene optimization, favoring geometric quality but incurring higher computation. Generalizability-based methods emerged to address the inefficiency of per-scene optimization, particularly when dealing with a limited number of views or even just one, where the efficacy of regularization techniques tends to diminish. Key developments include: PixelSplat: Proposed sampling Gaussians from dense probability distributions. Splatter Image: Introduced a 2D image-to-image network that maps an input image to a 3D Gaussian per pixel. Cost Volume Representations: Some approaches use cost volume representations to provide geometry cues, although this can be challenging with very few views. Future research directions include exploring adaptive mechanisms to control the trade-off between speed and geometric fidelity, such as learned confidence measures or context-aware prior selection. Additionally, extending these approaches to dynamic scenarios, handling temporal consistency and motion-induced artifacts, is an active area of interest. name: Sparse View Input Scalability
head: Arbitrary View Count Scalability, Progressive Multi-View Reconstruction
body: Sparse View Input Scalability is the capability of generalizable neural rendering methods to process an arbitrary number of input views, with reconstruction quality progressively improving as more views are added. It leverages cost volume representations as input to attribute prediction networks for Gaussians. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N input images. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian attributes predicted by a neural network, which are rendered via differentiable rasterization. Data Structures: Cost Volume: A representation brought into sparse view reconstruction to serve as input for the attribute prediction network. Steps: 1. Construct a cost volume representation from the input views. 2. Pass the cost volume to an attribute prediction network for Gaussians. 3. The network outputs Gaussian attributes, which are rasterized to produce the output image. Formulas: The Gaussian attributes A are predicted by the network f\theta from the cost volume C: A = f\theta(C) where C is the cost volume representation and A denotes the predicted Gaussian attributes. Parameters: Number of Views (N): The method supports an arbitrary number of input views, with experiments conducted using N \in [2, 8]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Few Views (N=2): The method produces plausible geometries using only two views, but accuracy is lower than with more views. Performance: On the DTU dataset (Scan105), the method produces plausible geometries with 2 views. Quality progressively improves and converges to a fairly low reconstruction error as views increase from 2 to 8. Strengths: Generalizable to unseen scenes; handles arbitrary view counts; produces smoother surfaces compared to density-based methods like MVSNerf. The capability to handle arbitrary view counts with progressive quality improvement was demonstrated in SparseNeuS, which showed results from 2 to 8 views on the DTU dataset. The specific integration of cost volume representations into Gaussian Splatting for sparse view reconstruction was introduced by MVSplat, building on Sparse Input Reconstruction via Generalizability and earlier generalizable reconstruction work. name: VolSplat Architecture and Training Pipeline
head: VolSplat
body: VolSplat is a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that regresses scene parameters from sparse multi-view images in a single pass, bypassing per-scene optimization. It distinguishes itself by lifting 2D features into a sparse 3D voxel grid via plane-sweep depth prediction and predicting exactly one Gaussian primitive per occupied voxel, ensuring scene-adaptive allocation with stable sparse decoding. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: N{\text{in}} = 6 input views at 256 \times 256 resolution. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}, each defined by a 38-dimensional parameter vector, for novel view synthesis. Data Structures: 1. Multi-scale Feature Maps: Extracted per view via a weight-sharing ResNet backbone. 2. Cost Volume: Constructed via plane-sweep with D = 128 inverse-depth candidates per reference view. 3. Sparse Voxel Grid: World-coordinate representation where only occupied cells are materialized, processed via MinkowskiEngine. 4. Gaussian Primitive Parameter Vector \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^{38}: Comprises opacity \alpha, center offset \Delta \mathbf{x}, anisotropic scale \mathbf{s}, quaternion rotation \mathbf{q}, and degree-2 spherical-harmonic color coefficients \mathbf{c}. Numbered Steps: 1. Extract multi-scale feature maps from each input view using a weight-sharing ResNet backbone. 2. Refine features via a cross-view interaction module using local window attention to enhance multi-view consistency. 3. Construct a cost volume for each reference view using a plane-sweep strategy with D = 128 inverse-depth candidates. 4. Perform local neighbor matching on the cost volume to predict robust depth maps. 5. Lift the 2D features into 3D space using the predicted depth maps, building the representation in world coordinates. 6. Process the lifted features as a sparse voxel set where only occupied cells are materialized, applying sparse 3D refinement via MinkowskiEngine. 7. Predict one Gaussian primitive per occupied voxel, outputting the 38-dimensional parameter vector \mathbf{p}. Formulas: The parameter vector \mathbf{p} is defined as: \mathbf{p} = [\alpha, \Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z, sx, sy, sz, qw, qx, qy, qz, c0, \dots, c{37}] where \alpha \in [0,1] is opacity, (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z) is the center offset, (sx, sy, sz) is the anisotropic scale, (qw, qx, qy, qz) is the quaternion rotation, and c0 \dots c{37} are the degree-2 spherical-harmonic color coefficients. Parameters: Inverse-depth candidates: 128 per reference view. Gaussian parameter vector dimension: 38. Input views per training sample: 6. Target views per training sample: 8. Input resolution: 256 \times 256 pixels. Optimizer: AdamW with decoupled weight decay. Learning rate: Two separate groups for the pretrained monocular branch and the remaining trainable parameters. Stability mechanism: Gradient clipping is enabled during training. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse grid initialization: Only occupied cells are materialized to avoid computational redundancy of a dense global grid. Depth prediction errors: Robust depth prediction via local neighbor matching is critical for accurate feature lifting. Anchor gap selection: The progressive expansion of the anchor-gap range during early training iterations is required for stable convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class VolSplatPipeline: def init(self, numdepthcandidates=128, inputresolution=(256, 256)): self.numdepthcandidates = numdepthcandidates self.inputresolution = inputresolution # Weight-sharing ResNet backbone for multi-scale feature extraction self.backbone = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(3, 64, 7, stride=2, padding=3, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(64), nn.ReLU(inplace=True)) # Cross-view interaction via local window attention self.crossviewattn = nn.MultiheadAttention(embeddim=256, numheads=8, batchfirst=True) # Depth prediction head self.depthhead = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(256, 128, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.Conv2d(128, 1, 3, padding=1)) # Sparse 3D refinement layers self.sparserefine = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv3d(256, 256, 3, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm3d(256), nn.ReLU(inplace=True)) # Gaussian parameter predictor self.gaussianhead = nn.Conv3d(256, 38, 1) def forward(self, inputviews): # inputviews: Tensor of shape (Nin, 3, 256, 256) # Step 1: Feature Extraction features = self.backbone(inputviews) # Shape: (Nin, C, H, W) # Step 2: Cross-View Interaction B, C, H, W = features.shape featflat = features.permute(0, 2, 3, 1).reshape(B, HW, C) refinedfeat, = self.crossviewattn(featflat, featflat, featflat) refinedfeatures = refinedfeat.reshape(B, H, W, C).permute(0, 3, 1, 2) # Step 3 & 4: Cost Volume Construction and Depth Prediction # Construct cost volume with 128 inverse-depth candidates # Perform local neighbor matching to predict depth maps depthmaps = [] for i in range(B): # name: VRP-UDF Training & Rendering Setup
head: UDF-Gaussian Joint Training, Volume Rendering Prior Network
body: This method uses a neural network-based volume rendering prior (VRP) to learn unsigned distance functions (UDFs) and guide 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization by providing dense queries around the UDF zero-level set. It addresses inaccurate surface reconstruction and depth estimation in Gaussian splatting by regularizing primitives with a differentiable UDF field, ensuring unbiased learning from ground truth UDFs and depths. Unlike sibling methods like MVSplat, it avoids standard SDF-based normal estimation ambiguities by explicitly excluding normals from the color network input. The approach builds on Neural Network and Feed-Forward Approaches by integrating implicit field priors into explicit Gaussian optimization. Inputs: Multi-view images, camera poses, and ground truth unsigned distance values or depth maps. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian primitives (position, scale, rotation, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) and the learned UDF and color fields. The volume rendering prior consists of four MLPs, all utilizing 256 hidden units: 1. Feature Network (f{w1}): 3 layers. Input: 3D coordinates. Output: feature vectors. 2. Weight Network (f{w2}): 6 layers with skip connections. Input: feature vectors and 3D coordinates. Output: weights for UDF and color prediction. 3. UDF Network (fu): 8 layers with skip connections. Input: feature vectors and 3D coordinates. Output: unsigned distance value. A Softplus activation is applied after the final layer to enforce non-negative outputs (d \ge 0). 4. Color Network (fc): 2 layers. Input: feature vectors and 3D coordinates. Normal vectors are explicitly excluded from the input because normals are ambiguous at the zero-level set due to UDF non-differentiability. Output: color values. The training process runs for 30,000 iterations total: 1. Initial Phase (Iterations 0–9,000): Standard Gaussian Splatting optimization proceeds without the UDF prior. 2. Prior Introduction (Iteration 9,000): Training of the UDF network (fu) and color network (fc) begins. The learning rate and decay scheduler for fu and fc follow previous works [1, 24], though exact numerical values are not specified. 3. Refinement Phase (Iterations 20,000–30,000): During the final 10,000 iterations, Gaussians are refined by casting rays with a batch size of 2,048, sampling 64 points along each ray. The UDF and color networks are queried at these points to compute volume rendering losses, which are backpropagated to update both Gaussian parameters and network weights. The following pseudocode outlines the joint training loop. Standard differentiable rendering primitives are assumed; steps not detailed in the sources are marked with comments. Unverified code. Initialize MLPs with 256 hidden units as specified in fw1 = MLP(layers=3, hidden=256) fw2 = MLP(layers=6, hidden=256, skipconnections=True) fu = MLP(layers=8, hidden=256, skipconnections=True) fc = MLP(layers=2, hidden=256) optgaussians = Optimizer(gaussians.parameters()) optnetworks = Optimizer([fw1, fw2, fu, fc].parameters()) for iteration in range(1, totaliterations + 1): batchcameras, batchimages = samplebatch(cameras, images) # Standard differentiable rasterization of Gaussians (not detailed in sources) renderedimages, rendereddepths = rendergaussians(gaussians, batchcameras) lossgs = computegaussianlosses(renderedimages, batchimages, rendereddepths) if iteration >= udfstartiter: # Configure sampling strategy based on phase if iteration >= refinementstartiter: batchsize = 2048 numsamples = 64 else: batchsize = 1024 # Default fallback not specified in sources numsamples = 32 # Default fallback not specified in sources # Sample points along rays as specified in samplepoints = getsamplepoints(gaussians, batchcameras, numsamples=numsamples) # Forward passes through prior networks features = fw1(samplepoints) weights = fw2(features, samplepoints) udfvalues = fu(features, samplepoints) udfvalues = softplus(udfvalues) # Enforce non-negativity colors = fc(features, samplepoints) # Normals excluded from input # Compute losses against ground truth UDFs and colors (not detailed in sources) lossudf = computeudfloss(udfvalues, groundtruthudfs) losscolor = computecolorloss(colors, groundtruthcolors) # Combine losses for backpropagation totalloss = lossgs + lossudf + losscolor optnetworks.zerograd() optgaussians.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optnetworks.step() optgaussians.step() else: optgaussians.zerograd() lossgs.backward() optgaussians.step() class MLP: def init(self, layers, hidden, skipconnections=False): self.layers = layers self.hidden = hidden self.skipconnections = skipconnections def call(self, x, args): # Standard linear transformation with activation; skip connections handled internally return x class Optimizer: def init(self, params): self.params = params def zerograd(self): for p in self.params: p.grad = 0.0 def step(self): for p in self.params: p.data -= 0.001 p.grad def samplebatch(cameras, images): return cameras[:1], images[:1] def rendergaussians(gaussians, cameras): return [], [] def computegaussianlosses(rendered, target, depth): return 0.0 def getsamplepoints(gaussians, cameras, numsamples): return [] def computeudfloss(udfpred, udfgt): return 0.0 def computecolorloss(colorpred, colorgt): return 0.0 Normal Ambiguity: Normal vectors must not be included in the input to the color network (fc) because the gradient is non-differentiable at the zero-level set of a UDF, making normals ambiguous and degrading color prediction. Sampling Inaccuracies: Random hierarchical sampling and the ill-defined nature of UDF fields near surfaces cause rendering inaccuracies, a common issue across volume rendering frameworks that leads to depth discrepancies even with theoretically unbiased mappings. Convergence Parameters: Excessively large convergence parameters (e.g., the "flip factor" in NeuralUDF) cause the UDF to flip into an SDF prematurely before the true surface, resulting in depth rendering errors. Time Complexity: The method adds significant computational overhead during the refinement phase due to forward passes through four MLPs (f{w1}, f{w2}, fu, fc) for every sample point. Training is fixed at 30,000 iterations, with the prior active for the latter 21,000 iterations. Memory Complexity: Memory usage increases due to the storage of the four MLPs (19 layers total with 256 hidden units) and the gradients for both the Gaussians and the networks. Performance: The method achieves the best accuracy among tested renderers for UDFs and SDFs. It outperforms baselines like NeUDF and VRPrior on complex indoor scenes and thin structures (e.g., eggshells, plant branches). Limitations: Practical inaccuracies persist due to sampling noise and UDF ill-definition near surfaces. It may struggle to capture extremely thin structures completely without advanced extraction techniques. The VRP-UDF method originates from the paper "VRP-UDF: Toward Unbiased Learning of Unsigned Distance Functions From Multi-View Images With Volume Rendering Priors". It builds on differentiable volume rendering and UDF learning, extending them to 3D Gaussian Splatting. The approach addresses limitations in previous UDF-based methods, specifically premature flipping and normal ambiguity, to enable high-fidelity reconstruction. It is applied to tasks requiring precise geometric details from multi-view images, such as digital heritage and complex indoor scene reconstruction. name: Decoupled Neural Fields
head: Decoupled geometry-appearance network, WildSplat Network Architecture
body: Decoupled Neural Fields is a feedforward neural network architecture that predicts pixel-aligned 3D Gaussians from unposed images by separating the representation of geometry and appearance into distinct branches. Unlike single-network baselines that predict all Gaussian parameters simultaneously, this decoupled approach prevents the interference between geometric and appearance features, thereby avoiding rendering artifacts such as gaps and holes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Unposed images of a scene, partitioned into context views (for encoding) and target views (for supervision). Output: A set of pixel-aligned 3D Gaussians, each defined by position, covariance, opacity, and view-dependent color. Data Structures: The architecture consists of two main branches: 1. Geometry Branch: Encoder: DINOv2-large. Embedding dimension: D = 1024. Transformer: L = 24 alternating-attention layers. 2. Appearance Branch: Extractor: Pretrained DINOv2-base model. Injector: Four identical blocks. Each block contains: AdaLN-Zero modulation layer. Cross-attention layer. Self-attention layer. MLP. Steps: 1. Geometry Encoding: Pass context images through the DINOv2-large encoder to obtain features with dimension D=1024. 2. Geometry Refinement: Process the encoded features through L=24 alternating-attention layers to refine geometric representations. 3. Appearance Extraction: Pass context images through the pretrained DINOv2-base model to extract appearance features. 4. Appearance Injection: Combine geometry and appearance features using the Appearance Injector. For each of the four blocks: a. Apply AdaLN-Zero modulation. b. Apply cross-attention to align appearance features with geometry. c. Apply self-attention to refine appearance features. d. Pass through an MLP. 5. Gaussian Prediction: Predict the parameters for pixel-aligned 3D Gaussians. View-dependent colors are parameterized using spherical harmonics of degree k=4. 6. Optimization: Optimize all network parameters except those in the geometry encoder (DINOv2-large). 7. Merging: Employ a voxel-based merging strategy to aggregate spatially redundant Gaussians during training and inference to optimize memory consumption. Formulas: View-dependent color: Parameterized with spherical harmonics of degree k=4. Training loss: \mathcal{L} = \lambda1 \mathcal{L}{\text{pose}} + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{\text{MSE}} + \lambda3 \mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}} + \lambda4 \mathcal{L}{\text{LPIPS}}, where \lambda1=10.0, \lambda2=10.0, \lambda3=1.0, and \lambda4=0.05. Parameters: Optimizer: Adam with \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.95. Learning Rate: 2 \times 10^{-5} for network backbones, 2 \times 10^{-4} for DPT heads. Hardware: Optimized across four NVIDIA RTX H20 GPUs. Pitfalls: Using a single neural field to concurrently represent geometric and appearance properties causes consistent degradation across all image quality metrics, resulting in compromised rendering fidelity and inaccurate geometry such as gaps and holes. The single neural field baseline requires a maximum hash size of 2^{18} to maintain experimental fairness, which leads to a slightly larger parameter count than the decoupled architecture. Memory: Employs a voxel-based merging strategy to aggregate spatially redundant Gaussians, optimizing memory consumption during training and inference. Performance: The decoupled approach avoids the degradation seen in single-field baselines, maintaining superior visual fidelity. Hardware: Implemented and optimized on four NVIDIA RTX H20 GPUs. Strengths: Prevents interference between geometry and appearance, leading to accurate geometry without gaps or holes. Limitations: Training requires four NVIDIA RTX H20 GPUs. Decoupled Neural Fields were introduced in the WildSplat paper as a method for feedforward Gaussian Splatting from unposed in-the-wild images. The architecture was designed to address the limitations of single-network approaches in predicting 3D Gaussians, specifically the trade-off between geometric accuracy and appearance quality. name: ClipGS
head: Clippable Gaussian Splatting
body: ClipGS is a Gaussian Splatting-based framework designed for the real-time interactive cinematic visualization of volumetric medical data with support for dynamic clipping planes. It solves the problem of maintaining rendering quality and continuity when a user interactively clips a 3D volume, addressing the artifacts caused by hard visibility truncations and the high computational cost of learning full deformation fields for the additional clipping dimension. It addresses the challenge of the introduced dimension transferring the 3D representation to a 4D representation problem, avoiding the high model capacity required by methods that learn a dense deformation field along the clipping dimension by instead modeling clipping plane interaction as a geometric visibility constraint managed via a learnable truncation scheme and an Adaptive Adjustment Model (AAM). ClipGS extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation to support 4D rendering (3D space + clipping plane parameter) by introducing two key components: Learnable Truncation (LT) for visibility control and an Adaptive Adjustment Model (AAM) for continuous deformation. Inputs: Volumetric medical data V (e.g., CT scans). Camera parameters: view direction \mathbf{v}i and projection matrices. Clipping plane parameter: defined by normal \boldsymbol{n} and distance to origin z. Ground-truth images \mathbf{C}{\text{gt}} generated from the volumetric data at specific camera views and clipping plane positions. Outputs: Rendered color image \mathbf{C} for the given view and clipping plane. Optimized 3D Gaussian primitives with attributes adjusted for the clipping context. The method operates on a set of N 3D Gaussian primitives. Each primitive i maintains the following attributes, optimized during training: Position: \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Rotation: \mathbf{r}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 (represented as a quaternion or axis-angle, decomposed into rotation matrix \boldsymbol{R}). Scale: si \in \mathbb{R} (or vector \boldsymbol{s}, decomposed into scaling matrix \boldsymbol{S}). Color: \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Opacity: \alphai \in \mathbb{R}. Learnable Truncation Attribute: mi \in \mathbb{R}, an optimizable scalar per Gaussian used to control visibility relative to the clipping plane. The AAM uses a shared MLP structure to predict deformations. It takes positional encoding of the Gaussian position \boldsymbol{\mu} and the clipping plane parameter z as input. A 3D Gaussian primitive is defined as: \mathcal{G}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{r}, s) = e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})} where the covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is decomposed into rotation \boldsymbol{R} and scaling \boldsymbol{S}: \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \boldsymbol{R} \boldsymbol{S} \boldsymbol{S}^T \boldsymbol{R}^T The projected 2D Gaussian \mathcal{G}'i is obtained by projecting the 3D Gaussian onto the image plane using camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters. Standard hard truncation (HT) uses the mean \boldsymbol{\mu} to determine visibility: if (\boldsymbol{\mu} \cdot \boldsymbol{n}) < z, the Gaussian is visible. This causes artifacts because Gaussians intersecting the clipping plane (within their confidence interval) may have means on either side, leading to discontinuous visibility changes. ClipGS introduces a "barycenter" offset \boldsymbol{\delta} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and defines the visibility condition based on the adjusted center: \mathcal{M} = (\boldsymbol{\mu} + \boldsymbol{\delta}) \cdot \boldsymbol{n} < z where \mathcal{M} \in \{0, 1\} is the visibility mask, \boldsymbol{n} is the clipping plane normal, and z is the distance to the origin. To make this differentiable, ClipGS introduces an optimizable scalar attribute mi for each Gaussian, where mi = (\boldsymbol{\mu}i + \boldsymbol{\delta}i) \cdot \boldsymbol{n}. The visibility function \mathcal{M} is approximated using a straight-through estimator with a sigmoid function: \mathcal{M} = \text{sg}(\mathbf{1}[\sigma(m - z) < \epsilon] - \sigma(m - z)) + \sigma(m - z) where: \sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid function. \mathbf{1}[\cdot] is the indicator function. \epsilon is a threshold hyperparameter (typical value: 0.5). \text{sg}(\cdot) is the stop-gradient operator. This allows gradients to flow through the sigmoid approximation during backpropagation while maintaining a step-like behavior for the forward pass. To ensure continuity across different clipping plane positions, ClipGS predicts dynamic deformations for visible Gaussians using an AAM. 1. Feature Extraction: The Gaussian position \boldsymbol{\mu} and clipping plane parameter z are passed through positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) and merged into a feature vector f via an MLP: f = \text{MLP}(\gamma(\boldsymbol{\mu}), \gamma(z)) 2. Deformation Prediction: Separate MLP heads \phi\mu, \phir, \phis predict the deformations for position, rotation, and scale: \Delta\boldsymbol{\mu} = \phi\mu(f), \quad \Delta\mathbf{r} = \phir(f), \quad \Delta s = \phis(f) 3. Rendering with Deformation: The final rendered color \mathbf{C} is computed by \alpha-blending the deformed Gaussians, weighted by the visibility mask \mathcal{M}i: \mathcal{C} = \sum{i=1}^N \mathcal{M}i Ti \alphai \mathcal{G}'i(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}i + \Delta\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \mathbf{r}i + \Delta\mathbf{r}i, si + \Delta si) \mathbf{c}i where Ti = \prod{j \in i-1} (1 - \mathcal{G}'j(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}i + \Delta\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \mathbf{r}i + \Delta\mathbf{r}i, si + \Delta si) \alphaj) is the accumulated transmittance. The optimization is performed in two steps: 1. Coarse Initialization (Learnable Truncation): Generate a sparse cinematic image sequence \{Ii\} from random camera views \mathbf{v}i and random clipping planes zi using a ray-tracing renderer. Randomly initialize N 3D Gaussians within a cube encompassing the scene (typical N=100,000). Optimize the Gaussian attributes and the learnable truncation attribute m for 7,000 iterations. Loss function: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda)\mathcal{L}1(\mathbf{C}, \mathbf{C}{\text{gt}}) + \lambda\mathcal{L}{\text{D-SSIM}}(\mathbf{C}, \mathbf{C}{\text{gt}}) where \lambda is the loss weight (typical value: 0.2). 2. Joint Optimization (AAM): Initialize the AAM parameters. Jointly optimize the Gaussian attributes, learnable truncation attributes, and AAM parameters for 33,000 iterations. This step refines rendering quality and ensures continuity in the clipping plane dimension. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class ClipGS: def init(self, numgaussians, scenebounds): """ Initialize ClipGS model. Args: numgaussians (int): Number of Gaussian primitives (e.g., 100,000). scenebounds (tuple): Bounding box of the scene for initialization. """ self.numgaussians = numgaussians # Initialize Gaussian attributes # Position: random within scene bounds self.mu = torch.rand(numgaussians, 3) (scenebounds[1] - scenebounds[0]) + scenebounds[0] # Rotation: random unit quaternion or axis-angle (simplified here as random 3D vector) self.r = torch.rand(numgaussians, 3) 2 torch.pi # Scale: random positive values self.s = torch.rand(numgaussians, 1) 0.1 + 0.01 # Color: random RGB self.c = torch.rand(numgaussians, 3) # Opacity: random initial opacity self.alpha = torch.rand(numgaussians, 1) 0.5 + 0.1 # Learnable Truncation attribute m self.m = torch.zeros(numgaussians, 1) # Adaptive Adjustment Model (AAM) self.aam = AdaptiveAdjustmentModel() def learnabletruncationmask(self, m, z, epsilon=0.5): """ Compute visibility mask using Learnable Truncation. Args: m (Tensor): Learnable truncation attribute (N, 1). z (float): Clipping plane distance to origin. epsilon (float): Threshold for sigmoid approximation. Returns: Tensor: Visibility mask (N, 1) with values in [0, 1]. """ # Sigmoid approximation sig = torch.sigmoid(m - z) # Indicator function (hard threshold) indicator = (sig < epsilon).float() # Straight-through estimator # Forward pass: use indicator (hard step) # Backward pass: use sigmoid gradient mask = indicator + (sig - indicator).detach() return mask def computedeformation(self, mu, z): """ Compute dynamic deformations using AAM. Args: mu (Tensor): Gaussian positions (N, 3). z (float): Clipping plane distance to origin. Returns: Tuple: Deformations (deltamu, deltar, deltas) """ # Positional encoding: standard high-frequency sine/cosine encoding for 3DGS # mupe = positionalencoding(mu) # zpe = positionalencoding(torch.tensor([z]).expand(mu.shape[0], -1)) # Merge and pass through MLP # f = self.aam(mupe, zpe) # Predict deformations # deltamu = self.aam.phimu(f) # deltar = self.aam.phir(f) # deltas = self.aam.phis(f) # Placeholder for standard PE and MLP forward pass return torch.zeroslike(mu), torch.zeroslike(mu), torch.zeroslike(mu) def render(self, cameraparams, clippingplanez, epsilon=0.5): """ Render the scene with clipping plane support. Args: cameraparams (dict): Camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters. clippingplanez (float): Clipping plane distance to origin. epsilon (float): Threshold for learnable truncation. Returns: Tensor: Rendered color image. """ # 1. Compute visibility mask mask = self.learnabletruncationmask(self.m, clippingplanez, epsilon) # 2. Compute deformations for visible Gaussians deltamu, deltar, deltas = self.computedeformation(self.mu, clippingplanez) # 3. Apply deformations mudeformed = self.mu + deltamu rdeformed = self.r + deltar sdeformed = self.s + deltas # 4. Project Gaussians to 2D and compute 2D Gaussian parameters # Standard 3DGS projection: compute 2D mean, covariance, and bounding box # projectedgaussians = projectgaussians(mudeformed, rdeformed, sdeformed, cameraparams) # 5. Rasterize and alpha-blend # Standard 3DGS rasterization: sort Gaussians by depth, iterate over pixels, blend # color = rasterizeandblend(projectedgaussians, self.c, self.alpha, mask, cameraparams) # Placeholder for standard 3DGS rasterization return torch.zeros(800, 800, 3) def trainstep(self, groundtruthimage, cameraparams, clippingplanez, lambdadssim=0.2): """ Perform one training step. Args: groundtruthimage (Tensor): Ground truth color image. cameraparams (dict): Camera parameters. clippingplanez (float): Clipping plane distance. lambdadssim (float): Weight for D-SSIM loss. Returns: float: Training loss. """ # Render current frame renderedimage = self.render(cameraparams, clippingplanez) # Compute L1 loss l1loss = torch.nn.functional.l1loss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage) # Compute D-SSIM loss # dssimloss = dssimlossfunction(renderedimage, groundtruthimage) dssimloss = torch.zeroslike(l1loss) # Placeholder for standard D-SSIM # Total loss loss = (1 - lambdadssim) l1loss + lambdadssim dssimloss # Backpropagate and optimize loss.backward() return loss.item() class AdaptiveAdjustmentModel(nn.Module): def init(self, inputdim=64, hiddendim=128, outputdim=3): super(AdaptiveAdjustmentModel, self).init() # MLP for feature extraction self.mlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(inputdim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU()) # Separate MLP heads for deformations self.phimu = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3) self.phir = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3) self.phis = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1) def forward(self, mupe, zpe): # Merge inputs f = torch.cat([mupe, zpe], dim=-1) f = self.mlp(f) return f \epsilon (Truncation threshold): Used in the learnable truncation sigmoid approximation. Typical value: 0.5. \lambda (Loss weight): Balances L1 and D-SSIM terms in the training loss. Typical value: 0.2. Initial Gaussian count (N): Number of points randomly initialized within a cube encompassing the scene. Typical value: 100,000. Training iterations: 7,000 iterations for the first step (LT only), followed by 33,000 iterations for joint optimization (LT + AAM). Hard Truncation Artifacts: Using the mean \boldsymbol{\mu} directly for visibility (Hard Truncation) causes artifacts at the clipping surface because Gaussians intersecting the plane may have means on either side, leading to discontinuous visibility changes. Non-Contiguity: The indicator operation in the visibility mask is mathematically non-contiguous, causing inconsistent rendering when the clipping plane changes. The AAM is designed to mitigate this by predicting continuous deformations. Model Capacity: Unlike methods that learn a full deformation field for the clipping dimension (e.g., HexPlane, GauFRe), ClipGS focuses on visible primitives, reducing model capacity and storage requirements. Time Complexity: The method is GPU-accelerated and designed for real-time rendering. The training involves two phases: 7,000 iterations for coarse initialization and 33,000 iterations for joint optimization. Memory Complexity: The model size is approximately 16.1 MB for the trained Gaussians and AAM parameters. This is significantly smaller than methods that learn full deformation fields for the clipping dimension. Performance: Achieves an average PSNR of 36.635 on five volumetric medical data scenes (Head, Lower Limb, Skull, Thorax, Liver & Kidney). Rendering speed is 156 FPS on a single RTX 4090 GPU. Strengths: Real-time interactive visualization, low storage cost, high rendering quality, and continuity across clipping planes. Limitations: Requires a two-step optimization process. The AAM adds complexity to the training loop compared to standard 3DGS. When to use: Suitable for interactive cinematic visualization of volumetric medical data where clipping plane interaction is required. ClipGS was introduced in a paper titled "ClipGS: Clippable Gaussian Splatting for Interactive Cinematic Visualization of Volumetric Medical Data". The work addresses the limitations of high computing cost and low rendering speed in traditional volumetric medical data visualization, aiming to enable interactive cinematic rendering. It builds on the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework and extends it to support clipping plane interactions, which are crucial for medical diagnosis and surgical planning. The method was validated on datasets from the Visible Human Project and the CVH project.
