name: DARBF-Splatting
head: DARB-Splatting, Decaying Anisotropic Radial Basis Functions Splatting
body: DARBF-Splatting replaces the standard Gaussian kernel in 3D Gaussian Splatting with a class of non-exponential, decaying anisotropic radial basis functions (DARBFs). It solves the limitation of the exponential family by allowing kernels like half-cosine or inverse multiquadric, which span larger regions with higher opacity for the same variance, thereby reducing the number of primitives needed and improving training efficiency. Unlike standard 3DGS, it introduces a scalar correction factor to approximate the closed-form integration shortcut of Gaussians, preserving computational efficiency while enabling differentiable rendering with non-Gaussian kernels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D primitives (positions, covariances, colors, opacities) initialized from an SfM pipeline (e.g., COLMAP). Output: A rendered 2D image and optimized primitive attributes via backpropagation. Data Structures: The primitive i retains the standard 3DGS structure but uses a DARBF kernel instead of a Gaussian: Position: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (symmetric positive definite), parameterized by rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{s}i as in [Parent]. Color: \mathbf{c}i (e.g., spherical harmonics coefficients). Method Steps: 1. 3D to 2D Projection: Transform the 3D primitive into the camera coordinate system. Project the 3D covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i to a 2D covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i by skipping the third row and column of the transformed 3x3 matrix. This bypasses costly integration, a property specific to the Gaussian family that DARBF-Splatting approximates. 2. Compute Mahalanobis Distance: For a pixel center x' in the 2D image plane, calculate the Mahalanobis distance dM from the projected primitive center \boldsymbol{\mu}' using the 2D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i: dM(x'; \boldsymbol{\mu}', \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i) = \sqrt{(x' - \boldsymbol{\mu}')^T (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i)^{-1} (x' - \boldsymbol{\mu}')} where \boldsymbol{\mu}' is the 2D projection of \mathbf{p}i. 3. Evaluate DARBF Kernel: Compute the kernel value K(dM) using a chosen DARBF function. The function must be non-negative, decaying, and anisotropic (via dM). Half-Cosine Kernel: K{hc}(dM) = \begin{cases} \cos\left(\frac{dM^2}{\xi}\right) & \text{if } dM^2 < \frac{\xi \pi}{2} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \xi > 0 is a shape parameter. Inverse Multiquadric (Inverse MQ): K{imq}(dM) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + dM^2}} Other DARBFs: Modified raised cosine, modular sinc. 4. Apply Correction Factor: Since non-Gaussian functions do not naturally integrate to a closed-form constant like Gaussians do during projection, apply a scalar correction factor \psi to the kernel value to approximate the Gaussian's integration shortcut: \sigmai(x') = \alphai \cdot \psi \cdot K(dM) The value of \psi is precomputed from closed-form regression experiments to ensure comparable accumulated opacity to Gaussians. 5. Rasterization and Blending: Sort primitives by depth [Parent]. For each pixel, accumulate color using alpha blending [Parent]: C(x') = \sum{i \in N} \mathbf{c}i \sigmai(x') \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \sigmaj(x')) where \sigmai(x') is the effective opacity contribution of primitive i at pixel x'. 6. Optimization: Backpropagate the pixel error between views and rasterized splats to optimize the primitives. Parameters: Kernel Type: Half-cosine, Inverse MQ, etc.. Shape Parameter (\xi): Controls the width of the half-cosine kernel. Correction Factor (\psi): Scalar precomputed from regression. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unbounded Functions: Growing functions cause instability and are omitted; only decaying functions are used. Integration Cost: Using functions outside the Gaussian family typically incurs costly integration. Precision: The half-cosine kernel has finite support (dM^2 < \frac{\xi \pi}{2}), which must be checked to avoid evaluating cosine outside the valid domain. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderdarbfsplat(primitives, cameraviewmatrix, imagedims): # primitives: list of dicts with keys 'p' (3,), 'cov' (3,3), 'alpha' (float), 'color' (3,), 'sh' (list) # cameraviewmatrix: 4x4 transformation to camera space # imagedims: (height, width) outcolor = np.zeros(imagedims + (3,)) outalpha = np.zeros(imagedims) # Step 1: Project 3D primitives to 2D and compute 2D covariance projectedprims = [] for prim in primitives: p3d = prim['p'] cov3d = prim['cov'] # Transform position and covariance to camera frame pcam = cameraviewmatrix[:3,:3] @ p3d + cameraviewmatrix[:3, 3] covcam = cameraviewmatrix[:3,:3] @ cov3d @ cameraviewmatrix[:3,:3].T # Skip third row and column for 2D projection cov2d = covcam[:2,:2] mu2d = pcam[:2] projectedprims.append({'mu': mu2d, 'cov': cov2d, 'alpha': prim['alpha'], 'color': prim['color'], 'sh': prim['sh']}) # Step 5 (partial): Sort primitives by depth for correct blending [Parent] projectedprims.sort(key=lambda p: p['mu'][2]) # Assuming z-depth in camera frame # Step 2-4: Evaluate kernel and blend per pixel for prim in projectedprims: mu = prim['mu'] cov = prim['cov'] alpha = prim['alpha'] color = prim['color'] # Compute bounding box for efficient rasterization bbox = computeboundingbox(mu, cov) for y in range(bbox.ymin, bbox.ymax): for x in range(bbox.xmin, bbox.xmax): xprime = np.array([x, y]) diff = xprime - mu[:2] # Mahalanobis distance squared dMsq = diff @ np.linalg.inv(cov) @ diff # Evaluate DARBF kernel (e.g., half-cosine) xi = 2.0 # shape parameter if dMsq < xi np.pi / 2: K = np.cos(dMsq / xi) else: K = 0.0 # Apply scalar correction factor psi = 1.5 # precomputed from regression sigma = alpha psi K # Alpha blending [Parent] outcolor[y, x] += color sigma (1.0 - outalpha[y, x]) outalpha[y, x] += sigma return outcolor Allows negative opacity values to cancel out artifacts. Negative Gaussian Splatting Wraps primitives around surfaces using a scaffold structure. Scaffold-GS Enforces geometric constraints on primitives. GeoGaussian Injects differentiable blur kernels into rasterization. Grid-based Blur Kernel Time and memory complexity: Training convergence is 34% faster than standard 3DGS with the half-cosine kernel. Memory usage is reduced by 15% compared to standard 3DGS with the half-cosine kernel. Measured performance: Achieves comparable PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS results to 3DGS on Mip-NeRF 360 scenes. Scaling: Wider-spread kernels (half-cosine, Inverse MQ) reduce the need for multiple splats to achieve the same accumulated value. Strengths and limitations: More efficient training and lower memory footprint. Requires precomputed correction factors for non-Gaussian kernels; not all DARBFs perform equally (e.g., radial cosine had lower SSIM than half-cosine in Table 6). When to use: When computational savings (training time, memory) are critical and comparable visual quality to 3DGS is acceptable. When not to use: Not given in the sources. DARBF-Splatting was introduced by Hashiru Pramuditha, Vinasirajan Viruthshaan, Vishagar Arunan, Saeedha Nazar, Sameera Ramasinghe, Simon Lucey, and Ranga Rodrigo from the University of Moratuwa and University of Adelaide. The work generalizes splatting techniques beyond the exponential family, addressing the underexplored area of non-Gaussian reconstruction kernels in 3D Gaussian Splatting. DARB-Splatting: Generalizing Splatting with Decaying Anisotropic Radial Basis Functions, https://doi.org/10.1109/WACV61042.2026.00438, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Grid-based Blur Kernel
head: Sharpness-indexed Blur Kernels, Trainable Grid-based Blur Kernels
body: Grid-based Blur Kernels address the challenge of modeling spatially-varying blurriness in radiance field optimization by replacing MLP-generated blur kernels with a set of learnable, indexed grid kernels. Unlike Negative Gaussian Splatting which modifies primitive attributes, or Scaffold-GS which constrains geometry, this method injects a differentiable blur convolution into the rendering pipeline to explicitly deblur or model defocus. It sets itself apart from previous works that use MLPs to generate kernels by allowing expressivity improvements via grid size expansion without additional computational cost for kernel generation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of training views (images), a precomputed sharpness level map L, and the number of blur kernels Nk. Outputs: A blurred image Ib that approximates the ground truth I{gt}, and optimized blur kernels \mathcal{B}. Data Structures: Blur Kernel Tensor \mathcal{B}: A tensor of shape \mathbb{R}^{N{img} \times Nk \times K \times K \times C}. N{img}: Number of training views. Nk: Number of unique sharpness groups (blur kernels). K: Kernel size (spatial dimension). C: Number of color channels. Note: The channel dimension C is often omitted for brevity in formulas. Sharpness Level Map L: A map where each pixel is assigned an integer value from 0 to Nk-1, indicating its sharpness group. Cropped Image I'c: A tensor of shape P' \times P' \times K \times K (plus channels) derived from the clean image Ic. Parameters: K: Kernel size. Typical value: 11. Nk: Number of blur kernels. Typical value: 400. Learning Rate: 0.05 for the kernel. Initialization: 2D Gaussian distribution. P': Patch size dimension. Typical value: 22 (patch size P=22). Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Sharpness Prior): Estimate a spatially varying defocus map for every training view using a Defocus Map Estimation Network (DMENet). Quantize this map uniformly into Nk values to create the sharpness level map L. Optionally, segment the scene based on depth information (e.g., from MIDAS) to assess focus levels within segments. This step is performed once before training, taking less than a couple of minutes. 2. Kernel Indexing: For each pixel x in a training view, determine its sharpness level Lx from the map L. Map this level to a specific blur kernel wx from the grid \mathcal{B} using a mapping function F: wx = F(\mathcal{B}, L, x) Here, F simply indexes \mathcal{B} using the view index and the sharpness level Lx. 3. Image Cropping: Crop the clean image Ic along height and width with stride 1 to obtain I'c of shape P' \times P' \times K \times K. This creates a local neighborhood window for each pixel in the target patch. 4. Blurred Image Convolution: Compute the blurred image Ib at pixel coordinates (h, w) by convolving the cropped clean image with the indexed kernel wx: Ib[h,w] = \sum{i=0}^{K} \sum{j=0}^{K} I'c[h,w,i,j] wx[h,w,i,j] where h, w are indices along the height and width of the image and blur kernels, respectively. 5. Optimization: Optimize both the blur kernels \mathcal{B} and the underlying neural fields (e.g., NeRF) jointly using the reconstruction loss: \mathcal{L}{recon} = ||Ib - I{gt}||2 where I{gt} is the ground truth image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def zeros(shape): """Returns a tensor of zeros with the given shape.""" if len(shape) == 1: return [0.0] shape[0] return [[0.0 for in range(shape[1])] for in range(shape[0])] def gridbasedblurkernelrendering(trainingviews, sharpnessmapL, B, K, Nk, Igt): """ trainingviews: List of clean image tensors Ic, shape (H, W, C). sharpnessmapL: Tensor of shape (Nimg, H, W) with integer values in [0, Nk-1]. B: Tensor of shape (Nimg, Nk, K, K, C). K: Kernel size. Nk: Number of blur kernels. Igt: Ground truth image tensor, shape (H, W, C). """ # Step 1: Preprocessing (sharpness map L) is assumed precomputed. HIGHSHARPNESSGROUPS = {i for i in range(100)} # 100 groups skipped per view for vidx in range(len(trainingviews)): Ic = trainingviews[vidx] H, W, C = Ic.shape Pprime = H # Assuming square patches where P' = H for simplicity # Step 3: Crop Ic with stride 1 to gather KxK neighborhoods # Icprime shape: (Pprime, Pprime, K+1, K+1, C) to match formula bounds 0..K Icprime = zeros((Pprime, Pprime, K + 1, K + 1, C)) for h in range(Pprime): for w in range(Pprime): hstart, hend = max(0, h - K // 2), min(H, h + K // 2 + 1) wstart, wend = max(0, w - K // 2), min(W, w + K // 2 + 1) patch = zeros((K + 1, K + 1, C)) phstart, pwstart = K // 2 - (h - hstart), K // 2 - (w - wstart) for pi in range(phstart, phstart + (hend - hstart)): for pj in range(pwstart, pwstart + (wend - wstart)): patch[pi, pj,:] = Ic[hstart + (pi - phstart), wstart + (pj - pwstart),:] Icprime[h, w,:,:,:] = patch Ib = zeros((Pprime, Pprime, C)) Lview = sharpnessmapL[vidx] # Step 4: Convolution with indexed kernels for h in range(Pprime): for w in range(Pprime): sharpnesslevel = Lview[h, w] if sharpnesslevel in HIGHSHARPNESSGROUPS: Ib[h, w,:] = Ic[h, w,:] # Pass-through for high sharpness continue # Step 2: Index blur kernel wx = B[vidx, sharpnesslevel,:,:,:] # Shape: (K, K, C) # Convolution: Ib[h,w] = sum{i=0}^{K} sum{j=0}^{K} I'c[h,w,i,j] wx[h,w,i,j] acc = zeros(C) for i in range(K + 1): for j in range(K + 1): for c in range(C): acc[c] += Icprime[h, w, i, j, c] wx[i, j, c] Ib[h, w,:] = acc # Step 5: Optimization loss = mseloss(Ib, Igt) # Backpropagate to update B and neural fields optimizer.step(loss) def mseloss(pred, target): """Computes Mean Squared Error loss.""" diffsq = zeroslike(pred, target) return sum(sum(sum(diffsq))) / (len(pred) len(pred[0]) len(pred[0][0])) def zeroslike(tensor1, tensor2): """Computes element-wise squared difference between two tensors.""" return [[(tensor1[i][j][k] - tensor2[i][j][k]) 2 for k in range(len(tensor1[i][j]))] for j in range(len(tensor1[0])) for i in range(len(tensor1))] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Sharpness Groups: Pixels in groups with high sharpness values (clear regions) skip convolution to save computation. The method skips convolution for pixels in 100 groups of each view with high sharpness values. Boundary Conditions: The cropping operation requires handling image boundaries. The sources do not specify a padding strategy, so standard practice involves zero-padding or replication. Initialization: Blur kernels are initialized with a 2D Gaussian distribution to provide a reasonable starting point for optimization. This variant refers to the preprocessing step used to generate the sharpness level map L. It estimates a spatially varying defocus map for every training view using DMENet, an end-to-end CNN framework. The defocus map is quantized uniformly into Nk values to create the sharpness level map L, which divides pixels into Nk groups based on their degree of sharpness. Additionally, the method may segment the scene based on depth information (from MIDAS) to assess the focus level within each segment, improving the extraction of sharp regions. This step is generic and can use any operator that reliably measures sharpness, but DMENet and MIDAS are the specific tools cited. A technique to predict a degradation kernel that accounts for differences between rendered and reference image patches, used to handle blur artifacts and defective training data. It grayscales and flattens rendered and reference patches, concatenates them, and feeds them into a shallow MLP to predict a kernel Bp and a blending weight \omegap. The final degradation kernel is computed as B{final} = \omegap Bp + (1 - \omegap) BI, where BI is an identity kernel. Choose this variant when training data contains defects or view-dependent inconsistencies that degrade rendering quality. It adds approximately 0.5 hours to a 200K iteration training run and yields a 0.5 PSNR improvement on the 'LivingRoom' dataset compared to pre-defined kernels. Time Complexity: The method reduces the number of required neighboring rays per ray compared to random ray sampling in NeRF, due to random patch sampling. The sharpness prior computation takes less than a couple of minutes and does not affect training or testing times. Memory Complexity: The blur kernel tensor \mathcal{B} has size N{img} \times Nk \times K \times K \times C. Performance: The method successfully renders clean images even from harshly defocused regions. It improves expressivity by increasing grid size without extra cost for kernel generation. Strengths: Joint optimization with neural fields allows rapid convergence. The grid-based approach is more efficient than MLP-based kernel generation. Limitations: Requires a preprocessing step for sharpness estimation. Performance depends on the accuracy of the defocus map estimation. The method originates from "Sharp-NeRF: Grid-based Fast Deblurring Neural Radiance Fields using Sharpness Prior". It was proposed to address the limitations of NeRF and its derivatives in handling defocus blur by leveraging a sharpness prior and grid-based blur kernels. The work contrasts with previous methods that used MLPs to generate blur kernels, offering a more scalable and expressive alternative. name: TideGS Trajectory Ordering
head: Clustered TSP ordering for 3DGS, Trajectory-aware view ordering
body:
TideGS Trajectory Ordering is a training strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces standard randomized view shuffling with a trajectory-aware ordered sequence of views to improve optimization stability and convergence for large-scale scenes. Unlike standard 3DGS which samples views with random shuffling, TideGS uses a clustered traveling-salesperson (TSP) ordering to preserve trajectory continuity, reducing gradient variation between consecutive steps. It builds on Base 3DGS Optimization by modifying the view sampling schedule while retaining the standard masked update mechanism. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of M training views with camera poses; the current state of Gaussian parameters 	heta; a fixed block size B. Outputs: A permutation \pi of view indices; updated parameters 	heta{t+1} after processing one epoch. Data Structures: 1. Spatial Blocks: Gaussians are partitioned into K spatial blocks using Morton-code ordering. Each block contains a fixed number of primitives B. The block-index universe is \mathcal{K} = \{0, \dots, K-1\}. These blocks serve as the basic unit for SSD–CPU–GPU streaming. Bit-packing details for Morton codes are Not given in the sources. 2. View Permutation: An ordered sequence \pi = (\pi1, \dots, \piM) generated by clustered TSP over camera poses. This is a permutation of view indices, not spatial blocks. 3. Active Set \mathcal{I}t: At iteration t, the set of Gaussian indices and parameter coordinates that are visible and selected for update after coarse-to-fine filtering. Numbered Steps: 1. Block Partitioning: Partition all Gaussian primitives into spatial blocks using Morton-code ordering. Each block k \in \mathcal{K} contains exactly B Gaussians. 2. Trajectory Construction: Apply a clustered traveling-salesperson (TSP) algorithm to the camera poses of the M training views to generate the permutation \pi = (\pi1, \dots, \piM). 3. Training Loop: Iterate through the views in the order defined by \pi. For each iteration t from 1 to M: a. Block Selection: Perform coarse block-wise frustum culling to select the working set of blocks Kt \subseteq \mathcal{K} relevant to the current view \pit. b. Active Set Determination: Perform coarse-to-fine filtering to determine the Gaussian-level active set \mathcal{I}t. Only Gaussians in the selected blocks that are visible in view \pit are included. c. Gradient Computation: Compute the photometric loss f{\pit}(	heta) and its gradient 
abla f{\pit}(	heta) for the active Gaussians. d. Masked Update: Update the parameters using the masked update rule: 	heta{t+1}^{(j)} =  egin{cases} 	hetat^{(j)} - \etat \cdot ut^{(j)}, & j \in \mathcal{I}t, \ 	hetat^{(j)}, & 	ext{otherwise,} \end{cases} where ut^{(j)} is the optimizer's update direction (e.g., Adam moments) and \etat is the learning rate. e. State Preservation: Parameters not in \mathcal{I}t are not updated, preserving their state and preventing interference from distant regions. Formulas: Objective Function: The goal is to minimize the average photometric loss over M training views: \min{	heta} F(	heta):=  rac{1}{M} \sum{i=1}^M fi(	heta) where fi(	heta) is the photometric loss for view i and 	heta \in \mathbb{R}^d is the concatenation of all Gaussian parameters. Gradient-Variation Surrogate: To analyze ordering stability, the following surrogate measures the squared norm difference between consecutive per-view gradients along the permutation \pi: V\pi(\{	hetat\}):= \sum{t=1}^{M-1} \left\| 
abla f{\pit}(	hetat) - 
abla f{\pi{t+1}}(	hetat) ight\|^2 This term is smaller for \pi{TSP} than for random permutations, indicating reduced gradient drift. Parameters: B: The fixed number of primitives (Gaussians) contained in each spatial block (typical value: e.g., B Gaussians). K: The total number of spatial blocks. M: The total number of training views. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stale Optimizer State: Sequentially correlated samples in non-shuffled training may introduce bias or cause optimizer state (e.g., momentum) to become stale or misaligned. Mitigation: The masked update in TideGS acts as a safeguard against stale optimizer state by updating optimizer state only on active coordinates, preventing distant regions from interfering with each other. Visibility Sparsity: Most parameters are untouched at each step. Inactive parameters are not repeatedly perturbed by unrelated views, and their update history is dominated by iterations where they are visible. An oracle-efficient active next-best-view selection framework for 3DGS that reduces computational cost by evaluating only a randomized subset of candidate views per iteration. It differs from TideGS by focusing on memory-efficient rendering and stochastic submodular optimization rather than trajectory-aware view ordering. Choose it when minimizing oracle complexity for view selection is the priority. Training-time techniques that replace randomized view shuffling with deterministic sequences to optimize Gaussian caching and reduce CPU optimizer communication overhead. Unlike TideGS which targets gradient stability via TSP ordering, these strategies focus on caching efficiency and CPU-side throughput. Choose them when CPU-bound optimizer performance is the bottleneck. Time Complexity: The TSP ordering is computed once during initialization. The training loop processes each view exactly once per epoch, similar to standard 3DGS, but with the overhead of block-wise frustum culling and Morton-code based spatial partitioning. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for spatial blocks and Morton codes. The out-of-core streaming capability allows handling large scenes by loading only active blocks into GPU memory. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces gradient drift; mitigates stale optimizer state through masked updates; enables scalable training via out-of-core optimization. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of TSP order; relies on visibility-induced sparsity for effectiveness. When to use: Large-scale scenes where standard random shuffling leads to unstable convergence or slow training. When not to use: Small scenes where random shuffling is sufficient and the overhead of TSP ordering is unjustified. TideGS was introduced in the paper "TideGS: Scalable Training of Over One Billion 3D Gaussian Splatting Primitives via Out-of-Core Optimization". It departs from standard randomized view order to address scalability and stability issues in large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting training. The method leverages empirical properties of visibility-induced sparsity and trajectory continuity to improve optimization. TideGS: Scalable Training of Over One Billion 3D Gaussian Splatting Primitives via Out-of-Core Optimization, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.20150, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: LiTe-GS
head: Oracle-Efficient NBV Selection for 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: LiTe-GS is an oracle-efficient active next-best-view (NBV) selection framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that reduces the computational cost of Fisher-information-based view selection by evaluating only a randomized subset of candidate views at each iteration rather than exhaustively scoring the full pool. It formulates NBV selection as the cardinality-constrained maximization of Fisher-information gain, leveraging stochastic submodular optimization to balance estimation accuracy with oracle efficiency, thereby achieving O(M \log(1/\epsilon)) oracle complexity independent of the selection cardinality K. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: H0: The prior block-diagonal Fisher information matrix obtained from an initial 3DGS reconstruction trained on a small set of seed views V0. Vc: A pool of M candidate viewpoints for acquisition. K: The selection cardinality, i.e., the number of views to select in each acquisition batch. \epsilon: An accuracy parameter controlling the trade-off between oracle efficiency and approximation quality. Outputs: S: A set of K selected views. Data Structures: Fisher Information Matrix (H): Stored as a block-diagonal matrix where each block corresponds to the parameters of an individual Gaussian primitive i \in \{1, \dots, N\}. Hv \approx \text{blkdiag}(Hv(\hat{\theta}1), Hv(\hat{\theta}2), \dots, Hv(\hat{\theta}N)). Each block Hv(\hat{\theta}i) is computed as \sigma^{-2} J{v,i}^\top J{v,i}, where J{v,i} is the Jacobian of the rendered observations for view v with respect to the parameters of Gaussian i. Priority Queue (Q): A max-priority queue storing candidate views from the current sampled subset P, ordered by their cached marginal gains \gammav. Formulas: 3D Gaussian Density: Gi(x) = \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} (x - \mui)^\top \Pii^{-1} (x - \mui) \right). Covariance Parameterization: \Pii = Ri Si Si^\top Ri^\top, where Ri \in SO(3) and Si is a scaling matrix. Image-Space Covariance: \Pi'i = JW \Pii W^\top J^\top, where W is the viewing transformation and J is the Jacobian of the projective transformation. Rendered Color: C = \sum{i \in N} ci \alphai (1 - \sum{j < i} \alphaj), where N is the set of Gaussians along the pixel’s viewing ray. Fisher Information for View v: Hv(\hat{\Theta}) \approx \sigma^{-2} \sum{\text{pixels}} Jv^\top Jv, where Jv = \frac{\partial fv}{\partial \Theta}|{\hat{\Theta}} is the Jacobian of the rendering function. Marginal Gain: \rho(\{v\} | Sq) is the marginal information gain computed via oracle evaluation, which constructs and accumulates the Fisher-information contribution Hv. The marginal gain is the reduction in uncertainty (increase in information) by adding view v to the selected set Sq. Subset Size: p = \frac{M}{K} \log \frac{1}{\epsilon}. Parameters: \epsilon: Typical value 0.1. Tested values include 0.1, 0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6. K: Tested values 3, 4, 6. \delta: Small regularization parameter for ill-conditioning, applied as H0 \leftarrow H0 + \delta I. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize selected set S = \emptyset. Initialize current information matrix H = H0. Precondition H0 by adding regularization: H0 \leftarrow H0 + \delta I. Initialize cached marginal gains \gammav \leftarrow \infty for all v \in Vc. 2. Iterative Selection (for q = 1 to K): Sample Subset: Sample a subset P \subset (Vc \setminus S) of size p = \frac{M}{K} \log \frac{1}{\epsilon}. Initialize Queue: Initialize a max-priority queue Q over views in P using their cached gains \gammav. Lazy Evaluation Loop: Repeat: Pop view v with the largest cached gain from Q. Oracle Evaluation: Recompute the true marginal gain \Deltav = \rho(\{v\} | Sq) by constructing and accumulating the Fisher information contribution Hv. Update cached gain \gammav \leftarrow \Deltav. Re-insert v into Q with updated priority \gammav. Until \gammav = \max{u \in P} \gammau (i.e., the popped view's true gain is greater than or equal to the cached gains of all other views in Q). Select and Update: Add selected view v to S: S \leftarrow S \cup \{v\}. Update information matrix: H \leftarrow H + Hv. 3. Return: Selected set S. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import random import heapq def logdet(M): """Computes the natural logarithm of the determinant of matrix M.""" return np.linalg.slogdet(M)[1] def computejacobian(view): """Computes the Jacobian Jv = d(fv)/d(Theta) for the given view.""" # Standard differentiable rendering computes this via backpropagation. return view.renderjacobian() def computefisherblock(jacobian, sigma2inv): """Computes Hv = sigma^-2 Jv^T Jv.""" return sigma2inv (jacobian.T @ jacobian) def liTegs(h0, candidateviews, k, epsilon, delta, sigma2inv): m = len(candidateviews) # Precondition H0 with regularization h = h0 + delta np.eye(h0.shape[0]) s = [] remainingviews = list(candidateviews) cachedgains = {v: float('inf') for v in candidateviews} for q in range(1, k + 1): # Sample subset P of size p psize = int((m / k) np.log(1 / epsilon)) psize = min(psize, len(remainingviews)) p = random.sample(remainingviews, psize) # Max-heap using negative gains heap = [(-cachedgains[v], v) for v in p] heapq.heapify(heap) selectedview = None while heap: neggain, v = heapq.heappop(heap) # Oracle evaluation: recompute true marginal gain jacobian = computejacobian(v) hv = computefisherblock(jacobian, sigma2inv) truegain = logdet(h) - logdet(h + hv) cachedgains[v] = truegain # Check if truegain >= max cached gain of remaining views in heap if heap: maxothercached = -heap[0][0] else: maxothercached = -float('inf') if truegain >= maxothercached: selectedview = v h = h + hv break else: heapq.heappush(heap, (-truegain, v)) if selectedview is None: selectedview = p[0] jacobian = computejacobian(selectedview) hv = computefisherblock(jacobian, sigma2inv) h = h + hv s.append(selectedview) remainingviews.remove(selectedview) return s Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-conditioning: The prior information matrix H0 can be ill-conditioned. This is handled by preconditioning with a small regularization parameter \delta: H0 \leftarrow H0 + \delta I. Subset Size: The subset size p depends on \epsilon. If \epsilon is large, p becomes small, potentially leading to poor selection quality if the subset does not contain informative views. Dynamic Resampling: LiTe-GS dynamically resamples candidate subsets at each acquisition step. This differs from Static-Subset Greedy (SSG), which samples once per stage. Dynamic resampling prevents the algorithm from being permanently restricted to a potentially unfavorable subset realization. A baseline method that uses the same Fisher-information-based objective but evaluates the full oracle over all candidate views at each iteration, resulting in higher oracle complexity. A baseline that samples a fixed subset of candidates once per acquisition stage and keeps it fixed, whereas LiTe-GS dynamically resamples candidate subsets at each acquisition step. Time and Memory Complexity: Oracle Complexity: Expected O(M \log(1/\epsilon)) oracle evaluations with respect to the number of candidate views M, independent of the selection cardinality K. Memory: The block-diagonal approximation of the Fisher information matrix makes storage tractable, scaling with the number of Gaussian primitives N but avoiding the full dense matrix. Measured Performance: On Blender (Ship) with K=6, \epsilon=0.1: 208 oracle evaluations, PSNR 25.49, SSIM 0.830, LPIPS 0.158. Increasing K from 3 to 6 increases POP-GS evaluations from 275 to 549, while LiTe-GS remains nearly constant (210, 209, 208). For fixed K=6, increasing \epsilon from 0.1 to 0.6 reduces evaluations from 208 to 44, yielding 80.42% and 91.99% reductions respectively. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significantly reduces oracle evaluations compared to exhaustive methods like POP-GS while maintaining comparable reconstruction quality. Provides an explicit trade-off between efficiency and accuracy via \epsilon. Limitations: Approximation quality depends on \epsilon. A fixed subset (SSG) can occasionally outperform LiTe-GS if the fixed subset is favorable, but LiTe-GS is more robust across different scenes due to dynamic resampling. LiTe-GS was proposed in the paper "LiTe-GS: Oracle-Efficient Next Best View Selection for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the computational bottleneck of information-driven view selection in 3DGS, where repeated evaluations of expensive information-gain oracles become prohibitive as the number of candidate views increases. The method leverages stochastic submodular optimization techniques to design an efficient active-view selection strategy. LiTe-GS: Oracle-Efficient Next Best View Selection for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30393, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: View Ordering Strategies
head: Camera Order, GS Count Order, TSP Order
body: View ordering strategies determine the sequence in which training views are processed during 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization to improve training efficiency and stability. Unlike randomized shuffling, these methods leverage geometric or visibility information to reduce communication overhead between CPU and GPU memory. They are primarily used in conjunction with Gaussian caching mechanisms to minimize redundant data transfers. Inputs: A set of training views V = \{v1, \dots, vN\}, their camera poses, and the current set of 3D Gaussians G. Outputs: A permutation \pi of view indices representing the processing order. The strategies operate by sorting the views based on specific criteria: 1. Random Order: Views are shuffled uniformly at random. 2. Camera Order: Views are sorted by the coordinate of their camera center along the scene’s principal axis. 3. GS Count Order: Views are sorted in descending order by the number of Gaussians visible in each view. Prioritizing views with higher Gaussian counts allows the CPU Adam optimizer to update a larger number of Gaussians earlier in the training process, thereby reducing its relative overhead. 4. TSP Order: Views are ordered using a Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) heuristic to find a sequence that maximizes the overlap of visible Gaussians between successive views. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility Computation: GS Count Order and TSP Order require computing view-Gaussian visibility, which adds preprocessing overhead. Scene Scale: In scenes with very low Gaussian sharing between images (low \rho), such as "BigCity," the benefits of TSP-based caching are reduced because fewer Gaussians are shared between successive views. Conversely, in scenes with high Gaussian density per image, such as "Bicycle," caching benefits are more significant. This is a combined optimization technique used in CLM that caches Gaussian parameters across views and applies TSP-based ordering to minimize redundant CPU-to-GPU transfers. By maintaining a cache of recently accessed Gaussians, the system avoids reloading them from CPU memory. When combined with TSP order, CLM reduces communication volume by 37% (in the Alameda scene) to 82% (in the BigCity scene) compared to naive offloading without caching. In scenes with low inter-image Gaussian sharing, the caching benefit is smaller, but the ordering still contributes to overall efficiency. Communication Reduction: CLM with Gaussian Caching and TSP Order significantly reduces the volume of parameters transferred from CPU to GPU memory compared to naive offloading. Overhead: GS Count Order and TSP Order require additional processing to compute visibility or solve the TSP problem, unlike Camera Order or Random Order. Performance: Training throughput varies by hardware and scene; CLM with TSP order improves throughput on RTX 2080 Ti and RTX 4090 compared to baselines. Scalability: Effectiveness scales with inter-image Gaussian overlap; in scenes with low sharing (low \rho) like BigCity, caching benefits diminish. These strategies were introduced in the context of CLM (CLM: Removing the GPU Memory Barrier for 3D Gaussian Splatting) to address the bottleneck of transferring Gaussian parameters between CPU and GPU memory during training. The ablation study in the source paper evaluates these ordering methods to isolate the impact of view sequence on communication volume and training speed. CLM: Removing the GPU Memory Barrier for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/3779212.3790140, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Gradient Computation and Back-Propagation
head: Backward Pass, Gradient Flow, Differentiable Rendering Gradients
body: Gradient Computation and Back-Propagation refers to the mechanism of calculating the derivatives of a rendering loss with respect to the learnable parameters of 3D Gaussian primitives (position, covariance, opacity, color, and spherical harmonic coefficients) to enable end-to-end optimization [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. It differs from standard rasterization by propagating gradients through the differentiable alpha-compositing equation and the 2D projection approximation, allowing the scene representation to be refined via gradient descent [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. The core challenge is efficiently computing these gradients on the GPU while managing memory constraints and numerical stability, leading to various optimizations such as per-splat parallelization, deferred back-propagation, and specialized gradient formulations for specific primitives like Skew-Normal Splatting [5989-parallelization-for-backpropagation.md][13506-deferred-back-propagation.md][10040-sns-backward-pass-with-intermediate-variable-q.md]. The fundamental mechanism relies on the differentiable alpha-compositing equation. For a pixel \mathbf{x}, the rendered color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}) is computed as: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{k=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}k \alphak(\mathbf{x}) Tk(\mathbf{x}) where \mathbf{c}k is the color of the k-th Gaussian, \alphak(\mathbf{x}) is its opacity at pixel \mathbf{x}, and Tk(\mathbf{x}) is the transmittance up to the k-th Gaussian: Tk(\mathbf{x}) = \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphaj(\mathbf{x})) The Gaussians are sorted by depth from closest to farthest [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. The gradient of the loss L with respect to the parameters \thetak of the k-th Gaussian is computed via the chain rule: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \thetak} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x})} \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \alphak(\mathbf{x})} \frac{\partial \alphak(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \thetak} The term \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \alphak(\mathbf{x})} represents the contribution of the k-th Gaussian to the pixel color gradient. It is computed efficiently using recursive accumulators traversed in reverse depth order to avoid O(N^2) complexity [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. Specifically: \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \alphak(\mathbf{x})} = Tk(\mathbf{x}) \mathbf{c}k - \alphak(\mathbf{x}) \sum{j=k+1}^{N} \mathbf{c}j \alphaj(\mathbf{x}) Tj(\mathbf{x}) \frac{1}{1-\alphak(\mathbf{x})} In practice, this is implemented by maintaining a running transmittance T and a running accumulated color C{acc} [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. The term \frac{\partial \alphak(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \thetak} depends on the parameterization: Opacity: \alphak is typically the sigmoid of a learnable scalar. The gradient is \frac{\partial \alphak}{\partial \text{opacity}{raw}} = \alphak (1 - \alphak) [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. 2D Projection: The 2D covariance \Sigma{2D} is derived from the 3D covariance \Sigma{3D} and the view matrix. The conic matrix C = \Sigma{2D}^{-1} is used for efficient evaluation. Gradients \frac{\partial \alphak}{\partial C} are computed based on the Gaussian PDF derivative [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. 3D Covariance: \Sigma{3D} is parameterized by scale and rotation (\Sigma{3D} = R S S^T R^T). Gradients flow to scale and rotation via the chain rule through \Sigma{3D} and then to \Sigma{2D} [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. Color/SH: \mathbf{c}k is computed from spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. Gradients flow directly to SH coefficients based on the basis function evaluation at the viewing direction [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. Parallelization for Backpropagation changes the backward pass parallelization strategy from per-pixel to per-splat to address training speed obstacles [5989-parallelization-for-backpropagation.md]. It derives faster, numerically equivalent solutions for gradient computation and attribute updates, yielding a 4–5× reduction in training time and lower compute and memory requirements compared to the standard approach [5989-parallelization-for-backpropagation.md]. Choose this when training speed is the primary bottleneck and the standard per-pixel atomic add operations cause synchronization bottlenecks. AbsGS addresses the "over-reconstruction" artifact in 3D Gaussian Splatting, where large Gaussians in high-frequency regions fail to split, resulting in blurry rendering [6127-absgs.md]. It replaces the standard view-space positional gradient with a homodirectional gradient that sums the absolute values of pixel-wise sub-gradients, preventing gradient collision where positive and negative components cancel each other out [6127-absgs.md]. Unlike standard 3D-GS, which requires lowering the densification threshold to catch these errors (causing memory overflow), AbsGS accurately identifies over-reconstructed Gaussians using fewer primitives, achieving higher quality with roughly half the memory consumption [6127-absgs.md]. Choose this when dealing with high-frequency details and memory constraints. Gradient-Weighted Feature Back-Projection is a training-free method for rendering feature fields in 3D Gaussian Splatting by aggregating 2D feature embeddings from training views into pre-trained 3D Gaussians [9769-gradient-weighted-feature-back-projection.md]. It solves the problem of assigning semantic or visual features to 3D Gaussians without the computational cost of training a separate feature field or distilling features from a 2D foundation model [9769-gradient-weighted-feature-back-projection.md]. Unlike training-based alternatives like Feature 3DGS, which require iterative optimization of feature parameters, this method computes features in a single pass using the rendering gradients as weights, offering a significant speedup while maintaining high-quality 3D segmentation results [9769-gradient-weighted-feature-back-projection.md]. Choose this for feature field reconstruction without iterative training. The SNS Backward Pass with Intermediate Variable Q computes exact gradients for 3D Skew-Normal Splatting (SNS) parameters by decoupling the complex interaction between rotation and scale matrices [10040-sns-backward-pass-with-intermediate-variable-q.md]. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) which computes gradients with respect to the inverse covariance matrix \Omega^{-1} before backpropagating to rotation R and scale S, this method introduces an intermediate variable Q = ARS to reformulate the 2D Skew-Normal density [10040-sns-backward-pass-with-intermediate-variable-q.md]. This allows for direct, closed-form gradient computation of the skew parameter k, the mean \mu, and the shape matrix Q, avoiding the high computational complexity of differentiating the coupled RS terms directly [10040-sns-backward-pass-with-intermediate-variable-q.md]. Choose this when using Skew-Normal Splatting primitives. Specular-Aware Gradient Gating is a training optimization technique for differentiable Gaussian splatting that suppresses specular reflection artifacts while preserving transmission details in semi-transparent scenes [13432-specular-aware-gradient-gating.md]. It differs from standard back-propagation by modulating the gradients of the transmission color component using a local variance-based gating factor, ensuring the forward pass remains unchanged [13432-specular-aware-gradient-gating.md]. Choose this when training scenes with significant specular highlights and semi-transparency. Deferred Back-propagation is a memory-efficient training technique that enables the optimization of radiance fields and Gaussian splats using full-resolution image losses (such as CNN-based style losses or global attention mechanisms) despite limited GPU memory [13506-deferred-back-propagation.md]. It solves the problem where standard differentiable rendering is too memory-intensive for full-resolution images, forcing a trade-off between resolution and the ability to compute complex, non-pixel-wise losses [13506-deferred-back-propagation.md]. Unlike sparse pixel sampling, which fails for global losses, or naive cropping, which breaks global consistency, DBP separates the forward pass from the backward pass, allowing full-resolution rendering without gradients followed by patch-wise re-rendering with gradients [13506-deferred-back-propagation.md]. Choose this when using global losses (e.g., LPIPS, Style Loss) that require full-resolution images. Weight Freezing by Mask is a gradient modification technique used during the optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting models to selectively disable updates for specific attributes [15877-weight-freezing-by-mask.md]. It solves the problem of unwanted parameter drift by zeroing out gradients for designated attributes (e.g., rotation, scale) via element-wise multiplication with a binary mask [15877-weight-freezing-by-mask.md]. It differs from AbsGS by applying a static or dynamic mask to the gradient tensor rather than modifying the gradient magnitude based on absolute values, and from Specular-Aware Gradient Gating by operating on attribute-level tensors rather than pixel-level contributions [15877-weight-freezing-by-mask.md]. Choose this when specific parameters need to be fixed or constrained during training. Softmax Depth Gradient Derivation computes the gradients for a depth rendering formulation that uses softmax scaling to bias accumulation toward high-weight Gaussians while allowing gradients to propagate to off-mode Gaussians [17405-softmax-depth-gradient-derivation.md]. It solves the problem of mode-selection depth, which restricts gradients to the single highest-weight Gaussian and fails when closer Gaussians are translucent [17405-softmax-depth-gradient-derivation.md]. Unlike mode-selection, this method approximates mode depth while maintaining gradient flow to all contributing Gaussians, modulated by a temperature parameter \beta [17405-softmax-depth-gradient-derivation.md]. Choose this when using softmax-based depth rendering. The 3D Gaussian Splatting backward pass computes the gradients of a rendering loss with respect to the learnable parameters of the 3D Gaussian primitives (position, covariance, opacity, color, and spherical harmonic coefficients) [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. It differs from standard rasterization by propagating gradients through the differentiable alpha-compositing equation and the 2D projection approximation, enabling end-to-end training of the scene representation [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. This is the standard baseline method for most 3DGS implementations. This family defines the gradient computation for opacity parameters in differentiable volume rendering, specifically addressing standard alpha-compositing, probabilistic masking, and Time-of-Flight (ToF) signal formation [22870-opacity-and-score-gradient-computation.md]. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting backpropagation by handling non-linear opacity interactions in ToF models [9733-tof-gradient-computation-for-gaussian-splatting.md] and explicit mask modulation [4254-maskgaussian-gradient-computation.md], as well as score-based probability gradients for triangle-soup representations [22870-opacity-and-score-gradient-computation.md]. Choose this when using non-standard opacity models like ToF or probabilistic masks. Faster-GS addresses oscillation in gradient updates for scaling and rotation parameters caused by a poorly conditioned learning rate ratio. It rescales the scaling gradient with the inverse of the current scale to stabilize convergence. This cuts training time by nearly half compared to standard 3DGS. During each training iteration, identify the cut set of Gaussians intersecting the current training view. Update only the parameters of this cut set. Gradients propagate to Gaussians in the middle of the hierarchy, diffusing across the entire structure over many iterations with diverse views. A gradient computation method using half-precision (FP16) arithmetic to optimize accuracy-throughput trade-off, omitting block-local reductions. It calculates \frac{\partial I}{\partial Mi} using Eqs. (3, 4, 5), \frac{\partial Mi}{\partial u} using Eq. (2) and bilinear interpolation, and \frac{\partial u}{\partial xi}, \frac{\partial v}{\partial xi}, \frac{\partial u}{\partial yi}, \frac{\partial v}{\partial yi}, \frac{\partial u}{\partial si}, \frac{\partial v}{\partial si}, \frac{\partial u}{\partial \thetai}, \frac{\partial v}{\partial \thetai} from Eq. (1). The gradient of image I w.r.t. primitive position xi is \frac{\partial I(x,y)}{\partial xi} = \frac{\partial I(x,y)}{\partial Mi(x,y)} \left( \frac{\partial Mi(x,y)}{\partial u} \frac{\partial u}{\partial xi} + \frac{\partial Mi(x,y)}{\partial v} \frac{\partial v}{\partial xi} \right). It differs from standard implementations by using half precision and omitting block-local reductions to align with accuracy-throughput goals. An optimization step where appearance features on each point are updated via backpropagation through the aggregation and rendering network. The gradient on point feature i is updated using the chain rule: \Delta Fi = -lr \times w(p,h,w)i \times g(p,h,w), where g(p,h,w) is the gradient from the loss function. A module integrated into DBP to maintain consistency between the forward-only rendering step and the gradient-based re-rendering step. Without Local Self-Attention, the rendered images between the first (Render w/o Grad) and second (Re-Render w/ Grad) steps of DBP are inconsistent, causing the loss from the forward-only pass to fail as a gradient guide, which drops PSNR after ~1,500 training steps. With Local Self-Attention, PSNR remains stable at 32.34 dB throughout training. Creates a zero tensor for 2D screen-space means with gradient tracking enabled, allowing gradients to flow back to 2D positions during backpropagation. Initialize screenspacepoints as a zero tensor with the same dtype and device as pc.getxyz, with requiresgrad=True. Attempt to retain gradients for screenspacepoints using retaingrad() to preserve intermediate gradients. retaingrad() may raise an exception in older PyTorch versions or specific execution contexts, requiring a try/except block to prevent crashes. Pre-optimization step for strategies, called only on the first view to retain gradients. Check if vi == 0 and gsplatstrategy is not None. Call gsplatstrategy.stepprebackward(splats, optimizers, strategystate, step, info). Computes the vector-Jacobian product (VJP) for the ray transform matrix in 2DGS, propagating gradients from 2D means back to ray transforms, quaternions, scales, and camera-space means. If vmeans2d[0] or vmeans2d[1] is non-zero, compute distance = raytransforms[6]^2 + raytransforms[7]^2 - raytransforms[8]^2. Compute f = 1/distance. Compute partial derivatives dpxdT00, dpxdT01, dpxdT02, dpydT10, dpydT11, dpydT12, dpxdT30, dpxdT31, dpxdT32, dpydT30, dpydT31, dpydT32 using f and raytransforms values. Accumulate gradients into vraytransforms using vmeans2d and the computed partial derivatives. Compute rotation matrix R from quat. Compute vM = P transpose(vraytransforms). Compute Wt = transpose(W). Compute vRS = Wt vM. Compute vtn = Wt vnormals. Compute tn = W R[2]. Compute cos = dot(-tn, meanc). Set multiplier = 1 if cos > 0 else -1. Multiply vtn by multiplier. Compute vR = mat3(vRS[0]scale[0], vRS[1]scale[1], vtn). Compute vquat using quattorotmatvjp. Compute vscale[0] = dot(vRS[0], R[0]), vscale[1] = dot(vRS[1], R[1]). Add vRS[2] to vmean. Split sequence to perform auto-back-propagation for one frame at a time. Back-propagation between frames is handled explicitly (see Algorithm 4, line 19). Keep all resources in CPU RAM. Only current frame and intermediate steps needed for auto-diff are moved to GPU. Naive auto-diff of full sequence requires recording all intermediate results, consuming excessive memory. Result is the same as full auto-diff, at least when using Equation (4) instead of the EMA version (Eq. (5)). Allow unlimited number of splats to have gradients. Vs Limited Gradients: Limiting gradients to front-most points (e.g., N=10) causes unstable optimization and severe quality degradation (11dB PSNR drop), whereas unlimited gradients maintain quality. A mechanism-analysis tool applied to center gradients before optimizer updates to scale orthogonal components based on structural confidence, though disabled in default configuration. Application timing: Applied after back-propagation of the joint loss, before the optimizer update and before estimating first- and second-order moments. Gradient modification: \tilde{g} = D g, where D = \text{diag}(d1, d2, d3) in the local PCA basis. di = 1 if \hat{C} < \tau (identity), else d{orth} = \alpha0 for orthogonal directions and d{allowed} = 1. \alpha0: Retention coefficient for the orthogonal direction. Range: 0 \le \alpha0 < 1. Preserves sufficient correction capacity for initialization errors. Directional projection does not stably translate into reconstruction-quality gains under the current protocol, so it is disabled in the default configuration. A method to scatter gradients from sorted rendering view back to canonical parameter buffer using a permutation \pi, avoiding data movement and keeping optimizer states aligned. Gradient scattering: \nabla \theta{\pi(i)} += gi, where gi is gradient of i-th sorted element, \pi(i) is canonical index. The 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) method, introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023, established the standard differentiable rendering pipeline for Gaussian primitives. The backward pass implementation, often encapsulated in a DiffRasterizer class, takes forward pass buffers and the upstream loss gradient to compute per-primitive gradients [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. Subsequent research has focused on optimizing this backward pass for speed (e.g., Parallelization for Backpropagation [5989-parallelization-for-backpropagation.md]), memory (e.g., Deferred Back-propagation [13506-deferred-back-propagation.md]), and specific artifact reduction (e.g., AbsGS [6127-absgs.md], Specular-Aware Gradient Gating [13432-specular-aware-gradient-gating.md]). The method is widely used in real-time radiance field rendering, neural rendering, and 3D reconstruction from images or video.
