name: Parallelization for Backpropagation
head: Per-splat Backpropagation
body: Parallelization for Backpropagation is a training optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that changes the backward pass parallelization strategy from per-pixel to per-splat to address training speed obstacles. It derives faster, numerically equivalent solutions for gradient computation and attribute updates, yielding a 4–5× reduction in training time and lower compute and memory requirements compared to the standard approach. The method restructures the backward pass to iterate over Gaussians rather than pixels, accumulating gradients directly per Gaussian to avoid synchronization bottlenecks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The set of N 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, camera parameters, and the gradient of the loss with respect to the rendered pixel colors \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{c}}. Output: The accumulated gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} for all Gaussian parameters \theta (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonic coefficients). Data Structures: Gaussian-to-Pixel Mapping: A list or sparse structure storing the set of screen-space pixels covered by each Gaussian, generated during the forward rasterization pass. Gradient Accumulator: A buffer matching the parameter layout of the Gaussians, initialized to zero for each processing unit. Steps: 1. Forward Rasterization: Project Gaussians to screen space and determine the set of pixels each Gaussian covers, storing the mapping for the backward pass. 2. Per-Splat Iteration: Iterate over each Gaussian g in the dataset. 3. Pixel Gradient Retrieval: For each pixel p covered by g, retrieve the pre-computed pixel loss gradient \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{c}p} from the forward pass output. 4. Jacobian Computation: Compute the derivative of the alpha-blended color at pixel p with respect to g's parameters, \frac{\partial \mathbf{c}p}{\partial \thetag}, using the differentiable rendering equations. 5. Gradient Accumulation: Update the gradient accumulator for g using the chain rule: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \thetag} \leftarrow \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \thetag} + \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{c}p} \frac{\partial \mathbf{c}p}{\partial \thetag}. 6. Numerical Optimization: Apply faster, numerically equivalent formulations for the Jacobian and attribute updates to reduce compute overhead. Formulas: The core update for a Gaussian g with parameters \thetag is: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \thetag} = \sum{p \in \text{covered}(g)} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{c}p} \frac{\partial \mathbf{c}p}{\partial \thetag} Where \frac{\partial \mathbf{c}p}{\partial \thetag} is the derivative of the alpha-blended color at pixel p with respect to the Gaussian's parameters. The per-splat approach computes this sum by iterating over g and then p, whereas the per-pixel approach iterates over p and then g, requiring atomic adds for \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \thetag} when multiple Gaussians contribute to the same pixel. Parameters: Bucket size: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Partial Buckets: If N is not a multiple of the processing unit size, the final iteration handles fewer Gaussians; handled gracefully by standard loop bounds. Precision: The method maintains numerical equivalence to the original backpropagation, so standard float32 precision is preserved. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def persplatbackward(gaussians, pixelgradients, cameraparams): # gaussians: list of objects with 'params' dict and 'coveredpixels' list # pixelgradients: 2D array of shape (H, W, 3) containing dL/dc # cameraparams: camera intrinsics and extrinsics globalgrads = [] for g in gaussians: # Initialize local gradient accumulator for this Gaussian's parameters localgrad = {k: [0.0] len(v) for k, v in g.params.items()} # Iterate over all pixels covered by this Gaussian for p in g.coveredpixels: # Retrieve pre-computed pixel loss gradient dLdcp = pixelgradients[p.y, p.x] # Compute Jacobian: derivative of alpha-blended color w.r.t Gaussian parameters # Standard differentiable splatting chain rule through opacity, # 2D covariance/conic matrix, 3D covariance, and spherical harmonics # The sources do not provide the exact Jacobian implementation details dCdTheta = [0.0] len(g.params['position']) # Accumulate gradient using chain rule: dL/dTheta += dL/dc dC/dTheta for paramname in localgrad: localgrad[paramname] = [a + b c for a, b, c in zip(localgrad[paramname], dCdTheta[paramname], dLdcp)] globalgrads.append(localgrad) return globalgrads The Per-Gaussian Backward Pass is a backward pass optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that parallelizes gradient computation over Gaussians rather than pixels to reduce atomic contention. It addresses the performance bottleneck of standard pixel-parallel backpropagation, where splats contributing to arbitrary numbers of pixels require frequent atomic operations for accumulation. By computing gradients per Gaussian instead of per tile, it reduces false sharing and atomic contention during z-order sorting. Time Complexity: Reduces training time by 4–5× compared to the standard per-pixel backpropagation. Memory Complexity: Requires lower compute and memory requirements than the standard approach. Strengths: Provides faster, numerically equivalent solutions for gradient computation and attribute updates. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in "Taming 3DGS: High-Quality Radiance Fields with Limited Resources" (2024) as part of a broader effort to optimize the 3D Gaussian Splatting training pipeline. It addresses the scalability issues of the original 3DGS method, which suffered from slow training times due to the inefficiencies of the per-pixel backward pass. Taming 3DGS: High-Quality Radiance Fields with Limited Resources, https://doi.org/10.1145/3680528.3687694, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Per-Gaussian Backward Pass
head: Tile-based backward pass
body: The Per-Gaussian Backward Pass is a backward pass optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that parallelizes gradient computation over Gaussians rather than pixels to reduce atomic contention. It addresses the performance bottleneck of standard pixel-parallel backpropagation, where splats contributing to arbitrary numbers of pixels require frequent atomic operations for accumulation. By computing gradients per Gaussian instead of per tile, it reduces false sharing and atomic contention during z-order sorting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The method takes the loss gradients with respect to rendered image pixels (\frac{\partial L}{\partial I}) and the forward pass state, including Gaussian parameters, tile assignments, and stored alpha blending states. Output: The method outputs the gradients with respect to Gaussian parameters, such as position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Data Structures: Alpha Blending State Buffer: A buffer stores the intermediate alpha blending state (accumulated opacity and color) at each non-empty pixel. This state is recorded after every 32nd splat in the respective tile list during the forward pass. Steps: 1. Forward Pass Recording: During the forward rasterization pass, for each tile, store the alpha blending state at each non-empty pixel after processing every 32nd Gaussian (splat) in the tile's sorted list. 2. Gradient Replay: For each Gaussian, threads compute gradients locally based on the stored alpha states and the final pixel gradients, avoiding global memory synchronization and atomic operations. 3. Parameter Update: Accumulate the computed gradients for the Gaussians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pergaussianbackward(tilegaussians, alphastates, pixelgradients, tileidx): """ tilegaussians: List of Gaussian parameters sorted by z-order for this tile. alphastates: 2D array [numpixels][numsteps] storing alpha blending state after every 32nd splat. pixelgradients: Gradient of loss w.r.t. final pixel colors [numpixels][3]. tileidx: Index of the current tile. """ numgaussians = len(tilegaussians) numpixels = len(pixelgradients) gradients = [None] numgaussians # Step 1: Forward pass recording is handled externally by storing states every 32 splats # Step 2 & 3: Gradient Replay and Parameter Update for gidx in range(numgaussians): gaussian = tilegaussians[gidx] stepidx = gidx // 32 for pidx in range(numpixels): # Standard rasterization coverage check if not gaussian.iscovered(pidx): continue # Retrieve stored alpha blending state (accumulated opacity and color) at this checkpoint alphastatebefore = alphastates[pidx][stepidx] # Compute gradient for this Gaussian using stored alpha state and final pixel gradient # Exact derivative formula depends on the forward alpha blending equation gradg = gaussian.opacity alphastatebefore.accumulatedopacity pixelgradients[pidx] if gradients[gidx] is None: gradients[gidx] = gradg else: gradients[gidx] += gradg return gradients Parameters: Bucket Size: 32 Gaussians (one GPU warp), matching the checkpoint interval. Tile Size: Typically 16x16 pixels (256 pixels). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: VRAM Usage: This approach increases VRAM usage due to the storage of alpha blending states. Precision: Storing intermediate alpha states may introduce precision issues if not handled carefully. Empty Pixels: Pixels not covered by any Gaussian in a bucket should be skipped to avoid unnecessary computation. Dynamically switches between rasterization implementations during the backward pass to minimize atomic contention and maximize thread utilization. It sets itself apart from static backward strategies by using a Thompson sampling scheduler to select the fastest implementation based on measured latency. Choose it when scene complexity or hardware configuration causes significant performance variance across different backward pass implementations. Parallelizes gradient computation over Gaussians rather than pixels to reduce atomic contention. It sets itself apart from standard pixel-parallel backpropagation by operating on fixed-size buckets of 32 Gaussians (one GPU warp), allowing threads to collaboratively replay the alpha blending process using warp-level primitives. Choose it when warp stalls from global memory synchronization are the primary bottleneck. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of required atomic operations by a factor equal to the number of pixels in each tile (256 for 16x16 tiles). Memory Complexity: Increases VRAM usage. Performance: On Mip-NeRF360 outdoor scenes (RTX 4090), training time decreases from 16m56s to 14m14s (1.20x speedup over base), but VRAM increases from 6.33GiB to 7.69GiB (1.20x increase) and Gaussian count from 3.87M to 3.89M. On RTX 5090, training takes 163 seconds on average, a 5× improvement over the original implementation. Strengths: Significantly reduces warp stalls and false sharing during z-order sorting. Limitations: Increased VRAM usage. The Per-Gaussian Backward Pass was introduced by Mallick et al. [56] (cited in) to address the computational suboptimality of atomic operations in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting backpropagation. Faster-GS: Analyzing and Improving Gaussian Splatting Optimization, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09999v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Scheduling for Backward Pass Implementations
head: Rasterization backward with adaptive scheduling, Thompson sampling scheduler for backward pass
body: This method minimizes atomic contention and maximizes thread utilization during the 3D Gaussian Splatting backward pass by dynamically switching between two distinct rasterization implementations. It sets itself apart from static backward strategies by using a Thompson sampling scheduler to select the fastest implementation based on measured latency, addressing performance variance across different scenes and hardware configurations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Projected Gaussians binned to tiles, tile pixel count P, Gaussian count N, subgroup size, and latency belief distributions. Output: Accumulated gradients for Gaussian parameters. Data Structures: Latency Beliefs: Two Beta distributions storing the estimated latency performance for Implementation 1 and Implementation 2. Shared Memory: Used in Implementation 2 to store pre-computed transmittance and derivatives. Parameters: Batch Size (S): Chosen by rounding up \sqrt{NP} to a multiple of subgroup size, capped at 128, where N is the number of Gaussians and P is the number of pixels in the tile. Gaussian Parameterization: Follows [LDC 25] to simplify opacity computation into matrix multiplication. Steps: 1. Initialize Latency Beliefs: Initialize Beta distributions for the latency of Implementation 1 and Implementation 2. 2. Select Implementation: Sample from both distributions and select the implementation with the highest sample value. 3. Execute Selected Implementation: If Implementation 1 is selected: 1. Launch one thread block per tile. 2. Calculate dynamic Gaussian batch size S = \min(128, \lceil \sqrt{NP} / \text{subgroup\size} \rceil \times \text{subgroup\size}). 3. Process Gaussians in batches of size S for each tile. If Implementation 2 is selected: 1. For a Gaussian batch, run a forward pass parallelized over pixels. 2. Compute transmittance and its derivative with respect to Gaussian parameters for each Gaussian-pixel pair. 3. Store these values in shared memory. 4. Run a backward pass parallelized over Gaussians. 5. Fetch pre-computed transmittance and derivatives from shared memory. 6. Compute accumulated gradients. 4. Update Latency Beliefs: Measure the actual latency of the selected implementation. Update the corresponding Beta distribution parameters based on the measured latency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random import time def selectimplementation(latencybeliefs): """Select implementation using Thompson sampling.""" samples = [random.betavariate(alpha, beta) for alpha, beta in latencybeliefs] return samples.index(max(samples)) def updatebelief(latencybeliefs, selectedimpl, latency): """Update latency belief based on measured latency.""" # Standard Bayesian update for minimization: lower latency increases confidence (alpha) alpha, beta = latencybeliefs[selectedimpl] latencybeliefs[selectedimpl] = [alpha + 1.0 / latency, beta] def implementation1(tilegaussians, P, subgroupsize, maxbatchsize): """Implementation 1: One thread block per tile, dynamic batch size.""" N = len(tilegaussians) if N == 0: return sqrtnp = math.sqrt(N P) S = math.ceil(sqrtnp / subgroupsize) subgroupsize S = min(S, maxbatchsize) for i in range(0, N, S): batch = tilegaussians[i:i+S] # Process batch: compute gradients and atomically accumulate to global memory pass def implementation2(tilegaussians, P, subgroupsize, maxbatchsize): """Implementation 2: Forward pass over pixels, backward pass over Gaussians, shared memory.""" N = len(tilegaussians) if N == 0: return sqrtnp = math.sqrt(N P) S = math.ceil(sqrtnp / subgroupsize) subgroupsize S = min(S, maxbatchsize) sharedmemory = [] for i in range(0, N, S): batch = tilegaussians[i:i+S] # Forward pass parallelized over pixels: compute transmittance and derivatives per Gaussian-pixel pair, store in sharedmemory pass # Backward pass parallelized over Gaussians: fetch from sharedmemory, compute accumulated gradients pass def runadaptivebackward(tilegaussians, P, subgroupsize, maxbatchsize, latencybeliefs): """Main function to run adaptive backward pass.""" selectedimpl = selectimplementation(latencybeliefs) starttime = time.perfcounter() if selectedimpl == 0: implementation1(tilegaussians, P, subgroupsize, maxbatchsize) else: implementation2(tilegaussians, P, subgroupsize, maxbatchsize) endtime = time.perfcounter() latency = endtime - starttime updatebelief(latencybeliefs, selectedimpl, latency) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Tile boundaries are handled via branchless ellipse range functions during projection, not during scheduling. Degenerate Input: If a tile has no Gaussians, both implementations return immediately. A scheduling mechanism that jointly adjusts the tile-wise pixel sampling rate (r{tile}) and the number of sampled views (K) over training iterations to allocate more computation during difficult stages and reduce it as optimization converges. It sets itself apart from static sampling strategies by dynamically scaling the view budget and pixel density based on reconstruction error and training progress, achieving a trade-off between training speed and reconstruction quality. When to choose it: Not given in the sources. Cooperative Scheduling and Synchronization addresses idle resources and gradient contention caused by uneven tile lists, variable pixel traversal, and backward propagation accumulation. It sets itself apart from static mapping strategies by dynamically redistributing work and organizing computation to minimize global atomic updates, replacing them with local reductions or cache-cooperative operations. When to choose it: Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Implementation 1 latency is approximately proportional to \frac{P+S}{P} \times \frac{N+S}{S}. Implementation 2 complexity is not explicitly given but targets improved thread utilization and reduced divergence. Memory Complexity: Implementation 2 requires shared memory for transmittance and derivatives, constraining batch or tile size based on hardware limits. Measured Performance: On NVIDIA RTX 3090, Implementation 2 is 20%-30% faster on the Mip-NeRF 360 bicycle scene, while Implementation 1 is faster on the garden scene. Scaling: Automatically adapts to different scenes and hardware via the Thompson sampling scheduler. Strengths: Reduces atomic contention, maximizes thread utilization, and automatically selects the optimal implementation per context. Limitations: Thompson sampling adds minimal overhead; gains depend on scene-specific performance variance. When to Use: Training 3D Gaussian Splatting models where backward pass performance varies across scenes or hardware. When Not to Use: When a single implementation is consistently faster across all scenarios, or scheduling overhead outweighs gains. This method was introduced in "VkSplat: High-Performance 3DGS Training in Vulkan Compute". It addresses high atomic contention and subgroup reduction in existing 3DGS training implementations. Implementation 1 is inspired by [MGK 24], while the overall approach improves upon [KKLD23] and [YLK 25] by dynamically selecting the best backward strategy. VkSplat: High-Performance 3DGS Training in Vulkan Compute, https://doi.org/10.2312/egs.20261024, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive View and Pixel Sampling Scheduling
head: Adaptive Scheduling of View Budget and Pixel Sampling, Sampled view number scheduling, Tile-wise pixel sampling rate scheduling, query sampling schedule
body: A scheduling mechanism that jointly adjusts the tile-wise pixel sampling rate (r{tile}) and the number of sampled views (K) over training iterations to allocate more computation during difficult stages and reduce it as optimization converges. It sets itself apart from static sampling strategies by dynamically scaling the view budget and pixel density based on reconstruction error and training progress, achieving a trade-off between training speed and reconstruction quality. Inputs and outputs: Inputs: Current iteration t, initial mean view error \bar{E}{init}, current mean view error \bar{E}t, densification/pruning cutoff iteration \tau{until}, tile sampling scale \lambda, minimum/maximum view budgets K{min}, K{max}, transition speed \alpha, and minimum/maximum sampling rates r{min}, r{max}. Outputs: Tile-wise pixel sampling rate r{tile}^{(t)} and sampled view number Kt for the current iteration. Data structures: No persistent data structures are required beyond scalar values for error tracking and iteration counters. The scheduler computes values on-the-fly. Numbered steps: 1. Compute Error Ratio (rt): Calculate the normalized error ratio by clipping the square root of the ratio of current error to initial error. rt = \text{clip}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\bar{E}t}{\bar{E}{init} + \epsilon}}, 0, 1\right) where \epsilon is a small constant for numerical stability. 2. Compute Sinusoidal Modulation (\phi(rt)): Apply a sinusoidal function to amplify sampling variation in the low-error regime. \phi(rt) = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} rt\right) This modulation is chosen because reconstruction error drops rapidly in early training and remains in a narrow range later, making sinusoidal modulation more sensitive to subtle differences than linear or exponential variants. 3. Compute Progress Coefficient (\rhot): Determine the annealing factor based on training progress relative to the densification phase. \rhot = 1 - \text{clip}\left(\frac{t}{\tau{until}}, 0, 1\right) This coefficient gradually reduces sampling intensity after the densification and pruning phase is complete. 4. Compute Tile-wise Pixel Sampling Rate (r{tile}^{(t)}): r{tile}^{(t)} = r{min} + (r{max} - r{min}) \left(1 - \rhot \phi(rt)\right) where r{min} = \lambda / K{max} and r{max} = \lambda / K{min}. 5. Compute Sampled View Number (Kt): Kt = \text{round}\left(K{min} + (K{max} - K{min}) e^{-\alpha(1 - \rhot \phi(rt))}\right) This formula exponentially decays the view budget as the term (1 - \rhot \phi(rt)) increases, shifting from global multi-view consistency to local refinement. Parameters: \lambda: Tile sampling scale. Typical value not given in the sources. K{min}, K{max}: Minimum and maximum number of sampled views. The source uses a range of 10 \to 3 (i.e., K{max}=10, K{min}=3). \alpha: Controls the transition speed of the view budget scheduling. Value not given in the sources. \tau{until}: The last iteration for densification and pruning. Value not given in the sources. \bar{E}{init}: Initial mean view error. Computed at the start of training. \bar{E}t: Current mean view error at iteration t. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeschedulingparams( t: int, tauuntil: int, Et: float, Einit: float, lambdascale: float, Kmin: int, Kmax: int, alpha: float, epsilon: float = 1e-6) -> tuple[float, int]: """ Computes the tile-wise pixel sampling rate and sampled view number for the current training iteration. Args: t: Current training iteration. tauuntil: Iteration after which densification/pruning stops. Et: Current mean view error. Einit: Initial mean view error. lambdascale: Tile sampling scale. Kmin: Minimum number of sampled views. Kmax: Maximum number of sampled views. alpha: Transition speed control for view budget. epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability. Returns: (rtile, Kt): Tile-wise pixel sampling rate and sampled view number. """ # Step 1: Compute Error Ratio # Clip the square root of the error ratio to [0, 1] errorratioraw = math.sqrt(Et / (Einit + epsilon)) rt = max(0.0, min(1.0, errorratioraw)) # Step 2: Compute Sinusoidal Modulation phirt = math.sin(math.pi / 2 rt) # Step 3: Compute Progress Coefficient # Clip t / tauuntil to [0, 1], then subtract from 1 progressratio = max(0.0, min(1.0, t / tauuntil)) rhot = 1.0 - progressratio # Step 4: Compute Sampling Rate Bounds rmin = lambdascale / Kmax rmax = lambdascale / Kmin # Step 5: Compute Tile-wise Pixel Sampling Rate # rtile = rmin + (rmax - rmin) (1 - rhot phi(rt)) modulationfactor = 1.0 - rhot phirt rtile = rmin + (rmax - rmin) modulationfactor # Step 6: Compute Sampled View Number # Kt = round(Kmin + (Kmax - Kmin) exp(-alpha modulationfactor)) viewbudget = Kmin + (Kmax - Kmin) math.exp(-alpha modulationfactor) Kt = round(viewbudget) return rtile, Kt Edge cases and pitfalls: Very small view budget: Setting K=1 degrades performance due to insufficient multi-view constraints. Large fixed budget: Using a large fixed budget (e.g., K=10) increases training time without quality gains. Division by zero: Ensure \bar{E}{init} + \epsilon > 0 to prevent division by zero in the error ratio calculation. Negative sampling rate: The clipping in rt and \rhot ensures the modulation factor stays within bounds, but implementation should verify r{tile} \ge 0. Time Complexity: The scheduling computation itself is O(1) per iteration. However, the method reduces the total training time by reducing the number of sampled views and pixels in later stages. The source reports a reduction in training time from 81s (linear schedule) to 77s (sinusoidal schedule) while improving PSNR. Memory Complexity: No additional memory overhead compared to static sampling, as it only computes scalar values. Measured Performance: On the tested scenes, the sinusoidal schedule achieved a PSNR of 27.57, SSIM of 0.794, and LPIPS of 0.256, outperforming linear (PSNR 27.35) and exponential (PSNR 27.27) schedules. Scaling: The method scales by reducing computation as the model converges, making it more efficient for long training runs. Strengths: Improves sensitivity to subtle reconstruction differences in the low-error regime; achieves best trade-off between speed and quality by gradually shifting from global multi-view consistency to local refinement. Limitations: Requires tracking initial and current mean view errors; sensitive to the choice of \alpha and \tau{until}. When to use: When training 3D Gaussian Splatting models and seeking to accelerate convergence without sacrificing quality, particularly when reconstruction error dynamics are non-linear. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited in the early stages and multi-view consistency is critical (avoid K=1). The method was introduced in the paper "TurboGS: Accelerating 3D Gaussian Splatting via Error-Guided Sparse Pixel Sampling and Optimization". It addresses the inefficiency of fixed sampling rates in 3D Gaussian Splatting training, where early iterations require dense sampling for global consistency and later iterations benefit from sparse sampling for local refinement. The sinusoidal modulation was found to outperform linear and exponential variants based on ablation studies. name: Cooperative Scheduling and Synchronization
head: Cooperative Scheduling, Synchronization for Backward Pass
body: Cooperative Scheduling and Synchronization addresses idle resources and gradient contention caused by uneven tile lists, variable pixel traversal, and backward propagation accumulation. It sets itself apart from static mapping strategies by dynamically redistributing work and organizing computation to minimize global atomic updates, replacing them with local reductions or cache-cooperative operations, contrasting with Adaptive View and Pixel Sampling Scheduling which optimizes sampling patterns rather than compute scheduling. The core mechanism relies on two primary optimizations to handle the irregularity of 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization: 1. Dynamic Work Redistribution: Static mappings of Gaussians to tiles or pixels are prone to warp divergence due to footprint coverage and early termination. Cooperative scheduling dynamically assigns tiles or Gaussians to threads/warps to balance the load, ensuring that resources remain active even when the number of pairs (N{pair}) and evaluations (N{eval}) is unchanged. 2. Local Gradient Reduction: Backward propagation requires accumulating gradients from many pixels into each Gaussian. Instead of performing frequent global atomic updates, these methods organize computation to combine gradients locally (within a warp, tile, or Gaussian-centric block) before writing the final result back to global memory. This reduces global atomic contention. Redistributes work through dynamic tile assignment and enables Gaussian parallel rendering inside a warp. Not given in the sources. See Balanced 3DGS. Uses parameter hoisting, warp culling, and coherent blending to reuse data and coordinate pixel processing within tiles. Not given in the sources. See Local-GS. Combines warp reduction with cache cooperation to reduce global atomic updates and contention during backward propagation. Not given in the sources. See DISTWAR. Organizes backward computation around Gaussians, combining gradients before writing them back, replacing some global updates with local reduction. Not given in the sources. See Taming 3DGS. Combines a refined Gaussian-centric backward pass with a parameter layout that keeps spatially nearby Gaussians close in memory, reducing global updates and enabling more regular reads. Not given in the sources. See Faster-GS. The concept emerged as a response to the inefficiencies of static rasterization schedules in 3D Gaussian Splatting. Uneven tile lists and variable pixel traversal leave GPU resources idle. The approach was developed by multiple independent research groups to optimize both forward and backward passes: Balanced 3DGS [15] introduced dynamic tile assignment. Local-GS [62] focused on warp-level coordination. DISTWAR [17] targeted backward propagation contention. Taming 3DGS [63] reorganized backward computation around Gaussians. Faster-GS [64] optimized parameter layout for spatial locality. These methods are cited in the broader survey "From Splats to Silicon: Rethinking Computational Efficiency of 3DGS". From Splats to Silicon: Rethinking Computational Efficiency of 3DGS, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06157, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Per-Gaussian Backward
head: Bucket-based backward, Mallick et al. backward
body: Per-Gaussian Backward is a backward pass optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that parallelizes gradient computation over Gaussians rather than pixels to reduce atomic contention. It differs from standard pixel-parallel backpropagation by operating on fixed-size buckets of 32 Gaussians (one GPU warp), allowing threads to collaboratively replay the alpha blending process using warp-level primitives. This approach significantly reduces warp stalls that occur when threads synchronize while loading alpha blending states from global memory. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Forward pass buffers storing intermediate color and transmittance after every 32nd Gaussian, the final number of contributing Gaussians per pixel, Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity, color), and tile definitions. Outputs: Gradients for Gaussian attributes written to global memory. Data Structures: 1. Intermediate Buffers: Allocated during the forward pass to store per-pixel state. intermediatecolor[tileid][pixel]: Accumulated color after every 32nd Gaussian. intermediatetransmittance[tileid][pixel]: Accumulated transmittance after every 32nd Gaussian. contributingcount[tileid][pixel]: Final number of contributing Gaussians per pixel. Size: Determined by the known lengths of the per-tile Gaussian lists. 2. Bucket: A group of 32 Gaussians associated with a single tile. 3. Shared Memory Buffer: Used by a warp (32 threads) to store alpha blending states (color/transmittance pairs) for the current bucket's pixels before they are needed. Numbered Steps: 1. Forward Pass Buffer Population: During the forward rendering pass, after processing every 32nd Gaussian in a tile's list, write the current accumulated color and transmittance for all pixels in that tile into the intermediate buffers. Also, write the final count of contributing Gaussians per pixel. 2. Bucket Launch: For each tile, launch a kernel block where each thread block (warp) handles one bucket of 32 Gaussians. 3. Thread Assignment: In a warp of 32 threads, thread i (where i \in [0, 31]) is responsible for computing the gradient contribution of the i-th Gaussian in the bucket across all pixels in the associated tile. 4. Shared Memory Pre-loading: All 32 threads in the warp collaboratively load a batch of alpha blending states into shared memory (one per thread) before they are needed. From that point on, the first thread in each warp reads the next state directly from shared memory instead of global memory. 5. Gradient Replay: Starting from the initial color and transmittance values stored in the buffers (or loaded into shared memory), the warp replays the blending process using warp-level primitives to efficiently compute the necessary gradients. 6. Atomic Accumulation: Each thread writes the accumulated gradients to global memory using atomics, as Gaussians can be inside multiple buckets across tiles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def PerGaussianBackward(bucketgaussians, tileid, intermediatecolor, intermediatetransmittance, sharedmem, gradientsglobal): threadid = getthreadid() # standard CUDA/OpenCL primitive gauss = bucketgaussians[threadid] pixelindices = getpixelindicesforgaussian(gauss, tileid) # standard rasterization query # 1. Collaborative shared memory load for p in pixelindices: sharedmem[threadid][p] = (intermediatecolor[tileid][p], intermediatetransmittance[tileid][p]) syncthreads() # warp barrier to ensure all loads complete # 2. Gradient replay using warp-level primitives colorgrad = 0.0 transgrad = 0.0 for p in pixelindices: c, t = sharedmem[threadid][p] # Replay blending process to compute gradients # The sources do not specify the exact chain-rule implementation for alpha blending gradients. dc = computealphablendinggradient(gauss, p, c, t) # standard chain-rule computation colorgrad += dc # 3. Atomic accumulation to global memory gradientsglobal[gauss.id].position += gauss.positiongrad gradientsglobal[gauss.id].covariance += gauss.covariancegrad gradientsglobal[gauss.id].opacity += gauss.opacitygrad gradientsglobal[gauss.id].color += colorgrad Parameters: Bucket Size: 32 Gaussians (one warp). Tile Size: Typically 16x16 pixels (256 pixels per tile). Shared Memory Usage: 32 entries per warp, each entry containing color and transmittance for the relevant pixel range. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Warp Stalls: If threads are synchronized while the first thread loads alpha blending state from global memory, the entire warp stalls. This is mitigated by collaborative loading into shared memory. Multiple Tile Membership: A single Gaussian may contribute to multiple tiles. Therefore, gradient accumulation must use atomic operations in global memory. Buffer Size: The intermediate buffers must be sized according to the maximum number of 32-Gaussian buckets in any tile. This is determined by the per-tile Gaussian list lengths. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians, but with a significantly reduced constant factor due to warp-level parallelism and reduced global memory traffic. Memory Complexity: Additional memory for intermediate buffers: O(T \cdot B \cdot P) where T is the number of tiles, B is the average number of buckets per tile, and P is the number of pixels per tile. Performance: The shared memory optimization improves kernel runtime by up to 2x compared to the original Mallick et al. implementation. Strengths: Reduces atomic contention by parallelizing over Gaussians; minimizes global memory latency through shared memory usage; efficient use of warp-level primitives. Limitations: Requires additional memory for intermediate buffers; complex implementation due to warp-level synchronization and shared memory management; Gaussians spanning multiple tiles still require atomic writes. Per-Gaussian Backward was proposed by Mallick et al. [56] as a key optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting training. It was later analyzed and improved by the Faster-GS team, who introduced the shared memory optimization to reduce warp stalls. The method is part of the broader effort to make differentiable volume rendering and radiance field optimization computationally efficient. Faster-GS: Analyzing and Improving Gaussian Splatting Optimization, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09999v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: AbsGS
head: Absolute Positional Gradients, Absgrad, Absolute Gaussian Splatting, Homodirectional view-space positional gradient
body: AbsGS addresses the "over-reconstruction" artifact in 3D Gaussian Splatting, where large Gaussians in high-frequency regions fail to split, resulting in blurry rendering. It replaces the standard view-space positional gradient with a homodirectional gradient that sums the absolute values of pixel-wise sub-gradients, preventing gradient collision where positive and negative components cancel each other out. Unlike standard 3D-GS, which requires lowering the densification threshold to catch these errors (causing memory overflow), AbsGS accurately identifies over-reconstructed Gaussians using fewer primitives, achieving higher quality with roughly half the memory consumption. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The standard 3D Gaussian Splatting training state (Gaussian parameters, camera poses, loss gradients \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{C}}) and the rasterization metadata (pixel coverage). Output: Updated Gaussian parameters after back-propagation, with densification decisions (split/clone) guided by the homodirectional gradient. Data Structures: The method modifies the gradient accumulation step within the backward pass. For each Gaussian Gi, a scalar value \hat{g}i (homodirectional gradient magnitude) is computed. This value is stored alongside the standard gradients. The parent article Gradient Computation and Back-Propagation defines the standard gradient tensor layout; AbsGS adds or replaces the magnitude check logic for the position parameters \mu. Parameters: Scale threshold (\tauS): Controls the maximum allowed scale for Gaussians to be eligible for splitting. Typical values tested: 0.01 and 0.001. Lowering \tauS improves quality but increases memory usage. Gradient threshold (\taup): The threshold for the homodirectional gradient to trigger a split. Since AbsGS yields larger gradient magnitudes than standard 3D-GS, \taup can be set higher than in standard 3D-GS to avoid noise. Typical value: 0.0008. absgrad flag: A boolean API flag to enable the absolute gradient accumulation in the rasterization call. Algorithm Steps: 1. Forward Pass: Render the image using standard differentiable rasterization [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md]. 2. Loss Computation: Compute the loss L between the rendered image and the ground truth. AbsGS may optionally use a high-pass filter on the residual before back-propagation to sharpen edges, though the core contribution is the gradient metric. 3. Back-Propagation: Compute the loss gradients with respect to the Gaussian parameters. Specifically, obtain the pixel-wise sub-gradients of the loss with respect to the view-space position \mu{i,x} and \mu{i,y} for all pixels j covered by Gaussian Gi. 4. Homodirectional Gradient Accumulation: For each Gaussian Gi, compute the homodirectional gradient \hat{g}i by summing the absolute values of the x and y components of the sub-gradients separately: \hat{g}i = \sum{j=1}^{m} \left( \left| \frac{\partial Lj}{\partial \mu{i,x}} \right| + \left| \frac{\partial Lj}{\partial \mu{i,y}} \right| \right) where m is the number of pixels covered by Gi. This avoids the cancellation effect of signed summation. 5. Densification Decision: Split: If Gi's scale exceeds \tauS AND \hat{g}i > \taup, select Gi for splitting. Clone: If Gi's opacity is below a threshold, select Gi for cloning. AbsGS recommends using the standard gradient (not homodirectional) for cloning decisions to follow the original 3D-GS strategy. 6. Update: Perform the split/clone operations and update parameters via optimizer step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computehomodirectionalgradient(gaussians, pixelgradients, coveragemask): """ Compute the homodirectional view-space positional gradient for each Gaussian. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives. pixelgradients: Tensor of shape (numpixels, 2) containing (dL/dmux, dL/dmuy) for each pixel. coveragemask: Sparse matrix or list of lists mapping each Gaussian to the indices of pixels it covers. Returns: homodirectionalgrads: Tensor of shape (numgaussians,) containing the sum of absolute sub-gradients for each Gaussian. """ numgaussians = len(gaussians) homodirectionalgrads = torch.zeros(numgaussians) for i in range(numgaussians): coveredpixelindices = coveragemask[i] if len(coveredpixelindices) == 0: continue # Get sub-gradients for covered pixels # pixelgradients[coveredpixelindices] has shape (m, 2) subgrads = pixelgradients[coveredpixelindices] # Sum absolute values of x and y components separately absdx = torch.sum(torch.abs(subgrads[:, 0])) absdy = torch.sum(torch.abs(subgrads[:, 1])) homodirectionalgrads[i] = absdx + absdy return homodirectionalgrads def densificationstep(gaussians, homodirectionalgrads, scalethreshold, gradthreshold): """ Determine which Gaussians to split based on homodirectional gradients. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives with 'scale' and 'opacity' attributes. homodirectionalgrads: Tensor of homodirectional gradient magnitudes. scalethreshold: Maximum scale allowed for splitting (tauS). gradthreshold: Gradient threshold for splitting (taup). Returns: splitindices: List of indices of Gaussians to split. """ splitindices = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): # Check scale constraint if g.scale > scalethreshold: # Check homodirectional gradient threshold if homodirectionalgrads[i] > gradthreshold: splitindices.append(i) return splitindices Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Collision: In standard 3D-GS, large Gaussians covering many pixels often have sub-gradients with mixed signs (positive and negative) in the view space. Summing these signed values leads to cancellation, resulting in a small total gradient that fails to exceed the densification threshold. AbsGS mitigates this by using absolute values. Memory Overflow: Simply lowering the gradient threshold \taup in standard 3D-GS to fix over-reconstruction is impractical. It selects many unnecessary Gaussians (noise), leading to significant memory consumption. On a single V100 GPU, lowering \taup below 0.0001 results in out-of-CUDA-memory errors. Clone vs. Split: AbsGS uses homodirectional gradients only for splitting. Cloning should follow the original 3D-GS strategy using standard gradients to maintain stability. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: AbsGS uses roughly half the memory of standard 3D-GS for comparable quality. This is because it avoids the explosion of Gaussians caused by lowering the threshold in standard 3D-GS. Time: The additional computation for absolute value summation is negligible compared to the rasterization and back-propagation steps. The reduction in the number of Gaussians can lead to faster training convergence and less memory pressure. Measured Performance: Mip-NeRF360: AbsGS-0004 (\tauS=0.01, \taup=0.0008) achieves SSIM 0.817, PSNR 27.38, LPIPS 0.212, Memory 374MB. AbsGS-0008 (\tauS=0.001, \taup=0.0008) achieves SSIM 0.815, PSNR 27.41, LPIPS 0.211, Memory 450MB. Tanks & Temples: AbsGS-0004 achieves SSIM 0.842, PSNR 23.64, LPIPS 0.190, Memory 159MB. AbsGS-0008 achieves SSIM 0.845, PSNR 23.54, LPIPS 0.183, Memory 202MB. Deep Blending: AbsGS-0004 achieves SSIM 0.902, PSNR 29.55, LPIPS 0.249, Memory 265MB. AbsGS-0008 achieves SSIM 0.903, PSNR 29.69, LPIPS 0.241, Memory 380MB. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Recovers fine details and sharpens edges in high-frequency regions. Reduces over-reconstruction artifacts. More memory-efficient than threshold-lowering strategies in 3D-GS. Easy to implement as a drop-in replacement for the gradient accumulation step. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \tauS and \taup. The absolute value operation may be less sensitive to the direction of error, potentially leading to over-splitting in some specific noise patterns if thresholds are not set correctly. AbsGS was introduced in the paper "AbsGS: Recovering Fine Details in 3D Gaussian Splatting". It builds upon the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework [17365-3d-gaussian-splatting.md] and addresses a specific flaw in its adaptive density control strategy: gradient collision. The method was developed to improve novel view synthesis quality, particularly for scenes with fine details like vegetation and textured surfaces, where standard 3D-GS tends to produce blurry results due to large, unsplit Gaussians. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) gsplat: An Open-Source Library for Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2409.06765, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) AbsGS: Recovering Fine Details in 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/3664647.3681361, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Gradient-Weighted Feature Back-Projection
head: Back-Projection Equation, Expected Feature Back-Projection, FBP, Feature Back-Projection
body: Gradient-Weighted Feature Back-Projection is a training-free method for feature field rendering in 3D Gaussian Splatting that back-projects 2D features into pre-trained 3D Gaussians using a weighted sum based on each Gaussian's influence (opacity and transmittance) in the final rendering. It aggregates 2D feature embeddings from training views into 3D Gaussian features by weighting the contribution of each Gaussian based on its influence on the rendered pixel, avoiding the need for distillation or feature field training. Compared to training-based alternatives like Feature 3DGS, which require iterative optimization of feature parameters, this method computes features in a single pass using the rendering gradients as weights, achieving a 10x speedup while maintaining high-quality 3D segmentation results. The method leverages the differentiable nature of the alpha-compositing equation to determine the influence of each Gaussian on the final rendered image. It back-projects 2D features (e.g., from LSeg or DINOv2) into 3D space by weighting the contribution of each Gaussian based on its opacity and transmittance. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians with fixed parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color) obtained from a standard 3DGS reconstruction. A set of V training views, each with a corresponding 2D feature map \mathbf{F}{2D} generated by a pre-trained model (e.g., LSeg or DINOv2). The camera parameters for each training view. Outputs: A feature vector \mathbf{f}k \in \mathbb{R}^D for each Gaussian k, where D is the feature dimension. Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian k stores its 3D feature vector \mathbf{f}k. Initially, this is zero. 2D Feature Map: For each view n, a 2D array \mathbf{F}{2D}(x, y, n) of shape H \times W \times D, where H, W are image dimensions. 1. Render and Compute Gradients: For each training view n: Render the scene using the current Gaussian parameters to obtain the rendered color \mathbf{C}n(x, y) and depth/alpha information. The rendering follows the standard alpha-compositing equation: \mathbf{C}n(x, y) = \sum{k=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}k \alphak(x, y, n) Tk(x, y, n) where \mathbf{c}k is the color of the k-th Gaussian, \alphak(x, y, n) is its opacity at pixel (x, y) in view n, and Tk(x, y, n) is the transmittance up to the k-th Gaussian: Tk(x, y, n) = \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphaj(x, y, n)) Compute the gradient of the rendered color with respect to the k-th Gaussian's color \mathbf{c}k. This gradient serves as the weight for back-projection: \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}n(x, y)}{\partial \mathbf{c}k} = \alphak(x, y, n) Tk(x, y, n) Let wk(x, y, n) = \alphak(x, y, n) Tk(x, y, n). 2. Accumulate Features: For each Gaussian k, accumulate the weighted 2D features from all views n where the Gaussian contributes to the pixel. Expected Feature Back-Projection (Normalized): \mathbf{f}k = \frac{\sum{n} \sum{(x,y) \in \text{pixels}} \mathbf{F}{2D}(x, y, n) wk(x, y, n)}{\sum{n} \sum{(x,y) \in \text{pixels}} wk(x, y, n)} Accumulated Feature Back-Projection (Unnormalized): \mathbf{f}k = \sum{n} \sum{(x,y) \in \text{pixels}} \mathbf{F}{2D}(x, y, n) wk(x, y, n) Note: If Euclidean normalization is applied to \mathbf{f}k after calculation, the normalized and unnormalized variants become equivalent. 3. Pruning: Calculate the numerator of the back-projection equation for each Gaussian. If the numerator is zero (indicating no influence on any screen pixel), prune the Gaussian or mark it as invalid to avoid division by zero or irrelevant data during inference. 4. Completion: The back-projection is completed in a single pass through all training views. No iterative optimization is required. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gradientweightedfeaturebackprojection(gaussians, views, D): """ gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: position (3,) scale (3,) rotation (4,) opacity (scalar) color (3,) feature (D,) # To be filled views: List of view dictionaries with attributes: cameraparams gtfeatures (H, W, D) # Pre-computed by featuremodel D: Integer, feature dimension. """ # Initialize accumulators for g in gaussians: g.featuresum = [0.0] D g.weightsum = 0.0 # Step 1 & 2: Render and Accumulate for view in views: # Forward pass computes alphak(x,y) and Tk(x,y) for each Gaussian at each pixel. # In practice, this is done via a tile-and-bin rasterization pipeline. # weights[k][y][x] = alphak(x,y) Tk(x,y) weights = computerenderingweights(gaussians, view.cameraparams, view.resolution) for k, g in enumerate(gaussians): w = weights[k] F2D = view.gtfeatures H, W, = F2D.shape for y in range(H): for x in range(W): alphaT = w[y][x] if alphaT > 0: for d in range(D): g.featuresum[d] += alphaT F2D[y][x][d] g.weightsum += alphaT # Step 3: Normalize and Prune for g in gaussians: if g.weightsum > 0: for d in range(D): g.feature[d] = g.featuresum[d] / g.weightsum else: g.feature = None g.ispruned = True return gaussians def computerenderingweights(gaussians, cameraparams, resolution): # Computes alphak(x,y) Tk(x,y) for all Gaussians and pixels. # The sources do not provide the rasterization implementation details. # This function projects 3D Gaussians to 2D, evaluates the Gaussian PDF, # and computes transmittance based on depth sorting. pass Feature Model: Pre-trained models such as LSeg or DINOv2 are used to generate \mathbf{F}{2D}. Rasterizer: The gsplat library is used for rendering. Hardware: Experiments are performed on NVIDIA A6000 GPU. Zero Influence: If a Gaussian has no influence on any pixel (numerator is zero), it should be pruned before inference to prevent division by zero or irrelevant data. Normalization: The normalized (expected) and unnormalized (accumulated) variants are equivalent if Euclidean normalization is applied to the result. This variant uses the back-projected features for semantic segmentation. It obtains feature vectors \{\mathbf{f}k\} \in \mathbb{R}^D for each Gaussian. A query embedding \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^D is extracted from a language query or another modality. Segmentation is performed by computing the similarity sim(\mathbf{f}k, \mathbf{q}) (typically cosine similarity) and thresholding: G = \{gk \mid \text{sim}(\mathbf{f}k, \mathbf{q}) > \theta\}, where \theta is a user-defined threshold. 2D segmentation masks are derived similarly by querying rendered 2D features. This variant encodes each object with a unique vector and back-projects these vectors into the 3D scene. Two approaches are used: 1. Orthogonal Encoding: Procedurally generated orthogonal vectors are assigned to objects to maximize separation. This is limited by the embedding dimension D. 2. Contrastive Encoding: Non-orthogonal vectors are made distinct through contrastive learning, which maximizes distance between different objects. The loss function is \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{classification}} + \mathcal{L}{\text{orthogonality}}, where \mathcal{L}{\text{classification}} = \text{CrossEntropy}(\hat{y}, y) and \mathcal{L}{\text{orthogonality}} = \|\mathbf{E}\mathbf{E}^T - \mathbf{I}\|F. This variant transfers annotated regions from source images to a target object. DINOv2 features are transferred to the target scene via back-projection. The closest matching source annotation for each Gaussian is identified by performing k-nearest neighbors (kNN) classification on the feature space. Time Complexity: The method requires a single pass through all training views. The feature back-projection process, including ground truth feature map generation, takes an average of 2–3 minutes. Inference Speed: Object segmentation (including text encoding and similarity calculation) takes 30 ms. Similarity calculation alone takes less than 1 ms. Speedup: The method achieves a 900x speedup compared to segmentation using masked gradients. It is 10x faster than Feature 3DGS (2.5 mins vs 20–30 mins for 7000 iterations) because it does not train a feature field. Memory: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Training-free, fast, scalable, high-quality 3D segmentation. Limitations: Requires pre-trained 3D Gaussians and 2D feature maps from training views. Performance depends on the quality of the 2D feature model. The method was introduced by Bharadwaj Amrutur and Shalabh Bhatnagar from the Indian Institute of Science. It addresses the limitations of training-based feature field rendering methods, which often perform poorly at 3D segmentation without post-processing. The approach leverages the gradient of the rendering equation to weight feature contributions, providing a computationally efficient alternative to distillation or feature field training. Gradient-Weighted Feature Back-Projection: A Fast Alternative to Feature Distillation in 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/3757377.3763926, fetched 2026-10-27

name: SNS Backward Pass with Intermediate Variable Q
head: SNS Gradient Computation, Skew-Normal 2D Gradient Computation
body: The SNS Backward Pass with Intermediate Variable Q computes exact gradients for 3D Skew-Normal Splatting (SNS) parameters by decoupling the complex interaction between rotation and scale matrices. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), which computes gradients with respect to the inverse covariance matrix \Omega^{-1} before backpropagating to rotation R and scale S, this method introduces an intermediate variable Q = ARS to reformulate the 2D Skew-Normal density. This allows for direct, closed-form gradient computation of the skew parameter k, the mean \mu, and the shape matrix Q, avoiding the high computational complexity of differentiating the coupled RS terms directly. The backward pass follows the standard 3DGS architecture, divided into a rendering stage and a preprocessing stage. The rendering stage evaluates shared auxiliary algebraic terms, and the preprocessing stage uses these terms to compute exact gradients for 3D learnable parameters using derived closed-form expressions. Inputs: Loss gradient w.r.t. rendered color: \frac{\partial L}{\partial C} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (per pixel). 2D pixel coordinate: u \in \mathbb{R}^2. 2D mean: \mu^{2D} \in \mathbb{R}^2. Intermediate shape matrix: Q \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}, where Q = ARS (A is projection, R rotation, S scale). Skew parameter: k \in \mathbb{R}^2. Opacity: o \in \mathbb{R}. Color: c \in \mathbb{R}^3. Transmittance up to previous Gaussian: T{k-1} = \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - aj(u)). Opacity gradient: \frac{\partial L}{\partial a}, computed by the standard alpha-compositing backward pass over sorted Gaussians. Outputs: Gradients: \frac{\partial L}{\partial c}, \frac{\partial L}{\partial o}, \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mu}, \frac{\partial L}{\partial Q}, \frac{\partial L}{\partial k}. Let \Delta = u - \mu^{2D} \in \mathbb{R}^2. Let \Omega^{2D} = Q Q^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2} be the 2D covariance matrix. Let G2(\Delta; \Omega^{2D}) = \frac{1}{2\pi \sqrt{\det(\Omega^{2D})}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} \Delta^\top (\Omega^{2D})^{-1} \Delta\right) be the standard 2D Gaussian component. Let \Phi(z) = \frac{1}{2} \left[ 1 + \text{erf}\left(\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \right] be the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution. Let m = m^{2D} = \frac{(\Omega^{2D})^{-1} Q k}{\sqrt{1 + k^\top k - k^\top Q^\top (\Omega^{2D})^{-1} Q k}} \in \mathbb{R}^2. Let D = \sqrt{1 + k^\top k - k^\top Q^\top (\Omega^{2D})^{-1} Q k}. The 2D Skew-Normal density is: SN^{2D}(u) = G2(\Delta; \Omega^{2D}) \cdot \Phi(m^\top \Delta) The opacity is a(u) = o \cdot SN^{2D}(u). To simplify gradient expressions, four auxiliary variables are computed in the rendering stage: 1. c\Delta = \Phi \cdot G2 \cdot (\Omega^{2D})^{-1} \Delta \in \mathbb{R}^2 2. M\Delta = \Phi \cdot G2 \cdot ((\Omega^{2D})^{-1} \Delta) ((\Omega^{2D})^{-1} \Delta)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2} 3. s\Delta = \frac{G2}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} (m^\top \Delta)^2 \right) \in \mathbb{R} 4. p\Delta = \frac{G2}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} (m^\top \Delta)^2 \right) \cdot (\Omega^{2D})^{-1} \Delta \in \mathbb{R}^2 1. Compute Gradient w.r.t. Skew-Normal Density: The gradient \frac{\partial L}{\partial a} is provided by the standard compositing backward pass. \frac{\partial L}{\partial SN^{2D}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial a} \cdot o 2. Compute Gradient w.r.t. Mean \mu^{2D}: Using the auxiliary variables c\Delta and s\Delta: \frac{\partial SN^{2D}}{\partial \mu^{2D}} = c\Delta - s\Delta \cdot m \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mu^{2D}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial SN^{2D}} \cdot \frac{\partial SN^{2D}}{\partial \mu^{2D}} 3. Compute Gradient w.r.t. Skew Parameter k: Using auxiliary variables p\Delta, m, k, Q, \Omega^{2D}, and scalar D: \frac{\partial SN^{2D}}{\partial k} = \frac{1}{D} Q^\top \left( p\Delta + (p\Delta^\top \Omega^{2D} m) \cdot m \right) - \frac{1}{D^2} \cdot (p\Delta^\top \Omega^{2D} m) \cdot k \frac{\partial L}{\partial k} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial SN^{2D}} \cdot \frac{\partial SN^{2D}}{\partial k} 4. Compute Gradient w.r.t. Shape Matrix Q: Using auxiliary variables M\Delta, p\Delta, m, k, Q, and scalar D: \frac{\partial SN^{2D}}{\partial Q} = \left( M\Delta - p\Delta m^\top - m p\Delta^\top - (p\Delta^\top \Omega^{2D} m) \cdot m m^\top \right) Q + \frac{1}{D} \left( p\Delta + (p\Delta^\top \Omega^{2D} m) \cdot m \right) k^\top \frac{\partial L}{\partial Q} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial SN^{2D}} \cdot \frac{\partial SN^{2D}}{\partial Q} 5. Compute Gradient w.r.t. Color c and Opacity o: \frac{\partial L}{\partial c} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial C} \cdot a(u) \cdot T{k-1} \frac{\partial L}{\partial o} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial C} \cdot SN^{2D}(u) \cdot T{k-1} 6. Map Q Gradients to R and S (Preprocessing Stage): Since Q = ARS, and A is constant, gradients w.r.t R and S are derived from \frac{\partial L}{\partial Q}. \frac{\partial L}{\partial S} = A^\top \frac{\partial L}{\partial Q} R^\top \frac{\partial L}{\partial R} = A^\top \frac{\partial L}{\partial Q} S^\top (Exact mapping depends on the parameterization of R and S; if R is a quaternion or axis-angle, further chain rule steps are required.) Returns: gradc, grado, gradmu, gradQ, gradk """ # 1. Basic quantities Delta = u - mu2d # Shape (2,) Omega2D = Q @ Q.T # Shape (2, 2) Omegainv = np.linalg.inv(Omega2D) # Gaussian component G2 detOmega = np.linalg.det(Omega2D) exponent = -0.5 (Delta @ Omegainv @ Delta) G2 = (1.0 / (2.0 np.pi np.sqrt(detOmega))) np.exp(exponent) # Skew term m numeratorm = Omegainv @ Q @ k Dsquared = 1.0 + k.T @ k - k.T @ Q.T @ Omegainv @ Q @ k D = np.sqrt(Dsquared) m = numeratorm / D # Phi(m^T Delta) z = m.T @ Delta Phi = 0.5 (1.0 + math.erf(z / math.sqrt(2.0))) # 2. Auxiliary Variables v = Omegainv @ Delta cdelta = Phi G2 v Mdelta = Phi G2 np.outer(v, v) sdelta = (G2 / math.sqrt(2.0 np.pi)) np.exp(-0.5 z2) pdelta = sdelta v # 3. Gradient w.r.t SN2D dLdSN2D = dLda o # 4. Gradient w.r.t mu2d dSN2Ddmu = cdelta - sdelta m gradmu = dLdSN2D dSN2Ddmu # 5. Gradient w.r.t k termpOmm = np.dot(pdelta, Omega2D @ m) term1 = pdelta + termpOmm m gradk = dLdSN2D ((1.0 / D) (Q.T @ term1) - (1.0 / D2) termpOmm k) # 6. Gradient w.r.t Q termmm = termpOmm np.outer(m, m) matrixpart = Mdelta - np.outer(pdelta, m) - np.outer(m, pdelta) - termmm gradQ = dLdSN2D (matrixpart @ Q + (1.0 / D) np.outer(term1, k)) # 7. Gradient w.r.t c and o SN2Dval = G2 Phi aval = o SN2Dval gradc = gradLC aval Tprev grado = gradLC SN2Dval Tprev return gradc, grado, gradmu, gradQ, gradk Singularity in D: If D \approx 0, the division by D and D^2 in gradients for k and Q becomes unstable. This occurs when 1 + k^\top k - k^\top Q^\top (\Omega^{2D})^{-1} Q k \approx 0. A small epsilon should be added to D or D^2 for numerical stability. Covariance Inversion: (\Omega^{2D})^{-1} must be computed stably. If \Omega^{2D} is near-singular, use a regularized inverse or SVD-based inversion. Sign of \mu Gradient: The derivation \frac{\partial \Delta}{\partial \mu^{2D}} = -I is critical. The final formula c\Delta - s\Delta m already incorporates this sign. Implementers must ensure they do not negate it again. Batching: The pseudocode assumes a single pixel. For batched rendering, operations must be vectorized (e.g., using np.einsum or batched matrix multiplications). Time Complexity: The auxiliary variables require O(1) operations per Gaussian per pixel (matrix inversions are 2 \times 2). The gradient computations are also O(1). This is comparable to standard 3DGS but avoids the iterative or complex chain-rule steps for R and S inversion. Memory Complexity: Requires storing auxiliary variables c\Delta, M\Delta, s\Delta, p\Delta per Gaussian per pixel during the rendering stage. This is slightly higher than standard 3DGS but allows for efficient reuse in the preprocessing stage. Strengths: Decouples R and S optimization, leading to more stable gradients for shape parameters. Provides closed-form solutions for skew parameter k, which is absent in standard 3DGS. Limitations: Requires careful handling of the skew parameter k and the intermediate variable Q. The complexity of the gradient expressions for Q is higher than standard 3DGS covariance gradients. The SNS (Skew-Normal Splatting) method was introduced to address the limitations of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting in modeling asymmetric shapes. Standard 3DGS uses symmetric 2D Gaussians, which cannot capture skewness. The SNS method introduces a 2D Skew-Normal distribution. The backward pass with intermediate variable Q was proposed to simplify the gradient computation for the shape parameters (rotation and scale) which are coupled in the covariance matrix. This approach was detailed in the paper "3D Skew-Normal Splatting". 3D Skew-Normal Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.15010, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Specular-Aware Gradient Gating
head: Partial stop-gradient mechanism for transmission
body: Specular-Aware Gradient Gating is a training optimization technique for differentiable Gaussian splatting that suppresses specular reflection artifacts while preserving transmission details in semi-transparent scenes. It differs from standard back-propagation by modulating the gradients of the transmission color component using a local variance-based gating factor, ensuring the forward pass remains unchanged. The method addresses the conflict in differentiable rendering where gradients from specular reflections often corrupt the learning of transmission components, leading to visual artifacts. It operates on the transmission color \mathbf{C}{\text{trans}} during the backward pass of the alpha-compositing pipeline. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Original transmission color \mathbf{C}{\text{trans}} (per pixel or per Gaussian contribution), gating strength hyperparameter k. Output: Gated transmission color \tilde{\mathbf{C}}{\text{trans}} used for gradient computation. Data Structures: \mathbf{C}{\text{trans}}: Tensor of color values (e.g., RGB). g: Scalar gating factor per pixel/region, derived from local variance. Steps: 1. Calculate Local Variance: Compute the variance of the transmission color \mathbf{C}{\text{trans}} within a 3 \times 3 spatial window. Let this variance be \sigma^2. 2. Compute Gating Factor: Calculate the gating factor g using the variance \sigma^2 and the hyperparameter k. The specific functional form mapping \sigma^2 and k to g is not detailed in the provided text. 3. Apply Partial Stop-Gradient: Compute the gated color \tilde{\mathbf{C}}{\text{trans}} using the formula below. Formula: \tilde{\mathbf{C}}{\text{trans}} = (1 - g)\cdot \texttt{sg}(\mathbf{C}{\text{trans}}) + g\cdot \mathbf{C}{\text{trans}} where: \texttt{sg}(\cdot) is the stop-gradient operator, which returns the input value but blocks gradient flow during back-propagation. g is the gating factor. \mathbf{C}{\text{trans}} is the original transmission color. \tilde{\mathbf{C}}{\text{trans}} is the value used for final composition and gradient calculation. Implementation Note: The operation ensures that \tilde{\mathbf{C}}{\text{trans}} \equiv \mathbf{C}{\text{trans}} during the forward pass, preventing visual artifacts, while scaling the backward gradients by g. In a deep learning framework, this is implemented by creating a new tensor for the backward pass where gradients are masked by g. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def specularawaregradientgating(Ctrans, k, windowsize=3): """ Applies specular-aware gradient gating to transmission color. Args: Ctrans: Tensor of transmission colors (H, W, C). k: Gating strength hyperparameter (float). windowsize: Size of the local variance window (int). Returns: Ctransgated: Tensor for backward pass with modulated gradients. """ # 1. Calculate local variance using a 3x3 window # Standard spatial variance calculation over the window localmean = spatialmean(Ctrans, windowsize) localmeansq = spatialmean(Ctrans 2, windowsize) sigmasq = localmeansq - localmean 2 # 2. Compute gating factor g based on variance and k # Exact formula from Eq. (5) is not provided in sources g = sigmasq / (sigmasq + k) # Placeholder mapping g = max(0.0, min(1.0, g)) # Clamp to [0, 1] # 3. Apply partial stop-gradient # Forward pass: identical to original transmission # Backward pass: gradients scaled by g Ctransgated = (1 - g) Ctrans.detach() + g Ctrans return Ctransgated def spatialmean(tensor, windowsize): # Standard spatial averaging operation # Implemented via convolution with a uniform kernel or pooling pass Parameters: k: Gating strength hyperparameter. Typical value: 4. Window size: 3 \times 3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Forward Pass Consistency: It is critical that the forward pass output \tilde{\mathbf{C}}{\text{trans}} is identical to \mathbf{C}{\text{trans}} to avoid visual artifacts. Gradient Scaling: The mechanism only affects the backward pass, scaling gradients by g. Missing Formula: The exact equation for g (Eq. 5) is not provided in the sources, requiring implementation inference or reference to the original paper. Performance: The method peaks at k=4, offering an optimal trade-off between suppressing specular artifacts and preserving transmission details. Scope: Evaluated on transparent regions across eight scenes. Limitations: The exact functional form of the gating factor calculation (Eq. 5) is not detailed in the provided sources, making full reproducibility dependent on external references. Specular-Aware Gradient Gating is part of the RT-Splatting method, which jointly models reflection and transmission with Gaussian Splatting. It was introduced to address the failure of baseline methods to simultaneously reconstruct surface reflections and transmission behind the surface. name: Deferred Back-propagation
head: Deferred Back-propagation for Generalizable Gaussians, Deferred Gradient Computation, Patch-wise Gradient Accumulation
body: Deferred Back-propagation is a memory-efficient training technique that enables the optimization of radiance fields and Gaussian splats using full-resolution image losses (such as CNN-based style losses or global attention mechanisms) despite limited GPU memory. It solves the problem where standard differentiable rendering is too memory-intensive for full-resolution images, forcing a trade-off between resolution and the ability to compute complex, non-pixel-wise losses. Unlike sparse pixel sampling, which fails for global losses, or naive cropping, which breaks global consistency, DBP separates the forward pass from the backward pass, allowing full-resolution rendering without gradients followed by patch-wise re-rendering with gradients. The method decouples the high-memory forward rendering pass from the backward gradient computation pass. It operates in two distinct stages per optimization step: a forward-only pass to generate the full-resolution image, and a patch-wise re-rendering pass to compute gradients. Inputs: Scene parameters (e.g., Gaussian attributes: position, covariance, color, opacity; or NeRF weights), camera poses, and a loss function L that depends on the full-resolution rendered image \mathbf{I}. Outputs: Updated scene parameters after gradient accumulation. Rendered Image Buffer (\mathbf{I}): A full-resolution image tensor (e.g., H \times W \times 3) storing the color values from the forward pass. Cached Gradient Buffer (\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{I}}): A tensor of the same shape as \mathbf{I}, storing the gradient of the loss with respect to the pixel colors. Patch Grid: The image is conceptually or explicitly divided into M \times M patches. 1. Forward Pass (No Gradients): Render the full-resolution image \mathbf{I} from the current scene parameters and camera poses. Auto-differentiation is disabled during this pass to minimize memory usage. 2. Loss Computation: Compute the loss L(\mathbf{I}) using the full-resolution image \mathbf{I}. Calculate the gradient of the loss with respect to the image pixels, \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{I}}, and cache this gradient tensor. 3. Patch-wise Re-rendering: Iterate over each patch p in the image grid: a. Define the spatial bounds of patch p. b. Re-render the pixels within patch p using the same scene parameters and camera poses, but with auto-differentiation enabled. c. Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the scene parameters \theta for this patch using the chain rule: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} \bigg|p = \sum{\mathbf{x} \in \text{patch } p} \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{I}(\mathbf{x})} \frac{\partial \mathbf{I}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \theta} where \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{I}(\mathbf{x})} is retrieved from the cached gradient buffer. d. Accumulate \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} \big|p into the global gradient buffer for \theta. 4. Parameter Update: Apply the accumulated gradients to update the scene parameters. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def deferredbackprop(sceneparams, cameraposes, lossfn, patchh, patchw, imgh, imgw, lr): """ sceneparams: Current scene parameters (Gaussians/NeRF weights) cameraposes: Camera poses for the current view lossfn: Function that takes an image and returns (loss, gradwrtimage) patchh, patchw: Height and width of each patch imgh, imgw: Full image height and width lr: Learning rate scalar """ # Stage 1: Forward pass without gradients fullimage = render(sceneparams, cameraposes, enablegrad=False) loss, gradimage = lossfn(fullimage) # Stage 2: Patch-wise re-rendering with gradients gradparams = zeroslike(sceneparams) for y in range(0, imgh, patchh): for x in range(0, imgw, patchw): yend = min(y + patchh, imgh) xend = min(x + patchw, imgw) patchgrad = gradimage[y:yend, x:xend,:] with torch.enablegrad(): # render is defined in the parent article [18365-3d-gaussian-splatting-backward-pass.md] patchimage = render(sceneparams, cameraposes, enablegrad=True, crop=(y, yend, x, xend)) localgrad = computegradients(patchimage, sceneparams, gradoutputs=patchgrad) gradparams += localgrad sceneparams -= lr gradparams return sceneparams Patch Size: Determines the trade-off between memory usage and overhead, with patches sized to fit within GPU memory limits during the differentiable re-rendering pass. Number of Patches (M \times M): In, the image is split into M \times M patches to maintain consistency with global self-attention mechanisms. Global Context Loss: In methods using self-attention (like), naive patch rendering breaks global attention. addresses this by using Local Self-Attention with cropped positional encodings to maintain consistency between full-image and patch-wise training. Inefficiency for Per-Pixel Losses: For simple per-pixel losses (L1/L2), sparse sampling is more efficient. DBP is specifically designed for CNN-based or global losses. Memory Complexity: The memory footprint is dominated by the largest patch re-rendering pass, not the full image. Time Complexity: The method requires two rendering passes per iteration: one forward pass (no gradients) and one backward pass (patch-wise with gradients). Performance: On a single RTX 3090 GPU, standard back-propagation limits training to 2 reference views at 384×496 resolution. DBP enables training with 5-7 reference views at the same resolution, improving PSNR by 1.37–3.02 dB. Strengths: Enables full-resolution training for memory-intensive losses (VGG, Gram matrix, global attention). Avoids the performance degradation associated with resolution reduction. Limitations: Increased training time due to double rendering. Requires careful implementation to ensure consistency between forward and backward passes. Not efficient for simple per-pixel losses where sparse sampling suffices. Deferred Back-propagation was introduced in the context of 3D stylization of radiance fields, specifically in the "ARF: Artistic Radiance Fields" paper. It was developed to overcome the memory limitations of volumetric rendering when applying CNN-based style losses (like VGG features) that require full-resolution images. The technique was later adapted for generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting (GGRt) to enable high-resolution training and inference under limited GPU memory.
